title: Latin Grammar
text:
⟦=⟧Preface Table of Contents Sections 1-179: Sounds Sections 180-396: Formation Sections 397-712: Inflection of Nouns Sections 713-1022: Inflection of Verbs Sections 1023-1713: Sentences Sections 1714-2299: Complex Sentences Sections 2300-2745: Appendix Index of Subjects Index of Latin Words Advertising
⟦#1⟧
Latin Grammar has two parts. I. The first part treats of words: (A.) their sound; (B.) their formation; (C.) their inflection. II. The second part shows how words are joined together in sentences.

title: Parts of Speech
text:
⟦#2⟧
The principal kinds of words or Parts of Speech are ⟦i:Nouns⟧, ⟦i:Verbs⟧, and ⟦i:Conjunctions⟧.
⟦#3⟧
I. Nouns are ⟦i:Substantive⟧ or ⟦i:Adjective⟧.
⟦#4⟧
(A.) Nouns Substantive, otherwise called Substantives, are divided, as to meaning, into ⟦i:Concrete⟧ and ⟦i:Abstract⟧.
⟦#5⟧
(1.) Concrete Substantives denote persons or things. Concrete Substantives are subdivided into ⟦i:Proper Names⟧, which denote individual persons or things: as, ⟦b:Cicerō⟧, ⟦i:Cicero⟧; ⟦b:Rōma⟧, ⟦i:Rome⟧; and ⟦i:Common Names⟧, otherwise called ⟦i:Appellatives⟧, which denote one or more of a class: as, ⟦b:homo⟧, ⟦i:man⟧; ⟦b:taurus⟧, ⟦i:bull⟧.
⟦#6⟧
Appellatives which denote a collection of single things are called ⟦i:Collectives⟧: as, ⟦b:turba⟧, ⟦i:crowd⟧; ⟦b:exercitus⟧, ⟦i:army⟧. Appellatives which denote stuff, quantity, material, things not counted, but having measure or weight, are called ⟦i:Material Substantives⟧: as, ⟦b:vīnum⟧, ⟦i:wine⟧; ⟦b:ferrum⟧, ⟦i:iron⟧; ⟦b:faba⟧, ⟦i:horsebeans⟧.
⟦#7⟧
(2.) Abstract Substantives denote qualities, states, conditions: as, ⟦b:rubor⟧, ⟦i:redness⟧; ⟦b:aequitās⟧, ⟦i:fairness⟧; ⟦b:sōlitūdō⟧, ⟦i:loneliness⟧.
⟦#8⟧
(B.) Nouns Adjective, otherwise called Adjectives, attached to substantives, describe persons or things: as, ⟦b:ruber⟧, ⟦i:red⟧; ⟦b:aequus⟧, ⟦i:fair⟧; ⟦b:sōlus⟧, ⟦i:alone⟧.
⟦#9⟧
Pronouns are words of universal application which serve as substitutes for nouns.
Thus, ⟦b:taurus⟧, ⟦i:bull⟧, names, and ⟦b:ruber⟧, ⟦i:red⟧, describes, particular things; but ⟦b:ego⟧, ⟦i:I⟧, is universally applicable to any speaker, and ⟦b:meus⟧, ⟦i:mine⟧, to anything belonging to any speaker.
⟦#10⟧
Adverbs are mostly cases of nouns used to denote manner, place, time or degree: as, ⟦b:subitō⟧, ⟦i:suddenly⟧; ⟦b:forās⟧, ⟦i:out of doors⟧; ⟦b:diū⟧, ⟦i:long⟧; ⟦b:valdē⟧, ⟦i:mightily⟧, ⟦i:very⟧.
⟦#11⟧
Prepositions are adverbs which are used to modify as prefixes the meaning of verbs, or to define more nicely the meaning of cases: as, ⟦b:vocō⟧, ⟦i:I call⟧, ⟦b:ēvocō⟧, ⟦i:I call out⟧; ⟦b:ex urbe⟧, ⟦i:from town⟧.
⟦#12⟧
II. Verbs are words which denote action, including existence or condition: as, ⟦b:regit⟧, ⟦i:he guides⟧; ⟦b:est⟧, ⟦i:he is⟧; ⟦b:latet⟧, ⟦i:he is hid⟧.
⟦#13⟧
III. Conjunctions connect sentences, nouns, or verbs: as, ⟦b:et⟧, ⟦i:and⟧; ⟦b:sed⟧, ⟦i:but⟧.
⟦#14⟧
Interjections are cries which express feeling, and are not usually a part of the sentence: as, ⟦b:ā⟧, ⟦i:ah⟧; ⟦b:heu⟧, ⟦i:alas⟧.
⟦#15⟧
There is no Article in Latin: thus, ⟦b:mēnsa⟧ may denote ⟦i:table⟧, ⟦i:a table⟧, or ⟦i:the table⟧.

title: Alphabet
text:
⟦#16⟧
In Cicero’s time, the sounds of the Latin language were denoted by twenty-one letters (⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 93).
⟦b:A⟧  a  ⟦i:ah⟧
⟦b:B⟧  be  ⟦i:bay⟧
⟦b:C⟧  ce  ⟦i:kay⟧
⟦b:D⟧  de  ⟦i:day⟧
⟦b:E⟧  e  ⟦i:eh⟧
⟦b:F⟧  ef  ⟦i:ef⟧
⟦b:G⟧  ge  ⟦i:gay⟧
⟦b:H⟧  ha  ⟦i:hah⟧
⟦b:I⟧  i  ⟦i:ee⟧
⟦b:K⟧  ka  ⟦i:kah⟧
⟦b:L⟧  el  ⟦i:el⟧
⟦b:M⟧  em  ⟦i:em⟧
⟦b:N⟧  en  ⟦i:en⟧
⟦b:O⟧  o  ⟦i:o⟧
⟦b:P⟧  pe  ⟦i:pay⟧
⟦b:Q⟧  qu  ⟦i:koo⟧
⟦b:R⟧  er  ⟦i:air⟧
⟦b:S⟧  es  ⟦i:ess⟧
⟦b:T⟧  te  ⟦i:tay⟧
⟦b:V⟧  u  ⟦i:oo⟧
⟦b:X⟧  ix  ⟦i:eex⟧
⟦/⟧
Character Name pronounced
The names given above are those employed by Roman grammarians. The sound indicated by ⟦i:-ay⟧ is only approximate; the true sound is that of the French ⟦i:ê⟧ in ⟦i:fête⟧; see ⟦r39:39⟧. The names of the letters are indeclinable; for their gender, see ⟦r412:412⟧.
⟦#17⟧
Two other letters were also in use to represent Greek sounds in Greek words; these were always called by their Greek names, and were placed at the end of the alphabet; they are ⟦b:Y⟧, named ⟦i:ü⟧ (⟦r42:42⟧), and ⟦b:Z⟧, named ⟦b:zēta⟧ (⟦r71:71⟧).
⟦#18⟧
Origin of the Alphabet. The Latin alphabet, which originally consisted of capitals only, was adapted from the alphabet of Chalcidian colonies in Italy.
⟦#19⟧
Spelling. The signs for the Greek sounds denoted by φ and χ, and perhaps also that for θ, these three sounds being unknown in Latin, were used as numerals (⟦r2407:2407⟧). In words borrowed from the Greek the Romans at first represented θ by ⟦b:t⟧, φ by ⟦b:p⟧, and χ by ⟦b:c⟧: as, ⟦b:tūs⟧, ⟦i:incense⟧, for θύος; ⟦b:Poenī⟧, ⟦i:Punians⟧, for Φοίνικες; ⟦b:calx⟧, ⟦i:chalk⟧, for χάλιξ. Occasionally also the Latin mute was doubled: as, ⟦b:struppus⟧, ⟦i:strap⟧, for στρόφος. Later, about the middle of the second century B.C., ⟦b:th⟧, ⟦b:ph⟧, and ⟦b:ch⟧ begin to be used: as, ⟦b:cothurnus⟧, ⟦i:boot⟧, for κόθορνος; ⟦b:amphora⟧, ⟦i:jar⟧, for ἀμφόρα; ⟦b:Achaea⟧ for Ἀχαιά. In some instances these aspirates were next introduced even into words purely Latin: as, ⟦b:chommodus⟧, ⟦i:affable⟧, for ⟦b:commodus⟧, an affectation ridiculed by Catullus (Cat. 84) and disapproved by Quintilian (1, 5, 20). But ⟦b:pulcher⟧, ⟦i:pretty⟧, is the usual spelling for ⟦b:pulcer⟧ (formed by the suffix ⟦b:-cro-⟧ from the stem of the verb ⟦b:poliō⟧, ⟦i:I polish⟧). Even Cicero (⟦i:O.⟧ 160) aspirated the ⟦b:c⟧ in this word as a concession to popular usage, as he did the ⟦b:t⟧ in ⟦b:Cethēgus⟧, ⟦b:Karthāgō⟧, and the ⟦b:p⟧ in ⟦b:triumphus⟧, while he retained the unaspirated explosive in the proper names ⟦b:Orcīvius⟧, ⟦i:name of a ‘gens,’⟧ ⟦b:Matō⟧, ⟦b:Otō⟧, ⟦b:Caepiō⟧, and in ⟦b:sepulcrum⟧, ⟦i:tomb⟧; ⟦b:corōna⟧, ⟦i:crown⟧; and ⟦b:lacrima⟧, ⟦i:tear⟧. In a similar manner Greek ρ was at first transcribed by ⟦b:r⟧: as, ⟦b:rumpia⟧, ⟦i:a kind of weapon⟧, for ῥομφαία; but later by ⟦b:rh⟧: as, ⟦b:rhētor⟧, ⟦i:rhetorician⟧, for ῥητωρ.
⟦#20⟧
The letters ⟦b:C⟧ (first written ⟦b:<⟧) and ⟦b:K⟧ were at an early period used promiscuously, and ⟦b:C⟧ stood for both unvoiced ⟦b:k⟧ and voiced ⟦b:g⟧: as, VIRCO, ⟦b:virgō⟧, ⟦i:virgin⟧. Afterwards ⟦b:K⟧ dropped out of general use except in the abbreviations ⟦b:K.⟧ or ⟦b:Kal.⟧ for ⟦b:kalendae⟧, ⟦i:first of the month⟧, and ⟦b:K.⟧ for the proper name ⟦b:Kaesō⟧ (Quint. 1, 7, 10). About 300 B.C. the sign ⟦b:<⟧ or ⟦b:C⟧ was used for the unvoiced ⟦i:k⟧ alone, while a separate sign, which became ⟦b:G⟧, was set apart for the voiced ⟦i:g⟧. But ⟦b:C⟧ continued to be used for ⟦i:g⟧ in the abbreviations ⟦b:C⟧ for ⟦b:Gāius⟧, ⟦b:Ↄ⟧ for ⟦b:Gāia⟧, and ⟦b:Cn.⟧ for ⟦b:Gnaeus⟧. Occasionally ⟦b:q⟧ is written for ⟦b:c⟧, almost always before the vowels ⟦b:o⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧: as, ⟦b:qum⟧ for ⟦b:cum⟧, ⟦i:with⟧; ⟦b:qolunt⟧ for ⟦b:colunt⟧, ⟦i:they cultivate⟧; ⟦b:peqūnia⟧, ⟦i:money⟧. But ordinarily ⟦b:q⟧ is found before unsyllabic (consonantal) ⟦b:u⟧ (⟦b:v⟧) only (⟦r22:22⟧).
⟦#21⟧
Before the introduction of ⟦b:Y⟧ and ⟦b:Z⟧ (⟦r17:17⟧), ⟦b:u⟧ was used for the Greek ⟦b:υ⟧: as, ⟦b:Burrus⟧, later ⟦b:Pyrrhus⟧ (Cic. ⟦i:O.⟧ 160); and ⟦b:s⟧, or, as a medial, ⟦b:ss⟧, for ⟦b:ζ⟧: as, ⟦b:sōna⟧, ⟦i:belt⟧, later ⟦b:zōna⟧; ⟦b:massa⟧, ⟦i:lump⟧, for μᾶζα; ⟦b:malacissō⟧, ⟦i:I soften⟧, for μαλακίζω. By a blunder, ⟦b:y⟧ was occasionally introduced in words of Latin origin: as, ⟦b:lacryma⟧, ⟦i:tear⟧, for ⟦b:lacrima⟧, which was wrongly supposed to be derived from Greek δάκρυ.
⟦#22⟧
The characters ⟦b:I⟧ and ⟦b:V⟧ represent not only the two vowels ⟦b:i⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧, but also their cognate semivowels (⟦r52:52⟧) ⟦b:i̭⟧ and ⟦b:ṷ⟧ (⟦r83:83⟧), called commonly ⟦i:consonant⟧ ⟦b:i⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧, but with less ambiguity ⟦i:unsyllabic⟧ ⟦b:i⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧ (⟦r82:82⟧; ⟦r83:83⟧). They are equivalent to the English ⟦i:y⟧ and ⟦i:w⟧ respectively.
⟦#23⟧
In words like ⟦b:maior⟧, simple ⟦b:i⟧ was commonly written for the sound of ⟦b:i̭i̭⟧ (153, 2; ⟦r82:82⟧; ⟦r83:83⟧). But Cicero in such cases wrote ⟦b:ii⟧: as, ⟦b:aiiō⟧, ⟦i:I say⟧, ⟦b:Maiia⟧, ⟦b:Troiia⟧ (Quint. 1, 4, 11). In the same way Lucretius spelled ⟦b:Graiiugenārum⟧, ⟦i:of Greek-born men⟧, and EIIVS, ⟦i:of him⟧, CVIIVS, ⟦i:whose⟧, occur in inscriptions. Sometimes the same sound is represented by a taller letter, ‘⟦i:i longa⟧,’ especially in the imperial age: as, maIor, ⟦i:greater⟧. There are also cases in which the two designations were confounded, a double ⟦b:i⟧ being written, and one or the other letter made taller: as, eiIvs or eIivs, ⟦i:of him⟧.
⟦#24⟧
The tall ⟦b:i⟧, ⟦b:I longa⟧, was used not only to represent unsyllabic ⟦b:i⟧ (⟦r22:22⟧), but, beginning with Sulla’s time, also for long vowel ⟦b:i⟧ (29, 2, ⟦i:b⟧): as, sIgna, ⟦i:signs⟧; qvInqve, ⟦i:five⟧. It also represents sometimes double ⟦b:i⟧: as, vIs for viīs, ⟦i:in the roads⟧. At the beginning of words it occurs without reference to quantity for both short and long ⟦b:i⟧, and, by mistake, ⟦b:I⟧ is elsewhere found for short ⟦b:i⟧.
⟦#25⟧
The emperor Claudius (A.D. 41-54) introduced a separate sign for unsyllabic ⟦b:u⟧ (⟦r22:22⟧), restricting the sign ⟦b:v⟧ to the vowel ⟦b:u⟧ (Quint. 1, 7, 26; Ta. 11, 14); but it did not become current.
⟦#26⟧
In schoolbooks and most texts of the authors, the vowel ⟦b:u⟧ is printed ⟦b:U⟧, ⟦b:u⟧, and the consonant ⟦b:V⟧, ⟦b:v⟧. A character, ⟦b:J⟧, ⟦b:j⟧, was introduced in the 17th century, to indicate the consonant ⟦b:i⟧. But this character is no longer usual in editions of the authors or in schoolbooks.
⟦#27⟧
The distinction between ⟦b:u⟧ and ⟦b:v⟧ is not always made very consistently: ⟦b:q⟧ has regularly, and ⟦b:g⟧ and ⟦b:s⟧ have sometimes, an aftersound of ⟦i:w⟧, best represented by ⟦b:v⟧; but the usual practice is to write ⟦b:u⟧, as in the following disyllables: ⟦b:quōrum⟧, ⟦i:of whom⟧; ⟦b:anguis⟧, ⟦i:snake⟧; ⟦b:suāvis⟧, ⟦i:sweet⟧. ⟦b:qu⟧ is always counted as a single sound (⟦r177:177⟧). See also ⟦r2504:2504⟧.
⟦#28⟧
For the intermediate sound (⟦r103:103⟧) between ⟦b:i⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧, as in the first syllable of ⟦b:lubet⟧, ⟦b:libet⟧, ⟦i:it pleases⟧, and in the second syllable of ⟦b:optimus⟧, ⟦b:optumus⟧, ⟦i:best⟧ (Quint. 1, 4, 8; 7, 21), the emperor Claudius invented a separate character. It failed of acceptance, as did also the sign which he attempted to introduce for ⟦b:ps⟧.
⟦#29⟧
The same characters were ordinarily used to denote both long and short vowels. But at different periods long vowels were sometimes indicated in inscriptions thus:
(1.) Long ⟦b:a⟧, ⟦b:e⟧, or ⟦b:u⟧ was sometimes doubled: as, AARA, ⟦i:altar⟧; PAASTORES, ⟦i:shepherds⟧; LEEGE, ⟦i:by law⟧; IVVS, ⟦i:right⟧. This doubling, which was never frequent, seems to have been introduced into Latin from the Oscan by the poet Accius. It occurs most frequently in inscriptions about the year 150 B.C., but sporadically much later: as, CONVENTVVS, ⟦i:of the assembly⟧; ARBITRATVV, ⟦i:by the decree⟧; and in other stems in ⟦b:-u-⟧ (⟦r593:593⟧).
(2.) Long ⟦b:i⟧ was often denoted (⟦i:a.⟧) By the spelling ⟦b:ei⟧ (after the pronunciation of this diphthong had been changed to ⟦b:ī⟧, ⟦r98:98⟧): as, DAREI, ⟦i:be given⟧; REDIEIT, ⟦i:hath come back⟧; INTERIEISTI, ⟦i:hast died⟧. Some Roman grammarians prescribed this spelling for every long ⟦b:i⟧; others tried to regulate the use of ⟦b:ei⟧ for ⟦b:ī⟧ by special rules. At the end of the republic, the spelling EI had given way to uniform I. (⟦i:b.⟧) Since the time of Sulla, by a taller letter (‘⟦i:i longa⟧’): as, fIxa, ⟦i:fastened⟧ (⟦r23:23⟧, ⟦r24:24⟧).
(3.) A mark called an ⟦i:apex⟧ () was often put over a long vowel: as, FE͆CIT, ⟦i:made⟧; HORTE͆NSIVS; DVV͆MVIRATVS, ⟦i:duumvirate⟧. The apex was written ´ in the imperial age; the form -, which occurs in an inscription, was adopted by the grammarians, and is still in use to mark the long vowels. It may be mentioned that inscriptions which employ the apex are by no means consistent in its use, and that late inscriptions have it over short and long vowels, apparently for decorative purposes. Quintilian 1, 7, 2 prescribes it only for cases which otherwise might be ambiguous: as, MÁLVS (⟦b:mālus⟧), ⟦i:mast⟧, to distinguish it from MALVS (⟦b:malus⟧), ⟦i:bad⟧.
⟦#30⟧
In schoolbooks, a long vowel is indicated by a horizontal line over it: as, ⟦b:āra⟧, ⟦i:altar⟧; ⟦b:mēnsis⟧, ⟦i:month⟧; ⟦b:ōrdō⟧, ⟦i:series⟧. A short vowel is sometimes indicated by a curved mark: as, ⟦b:pĕr⟧, ⟦i:through⟧; ⟦b:dŭx⟧, ⟦i:leader⟧; but this mark is unnecessary if long vowels are systematically marked. Usually the quantity of the vowels in each word is definitely fixed; but in a few cases the same vowel may be now short, now long, as in English the ⟦i:ee⟧ of ⟦i:been⟧ is pronounced long by some (⟦i:bean⟧), short by others (⟦i:bin⟧). Thus (⟦r2446:2446⟧) ⟦b:mihi⟧, ⟦b:ibi⟧ were sometimes pyrrhics (⏖, ⟦r2522:2522⟧), sometimes iambi (⏑-, ⟦r2521:2521⟧). See for other cases ⟦r134:134⟧, ⟦r2443:2443⟧, ⟦r2452:2452⟧, ⟦r2453:2453⟧. Such vowels of variable quantity are termed ⟦i:common⟧ and marked ⏓ or ⏒: as ⟦b:mihī̆⟧, ⟦i:to me⟧ (⟦r2514:2514⟧).

title: Pronunciation
text:
⟦#31⟧
The pronunciation of Latin sounds may be approximately determined: (⟦i:a⟧) from the description of the native grammarians and incidental allusions in other Latin authors; (⟦i:b⟧) from variations in spelling; (⟦i:c⟧) from the Greek transliteration of Latin words; (⟦i:d⟧) from the Latin transliteration of foreign words; (⟦i:e⟧) from the development of the sounds in languages derived from the Latin.

title: Vowels
text:
⟦#32⟧
Vowels are sounds which are produced by the vibrations of the vocal chords (this may be easily felt by placing a finger on the throat at the Adam’s apple) and without any audible friction or any obstruction anywhere in the passage above the vocal chords. The difference in the sound of the vowels is due to the different shape which the position of the tongue and the lips gives in each case to the cavity of the mouth. During the pronunciation of pure vowels no air escapes through the nose.
⟦#33⟧
The simple vowels, ⟦b:a⟧, ⟦b:e⟧, ⟦b:i⟧, ⟦b:o⟧, ⟦b:u⟧ (⟦b:y⟧), are either ⟦i:long⟧ or ⟦i:short⟧. The sound of a long vowel is considered to be twice the length of that of a short.
⟦#34⟧
That a long vowel is equal to two shorts is a rule of metrical theory (see ⟦r2515:2515⟧). In actual pronunciation, there were undoubtedly various degrees of length, as in English: e.g., ⟦i:sea⟧, ⟦i:seize⟧ (long), ⟦i:cease⟧ (half-long).
The quantity of vowels must in general be learned by observation; but some convenient helps for the memory may be found in ⟦r2429:2429⟧; and the quantity of many vowels may be ascertained by the general principles given in ⟦r35:35⟧ and ⟦r36:36⟧. Except in the case of ⟦i:Hidden Quantity⟧ (⟦r2459:2459⟧), the quantity of vowels is in general ascertained from verse. But some information may also be gleaned from such rhetorical prose as exhibits well defined habits in the rhythmical endings selected for sentences (⟦b:clausulae⟧, Cic. ⟦i:O.⟧ 191-226).

title: Short Vowels
text:
⟦#35⟧
A vowel is short:
(1.) Before another vowel or ⟦b:h⟧ (⟦r124:124⟧): as, ⟦b:eōs⟧, ⟦b:ēvehō⟧; compare ⟦b:taceō⟧ with ⟦b:tacēre⟧. For exceptions in classical Latin, see ⟦r127:127⟧; for exceptions in early Latin see ⟦r126:126⟧.
(2.) Before ⟦b:nt⟧ and ⟦b:nd⟧ (⟦r128:128⟧) if not the result of contraction: as, ⟦b:calendae⟧, ⟦b:centum⟧; compare ⟦b:amant⟧, ⟦b:amandus⟧, with ⟦b:amāre⟧.
(3.) Before final ⟦b:t⟧ and ⟦b:m⟧, and, in words of more than one syllable, before final ⟦b:r⟧ and ⟦b:l⟧ (⟦r132:132⟧): compare ⟦b:amat⟧, ⟦b:amem⟧, with ⟦b:amās⟧ and ⟦b:amēs⟧.

title: Long Vowels
text:
⟦#36⟧
All vowels are long which are:
(1) Weakened from a diphthong (⟦r96:96-101⟧; ⟦r108:108⟧), or which are the result of contraction (⟦r118:118⟧): as, ⟦b:concīdō⟧ from ⟦b:caedō⟧; ⟦b:cōgō⟧ from ⟦b:co-agō⟧.
(2) Lengthened by compensation (⟦r121:121⟧): as, ⟦b:quīnī⟧ for ⟦b:*quincnī⟧.
(3) Before ⟦b:nf⟧, ⟦b:ns⟧, often before ⟦b:nc⟧ followed by a consonant, and, in some cases, before ⟦b:gn⟧ (⟦r122:122⟧).

title: Pronunciation of Vowels
text:
⟦#37⟧
The following English sounds come nearest to the Latin pronunciation of the vowels:
⟦#38⟧
Long vowels. ⟦b:ā⟧ had the sound of ⟦i:a⟧ in ⟦i:father⟧; ⟦b:ē⟧ that of ⟦i:a⟧ in ⟦i:fate⟧ (but see ⟦r39:39⟧); ⟦b:ī⟧ that of ⟦i:i⟧ in ⟦i:machine⟧; ⟦b:ō⟧ that of ⟦i:o⟧ in ⟦i:tone⟧; ⟦b:ū⟧ that of ⟦i:u⟧ in ⟦i:rule⟧.
⟦#39⟧
It must be noted, however, that all English long vowels, save ⟦i:a⟧ as in ⟦i:father⟧, are more or less diphthongal, that is, they become gradually closer (⟦r46:46⟧); ⟦i:a⟧ in ⟦i:fate⟧ ends in a vanishing sound of ⟦i:ee⟧ (not heard in the ⟦i:ê⟧ of French ⟦i:fête⟧), and ⟦i:o⟧ in ⟦i:no⟧ ends in the sound of ⟦i:oo⟧. Similarly the long ⟦i:e⟧ sound in ⟦i:he⟧ becomes closer and ends in a sound similar to the ⟦i:y⟧ in ⟦i:year⟧. In Latin all long vowels had one sustained sound.
⟦#40⟧
Short vowels. ⟦b:a⟧ sounded approximately like the English ⟦i:a⟧ in the first syllable of ⟦i:aha⟧; ⟦b:e⟧, ⟦b:i⟧, ⟦b:o⟧, and ⟦b:u⟧ sounded like ⟦i:e⟧ in ⟦i:step⟧, ⟦i:i⟧ in ⟦i:pit⟧, ⟦i:o⟧ in ⟦i:obey⟧, and ⟦i:u⟧ in ⟦i:pull⟧ respectively.
⟦#41⟧
Latin short ⟦b:a⟧ did not differ, except in quantity, from long ⟦b:ā⟧; it never had the ‘flat’ sound of English ⟦i:a⟧ in ⟦i:pat⟧. In the case of the other vowels, ⟦b:i⟧, ⟦b:e⟧, ⟦b:o⟧, and ⟦b:u⟧, the long vowels were closer (⟦r46:46⟧) than the short ones. This is the same difference which the English shows in ⟦i:keen⟧ (long and close) and ⟦i:kin⟧ (short and open); ⟦i:pool⟧ (long and close) and ⟦i:pull⟧ (short and open). For this reason, open ⟦b:i⟧ is sometimes represented by ⟦b:e⟧ in inscriptions: as, ANEMA for ⟦b:anima⟧, ⟦i:soul⟧; and ⟦b:vea⟧ was the rustic pronunciation for ⟦b:via⟧, ⟦i:road⟧ (Varro, ⟦i:R. R.⟧ 1, 2, 14).
⟦#42⟧
⟦b:Y⟧, which was a sound borrowed from the Greek (⟦r17:17⟧), sounded like German ⟦i:ü⟧. The sound, which is missing in English, is formed with the tongue in position for ⟦i:i⟧ (in ⟦i:kin⟧) and the lips rounded as for ⟦i:oo⟧ (in ⟦i:moon⟧).

title: Classification of Vowels
text:
⟦#43⟧
Vowels are divided according to the position of the tongue. Latin ⟦b:i⟧ and ⟦b:e⟧ are called ⟦i:front vowels⟧, because the front part of the tongue is elevated. This elevation is greater for ⟦b:i⟧ than for ⟦b:e⟧. Latin ⟦b:o⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧ are called ⟦i:back vowels⟧, because they require an elevation of the rear part of the tongue. This elevation is greater for ⟦b:u⟧ than for ⟦b:o⟧. Latin ⟦b:a⟧ holds an intermediate position, no part of the tongue being raised, while the front part is depressed.
⟦#44⟧
In the formation of ⟦b:i⟧ and ⟦b:e⟧, the tongue approaches the hard palate; hence these two vowels are also called ⟦i:palatal vowels⟧. Similarly, ⟦b:o⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧ are called ⟦i:velar⟧ or ⟦i:guttural vowels⟧, because in their formation the tongue approaches the soft palate (⟦b:vēlum palātī⟧).
⟦#45⟧
⟦b:o⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧ require a rounding of the lips (⟦b:labia⟧); hence they are called ⟦i:labial vowels⟧. The same is true for ⟦b:y⟧.
⟦#46⟧
Comparing the vowels in English ⟦i:keen⟧ and ⟦i:kin⟧, it will be noted that the passage between the tongue and the hard palate is narrower in the former than in the latter case. The ⟦i:ee⟧ in ⟦i:keen⟧ is therefore said to be a ⟦i:narrow⟧ or ⟦i:close⟧ vowel, while the ⟦i:i⟧ in ⟦i:kin⟧ is ⟦i:wide⟧ or ⟦i:open⟧. See ⟦r41:41⟧.

title: Diphthongs
text:
⟦#47⟧
Two unlike (⟦r43:43-46⟧) vowels pronounced under one stress and as one syllable form a ⟦i:Diphthong⟧. All diphthongs are long.
In all diphthongs the transition from one vowel to the other is gradual. A diphthong is, therefore, not formed simply by pronouncing two vowels in succession, but the vocal organs pass through all the intermediate positions and consequently the sound is constantly changing.
⟦#48⟧
In their origin diphthongs are of two kinds: (⟦i:a.⟧) primitive diphthongs: as in ⟦b:foedus⟧, ⟦i:treaty⟧; ⟦b:aurum⟧, ⟦i:gold⟧; or (⟦i:b.⟧) secondary diphthongs, the result of vowels meeting in formation, composition, or inflection: see ⟦r120:120⟧.
⟦#49⟧
The diphthongs which occur in classical Latin are ⟦b:au⟧, ⟦b:ae⟧, ⟦b:oe⟧, and the rare ⟦b:ui⟧ and ⟦b:eu⟧.
⟦b:au⟧ sounded like ⟦i:ou⟧ in ⟦i:house⟧. ⟦b:ae⟧ had the sound of short Latin ⟦b:a⟧ rapidly combined with the sound of ⟦i:e⟧ in English ⟦i:men⟧. But it is the common practice now to give to ⟦b:ae⟧ the sound of ⟦i:ay⟧ or ⟦i:ai⟧ in ⟦i:ay⟧, ⟦i:aisle⟧, although the difference between Latin ⟦b:ae⟧ and the earlier ⟦b:ai⟧ from which it descended is thus obliterated. ⟦b:oe⟧ had the sound of short Latin ⟦b:o⟧ rapidly followed by the sound of ⟦i:e⟧ in English ⟦i:men⟧. But it is now customary not to distinguish between Latin ⟦b:oe⟧ and ⟦b:oi⟧, and to give to both the sound of ⟦i:oi⟧ in ⟦i:boil⟧. ⟦b:ui⟧ is pronounced by combining Latin short ⟦b:u⟧ and ⟦b:i⟧ (⟦r40:40⟧, ⟦r41:41⟧) with the stress on the ⟦b:i⟧ like French ⟦i:oui⟧; ⟦b:eu⟧ by combining Latin short ⟦b:e⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧ with stress on the ⟦b:u⟧.
⟦#50⟧
Besides these, the following diphthongs occur in the older inscriptions: ⟦b:ai⟧ pronounced as ⟦i:ai⟧ in ⟦i:aisle⟧; ⟦b:ei⟧ as ⟦i:ei⟧ in ⟦i:eight⟧; ⟦b:oi⟧ as ⟦i:oi⟧ in ⟦i:boil⟧; and ⟦b:ou⟧ which sounded very much like the final ⟦i:o⟧ in ⟦i:no⟧, ⟦i:go⟧, which is really a diphthong (see ⟦r39:39⟧).

title: Consonants
text:
⟦#51⟧
Consonants are formed by stopping the breath somewhere in the cavity of the mouth or by squeezing it through a narrow channel or aperture.
⟦#52⟧
Semivowels. There is no sharp line of demarcation between consonants and vowels. Some vowels in unsyllabic function (⟦r82:82⟧, ⟦r83:83⟧) notably ⟦b:i⟧ (⟦i:i̭⟧) and ⟦b:u⟧ (⟦i:ṷ⟧) (corresponding to English ⟦i:y⟧ and ⟦i:w⟧), though usually classed as consonants, are so closely related to the vowels that they are termed semivowels (⟦r2504:2504⟧). To these may be added also the liquids ⟦b:l⟧ and ⟦b:r⟧. Contact of the semivowels ⟦b:i⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧ with their corresponding vowels ⟦b:i⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧ is avoided in classical times. See for ⟦b:-vu-⟧ 107, ⟦i:c⟧; for ⟦b:-quu-⟧ ⟦r157:157⟧; and for ⟦b:-i̭i-⟧ 104, ⟦i:c⟧ (on ⟦b:obi̭iciō⟧); ⟦r458:458⟧ (⟦b:Bōī⟧ for ⟦b:*Bōi̭ī⟧). See 153, 3.

title: Pronunciation of Consonants
text:
⟦#53⟧
Most of the consonants are pronounced as in English. The following points must be noticed:
⟦#54⟧
⟦b:b⟧ before ⟦b:a⟧ surd, as ⟦b:s⟧ or ⟦b:t⟧, has the sound of ⟦b:p⟧. The spelling ⟦b:b⟧ is here simply etymological: as, ⟦b:abs⟧, pronounced ⟦i:aps⟧ (the ⟦b:b⟧ retained in spelling because of ⟦b:ab⟧); ⟦b:urbs⟧, pronounced ⟦i:urps⟧ (the ⟦b:b⟧ retained because of the oblique cases ⟦b:urbis⟧, ⟦b:urbī⟧, etc.); ⟦b:obterō⟧, pronounced ⟦i:opterō⟧ (Quint. 1, 7, 7), where the spelling of the preposition ⟦b:ob⟧ was kept (⟦r164:164⟧).
⟦#55⟧
⟦b:c⟧ has always the sound of English ⟦i:k⟧.
⟦#56⟧
⟦b:d⟧ before the surd ⟦b:s⟧ is pronounced ⟦b:t⟧; the spelling ⟦b:d⟧ is preserved for etymological reasons only: as, ⟦b:adsum⟧, pronounced ⟦i:atsum⟧.
⟦#57⟧
⟦b:g⟧ always has the sound of English ⟦i:g⟧ in ⟦i:go⟧, never that of ⟦i:g⟧ in ⟦i:gentle⟧. ⟦b:gu⟧, when it makes one syllable with the following vowel, is pronounced like English ⟦i:gw⟧: as, ⟦b:sanguine⟧ like ⟦i:sanguine⟧.
⟦#58⟧
⟦b:h⟧ has a weak sound as ⟦i:h⟧ in British English (Southern), and by some was not counted as a consonant. Consequently the same uncertainty existed as to initial ⟦b:h⟧. The omission of initial ⟦b:h⟧ is recognized in classical Latin for ⟦b:ānser⟧ (originally ⟦b:*hānser⟧). Elsewhere the omission of initial ⟦b:h⟧ in spelling, as ⟦b:ostia⟧ for ⟦b:hostia⟧, is rare until the third century A.D.
Very rarely ⟦b:h⟧ is written between two vowels to denote that each should be pronounced separately (like our diaeresis in ⟦i:coëxtensive⟧): as, ⟦b:ahēneus⟧, ⟦i:bronze⟧, with ⟦b:aē⟧ separate (116 ⟦i:a⟧); but ⟦b:aes⟧, ⟦i:bronze⟧, with diphthongal ⟦b:ae⟧.
⟦#59⟧
Unsyllabic (⟦r22:22⟧) or consonant ⟦b:i⟧ has the sound of English ⟦i:y⟧ in ⟦i:year⟧.
⟦#60⟧
There were two varieties of ⟦b:l⟧. One was like the English ⟦i:l⟧, guttural in character, because in its pronunciation not only the blade (front part) of the tongue touched the gums, but in addition to this the rear part of the tongue was elevated toward the soft palate. The other ⟦b:l⟧ was purely dental, and formed without such back elevation. This second variety appeared in the combination ⟦b:ll⟧, or whenever ⟦b:l⟧ was followed by the front vowels (⟦r43:43⟧) ⟦b:e⟧ or ⟦b:i⟧, or when it was final. Elsewhere ⟦b:l⟧ was guttural.
⟦#61⟧
From the earliest times final m in unaccented syllables had a faint sound or was even inaudible (Quint. 9, 4, 39). Consequently it is often omitted in writing in the older inscriptions both before an initial vowel or consonant: as, POCOLO for ⟦b:pōcolom⟧; OINO for ⟦b:oinom⟧ (⟦b:ūnum⟧), and the grammarian Verrius Flaccus proposed to write only half an ⟦b:M⟧ for final ⟦b:m⟧ before a vowel. In prosody, therefore, final ⟦b:m⟧ did not prevent elision (⟦r2493:2493⟧). The same is seen in prose in cases like ⟦b:animadvertō⟧, ⟦i:I pay heed to⟧, from ⟦b:animum advertō⟧, ⟦i:I turn my mind toward⟧ (⟦r395:395⟧); ⟦b:vēnīre⟧, ⟦i:to be sold⟧ for ⟦b:vēnum īre⟧, ⟦i:to go to sale⟧ (⟦r1165:1165⟧). But in monosyllables where ⟦b:m⟧ closes the accented syllable, it did not vanish (⟦r2494:2494⟧, ⟦r2495:2495⟧), and this difference in the treatment of final ⟦b:m⟧ is reflected in the Romance languages.
⟦#62⟧
⟦b:n⟧ stands for two sounds. It represents the dental nasal, as ⟦i:n⟧ in English ⟦i:now⟧. But before the gutturals ⟦b:k⟧, ⟦b:c⟧, ⟦b:g⟧, ⟦b:q⟧, and the compound ⟦b:x (= cs)⟧, it represents the guttural nasal which is written ⟦i:ng⟧ in English ⟦i:sing⟧, ⟦i:wrong⟧. This second n is sometimes called ⟦b:n adulterīnum⟧ or ‘spurious ⟦b:n⟧,’ thus: ⟦b:nc⟧ (in ⟦b:avunculus⟧) as in ⟦i:uncle⟧; ⟦b:ng⟧ (in ⟦b:angulus⟧) as in ⟦i:angle⟧; ⟦b:ngu⟧ (in ⟦b:sanguine⟧) as in ⟦i:sanguine⟧; ⟦b:nqu⟧ (in ⟦b:inquit⟧) as ⟦i:inkw⟧ in ⟦i:inkwiper⟧; ⟦b:nx⟧ (in ⟦b:pīnxit⟧) as in ⟦i:lynx⟧.
⟦#63⟧
Dental ⟦b:n⟧ before ⟦b:s⟧ had a reduced sound, and is therefore sometimes omitted in writing: as, CESOR for ⟦b:cēnsor⟧; COSOL for ⟦b:cōnsul⟧, in older inscriptions; and ⟦b:fōrmōsus⟧ by the side of ⟦b:fōrmōnsus⟧; ⟦b:vīcēsimus⟧ by the side of ⟦b:vīcēnsimus⟧, Cicero omitted the ⟦b:n⟧ in the adjective suffix ⟦b:-ēnsis⟧: as, ⟦b:forēsia⟧, ⟦i:of the forum⟧; ⟦b:hortēsia⟧, ⟦i:garden plants⟧.
⟦#64⟧
⟦b:q⟧, in classical Latin, appears only in the combination ⟦b:qu⟧, sounded like English ⟦i:qu⟧ or ⟦i:kw⟧ (⟦r27:27⟧). ⟦b:r⟧ was trilled.
⟦#65⟧
⟦b:s⟧, in classical Latin was always unvoiced (surd, ⟦r75:75⟧) like English ⟦i:s⟧ in ⟦i:so⟧, ⟦i:sin⟧, never voiced (sonant, ⟦r75:75⟧) as English ⟦i:s⟧ in ⟦i:ease⟧. ⟦b:su⟧, when it makes one syllable with the following vowel, is like ⟦i:sw⟧ in ⟦i:sweet⟧ (⟦r27:27⟧).
⟦#66⟧
In old Latin, final ⟦b:s⟧ after a short vowel and before a consonant seems to have been reduced in sound or to have disappeared altogether. In the older inscriptions it is often omitted in the ending of the nominative singular ⟦b:-us⟧, and in the pre-Ciceronian poets final ⟦b:s⟧ often does not make position (⟦r2468:2468⟧). But such omission was considered vulgar in Cicero’s time (Cic. ⟦i:O.⟧ 161; Quint. 9, 4, 38).
⟦#67⟧
In the archaic period Latin ⟦b:s⟧ stood also for the voiced sibilant (English ⟦i:s⟧ in ⟦i:ease⟧, ⟦i:z⟧ in ⟦i:zeal⟧), as in ASA, ⟦i:altar⟧ (⟦r154:154⟧).
⟦#68⟧
⟦b:t⟧ is always sounded as in ⟦i:time⟧, never as in ⟦i:nation⟧. The pronunciation of ⟦b:ci⟧ and ⟦b:ti⟧ with the ⟦b:c⟧ and ⟦b:t⟧ as sibilants (as in English ⟦i:cinder⟧, ⟦i:nation⟧) is very late.
⟦#69⟧
⟦b:v⟧ is like the English ⟦i:w⟧.
⟦#70⟧
⟦b:x⟧ is a compound consonant, standing for ⟦b:cs⟧, and so sounded, never as English ⟦i:gs⟧ or ⟦i:gz⟧.
⟦#71⟧
⟦i:z⟧, being a Greek sound, should have retained its Greek pronunciation. This differed in the different dialects; in the Attic of the fourth century B.C. it was approximately that of English ⟦i:z⟧ in ⟦i:zeal⟧, while its earlier value was ⟦i:zd⟧. The Romans had great difficulty in pronouncing this sound (Quint. 12, 10, 27 f.), but the grammarian Velius Longus expressly states that it should not be pronounced as a compound sound (⟦i:zd⟧).
⟦#72⟧
About 100 B.C. the combinations ⟦b:ch⟧, ⟦b:ph⟧, and ⟦b:th⟧ were introduced in Greek words to represent χ, φ, and θ; as ⟦b:Philippus⟧, for the older PILIPVS. Somewhat later these combinations were in general use in some Latin words (⟦r19:19⟧). ⟦b:ch⟧ is thought to have been pronounced like ⟦i:kh⟧ in ⟦i:blockhead⟧, ⟦b:ph⟧ as in ⟦i:uphill⟧, and ⟦b:th⟧ as in ⟦i:hothouse⟧. But in practice ⟦b:ch⟧ is usually sounded as in the German ⟦i:machen⟧ or ⟦i:ich⟧, ⟦b:ph⟧ as in ⟦i:graphic⟧, and ⟦b:th⟧ as in ⟦i:pathos⟧.

title: Classification of Consonants
text:
⟦#73⟧
Explosives. Consonants which are formed by stopping the breath in the oral cavity and then suddenly removing the obstruction are called ⟦i:explosives⟧. They cannot be prolonged in sound. They are: ⟦b:c⟧, ⟦b:k⟧, ⟦b:q⟧, ⟦b:g⟧; ⟦b:t⟧, ⟦b:d⟧; ⟦b:p⟧, ⟦b:b⟧. These are often called ⟦i:mutes⟧.
⟦#74⟧
Continuants. Consonants which may be prolonged in sound are called ⟦i:continuants⟧. They are: unsyllabic (⟦r83:83⟧) ⟦b:i⟧ (⟦r59:59⟧) and ⟦b:u⟧ (⟦r66:66⟧); ⟦b:l⟧ (⟦r60:60⟧), ⟦b:r⟧; ⟦b:l⟧, ⟦b:s⟧, ⟦b:f⟧; ⟦b:n⟧ (⟦r62:62⟧), ⟦b:m⟧.
⟦#75⟧
Voiced and Unvoiced. If during the emission of breath the vocal chords vibrate (⟦r32:32⟧), the consonant is said to be ⟦i:voiced⟧ or ⟦i:sonant⟧: ⟦b:g⟧; ⟦b:d⟧; ⟦b:b⟧; ⟦b:n⟧ (⟦r62:62⟧), ⟦b:m⟧; ⟦b:l⟧ (⟦r60:60⟧), ⟦b:r⟧; unsyllabic (⟦r83:83⟧) ⟦b:i⟧ (⟦r59:59⟧) and ⟦b:u⟧ (⟦r69:69⟧); otherwise it is said to be ⟦i:unvoiced⟧ or ⟦i:surd⟧: ⟦b:c⟧, ⟦b:k⟧, ⟦b:q⟧; ⟦b:t⟧; ⟦b:p⟧; ⟦b:h⟧, ⟦b:s⟧, ⟦b:f⟧.
⟦#76⟧
Nasals. In the majority of consonants, the breath escapes through the cavity of the mouth, and the cavity of the nose is closed in the rear by means of the raised soft palate. Those consonants in which the breath escapes through the nose, while the oral cavity is closed, are called ⟦i:nasals⟧: as, ⟦b:n⟧, ⟦b:m⟧, ⟦b:n adulterīnum⟧ (see ⟦r62:62⟧).
⟦#77⟧
Classification according to place of formation. Consonants are further divided according to the place where the breath is stopped or squeezed. (1.) If the breath is stopped by the lips, as in ⟦b:p⟧, ⟦b:b⟧, ⟦b:m⟧, or squeezed through the lips, as in ⟦b:v⟧ (English ⟦i:w⟧), we speak of ⟦i:labials⟧. (2.) If the breath is forced through an opening between the upper teeth and the lower lip, as in ⟦b:f⟧, we speak of a ⟦i:labiodental⟧. (3.) Sounds which are produced by the point of the tongue touching the upper gums and teeth, as ⟦b:t⟧, ⟦b:d⟧, ⟦b:n⟧, ⟦b:r⟧, or by the formation of a narrow median channel in the same place, like ⟦b:s⟧, or of a lateral channel, like ⟦b:l⟧ (⟦r60:60⟧), are called ⟦i:dentals⟧. (4.) ⟦i:Palatals⟧ are formed by an elevation of the front part of the tongue against the forward section of the palate, like ⟦b:i⟧ consonant (English ⟦i:y⟧). (5.) If the back of the tongue touches or approaches the rear part of the palate as in ⟦b:k⟧, ⟦b:q⟧, ⟦b:c⟧, ⟦b:g⟧, ⟦b:n adulterīnum⟧ (English ⟦i:ng⟧ in ⟦i:sing⟧), and ⟦b:l⟧ (⟦r60:60⟧), we speak of ⟦i:gutturals⟧ (⟦i:velars⟧); see ⟦r44:44⟧.
⟦#78⟧
Spirants. Sounds which are produced by friction of the breath are called ⟦i:spirants⟧: as, ⟦b:s⟧, ⟦b:f⟧, and ⟦b:h⟧.
⟦#79⟧
Sibilants. On account of its hissing sound, ⟦b:s⟧ is called a sibilant. English ⟦i:s⟧, ⟦i:z⟧, ⟦i:th⟧ are sibilants.
⟦#80⟧
Doubling of Consonants. In English, double consonants as the ⟦i:tt⟧, ⟦i:nn⟧, ⟦i:pp⟧, ⟦i:mm⟧ in ⟦i:motto⟧, ⟦i:Anna⟧, ⟦i:tapping⟧, ⟦i:grammar⟧, are sounded exactly like the corresponding single consonants in ⟦i:cot⟧, ⟦i:pan⟧, ⟦i:tap⟧, ⟦i:ram⟧. In Latin, on the other hand, double consonants (⟦b:geminātae⟧) were pronounced as they are in modern Italian. In the case of explosives (⟦r73:73⟧), as in ⟦b:mitto⟧, after the tongue had come in contact with the roof of the mouth (= first ⟦b:t⟧) a short pause ensued before the explosion took place (= second ⟦b:t⟧). In the case of continuants (⟦r74:74⟧), as in ⟦b:summus⟧, ⟦b:Apollo⟧, the ⟦b:mm⟧ or ⟦b:ll⟧ was sounded appreciably longer than a single ⟦b:m⟧ or ⟦b:l⟧, and at the beginning of the second half of the long continuant there was a slight increase of force.
⟦#81⟧
Consonants were not doubled in writing till after 200 B.C.: as, FVISE for ⟦b:fuisse⟧, ⟦i:to have been⟧, and for more than a century afterward the usage is variable: as, in the same inscription, ESSENT, ⟦i:they might be⟧, by the side of SVPERASES, ⟦i:thou mayest have conquered⟧; but it must not be inferred that they were pronounced as single consonants.

title: Syllabic and Unsyllabic Function
text:
⟦#82⟧
Whenever two or more sounds are combined in a syllable, one of them excels in acoustic prominence: as, ⟦i:a⟧ in English ⟦i:pat⟧; ⟦i:n⟧ in the group ⟦i:pnd⟧ in ⟦i:opnd⟧ (⟦i:opened⟧); ⟦i:l⟧ in the group ⟦i:tld⟧ in ⟦i:bottld⟧ (⟦i:bottled⟧); and ⟦i:s⟧ in the group ⟦i:pst⟧. This sound is said to have ⟦i:syllabic function⟧ or to be ⟦i:syllabic⟧; in the examples given, ⟦i:a⟧, ⟦i:n⟧, ⟦i:l⟧, and ⟦i:s⟧ are respectively syllabic. All the other members of each group are termed ⟦i:unsyllabic⟧.
⟦#83⟧
Vowels are almost always used in syllabic function. When, in rare cases, they are unsyllabic, this fact is usually indicated in phonetic works by an inverted half-circle, ̭, placed under the vowel; so in the case of diphthongs to indicate the subordinate member: as ⟦b:ai̭⟧, ⟦b:oḙ⟧, ⟦b:ṷi⟧ (⟦r49:49⟧). Latin ⟦b:omnia⟧ and English ⟦i:glorious⟧, when pronounced as words of two syllables, would be written ⟦b:omni̭a⟧ (⟦r2503:2503⟧), ⟦i:glori̭ous⟧. When sounds other than vowels have, in rare cases, syllabic function, this fact is noted in phonetic works by a point, . , or circle, ˳ , under the letter: as, Latin ⟦b:*agṛs⟧, ⟦b:*agr̥s⟧ (111, ⟦i:b⟧), English ⟦i:opṇd⟧, ⟦i:opn̥d⟧.

title: Accent
text:
⟦#84⟧
The relative force with which the different syllables of a word are uttered varies. Such variation in emphasis is called ⟦i:stress accentuation⟧.
The degrees of stress are really infinite, but for practical purposes it is sufficient to distinguish between (1.) the strongest stress (chief accent); (2.) a weaker stress (secondary accent); and (3.) absence of stress (atonic syllable). In the English ⟦i:contradict⟧, the last syllable has the chief accent, a secondary accent falls on the first, and the second syllable is unstressed.
⟦#85⟧
It is not customary to indicate the place of accents in Latin by special signs. When, for special reasons, signs are used, ´ denotes the chief accent, ` the secondary accent, while the unstressed syllables are left unmarked.

title: The Classical Accent
text:
⟦#86⟧
In classical Latin the place of the chief accent may be determined by the following rules.
(1.) Words of two syllables have the accent on the penult (⟦r175:175⟧): as,
⟦b:hómo⟧; ⟦b:ā́cer⟧.
(2.) Words of more than two syllables have the accent on the penult when that syllable is long (⟦r177:177⟧); otherwise on the antepenult: as,
⟦b:palū́ster⟧, ⟦b:onústus⟧ (⟦r177:177⟧); ⟦b:mulíebris⟧, ⟦b:génetrīx⟧ (⟦r178:178⟧); ⟦b:árborēs⟧, ⟦b:árbutus⟧, ⟦b:gladíolus⟧.
⟦#87⟧
A short penult retains the accent in the genitive and vocative with a single ⟦b:ī⟧ from stems in ⟦b:-io-⟧ (⟦r456:456⟧, ⟦r459:459⟧): as, genitive, ⟦b:cōnsílī⟧; ⟦b:impérī⟧; genitive or vocative, ⟦b:Vergílī⟧; ⟦b:Valérī⟧; ⟦b:Mercúrī⟧. For ⟦b:calefácis⟧, &c., see ⟦r394:394⟧.
⟦#88⟧
In a few words which have lost a syllable the accent is retained on the last syllable; such are (1.) compounds of the imperatives ⟦b:dīc⟧ and ⟦b:dūc⟧ (⟦r113:113⟧): as, ⟦b:ēdū́c⟧; (2.) nominatives of proper names in ⟦b:-ās⟧ and ⟦b:-īs⟧ for ⟦b:-ātis⟧ and ⟦b:-ītis⟧: as, ⟦b:Arpīnā́s⟧, for ⟦b:Arpīnā́tis⟧; ⟦b:Laenā́s⟧; ⟦b:Maecēnā́s⟧; ⟦b:Quirī́s⟧; ⟦b:Samnī́s⟧; also ⟦b:nostrā́s⟧, ⟦b:vostrā́s⟧; (3.) words compounded with the abbreviated (⟦r113:113⟧) enclitics ⟦b:-c⟧ for ⟦b:-ce⟧ and ⟦b:-n⟧ for ⟦b:-ne⟧: as, ⟦b:illī́c⟧; ⟦b:tantṓn⟧; ⟦b:audīstī́n⟧ (for the shortening of the final syllable: as, ⟦b:vidén⟧, ⟦i:dost see?⟧, see ⟦r129:129⟧); (4.) ⟦b:audī́t⟧, contracted from ⟦b:audīvit⟧ (⟦r154:154⟧, ⟦r893:893⟧). The Latin grammarians prescribe the circumflex (⟦r90:90⟧) for all these long syllables.

title: Earlier Recessive Accent
text:
⟦#89⟧
In the preliterary period of the Latin language, the accent tended to go as far from the end of the word as possible (⟦i:recessive accent⟧). Thus, while the classical accentuation is ⟦b:inimī́cus⟧, the older period accented ⟦b:ínimīcus⟧. In literary Latin this early recessive accent has survived, only in Plautus’s accentuation of words of the form ⏑ ⏑ ⏑ ⏓ (proceleusmatic or fourth paeon, see ⟦r2521:2521⟧), in which he stresses the first syllable: as, ⟦b:fácilius⟧ (classical ⟦b:facílius⟧); ⟦b:vóluerat⟧ (classical ⟦b:volúerat⟧). But in many instances the early recessive accent may be traced in literary Latin by the phonetic changes which it produced (⟦r102:102 ff.⟧).
⟦#90⟧
Musical element. The native Latin grammarians slight the stress accentuation and pay much attention instead to the variations in pitch. But they are so greatly dependent on their Greek models that they are unsafe guides in this matter. It is, however, probable that a stressed vowel was uttered on a higher key (acute) than an unstressed vowel (grave), and that in certain syllables the long, accented vowel showed a rise and fall (circumflex): as, ⟦b:illîc⟧ (⟦r88:88⟧).
⟦#91⟧
The force of the Latin stress accent must have varied at different periods and in different localities, as it now varies in the Romance countries. The early recessive accent seems to have been fairly emphatic; but the stress in classical Latin was probably weak and the difference between accented and unaccented syllables was much less marked than it is in English.

title: Proclitics and Enclitics
text:
⟦#92⟧
⟦b:Proclitics⟧ are unaccented words which are pronounced as a part of the following word; they are: (1.) The relative and indefinite pronouns and their derivatives; (2.) Prepositions.
(⟦i:a.⟧) Thus, ⟦b:quō diē⟧, pronounced ⟦b:quōdíē⟧; ⟦b:quī vīxit⟧, ⟦b:quīvī́xit⟧; ⟦b:genus unde Latīnum⟧, ⟦b:génus undeLatī́num⟧. Similarly ⟦b:quamdíū⟧, ⟦i:as long as⟧; ⟦b:iamdíū⟧, ⟦i:this long time⟧. A distinction is thus made between the interrogative ⟦b:quālis⟧ (⟦r1526:1526⟧), which is accented, and the relative ⟦b:quālis⟧ (⟦r1831:1831⟧) which is proclitic (Quint. 1, 5, 26); cf. the English ⟦i:who⟧, which is accented when interrogative, and proclitic when relative. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:circum lītora⟧, pronounced ⟦b:circumlī́tora⟧; ⟦b:ab ōrīs⟧, pronounced ⟦b:abōrīs⟧ (Quint. 1, 5, 27); in inscriptions and manuscripts prepositions are often united in writing with the following word. Phrases like ⟦b:extemplō⟧, ⟦i:suddenly⟧, ⟦b:invicem⟧ (⟦r94:94⟧), ⟦i:in turn⟧, are commonly written and accented as one word. But the preposition is accented when it is followed by a monosyllabic unemphatic (and therefore enclitic) personal pronoun: as, ⟦b:ín mē⟧; ⟦b:ábs tē⟧ (but ⟦b:abs tḗ⟧, if ⟦b:tē⟧ is emphatic). All prepositions used as adverbs (⟦r1402:1402⟧) have an independent accent.
⟦#93⟧
Enclitics are words which have no accent of their own, but are pronounced as a part of the word preceding. This increase of the number of syllables produced certain accentual changes, all the details of which are not clear. When the enclitic was monosyllabic the place of the accent seems to have been determined as in ⟦r86:86⟧; thus ⟦b:vídēs⟧, but ⟦b:vidḗsne⟧; ⟦b:Látiō⟧, but ⟦b:Latiṓque⟧. Again, when by the addition of a monosyllabic enclitic the accent falls on the fourth syllable from the end, a secondary (⟦r84:84⟧, ⟦r85:85⟧) accent was probably placed on the penult: as, ⟦b:perī́cula⟧, but ⟦b:perī́culàque⟧. The Roman grammarians agree, however, in demanding that everywhere the syllable preceding the enclitics ⟦b:-que⟧, ⟦b:-ne⟧, ⟦b:-ve⟧, and ⟦b:-ce⟧ should be accented. In ⟦b:deinde⟧ and ⟦b:subinde⟧ there is authority for placing the accent on the first syllable.
Enclitics are: (1.) Unemphatic personal and indefinite pronouns: as, ⟦b:in mē⟧, pronounced, ⟦b:ínmē⟧; ⟦b:dā mihi⟧, ⟦b:dā́mihi⟧; ⟦b:sīc tibi⟧, ⟦b:sī́ctibi⟧; ⟦b:sī quis⟧, ⟦b:sī́quis⟧; ⟦b:nē quid⟧, ⟦b:nḗquid⟧. (2.) Verbs when used as auxiliaries: as, ⟦b:possum⟧ for ⟦b:pót(e) sum⟧ (⟦r752:752⟧); ⟦b:quī́ libet⟧ (⟦r2401:2401⟧); ⟦b:vidḗlicet⟧, ⟦b:īlicet⟧, ⟦b:scīlicet⟧ (⟦r712:712⟧); ⟦b:quámvīs⟧ (⟦r1903:1903⟧); the forms of ⟦b:esse⟧ in compound tenses (⟦r719:719⟧), so that ⟦b:est⟧ is frequently combined, even in writing, with the preceding past participle (⟦r747:747⟧). (3.) The particles ⟦b:-ne⟧ (⟦b:-n⟧), ⟦b:-ve⟧, and ⟦b:-ce⟧ (⟦b:-c⟧): as, ⟦b:satísne⟧ or shortened ⟦b:satín⟧; ⟦b:Hyrcānīsve Arabī́sve⟧; ⟦b:istī́ce⟧ or shortened ⟦b:istîc⟧ (⟦r90:90⟧), ⟦b:adhûc⟧ (⟦r90:90⟧). (4.) The copulative conjunction ⟦b:-que⟧: as, ⟦b:Latiṓque⟧, ⟦b:līmináque⟧. (5.) The preposition ⟦b:cum⟧ when it follows (⟦r1435:1435⟧) its case. (6.) The particle ⟦b:quidem⟧: as, ⟦b:sī quidem⟧, ⟦b:síquidem⟧ (⟦r131:131⟧). (7.) Other enclitics are: ⟦b:-met⟧ (⟦r650:650⟧): as, ⟦b:egómet⟧; ⟦b:-dem⟧: as, ⟦b:ibídem⟧; ⟦b:-nam⟧: as, ⟦b:ubínam⟧; ⟦b:-dum⟧ (⟦r1573:1573⟧): as, ⟦b:agédum⟧; ⟦b:-inde⟧: as, ⟦b:déinde⟧, ⟦b:próinde⟧ (which are disyllabic in verse), and ⟦b:súbinde⟧; ⟦b:-tum⟧; as, ⟦b:etiámtum⟧; ⟦b:-per⟧: as, ⟦b:parúmper⟧; the vocative when it was closely joined to the preceding word, e.g. an imperative: as, ⟦b:dī́c puer⟧ (⟦r106:106⟧).
⟦#94⟧
Two words expressing what is really one single idea are often bound together by ⟦i:one⟧ accent, one of them acting the part of either a proclitic or enclitic.
Thus, with the earlier recessive accent (⟦r89:89⟧), ⟦b:Iū́piter⟧ (⟦r133:133⟧; ⟦r389:389⟧; originally a vocative which came to be used as nominative; for the change of ⟦b:pater⟧ to ⟦b:piter⟧ see ⟦r104:104⟧); ⟦b:ínvicem⟧, ⟦i:in turn⟧; ⟦b:dḗnuō⟧ for ⟦b:dḗ nóvō⟧ (⟦r106:106⟧); with the later, classical accent, ⟦b:lēgislā́tor⟧, ⟦b:paterfamíliās⟧, ⟦b:orbisterrā́rum⟧, ⟦b:extémplō⟧, ⟦b:imprī́mīs⟧. When unemphatic ⟦b:ille⟧ and ⟦b:iste⟧ preceded their noun and had practically the value of our definite article they formed a unit with the following noun and thus the accent might fall on their last syllable: as, ⟦b:illé pater⟧, ⟦b:isté canis⟧. This use is particularly common in vulgar and late Latin (see ⟦r112:112⟧).

title: Change of Diphthongs in Accented Syllables
text:
⟦#95⟧
Of the six original diphthongs ⟦b:au⟧, ⟦b:ou⟧, ⟦b:eu⟧, and ⟦b:ai⟧, ⟦b:oi⟧, ⟦b:ei⟧, the only one which preserved its original sound in the classical period is ⟦b:au⟧. Of the rest only ⟦b:ae⟧ (for older ⟦b:ai⟧) and, in a few words, ⟦b:oe⟧ (for older ⟦b:oi⟧) remained diphthongs; all the others had become monophthongs.
⟦#96⟧
Change of ⟦b:ai⟧. ⟦b:ai⟧ is common in inscriptions: as, AIDILIS, PRAITOR. Toward the end of the republic the two elements of the diphthong had been partially assimilated to ⟦b:ae⟧ (⟦r49:49⟧): as, ⟦b:aedīlis⟧ (Quint. 1, 7, 18). This is its pronunciation in the classical period. Between 130 and 100 B.C. ⟦b:ai⟧ is displaced by ⟦b:ae⟧ in public documents; but the old-fashioned ⟦b:ai⟧ was often retained in private inscriptions. Still later the two elements completely converged to ⟦b:ē⟧. In provincial Latin ⟦b:ē⟧ is found as early as 200 B.C.: as, CESVLA for CAESVLLA; in Rome itself the pronunciation ‘Cēcilius’ for ⟦b:Caecilius⟧, and ‘⟦b:prētor⟧’ for ⟦b:praetor⟧ was derided as boorish; but by 71 A.D. ⟦b:ae⟧ was verging toward ⟦b:ē⟧ even in the court language: the coins of Vespasian have IVDEA as well as IVDAEA. In the 3d and 4th century A.D. ⟦b:ē⟧ became the prevalent sound.
⟦#97⟧
Change of ⟦b:au⟧. The diphthong ⟦b:au⟧, which was preserved in educated speech, was changed to ⟦b:ō⟧ in rustic and colloquial pronunciation (see the anecdote related by Suetonius, ⟦i:Vesp.⟧ 22): as, ⟦b:cōpō⟧, ⟦i:innkeeper⟧, for ⟦b:caupō⟧; ⟦b:plōstrum⟧ for ⟦b:plaustrum⟧ (⟦i:barge⟧), ⟦i:cart⟧: ⟦b:Clōdius⟧ for ⟦b:Claudius⟧. Some of these gained literary currency: as, ⟦b:cōdex⟧, ⟦i:book⟧, ⟦b:caudex⟧, ⟦i:block⟧; ⟦b:fōcāle⟧, ⟦i:neckcloth⟧, ⟦b:faucēs⟧, ⟦i:throat⟧. The form ⟦b:sōdēs⟧ (⟦r1572:1572⟧) for ⟦b:si̭ audēs⟧ = ⟦b:sī audēs⟧ (Cic. ⟦i:O.⟧ 154) is a colloquialism.
⟦#98⟧
Change of ⟦b:ei⟧. ⟦b:ei⟧ as a genuine diphthong is common in old inscriptions: as, SEI; SEIVE; ADEITVR; DEIXERVNT; FEIDA. In classical Latin it has passed into ⟦b:ī⟧: thus, ⟦b:sī⟧, ⟦i:if⟧; ⟦b:sīve⟧, ⟦i:either⟧; ⟦b:adītur⟧, ⟦i:is approached⟧; ⟦b:dīxērunt⟧, ⟦i:they said⟧; fīda, ⟦i:faithful⟧. An intermediate stage between the old diphthong ⟦b:ei⟧ and the classical ⟦b:ī⟧ was a very close (⟦r46:46⟧) ⟦b:ē⟧: as, PLOIRVME (⟦r465:465⟧) for ⟦b:plūrimī⟧; IOVRE (⟦r501:501⟧, ⟦r507:507⟧) for ⟦b:iūrī⟧. For the orthographical use of ⟦b:ei⟧ as a spelling for the long ⟦b:ī⟧-sound, see ⟦r29:29⟧.
⟦#99⟧
Change of ⟦b:oi⟧. The development of ⟦b:oi⟧ was parallel to that of ⟦b:ai⟧. It first passed into ⟦b:oe⟧: as, COIRAVERVNT and COERAVERVNT, ⟦i:they cared⟧; OITILE, ⟦i:useful⟧, and OETI, ⟦i:to use⟧; LOIDOS and LOEDOS, ⟦i:play⟧,—all in old Latin. In classical Latin it has further been changed in accented syllables to ⟦b:ū⟧: as, ⟦b:cūrāvērunt⟧, ⟦b:ūtile⟧, ⟦b:ūtī⟧, ⟦b:lūdus⟧. But ⟦b:oe⟧ was retained in classical Latin (1.) when a secondary diphthong (⟦r48:48⟧), the result of contraction (⟦r120:120⟧), and (2.) in a few words like ⟦b:foedus⟧, ⟦i:treaty⟧, perhaps as an archaizing, legal term; ⟦b:foedus⟧, ⟦i:ugly⟧; ⟦b:poena⟧, ⟦i:penalty⟧, perhaps through the influence of Greek ποινή (in the verb ⟦b:pūnīre⟧, ⟦i:to punish⟧, the regular ⟦b:ū⟧ appears); ⟦b:proelium⟧, ⟦i:skirmish⟧; ⟦b:foetor⟧, ⟦i:stench⟧; and ⟦b:moenia⟧, ⟦i:walls⟧, perhaps because there was a word ⟦b:mūnia⟧, ⟦i:services⟧. The connection of ⟦b:nōn⟧, ⟦i:not⟧, with ⟦b:noenum⟧ (⟦r455:455⟧; ⟦r1444:1444⟧; ⟦r699:699⟧) is difficult because of the unusual development of ⟦b:oe⟧ to ⟦b:o⟧, for which the Praenestine form CORAVERONT is the only parallel.
⟦#100⟧
Change of ⟦b:ou⟧. ⟦b:ou⟧, found in inscriptions down to about 90 B.C., passed, in classical Latin, into ⟦b:ū⟧: as, POVBLICOM, NOVNTIATA, IOVDEX; later ⟦b:pūblicum⟧, ⟦i:public⟧, ⟦b:nūntiāta⟧, ⟦i:notified⟧, ⟦b:iūdex⟧, ⟦i:judge⟧.
⟦#101⟧
Change of ⟦b:eu⟧. Primitive (⟦r48:48⟧) ⟦b:eu⟧ appears in classical Latin only in the interjections ⟦b:eu⟧, ⟦b:heu⟧, ⟦b:ē̆heu⟧, ⟦b:heus⟧. Every other original ⟦b:eu⟧ had, even in old Latin, passed into ⟦b:ou⟧ and developed like the latter: as, ⟦b:*neumen⟧ (Greek νεῦμα) became first ⟦b:*noumen⟧, then (⟦r100:100⟧) ⟦b:nūmen⟧. With the exceptions noted above, the diphthong ⟦b:eu⟧, as it appears in Latin, is always of secondary origin (⟦r48:48⟧), the result of the two vowels ⟦b:e⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧ meeting in composition: as, ⟦b:neu⟧, ⟦i:neither⟧, from ⟦b:nē-ve⟧; ⟦b:neutiquam⟧, from ⟦b:nē⟧ and ⟦b:utiquam⟧ (⟦r124:124⟧).

title: Weakening in Unaccented Syllables
text:
⟦#102⟧
The vowel of an unstressed (atonic) syllable is often weakened, changing its quantity or quality or both. This is especially the case in syllables immediately preceded by the chief accent (⟦i:posttonic syllables⟧). The following changes took place at an early period when Latin still possessed the old, recessive accent (⟦r89:89⟧).

title: Weakening of Simple Vowels in Medial Syllables
text:
⟦#103⟧
(⟦i:a.⟧) Atonic medial ⟦b:e⟧ before a single consonant was weakened (with the exceptions given under ⟦i:b.⟧) to ⟦b:i⟧: as, ⟦b:cólligō⟧, ⟦i:collect⟧, from ⟦b:legō⟧; ⟦b:óbsideō⟧, ⟦i:besiege⟧, from ⟦b:sedeō⟧; ⟦b:cértāminis⟧, ⟦i:of the contest⟧, from ⟦b:certāmen⟧ (⟦r224:224⟧); ⟦b:flāminis⟧, from ⟦b:flāmen⟧ (⟦r470:470⟧). And so probably ⟦b:hic⟧ (⟦r664:664⟧) arose from ⟦b:*hec⟧ or ⟦b:*hoc⟧ (105, ⟦i:g⟧) when used as proclitic (⟦r92:92⟧). Before the labials ⟦b:p⟧, ⟦b:b⟧, ⟦b:f⟧, and ⟦b:m⟧ this weakened sound was intermediate between ⟦b:i⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧ (⟦r28:28⟧), and both spellings occur: as, ⟦b:quadripēs⟧ and ⟦b:quadrupēs⟧, ⟦i:four-footed⟧; ⟦b:alimentum⟧, ⟦i:nourishment⟧; ⟦b:monumentum⟧, ⟦i:monument⟧. The choice of ⟦b:i⟧ or ⟦b:u⟧ was probably governed by the quality of the stressed vowel in the preceding syllable: viz., ⟦b:u⟧ after ⟦b:o⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧, and ⟦b:i⟧ after ⟦b:a⟧, ⟦b:e⟧, and ⟦b:i⟧. But such distinction is only imperfectly maintained in classical Latin.
(⟦i:b.⟧) But before two consonants, before ⟦b:r⟧, before vowels, and after ⟦b:i⟧, atonic ⟦b:e⟧ does not change: as, ⟦b:lévāmentum⟧ (⟦r224:224⟧), but ⟦b:lévāminis⟧, ⟦i:of consolation⟧; ⟦b:óbsessus⟧ (but ⟦b:óbsideō⟧), ⟦i:possessed⟧; ⟦b:sócietās⟧, ⟦i:society⟧, from the stem ⟦b:socie-⟧ (but ⟦b:nóvitās⟧ from the stem ⟦b:nove-⟧); ⟦b:géneris⟧, ⟦i:of the kind⟧; ⟦b:ádeunt⟧, ⟦i:they approach⟧.
⟦#104⟧
(⟦i:c.⟧) Atonic medial ⟦b:a⟧, except in the cases mentioned below under (⟦i:d.⟧), (⟦i:e.⟧), and (⟦i:f.⟧), was first weakened to ⟦b:e⟧ and then underwent the same changes as atonic medial ⟦b:e⟧ (⟦r103:103⟧): as (before single consonants), ⟦b:cṓnficiō⟧, ⟦i:accomplish⟧, from ⟦b:faciō⟧; ⟦b:ī́nsiliō⟧, ⟦i:jump in⟧, from ⟦b:saliō⟧ (⟦r1019:1019⟧); ⟦b:rédditus⟧, ⟦i:restored⟧, from ⟦b:datus⟧; ⟦b:trícipitem⟧, ⟦i:three-headed⟧, from ⟦b:*trícapitem⟧ (⟦b:caput⟧), Cic. ⟦i:O.⟧ 159; ⟦b:occiput⟧, ⟦i:back of the head⟧, and ⟦b:sinciput⟧, ⟦i:jole⟧ (⟦r478:478⟧). In compounds of ⟦b:iaciō⟧ (⟦r940:940⟧), ⟦b:-iaciō⟧ is weakened in early Latin to ⟦b:-ieciō⟧ (as, ⟦b:conieciō⟧, ⟦r940:940⟧), but later to ⟦b:-iciō⟧ (as, ⟦b:subiciō⟧). This last form may be due to syncope (111, ⟦i:a⟧) of the radical ⟦b:a⟧. The spelling ⟦b:-iiciō⟧ (as, ⟦b:subiiciō⟧) is late and faulty (⟦r52:52⟧). It does not occur in republican inscriptions and owes its origin to a confusion of the two forms ⟦b:conieciō⟧ and ⟦b:coniciō⟧. (On the quantity of the vowel of the prepositions in these compounds of ⟦b:iaciō⟧, see ⟦r122:122⟧ ⟦i:e⟧); (before ⟦b:p⟧, ⟦b:b⟧, ⟦b:f⟧, ⟦b:m⟧) ⟦b:áccipiō⟧, ⟦i:accept⟧, and ⟦b:óccupō⟧, ⟦i:occupy⟧, from ⟦b:capiō⟧; ⟦b:cóntubernālis⟧, ⟦i:room-mate⟧, from ⟦b:taberna⟧; ⟦b:ábripiō⟧, ⟦i:to snatch away⟧, from ⟦b:rapiō⟧; (before two consonants) ⟦b:pépercī⟧, ⟦i:I have spared⟧, from ⟦b:parcō⟧; ⟦b:áccentus⟧, ⟦i:accent⟧, from ⟦b:cantus⟧; (before ⟦b:r⟧) ⟦b:péperī⟧, ⟦i:I brought forth⟧, from ⟦b:pariō⟧.
(⟦i:d.⟧) But an ⟦b:a⟧ in the preceding syllable may protect the atonic ⟦b:a⟧: as, ⟦b:ádagiō⟧, ⟦b:ádagium⟧, ⟦i:proverb⟧, but ⟦b:prṓdigium⟧, ⟦i:miracle⟧ (⟦r144:144⟧).
(⟦i:e.⟧) Atonic medial ⟦b:a⟧ before the guttural nasal (⟦r62:62⟧) ⟦b:n⟧ followed by ⟦b:g⟧ changed to ⟦b:i⟧ (⟦r138:138⟧): as, ⟦b:áttingō⟧, ⟦i:touch⟧, from ⟦b:tangō⟧.
(⟦i:f.⟧) Atonic medial ⟦b:a⟧ before ⟦b:l⟧ followed by any consonant save ⟦b:l⟧ changed to ⟦b:u⟧ (both ⟦b:l⟧ and ⟦b:u⟧ being guttural, ⟦r60:60⟧, ⟦r44:44⟧): as, ⟦b:éxsultāre⟧, ⟦i:to leap up⟧, from ⟦b:saltāre⟧; but ⟦b:féfellī⟧, ⟦i:I deceived⟧, from ⟦b:fallō⟧.
⟦#105⟧
(⟦i:g.⟧) Atonic medial ⟦b:o⟧, when followed by a single consonant, first changed to ⟦b:e⟧ and then underwent all further changes of medial atonic ⟦b:e⟧: as, ⟦b:hóminis⟧, from ⟦b:*homon-is⟧ (⟦r485:485⟧); ⟦b:ímāginis⟧, for ⟦b:*imāgonis⟧, ⟦r226:226⟧ (nominative ⟦b:imāgō⟧, ⟦r485:485⟧); ⟦b:cúpīdinis⟧, for ⟦b:*cupīdonis⟧, ⟦r225:225⟧, (nominative ⟦b:cupīdō⟧, ⟦r485:485⟧); ⟦b:vírginis⟧, for ⟦b:*virgonis⟧ (nominative ⟦b:virgō⟧, ⟦r470:470⟧); ⟦b:ī́licō⟧, from ⟦b:*in-slocō⟧, ⟦i:on the spot⟧ (169, 4).
(⟦i:h.⟧) Before two consonants or before guttural ⟦b:l⟧ (⟦r60:60⟧) atonic medial ⟦b:o⟧ changed to ⟦b:u⟧: as, ⟦b:éuntis⟧, from ⟦b:*éontis⟧ (Greek ἴοντος); ⟦b:sēdulō⟧, from ⟦b:sē dolō⟧ (⟦r1417:1417⟧). But a preceding ⟦b:v⟧ or ⟦b:u⟧ protects ⟦b:o⟧ (107, ⟦i:c⟧).
(⟦i:i.⟧) Before ⟦b:r⟧, atonic medial ⟦b:o⟧ was retained: as, ⟦b:témporis⟧, ⟦i:of time⟧; except when ⟦b:u⟧ in the preceding syllable induced a change to ⟦b:u⟧: as, ⟦b:fúlguris⟧, ⟦i:of lightning⟧ (for the ⟦b:-r⟧ in the nominative singular ⟦b:fulgur⟧ instead of ⟦b:-s⟧, see ⟦r154:154⟧).
⟦#106⟧
(⟦i:k.⟧) Medial ⟦b:-av-⟧, ⟦b:-ov-⟧, and ⟦b:-iv-⟧ in posttonic syllables were weakened to ⟦b:u⟧: as, ⟦b:dḗnuō⟧ from ⟦b:dḗnovō⟧ (⟦r94:94⟧); ⟦b:ábluō⟧ from ⟦b:ablavō⟧. The form ⟦b:puer⟧, ⟦i:boy⟧, arose from the older POVER in enclitic vocatives (⟦r93:93, 7⟧) and was thence transferred to the nominative like ⟦b:piter⟧ in ⟦b:Iūpiter⟧ (⟦r94:94⟧).

title: Weakening of Simple Vowels in Final Syllables
text:
⟦#107⟧
(⟦i:a.⟧) In final syllables unaccented original ⟦b:e⟧ before ⟦b:s⟧ and ⟦b:t⟧ was weakened to ⟦b:i⟧: as, ⟦b:salūtis⟧, ⟦i:of safety⟧, from older ⟦b:salūtes⟧ (⟦r507:507⟧).
(⟦i:b.⟧) Final ⟦b:i⟧ became ⟦b:e⟧: as, ⟦b:ante⟧ for ⟦b:*anti⟧ (Greek ἀντί and ⟦b:anti-cipāre⟧); nominative singular ⟦b:mare⟧, from the stem ⟦b:mari-⟧ (⟦r526:526⟧).
(⟦i:c.⟧) In final syllables ⟦b:o⟧ before consonants changed to ⟦b:u⟧ except when preceded by ⟦b:u⟧ or ⟦b:v⟧: as, ⟦b:fīlius⟧, ⟦i:son⟧, for old Latin ⟦b:fīlios⟧ (⟦r452:452⟧); ⟦b:ferunt⟧, ⟦i:they carry⟧, for older ⟦b:feront⟧; ⟦b:femur⟧, ⟦i:thigh⟧, nomin. sg. from the stem ⟦b:femor-⟧ (⟦r489:489⟧); ⟦b:genus⟧, ⟦i:kind⟧, for ⟦b:*genos⟧, Greek γένος; but ⟦b:vīvont⟧, ⟦i:they live⟧; ⟦b:salvom⟧, ⟦i:safe⟧. Not long before the beginning of our era ⟦b:o⟧ here also changed to ⟦b:u⟧ and appears to have coalesced with the preceding ⟦b:v⟧ (Quint. 1, 7, 26): as, in inscriptions: INGENVS (nomin. sg.) for ⟦b:ingenuos⟧; SERVM, ⟦i:slave⟧ (acc. sg.), for ⟦b:servom⟧; NOVM for ⟦b:novom⟧, ⟦i:something new⟧; so also ⟦b:boum⟧, ⟦i:oxen⟧ (gen. pl.), for ⟦b:bovom⟧ (⟦r494:494⟧). But inasmuch as the majority of forms in the paradigms of these words retained their ⟦b:v⟧, it was restored in most cases, by analogy, to the forms which had lost it: as, ⟦b:servum⟧ for ⟦b:serum⟧, because of ⟦b:servī⟧, ⟦b:servō⟧, etc.; ⟦b:vīvunt⟧ for ⟦b:vīunt⟧, because of ⟦b:vīvō⟧, ⟦b:vīvis⟧, ⟦b:vīvit⟧, etc.
(⟦i:d.⟧) When the stems ⟦b:fac-⟧ (⟦b:facere⟧, ⟦i:do⟧), ⟦b:cap-⟧ (⟦b:capere⟧, ⟦i:take⟧) appear as second members of compounds, their ⟦b:a⟧ changes in final syllables to ⟦b:e⟧: as, ⟦b:artifex⟧, ⟦i:artisan⟧; ⟦b:auceps⟧, ⟦i:bird-catcher⟧. After the analogy of these words, compounds with ⟦b:dīcere⟧ and ⟦b:īre⟧ have ⟦b:e⟧ in the nom. sg.: as, ⟦b:iūdex⟧, ⟦b:iūdicis⟧, ⟦i:judge⟧ (from ⟦b:iūs⟧ and ⟦b:dīcere⟧); ⟦b:comes⟧, ⟦i:companion⟧ (from ⟦b:com⟧, ⟦i:with⟧, and ⟦b:īre⟧); see ⟦r136:136⟧, 2.

title: Weakening of Diphthongs in Unaccented Syllables
text:
⟦#108⟧
Diphthongs, whether medial or final, are treated alike in atonic syllables.
(⟦i:a.⟧) Atonic ⟦b:ei⟧, ⟦b:oi⟧, and ⟦b:ai⟧ (⟦b:ae⟧) became ⟦b:ī⟧: as, ⟦b:lupī⟧, ⟦i:wolves⟧ (nom. pl.), for ⟦b:*lupoi⟧ (Gr. λύκοι); ⟦b:bellī⟧, ⟦i:in war⟧ (loc. sg., ⟦r460:460⟧, ⟦r1338:1338⟧), for ⟦b:*bellei⟧ (Greek οἴκει) or ⟦b:*belloi⟧ (Greek οἴκοι); ⟦b:éxīstimō⟧, ⟦i:I consider⟧, from ⟦b:aestimō⟧; ⟦b:cóncīdō⟧, ⟦i:I strike down⟧, from ⟦b:caedō⟧; Cicero, ⟦i:O.⟧ 159, mentions ⟦b:inīcum⟧, ⟦i:unfair⟧, for ⟦b:*ínaecum⟧, and ⟦b:concīsum⟧ for ⟦b:*cóncaesum⟧; so also, probably, ⟦b:hīc⟧, ⟦i:this⟧, arose from ⟦b:hoic⟧ (⟦r662:662⟧) when used as a proclitic (⟦r92:92⟧).
(⟦i:b.⟧) Atonic ⟦b:ou⟧ and ⟦b:au⟧ became ⟦b:ū⟧: as, ⟦b:ínclūdō⟧, ⟦i:I include⟧, from ⟦b:claudō⟧; ⟦b:áccūsāre⟧, ⟦i:to accuse⟧, from ⟦b:causa⟧.
⟦#109⟧
There are not a few cases in which the atonic vowel does not conform to the rules given above (⟦r102:102-108⟧). These are usually compounds which show the vowel of the simple verb. Some of these were formed at a time when the early recessive accent was no longer in force and consequently there was no cause for weakening; in others the vowel of the simple verb was by analogy substituted for the weakened vowel of the compound: as, ⟦b:appetō⟧, ⟦i:I strive after⟧, from ⟦b:petō⟧, which ought to have ⟦b:i⟧ like ⟦b:colligō⟧, ⟦i:collect⟧, from ⟦b:legō⟧; ⟦b:intermedius⟧, ⟦i:intermediate⟧, but ⟦b:dīmidius⟧, ⟦i:half⟧; ⟦b:dēfraudāre⟧, ⟦i:to cheat⟧, by the side of ⟦b:dēfrūdāre⟧ from ⟦b:fraudāre⟧; instead of the common ⟦b:redarguō⟧, ⟦i:I refute⟧, Scipio Africanus minor Pauli filius (185-129 B.C.) said ⟦b:rederguō⟧, and ⟦b:pertīsum⟧ for ⟦b:pertaesum⟧, but both Cicero (⟦i:O.⟧ 159) and Lucilius discountenance ⟦b:pertīsum⟧ as the sign of a pedantic prig. In a few cases the reverse process took place, and the weakened vowel which arose in the compound was transferred to the simple verb: as, ⟦b:clūdō⟧, ⟦i:I close⟧ (⟦r958:958⟧), for ⟦b:claudō⟧, which owes its ⟦b:ū⟧ to compounds like ⟦b:occlūdō⟧. For a case where the vowel of the preceding syllable acted as a stay to the expected change, see ⟦r104:104⟧, ⟦i:d⟧.

title: Loss in Unaccented Syllables
text:
⟦#110⟧
Only vowels which are short and atonic may be lost. The loss of a medial vowel is called ⟦i:Syncope⟧; of an initial vowel, ⟦i:Aphaeresis⟧; of a final vowel ⟦i:Apocope⟧.
⟦#111⟧
Syncope. (⟦i:a.⟧) Loss of a posttonic vowel, entailing the loss of a syllable, occurs in ⟦b:ardus⟧ (Lucil.; for ⟦b:ă⟧ see ⟦r128:128⟧) for the common ⟦b:āridus⟧, ⟦i:dry⟧; ⟦b:caldus⟧ by the side of ⟦b:calidus⟧, ⟦i:warm⟧ (Quint. 1, 6, 19); ⟦b:reppulī⟧, ⟦i:I pushed back⟧, and ⟦b:rettulī⟧, ⟦i:I carried back⟧, stand for ⟦b:*répepulī⟧ and ⟦b:*rétetulī⟧ (⟦r861:861⟧); ⟦b:pergō⟧, ⟦i:I proceed⟧, stands for ⟦b:*perregō⟧ from ⟦b:regō⟧ (cf. ⟦b:cor-rigō⟧, ⟦b:ē-rigō⟧, where the ⟦b:e⟧ is weakened, ⟦r103:103⟧, and ⟦b:porrigō⟧, ⟦b:porgō⟧, where it is either weakened or lost), hence it forms its perfect ⟦b:perrēxī⟧ (⟦r953:953⟧): ⟦b:pōnō⟧, ⟦i:I place⟧, is for ⟦b:*posnō⟧ (⟦r170:170, 2⟧) from ⟦b:*po-sinō⟧ (⟦r112:112⟧), hence it forms its past participle ⟦b:positus⟧ (⟦r972:972⟧); for ⟦b:iūrgō⟧, ⟦i:I blame⟧. Plautus has ⟦b:iūrigō⟧; ⟦b:*ūsūripō⟧ (from ⟦b:ūsus⟧ and ⟦b:rapere⟧) yields ⟦b:ūsurpō⟧, ⟦i:I utilize⟧; ⟦b:*gāvideō⟧, hence ⟦b:gāvīsus⟧ (⟦r801:801⟧), gives ⟦b:gaudeo⟧, ⟦i:I rejoice⟧, converting ⟦b:āṷ⟧ to ⟦b:aṷ⟧ before the following ⟦b:d⟧ (⟦r128:128⟧); in a similar way ⟦b:auceps⟧, ⟦i:bird-catcher⟧, is formed from ⟦b:*aviceps⟧ (⟦b:avis⟧, ⟦i:bird⟧, and ⟦b:capere⟧, ⟦i:catch⟧); ⟦b:claudere⟧, ⟦i:lock⟧, from ⟦b:*clāvidere⟧ (⟦b:clāvis⟧, ⟦i:key⟧); ⟦b:aetās⟧, ⟦i:age⟧, for ⟦b:áevitās⟧ (⟦r262:262⟧); ⟦b:praecō⟧, ⟦i:herald⟧, for ⟦b:*práevicō⟧ (105, ⟦i:g⟧) ⟦b:prae-vocō⟧ (⟦r211:211⟧); also with change of ⟦b:ou⟧ to ⟦b:ū⟧ (⟦r100:100⟧), ⟦b:prūdēns⟧, ⟦i:prudent⟧, for ⟦b:*proudēns⟧ from ⟦b:providēns⟧, ⟦i:foreseeing⟧; ⟦b:nūper⟧, ⟦i:lately⟧, from ⟦b:*noviper⟧; ⟦b:nūntius⟧, ⟦i:messenger⟧, from ⟦b:*noventius⟧ (⟦r333:333⟧); ⟦b:iūcundus⟧, ⟦i:joyful⟧, from ⟦b:iuvicundus⟧ (Cic. ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 14). But forms like ⟦b:pōclum⟧, ⟦i:cup⟧, ⟦b:saeclum⟧, ⟦i:age⟧, do not belong here, as they are original and not derived by syncope from ⟦b:pōculum⟧, ⟦b:saeculum⟧; cf. ⟦r172:172⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) Where, through the loss of a vowel, ⟦b:l⟧ or ⟦b:r⟧ would come to stand between two consonants, or where they would be final and preceded by a consonant, ⟦b:l⟧ and ⟦b:r⟧ become syllabic (⟦r83:83⟧) and the syllable is thus maintained. Syllabic ⟦b:l⟧ is represented by ⟦b:ul⟧, syllabic ⟦b:r⟧ by ⟦b:er⟧ (⟦r172:172, 3⟧). The development of such intercalary vowels as ⟦b:u⟧ before ⟦b:l⟧ and ⟦b:e⟧ before ⟦b:r⟧ is called ⟦i:Anaptyxis⟧ (⟦r172:172⟧). Thus, ⟦b:*sacri-dōts⟧ (cf. ⟦b:sacri-legium⟧) became first ⟦b:*sacr̥dōts⟧ by syncope, then ⟦b:sacerdōs⟧, ⟦i:priest⟧, by anaptyxis; ⟦b:*ācribus⟧ (cf. ⟦b:ācri-mōnia⟧, ⟦i:pungency⟧) first became ⟦b:*ācr̥bus⟧ then ⟦b:ācerbus⟧, ⟦i:pungent⟧; ⟦b:*agrilos⟧ (⟦r267:267⟧, cf. ⟦b:agri-cola⟧, ⟦i:farmer⟧) became first ⟦b:*agr̥los⟧, then ⟦b:*agerlos⟧, and finally, by assimilation of the ⟦b:r⟧ to ⟦b:l⟧ (⟦r166:166, 7⟧), ⟦b:agellus⟧, ⟦i:small field⟧; from ⟦b:*dis-ficilter⟧ (adverb from ⟦b:dis-⟧ and ⟦b:facilis⟧) arose ⟦b:*difficl̥ter⟧ and ⟦b:difficulter⟧, ⟦i:with difficulty⟧. The nominative sg. of the following words is to be explained thus. ⟦b:ager⟧ (⟦r451:451⟧) was originally ⟦b:*agros⟧ (cf. Greek ἄγρος), which changed successively to ⟦b:*agr̥s⟧, ⟦b:*agers⟧, and ⟦b:ager⟧ (for the loss of ⟦b:-s⟧ see ⟦r171:171, 1 and 3⟧). Similarly ⟦b:*ācris⟧, passing through the stages of ⟦b:*ācr̥s⟧, ⟦b:*ācers⟧, became ⟦b:ācer⟧ (⟦r627:627⟧), and ⟦b:*famlos⟧ by way of ⟦b:*faml̥s⟧, ⟦b:*famuls⟧, became ⟦b:famul⟧ (⟦r455:455⟧), to which later the common ending of nouns of the ⟦b:o-⟧declension was added, giving ⟦b:famulus⟧.
⟦#112⟧
Aphaeresis. Aphaeresis hardly occurs in literary Latin. In the pronoun ⟦b:iste⟧ the initial ⟦b:i⟧ is sometimes dropped (⟦r667:667⟧); this loss implies an accented ultima (⟦r94:94⟧). A trace of prehistoric aphaeresis is found in the prefix ⟦b:po-⟧ for ⟦b:*apo⟧ (Greek ἀπό) in ⟦b:pōnō⟧, ⟦i:I place⟧, for ⟦b:po-s(i)nō⟧ (111, ⟦i:a⟧).
⟦#113⟧
Apocope. Under the same conditions under which a medial vowel was syncopated, the final vowel of a word which stood in close union with the following word, as a preposition with its noun, was lost. In this way ⟦b:*peri⟧ (Greek περί) became ⟦b:per⟧; ⟦b:*apo⟧ (Greek ἀπό) became ⟦b:ap⟧, ⟦b:ab⟧ (⟦r164:164, 2⟧); ⟦b:*eti⟧ (Greek ἔτι) became ⟦b:et⟧. Similarly the final ⟦b:-e⟧ of the enclitics ⟦b:-ce⟧, ⟦b:-ne⟧, ⟦i:not⟧, and ⟦b:-ne⟧ interrogative was lost: ⟦b:*sī-ce⟧ became ⟦b:sīc⟧, ⟦i:so⟧; ⟦b:*quī-ne⟧, ⟦b:quīn⟧, ⟦i:why not⟧; ⟦b:habēsne⟧, ⟦b:haben⟧, ⟦i:hast thou⟧; the imperatives ⟦b:dīc⟧, ⟦i:say⟧, ⟦b:dūc⟧, ⟦i:lead⟧, and ⟦b:fac⟧, ⟦i:do⟧, stand for earlier ⟦b:dīce⟧, ⟦b:dūce⟧, ⟦b:face⟧ (⟦r846:846⟧); the shortened form ⟦b:em⟧ for ⟦b:eme⟧ (imperative of ⟦b:emere⟧, ⟦i:take⟧) has been turned into an interjection (⟦r1149:1149⟧). In the same way ⟦b:nec⟧ arose by the side of ⟦b:neque⟧; ⟦b:ac⟧ by the side of ⟦b:atque⟧ (⟦r158:158⟧). Final ⟦b:-e⟧ has also been dropped in the nominative sg. of a number of polysyllabic neuter stems in ⟦b:-āli⟧ and ⟦b:-āri⟧ (⟦r546:546⟧): as, ⟦b:animal⟧, ⟦i:animal⟧, for ⟦b:*animāle⟧, ⟦b:exemplar⟧, ⟦i:pattern⟧, for ⟦b:*exemplāre⟧. See ⟦r536:536⟧, ⟦r537:537⟧. It must, however, be remembered that in most of the cases given the loss of a final vowel would also result from elision (⟦r119:119⟧) before the initial vowel of the following word.

title: Combination of Adjacent Vowels
text:
⟦#114⟧
Hiatus. A succession of two vowel sounds not making a diphthong is called ⟦i:Hiatus⟧.
When in the formation of words by means of suffixes or prefixes or through the loss of an intervening consonant, two vowels come into contact within a word we speak of ⟦i:internal hiatus⟧; the term ⟦i:external hiatus⟧ comprises those cases where, in connected discourse, the final vowel of one word comes into contact with the initial vowel of the following word. For the latter kind, see ⟦r2474:2474⟧.
⟦#115⟧
The treatment of vowels in internal hiatus is four-fold: (1.) The hiatus may remain; (2.) the two vowels may be fused into one (⟦i:Contraction⟧); (3.) one of the two vowels may be dropped (⟦i:Elision⟧); and (4.) the two vowels may be combined into a diphthong.
⟦#116⟧
Hiatus is maintained (⟦i:a.⟧) between two adjacent vowels the second of which is long and accented (according to the classical accentuation): as, ⟦b:coḗgi⟧, ⟦i:I forced⟧, and ⟦b:coā́ctus⟧, ⟦i:forced⟧ (⟦r937:937⟧); but ⟦b:cōgō⟧ (⟦r118:118, 3⟧). For ⟦b:coepi⟧, instead of ⟦b:coḗpī⟧, ⟦i:I began⟧, see ⟦r120:120⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) In many prepositional compounds when the members were still felt to be independent: as, ⟦b:praeesse⟧ (the contracted form ⟦b:praesse⟧ is found in inscriptions); ⟦b:dēerunt⟧, ⟦i:they will be wanting⟧, by the side of ⟦b:dērunt⟧; ⟦b:coalēscō⟧, ⟦i:grow together⟧ (the contracted form ⟦b:cōlēscō⟧ appears in Varro); ⟦b:cooptāre⟧, ⟦i:coöpt⟧, ⟦b:cooperiō⟧, ⟦i:I cover up⟧ (by the side of rare ⟦b:cōptāre⟧, ⟦b:cōperīre⟧); ⟦b:coïtus⟧, ⟦i:meeting⟧, by the side of ⟦b:coetus⟧ (⟦r120:120⟧).
(⟦i:c.⟧) A comparatively large number of vowel combinations remain unchanged: as ⟦b:ea⟧ and ⟦b:eā⟧ in ⟦b:eam⟧, ⟦i:her⟧, and ⟦b:meā⟧, ⟦i:by my⟧ (fem. sing.); ⟦b:ia⟧ and ⟦b:iā⟧ in ⟦b:māria⟧, ⟦i:seas⟧, ⟦b:viātōris⟧, ⟦i:of the traveller⟧; ⟦b:ua⟧ and ⟦b:uā⟧ in ⟦b:bēlua⟧, ⟦i:monster⟧, ⟦b:suā⟧, ⟦i:through her⟧ (fem. sg.); ⟦b:iē⟧ in ⟦b:quiēs⟧, ⟦i:quiet⟧; ⟦b:uē⟧ in ⟦b:luēs⟧, ⟦i:pestilence⟧; ⟦b:eī⟧ in ⟦b:meī⟧, ⟦i:of me⟧; ⟦b:uī⟧ in ⟦b:tuī⟧, ⟦i:of thee⟧; ⟦b:eō⟧ in ⟦b:meō⟧, ⟦i:by my⟧ (masc. sing.).
⟦#117⟧
Synizesis. In these combinations the first vowel is sometimes made unsyllabic (⟦r83:83⟧). This is called ⟦i:synizesis⟧ (⟦r2499:2499⟧) and is not rare in poets, being often the only means of adapting a word to the requirements of certain metres. Thus, ⟦b:fortuītus⟧ (- ⏑ - ⏓) must appear in a hexameter as ⟦b:fortvītus⟧ (⟦b:fortṷītus⟧). See ⟦r2499:2499⟧, ⟦r2503:2503⟧.
⟦#118⟧
Contraction. (1.) Two like vowels may unite in one long vowel; rapidity of utterance was favourable to such fusion. In compounds, the desire to keep the members distinct often prevented it. So always ⟦b:nēmō⟧, ⟦i:nobody⟧, for ⟦b:*neemō⟧ from ⟦b:*ne-hemō⟧, ⟦i:no man⟧ (for the loss of ⟦b:h⟧, see ⟦r58:58⟧, ⟦r150:150⟧; for ⟦b:e⟧ in ⟦b:*hemō⟧, see ⟦r144:144⟧); and by the side of the open forms, ⟦b:nīl⟧ from ⟦b:nihil⟧, ⟦i:nothing⟧; ⟦b:vēmēns⟧ from ⟦b:vehemēns⟧, ⟦i:rapid⟧ (connected with the verb ⟦b:vehō⟧); rarely ⟦b:dērunt⟧, ⟦i:they will be wanting⟧, and ⟦b:dēsse⟧, ⟦i:to be wanting⟧, for ⟦b:dēerunt⟧, ⟦b:dēesse⟧; ⟦b:dēlēram⟧, ⟦i:I had destroyed⟧, from ⟦b:*dēlēeram⟧ for ⟦b:dēlēveram⟧ (for the loss of ⟦b:v⟧, see ⟦r153:153⟧), see ⟦r890:890⟧; ⟦b:passūm⟧, ⟦i:of paces⟧, for ⟦b:passuum⟧ (⟦r591:591⟧).
(2.) A diphthong absorbs the following vowel: as, ⟦b:praetor⟧, older ⟦b:praitor⟧, ⟦i:praetor⟧, from ⟦b:*prai-itor⟧, ⟦i:who goes before⟧; inscriptions show ⟦b:praerunt⟧ for ⟦b:praeerunt⟧, ⟦i:they will be before⟧; for ⟦b:praebēre⟧, ⟦i:to furnish⟧, the open form ⟦b:praehibēre⟧ occurs in Plautus (⟦r1004:1004⟧).
(3.) If two unlike vowels are contracted at all, they usually unite in the long sound of the first vowel. Thus, ⟦b:o⟧ and ⟦b:a⟧ yield ⟦b:ō⟧: as, ⟦b:cōgō⟧, ⟦i:I force⟧, from ⟦b:co-agō⟧; ⟦b:cōgitō⟧, ⟦i:I think⟧, from ⟦b:co-agitō⟧. Similarly Varro has ⟦b:cōlēscat⟧, ⟦i:it may combine⟧, for ⟦b:co-alēscat⟧. ⟦b:o⟧ and ⟦b:e⟧ yield ⟦b:ō⟧: as, ⟦b:prōmō⟧, ⟦i:bring out⟧, ⟦b:cōmō⟧, ⟦i:put up⟧, for ⟦b:pro-emō⟧, ⟦b:co-emō⟧ (⟦r953:953⟧). ⟦b:ē⟧ and ⟦b:a⟧ yield ⟦b:ē⟧: as, ⟦b:dēgō⟧, ⟦i:I pass away⟧, from ⟦b:dē-agō⟧ (⟦r937:937⟧). ⟦b:i⟧ and ⟦b:e⟧ in the termination of the vocative of ⟦b:-io-⟧ stems probably contracted to ⟦b:-ī⟧; as ⟦b:fīlī⟧ from ⟦b:*fīlie⟧, ⟦r459:459⟧. But in denominative (⟦r365:365⟧) and other verbs of the first conjugation ⟦b:ā⟧ and ⟦b:ō⟧ contract into ⟦b:ō⟧: as, ⟦b:amō⟧, ⟦i:I love⟧, from ⟦b:*amā-ō⟧ (cf. Greek τιμά·ω); and ⟦b:ā⟧ and ⟦b:ē⟧ into ⟦b:ē⟧: as, ⟦b:amēs⟧, ⟦i:thou mayest love⟧, for ⟦b:*amā-ēs⟧.
⟦#119⟧
Elision. Only rarely the first of two successive vowels is dropped: as, ⟦b:nūllus⟧, ⟦i:no⟧, for ⟦b:*ne-ūllus⟧; likewise the final vowel of the first member of nominal compounds: as, ⟦b:multangulus⟧, ⟦i:with many corners⟧, for ⟦b:*multi-angulus⟧ (cf. ⟦b:multi-cavus⟧, ⟦i:with many holes⟧); ⟦b:flexanimus⟧, ⟦i:heart-rending⟧, for ⟦b:*flexi-animus⟧ (cf. ⟦b:flexi-pēs⟧, ⟦i:with bent feet⟧).
⟦#120⟧
Combination into diphthongs. The union of two successive vowels into a diphthong is equally rare: ⟦b:o⟧ and ⟦b:i⟧ are combined to ⟦b:oi⟧, ⟦b:oe⟧, in ⟦b:coetus⟧, ⟦i:meeting⟧, by the side of the open form ⟦b:coïtus⟧ (116, ⟦i:b⟧); the perfect ⟦b:coepī⟧ (⟦r812:812⟧), ⟦i:I began⟧, owes its diphthong ⟦b:oe⟧ to forms in which the ⟦b:e⟧ was short and unaccented, such as the rare present forms ⟦b:coepiō⟧ for ⟦b:có-ĕpiō⟧ (⟦r813:813⟧); for ⟦b:coḗpi⟧ (⟦r813:813⟧, ⟦r863:863⟧) would have remained unchanged (116, ⟦i:a⟧). ⟦b:neuter⟧, with the accent on the ⟦b:e⟧, was pronounced as three syllables, later ⟦b:eu⟧ became diphthongal; ⟦b:neutiquam⟧ with synizesis (⟦r117:117⟧) of ⟦b:e⟧. ⟦b:e⟧ and ⟦b:ī̆⟧ sometimes contract to ⟦b:e͡i⟧ in ⟦b:rēi⟧ (⟦r601:601⟧, ⟦r602:602⟧) and in ⟦b:de͡inde⟧, ⟦b:dēin⟧ in the classic poets.

title: Lengthening
text:
⟦#121⟧
Compensative lengthening. When certain groups of consonants are simplified by the dropping of a consonant, its time is absorbed by a preceding short vowel, which thereby becomes long. This is called ⟦i:Compensation⟧. In many cases compensative lengthening is due to the loss of a preliterary sonant ⟦b:s⟧ (⟦r170:170, 2⟧): as,
⟦b:cānus⟧, ⟦i:gray⟧, from ⟦b:*casnus⟧ (cf. ⟦b:cas-cus⟧, ⟦i:very old⟧). See for other cases of this lengthening, 170, 5, ⟦b:quīnī⟧, for ⟦b:*quincnī⟧; 170, 6, ⟦b:īgnōscō⟧, for ⟦b:*in-gnōscō⟧.
⟦#122⟧
Induced lengthening. Before certain groups of consonants short vowels have a tendency to become long: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) The prefixes ⟦b:in-⟧ and ⟦b:con-⟧ before ⟦b:s⟧ or ⟦b:f⟧ lengthened their vowels in classical Latin (Cic. ⟦i:O.⟧ 159): as, ⟦b:īnsānus⟧, ⟦i:mad⟧; ⟦b:īnfēlīx⟧, ⟦i:unhappy⟧; ⟦b:cōnsuēvit⟧, ⟦i:he grew used to⟧; ⟦b:cōnfēcit⟧, ⟦i:he accomplished⟧. Elsewhere also the vowel before ⟦b:ns⟧ and ⟦b:nf⟧ appears to have been lengthened: as, ⟦b:fōns⟧, ⟦i:fountain⟧; ⟦b:pēnsus⟧, ⟦i:weighty⟧ (Gell. 9, 6); ⟦b:forēnsis⟧, ⟦i:forensic⟧; ⟦b:cēnsor⟧, ⟦i:censor⟧; ⟦b:mēnsa⟧, ⟦i:table⟧; ⟦b:mēnsis⟧, ⟦i:mouth⟧; ⟦b:Valēns⟧; ⟦b:Clēmēns⟧; the ⟦b:o⟧ of ⟦b:īnsons⟧, ⟦i:guiltless⟧, however, is marked as short by the grammarian Probus.
(⟦i:b.⟧) A similar lengthening of the vowel before ⟦b:nc⟧ followed by ⟦b:t⟧ or ⟦b:s⟧ appears: as, ⟦b:ūnctus⟧, ⟦i:anointed⟧, from ⟦b:unguō⟧ (Gell. 9, 6); ⟦b:iūnctus⟧, ⟦i:joined⟧, from ⟦b:iungō⟧ (⟦r954:954⟧), ⟦b:coniūnx⟧, ⟦i:spouse⟧, genit. ⟦b:coniugis⟧ (⟦r472:472⟧); ⟦b:quīnctus⟧, ⟦i:fifth⟧, whence ⟦b:quīntus⟧ (⟦r170:170, 4⟧) and ⟦b:quīnque⟧, ⟦i:five⟧, derive their ⟦b:ī⟧; ⟦b:sānctus⟧, ⟦i:hallowed⟧.
(⟦i:c.⟧) Spellings like sIgnvm, ⟦i:sign⟧ (well supported in inscriptions), and dIgne, ⟦i:worthily⟧ (less well supported) show that ⟦b:i⟧ was at times lengthened before ⟦b:gn⟧. The grammarian Priscian demands this lengthening for all vowels preceding the ending ⟦b:-gnus⟧, ⟦b:-gna⟧, ⟦b:-gnum⟧.
(⟦i:d.⟧) A lengthened vowel before ⟦b:r⟧ followed by a consonant is also certain for some words like ⟦b:ōrdō⟧, ⟦i:order⟧; ⟦b:fōrma⟧, ⟦i:shape⟧.
(⟦i:e.⟧) Some speakers appear to have lengthened the vowel of prepositions like ⟦b:con-⟧, ⟦b:sub-⟧, ⟦b:ob-⟧, in the compounds of ⟦b:iaciō⟧ (104, ⟦i:c⟧); as ⟦b:ōbicit⟧. This practice, which is disapproved by Gellius (⟦r4:4⟧, ⟦r17:17⟧), probably arose from the transfer by analogy of the quantity of the first syllable in forms like ⟦b:conieciant⟧ (⟦r940:940⟧) to that of the shortened form. In the same way the occasional spelling CÓNIV́NX, ⟦i:spouse⟧, for ⟦b:coniūnx⟧, may owe its long ⟦b:ō⟧ to the analogy of ⟦b:cōiunx⟧, CÓIVGI (⟦r170:170, 6⟧).
(⟦i:f.⟧) Many verb stems ending in ⟦b:-g⟧ have a long vowel in the past participle before the suffix ⟦b:-to-⟧: as, ⟦b:tēctus⟧, ⟦i:covered⟧, from ⟦b:tego⟧ (⟦r916:916⟧); ⟦b:tāctus⟧, ⟦i:touched⟧, from ⟦b:tangō⟧ (⟦r925:925⟧); ⟦b:pāctus⟧, ⟦i:fixed⟧, from ⟦b:pangō⟧ (⟦r925:925⟧); ⟦b:fīctus⟧, ⟦i:moulded⟧, from ⟦b:fingō⟧ (⟦r954:954⟧); ⟦b:pīctus⟧, ⟦i:painted⟧, from ⟦b:pingō⟧. The evidence for ⟦b:ā⟧ in ⟦b:maximus⟧ is very scanty: one case of A with the apex (⟦r29:29, 3⟧) in a faulty inscription.
(⟦i:g.⟧) Of the induced lengthenings enumerated above, only those given in (⟦i:a.⟧) (⟦i:b.⟧) (⟦i:f.⟧) seem to have been universal in classical Latin. The rest appear to have been local peculiarities, which, while making inroads upon the literary language, never gained full recognition.
⟦#123⟧
(1.) Analogical lengthening. In noun stems in ⟦b:-o⟧ the stem vowel is lengthened in the genitive plural ⟦b:-ōrum⟧ (⟦r449:449⟧, ⟦r462:462⟧), by analogy to the stems in ⟦b:-ā⟧ (⟦r435:435⟧): as, ⟦b:servōrum⟧, ⟦i:of slaves⟧, like ⟦b:mēnsārum⟧, ⟦i:of tables⟧. For other cases see ⟦r122:122⟧, ⟦i:e⟧.
(2.) Metrical lengthening. On the lengthening of a vowel (or a syllable) under the influence of verse-ictus, see ⟦r2505:2505⟧.

title: Shortening
text:
⟦#124⟧
A vowel originally long is regularly shortened in classical Latin before another vowel, even though an ⟦b:h⟧ intervene: as,
⟦b:taceō⟧, ⟦i:I am silent⟧, from the stem ⟦b:tacē-⟧ (⟦r365:365⟧); ⟦b:seorsum⟧, ⟦i:apart⟧, ⟦b:deorsum⟧, ⟦i:downward⟧, from ⟦b:sē(v)orsum⟧, ⟦b:dē(v)orsum⟧ (⟦r153:153⟧).
⟦#125⟧
In simple words a diphthong occurs before a vowel only in one or two proper names: as, ⟦b:Gnaeus⟧, ⟦b:Annaeus⟧, in which it remains long, and in Greek words. But the diphthong ⟦b:ae⟧ of the prefix ⟦b:prae⟧ is sometimes shortened before a vowel: as, ⟦b:pra͝eacūtus⟧; ⟦b:pra͝eeunt⟧; ⟦b:pra͝ehibeō⟧; hence ⟦b:prehendō⟧ for ⟦b:*prae-hendō⟧. Sometimes it coalesces with a following vowel: as, ⟦b:pra͡e͡optāvīstī⟧.
⟦#126⟧
An increased tendency to shorten a long vowel before another vowel can be traced in the history of the language: thus, classical ⟦b:fuī⟧, ⟦i:I was⟧, for Plautus’s ⟦b:fūī⟧ (⟦r750:750⟧); ⟦b:clueō⟧, ⟦i:I am called⟧, for Plautus’s ⟦b:clūeō⟧; perfect ⟦b:pluit⟧, ⟦i:it rained⟧, for Varro’s ⟦b:plūit⟧ (cf. ⟦b:plūvit⟧, ⟦r823:823⟧, ⟦r947:947⟧); ⟦b:pius⟧, ⟦i:pious⟧, for Ennius’s ⟦b:pīus⟧; see also ⟦r765:765⟧.
⟦#127⟧
But even in classical Latin there are cases where a vowel before another vowel remains long: thus,
(1.) Regularly, the ⟦b:ī⟧ of ⟦b:fīō⟧, ⟦i:I am made⟧, except before ⟦b:-er-⟧, as in ⟦b:fierem⟧ (⟦r788:788⟧, ⟦r789:789⟧).
(2.) In ⟦b:dīus⟧, ⟦i:godly⟧, for ⟦b:dīvus⟧ (⟦r153:153⟧), and the old ablatives ⟦b:dīū⟧, ⟦b:dīō⟧, ⟦i:open sky⟧ (used only in the expression ⟦b:sub dīū⟧, ⟦b:sub dīō⟧, i.e. ⟦b:sub dīvō⟧).
(3.) In the ending ⟦b:ēī⟧ of the genitive and dative sg. of stems in ⟦b:-ē-⟧ (⟦r601:601⟧) when an ⟦b:i⟧ precedes: as, ⟦b:diēī⟧, ⟦i:of a day⟧, ⟦b:aciēī⟧, ⟦i:of the battle line⟧, but ⟦b:reī⟧, ⟦i:of the thing⟧, for older ⟦b:rēī⟧.
(4.) It may be mentioned here that ⟦b:rēī⟧ is said to occur in verse 6 times (Plaut. G. 2, Lucr. G. 2, D. 2); ⟦b:reī⟧ 9 times (Plaut. G. 2, Ter. G. 4, D. 1, Juv. G. 1, Sulp. Apoll. G. 1); ⟦b:re͞i⟧ 27 times (Plaut. G. 2, D. 3, Enn. D. 1, Ter. G. 9, D. 8, Lucil. G. 1, D. 1, Lucr. G. 2). ⟦b:fidēī⟧ G. 3 times (Plaut., Enn., Lucr.); ⟦b:fideī⟧ 11 times (Enn. D. 1, Man. G. 2, D. 1, Sil. G. 4, D. 1, Juv. G. 2); ⟦b:fidēi⟧ 5 times (Ter. G. 1, D. 3, Hor. 1). ⟦b:ēī⟧ 35 times (Plaut. 18, Ter. 8, Lucr. 9); ⟦b:eī⟧ some 17 times (Plaut. 12, Ter. 2, German. 1, Ter. Maur. 2); ⟦b:ēi⟧ 23 times (Plaut. 11, Ter. 8, Lucil. 3, Cat. 1).
(5.) ⟦b:Gāius⟧ retains its ⟦b:ā⟧ before the vowel ⟦b:i⟧: thus, ⟦b:Gāius⟧ (trisyllabic).
(6.) In the pronominal genitives in ⟦b:-ī̆us⟧ (⟦r618:618⟧), the quantity of ⟦b:i⟧ varied. The older dramatists use ⟦b:ī⟧; later, ⟦b:ī⟧ was shortened, but variations in its quantity seem to have continued until long after the end of the republic; Cicero, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 3, 183, measures ⟦b:illius⟧; Quintilian 1, 5, 18 ⟦b:ūnīus⟧; the grammarian Priscian prescribes ⟦b:-īus⟧ for all except ⟦b:alterius⟧, which should always have ⟦b:i⟧, and ⟦b:utrius⟧, in which the ⟦b:i⟧ is common (⟦r30:30⟧). In verse the ⟦b:i⟧ is often short, except in ⟦b:neutrīus⟧; ⟦b:utriusque⟧ has always short ⟦b:i⟧.
(7.) The penult is long in the endings ⟦b:-āī⟧, ⟦b:-āīs⟧, ⟦b:-ōī⟧, ⟦b:-ōīs⟧, and ⟦b:-ēī⟧, ⟦b:-ēīs⟧, from stems in ⟦b:-āio-⟧, ⟦b:-ōio-⟧, and ⟦b:-ēio-⟧ (⟦r458:458⟧) or ⟦b:-iā-⟧ (⟦r437:437⟧): as, ⟦b:Gāī⟧, ⟦b:Bōī⟧, ⟦b:Pōmpēī⟧, ⟦b:plēbēī⟧: ⟦b:Gāīs⟧, ⟦b:Bōīs⟧, ⟦b:Pompēīs⟧, ⟦b:plēbēīs⟧, ⟦b:Bāīs⟧; ⟦b:aulāī⟧, ⟦b:pictāī⟧.
(8.) ⟦b:Dī̆ana⟧ has ⟦b:ĭ⟧ as often as ⟦b:ī⟧. ⟦b:ohē⟧ has ⟦b:ŏ̄⟧; ⟦b:ē̆heu⟧ has ⟦b:ĕ⟧ in comedy, otherwise ⟦b:ē⟧.
(9.) In many Greek words a long vowel comes before another vowel; as, ⟦b:āēr⟧, ⟦b:Aenēās⟧, ⟦b:Mēdēa⟧. But early importations from Greek followed the general rule and shortened the vowel: as, ⟦b:platĕa⟧ (πλατεῖα), ⟦b:balinĕum⟧, ⟦b:balnĕum⟧ (βαλανεῖον).
⟦#128⟧
A long vowel preceding unsyllabic ⟦b:i̭⟧ or ⟦b:ṷ⟧ followed by a consonant is shortened: as, ⟦b:gaudeō⟧ for ⟦b:*gāudeō⟧ (cf. ⟦b:gāvīsus⟧, ⟦r111:111⟧); ⟦b:claudo⟧ for ⟦b:clāudō⟧ (cf. ⟦b:clāṷis⟧, ⟦r111:111⟧).
Similarly a long vowel (unless long by contraction: as, ⟦b:nūntius⟧, ⟦r111:111⟧, ⟦i:a⟧, ⟦b:cōntiō⟧) preceding a liquid or nasal followed by a consonant is shortened: as, syncopated ⟦b:ardus⟧ from ⟦b:āridus⟧ (⟦r111:111⟧), ⟦b:habentem⟧, from the stem ⟦b:habē-⟧. For cases of induced lengthening of the vowel before ⟦b:n⟧ followed by certain consonants, see ⟦r122:122⟧.
⟦#129⟧
Iambic shortening. The law of iambic shortening (⟦r2470:2470⟧) produced a number of important changes: thus,
(1.) In old dramatic verse iambic words (⏑ –) often shorten the long vowel. The poets after Plautus and Terence preserve the long vowel.
(⟦i:a.⟧) Nouns; G. ⟦b:eri⟧, ⟦b:boni⟧, ⟦b:preti⟧. D. ⟦b:cani⟧, ⟦b:ero⟧, ⟦b:malo⟧. L. ⟦b:domi⟧, ⟦b:heri⟧. Ab. ⟦b:levi⟧, ⟦b:manu⟧, ⟦b:domo⟧, ⟦b:bona⟧, ⟦b:fide⟧. Plural: N. ⟦b:fores⟧, ⟦b:viri⟧. D., Ab. ⟦b:bonis⟧. Ac. ⟦b:foris⟧, ⟦b:viros⟧, ⟦b:bonas⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) Verbs: ⟦b:eo⟧, ⟦b:volo⟧, ⟦b:ago⟧; ⟦b:ero⟧, ⟦b:dabo⟧; ⟦b:vides⟧; ⟦b:loces⟧; ⟦b:voles⟧; ⟦b:dedi⟧, ⟦b:dedin⟧; ⟦b:roga⟧, ⟦b:veni⟧; later poets sometimes retain ⟦b:cave⟧, ⟦b:vale⟧, and ⟦b:vide⟧. The vowel may also be shortened when ⟦b:-n⟧ (⟦r1503:1503⟧) is added and ⟦b:s⟧ is dropped before ⟦b:-n⟧ (⟦r170:170, 2⟧): ⟦b:rogan⟧, ⟦b:abin⟧; ⟦b:viden⟧ is also retained by later poets.
(2.) In a few pyrrhic words (⏑ ⏑) in ⟦b:-i⟧, which were originally iambic (⏑ –), the poets in all periods retained final ⟦b:-ī⟧ at pleasure: these are,
⟦b:mihī̆⟧, ⟦b:tibī̆⟧, ⟦b:sibī̆⟧; ⟦b:ibī̆⟧, ⟦b:ubī̆⟧; also ⟦b:alicubī̆⟧. The ⟦b:i⟧ of ⟦b:bi⟧ is always short in ⟦b:nēcubi⟧ and ⟦b:sīcubi⟧, and usually in ⟦b:ubinam⟧, ⟦b:ubivīs⟧, and ⟦b:ubicumque⟧; ⟦b:ibidem⟧ is used by the dramatists, ⟦b:ibīdem⟧ in hexameter. ⟦b:ubīque⟧ has always ⟦b:ī⟧.
⟦#130⟧
The following instances show that this law operated in prose speech also:
(1.) In iambic words of the ⟦b:ā-⟧ declension (⟦r432:432⟧) the final ⟦b:-ā⟧ of the nominative singular was shortened; hence ⟦b:*equā⟧ became ⟦b:equa⟧, ⟦i:mare⟧. From these iambic words short final ⟦b:-a⟧ spread so that all stems in ⟦b:-ā-⟧ shorten the final ⟦b:ā⟧ of the nom. sg. (⟦r434:434⟧).
(2.) The final ⟦b:-a⟧ in the nominative plural of neuter nouns of the ⟦b:o-⟧ declension (⟦r446:446⟧), which appears in ⟦b:trīgintā⟧, ⟦i:thirty⟧, was likewise shortened, first in iambic words like ⟦b:iuga⟧, ⟦i:yokes⟧, ⟦b:bona⟧, ⟦i:goods⟧, then everywhere (⟦r461:461⟧).
(3.) This law explains the short final vowel in ⟦b:homo⟧ (⟦r2442:2442⟧) by the side of ⟦b:sermō⟧ (2437, ⟦i:c⟧) and similar cases, like the adverbs ⟦b:modo⟧, ⟦b:cito⟧ (⟦r2442:2442⟧), ⟦b:bene⟧, ⟦b:male⟧ (⟦r2440:2440⟧). In the same way arose the short final ⟦b:o⟧ of the first person in conjugation (⟦r2443:2443⟧): as, ⟦b:volo⟧, ⟦b:dabo⟧, ⟦b:dīxero⟧ by the side of ⟦b:scrībō⟧; so also ⟦b:viden⟧ for ⟦b:vidēn⟧ (129, 1; 170, 2).
(4.) Of imperatives only ⟦b:puta⟧, used adverbially (2438, ⟦i:c⟧), ⟦b:ave⟧, ⟦b:have⟧ (⟦r805:805⟧; Quint. i, 6, 21; but Martial scans ⟦b:havē⟧) as a salutation and ⟦b:cave⟧, used as an auxiliary (⟦r1711:1711⟧), show the short final vowel in classical Latin. Elsewhere the long vowel has been restored, as ⟦b:amā⟧, ⟦b:monē⟧ (⟦r845:845⟧).
(5.) According to this rule ⟦b:calēfaciō⟧, ⟦b:malēdīcō⟧ changed to ⟦b:calefaciō⟧, ⟦b:maledīcō⟧.
⟦#131⟧
A long final vowel is shortened when an enclitic is added to the word: as ⟦b:siquidem⟧ from ⟦b:sī⟧; ⟦b:quoque⟧ from ⟦b:quō⟧.
⟦#132⟧
A long vowel is regularly shortened, in the classical period, before final ⟦b:-t⟧ and ⟦b:-m⟧ and, in words of more than one syllable, also before final ⟦b:r⟧ and ⟦b:l⟧.
Thus, ⟦b:soror⟧, ⟦i:sister⟧, for Plautus’s ⟦b:sorōr⟧, from the stem ⟦b:sorōr-⟧ (⟦r487:487⟧); ⟦b:ūtar⟧, ⟦i:I may use⟧, for Plautus’s ⟦b:ūtār⟧ (cf. ⟦b:ūtāris⟧); ⟦b:bacchanal⟧ for Plautus’s ⟦b:bacchanāl⟧; ⟦b:animal⟧, ⟦b:exemplar⟧ from the stems ⟦b:animāl-⟧ (⟦r530:530⟧) and ⟦b:exemplār-⟧ (⟦r537:537⟧); but the long vowel is retained in the monosyllables ⟦b:fūr⟧, ⟦i:thief⟧, ⟦b:sōl⟧, ⟦i:sun⟧; ⟦b:pōnēbat⟧, ⟦i:he placed⟧, for Plautus’s ⟦b:pōnēbāt⟧ (cf. ⟦b:pōnēbās⟧); ⟦b:iūbet⟧, ⟦i:he commanded⟧, for Plautus’s ⟦b:iūbēt⟧; ⟦b:eram⟧, ⟦i:I was⟧, but ⟦b:erās⟧; ⟦b:rēxerim⟧, ⟦i:I may have ruled⟧, but ⟦b:rēxerīs⟧ (⟦r877:877⟧); ⟦b:-um⟧ in the genitive plural of ⟦b:-o-⟧ stems is for ⟦b:-ūm⟧ (⟦r462:462⟧); ⟦b:mēnsam⟧, ⟦i:table⟧, for ⟦b:*mēnsām⟧ from the stem ⟦b:mensā-⟧; ⟦b:rem⟧, from ⟦b:rē-⟧ (⟦b:rēs⟧), ⟦b:spem⟧ from ⟦b:spē-⟧ (⟦b:spēs⟧).

title: Transfer of Quantity
text:
⟦#133⟧
(1.) In a few cases the length of the vowel has been transferred to the following consonant, the length of which is then indicated by doubling it (⟦r81:81⟧): as, ⟦b:littera⟧ for ⟦b:lītera⟧, LEITERAS; ⟦b:Iuppiter⟧ for ⟦b:Iūpiter⟧; ⟦b:parricīda⟧ for ⟦b:pāri-cīda⟧, ⟦i:murder of a member of the same clan⟧ (⟦b:*pāro-⟧, ⟦i:member of a clan⟧, Doric πᾶός, ⟦i:a relative⟧); ⟦b:cuppa⟧ for ⟦b:cūpa⟧, ⟦i:barrel⟧. The legal formula ⟦i:sī pāret⟧, ⟦i:if it appear⟧, was vulgarly pronounced ⟦b:sī parret⟧ (Festus).
(2.) Since the doubled unsyllabic ⟦b:i⟧ (⟦b:i̭⟧) between vowels (⟦r23:23⟧; 166, 9; 153, 2) is commonly written single, the ⟦i:vowel⟧ preceding it is often erroneously marked long: as, ⟦b:āiō⟧ wrongly for ⟦b:aiō⟧, ⟦i:i.e.⟧ ⟦b:ai̭i̭ō⟧, ⟦i:I say⟧; ⟦b:māior⟧ wrongly for ⟦b:maior⟧, ⟦i:i.e.⟧ ⟦b:mai̭i̭or⟧, ⟦i:greater⟧; ⟦b:pēior⟧ wrongly for ⟦b:peior⟧, ⟦i:i.e.⟧ ⟦b:pei̭i̭or⟧, ⟦i:worse⟧; ⟦b:ēius⟧, ⟦i:of him⟧, ⟦b:cūius⟧, ⟦i:of whom⟧, ⟦b:hūius⟧, ⟦i:of him⟧, all wrongly for ⟦b:eius⟧, ⟦b:cuius⟧, ⟦b:huius⟧ ⟦i:i.e.⟧ ⟦b:ei̭i̭us⟧, ⟦b:cui̭i̭us⟧, ⟦b:huii̭us⟧ (⟦r153:153, 2⟧). In all these words the first ⟦i:syllable⟧ was long but not the vowel.

title: Variations of Quantity
text:
⟦#134⟧
