The accusative ⟦b:domum⟧ or ⟦b:domōs⟧ sometimes has an attribute, usually a possessive pronoun: as, ⟦b:domum suam quemque revertī⟧, 2, 10, 4, ⟦i:for every man to go back to his home⟧. ⟦b:alius alium domōs suās invītant⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 66, 3, ⟦i:they invite each other to their homes⟧. ⟦b:aurum domum rēgiam comportant⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 76, 6, ⟦i:they bring all the gold to the house royal⟧. ⟦b:cum domum rēgis dēvertissēs⟧, ⟦i:D.⟧ 17, ⟦i:when you went to stay at the king’s palace⟧. The preposition ⟦b:in⟧ is sometimes used when the attribute is a genitive or a possessive pronoun, and commonly when it is any adjective but a possessive pronoun.
⟦#1165⟧
(3.) In old Latin, ⟦b:exsequiās⟧ and ⟦b:īnfitiās⟧ are also used with ⟦b:eō⟧, and sometimes ⟦b:malam crucem⟧ and ⟦b:malam rem⟧, though these last more commonly have ⟦b:in⟧: as,
⟦b:exsequiās Chremētī īre⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 1026, ⟦i:to go to Chremes’s funeral⟧. ⟦b:ut eās malam crucem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 328, ⟦i:that thou mayst get thee to the accursed cross⟧. Later writers, as Nepos, Livy, and Quintilian, use ⟦b:īnfitiās eō⟧ again, and, from Sallust on, ⟦b:vēnum eō⟧ and ⟦b:vēnum dō⟧ sometimes occur for ⟦b:vēneō⟧ and ⟦b:vēndō⟧.
⟦#1166⟧
With the accusative in ⟦b:-tum⟧ (or ⟦b:-sum⟧), called the supine, the idea of ‘aim’ passes over into that of ‘purpose:’ as ⟦b:mīlitātum abiīt⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 117, ⟦i:he’s gone away a soldiering⟧ (⟦r2270:2270⟧).

title: Object and Predicate
text:
⟦#1167⟧
Many verbs may take two accusatives, an object and a predicate.
Such are verbs signifying ⟦i:make⟧, ⟦i:keep⟧, ⟦i:choose⟧, ⟦i:name⟧ or ⟦i:call⟧, ⟦i:have⟧, ⟦i:think⟧, ⟦i:recognize⟧ or ⟦i:find⟧, ⟦i:show oneself⟧, &c., &c.: as, ⟦b:longiōrem mēnsem faciunt⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 129, ⟦i:they make the month longer⟧. ⟦b:eum certiōrem faciunt⟧, 5, 37, 7, ⟦i:they let him know⟧. ⟦b:Ancum Mārcium rēgem populus creāvit⟧, L. 1, 32, 1, ⟦i:the people made Ancus Marcius king⟧. ⟦b:mē cēpēre arbitrum⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 500, ⟦i:they’ve chosen me as referee⟧. ⟦b:Duellium ‘Bellium’ nōmināvērunt⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 153, ⟦i:Duellius they named ‘Bellius.’⟧ ⟦b:vīcīnam Capreīs insulam ‘Aprāgopolim’ appellābat⟧, Suet. ⟦i:Aug.⟧ 98, ⟦i:the island next to Capreae he called ‘the Castle of Indolence.’⟧ ⟦b:conlēgās adiūtōrēs habēbat⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 87, ⟦i:he had his colleagues as assistants⟧. ⟦b:tē sapientem exīstimant⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 6, ⟦i:they consider you a sage⟧. ⟦b:quem virum P. Crassum vīdimus⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 61, ⟦i:what a man we saw in Crassus⟧. ⟦b:sevērum mē praebeō⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 12, ⟦i:I show myself stern⟧. In the passive both the object and the predicate become nominatives: as, ⟦b:Caesar certior factus est⟧, 3, 19, 5, ⟦i:Caesar was informed⟧.
⟦#1168⟧
In the sense of ⟦i:consider as equivalent to⟧, ⟦b:dūcō⟧ and ⟦b:habeō⟧, less frequently ⟦b:putō⟧, have the ablative with ⟦b:prō⟧. Other constructions with these and the above verbs may be found in the dictionary.

title: Person and Thing
text:
⟦#1169⟧
(1.) Some verbs of teaching and hiding, demanding and questioning, may take two accusatives, one of a person and one of a thing.
The commonest of these verbs are ⟦b:doceō⟧ and its compounds, and ⟦b:cēlō⟧; ⟦b:flāgitō⟧, ⟦b:ōrō⟧, ⟦b:poscō⟧, and ⟦b:rogō⟧, ⟦b:interrogō⟧. The thing is usually the neuter of a pronoun or enumerative word (⟦r1144:1144⟧): as, (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:peior magister tē istaec docuit, nōn ego⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 163, ⟦i:a worse instructor taught thee that, not I⟧. ⟦b:quid tē litterās doceam?⟧ ⟦i:Pis.⟧ 73, ⟦i:why should I teach you your A B C’s?⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:nōn tē cēlāvī sermōnem T. Ampiī⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 16, 3, ⟦i:I have not kept you in the dark about the talk with Ampius⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:interim cōtīdiē Caesar Aeduōs frūmentum flāgitāre⟧, 1, 16, 1, ⟦i:meantime Caesar every day a dunning the Aeduans for the grain⟧. ⟦b:Mīlēsiōs nāvem poposcit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 86, ⟦i:he called on the Miletus people for a vessel⟧. ⟦b:quid me istud rogās?⟧ ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 5, 83, ⟦i:why do you ask me that?⟧ ⟦b:Racilius mē sententiam rogāvit⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 2, 1, 3, ⟦i:Racilius asked me my opinion⟧.
⟦#1170⟧
With ⟦b:doceō⟧, meaning ⟦i:inform⟧, ⟦b:cēlō⟧, ⟦b:rogō⟧, and ⟦b:interrogō⟧, the ablative of the thing with ⟦b:dē⟧ is also used. And with ⟦b:flāgitō⟧ and ⟦b:poscō⟧, sometimes the ablative of the person with ⟦b:ab⟧, with ⟦b:cēlō⟧ the ablative of the person with ⟦b:dē⟧.
⟦#1171⟧
In the passive the person becomes the subject, and the accusative of a neuter pronoun or adjective is retained: as,
⟦b:nōsne hoc cēlātōs tam diū⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 645, ⟦i:for us not to be told of this so long⟧; rarely with reversed construction: ⟦b:quōr haec cēlāta mē sunt?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 490, ⟦i:why was this hid from me?⟧ Accusatives of appellatives are rare: as, ⟦b:omnīs mīlitiae artīs ēdoctus fuerat⟧, L. 25, 37, 3, ⟦i:he had been thoroughly taught all the arts of war⟧. ⟦b:interrogātus sententiam⟧, L. 36, 7, 1, ⟦i:being asked his opinion⟧. Other constructions of ⟦b:doctus⟧, and of the passive of ⟦b:cēlō⟧, ⟦b:flāgitō⟧, ⟦b:poscō⟧, ⟦b:rogō⟧ and ⟦b:interrogō⟧, may be found in the dictionary.
⟦#1172⟧
(2.) Verbs of wishing, reminding, inducing, and accusing, and some others, also sometimes take an accusative of the person and one of the thing.
Such are ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:moneō⟧ and its compounds, ⟦b:hortor⟧ and ⟦b:cōgō⟧; ⟦b:accūsō⟧, ⟦b:arguō⟧, ⟦b:īnsimulō⟧, ⟦b:obiūrgō⟧. The thing is usually the neuter of a pronoun or enumerative word (⟦r1144:1144⟧): as, ⟦b:quid mē voltis?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Mer.⟧ 868, ⟦i:what do you want of me?⟧ ⟦b:illud tē esse admonitum velim⟧, ⟦i:Cael.⟧ 8, ⟦i:on this point I want you to be reminded⟧ (⟦r1171:1171⟧). In old Latin, accusatives of appellatives also are thus used, and sometimes also with ⟦b:dōnō⟧ and ⟦b:condōnō⟧.
⟦#1173⟧
(3.) The defining accusative is sometimes combined with an accusative of the person: as, ⟦b:tam tē bāsia multa bāsiāre⟧, Cat. 7, 9, ⟦i:thee to kiss so many kisses⟧ (⟦r1140:1140⟧). But usually with an accusative of the person, the ablative takes the place of the defining accusative: as, ⟦b:ōdissem tē odiō Vatīniānō⟧, Cat. 14, 3, ⟦i:I should hate thee with a Vatinian hate⟧.

title: Object and Extent, Duration, or Aim
text:
⟦#1174⟧
The accusative of extent or duration, or of aim of motion is often combined with that of the object: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:mīlia passuum decem novem mūrum perdūcit⟧, 1, 8, 1, ⟦i:he makes a wall nineteen miles⟧ (⟦r1151:1151⟧). ⟦b:mātrōnae annum eum lūxērunt⟧, L. 2, 7, 4. ⟦i:the married women wore mourning for him a year⟧ (⟦r1151:1151⟧). (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:Ancus multitūdinem omnem Rōmam trādūxit⟧, L. 1, 33, 1, ⟦i:Ancus moved the whole population over to Rome⟧ (⟦r1157:1157⟧). ⟦b:eōs domum remittit⟧, 4, 21, 6, ⟦i:he sends them home again⟧ (⟦r1162:1162⟧). For other combinations, see ⟦r1138:1138⟧, ⟦r1198:1198⟧, and 2270.

title: The Dative
text:
⟦#1175⟧
The dative denotes that for or to which a thing is or is done, and either accompanies single words, such as verbs, adjectives, sometimes adverbs, rarely substantives, or serves to modify the entire sentence. It has two principal uses.
⟦#1176⟧
I. The dative is used as a complement. Complements may be roughly distinguished as essential or optional. But these two complements are not always separated by a sharp line, and the same dative may sometimes be referred indifferently to either head.
⟦#1177⟧
(1.) The Essential Complement is a dative of the person or thing added to an idea which is felt as incomplete without the dative (⟦r1180:1180⟧).
Thus, ⟦b:pāret⟧, ⟦i:he is obedient⟧, is a statement which is felt as incomplete without a dative added to denote what it is he is obedient to, in the sentence ⟦b:pāret senātuī⟧, ⟦i:he is obedient to the senate⟧. But when stress is put on the action merely, without reference to its bearing, such a verb may be used without a dative: as, ⟦b:pāret⟧, ⟦i:he is obedient⟧, ⟦i:he yields obedience⟧.
⟦#1178⟧
(2.) The Optional Complement, that is, the dative of interest, advantage, or disadvantage, adds something to an idea that is already complete in itself (⟦r1205:1205⟧).
Thus, ⟦b:carmina cantō⟧, ⟦i:I chant verses⟧, is a statement entirely complete in itself; it may be modified or not, at option, by a dative, thus: ⟦b:carmina virginibus puerīsque cantō⟧, ⟦i:verses for maids and boys I chant⟧.
⟦#1179⟧
II. The dative of certain substantives is used predicatively (⟦r1219:1219⟧).
⟦#1180⟧
Many verbs require a dative to complete their meaning.

title: The Complementary Dative: With Verbs of Intransitive Use
text:
⟦#1181⟧
(1.) Many verbs of intransitive use, particularly such as denote a state, disposition, feeling, or quality, take the dative: as,
⟦b:quodne vōbīs placeat, displiceat mihī?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 614, ⟦i:shall that which pleases you, displeasing be to me?⟧ ⟦b:sī Asiciō causa plūs prōfuit quam invidia nocuit⟧, ⟦i:Cael.⟧ 23, ⟦i:if his case has been more helpful to Asicius than the hostility has been damaging⟧. ⟦b:imperat aut servit collēcta pecūnia cuique⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 10, 47, ⟦i:for every man his garnered hoard or master is or slave⟧. ⟦b:nōnne huic lēgī resistētis?⟧ ⟦i:Agr.⟧ 2, 85, ⟦i:will you not stand out against this law?⟧ ⟦b:gymnasiīs indulgent Graeculī⟧, Traj. in Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 40 [49], 2, ⟦i:our Greek cousins are partial to gymnasiums⟧. ⟦b:īgnōscās velim huic festīnātiōnī meae⟧, in a letter, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 5, 12, 1, ⟦i:please excuse haste⟧. ⟦b:huic legiōnī Caesar cōnfīdēbat maximē⟧, 1, 40, 15, ⟦i:Caesar trusted this legion most of all⟧. ⟦b:an C. Trebōniō ego persuāsī? cui nē suādēre quidem ausus essem⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 27, ⟦i:or was it I that brought conviction to Trebonius? a man to whom I should not have presumed even to offer advice⟧. In the passive, such verbs are used impersonally, the dative remaining (⟦r1034:1034⟧); personal constructions are rare and poetical.
⟦#1182⟧
This dative is used with such verbs or verbal expressions as mean ⟦i:am pleasing⟧ or ⟦i:displeasing⟧, ⟦i:helpful⟧ or ⟦i:injurious⟧, ⟦i:command⟧, ⟦i:yield⟧, or ⟦i:am obedient⟧, ⟦i:am friendly⟧, ⟦i:partial⟧, or ⟦i:opposed⟧; ⟦i:spare⟧, ⟦i:pardon⟧, ⟦i:threaten⟧, ⟦i:trust⟧, ⟦i:advise⟧, ⟦i:persuade⟧, ⟦i:happen⟧, ⟦i:meet⟧. But the English translation is not a safe guide: many of the verbs used with a dative are represented transitively in English; and some verbs of the meanings above are used transitively in Latin: as, ⟦b:dēlectō⟧, ⟦b:iuvō⟧, ⟦b:laedō⟧, &c., &c.
⟦#1183⟧
The dative is rarely used with a form of ⟦b:sum⟧ and a predicate noun corresponding in meaning with the verbs above (⟦r1181:1181⟧): as, ⟦b:quid mihi scelestō tibī̆ erat auscultātiō?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 502, i.e. ⟦b:quid tibī̆ auscultābam?⟧ ⟦i:why did I, ill-starred wretch, lend ear to thee?⟧ ⟦b:quī studiōsus re͡i nūllī aliaest⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 802, i.e. ⟦b:quī studet⟧, ⟦i:who lends his soul to nothing else⟧. Or immediately with a noun: as, ⟦b:servitūs opulentō hominī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 166, ⟦i:slavery to a millionaire⟧. ⟦b:optemperātiō lēgibus⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 1, 42, ⟦i:obedience to the laws⟧. ⟦b:aemula labra rosīs⟧, Mart. 4, 42, 10, ⟦i:lips rivalling the rose⟧.
⟦#1184⟧
Some verbs have a variable use without any difference of meaning: thus, ⟦b:cūrō⟧, ⟦b:decet⟧, and ⟦b:vītō⟧, have sometimes the dative in old Latin, but usually the accusative. In Cicero, ⟦b:adūlor⟧ has the accusative; from Nepos on, the dative as well. ⟦b:medeor⟧, ⟦b:medicor⟧, and ⟦b:praestōlor⟧ take either the accusative or the dative.
⟦#1185⟧
Some verbs have an accusative with one meaning, a dative of the complement, essential or optional, with another: see ⟦b:aemulor⟧, ⟦b:caveō⟧, ⟦b:comitor⟧, ⟦b:cōnsulō⟧, ⟦b:conveniō⟧, ⟦b:cupiō⟧, ⟦b:dēspērō⟧, ⟦b:maneō⟧, ⟦b:metuō⟧, ⟦b:moderor⟧, ⟦b:prōspiciō⟧, ⟦b:temperō⟧, ⟦b:timeō⟧, and the different uses of ⟦b:invideō⟧, in the dictionary.
⟦#1186⟧
In poetry, verbs of union, of contention, and of difference, often take a dative: as, (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:haeret laterī lētālis harundō⟧, V. 4, 73, ⟦i:sticks to her side the deadly shaft⟧. So with ⟦b:coëō⟧, ⟦b:concurrō⟧, ⟦b:haereō⟧, and similarly with ⟦b:iungō⟧, ⟦b:misceō⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:quid enim contendat hirundō cycnīs?⟧ Lucr. 3, 6, ⟦i:for how can swallow cope with swans?⟧ So with ⟦b:bellō⟧, ⟦b:certō⟧, ⟦b:contendō⟧, ⟦b:pugnō⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:īnfīdō scurrae distābit amīcus⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 18, 4, ⟦i:a friend will differ from a faithless hanger-on⟧. So with ⟦b:differō⟧, ⟦b:discrepō⟧, ⟦b:dissentiō⟧, ⟦b:distō⟧.
⟦#1187⟧
A verb often takes the dative, when combined with ⟦b:adversum⟧, ⟦b:obviam⟧, or ⟦b:praestō⟧, also with ⟦b:bene⟧, ⟦b:male⟧, or ⟦b:satis⟧, and the like: as,
⟦b:fit ob viam Clōdiō⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 29, ⟦i:he runs across Clodius⟧. ⟦b:cui bene dīxit umquam bonō?⟧ ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 110, ⟦i:for what patriot had he ever a good word?⟧ ⟦b:nōs, virī fortēs, satis facere rē̆ī pūblicae vidēmur⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 2, ⟦i:we doughty champions flatter ourselves we are doing our whole duty by the state⟧. Similarly with verbs of transitive use.
⟦#1188⟧
(2.) Many verbs of intransitive use compounded with a preposition take a dative connected in sense with the preposition: as,
⟦b:manus extrēma nōn accessit operibus eius⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 126, ⟦i:the last touch was not put upon his works⟧. ⟦b:omnibus adfuit hīs pugnīs Dolābella⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 75, ⟦i:Dolabella was on hand in all these battles⟧. ⟦b:pontō nox incubat ātra,⟧ V. 1, 89, ⟦i:over the deep, night broodeth black⟧. ⟦b:cōgnitiōnibus dē Chrīstiānīs interfuī numquam⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep. ad Trai.⟧ 96 [97], 1, ⟦i:I have never been to any of the trials of the Christians⟧.
⟦#1189⟧
The prepositions are chiefly ⟦b:ad⟧, ⟦b:ante⟧, ⟦b:com-⟧, ⟦b:in⟧, ⟦b:inter⟧, ⟦b:ob⟧, ⟦b:prae⟧, ⟦b:sub⟧, or ⟦b:super⟧. In many compounds of these prepositions, however, the dative is due to the general meaning of the verb, as in ⟦b:cōnfīdit mihī̆⟧, ⟦i:he puts all trust in me⟧ (⟦r1181:1181⟧), as contrasted with ⟦b:cōnsentit mihī̆⟧, ⟦i:he feels with me⟧, nearly equivalent to ⟦b:sentit mēcum⟧ (⟦r1188:1188⟧).
⟦#1190⟧
Instead of the dative, such verbs often have a prepositional construction, particularly when place, literal or figurative, is distinctly to be expressed: as,
⟦b:accēdere in fūnus⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 2, 66, ⟦i:to go to a funeral⟧. ⟦b:in morbum incidit⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 175, ⟦i:he fell ill⟧.
⟦#1191⟧
Some verbs of intransitive use take, when compounded, either the dative or the accusative. See ⟦b:adiaceō⟧, ⟦b:antecēdō⟧, ⟦b:anteeō⟧, ⟦b:praecurrō⟧, ⟦b:praestō⟧, ⟦b:incēdō⟧, ⟦b:inlūdō⟧, ⟦b:īnsultō⟧, ⟦b:invādō⟧, in the dictionary. And some compounds acquire a transitive use altogether, as ⟦b:obeō⟧, ⟦b:oppugnō⟧: see ⟦r1137:1137⟧.

title: The Complementary Dative: With Verbs of Transitive Use
text:
⟦#1192⟧
(1.) Many verbs of transitive use take the dative: as,
⟦b:ē̆ī fīliam suam in mātrimōnium dat⟧, 1, 3, 5, ⟦i:he gives this person his own daughter in marriage⟧. ⟦b:decima legiō ē̆ī grātiās ēgit⟧, 1, 41, 1, ⟦i:the tenth legion gave him thanks⟧. ⟦b:huic fert subsidium Puliō⟧, 5, 44, 13, ⟦i:to him Pulio brings aid⟧. ⟦b:multīs idem minātur Antōnius⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 11, 2, ⟦i:to many Antony threatens the same⟧. ⟦b:reliquī sēsē fugae mandārunt⟧, 1, 12, 3, ⟦i:the rest betook themselves to flight⟧. ⟦b:commendō vōbīs meum parvum fīlium⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 23, ⟦i:unto your keeping do I commit the little son of mine⟧. ⟦b:multī sē aliēnissimīs crēdidērunt⟧, 6, 31, 4, ⟦i:many people put themselves in the hands of utter strangers⟧. ⟦b:equitēs imperat cīvitātibus⟧, 6, 4, 6, ⟦i:he issues orders to the communities for horse⟧.
⟦#1193⟧
This dative is used with such verbs as ⟦b:dō⟧, ⟦b:trādō⟧, ⟦b:tribuō⟧, ⟦b:dīvidō⟧, ⟦b:ferō⟧, ⟦b:praebeō⟧, ⟦b:praestō⟧, ⟦b:polliceor⟧, ⟦b:prōmittō⟧, ⟦b:dēbeō⟧, ⟦b:negō⟧, ⟦b:mōnstrō⟧, ⟦b:dīcō⟧, ⟦b:nārrō⟧, ⟦b:mandō⟧, ⟦b:praecipiō⟧, &c., &c. In the passive construction, the accusative becomes nominative, the dative remaining.
⟦#1194⟧
(2.) Many verbs of transitive use compounded with a preposition take a dative connected in sense with the preposition: as,
⟦b:nihil novī vōbīs adferam⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 1, 21, ⟦i:I shall not lay any novelty before you⟧. ⟦b:lēgēs omnium salūtem singulōrum salūtī antepōnunt⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 3, 64, ⟦i:the law always puts the general safety before the safety of the individual⟧. ⟦b:timōrem bonīs iniēcistis⟧, ⟦i:Agr.⟧ 1, 23, ⟦i:you have struck terror into the hearts of patriots⟧. ⟦b:nōluērunt ferīs corpus obicere⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 71, ⟦i:they would not cast his person before ravenous beasts⟧. ⟦b:nēminem huic praeferō⟧, N. 8, 1, 1, ⟦i:there is nobody I put before him⟧. ⟦b:hībernīs Labiēnum praeposuit⟧, 1, 54, 2, ⟦i:he put Labienus over the winter-quarters⟧. ⟦b:anitum ōva gallīnīs saepe suppōnimus⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 124, ⟦i:we often put ducks’ eggs under hens⟧.
⟦#1195⟧
The prepositions are ⟦b:circum⟧, ⟦b:dē⟧, ⟦b:ex⟧, ⟦b:post⟧, or those named in 1189. In many compounds of transitive use, however, the dative is due to the general meaning of the verb, as with those spoken of in 1189.
⟦#1196⟧
With these verbs, a prepositional construction is often used, as with the verbs of intransitive use (⟦r1190:1190⟧): as,
⟦b:iam diū nihil novī ad nōs adferēbātur⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 14, ⟦i:no news has got to us this long time⟧. For compounds of ⟦b:circum⟧ and ⟦b:trāns⟧ with two accusatives, see ⟦r1138:1138⟧.
⟦#1197⟧
Verbs of transitive use compounded with ⟦b:com-⟧ have oftener the ablative with ⟦b:cum⟧: as, ⟦b:cōnferte hanc pācem cum illō bellō⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 115, ⟦i:just compare this peace with that war⟧. See also in the dictionary, ⟦b:coniungō⟧ and ⟦b:compōnō⟧; also the indirect compounds ⟦b:comparō⟧, ⟦i:compare⟧, from ⟦b:compār⟧, and ⟦b:commūnicō⟧.
⟦#1198⟧
With a few compounds of ⟦b:ad⟧ or ⟦b:in⟧, a second accusative is exceptionally used: as, ⟦b:arbitrum illum adēgit⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 66, ⟦i:he had the other man up before a daysman⟧. So with ⟦b:inmittō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 548, ⟦b:īnsinuō⟧, Lucr. 1, 116, &c., &c. Regularly with ⟦b:animum advertō⟧: as, ⟦b:animum advertī columellam⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 65, ⟦i:I noticed a modest shaft⟧. ⟦b:quā rē animum adversā⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 80, 4, ⟦i:this fact being paid heed to⟧: compare 1138.
⟦#1199⟧
A few compound verbs admit either the dative of the person or thing and accusative of the thing, or the accusative of the person or thing and ablative of the thing; such are ⟦b:adspergō⟧ and ⟦b:īnspergō⟧, ⟦b:circumdō⟧, ⟦b:circumfundō⟧, ⟦b:exuō⟧ and ⟦b:induō⟧, ⟦b:impertiō⟧, ⟦b:interclūdō⟧; also the uncompounded ⟦b:dōnō⟧: as, ⟦b:praedam mīlitibus dōnat⟧, 7, 11, 9, ⟦i:he presents the booty to the soldiers⟧. ⟦b:scrībam tuum ānulō dōnāstī⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 185, ⟦i:you presented your clerk with a ring⟧. For the different constructions of ⟦b:interdīcō⟧, see the dictionary.

title: The Dative with Adjectives
text:
⟦#1200⟧
The dative with many adjectives and some adverbs denotes that to which the quality is directed.
Such have the meaning of ⟦i:useful⟧, ⟦i:necessary⟧, ⟦i:fit⟧, ⟦i:easy⟧, ⟦i:agreeable⟧, ⟦i:known⟧, ⟦i:near⟧, ⟦i:belonging⟧, ⟦i:friendly⟧, ⟦i:faithful⟧, ⟦i:like⟧, and most of their opposites; the adjective is often predicative: as, ⟦b:vēr ūtile silvīs⟧ (⟦r1036:1036⟧), V. ⟦i:G.⟧ 2, 323, ⟦i:the spring is good for woods⟧. ⟦b:est senātōrī necessārium nōsse rem pūblicam⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 3, 41, ⟦i:for a senator it is indispensable to be conversant with government⟧. ⟦b:ōrātiōnis genus pompae quam pugnae aptius⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 42, ⟦i:a style better suited to the parade than to the field⟧. ⟦b:convenienter nātūrae vīvere⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 13, ⟦i:to live in touch with nature⟧.
⟦#1201⟧
Some adjectives of this class have the dative of a person, the accusative with ⟦b:ad⟧ of a thing: so ⟦b:accommodātus⟧, ⟦b:aptus⟧, ⟦b:idōneus⟧, ⟦b:necessārius⟧, and ⟦b:ūtilis⟧; and some denoting feeling have also the accusative with a preposition: ⟦b:aequus⟧, ⟦b:inīquus⟧, ⟦b:fidēlis⟧ with ⟦b:in⟧, ⟦b:benevolus⟧ with ⟦b:ergā⟧, and ⟦b:impius⟧ with ⟦b:adversus⟧. ⟦b:propior⟧ and ⟦b:proximus⟧ sometimes accompany an accusative, like ⟦b:prope⟧, ⟦b:propius⟧, and ⟦b:proximē⟧.
⟦#1202⟧
The adjectives ⟦b:commūnis⟧, ⟦b:proprius⟧ or ⟦b:aliēnus⟧, ⟦b:sacer⟧, ⟦b:tōtus⟧, often accompany the construction of the genitive of the owner: see ⟦r1238:1238⟧. For ⟦b:aliēnus⟧ with the ablative, see ⟦r1306:1306⟧. Sometimes ⟦b:aliēnus⟧ has the ablative with ⟦b:ab⟧.
⟦#1203⟧
Some adjectives denoting relationship, connection, friendship or hostility, become substantives, and as such, admit the genitive also (⟦r1103:1103⟧): such are (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:adfīnis⟧, ⟦b:cōgnātus⟧; (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:aequālis⟧, ⟦b:familiāris⟧, ⟦b:fīnitimus⟧, ⟦b:pār⟧ and ⟦b:dispār⟧, ⟦b:propīnquus⟧, ⟦b:vīcīnus⟧; (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:adversārius⟧, ⟦b:amīcus⟧, ⟦b:inimīcus⟧, ⟦b:necessārius⟧.
⟦#1204⟧
In Plautus and Terence, ⟦b:similis⟧, ⟦i:the like⟧, ⟦i:the counterpart⟧, and its compounds, regularly take the genitive. The dative, as well as the genitive, is also used from Ennius on, particularly of a limited or approximate likeness: see the dictionary.

title: The Optional Complement
text:
⟦#1205⟧
The dative of a person or thing interested, benefited, harmed, may be added at option to almost any verb: as,
⟦b:cōnservāte parentī fīlium, parentem fīliō⟧, ⟦i:Cael.⟧ 80, ⟦i:save the son for the father, the father for the son⟧. ⟦b:mea domus tibī̆ patet, mihī̆ clausa est⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 145, ⟦i:the very house I own is open for you, is shut upon me⟧. ⟦b:cui flāvam religās comam, simplex munditiīs?⟧ H. 1, 5, 4, ⟦i:for whom bind’st thou in wreaths thy golden hair, plain in thy neatness?⟧ ⟦b:nōn audēret facere haec viduae mulierī, quae in mē fēcit⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 953, ⟦i:he durst not to an unprotected female do what he hath done towards me⟧.
⟦#1206⟧
The place of a verb with the dative of interest is sometimes filled by an interjection, ⟦b:ecce⟧, ⟦b:ei⟧, ⟦b:em⟧, or ⟦b:vae⟧: as, ⟦b:ei mihi quālis erat⟧, E. 1, 7, V. 2, 274, ⟦i:ah me, how ghastly he did look⟧. ⟦b:vae vīctīs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 1317, said by Brennus, 390 B.C., L. 5, 48, 9, ⟦i:woe worth the worsted⟧. ⟦b:vae capitī atque aetātī tuae⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 375, ⟦i:a murrain on thy head and life⟧.
⟦#1207⟧
The dative is often added to the entire sentence, where either a genitive or a possessive pronoun limiting a substantive might be used.
In such cases the dative expresses interest, advantage, or disadvantage, while the genitive would simply indicate the owner or the object: as, ⟦b:trānsfīgitur scūtum Puliōni⟧, 5, 44, 7, ⟦i:unfortunately for Pulio, his shield gets pierced through and through⟧. ⟦b:mīlitantī in Hispāniā pater ē̆ī moritur⟧, L. 29, 29, 6, ⟦i:while serving in Spain he had the misfortune to lose his father⟧. ⟦b:huic ego mē bellō ducem profiteor⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 11, ⟦i:I here proclaim myself captain for this war⟧. ⟦b:sēsē Caesarī ad pedēs prōiēcērunt⟧, 1, 31, 2, ⟦i:they cast themselves at Caesar’s feet⟧. ⟦b:nostrīs mīlitibus spem minuit⟧, 5, 33, 5, ⟦i:it dashed the hopes of our soldiers⟧. ⟦b:extergē tibi manūs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 267, ⟦i:wipe off thy hands⟧. ⟦b:vellunt tibi barbam lascīvī puerī⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 3, 133, ⟦i:the wanton gamins pull thy beard, poor soul⟧.
⟦#1208⟧
This dative is sometimes detached from the verb, and used immediately with a substantive, instead of the genitive: as, ⟦b:Philocōmasiō custōs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 271, ⟦i:the keeper for Philocomasium⟧. ⟦b:rēctor iuvenī⟧, Ta. 1, 24, ⟦i:a mentor for the young man⟧. So particularly with a gerundive in official expressions: as, ⟦b:cūrātor mūrīs reficiendīs⟧, ⟦i:OG.⟧ 19, ⟦i:commissioner for rebuilding the walls⟧.
⟦#1209⟧
Verbs of warding off sometimes take a dative, especially in poetry, also those of robbing and ridding: as, (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:hunc quoque arcēbis gravidō pecorī⟧, V. ⟦i:G.⟧ 3, 154, ⟦i:him also wilt thou for the pregnant herd keep far⟧. ⟦b:sōlstitium pecorī dēfendite⟧. V. ⟦i:E.⟧ 7, 47, ⟦i:the summer’s heat keep distant for the flock⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:torquem dētrāxit hostī⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 1, 35, ⟦i:he pulled a torque away from his enemy⟧. ⟦b:ēripiēs mihī̆ hunc errōrem⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 10, 4, 6, ⟦i:you will rid me of this mistake⟧.
⟦#1210⟧
With verbs of motion the dative of the person interested denotes in poetry the end of motion also: as, ⟦b:multōs Danaūm dēmittimus Orcō⟧, V. 2, 398, ⟦i:we send down many a Danaan for the nether king⟧. So also the dative of personified words of place: as, ⟦b:it clāmor caelō⟧, V. 5, 451, ⟦i:up goes a shout for heaven⟧, i.e. ⟦i:heaven hears a shout⟧. ⟦b:sēdibus hunc refer ante suīs⟧, V. 6, 152, ⟦i:first bear him duly to his place of rest⟧, i.e. let his expectant grave receive him.

title: The Emotional Dative
text:
⟦#1211⟧
The dative of the personal pronoun is often used with expressions of emotion, interest, surprise, or derision: as,
⟦b:quid mihi Celsus agit?⟧ H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 3, 15, ⟦i:how fares me Celsus?⟧ ⟦b:Tongilium mihī̆ ēdūxit⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 4, ⟦i:he took out Tongilius, bless my soul⟧. ⟦b:at tibī̆ repente, cum minimē exspectārem, vēnit ad mē Canīnius māne⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 9, 2, 1, ⟦i:but bless you, sir, when I least dreamt of it, who should drop in on me all at once but Caninius, bright and early⟧.

title: The Dative of the Possessor
text:
⟦#1212⟧
The dative is used with forms of ⟦b:sum⟧ to denote the possessor: as,
⟦b:est hominī cum deō similitūdō⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 1, 25, ⟦i:man has a resemblance to god⟧. ⟦b:an nescīs longās rēgibus esse manūs?⟧ O. ⟦i:E.⟧ 16, 166, ⟦i:dost possibly not know kings have long arms?⟧ ⟦b:suos quoique mōs⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 454, ⟦i:to every man his own pet way⟧. So also with the compounds ⟦b:absum⟧, ⟦b:dēsum⟧, ⟦b:supersum⟧: as, ⟦b:hoc ūnum Caesarī dēfuit⟧, 4, 26, 5, ⟦i:this was all Caesar lacked⟧.
⟦#1213⟧
(1.) With ⟦b:mihī̆ est nōmen⟧, the name is put either in the dative or in the nominative: as,
⟦b:mihī̆ nomen est Iūliō⟧, or ⟦b:mihī̆ nōmen est Iūlius⟧, Gell. 15, 29, 1, ⟦i:my name is Julius⟧. In old Latin and in Sallust, the dative: as, ⟦b:nōmen Mercuriōst mihī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am. prol.⟧ 19, ⟦i:my name is Mercury⟧; later the nominative: as, ⟦b:canibus pigrīs nōmen erit Pardus, Tigris, Leo⟧, J. 8, 34, ⟦i:the craven cur shall sport the name of ‘Lion, Tiger, Pard.’⟧ Cicero uses the nominative or rarely the dative, Livy oftener the dative than the nominative. Tacitus puts adjectives in the dative, substantives in the nominative, rarely in the genitive. Caesar does not use the construction.
⟦#1214⟧
(2.) With the actives ⟦b:nōmen dō⟧, ⟦b:indō⟧, ⟦b:pōnō⟧, ⟦b:tribuō⟧, &c., the name may be in the dative or in the accusative; with the passive of these expressions, the name may be in the dative or in the nominative: as,
⟦b:quī tibi nōmen īnsānō posuēre⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 3, 47, ⟦i:who’ve put on thee the nickname Crank⟧. ⟦b:quī fīliīs Philippum atque Alexandrum nōmina inposuerat⟧, L. 35, 47, 5, ⟦i:who had given his sons the names Philip and Alexander⟧. A genitive dependent on ⟦b:nōmen⟧ is used once by Tacitus and in very late Latin.
⟦#1215⟧
With a gerundive, the dative of the possessor denotes the person who has the action to do: see ⟦r2243:2243⟧. For the ablative with ⟦b:ab⟧, or for ⟦b:habeō⟧, see ⟦r2243:2243⟧, ⟦r2245:2245⟧.
⟦#1216⟧
This dative is sometimes used with the perfect participle, and the tenses formed with it: as, ⟦b:mihī̆ est ēlabōrātum⟧, ⟦i:Caecil.⟧ 40, ⟦i:I have it all worked out⟧. ⟦b:carmina nūlla mihī sunt scrīpta⟧, O. ⟦i:Tr.⟧ 5, 12, 35, ⟦i:no poetry have I ready made⟧. Rarely with passives of the present system: as, ⟦b:nūlla placēre diū nec vīvere carmina possunt, quae scrībuntur aquae pōtōribus⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 19, 2, ⟦i:no verse can take or be longlived that by teetotallers is writ⟧.

title: The Dative of Relation
text:
⟦#1217⟧
The dative may denote the person viewing or judging: as,
⟦b:eris mihi magnus Apollō⟧, V. ⟦i:E.⟧ 3, 104, ⟦i:thou shalt to me the great Apollo be⟧. ⟦b:Quīntia fōrmōsa est multīs, mihi candida, longa, rēcta est⟧, Cat. 86, 1, ⟦i:in many eyes is Quintia fair, to me she’s bonny, tall, and straight⟧. From Caesar on, participles are often used to denote the person viewing or judging: as, ⟦b:est urbe ēgressīs tumulus⟧, V. 2, 713, ⟦i:there is, as you get out of town, a mound⟧. ⟦b:in ūniversum aestimantī⟧, Ta. ⟦i:G.⟧ 6, ⟦i:looking at it generally⟧.
⟦#1218⟧
In imitation of a Greek idiom, ⟦b:volēns⟧, ⟦b:cupiēns⟧, or ⟦b:invītus⟧, is used by Sallust and Tacitus in agreement with a dative dependent on a form of ⟦b:sum⟧, the combination being equivalent to a subject with a form of ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:cupiō⟧, or ⟦b:invītus sum⟧, respectively: as, ⟦b:cēterīs remanēre volentibus fuit⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 3, 43, i.e. ⟦b:cēterī remanēre voluērunt⟧, ⟦i:the rest were minded to bide where they were⟧. Once in Livy.

title: The Dative of Tendency or Result
text:
⟦#1219⟧
(1.) Certain datives are used with a form of ⟦b:sum⟧ to denote what a thing tends to, proves, or is. This dative is generally accompanied by a dative of the person interested: as,
⟦b:auxiliō īs fuit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am. prol.⟧ 92, ⟦i:he was a help to them⟧. ⟦b:odiō sum Rōmānīs⟧, L. 35, 19, 6, ⟦i:I am an abomination in the eyes of Rome⟧. ⟦b:potestne bonum cuiquam malō esse?⟧ ⟦i:Par.⟧ 7, ⟦i:can good prove bad for any human being?⟧ ⟦b:L. Cassius identidem quaerere solēbat, cui bonō fuisset⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 84, ⟦i:Cassius used to ask for ever and ever, who the person benefited was⟧, or ⟦i:who the gainer was⟧. ⟦b:nēminī meus adventus labōrī aut sūmptuī fuit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 16, ⟦i:my visit did not prove a bother or an expense to a soul⟧. ⟦b:rēs et fortūnae tuae mihī̆ maximae cūrae sunt⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 6, 5, 1, ⟦i:your money-matters are an all-absorbing interest to me⟧.
⟦#1220⟧
There are many of these datives, mostly abstracts and all singular, some of the commonest are ⟦b:cūrae⟧, ⟦b:ūsuī⟧, ⟦b:praesidiō⟧, ⟦b:cordī⟧, ⟦b:odiō⟧, ⟦b:auxiliō⟧, ⟦b:impedīmentō⟧, ⟦b:salūtī⟧, ⟦b:voluptātī⟧. The adjectives ⟦b:magnus⟧, ⟦b:maior⟧, ⟦b:maximus⟧, or ⟦b:tantus⟧ and ⟦b:quantus⟧, are sometimes used in agreement with them; and the dative ⟦b:frūgī⟧ sometimes has ⟦b:bonae⟧.
⟦#1221⟧
Instead of the dative of tendency, a predicative nominative or accusative is rarely used: thus, ⟦b:possessiōnem līberam Dardaniae sōlāciō fore⟧, L. 40, 57, 9, ⟦i:that the unrestricted occupancy of Dardania would prove comforting⟧, but, ⟦b:domestica quiēs sōlācium fuit⟧, L. 6, 30, 9, ⟦i:the peace that prevailed at home was a solid comfort⟧. Prepositional expressions with ⟦b:prō⟧ and ⟦b:in⟧ also occur.
⟦#1222⟧
(2.) The dative is also used with a few verbs of considering or accounting to denote what a thing is accounted.
So with such verbs as ⟦b:dō⟧, ⟦b:dūcō⟧, ⟦b:habeō⟧, ⟦b:tribuō⟧, and ⟦b:vertō⟧: as, ⟦b:vitiō mihī̆ dant, quod mortem hominis necessāriī graviter ferō⟧, Matius in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 11, 28, 2, ⟦i:the world scores it against me that I take the murder of a near and dear friend to heart⟧. ⟦b:postquam paupertās probrō habērī coepit⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 12, 1, ⟦i:after lack of wealth began to count as a stigma⟧.

title: The Dative of Purpose or Intention
text:
⟦#1223⟧
A few datives are used to denote what a thing is intended to be. This dative is generally accompanied by a dative of the person interested.
So (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:dōnō⟧ and ⟦b:mūnerī⟧: as, ⟦b:ēmit eam dōnō mihī̆⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 135, ⟦i:he bought her as a gift for me⟧. ⟦b:centum bovēs mīlitibus dōnō dedit⟧, L. 7, 37, 3, ⟦i:he gave the soldiers a hundred oxen as a present⟧. Also (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:auxiliō⟧, ⟦b:praesidiō⟧, and ⟦b:subsidiō⟧, used of military operations, chiefly with verbs of motion: as, ⟦b:iī, quī praesidiō contrā castra erant relictī, subsidiō suīs iērunt⟧, 7, 62, 8, ⟦i:the men that had been left as a protection against the camp, went as a reinforcement to their own side⟧.
⟦#1224⟧
For the datives ⟦b:dōnō⟧ and ⟦b:mūnerī⟧, a predicative nominative or accusative is sometimes used: as, ⟦b:corōnam Iovī dōnum in capitōlium mittunt⟧, L. 2, 22, 6, ⟦i:they send a crown to the capitol as a present for Jupiter⟧. Prepositional expressions are also used for ⟦b:auxiliō⟧, &c.: as, ⟦b:ad praesidium⟧, L. 3, 5, 3, ⟦b:in praesidium⟧, L. 31, 16, 7, ⟦i:for protection⟧, ⟦b:auxiliī causā⟧, L. 2, 24, 4, ⟦i:to help⟧.
⟦#1225⟧
The dative ⟦b:receptuī⟧ is also used in military language to denote purpose: as, ⟦b:Caesar receptuī canī iussit⟧, 7, 47, 1, ⟦i:Caesar ordered the retreat sounded⟧. ⟦b:Quīnctius receptuī canere iussit⟧, L. 34, 39, 13. This dative is sometimes attached immediately to a substantive: as, ⟦b:receptuī sīgnum⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 13, 15, ⟦i:the trumpet for retreat⟧.

title: The Genitive
text:
⟦#1226⟧
The genitive is principally used with nouns, less frequently with verbs. Sometimes even when it seems to be dependent on a verb, it really depends on a substantive understood, or on a noun virtually contained or implied in the verb. Some verbs require an accusative also, in addition to the genitive.

title: The Genitive with Substantives
text:
⟦#1227⟧
A substantive is often limited by another substantive in the genitive.
The things denoted by the two words are usually distinct: as, ⟦b:metus hostium⟧, ⟦i:the fear of the enemy⟧, i.e. either (⟦i:a.⟧) which they feel (⟦r1231:1231⟧), or (⟦i:b.⟧) which is felt towards them (⟦r1260:1260⟧); ⟦b:magnī ponderis saxa⟧, ⟦i:stones of great weight⟧ (⟦r1239:1239⟧). Sometimes, however, they are more or less the same: as, ⟦b:mīlitum pars⟧, ⟦i:part of the soldiers⟧ (⟦r1242:1242⟧); ⟦b:magna multitūdō perditōrum hominum⟧, ⟦i:a perfect swarm of desperadoes⟧ (⟦r1255:1255⟧).
⟦#1228⟧
Two or even three genitives expressing different relations, sometimes limit one substantive: as, ⟦b:superiōrum diērum Sabīnī cunctātiō⟧, 3, 18, 6, ⟦i:Sabinus’s dilatoriness in days preceding⟧. ⟦b:eōrum diērum cōnsuētūdine itineris nostrī exercitūs perspectā⟧, 2, 17, 2, ⟦i:studying up the order of march followed by our army in those days⟧.
⟦#1229⟧
The limited substantive is often omitted, when it is obvious from the context: as, ⟦b:ventum erat ad Vestae⟧, sc. ⟦b:aedem⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 9, 35, ⟦i:to Vesta’s were we come⟧, i.e. to her temple. ⟦b:aberam bīduī⟧, sc. ⟦b:iter⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 5, 17, 1, ⟦i:I was two days distant⟧. Usually so, when it is expressed with another genitive, which generally precedes: as, ⟦b:quis est, quī possit cōnferre vītam Trebōnī cum Dolābellae?⟧ ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 11, 9, ⟦i:who is there that can compare the life of Trebonius with Dolabella’s?⟧
⟦#1230⟧
Instead of the genitive depending on a substantive, an equivalent adjective or a prepositional expression is often used. Such substitutions will be mentioned below in their appropriate places.
⟦#1231⟧
The relations expressed by the limiting genitive vary very much according to the context. These relations may be put in classes, as below (⟦r1232:1232-1260⟧). But it must be remembered that as the genitive connects substantives in a loose way, the same construction may sometimes be referred to more than one head.

title: The Genitive of the Subject, Cause, Origin, or Owner
text:
⟦#1232⟧
(1.) The genitive is used to denote that which does the action, or which causes, originates, or possesses the object designated by the substantive it limits: as,
⟦b:metus hostium⟧, Gell. 9, 12, 13, ⟦i:the fear of the enemy⟧, i.e. which they feel. ⟦b:adventus Caesaris⟧, 6, 41, 4, ⟦i:the arrival of Caesar⟧. ⟦b:bellum Venetōrum⟧, 3, 16, 1, ⟦i:the war with the Venetans⟧. ⟦b:illud Solōnis⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 50, ⟦i:Solon’s memorable words⟧. ⟦b:Canachī sīgna⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 70, ⟦i:statues by Canachus⟧. ⟦b:Cupīdinis sīgnum⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 135, ⟦i:the statue representing Cupid⟧. ⟦b:huius sīgnīs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 9, ⟦i:with statues belonging to this man⟧. ⟦b:pācem Ariovistī⟧, 1, 37, 2, ⟦i:a peaceful policy on Ariovistus’s part⟧. ⟦b:Cannārum pugna⟧, L. 23, 43, 4, ⟦i:the battle of Cannae⟧ (⟦r1427:1427⟧). ⟦b:abacī vāsa omnia⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 35, ⟦i:all the vessels on the sideboard⟧. ⟦b:prīdiē eius diēī⟧, 1, 47, 2, ⟦i:the day before that day⟧ (⟦r1413:1413⟧). ⟦b:labrōrum tenus⟧, Lucr. 1, 940, ⟦i:the length of the lips⟧ (⟦r1420:1420⟧).
⟦#1233⟧
Instead of the genitive, an adjective is often used to express such relations; less frequently a prepositional construction: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:odium paternum⟧, N. 23, 1, 3, ⟦i:the hatred felt by his father⟧. ⟦b:servīlī tumultū⟧, 1, 40, 5, ⟦i:in the slave insurrection⟧. ⟦b:bellō Cassiānō⟧, 1, 13, 2, ⟦i:in the war with Cassius⟧. ⟦b:illud Cassiānum, cui bonō fuerit⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 35, ⟦i:Cassius’s test question, ‘who the gainer was.’⟧ ⟦b:erīlis patria⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 170, ⟦i:my master’s birthplace⟧. ⟦b:intrā domesticōs parietēs⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 1, ⟦i:within the walls of our houses⟧. So usually with names of countries and of towns: as, ⟦b:anus Corinthia⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 600, ⟦i:an old woman of Corinth⟧. ⟦b:pugna Cannēnsis⟧, L. 22, 50, 1, ⟦i:the battle of Cannae⟧. Often in a generalizing sense: as, ⟦b:paternus māternusque sanguī̆s⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 66, ⟦i:the blood of a father and of a mother⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:ad Cannās pugnam⟧, L. 22, 58, 1, ⟦i:the battle of Cannae⟧.
⟦#1234⟧
The possessive pronoun is regularly used instead of the possessive genitive of a personal or reflexive pronoun (⟦r1230:1230⟧): as,
⟦b:mea domus⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 145, ⟦i:my own house⟧. ⟦b:in tuā quādam epistolā⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 9, 10, 3, ⟦i:in a letter of yours⟧. But sometimes, for emphasis, the genitive of the personal or reflexive is used: as, ⟦b:magnō suī cum perīculō⟧, 4, 28, 2, ⟦i:with great personal risk⟧; commonly so with ⟦b:omnium⟧ or ⟦b:utriusque⟧: as, ⟦b:voluntātī vestrūm omnium pāruī⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 3, 208, ⟦i:I yielded to your joint wish⟧; see however 1235.
⟦#1235⟧
A word in apposition with the possessive pronoun is put in the genitive: as, ⟦b:meā ūnīus operā⟧, ⟦i:Pis.⟧ 6, ⟦i:by my sole instrumentality⟧. ⟦b:ad vestram omnium caedem⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 4, ⟦i:for the murder of you all⟧ (⟦r1230:1230⟧). So particularly ⟦b:ipse⟧, ⟦b:omnis⟧, ⟦b:sōlus⟧, and ⟦b:ūnus⟧.
⟦#1236⟧
The genitive is often used predicatively with verbs meaning ⟦i:am⟧, ⟦i:belong⟧, ⟦i:become⟧, ⟦i:make⟧, ⟦i:seem⟧, ⟦i:am accounted⟧, &c., &c.: as,
⟦b:litterāriī ista sunt lūdī⟧, Quint. 1, 4, 27, ⟦i:such questions belong to the infant school⟧. ⟦b:hīc versus Plautī nōn est, hīc est⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 9, 16, 4, ⟦i:this line is not Plautus’s, this one is⟧. ⟦b:omnia, quae mulieris fuērunt, virī fīunt⟧, ⟦i:Top.⟧ 23, ⟦i:everything which was the woman’s becomes the man’s⟧. ⟦b:neque sē iūdicāre Galliam potius esse Ariovistī quam populī Rōmānī⟧, 1, 45, 1, ⟦i:and that he did not think Gaul was any more Ariovistus’s than it was the Romans’⟧. ⟦b:hostiumst potīta⟧, Pl. ⟦i:E.⟧ 562, ⟦i:into the foemen’s hands she fell⟧.
⟦#1237⟧
The possessive genitive of a person or of an abstract is particularly common when the subject of the verb is an infinitive or sentence: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:scyphīs pugnāre Thrācum est⟧, H. 1, 27, 1, ⟦i:to fight with bowls is Vandal work⟧. ⟦b:erat āmentis, cum aciem vidērēs, pācem cōgitāre⟧, ⟦i:Lig.⟧ 28, ⟦i:it was a madman’s act, dreaming of peace when you saw the troops in battalia⟧. ⟦b:temporī cēdere semper sapientis est habitum⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 4, 9, 2, ⟦i:shaping your course to circumstance has always passed as the sign of a wise man⟧. ⟦b:mentīrī nōn est meum⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 549, ⟦i:telling lies is not my style⟧ (⟦r1234:1234⟧). (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:nōn est pudōris meī, mē prōpugnātōrem P. Scīpiōnis profitērī⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 80, ⟦i:it is not in keeping with my delicacy to set up as the champion of Scipio⟧. ⟦b:hārum rērum esse dēfēnsōrem magnī animī est⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 99, ⟦i:to be the defender of these interests takes heroism⟧. ⟦b:hoc sentīre prūdentiae est, facere fortitūdinis⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 86, ⟦i:to think thus shows wisdom, to act thus, courage⟧. ⟦b:negāvit mōris esse Graecōrum, ut in convīviō virōrum accumberent mulierēs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 66, ⟦i:he said it was not manners among the Greeks to have women at table at a men’s dinner-party⟧.
⟦#1238⟧
With the possessive genitive, the limited substantive is sometimes defined by ⟦b:commūnis⟧, ⟦b:proprius⟧ or ⟦b:aliēnus⟧, ⟦b:sacer⟧, or ⟦b:tōtus⟧ added: as, ⟦b:hoc proprium virtūtis exīstimant⟧, 6, 23, 2, ⟦i:this they consider a special characteristic of bravery⟧. ⟦b:omnia quae nostra erant propria⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 150, ⟦i:everything which was our peculiar property⟧ (⟦r1234:1234⟧). ⟦b:illa īnsula eōrum deōrum sacra putātur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 48, ⟦i:that island is considered the hallowed property of those gods⟧. ⟦b:iam mē Pompēī tōtum esse scīs⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 13, 2, ⟦i:you are aware that I am become Pompey’s, out and out⟧.

title: The Genitive of Quality
text:
⟦#1239⟧
(2.) The genitive with an adjective in agreement is used to denote quality, either attributively or predicatively: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) Attributively: ⟦b:magnī ponderis saxa⟧, 2, 29, 3, ⟦i:stones of great weight⟧. ⟦b:summae speī adulēscentēs⟧, 7, 63, 9, ⟦i:young men of high promise⟧. ⟦b:diērum vīgintī supplicātiō⟧, 4, 38, 5, ⟦i:a twenty day thanksgiving⟧. ⟦b:bēlua multōrum es capitum⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 1, 76, ⟦i:a many-headed beast art thou⟧. ⟦b:eius modī cōnsilium⟧, 5, 29, 5, ⟦i:such a plan⟧. ⟦b:dēmittō auriculās ut inīquae mentis asellus⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 9, 20, ⟦i:I drop my ears like Neddy in the sulks⟧ (⟦r269:269⟧). ⟦b:vāllō pedum IX⟧, 5, 42, 1, ⟦i:with a nine foot palisade⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) Predicatively: ⟦b:magnae habitus auctōritātis⟧, 7, 77, 3, ⟦i:passing for a man of great influence⟧. ⟦b:flūminis erat altitūdō circiter pedum trium⟧, 2, 18, 3, ⟦i:the depth of the river was about three feet⟧. The genitive of quality resembles the ablative of quality (⟦r1375:1375⟧); the two are sometimes combined: as, ⟦b:hominem maximī corporis terribilīque faciē⟧, N. 15, 4, 1, ⟦i:a man of gigantic frame and with an awe-inspiring presence⟧. But the genitive is common in designations of size and number.
⟦#1240⟧
A substantive expressing quality with ⟦b:aequus⟧, ⟦b:pār⟧, ⟦b:similis⟧, or ⟦b:dissimilis⟧ in agreement, is put not in the genitive, but in the ablative, by Cicero, Caesar, Nepos, and Livy.

title: The Partitive Genitive
text:
⟦#1241⟧
(3.) The partitive genitive denotes a whole of which the limited substantive denotes a part. There are two kinds of partitive genitive, the numerical and the quantitative: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:mīlitum pars⟧, 6, 40, 8, ⟦i:part of the soldiers⟧, numerical partitive (⟦r1242:1242⟧). (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:multum aestātis⟧, 5, 22, 4, ⟦i:much of the summer⟧, quantitative partitive (⟦r1247:1247⟧).
⟦#1242⟧
(a.) The numerical partitive is a plural or a collective, limiting a word expressing part of the number: as,
⟦b:mīlitum pars⟧, 6, 40, 8, ⟦i:part of the soldiers⟧. ⟦b:pars equitātūs⟧, 4, 16, 2, ⟦i:part of the cavalry⟧. ⟦b:alter cōnsulum⟧, L. 6, 35, 5, ⟦i:one of the two consuls⟧. ⟦b:uter est īnsānior hōrum?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 3, 102, ⟦i:which of these two is crazier?⟧ ⟦b:eōrum neuter⟧, ⟦i:Pis.⟧ 62, ⟦i:neither of the two⟧. ⟦b:multae istārum arborum⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 59, ⟦i:many of the trees you see there⟧. ⟦b:quis omnium mortālium?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 179, ⟦i:who among all the sons of men?⟧ ⟦b:nēmō nostrūm⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 55, ⟦i:not one of us⟧. ⟦b:nihil hōrum⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 138, ⟦i:none of these things⟧. ⟦b:Stertinius, sapientum octāvus⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 3, 296, ⟦i:Stertinius, of sages eighth⟧. ⟦b:ō maior iuvenum⟧, H. ⟦i:AP.⟧ 366, ⟦i:O elder of the youths⟧. ⟦b:hōrum omnium fortissimī sunt Belgae⟧, 1, 1, 3, ⟦i:of all these the stoutest fighters are the Belgians⟧. Also with superlative adverbs: as, ⟦b:deōrum maximē Mercurium colunt⟧, Ta. ⟦i:G.⟧ 9, ⟦i:of the gods, they revere Mercury most⟧. ⟦b:minumē gentium⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 690, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 625, ⟦i:no, never in the world⟧.
⟦#1243⟧
⟦b:uterque⟧, ⟦i:each⟧, ⟦i:both⟧, often takes the genitive plural of a pronoun: as, ⟦b:quōrum uterque⟧, ⟦b:uterque eōrum⟧, ⟦b:hōrum⟧, ⟦b:nostrūm⟧, &c.; sometimes of a substantive and pronoun combined: as, ⟦b:utriusque hārum rērum⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 65, ⟦i:of each of these things⟧. ⟦b:quārum cīvitātum utraque⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 56, ⟦i:each of these communities⟧. With a substantive alone, it is oftener attributive: as, ⟦b:uterque dux⟧, ⟦i:Marc.⟧ 24, ⟦i:each commander⟧; and sometimes with neuter pronouns: as, ⟦b:quod utrumque⟧, Brut. in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 11, 1, 1, N. 25, 2, 4. The plural ⟦b:utrīque⟧ is used both ways: as, ⟦b:ab utrīsque vestrūm⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 11, 21, 5, and ⟦b:ab utrīsque nōbīs⟧, Brut. in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 11, 20, 3.
⟦#1244⟧
The plurals ⟦b:tot⟧, ⟦b:totidem⟧, and ⟦b:quot⟧, are not used partitively, and ⟦b:omnēs⟧ and ⟦b:cūnctī⟧ only so by poets and late prose writers. ⟦b:plērīque⟧ is used either way, in agreement, or with the genitive.
⟦#1245⟧
The numerical partitive is exceptionally used in poetry with the positive of a descriptive adjective: as, ⟦b:sāncte deōrum⟧, V. 4, 576, ⟦i:thou holy of the gods⟧. And in late prose, particularly with words denoting a class of persons: as, ⟦b:cum dēlēctīs peditum⟧, L. 26, 5, 3, ⟦i:with the pick of the infantry⟧. ⟦b:levīs cohortium⟧, Ta. 3, 39, ⟦i:the light-armed of the cohorts⟧.
⟦#1246⟧
Instead of the numerical partitive, a prepositional expression with ⟦b:ante⟧, ⟦b:inter⟧, or ⟦b:in⟧, or with ⟦b:ex⟧ or ⟦b:dē⟧, is sometimes used: as, ⟦b:ante aliōs acceptissimus⟧, L. 1, 15, 8, ⟦i:most welcome before others⟧. So particularly ⟦b:quīdam⟧ and ⟦b:ūnus⟧, ⟦b:duo⟧, ⟦b:trēs⟧, with ⟦b:ex⟧ or ⟦b:dē⟧: as, ⟦b:quīdam ex hīs⟧, 2, 17, 2, ⟦i:one of these⟧. ⟦b:ūnus dē multīs⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 66, ⟦i:one of the common herd⟧. But ⟦b:ūnus⟧ sometimes has the genitive: as, ⟦b:ūnus multōrum⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 9, 71. And usually so in a series, when ⟦b:ūnus⟧ is followed by ⟦b:alter⟧, ⟦b:alius⟧, ⟦b:tertius⟧, &c.
⟦#1247⟧
(b.) The quantitative partitive is usually a singular, limiting a neuter singular word denoting amount. The limited word is either a nominative, or an accusative without a preposition. This genitive often borders very closely on the genitive of definition (⟦r1255:1255⟧): as,
⟦b:multum aestātis⟧, 5, 22, 4, ⟦i:much of the summer⟧. ⟦b:amplius obsidum⟧, 6, 9, 7, ⟦i:something more extensive in the way of hostages⟧. ⟦b:minus dubitātiōnis⟧, 1, 14, 1, ⟦i:less of hesitation⟧. ⟦b:quam minimum spatiī⟧, 3, 19, 1, ⟦i:as little time as possible⟧. ⟦b:id aetātis⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 207, ⟦i:at that time of life⟧. ⟦b:id temporis⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 5, 1, ⟦i:at that time of day⟧. ⟦b:quid causae est?⟧ ⟦i:Ac.⟧ 1, 10, ⟦i:what earthly reason is there?⟧ ⟦b:hoc litterulārum⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 12, 1, 1, ⟦i:this apology for a letter⟧, or ⟦i:this hasty line⟧. ⟦b:hoc sibī̆ sōlācī prōpōnēbant⟧, 7, 15, 2, ⟦i:they laid this flattering unction to their souls⟧.
⟦#1248⟧
Such neuters are: ⟦b:multum⟧, ⟦b:plērumque⟧, ⟦b:plūrimum⟧, ⟦b:amplius⟧, ⟦b:plūs⟧, ⟦b:paulum⟧, ⟦b:minus⟧, ⟦b:minimum⟧, ⟦b:tantum⟧, ⟦b:quantum⟧, ⟦b:tantundem⟧, ⟦b:nimium⟧; in poetry and late prose, also many other adjectives singular and plural. Furthermore, ⟦b:id⟧, ⟦b:hoc⟧, ⟦b:illud⟧, ⟦b:quod⟧, ⟦b:quid⟧, &c., and ⟦b:nihil⟧; also ⟦b:abunde⟧, ⟦b:adfatim⟧, ⟦b:largiter⟧, ⟦b:nimis⟧, ⟦b:partim⟧, ⟦b:parum⟧, and ⟦b:satis⟧.
⟦#1249⟧
A few adjectives of place and time indicating a particular part of an object, are commonly used in immediate agreement with their substantives: as,
⟦b:summus mōns⟧, 1, 22, 1, ⟦i:the highest part of the mountain⟧, or ⟦i:the mountain-top⟧. ⟦b:extrēmā hieme, mediā aestāte⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 35, ⟦i:at the end of the winter, in midsummer⟧. Such are: ⟦b:prīmus⟧, ⟦b:intimus⟧, ⟦b:medius⟧, ⟦b:extrēmus⟧, ⟦b:postrēmus⟧, ⟦b:ūltimus⟧, ⟦b:summus⟧, ⟦b:īnfimus⟧, ⟦b:īmus⟧, ⟦b:reliquus⟧. But the neuter is sometimes used partitively: as, ⟦b:aestātis extrēmum erat⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 90, 1, ⟦i:it was the end of summer⟧. ⟦b:summa pectoris⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 1, 9, 15, ⟦i:the upper parts of the breast⟧.
⟦#1250⟧
The limiting genitive is often the neuter singular of an adjective used substantively: as,
⟦b:aliquid bonī⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 398, ⟦i:something good⟧. ⟦b:aliquid malī⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 999, ⟦i:something bad⟧. ⟦b:numquid tandem novī?⟧ ⟦i:Br.⟧ 10, ⟦i:nothing new, pray?⟧ This use is ordinarily confined to stems in ⟦b:-o-⟧; rarely otherwise: as, ⟦b:plūs inānis⟧, Lucr. 1, 365, ⟦i:more of the void⟧: and usually only when joined with an ⟦b:-o-⟧ stem: as, ⟦b:nihil solidī, nihil ēminentis⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 75, ⟦i:no solidity, no projection⟧.
⟦#1251⟧
The partitive construction sometimes extends to the predicate: as, ⟦b:id erit sīgnī mē invītum facere⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 83, ⟦i:this will be something of an indication that I act with reluctance⟧; ⟦b:sīgnī⟧ is here in the predicate, and yet made dependent on ⟦b:id⟧. ⟦b:quid ergō est tuī cōnsulī?⟧ Brut. in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 11, 1, 3, ⟦i:what then is your advice?⟧ ⟦b:quid suī cōnsilī sit ostendit⟧, 1, 21, 2, ⟦i:he explains what his plan is⟧. ⟦b:quid est enim huic reliquī?⟧ ⟦i:Sull.⟧ 89, ⟦i:for what is there left for my client?⟧ ⟦b:hī mīlitēs nihil reliquī victīs fēcēre⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 11, 7, ⟦i:these soldiers left nothing over to the conquered⟧. ⟦b:nihil ad celeritātem sibī̆ reliquī fēcērunt⟧, 2, 26, 5, ⟦i:as for speed, they left no effort unspared⟧.
⟦#1252⟧
The accusative with a preposition also sometimes has the genitive, as, ⟦b:in id redāctus sum locī⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 979, ⟦i:I am reduced to such a strait⟧. ⟦b:ad id locī⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 45, 3, ⟦i:to that spot⟧. ⟦b:ad id locōrum⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 63, 6, ⟦i:up to that time⟧. ⟦b:in multum diēī⟧, L. 9, 44, 11, ⟦i:till late in the day⟧. In Cicero, also the ablatives ⟦b:eō⟧, ⟦b:eōdem⟧, and ⟦b:quō⟧, with ⟦b:locī⟧: as, ⟦b:eō locī⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 68, ⟦i:in that position⟧. And in later writers, other ablatives, with or without a preposition, also have a genitive.
⟦#1253⟧
Some appellatives of place are put in the genitive with adverbs of place: as, ⟦b:ubinam gentium?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Mer.⟧ 434, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 9, ⟦i:where in the world?⟧ ⟦b:nusquam gentium⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 540, ⟦i:nowhere in the world⟧. Similarly, ⟦b:locī⟧ with adverbs of time or order, as with ⟦b:intereā⟧ in Plautus and Terence, ⟦b:postideā⟧ in Plautus, ⟦b:posteā⟧ in Sallust, and ⟦b:inde⟧ in Lucretius; also ⟦b:locōrum⟧ with ⟦b:adhūc⟧ and ⟦b:postid⟧ in Plautus.
⟦#1254⟧
In Sallust, Livy, and Tacitus, genitives of abstracts are used with the adverbs ⟦b:eō⟧, ⟦b:quō⟧, and ⟦b:hūc⟧: as, ⟦b:eō miseriārum⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 14, 3, ⟦i:to that pitch of distress⟧. Ones with ⟦b:ut⟧: ⟦b:ut quisque audentiae habuisset, adcurrerent⟧, Ta. 15, 53, ⟦i:they should run up, with a speed commensurate in every case to their daring⟧.

title: The Genitive of Definition
text:
⟦#1255⟧
(4.) The genitive is used to define that of which a thing consists: as,
⟦b:magna multitūdō perditōrum hominum⟧, 3, 17, 4, ⟦i:a perfect swarm of desperadoes⟧. ⟦b:innumerābile pondus aurī⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 93, ⟦i:a weight of gold too great to count⟧. ⟦b:mīlle numerō nāvium clāssem⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 48, ⟦i:an armada a thousand sail strong⟧.
⟦#1256⟧
The genitive of an explicit word containing the leading idea is sometimes used to define a more general word; as,
⟦b:praedae pecudum hominumque⟧, L. 24, 20, 5, ⟦i:booty consisting of cattle and human beings⟧. ⟦b:pignora coniugum ac līberōrum⟧, L. 2, 1, 5, ⟦i:pledges in the shape of wives and children⟧. ⟦b:cōnfīsus mūnītiōne fossae⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 42, 3, ⟦i:relying on the defensive works in the shape of a moat⟧. Rarely in poetry and late prose, the proper name of a place, with ⟦b:urbs⟧, ⟦b:prōmunturium⟧, &c.: as, ⟦b:urbem Patavī⟧, V., 1, 247, ⟦i:the city of Patavium⟧ (⟦r1045:1045⟧). Particularly with the words ⟦b:vōx⟧, ⟦b:nōmen⟧, ⟦b:genus⟧, and especially ⟦b:causa⟧: as, ⟦b:haec vōx voluptātis⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 6, ⟦i:this word ‘pleasure.’⟧ ⟦b:nōmen amīcitiae⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 78, ⟦i:the name ‘friendship.’⟧ Compare ⟦b:nōmen frāternum⟧, 1, 36, 5, ⟦i:the name of brothers⟧ (⟦r1233:1233⟧). ⟦b:haec īgnōminiae causa⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 120, ⟦i:this reason, namely the censor’s stigma⟧. ⟦b:parvulae causae vel falsae suspīciōnis vel terrōris repentīnī⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 72, 4, ⟦i:insignificant causes, as for instance ungrounded suspicion or a panic⟧. ⟦b:propter eam causam sceleris istīus⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 113, ⟦i:for this reason, namely the crime of the defendant⟧.
⟦#1257⟧
The genitive of definition is very common with ⟦b:causā⟧, less common with ⟦b:grātiā⟧, to define what the motive or cause is: as,
⟦b:amīcitiae causā⟧, 1, 39, 2, ⟦i:from motives of friendship⟧. Compare ⟦b:vestrā magis hoc causā volēbam, quam meā⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 164, ⟦i:I wished this more for your sake than for my own⟧ (⟦r1234:1234⟧). ⟦b:honestātis amplitūdinisque grātiā⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 15, ⟦i:in compliment to their respectability and high social standing⟧. So also sometimes with ⟦b:nōmine⟧, and in old or official Latin, with ⟦b:ergō⟧.
⟦#1258⟧
Conversely, the genitive of a generic word denoting a person is sometimes added to a leading word defining the kind of a person: as, ⟦b:frūstum puerī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 849, ⟦i:thou bit of a boy⟧. ⟦b:mōnstrum hominis⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 696, ⟦i:thou fiend in human shape⟧. ⟦b:quaedam pestēs hominum⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 5, 8, 2, ⟦i:some regular plagues in the shape of men⟧.
⟦#1259⟧
⟦b:quidquid est⟧, ⟦b:quantum est⟧, ⟦b:quod est⟧, or ⟦b:quodcumque est⟧, with a genitive, is equivalent to an emphatic ⟦b:omnis⟧: as, ⟦b:quidquid patrum est⟧, L. 3, 17, 5, ⟦i:whatever there is in the shape of senators⟧, i.e. ⟦i:every single senator⟧. ⟦b:quod est pecūniae, trādit⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 20, 8, ⟦i:what there is in the-way of money, he hands over⟧. Similarly ⟦b:tantum⟧ for ⟦b:tot⟧: as, ⟦b:tantum hominum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 619, ⟦i:such a mass of men⟧.

title: The Objective Genitive
text:
⟦#1260⟧
(5.) The objective genitive denotes the object of the action expressed in the limited substantive: as,
⟦b:metus hostium⟧, Gell. 9, 12, 13, ⟦i:the fear of the enemy⟧, i.e. which is felt towards them. ⟦b:vēnditiō bonōrum⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 110, ⟦i:sale of the goods⟧. ⟦b:lūctū fīlī⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 193, ⟦i:from grief for his son⟧. This construction is freely used, even when the parallel verb has a dative, an ablative, or a prepositional expression: as, ⟦b:fīdūciā locī⟧, 7, 19, 2, ⟦i:from confidence in the position⟧. ⟦b:līberātiōnem culpae⟧, ⟦i:Lig.⟧ 1, ⟦i:acquittal from guilt⟧. ⟦b:mīlitiae vacātiōnem⟧, 6, 14, 1, ⟦i:exemption from military service⟧. ⟦b:opīniōne trium legiōnum dēiectus⟧, 5, 48, 1, ⟦i:disappointed in his hope of three legions⟧. ⟦b:deōrum opīniō⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 30, ⟦i:a conception of the gods⟧. ⟦b:miserrima est contentiō honōrum⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 87, ⟦i:a scramble for office is a pitiful thing⟧.
⟦#1261⟧
Instead of the objective genitive, a prepositional expression is sometimes used with greater precision: as,
⟦b:metus ā vī atque īrā deōrum⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 45, ⟦i:fear of the might and wrath of the gods⟧. So especially the accusative, usually denoting a person, with ⟦b:in⟧, ⟦b:ergā⟧, or ⟦b:adversus⟧, combined with substantives denoting feeling: as, ⟦b:odium in hominum ūniversum genus⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 4, 25, ⟦i:hatred to all mankind⟧. ⟦b:vestra ergā mē voluntās⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 1, ⟦i:your good-will towards me⟧.
⟦#1262⟧
A possessive pronoun or adjective is sometimes used for the objective genitive: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:odiō tuō⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 1016, ⟦i:from hate to thee⟧. ⟦b:tuā fīdūciā⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 176, ⟦i:from his reliance on you⟧. ⟦b:aspectūque suō⟧, Lucr. 1, 91, ⟦i:and at the sight of her⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:metus hostīlis⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 41, 2, ⟦i:fear felt of the enemy⟧. ⟦b:servīlis percontātiō⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 327, ⟦i:crossquestioning of the servant-girls⟧. ⟦b:firmus adversus mīlitārem largītiōnem⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 2, 82, ⟦i:dead-set against any largess to the military⟧.

title: The Genitive with Adjectives
text:
⟦#1263⟧
(1.) The genitive is used with many adjectives to denote the object.
Such are chiefly adjectives meaning (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦i:desirous⟧, (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦i:knowing⟧, or ⟦i:remembering⟧, (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦i:participating⟧, ⟦i:controlling⟧, or ⟦i:guilty⟧, (⟦i:d.⟧) ⟦i:full⟧, and most of their opposites: as, (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:aurī cupidus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 179, ⟦i:eager for gold⟧. ⟦b:sapientiae studiōsōs, id est enim philosophōs⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 9, ⟦i:devotees of wisdom, for that is what ‘philosophers’ means⟧. So also ⟦b:aemulus⟧, ⟦b:avidus⟧, ⟦b:fastīdiōsus⟧, ⟦b:invidus⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:gnārus rē̆ī pūblicae⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 228, ⟦i:familiar with government⟧. ⟦b:rē̆ī mīlitāris perītissimus⟧, 1, 21, 4, ⟦i:a master of the art military⟧. ⟦b:hominēs adulēscentulōs, inperītōs rērum⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 910, ⟦i:mere hobbledehoys, not up in the world’s ways⟧. ⟦b:imperītus mōrum⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 143, ⟦i:behind the times⟧. ⟦b:immemor beneficiōrum, memor patriae⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 27, ⟦i:forgetful of kindnesses, never forgetting his country⟧. So also ⟦b:cōnscius⟧, ⟦b:cōnsultus⟧, ⟦b:īnscius⟧, ⟦b:īnsolēns⟧, ⟦b:īnsolitus⟧, ⟦b:īnsuētus⟧, ⟦b:iēiūnus⟧, ⟦b:prōvidus⟧, ⟦b:prūdēns⟧, ⟦b:rudis⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:praedae participēs⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 82, 1, ⟦i:sharing in the booty⟧. ⟦b:manifestus tantī sceleris⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 35, 8, ⟦i:caught in committing this atrocious crime⟧. ⟦b:expers glōriae⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 57, ⟦i:without a share in the glory⟧. So also ⟦b:adfīnis⟧, ⟦b:compos⟧, ⟦b:cōnsors⟧, ⟦b:exhērēs⟧, ⟦b:potēns⟧, ⟦b:reus⟧. (⟦i:d.⟧) ⟦b:negōtī plēnus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 380, ⟦i:full of business⟧. ⟦b:fōns plēnissimus piscium⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 118, ⟦i:a fountain swarming with fish⟧. ⟦b:refertō praedōnum marī⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 31, ⟦i:when the sea was crammed with corsairs⟧. So also ⟦b:fertilis⟧, ⟦b:inops⟧, ⟦b:līberālis⟧, ⟦b:nūdus⟧, ⟦b:prōfūsus⟧.
⟦#1264⟧
In poetry and late prose, a great many other adjectives of these meanings, besides those mentioned above, are also used with the genitive. Such are principally: (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:avārus⟧, ⟦b:cūriōsus⟧, ⟦b:incūriōsus⟧, ⟦b:sēcūrus⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:nescius⟧, ⟦b:praesāgus⟧, ⟦b:praescius⟧, ⟦b:scītus⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:exsors⟧, ⟦b:immūnis⟧, ⟦b:impos⟧, ⟦b:impotēns⟧, ⟦b:innocēns⟧, ⟦b:innoxius⟧, ⟦b:īnsōns⟧, ⟦b:noxius⟧, ⟦b:suspectus⟧. (⟦i:d.⟧) ⟦b:abundāns⟧, ⟦b:dīves⟧, ⟦b:egēnus⟧, ⟦b:inānis⟧, ⟦b:indigus⟧, ⟦b:largus⟧, ⟦b:parcus⟧, ⟦b:pauper⟧, ⟦b:prōdigus⟧, ⟦b:sterilis⟧, ⟦b:vacuus⟧.
⟦#1265⟧
With ⟦b:cōnscius⟧ and the genitive of a thing, the dative of a person is sometimes added: as, ⟦b:tot flāgitiōrum exercituī meō cōnscius⟧, Ta. 1, 43, ⟦i:a participant with my army in so many outrages⟧. Sometimes ⟦b:cōnscius⟧ has the dative of a thing: as, ⟦b:mēns cōnscia factīs⟧, Lucr. 3, 1018, ⟦i:the mind of guilt aware⟧.
⟦#1266⟧
(2.) The genitive of the object is often used with present participles which express permanent condition.
These participles are chiefly from verbs which have a transitive use. Not common in old Latin: as, ⟦b:amantem uxōris⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 857, ⟦i:devoted to his wife⟧, ⟦b:fugitāns lītium⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 623, ⟦i:inclined to dodge a suit at law⟧. Very common in Cicero: as, ⟦b:semper appetentēs glōriae praeter cēterās gentīs fuistis⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 7, ⟦i:you have always been more hungry for glory than any other nation⟧. Especially in set expressions: as, ⟦b:homo amantissimus patriae⟧, ⟦i:Sull.⟧ 34, ⟦b:vir amantissimus rē̆ī pūblicae⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 13, ⟦i:ever a devoted patriot⟧. ⟦b:negōtī gerentēs⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 97, ⟦i:business men⟧. ⟦b:aliēnī appetēns⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 135, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 5, 4, ⟦i:always hankering after other people’s things⟧. In Caesar seldom: as, ⟦b:fugiēns labōris⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 69, 3, ⟦i:apt to shirk exertion⟧.
⟦#1267⟧
The genitive is hardly ever found with adjectives in ⟦b:-āx⟧ (⟦r284:284⟧): as, ⟦b:huius re͡i mendācem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 855, ⟦i:untruthful in this point⟧. But in poetry, from Vergil and Horace on, and in late prose, a few genitives occur with adjectives whose parallel verbs have a transitive use, such as ⟦b:capāx⟧, ⟦b:edāx⟧, ⟦b:tenāx⟧, &c.: as, ⟦b:tempus edāx rērum⟧, O. 15, 234, ⟦i:thou all-devourer—time⟧.
⟦#1268⟧
Some of the adjectives which usually take the genitive have occasionally other constructions.
Thus, with ⟦b:adfīnis⟧ the dative also occurs (⟦r1200:1200⟧), rarely with ⟦b:aemulus⟧ (⟦r1183:1183⟧); the ablative with adjectives of fulness, as ⟦b:dīves⟧, ⟦b:plēnus⟧, and ⟦b:refertus⟧ (⟦r1387:1387⟧); ⟦b:iūre⟧ with ⟦b:cōnsultus⟧ and ⟦b:perītus⟧ (⟦r1385:1385⟧). For ⟦b:vacuus⟧, &c., see ⟦r1306:1306⟧. Prepositional constructions also occur with these adjectives, such as the accusative with ⟦b:ad⟧ or ⟦b:in⟧, or the ablative with ⟦b:ab⟧, ⟦b:dē⟧, or ⟦b:in⟧: see the dictionary.
⟦#1269⟧
For the genitive, with words denoting relationship, connection, friendship, or hostility, see ⟦r1203:1203⟧; with ⟦b:similis⟧, 1204. With ⟦b:dignus⟧ and ⟦b:indignus⟧, ⟦i:worthy⟧ and ⟦i:unworthy⟧, the ablative is regularly used (⟦r1392:1392⟧); rarely the genitive: as, ⟦b:nōn ego sum dignus salūtis?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 1153, ⟦i:don’t I deserve a greeting too?⟧ ⟦b:indignus avōrum⟧, V. 12, 649, ⟦i:unworthy of my sires⟧.
⟦#1270⟧
(3.) In poetry and late prose, the genitive is used very freely with many adjectives of various meanings, often merely to indicate what they apply to: as,
⟦b:nēmō mīlitāris rē̆ī callidior habēbātur⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 2, 32, ⟦i:at soldiering nobody was thought to have a greater knack⟧. ⟦b:vetus operis ac labōris⟧, Ta. 1, 20, ⟦i:an old hand at the toil and moil of army life⟧. ⟦b:aevī mātūrus Acestēs⟧, V. 5, 73, ⟦i:Acestes, ripe in years⟧. ⟦b:sērī studiōrum⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 10, 21, ⟦i:what laggards at your books⟧. ⟦b:integer vītae scelerisque pūrus⟧, H. 1, 22, 1, ⟦i:the man unspotted in his life and clean of sin⟧. ⟦b:fessī rērum⟧, V. 1, 178, ⟦i:in travail spent⟧. ⟦b:satin tū sānu’s mentis aut animī tuī?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 454, ⟦i:art thou quite right in thy five wits?⟧ (⟦r1339:1339⟧).

title: Verbs Of Valuing
text:
⟦#1271⟧
A few neuter adjectives of quantity are put in the genitive with verbs of valuing to denote the amount of estimation; such genitives are:
⟦b:magnī⟧, ⟦b:plūris⟧, ⟦b:plūrimī⟧; ⟦b:parvī⟧, ⟦b:minōris⟧, ⟦b:minimī⟧; ⟦b:tantī⟧, ⟦b:quantī⟧.
⟦/⟧
The verbs with which these genitives are used are ⟦b:aestimō⟧, ⟦b:dūcō⟧, ⟦b:faciō⟧, ⟦b:habeō⟧, ⟦b:pendō⟧, ⟦b:putō⟧, and ⟦b:sum⟧; rarely ⟦b:exīstimō⟧: as, ⟦b:magnī opera eius aestimāta est⟧, N. 24, 1, 2, ⟦i:his services were rated high⟧. ⟦b:nōn magnī pendō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 460, ⟦i:I don’t care much⟧. ⟦b:sua parvī pendere⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 12, 2, ⟦i:a setting small store by what they had of their own⟧. ⟦b:Verrēsne tibī̆ tantī fuit?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 77, ⟦i:was Verres so important in your eyes?⟧ ⟦b:est mihī̆ tantī⟧. ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 15, ⟦i:it is well worth my while⟧. ⟦b:quantī is ā cīvibus suīs fieret īgnōrābās?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 19, ⟦i:did not you know how the man was prized by his own townsmen?⟧ Rarely ⟦b:maximī⟧: as, ⟦b:maximī aestimāre⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 159, ⟦i:to think all the world of⟧.
⟦#1272⟧
In expressions of worthlessness, other genitives are also used thus; such are ⟦b:nihilī⟧, or, usually with a negative, ⟦b:āssis⟧, ⟦b:floccī⟧, ⟦b:naucī⟧, ⟦b:pilī⟧, ⟦b:teruncī⟧: as, ⟦b:nōn āssis facis?⟧ Cat. 43, 13, ⟦i:car’st not a doit?⟧ So also ⟦b:huius⟧: as, ⟦b:huius nōn faciam⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 163, ⟦i:I shall not care a snap⟧.
⟦#1273⟧
With ⟦b:aestimō⟧, the ablatives ⟦b:magnō⟧ and ⟦b:permagnō⟧ are sometimes used: as, ⟦b:quid? tū ista permagnō aestimās?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 13, ⟦i:tell me, do you rate that sort of thing very high yourself?⟧ Compare 1390.
⟦#1274⟧
The genitives ⟦b:tantī⟧ and ⟦b:quantī⟧, ⟦b:plūris⟧ and ⟦b:minōris⟧ are also used with verbs of buying and selling, hiring and letting, and costing. But other words are put in the ablative with these verbs: see ⟦r1391:1391⟧. For ⟦b:magnī⟧, &c., with ⟦b:rēfert⟧ and ⟦b:interest⟧, see ⟦r1279:1279⟧.
⟦#1275⟧
A similar genitive occurs in one or two set forms, such as ⟦b:aequī bonīque dīcō⟧, or ⟦b:faciō⟧, ⟦b:aequī faciō⟧, and ⟦b:bonī cōnsulō⟧: as, ⟦b:istūc, Chremēs, aequī bonīque faciō⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 787, ⟦i:I count that, Chremes, fair and good⟧. ⟦b:aequī istūc faciō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 784, ⟦i:that’s all the same to me⟧.

title: The Verbs rēfert and interest
text:
⟦#1276⟧
⟦b:rēfert⟧ and ⟦b:interest⟧, ⟦i:it concerns⟧, are much alike in meaning and in construction. But the use of ⟦b:rēfert⟧ is characteristic of old Latin and poetry; in prose from Cicero on it is almost supplanted by ⟦b:interest⟧, especially where persons are concerned.
⟦#1277⟧
(1.) With ⟦b:rēfert⟧ and ⟦b:interest⟧, a first or second person concerned is denoted by the possessive pronoun forms ⟦b:meā⟧, ⟦b:tuā⟧, ⟦b:nostrā⟧, ⟦b:vestrā⟧; and, from Cicero on, the third person reflexive by ⟦b:suā⟧: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:quid id rēfert meā?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Cur.⟧ 395, ⟦i:what’s that to me?⟧ ⟦b:tuā istūc rēfert maxumē⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 319, ⟦i:that is of most concern to thee⟧. ⟦b:nōn suā rēferre⟧, ⟦i:Quinct.⟧ 19, ⟦i:that it did not concern him⟧. ⟦b:nōn nostrā magis quam vestrā rēfert vōs nōn rebellāre⟧, L. 34, 17, 7, ⟦i:it is not more for our interest than for your own that you should not make war again⟧. Without the verb: as, ⟦b:quid istūc nostrā⟧, or ⟦b:quid id nostrā?⟧ T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 800, 940, ⟦i:what’s that to us?⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:tuā et meā maximē interest tē valēre⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 4, 4, ⟦i:your health is a matter of the highest importance to you and to me⟧. ⟦b:vestrā hōc maximē interest⟧, ⟦i:Sull.⟧ 79, ⟦i:this is of vital moment to you⟧.
⟦#1278⟧
(2.) With ⟦b:interest⟧, from Cicero on, a third person or thing concerned is denoted by the genitive. Also with ⟦b:rēfert⟧, a few times from Sallust on: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:quid eius intererat?⟧ ⟦i:RA.⟧ 96, ⟦i:what concern was it of his?⟧ ⟦b:interesse rē̆ī pūblicae sē cum Pompēiō colloquī⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 24, 5, ⟦i:that it was of importance to the common weal that he should have a parley with Pompey⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:faciundum aliquid, quod illōrum magis quam suā rētulisse vidērētur⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 111, 1, ⟦i:that he must do something which should seem more for the other side’s good than his own⟧. For the accusative with ⟦b:ad⟧ with these verbs, or for the dative with ⟦b:rēfert⟧, see the dictionary.
⟦#1279⟧
The matter of concern is expressed by a sentence or infinitive, or by a neuter pronoun; rarely by an appellative: as, ⟦b:nōn quō meā interesset locī nātūra⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 3, 19, 1, ⟦i:not that the character of the place concerned me⟧. The degree of concern is expressed by an adverb, as ⟦b:magnopere⟧, by a neuter accusative, as ⟦b:multum⟧, or by a genitive of estimation, ⟦b:magnī⟧, ⟦b:permagnī⟧, ⟦b:plūris⟧, ⟦b:parvī⟧, ⟦b:tantī⟧, ⟦b:quantī⟧ (⟦r1271:1271⟧).

title: Judicial Verbs
text:
⟦#1280⟧
Verbs of accusing, convicting, condemning, and acquitting, take a genitive of the charge: as,
⟦b:C. Verrem īnsimulat avāritiae⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 128, ⟦i:he charges Verres with avarice⟧. ⟦b:accūsātus est prōditiōnis⟧, N. 1, 7, 5, ⟦i:he was charged with treason⟧. ⟦b:capitis arcēssere⟧, ⟦i:D.⟧ 30, ⟦i:accuse on a capital charge⟧. ⟦b:prōditiōnis damnātus est⟧, N. 2, 8, 2, ⟦i:he was convicted of treason⟧. ⟦b:Pollis pecūniae pūblicae est condemnātus⟧, ⟦i:Flacc.⟧ 43, ⟦i:Pollis was condemned for embezzlement of government money⟧. ⟦b:maiestātis absolūtī sunt permultī⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 116, ⟦i:a good many were acquitted of high treason⟧. With this genitive, an ablative, ⟦b:crīmine⟧, ⟦b:iūdiciō⟧, ⟦b:nōmine⟧, or ⟦b:lēge⟧, is sometimes expressed (⟦r1377:1377⟧): as, ⟦b:nē quem umquam innocentem iūdiciō capitis arcēssās⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 2, 51, ⟦i:that you are never to accuse any innocent man on a charge affecting his status as a citizen⟧.
⟦#1281⟧
The charge is sometimes denoted by a prepositional construction: as, ⟦b:sescentī sunt, quī inter sīcāriōs et dē venēficiīs accūsābant⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 90, ⟦i:there are hundreds and hundreds that brought charges of murder, by steel and by poison⟧. So also ⟦b:dē āleā⟧, ⟦i:of gambling⟧, in Cicero regularly ⟦b:dē pecūniīs repetundīs⟧, ⟦i:of extortion⟧, and necessarily ⟦b:dē vī⟧, ⟦i:of an act of violence⟧, as ⟦b:vīs⟧ has no genitive. For the neuter accusative, see ⟦r1172:1172⟧.
⟦#1282⟧
The penalty also is sometimes denoted by the genitive: as, ⟦b:cupiō octuplī damnārī Aprōnium⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 28, ⟦i:I want to have Apronius condemned to a payment of eightfold⟧. ⟦b:damnātusque longī Sīsyphus Aeolidēs labōris⟧, H. 2, 14, 19, ⟦i:and Sisyphus the Aeolid, amerced with penance long⟧. Sometimes by the ablative: as, ⟦b:capite⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 109. So usually from Livy on, when the penalty is a definite sum of money or fractional part of a thing.

title: Impersonal Verbs of Mental Distress
text:
⟦#1283⟧
A genitive of the thing, commonly with an accusative of the person, is used with five impersonals of mental distress:
⟦b:miseret⟧, ⟦b:paenitet⟧, ⟦b:piget⟧, ⟦b:pudet⟧, ⟦b:taedet⟧: as,
⟦b:tu͡i mē miseret, me͡i piget⟧, E. in ⟦i:Div.⟧ 1, 66, ⟦i:I pity thee, I loathe myself⟧. ⟦b:frātris mē pudet pigetque⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 391, ⟦i:my brother stirs my shame and my disgust⟧. ⟦b:mī pater, mē tu͡i pudet⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 681, ⟦i:dear father, in thy presence I’m abashed⟧. ⟦b:galeātum sēro duellī paenitet⟧, J. 1, 169, ⟦i:too late, with casque on head, a combatant repenteth him of war⟧. So also ⟦b:miserētur⟧, and in old Latin inceptively, ⟦b:miserēscit⟧, ⟦b:commiserēscit⟧.
⟦#1284⟧
These verbs sometimes have a sentence or a neuter pronoun as subject: as, ⟦b:nōn tē haec pudent?⟧ T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 754, ⟦i:does not this make thee blush for shame?⟧ Rarely an appellative: as, ⟦b:mē quidem haec condiciō nōn paenitet⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 51, ⟦i:for my part, with my wedded state I’m well content⟧. Or a person: as, ⟦b:pudeō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cas.⟧ 877, ⟦i:I feel ashamed⟧. For participles and gerundives, see ⟦r817:817⟧.
⟦#1285⟧
The genitive is used with the personals ⟦b:misereor⟧ or ⟦b:misereō⟧, and in poetry with ⟦b:miserēscō⟧: as,
⟦b:aliquandō miserēminī sociōrum⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 72, ⟦i:do take pity on your allies, it is high time⟧. ⟦b:nēminis miserēre certumst, quia me͡i miseret nēminem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 764, ⟦i:I’m bound to care for nobody, as no one cares for me⟧. ⟦b:Arcadiī miserēscite rēgis⟧, V. 8, 573, ⟦i:take pity on the king of Arcady⟧.
⟦#1286⟧
Personal verbs of desiring, loathing, admiring, and dreading, sometimes take the genitive: as, ⟦b:pol, quamquam domī cupiō, opperiar⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 841, ⟦i:although I yearn for home, I vow I’ll wait⟧ (⟦r1263:1263⟧). ⟦b:fastīdit meī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 245, ⟦i:he views me with disdain⟧ (⟦r1263:1263⟧). ⟦b:iūstitiaene prius mīrer, bellīne labōrum?⟧ V. 11, 126, ⟦i:thy justice first shall I admire? thy toils in war?⟧ ⟦b:nē tuī quidem testimōnī veritus⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 8, 4, 1, ⟦i:not having any awe about your recommendation either⟧.

title: Verbs of Memory
text:
⟦#1287⟧
The genitive is used with verbs of remembering and forgetting when they denote an inherent state of memory or of forgetfulness: as,
⟦b:faciam ut meī meminerīs dum vītam vīvās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 494, ⟦i:I’ll make you remember me as long as you live⟧. ⟦b:num potuī magis oblīvīscī temporum meōrum, meminisse āctiōnum?⟧ ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 1, 9, 8, ⟦i:could I have been more forgetful of my present interests, more mindful of my past career?⟧ ⟦b:reminīscerētur incommodī populī Rōmānī⟧, 1, 13, 4, ⟦i:he had better bear in mind the rebuff dealt out to Rome⟧. ⟦b:oblītusque meōrum oblīvīscendus et illīs⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 11, 10, ⟦i:of friends forgetful and by friends forgot⟧. See ⟦r1263:1263⟧.
⟦#1288⟧
The accusative is used with these verbs when they denote the mere intellectual exercise of memory or a failure to remember: as,
⟦b:equid meministī tu͡om parentum nōmina?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 1062, ⟦i:do you remember your parents’ names?⟧ ⟦b:Cinnam meminī vīdī Sūllam⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 5, 17, ⟦i:I can remember Cinna, I have seen Sulla⟧. ⟦b:utinam mēmet possim oblīscier!⟧ Accius ap. Non. 500, 5, ⟦i:oh that myself I could forget!⟧ ⟦b:subitō tōtam causam oblītus est⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 217, ⟦i:suddenly he forgot the whole case⟧.
⟦#1289⟧
⟦b:recordor⟧ has once the genitive (⟦i:Pis.⟧ 12), but from its meaning ⟦i:bring to heart⟧ it is naturally found oftener with the accusative. With it and with ⟦b:meminī⟧, the ablative with ⟦b:dē⟧ also occurs. The rare ⟦b:reminīscor⟧ has the genitive once each in Caesar and Nepos; twice later; oftener the accusative. Neuter pronouns are in the accusative with all these verbs.
⟦#1290⟧
The impersonal ⟦b:venit in mentem⟧ also takes the genitive: as, ⟦b:venit mihī̆ Platōnis in mentem⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 5, 2, ⟦i:Plato comes into my head⟧; very exceptionally the ablative with ⟦b:dē⟧. But the verb in this combination is often used personally, with the thing occurring to the mind as the subject, and regularly in Cicero, when it is ⟦b:rēs⟧ or ⟦b:genus⟧, or a neuter pronoun.
⟦#1291⟧
Verbs of reminding take the accusative of a person and sometimes with it the genitive of a thing: as,
⟦b:admonēbat alium egestātis, alium cupiditātis suae⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 21, 4, ⟦i:he reminded one man of his beggary, another of his greed⟧. So also ⟦b:commoneō⟧, ⟦b:commonē̆faciō⟧, and, in Tacitus only, ⟦b:moneō⟧. Oftener however the thing is in the ablative with ⟦b:dē⟧, or, if it is a neuter pronoun or adjective, in the accusative (⟦r1172:1172⟧). Rarely a substantive equivalent to a neuter pronoun: as, ⟦b:eam rem nōs locus admonuit⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 79, 1, ⟦i:the place has reminded me of that⟧.

title: Verbs of Participation and Mastery
text:
⟦#1292⟧
Verbs of participation and mastery sometimes take the genitive in old Latin and in poetry: as, ⟦b:servom su͡i participat cōnsilī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cist.⟧ 163, ⟦i:she makes a slave a sharer in her plot⟧ (⟦r1263:1263⟧). ⟦b:quā Daunus agrestium rēgnāvit populōrum⟧, H. 3, 30, 11, ⟦i:where Daunus was the lord of rural folk⟧ (⟦r1260:1260⟧). So, even in prose, ⟦b:potior⟧, which usually has the ablative (⟦r1379:1379⟧): as, ⟦b:totīus Galliae sēsē potīrī posse spērant⟧, 1, 3, 8, ⟦i:they hope they can get the mastery over the whole of Gaul⟧. Especially with persons, or with the genitive plural ⟦b:rērum⟧: ⟦b:rērum potior⟧, ⟦i:get to be⟧, or often, ⟦i:am, master of the situation⟧, or ⟦i:I am monarch of all I survey⟧. Similarly in Tacitus ⟦b:apīscor⟧, ⟦b:adipīscor⟧: as, ⟦b:arma, quīs Servius Galba rērum adeptus est⟧, Ta. 3, 55, ⟦i:the war by which Galba became master of the throne⟧. In Plautus ⟦b:crēdō⟧ sometimes has the genitive of a thing and dative of a person.

title: Verbs of Fulness and Want
text:
⟦#1293⟧
The genitive is sometimes used with verbs of filling, abounding, and lacking, as it is with the corresponding adjectives (⟦r1263:1263⟧): as,
⟦b:convīvium vīcīnōrum cōtīdiē compleō⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 46, ⟦i:I fill out a dinner-party every day with neighbours⟧. ⟦b:haec rēs vītae mē, soror, saturant⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 18, ⟦i:these things, my sister, sicken me of life⟧. ⟦b:terra ferārum nunc etiam scatit⟧, Lucr. 5, 39, ⟦i:still teems the earth with ravin beasts⟧. So with ⟦b:egeō⟧ sometimes: as, ⟦b:egeō cōnsilī⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 7, 22, 2, ⟦i:I am in need of some advice⟧. And usually with ⟦b:indigeō⟧: as, ⟦b:hoc bellum indiget celeritātis⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 6, 7, ⟦i:this war requires rapid action⟧. But, from Livy on, the ablative is commoner with ⟦b:indigeō⟧: see ⟦r1305:1305⟧.
⟦#1294⟧
With verbs of separating and abstaining, the ablative is regularly used (⟦r1302:1302⟧). But the genitive is sometimes found in poetry: as, ⟦b:mē omnium labōrum levās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 247, ⟦i:thou riddest me of all my woes⟧. ⟦b:abstinētō īrārum calidaeque rixae⟧, H. 3, 27, 69, ⟦i:from bursts of rage keep thou and hot affray⟧.

title: The Genitive of Exclamation
text:
⟦#1295⟧
In poetry, the genitive with an adjective in agreement occurs two or three times in exclamation: as, ⟦b:foederis heu tacitī⟧, Prop. 5, 7, 21, ⟦i:alas, that secret covenant⟧. Usually the nominative (⟦r1117:1117⟧), or the accusative (⟦r1149:1149⟧).

title: The Ablative
text:
⟦#1296⟧
The ablative is used principally with verbs and their participles, or with adjectives, and consists of three cases that were originally distinct.
⟦#1297⟧
I. The Ablative proper denotes that from which something parts or proceeds (⟦r1302:1302⟧).
The ablative proper is often accompanied by the prepositions ⟦b:ab⟧, ⟦b:dē⟧, ⟦b:ex⟧, ⟦b:prae⟧, ⟦b:prō⟧, ⟦b:sine⟧, or ⟦b:tenus⟧.
⟦#1298⟧
With the ablative proper two other cases, originally distinct, a locative case and an instrumental case, were confounded, and merged under the common name of the ablative.
⟦#1299⟧
II. The Locative case denotes the place in, at, or on which action occurs. A few forms of the locative proper are still preserved (⟦r1331:1331⟧). But the place where is ordinarily denoted by the locative ablative (⟦r1342:1342⟧).
The locative ablative is often accompanied by the prepositions ⟦b:in⟧ or ⟦b:sub⟧.
⟦#1300⟧
III. The Instrumental case denotes that by which or with which a main person or thing is attended (⟦r1356:1356⟧).
The instrumental ablative is often accompanied by the prepositions ⟦b:cum⟧ or ⟦b:cōram⟧.
⟦#1301⟧
The ablative or locative is sometimes attached immediately to a substantive.
Thus, (⟦i:a.⟧) sometimes to a substantive which denotes or implies action: as, ⟦b:interitus ferrō⟧, ⟦i:destruction with the sword⟧, like ⟦b:intereō ferrō⟧; see ⟦r1307:1307⟧, ⟦r1331:1331⟧, 1342, 1376, 1377. (⟦i:b.⟧) In constructions in which the ablative is due to an older combination with a verb: as, ⟦b:vir singulārī virtūte⟧, ⟦i:a man of unexampled bravery⟧. See ⟦r1309:1309⟧ and ⟦r1375:1375⟧.

title: The Ablative of Separation and Want, and of Departure
text:
⟦#1302⟧
Verbs of separation take an ablative of the thing from which separation takes place: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:caruit forō posteā Pompēius, caruit senātū, caruit pūblicō⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 18, ⟦i:after that Pompey had to keep away from the market place, from the senate, from highways and byways⟧. ⟦b:adhūc Q. Ligārius omnī culpā vacat⟧, ⟦i:Lig.⟧ 4, ⟦i:thus far Ligarius proves devoid of any guilt⟧. ⟦b:egeō cōnsiliō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 15, 1, A, 5, ⟦i:I need advice⟧ (⟦r1305:1305⟧). (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:Ītaliā prohibētur: nōn tū eum patriā prīvāre, quā caret, sed vītā vīs⟧, ⟦i:Lig.⟧ 11, ⟦i:he is kept out of Italy; you want to deprive him not of his country, from which he is debarred, but of life⟧. ⟦b:līberēmus cūrā populum Rōmānum⟧, L. 39, 51, 9, Hannibal’s words when he took poison, 183 B.C., ⟦i:let me relieve Rome of anxiety⟧.
⟦#1303⟧
This ablative is used (⟦i:a.⟧) with such verbs as mean ⟦i:abstain⟧, ⟦b:abstineō⟧, ⟦b:dēsistō⟧, ⟦b:supersedeō⟧; ⟦i:am devoid of⟧, ⟦b:careō⟧, ⟦b:vacō⟧; ⟦i:need⟧, ⟦b:egeō⟧; and in addition to the accusative of the object, (⟦i:b.⟧) with verbs used transitively, such as mean ⟦i:keep off⟧, ⟦b:arceō⟧, ⟦b:exclūdō⟧ and ⟦b:interclūdō⟧, ⟦b:prohibeō⟧; ⟦i:drive away⟧, ⟦i:remove⟧, ⟦b:pellō⟧, ⟦b:moveō⟧, and their compounds; ⟦i:free⟧, ⟦b:expediō⟧, ⟦b:līberō⟧, ⟦b:levō⟧, ⟦b:solvō⟧ and ⟦b:exsolvō⟧; ⟦i:deprive⟧, ⟦b:orbō⟧, ⟦b:prīvō⟧, ⟦b:spoliō⟧, ⟦b:nūdō⟧, ⟦b:fraudō⟧.
⟦#1304⟧
A preposition, ⟦b:ab⟧ or ⟦b:ex⟧, is often used with these verbs, and regularly when the ablative denotes a person. But ⟦b:careō⟧ and ⟦b:egeō⟧, and ⟦b:exsolvō⟧ and ⟦b:levō⟧, never have a preposition.
⟦#1305⟧
With ⟦b:egeō⟧, the genitive is sometimes used, and often with ⟦b:indigeō⟧: see ⟦r1293:1293⟧. Also in poetry, with verbs of abstaining and separating: see ⟦r1294:1294⟧.
⟦#1306⟧
The ablative of separation is sometimes used with such adjectives as ⟦b:aliēnus⟧, ⟦b:expers⟧, ⟦b:līber⟧, ⟦b:nūdus⟧, ⟦b:vacuus⟧, &c.: as, ⟦b:negant id esse aliēnum maiestāte deōrum⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 105, ⟦i:they maintain that this is not at variance with the greatness of the gods⟧. ⟦b:vacuī cūrīs⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 46, ⟦i:devoid of cares⟧. ⟦b:arce et urbe orba sum⟧, E. ⟦i:Tr.⟧ 114, ⟦i:of tower and town bereft am I⟧. But sometimes the genitive: see ⟦r1263:1263⟧ and ⟦r1264:1264⟧; sometimes also prepositional constructions: for these, and particularly for the different constructions of ⟦b:aliēnus⟧, see the dictionary.

title: Town and Island Names
text:
⟦#1307⟧
(1.) Proper names of towns and of little islands are put in the ablative with verbs of motion, to denote the place from which motion proceeds: as,
⟦b:Dāmarātus fūgit Tarquiniōs Corinthō⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 109, ⟦i:Damaratus ran away from Corinth to Tarquinii⟧. ⟦b:sīgnum Carthāgine captum⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 82, ⟦i:the statue carried off from Carthage⟧. ⟦b:Megaribus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 137, ⟦i:from Megara⟧. ⟦b:Lēmnō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tru.⟧ 90, ⟦i:from Lemnos⟧. ⟦b:Rōmā accēperam litterās⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 5, 8, 2, ⟦i:I had got a letter from Rome⟧. Rarely with a substantive of motion (⟦r1301:1301⟧): as, ⟦b:dē illīus Alexandrēā discessū⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 11, 18, 1, ⟦i:about his departure from Alexandrea⟧. Also in dating letters: as, ⟦b:V kal. Sextīl., Rēgiō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 7, 19, ⟦i:Regium, 28 July⟧; less often the locative: as, ⟦b:Īdibus Iūniīs, Thessalonīcae⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 1, 3, 10, ⟦i:Thessalonica, 13 June⟧. Like a town name: ⟦b:Ācherunte⟧, poet. in ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 37, ⟦i:from Acheron⟧. With an attribute: ⟦b:ipsā Samō⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 51, ⟦i:from Samos itself⟧. ⟦b:Teānō Sidicīnō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 8, 11, B, 2, ⟦i:from Sidicinian Teanum⟧.
⟦#1308⟧
Singular town or island names sometimes have ⟦b:ex⟧ in old Latin: thus, ⟦b:Carystō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 730, ⟦i:from Carystus⟧, or, ⟦b:ex Carystō⟧, ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 737, indifferently. ⟦b:ex Andrō⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 70, ⟦i:from Andros⟧. In classical Latin, town names rarely have ⟦b:ab⟧: as, ⟦b:ab Athēnīs proficīscī⟧, Serv. in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 4, 12, 2, ⟦i:to start from Athens⟧; chiefly of neighbourhood: as, ⟦b:ab Gergoviā⟧, 7, 43, 5: 7, 59, 1, ⟦i:from camp at Gergovia⟧; or direction: as, ⟦b:ā Salōnīs ad Ōricum⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 8, 4, ⟦i:from Salonae to Oricum⟧; regularly with ⟦b:longē⟧: as, ⟦b:longē ā Syrācūsīs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 107, ⟦i:far from Syracuse⟧.
⟦#1309⟧
The ablative of a town or country name is rarely attached immediately to a substantive, to denote origin: as, ⟦b:Periphanēs Rhodō mercātor dīves⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 499, ⟦i:Periphanes from Rhodes a chapman rich⟧. ⟦b:videō ibī̆ hospitem Zacynthō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Mer.⟧ 940, ⟦i:I see the friend there from Zacynthus⟧. Rarely in Cicero: as, ⟦b:Teānō Āpulō laudātōrēs⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 197, ⟦i:eulogists from Apulian Teanum⟧; in Caesar twice.
