In Livy with ⟦b:ab⟧ only: as, ⟦b:Turnus ab Arīciā⟧, L. 1, 50, 3, ⟦i:Turnus from Aricia⟧. But the Roman tribe one belongs to, is regularly in the ablative: as, ⟦b:Q. Verrem Rōmiliā,⟧ sc. ⟦b:tribū⟧, ⟦i:V. a. pr.⟧ 1, 23, ⟦i:Verres of the tribe Romilia⟧.
⟦#1310⟧
With a verb, country names regularly have a preposition, and always in Cicero, Sallust, and Livy: as, ⟦b:ē Ciliciā dēcēdēns⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 1, ⟦i:going away from Cilicia⟧. The ablative alone is rare: as, ⟦b:Aegyptō adveniō domum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 440, ⟦i:from Egypt I come home⟧. Chiefly in Tacitus: as, ⟦b:Aegyptō remeāns⟧, 2, 69, ⟦i:coming back from Egypt⟧. In Caesar, by attraction: ⟦b:cōgēbantur Corcȳrā atque Acarnāniā pābulum supportāre⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 58, 4, ⟦i:they were forced to fetch fodder from Corcyra and even Acarnania⟧.
⟦#1311⟧
(2.) The ablatives ⟦b:domō⟧ and ⟦b:rūre⟧, and in poetry ⟦b:humō⟧, are used like proper names of towns: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:domō excesserant⟧, 4, 14, 5, ⟦i:they had gone away from home⟧. Also metaphorically: as, ⟦b:domō doctus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Mer.⟧ 355, ⟦i:by home-experience taught⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:rūre rediīt uxor mea⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Mer.⟧ 705, ⟦i:my wife’s come back from out of town⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:humō⟧, in Vergil first: as, ⟦b:vix oculōs attollit humō⟧, O. 2, 448, ⟦i:scarce from the ground her eyes she lifts⟧.

title: The Ablative of Source, Stuff, or Material
text:
⟦#1312⟧
The verb ⟦b:nāscor⟧ and participles of origin take an ablative to denote parentage or rank in life.
Such participles are: ⟦b:nātus⟧, ⟦b:prōgnātus⟧, and ⟦b:ortus⟧; in poetry and late prose, also ⟦b:crētus⟧, ⟦b:ēditus⟧, ⟦b:generātus⟧, ⟦b:genitus⟧, ⟦b:satus⟧, and ⟦b:oriundus⟧: as, (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:Rōmulus deō prōgnātus⟧, L. 1, 40, 3, ⟦i:Romulus, sprung from a god⟧. ⟦b:dīs genite⟧, V. 9, 642, ⟦i:thou sired of gods⟧. Of a parent, ⟦b:ex⟧ is sometimes used: as ⟦b:ex mē hic nātus nōn est⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 40, ⟦i:he’s not my son⟧; and of remoter ancestors, ⟦b:ab⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:locō nātus honestō⟧, 5, 45, 2, ⟦i:respectably descended⟧. ⟦b:summō locō nātus⟧, 5, 25, 1, ⟦i:of high birth⟧, ⟦b:familiā antīquissimā nātum⟧, 7, 32, 4, ⟦i:a member of an old family⟧. Rarely with ⟦b:dē⟧: as, ⟦b:quō dē genere gnātust Philocratēs?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 277, ⟦i:what is the parentage of Philocrates?⟧
⟦#1313⟧
The ablative with an attribute, attached to a substantive, sometimes denotes stuff or material: as, ⟦b:aere cavō clipeum⟧, V. 3, 286, ⟦i:a targe of hallow bronze⟧. ⟦b:perennī fronde corōnam⟧, Lucr. 1, 118, ⟦i:a crown of amaranthine leaf⟧. ⟦b:solidōque adamante columnae⟧, V. 6, 552, ⟦i:and pillars of the solid adamant⟧. This construction borders closely on the ablative of quality (⟦r1375:1375⟧). Rarely without an attribute: as, ⟦b:pīctās abiete puppīs⟧, V. 5, 663, ⟦i:painted sterns of fir⟧.
⟦#1314⟧
A substantive denoting stuff or material is generally put in the ablative with ⟦b:dē⟧ or ⟦b:ex⟧; thus,
(⟦i:a.⟧) Directly with a substantive: ⟦b:pōcula ex aurō⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 62, ⟦i:cups of gold⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) Oftener with an auxiliary verb or participle: ⟦b:sīgnum erat hoc Cupīdinis ē marmore⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 5, ⟦i:this statue of Cupid was made of marble⟧. ⟦b:scūtīs ex cortice factīs⟧, 2, 33, 2, ⟦i:with long shields made out of bark⟧. ⟦b:ex ūnā gemmā pergrandī trūlla excavāta⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 62, ⟦i:a ladle scooped out of a single enormous semi-precious stone⟧.
⟦#1315⟧
The ablative with forms of ⟦b:faciō⟧ and ⟦b:sum⟧ denotes that with which or to which something is done: as, ⟦b:quid hōc homine faciās?⟧ ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 29, ⟦i:what can you do with such a fellow?⟧ ⟦b:quid mē fīet?⟧ T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 709, ⟦i:what will become of me?⟧ But often the dative (⟦r1205:1205⟧): as, ⟦b:quid tibī̆ faciam?⟧ ⟦i:Att.⟧ 7, 3, 2, ⟦i:what shall I do to you?⟧ Or the ablative with ⟦b:dē⟧: as, ⟦b:dē frātre quid fīet?⟧ T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 996, ⟦i:as to my brother, what will come to pass?⟧

title: The Ablative of Cause, Influence, or Motive
text:
⟦#1316⟧
The ablative is used to denote cause, influence, or motive: as,
⟦b:madeō metū⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 395, ⟦i:I’m drenched with dread⟧. ⟦b:tū imprūdentiā lāberis⟧, ⟦i:Mur.⟧ 78, ⟦i:you, sir, slip from inadvertence⟧. ⟦b:maerōre et lacrimīs cōnsenēscēbat⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 13, ⟦i:she just pined away in sorrow and tears⟧. ⟦b:īrā incendor⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 201, ⟦i:I’m getting hot with wrath⟧. ⟦b:premor lūctū⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 3, 22, 3, ⟦i:I am bowed down with grief⟧. ⟦b:quod ego nōn superbiā faciēbam⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 99, ⟦i:I did not act thus from superciliousness, not I⟧. ⟦b:nōn movētur pecūniā⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 18, ⟦i:he is not moved by money⟧. ⟦b:boat caelum fremitū virūm⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 232, ⟦i:the welkin rings with roar of men⟧. ⟦b:dēlictō dolēre, corrēctiōne gaudēre⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 90, ⟦i:be pained by the sin, take pleasure in the reproof⟧. ⟦b:aetāte nōn quīs optuērier⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 840, ⟦i:owing to age thou canst not see⟧. ⟦b:Iovis iussū veniō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am. prol.⟧ 19, ⟦i:at Jove’s behest I come⟧. ⟦b:Sēiānus nimiā fortūnā sōcors⟧, Ta. 4, 39, ⟦i:Sejanus giddy with over-prosperity⟧. ⟦b:ferōx praedā glōriāque exercitus⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 1, 51, ⟦i:the army flushed with booty and glory⟧. ⟦b:exercitūs nostrī interitus ferrō⟧, ⟦i:Pis.⟧ 40, ⟦i:the annihilation of our army by the sword⟧ (⟦r1301:1301⟧).
⟦#1317⟧
Instead of the ablative, other constructions often occur, especially with verbs used transitively; such are:
(⟦i:a.⟧) Prepositional phrases with ⟦b:dē⟧ or ⟦b:ex⟧, in Varro and Livy with ⟦b:ab⟧; also with ⟦b:ob⟧, ⟦b:per⟧, or ⟦b:propter⟧: as, ⟦b:multī in oppidum propter timōrem sēsē recipiunt⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 35, 6, ⟦i:a good many retreated to the town from fear⟧. Sometimes with ⟦b:prae⟧: as, ⟦b:prae amōre exclūstī hunc forās⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 98, ⟦i:it was for love you turned him out of doors⟧: in classical Latin, usually of hindrance: as, ⟦b:sōlem prae iaculōrum multitūdine nōn vidēbitis⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 101, ⟦i:you won’t see the sun for the cloud of javelins⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) Circumlocutions with ⟦b:causā⟧, less frequently with ⟦b:grātiā⟧ (⟦r1257:1257⟧). (⟦i:c.⟧) Ablatives absolute, or participles, particularly auxiliary participles with an ablative to express cause, oftener motive, such as ⟦b:captus⟧, ⟦b:ductus⟧, ⟦b:excitātus⟧ or ⟦b:incitātus⟧, ⟦b:impulsus⟧, ⟦b:incēnsus⟧, ⟦b:īnflammātus⟧, ⟦b:mōtus⟧, ⟦b:perterritus⟧: as, ⟦b:nōnnūllī pudōre adductī remanēbant⟧, 1, 39, 3, ⟦i:some stuck by from shame⟧.
⟦#1318⟧
The person by whom the action of a passive verb is done, is denoted by the ablative with ⟦b:ab⟧ or ⟦b:ā⟧. Also occasionally with verbs equivalent to a passive, such as ⟦b:cadō⟧, ⟦b:intereō⟧, ⟦b:pereō⟧, ⟦b:vēneō⟧, &c., &c. Things or animals are sometimes represented as persons by the use of ⟦b:ab⟧: as, ⟦b:animus bene īnfōrmātus ā nātūrā⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 13, ⟦i:a soul meetly fashioned by dame nature⟧. See ⟦r1476:1476⟧-1478.
⟦#1319⟧
In poetry, an ablative denoting a person, with an adjective in agreement, is sometimes equivalent to an expression with an abstract substantive: as, ⟦b:et adsiduō ruptae lēctōre columnae⟧, J. 1, 13, ⟦i:and pillars by persistent reader riven⟧, i.e. ⟦b:adsiduitāte lēctōris⟧, or ⟦b:adsiduā lēctiōne⟧. ⟦b:cūrātus inaequālī tōnsōre capillōs⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 1, 94, ⟦i:my locks by unsymmetric barber trimmed⟧.

title: The Ablative of Comparison
text:
⟦#1320⟧
(1.) The ablative may be used with a comparative adjective, when the first of two things compared is in the nominative, or is a subject-accusative.
Such an ablative is translated by ⟦i:than⟧: as, (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:lūce sunt clāriōra nōbīs tua cōnsilia⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 6, ⟦i:your schemes are plainer to us than day⟧. ⟦b:ō mātre pulchrā fīlia pulchrior⟧, H. 1, 16, 1, ⟦i:O daughter fairer than a mother fair⟧. Particularly in sentences of negative import: as, ⟦b:quis Karthāginiēnsium plūris fuit Hannibale?⟧ ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 142, ⟦i:of all the sons of Carthage, who was rated higher than Hannibal?⟧ ⟦b:nec mihī̆ est tē iūcundius quicquam nec cārius⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 10, 1, ⟦i:and there is nothing in the world nearer and dearer to me than you⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:illud cōgnōscēs profectō, mihī̆ tē neque cāriōrem neque iūcundiōrem esse quemquam⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 3, 2, ⟦i:one thing I am sure you will see, that there is nobody nearer and dearer to me than you⟧.
⟦#1321⟧
(2.) The ablative of comparison is similarly used when the first member of comparison is an accusative of the object: as,
⟦b:exēgī monumentum aere perennius⟧, H. 3, 30, 1, ⟦i:I have builded up a monument more durable than bronze⟧. Particularly so in sentences of negative import: as, ⟦b:hōc mihī̆ grātius facere nihil potes⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 13, 44, ⟦i:you can do nothing for me more welcome than this⟧. Also with predicate adjectives dependent on a verb of thinking (⟦r1167:1167⟧): as, ⟦b:Hērodotum cūr vērāciōrem dūcam Enniō?⟧ ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 116, ⟦i:why should I count Herodotus any more truthful than Ennius?⟧ Regularly when the second member of comparison is a relative: as, ⟦b:quā pecude nihil genuit nātūra fēcundius⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 160, ⟦i:nature has created nothing more prolific than this animal⟧, i.e. the sow.
⟦#1322⟧
(3.) In poetry, the ablative of comparison may be used with the first member of comparison in any case: as, ⟦b:Lūcīlī rītū, nostrūm meliōris utrōque⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 1, 29, ⟦i:after Lucilius’s way, a better man than thou or I⟧.
⟦#1323⟧
(4.) In sentences of negative import, the ablative is sometimes used with ⟦b:alter⟧ and ⟦b:alius⟧, as with a comparative: as, ⟦b:neque mēst alter quisquam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 492, ⟦i:and there’s no other man than I⟧. ⟦b:nec quicquam aliud lībertāte commūnī quaesīsse⟧, Brut. and Cass. in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 11, 2, 2, ⟦i:and to have aimed at nothing else than freedom for all⟧. But in prose, ⟦b:quam⟧ is commonly used.
⟦#1324⟧
(1.) The second member of comparison is often introduced by ⟦b:quam⟧, ⟦i:than⟧, or in poetry by ⟦b:atque⟧ or ⟦b:ac⟧. This member, whatever the case of the first member, is sometimes made the subject of a form of ⟦b:sum⟧ in a new sentence: as,
⟦b:meliōrem quam ego sum suppōnō tibī̆⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cur.⟧ 256, ⟦i:I give you as a substitute a better than I am myself⟧. ⟦b:verba M. Varrōnis, hominis quam fuit Claudius doctiōris⟧, Gell. 10, 1, 4, ⟦i:the words of Varro, a better scholar than Claudius ever was⟧. ⟦b:ut tibī̆ maiōrī quam Āfricanus fuit, mē adiūnctum esse patiāre⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 5, 7, 3, ⟦i:so that you will allow me to be associated with you, a bigger man than Africanus ever was⟧.
⟦#1325⟧
(2.) When the first member is in the nominative or accusative, ⟦b:quam⟧ is commonly a mere coordinating word, with both members in the same case: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:plūris est oculātus testis ūnus quam aurītī decem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tru.⟧ 490, ⟦i:a single witness with an eye rates higher than a dozen with the ear⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:tū velim exīstimēs nēminem cuiquam neque cāriōrem neque iūcundiōrem umquam fuisse quam tē mihī̆⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 1, 9, 24, ⟦i:I hope you will be convinced that nobody was ever nearer and dearer to anybody than you to me⟧.
⟦#1326⟧
An introductory ablative of a demonstrative or relative pronoun sometimes precedes the construction with ⟦b:quam⟧: as, ⟦b:quid hōc est clārius, quam omnīs Segestae mātrōnās et virginēs convēnisse?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 77, ⟦i:what fact is there better known than this, to wit, that all the women in Segesta, married and single, came streaming together?⟧
⟦#1327⟧
The ablative is sometimes used with comparative adverbs also.
So particularly in sentences of negative import: as, ⟦b:nihil lacrimā citius ārēscit⟧, Corn. 2, 50, ⟦i:nothing dries up quicker than a tear⟧. Less frequently in positive sentences in prose: as, ⟦b:fortūna, quae plūs cōnsilīs hūmānīs pollet, contrāxit certāmen⟧, L. 44, 40, 3, ⟦i:fortune, who is mightier than the devices of man, precipitated the engagement⟧. Very commonly, however, ⟦b:quam⟧ is used with comparative adverbs.
⟦#1328⟧
Designations of number or extent are often qualified by ⟦b:amplius⟧, ⟦b:longius⟧, or ⟦b:plūs⟧, ⟦i:over⟧, or by ⟦b:minus⟧, ⟦i:under⟧.
The word thus qualified is put in the case which the context would require without any such qualification: as, ⟦b:plūs septingentī captī⟧, L. 41, 12, 8, ⟦i:over seven hundred were taken prisoners⟧. ⟦b:tēcum plūs annum vīxit⟧, ⟦i:Q.⟧ 41, ⟦i:he lived with you over a year⟧ (⟦r1151:1151⟧). ⟦b:cum equīs plūs quīngentīs⟧, L. 40, 32, 6, ⟦i:with over five hundred horses⟧. Less frequently with ⟦b:quam⟧. When these words are felt as real substantives in the nominative or accusative, the ablative of comparison may be used (⟦r1320:1320⟧): as, ⟦b:plūs trīduō⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 74, ⟦i:more than three days⟧.
⟦#1329⟧
In expressions of age with ⟦b:nātus⟧, the adjectives ⟦b:maior⟧ and ⟦b:minor⟧ are used as well as ⟦b:amplius⟧ and ⟦b:minus⟧, and with the same construction (⟦r1328:1328⟧): as, ⟦b:annōs nātus maior quadrāgintā⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 39, ⟦i:over forty years old⟧. For other constructions, see the dictionary. Similarly ⟦b:conlēctus aquae digitum nōn altior ūnum⟧, Lucr. 4, 414, ⟦i:a pool no deeper than a finger’s breadth⟧ (⟦r1130:1130⟧). But commonly with comparative adjectives of extent, ⟦b:quam⟧ is used, or the ablative (⟦r1320:1320⟧): as, ⟦b:palūs nōn lātior pedibus quīnquāgintā⟧, 7, 19, 1, ⟦i:a marsh not wider than fifty feet⟧.
⟦#1330⟧
With a comparative adjective or adverb, the ablatives ⟦b:opīniōne⟧, ⟦b:exspectātiōne⟧, and ⟦b:spē⟧, and some others, chiefly in poetry, take the place of a sentence with ⟦b:quam⟧: as,
⟦b:opīniōne melius⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cas.⟧ 338, ⟦i:better than you thought⟧. ⟦b:minōra opīniōne⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 31, 5, ⟦i:more insignificant than is thought⟧. ⟦b:lātius opīniōne dissēminātum est hoc malum⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 6, ⟦i:this infection is more sweeping than anybody dreams⟧. ⟦b:spē omnium sērius⟧, L. 2, 3, 1, ⟦i:later than was generally expected⟧.

title: The Locative Proper
text:
⟦#1331⟧
(1.) Singular proper names of towns and of little islands are put in the locative to denote the place in or at which action occurs: as,
⟦b:quid Rōmae faciam? mentīrī nescio⟧, J. 3, 41, ⟦i:what can I do in Rome? I don’t know how to lie⟧. ⟦b:Corinthī et Karthāginī⟧, ⟦i:Agr.⟧ 2, 90, ⟦i:at Corinth and at Carthage⟧. ⟦b:Lacedaemonī⟧, N. ⟦i:praef.⟧ 4, ⟦i:in Lacedaemon⟧. ⟦b:Tīburī⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 16, 3, 1, ⟦i:at Tibur⟧. ⟦b:Rhodī⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 4, 7, 4, ⟦i:at Rhodes⟧. ⟦b:mānsiōnēs diutinae Lēmnī⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 1012, ⟦i:protracted stays at Lemnos⟧ (⟦r1301:1301⟧). Sometimes in dates: as, ⟦b:data Thessalonīcae⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 3, 20, 3, ⟦i:given at Thessalonica⟧ (⟦r1307:1307⟧). The locative rarely means ⟦i:near⟧: as, ⟦b:Antiī⟧, L. 22, 1, 10, ⟦i:round about Antium⟧. In Plautus only two singular town names with consonant stems occur, and these regularly in the locative, ⟦b:Carthāginī⟧ and ⟦b:Sicyōnī⟧, three times each; once in a doubtful example, ⟦b:Sicyōne⟧, ⟦i:Cist.⟧ 128. Terence has no examples of these stems. From Cicero on, the locative ablative is commoner with them (⟦r1343:1343⟧).
⟦#1332⟧
With an adjective attribute also, the locative is used: as, ⟦b:Teānī Āpulī⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 27, ⟦i:at the Apulian Teanum⟧. ⟦b:Suessae Auruncae⟧, L. 32, 9, 3, ⟦i:at the Auruncan Suessa⟧. The appellative ⟦b:forum⟧, ⟦i:market place⟧, used, with an attribute, as a proper name, is sometimes put in the accusative with ⟦b:ad⟧: as, ⟦b:Claternae, ad Forum Cornēlium⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 12, 5, 2, ⟦i:at Claterna and at Forum Cornelium⟧; sometimes in the locative ablative: ⟦b:Forō Iūlī⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 5, 19, 7.
⟦#1333⟧
When the locative is further explained by an appellative following, the appellative is put in the locative ablative, either alone, or with ⟦b:in⟧: as, ⟦b:Antiochīae, celebrī quondam urbe⟧, ⟦i:Arch.⟧ 4, ⟦i:at Antioch, once a bustling town⟧. ⟦b:Neāpolī, in celeberrimō oppidō⟧, ⟦i:RabP.⟧ 26, ⟦i:at Neapolis, a town swarming with people⟧. An appellative in the ablative with ⟦b:in⟧ may be further defined by a proper name in the locative: as, ⟦b:duābus in īnsulīs, Melitae et Samī⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 184, ⟦i:in two islands—at Melita and Samos⟧. ⟦b:in oppidō, Antiochīae⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 5, 18, 1, ⟦i:within town walls—at Antioch⟧. ⟦b:in sēcessū, Apollōniae⟧, Suet. ⟦i:Aug.⟧ 94, ⟦i:out of town—at Apollonia⟧. Or in the ablative: as, ⟦b:in oppidō Citiō⟧, N. 5, 3, 4, ⟦i:in the town of Citium⟧. ⟦b:in urbe Rōmā⟧, L. 39, 14, 7, ⟦i:in the city of Rome⟧.
⟦#1334⟧
In Plautus, singular town names with stems in ⟦b:-ā-⟧ or ⟦b:-o-⟧ are put in the locative ten or twelve times, in the ablative with ⟦b:in⟧ some fifteen times. Three such have only ⟦b:in⟧, never the locative: ⟦b:in Anactoriō⟧, ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 896, ⟦b:in Seleuciā⟧, ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 901, ⟦b:in Spartā⟧, ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 663; furthermore, ⟦b:in Epidamnō⟧, ⟦i:Men.⟧ 267, 380 twice, ⟦b:in Ephesō⟧, ⟦i:B.⟧ 309, ⟦i:MG.⟧ 441, 778, and ⟦b:in Epidaurō⟧, ⟦i:Cur.⟧ 341, 429, ⟦i:E.⟧ 540, 541, 554, but also ⟦b:Epidamnī⟧, ⟦i:Men. prol.⟧ 51, ⟦b:Ephesī⟧, ⟦i:B.⟧ 336, 1047, ⟦i:MG.⟧ 648, and ⟦b:Epidaurī⟧, ⟦i:E.⟧ 636. Terence, who has only ⟦b:-o-⟧ stems, uses the locative six times, the ablative with ⟦b:in⟧ four times: only with ⟦b:in⟧: ⟦b:in Andrō⟧, ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 931, ⟦b:in Imbrō⟧, ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 171. Furthermore ⟦b:in Lēmnō⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 873, 1004 but also ⟦b:Lēmnī⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 680, 942, 1013. Also ⟦b:Mīlētī⟧, ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 654, ⟦b:Rhodī⟧, ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 107, ⟦b:Sūniī⟧, ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 519.
⟦#1335⟧
A town name is sometimes put in the ablative with ⟦b:in⟧ by assimilation with a parallel ⟦b:in⟧: as, ⟦b:in Illyricō, in ipsā Alexandrēā⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 11, 16, 1, ⟦i:in Illyricum, and at Alexandrea itself⟧. ⟦b:Antiochum in Syriā, Ptolemaeum in Alexandrīā esse⟧, L. 42, 26, 7. ⟦i:that Antiochus was in Syria, Ptolemy at Alexandria⟧. ⟦b:in mōnte Albānō Lāvīniōque⟧, L. 5, 52, 8, ⟦i:on the Alban mount and at Lavinium⟧. Also without assimilation: as, ⟦b:nāvis et in Caiētā est parāta nōbīs et Brundusiī⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 8, 3, 6, ⟦i:we have a vessel all chartered, one in Cajeta and one at Brundusium⟧. ⟦b:in Hispalī⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 18, 1, ⟦i:in Hispalis⟧.
⟦#1336⟧
With country names, the locative is very exceptional: as, ⟦b:Chersonēsī⟧, N. 1, 2, 4, ⟦i:at the Peninsula⟧. ⟦b:Aegyptī⟧, Val. M. 4, 1, 15, ⟦i:in Egypt⟧. Similarly ⟦b:Accheruntī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 689, 998, ⟦i:Mer.⟧ 606, ⟦i:Tru.⟧ 749, ⟦i:in Acheron⟧; ⟦b:Accherunte⟧ however once: ⟦b:Accheruntest⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 431. In Sallust, ⟦b:Rōmae Numidiaeque⟧, ⟦i:I.⟧ 33, 4, with assimilation of ⟦b:Numidiae⟧ to ⟦b:Rōmae⟧.
⟦#1337⟧
(2.) The locatives ⟦b:domī⟧, ⟦b:rūrī⟧, ⟦b:humī⟧, and rarely ⟦b:orbī⟧, are used like proper names of towns: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:cēnābō domī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 482, ⟦i:I shall dine at home⟧. Metaphorically, ⟦b:domī est⟧, ⟦b:nāscitur⟧, or ⟦b:habeō⟧, ⟦i:I can get at home⟧, ⟦i:I need not go abroad for⟧, or ⟦i:I have in plenty⟧: as, ⟦b:id quidem domī est⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 10, 14, 2, ⟦i:as for that, I have it myself⟧. With a possessive pronoun or ⟦b:aliēnus⟧ in agreement, either the locative is used, or the ablative with ⟦b:in⟧; for ⟦b:domuī⟧, as, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 99, see ⟦r594:594⟧; with other adjectives the ablative with ⟦b:in⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:rūrī⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 363, ⟦i:up in the country⟧; for ⟦b:rūre⟧, see ⟦r1344:1344⟧ and ⟦r1345:1345⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:humī⟧, ⟦i:on the ground⟧, or ⟦i:to the ground⟧, in Terence first: as, ⟦b:hunc ante nostram iānuam appōne :: obsecrō, humīne?⟧ T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 724, ⟦i:set down this baby at our door :: good gracious; on the ground?⟧ ⟦b:iacēre humī⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 26, ⟦i:sleeping on bare ground⟧. (⟦i:d.⟧) ⟦b:orbī⟧ with ⟦b:terrae⟧ or ⟦b:terrārum⟧: as, ⟦b:amplissimum orbī terrārum monumentum⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 82, ⟦i:the grandest monument in the wide wide world⟧.
⟦#1338⟧
The locatives ⟦b:bellī⟧, older ⟦b:du͡ellī⟧, and ⟦b:mīlitiae⟧ are sometimes used in contrast with ⟦b:domī⟧: as, ⟦b:domī du͡ellīque⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap. prol.⟧ 68, ⟦b:domī bellīque⟧, L. 2, 50, 11, ⟦b:domī mīlitiaeque⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 55, ⟦b:mīlitiae et domī⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 495, ⟦i:at home and in the field⟧. Rarely without ⟦b:domī⟧: as, ⟦b:bellī⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 2, 56, ⟦b:mīlitiae⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 84, 2.
⟦#1339⟧
(3.) Other appellatives rarely have the locative: as, ⟦b:proxumae vīcīniae⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 205, ⟦i:MG.⟧ 273, ⟦i:in the next neighbourhood⟧. ⟦b:terrae⟧, L. 5, 51, 9, ⟦i:in the earth⟧. With verbs of suspense, doubt, and distress, and with many adjectives, ⟦b:animī⟧, ⟦i:in soul⟧, is not infrequent; and ⟦b:animī⟧ being mistaken for a genitive, ⟦b:mentis⟧ is also used: as, ⟦b:dēsipiēbam mentis⟧, Pl. ⟦i:E.⟧ 138, ⟦i:I was beside myself⟧. Oftener ⟦b:animō⟧ (⟦r1344:1344⟧).
⟦#1340⟧
Many original locatives have become set as adverbs: as, ⟦b:peregrī⟧, ⟦i:abroad⟧. Particularly of pronouns: as, ⟦b:illī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 249, ⟦i:off there⟧, oftener ⟦b:illīc⟧; ⟦b:istī⟧ or ⟦b:istīc⟧, ⟦b:hīc⟧; sometimes further defined by an added expression: as, ⟦b:hīc vīcīniae⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 95, ⟦i:here in the neighbourhood⟧. ⟦b:hīc proxumae vīcīniae⟧, ⟦i:MG.⟧ 273, ⟦i:here in the house next door⟧. ⟦b:hīc in Veneris fānō me͡a͡e vīcīniae⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 613, ⟦i:here, in the shrine of Venus, in my neighbourhood⟧. ⟦b:hīc Rōmae⟧, ⟦i:Arch.⟧ 5, ⟦i:here in Rome⟧.
⟦#1341⟧
The locative proper sometimes denotes time when: as, ⟦b:lūcī⟧, ⟦i:by light⟧, ⟦b:temperī⟧, ⟦i:betimes⟧, ⟦b:herī⟧ or ⟦b:here⟧, ⟦i:yesterday⟧, ⟦b:vesperī⟧, ⟦i:at evening⟧, ⟦b:herī vesperī⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 13, ⟦i:last evening⟧. In Plautus, ⟦b:diē septimī⟧, ⟦i:Men.⟧ 1156, ⟦i:Per.⟧ 260, ⟦i:on the seventh day⟧, ⟦b:māne sānē septimī⟧, ⟦i:Men.⟧ 1157, ⟦i:bright and early on the seventh⟧, ⟦b:diē crāstinī⟧, ⟦i:Most.⟧ 881, ⟦i:tomorrow⟧. Often with an adjective juxtaposed: as, ⟦b:postrīdiē⟧, ⟦i:the day after⟧, ⟦b:postrīdiē māne⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 11, 6, 1, ⟦i:early next day⟧, ⟦b:cōtīdiē⟧, ⟦i:each day⟧, ⟦i:daily⟧, ⟦b:prīdiē⟧, ⟦i:the day before⟧.

title: Place in, on, or at which
text:
⟦#1342⟧
(1.) Plural proper names of towns and of little islands are put in the locative ablative to denote the place in or at which action occurs: as,
⟦b:mortuus Cūmīs⟧, L. 2, 21, 5, ⟦i:he died at Cumae⟧. ⟦b:Athēnīs tenue caelum, crassum Thēbīs⟧, ⟦i:Fat.⟧ 7, ⟦i:in Athens the air is thin, at Thebes it is thick⟧. ⟦b:locus ostenditur Capreīs⟧, Suet. ⟦i:Tib.⟧ 62, ⟦i:the place is pointed out at Capreae⟧. Rarely with substantives of action (⟦r1301:1301⟧): as, ⟦b:mānsiō Formiīs⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 9, 5, 1, ⟦i:the stay at Formiae⟧. With an attribute: ⟦b:Athēnīs tuīs⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 16, 6, 2, ⟦i:in your darling Athens⟧. ⟦b:Curibus Sabīnīs⟧, L. 1, 18, 1, ⟦i:at the Sabine Cures⟧.
⟦#1343⟧
(2.) Singular proper names of towns with consonant stems are oftener put in the locative ablative than in the locative proper: as,
⟦b:adulēscentium gregēs Lacedaemone vīdimus⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 77, ⟦i:we have seen the companies of young men in Lacedaemon⟧. ⟦b:Karthāgine⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 16, 4, 2, ⟦i:at Carthage⟧. ⟦b:Tībure⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 8, 12, ⟦i:at Tibur⟧. ⟦b:Nārbōne⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 76, ⟦i:at Narbo⟧. See ⟦r1331:1331⟧. So also ⟦b:Acherunte⟧, Lucr. 3, 984, ⟦i:in Acheron⟧. ⟦b:Calydōne et Naupāctō⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 35, 1, ⟦i:at Calydon and Naupactus⟧, with ⟦b:Naupāctō⟧ attracted by ⟦b:Calydōne⟧. With an attribute: ⟦b:Carthāgine Novā⟧, L. 28, 17, 11, ⟦i:at New Carthage⟧. ⟦b:Acherunte profundō⟧, Lucr. 3, 978, ⟦i:in vasty Acheron⟧.
⟦#1344⟧
(3.) A few general appellatives are used in the locative ablative without an attribute, especially in set expressions, to denote the place where: as,
⟦b:terrā marīque⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 48, ⟦i:by land and sea⟧; less commonly ⟦b:marī atque terrā⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 53, 2, ⟦i:by sea and land⟧. ⟦b:dextrā Pīraeus, sinistrā Corinthus⟧, Cael. in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 4, 5, 4, ⟦i:Piraeus on the right, Corinth on the left⟧. Rarely, ⟦b:rūre⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cas.⟧ 110, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 7, 1, ⟦i:in the country⟧, for ⟦b:rūrī⟧ (⟦r1337:1337⟧). So ⟦b:animō⟧, ⟦b:animīs⟧, with verbs of feeling: as, ⟦b:angor animō⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 7, ⟦i:I am distressed in soul⟧, or ⟦i:I am heart-broken⟧. Metaphorically: ⟦b:locō⟧, (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦i:in the right place⟧, also ⟦b:suō locō⟧, or ⟦b:in locō⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:locō⟧, ⟦i:instead⟧; ⟦b:numerō⟧, ⟦i:in the category⟧, both with a genitive. ⟦b:prīncipiō⟧, ⟦b:initiō⟧, ⟦i:in the beginning⟧.
⟦#1345⟧
Certain appellatives, with an attribute, often denote the place where by the locative ablative; so especially ⟦b:locō⟧, ⟦b:locīs⟧, ⟦b:rūre⟧, ⟦b:librō⟧, ⟦b:librīs⟧, ⟦b:parte⟧, ⟦b:partibus⟧: as, ⟦b:remōtō, salūbrī, amoenō locō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 7, 20, 2, ⟦i:in a sequestered, healthy, and picturesque nook⟧. ⟦b:idōneō locō⟧, 3, 17, 5, ⟦i:in an advantageous spot⟧. ⟦b:inīquō locō⟧, 5, 51, 1, ⟦i:on unsuitable ground⟧. ⟦b:campestribus ac dēmissīs locīs⟧, 7, 72, 3, ⟦i:in level and sunken places⟧. ⟦b:rūre meō⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 15, 17, ⟦i:at my own country box⟧. ⟦b:rūre paternō⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 18, 60, J. 6, 55, ⟦i:on the ancestral farm⟧. ⟦b:aliō librō⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 2, 31, ⟦i:in another book⟧.
⟦#1346⟧
Substantives are often used in the locative ablative with ⟦b:tōtus⟧ in agreement, less often with ⟦b:cūnctus⟧, ⟦b:omnis⟧, or ⟦b:medius⟧, to denote the place where: as, ⟦b:tōtā Galliā⟧, 5, 55, 3, ⟦i:all over Gaul⟧. ⟦b:tōtīs trepidātur castrīs⟧, 6, 37, 6, ⟦i:there is a panic all over the camp⟧. ⟦b:omnibus oppidīs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 136, ⟦i:in all the towns⟧. ⟦b:omnibus oppidīs maritimīs⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 5, 1, ⟦i:in all the seaports⟧. ⟦b:mediā urbe⟧, L. 1, 33, 8, ⟦i:in the heart of Rome⟧. But sometimes ⟦b:in⟧ is used, or the accusative with ⟦b:per⟧.
⟦#1347⟧
(4.) With country names and most appellatives, the place where is generally expressed by the ablative with ⟦b:in⟧. But even without an attribute, the ablative alone is sometimes used, especially in poetry: as,
⟦b:Ītaliā⟧, V. 1, 263, ⟦i:in Italy⟧, ⟦b:lītore⟧, V. 1, 184, ⟦i:upon the beach⟧, ⟦b:corde⟧, V. 1, 209, ⟦i:in heart⟧, ⟦b:pectore⟧, V. 1, 657, ⟦i:in breast⟧, ⟦b:thalamō⟧, H. 1, 15, 16, ⟦i:in bower⟧, ⟦b:umerō⟧, V. 1, 501, ⟦i:on shoulder⟧, ⟦b:Ēsquiliīs⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 63, ⟦i:on the Esquiline⟧. Once in Plautus ⟦b:Ālide⟧, ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 330, ⟦i:in Elis⟧, but eight times ⟦b:in Ālide⟧.
⟦#1348⟧
The locative ablative is sometimes used with such verbs as ⟦b:teneō⟧ and ⟦b:recipiō⟧: as, (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:Ariovistus exercitum castrīs continuit⟧, 1, 48, 4, ⟦i:Ariovistus kept his infantry in camp⟧. ⟦b:oppidō sēsē continēbant⟧, 2, 30, 2, ⟦i:they kept inside the town⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:oppidīs recipere⟧, 2, 3, 3, ⟦i:to receive inside their towns⟧. ⟦b:rēx ecquis est, qui senātōrem tēctō ac domō nōn invītet?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 25, ⟦i:is there a monarch in the wide world that would not welcome a senator to house and home?⟧
⟦#1349⟧
The locative ablative is used with ⟦b:fīdō⟧ and ⟦b:cōnfīdō⟧, ⟦b:glōrior⟧, ⟦b:laetor⟧, ⟦b:nītor⟧, ⟦b:stō⟧, and with ⟦b:frētus⟧: as, ⟦b:barbarī cōnfīsī locī nātūrā in aciē permānsērunt⟧, 8, 15, 1, ⟦i:the natives, trusting in the nature of their position, kept their stand in battle array⟧. ⟦b:superiōribus vīctōriis frētī⟧, 3, 21, 1, ⟦i:relying on their former victories⟧. For other constructions with these words, see the dictionary.

title: Time at which or Time within which
text:
⟦#1350⟧
(1.) The locative ablative is used to denote the point of time at which action occurs.
So particularly of substantives denoting periods or points of time, thus: ⟦b:hieme⟧, 5, 1, 1, ⟦i:in the winter⟧. ⟦b:Kalendīs⟧, H. ⟦i:Epod.⟧ 2, 70, ⟦i:upon the first⟧, i.e. of the month. Generally with an attribute: as, ⟦b:prīmō vēre⟧, 6, 3, 4, ⟦i:in the first month of spring⟧. ⟦b:Mārtiīs Kalendīs⟧, H. 3, 8, 1, ⟦i:upon the first of March⟧. With a parallel locative (⟦r1341:1341⟧): ⟦b:vesperī eōdem diē⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 8, 5, 1, ⟦i:the evening of the same day⟧.
⟦#1351⟧
Words not in themselves denoting periods or points of time, are in the same way put in the ablative: as,
⟦b:patrum nostrōrum memoriā⟧, 1, 12, 5, ⟦i:in the memory of our fathers⟧. ⟦b:nōn modo illīs Pūnicīs bellīs, sed etiam hāc praedōnum multitūdine⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 103, ⟦i:not only in the Punic wars of yore, but also in the present swarm of pirates⟧. ⟦b:proxumīs comitiīs⟧, 7, 67, 7, ⟦i:at the last election⟧. ⟦b:spectāculīs⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 2, 19, 3, ⟦i:at the shows⟧. Especially substantives of action in ⟦b:-tus⟧ or ⟦b:-sus⟧ (⟦r235:235⟧): as, ⟦b:sōlis occāsū⟧, 1, 50, 3, ⟦i:at sunset⟧. ⟦b:adventū in Galliam Caesaris⟧, 5, 54, 2, ⟦i:at Caesar’s arrival in Gaul⟧. ⟦b:eōrum adventū⟧, 7, 65, 5, ⟦i:after these people came⟧. ⟦b:discessū cēterōrum⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 7, ⟦i:when the rest went away⟧.
⟦#1352⟧
(2.) The locative ablative is used to denote the space of time within which action occurs: as,
⟦b:paucīs diēbus opus efficitur⟧, 6, 9, 4, ⟦i:the job is finished up in a few days⟧. ⟦b:tribus hōris Aduātucam venīre potestis⟧, 6, 35, 8, ⟦i:in three hours you can get to Aduatuca⟧. ⟦b:quae hīc mōnstra fīunt, annō vix possum ēloquī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 505, ⟦i:what ghost-transactions take place here I scarce could tell you in a year⟧. ⟦b:cum ad oppidum Senonum Vellaunodūnum vēnisset, id bīduō circumvāllāvit⟧, 7, 11, 1, ⟦i:arriving at Vellaunodunum, a town of the Senons, in two days time he invested it⟧. ⟦b:quicquid est, bīduō sciēmus⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 9, 14, 2, ⟦i:whatever it may be, we shall know in a couple of days⟧.
⟦#1353⟧
The ablative of the time at or within which action occurs is sometimes accompanied by ⟦b:in⟧: as, ⟦b:in bellō⟧, 6, 1, 3, ⟦i:in the war⟧. ⟦b:in tempore⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 364, ⟦i:in the nick of time⟧. ⟦b:in adulēscentiā⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 410, ⟦i:in my young days⟧. ⟦b:in tālī tempore⟧, Lucr. 1, 93, L. 22, 35, 7, ⟦i:in such a stress, at such an hour⟧. ⟦b:in hōc trīduō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 316, ⟦i:within the next three days⟧. Especially of repeated action, in the sense of ⟦i:a⟧ or ⟦i:every⟧, with numerals: as, ⟦b:ter in annō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 1127, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 132, ⟦i:three times a year⟧. ⟦b:in hōrā saepe ducentōs versūs dictābat⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 4, 9, ⟦i:two hundred verses in an hour he’d often dictate off⟧. But occasionally without ⟦b:in⟧: as, ⟦b:mē deciēns diē ūnō extrūdit aedibus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 70, ⟦i:ten times a day he thrusts me from the house⟧. ⟦b:septiēns diē⟧, L. 28, 6, 10, ⟦i:seven times a day⟧.
⟦#1354⟧
An ablative of the time within which action occurs is sometimes followed by a relative pronoun sentence, with the relative pronoun likewise in the ablative: as, ⟦b:quadrīduō, quō haec gesta sunt, rēs ad Chrȳsogonum dēfertur⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 20, ⟦i:within the four days space in which this occurred, the incident is reported to Chrysogonus⟧, i.e. four days after this occurred. ⟦b:diēbus decem, quibus māteria coepta erat conportārī, omnī opere effectō⟧, 4, 18, 1, ⟦i:the job being all done ten days after the carting of the stuff had begun⟧.
⟦#1355⟧
The ablative is exceptionally used to denote duration of time: as,
⟦b:tōtā nocte continenter iērunt⟧, 1, 26, 5, ⟦i:they went on and on all night without interruption⟧. Regularly, however, the accusative (⟦r1151:1151⟧); but the ablative is common in inscriptions.

title: The Ablative of Accompaniment
text:
⟦#1356⟧
A few indefinite designations of military forces denote accompaniment by the ablative alone, or oftener with ⟦b:cum⟧: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:ad castra Caesaris omnibus cōpiīs contendērunt⟧, 2, 7, 3, ⟦i:they marched upon Caesar’s camp with all their forces⟧. ⟦b:omnibus cōpiīs ad Ilerdam proficīscitur⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 41, 2, ⟦i:he marches before Ilerda, horse, foot, and dragoons⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:is cīvitātī persuāsit, ut cum omnibus cōpiīs exīrent⟧, 1, 2, 1, ⟦i:well, this man induced the community to emigrate in a body, bag and baggage⟧.
⟦#1357⟧
The participles ⟦b:iūnctus⟧ and ⟦b:coniūnctus⟧ take the ablative of the thing joined with: as, ⟦b:dēfēnsiōne iūncta laudātiō⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 162, ⟦i:a eulogy combined with a defence⟧. But sometimes the ablative with ⟦b:cum⟧ is used, or the dative (⟦r1186:1186⟧).

title: The Ablative of Manner
text:
⟦#1358⟧
(1.) Certain substantives without an attribute are put in the ablative alone to denote manner; but usually substantives without an attribute have ⟦b:cum⟧.
(⟦i:a.⟧) Such adverbial ablatives are ⟦b:iūre⟧ and ⟦b:iniūriā⟧, ⟦b:ratiōne et viā⟧, ⟦b:silentiō⟧, ⟦b:vitiō⟧, ⟦b:ōrdine⟧, ⟦b:sponte⟧, ⟦b:cōnsuētūdine⟧, &c.: as, ⟦b:Arātus iūre laudātur⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 2, 81, ⟦i:Aratus is justly admired⟧. ⟦b:iniūriā suspectum⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 17, ⟦i:wrongfully suspected⟧. ⟦b:in omnibus, quae ratiōne docentur et viā⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 116, ⟦i:in everything that is taught with philosophic method⟧. ⟦b:silentiō ēgressus⟧, 7, 58, 2, ⟦i:going out in silence⟧. ⟦b:cēnsōrēs vitiō creātī⟧, L. 6, 27, 5, ⟦i:censors irregularly appointed⟧. ⟦b:ōrdine cūncta exposuit⟧, L. 3, 50, 4, ⟦i:he told the whole story from beginning to end⟧, i.e. with all the particulars. (⟦i:b.⟧) With ⟦b:cum⟧: ⟦b:face rem hanc cum cūrā gerās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 198, ⟦i:see that this job with care thou dost⟧. ⟦b:cum virtūte vīvere⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 3, 29, ⟦i:to live virtuously⟧.
⟦#1359⟧
(2.) The ablative of a substantive with an attribute is often used to denote manner, sometimes with ⟦b:cum⟧: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:ī pede faustō⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 2, 2, 37, ⟦i:go with a blessing on thy foot⟧. ⟦b:dat sonitū magnō strāgem⟧, Lucr. 1, 288, ⟦i:it deals destruction with a mighty roar⟧. ⟦b:ferārum rītū sternuntur⟧, L. 5, 44, 6, ⟦i:they throw themselves down beast-fashion⟧. ⟦b:apis Matīnae mōre modōque operōsa carmina fingō⟧, H. 4, 2, 27, ⟦i:in way and wise of Matin bee laborious lays I mould⟧. ⟦b:‘indoctus’ dīcimus brevī prīmā litterā, ‘īnsānus’ prōductā, ‘inhūmānus’ brevī, ‘īnfēlīx’ longā⟧. ⟦i:O.⟧ 159, ⟦i:we pronounce⟧ ⟦b:indoctus⟧ ⟦i:with the first letter short⟧, ⟦b:īnsānus⟧ ⟦i:with it long⟧, ⟦b:inhūmānus⟧ ⟦i:with it short⟧, ⟦b:īnfēlīx⟧ ⟦i:with it long⟧ (⟦r167:167⟧). ⟦b:ternō cōnsurgunt ōrdine rēmī⟧, V. 5, 120, ⟦i:with triple bank each time in concert rise the oars⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:Allobroges magnā cum cūrā suōs fīnēs tuentur⟧, 7, 65, 3, ⟦i:the Allobrogans guard their own territory with great care⟧.
⟦#1360⟧
With a substantive meaning ⟦i:way⟧ or ⟦i:manner⟧, as ⟦b:modō⟧, ⟦b:rītū⟧, &c., ⟦i:feeling⟧ or ⟦i:intention⟧, as ⟦b:hāc mente⟧, ⟦b:aequō animō⟧, ⟦i:condition⟧, as ⟦b:eā condiciōne⟧, or a part of the body, as in ⟦b:nūdō capite⟧, ⟦i:bareheaded⟧, ⟦b:cum⟧ is not used.
⟦#1361⟧
Other expressions denoting manner, particularly prepositional expressions with ⟦b:per⟧, may be found in the dictionary: as, ⟦b:per dolum⟧, 4, 13, 1, ⟦i:by deceit⟧, ⟦b:per iocum⟧, ⟦i:Agr.⟧ 2, 96, ⟦i:in fun⟧, ⟦b:per litterās⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 5, 21, 13, ⟦i:by letter⟧, ⟦i:in writing⟧, ⟦b:per vim⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 32, ⟦i:violently⟧, ⟦b:per praestigiās⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 53, ⟦i:by some hocus pocus or other⟧, &c., &c. Sometimes the ablative with ⟦b:ex⟧.

title: The Ablative Absolute
text:
⟦#1362⟧
(1.) The ablative of a substantive, with a predicate participle in agreement, is used to denote an attendant circumstance of an action.
In this construction, which is called the ⟦i:Ablative Absolute⟧, (⟦i:a.⟧) the present participle is sometimes used: as, ⟦b:nūllō hoste prohibente incolumem legiōnem in Nantuātīs perdūxit⟧, 3, 6, 5, ⟦i:with no enemy hindering, he conducted the legion in safety to the Nantuates⟧. Much oftener, however, (⟦i:b.⟧) the perfect participle: as, ⟦b:hōc respōnsō datō discessit⟧, 1, 14, 7, ⟦i:this answer given he went away⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) The future participle is also used in the ablative absolute from Livy on: as, ⟦b:hospite ventūrō, cessābit nēmo tuōrum⟧, J. 14, 59, ⟦i:a visitor to come, your slaves will bustle each and all⟧.
⟦#1363⟧
A predicate ablative with a participle meaning ⟦i:made⟧, ⟦i:kept⟧, ⟦i:chosen⟧, or the like, occurs in Cicero, Caesar, Nepos, and Livy, but is rare (⟦r1167:1167⟧): as, ⟦b:Dolābellā hoste dēcrētō⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 11, 16, ⟦i:Dolabella having been voted an enemy of the state⟧.
⟦#1364⟧
The perfect participles of deponents used actively in the ablative absolute, are chiefly those of intransitive use, such as ⟦b:nātus⟧, ⟦b:mortuus⟧, ⟦b:ortus⟧, ⟦b:profectus⟧. From Sallust on, other perfect deponent participles also are used actively with an accusative. Cicero and Caesar use a few deponent participles, such as ⟦b:ēmeritus⟧, ⟦b:pactus⟧, ⟦b:partītus⟧, ⟦b:dēpopulātus⟧, as passives, and later authors use many other participles so.
⟦#1365⟧
(2.) The ablative of a substantive, with a predicate noun in agreement, is often used to denote an attendant circumstance of an action: as,
⟦b:brevitātem secūtus sum tē magistrō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 11, 25, 1, ⟦i:I aimed at brevity with you as a teacher⟧. ⟦b:nātus dīs inimīcīs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 563, ⟦i:born under wrath of gods⟧. ⟦b:M. Messālā et M. Pīsōne cōnsulibus⟧, 1, 2, 1, ⟦i:in the consulship of Messala and Piso⟧. ⟦b:istō praetōre vēnit Syrācūsās⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 61, ⟦i:in the defendant’s praetorship he came to Syracuse⟧.
⟦#1366⟧
The nominative ⟦b:quisque⟧, ⟦b:plerīque⟧, or ⟦b:ipse⟧, sometimes accompanies the ablative absolute: as, ⟦b:causā ipse prō sē dictā, damnātur⟧, L. 4, 44, 10, ⟦i:he is condemned after pleading his case in person⟧.
⟦#1367⟧
The ablative absolute may denote in a loose way various relations which might be more distinctly expressed by subordinate sentences.
So particularly: (⟦i:a.⟧) Time: as, ⟦b:tertiā initā vigiliā exercitum ēdūcit⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 54, 2, ⟦i:at the beginning of the third watch he leads the army out⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) Cause or means: as, ⟦b:C. Flāminium Caelius religiōne neglēctā cecidisse apud Trāsumēnum scrībit⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 8, ⟦i:Caelius writes that Flaminius fell at Trasumene in consequence of his neglect of religious observances⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) Concession: as, ⟦b:id paucīs dēfendentibus expugnāre nōn potuit⟧, 2, 12, 2, ⟦i:though the defenders were few, he could not take it by storm⟧. (⟦i:d.⟧) Hypothesis: as, ⟦b:quae potest esse vītae iūcunditās sublātīs amīcitiīs?⟧ ⟦i:Pl.⟧ 80, ⟦i:what pleasure can there be in life, if you take friendships away?⟧ (⟦i:e.⟧) Description: as, ⟦b:domum vēnit capite obvolūtō⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 77, ⟦i:he came home with his head all muffled up⟧.
⟦#1368⟧
It may be seen from the examples above that a change of construction is often desirable in translating the ablative absolute. Particularly so in many set idiomatic expressions: as, ⟦b:nūllā interpositā morā⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 75, 1, ⟦i:without a moment’s delay⟧, ⟦i:instantly⟧. ⟦b:equō admissō⟧, 1, 22, 2, ⟦b:equō citātō⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 96, 3, ⟦i:full gallop⟧. ⟦b:clāmōre sublātō⟧, 7, 12, 5, ⟦i:with a round of cheers⟧. ⟦b:bene rē gestā salvos redeō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 1182, ⟦i:crowned with success I come back safe and sound⟧.
⟦#1369⟧
The substantive of the ablative absolute usually denotes a different person or thing from any in the main sentence. But exceptions to this usage sometimes occur: as,
⟦b:quibus audītīs, eōs domum remittit⟧, 4, 21, 6, ⟦i:after listening to these men, he sends them home again⟧. ⟦b:sī ego mē sciente paterer⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 559, ⟦i:if I should wittingly myself allow⟧, more emphatic than ⟦b:sciēns⟧. ⟦b:sē iūdice nēmo nocēns absolvitur⟧, J. 13, 2, ⟦i:himself the judge, no criminal gets free⟧.
⟦#1370⟧
Two ablatives absolute often occur together, of which the first indicates the time, circumstances, or cause of the second: as, ⟦b:exaudītō clāmōre perturbātīs ōrdinibus⟧, 2, 11, 5, ⟦i:the ranks being demoralized from hearing the shouts⟧. ⟦b:cōnsūmptīs omnibus tēlīs gladiīs dēstrictīs⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 46, 1, ⟦i:drawing their swords after expending all their missiles⟧.
⟦#1371⟧
The substantive is sometimes omitted in the ablative absolute, particularly when it is a general word for a person or a thing which is explained by a relative: as, ⟦b:praemissīs, quī repūrgārent iter⟧, L. 44, 4, 11, ⟦i:sending sappers and miners ahead to clear a way⟧. ⟦b:relātīs ōrdine, quae vīdissent⟧, L. 42, 25, 2, ⟦i:telling circumstantially all they had seen⟧.
⟦#1372⟧
The ablative neuter of some perfect participles is used impersonally (⟦r1034:1034⟧). This use is rare in old Latin, in classical Latin commonest in Cicero, and afterwards in Livy: as, ⟦b:auspicātō⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 11, ⟦i:with auspices taken⟧. ⟦b:sortītō⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 126, ⟦i:lots being drawn⟧, or ⟦i:by lot⟧. Such ablatives readily become adverbs (⟦r704:704⟧). Substantives are also sometimes used alone: as, ⟦b:austrō⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 58, ⟦i:when the wind is south⟧. ⟦b:tranquillitāte⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 8, 20, 6, ⟦i:when it is calm⟧. ⟦b:serēnō⟧, L. 37, 3, 3, ⟦i:the day being clear⟧.
⟦#1373⟧
The ablative neuter of some perfect participles is occasionally used in agreement with a sentence or an infinitive: as, ⟦b:cōgnitō vīvere Ptolomaeum⟧, L. 33, 41, 5, ⟦i:it being known that Ptolomy was alive⟧. This construction is not used in old Latin, and is rare in classical Latin, but common in Livy and Tacitus. So adjectives also: as, ⟦b:incertō quid vītārent⟧, L. 28, 36, 12, ⟦i:it not being obvious what they were to steer clear of⟧.
⟦#1374⟧
The ablative absolute is sometimes attended, especially in Livy and Tacitus, by an explanatory word, such as ⟦b:etsī⟧, ⟦b:tamen⟧, ⟦b:nisi⟧, ⟦b:quasi⟧, ⟦b:quamquam⟧, or ⟦b:quamvīs⟧: as, ⟦b:etsī aliquō acceptō dētrīmentō, tamen summā exercitūs salvā⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 67, 5, ⟦i:though with some loss, yet with the safety of the army as a whole⟧.

title: The Ablative of Quality
text:
⟦#1375⟧
The ablative with an adjective in agreement or with a limiting genitive is used to denote quality, either predicatively or attributively: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) Predicatively: ⟦b:capillō sunt prōmissō⟧, 5, 14, 3, ⟦i:they have long hair⟧, or ⟦i:let their hair grow long⟧. ⟦b:singulārī fuit industriā⟧, N. 24, 3, 1, ⟦i:he had unparalleled activity⟧. ⟦b:animō bonō’s⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 732, ⟦i:be of good cheer⟧. ⟦b:ad flūmen Genusum, quod rīpīs erat impedītīs⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 75, 4, ⟦i:to the river Genusus, which had impracticable banks⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) Attributively: ⟦b:difficilī trānsitū flūmen rīpīsque praeruptīs⟧, 6, 7, 5, ⟦i:a river hard to cross and with steep banks⟧. ⟦b:interfectus est C. Gracchus, clārissimō patre, avō, maiōribus⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 4, ⟦i:Gracchus was done to death, a man with an illustrious father, grandfather, and ancestors in general⟧ (⟦r1044:1044⟧). ⟦b:bōs cervī figūrā⟧, 6, 26, 1, ⟦i:an ox with the shape of a stag⟧. Compare the genitive of quality (⟦r1239:1239⟧).

title: The Ablative of the Route taken
text:
⟦#1376⟧
The instrumental ablative is used with verbs of motion to denote the route taken: as,
⟦b:Aurēliā viā profectus est⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 6, ⟦i:he has gone off by the Aurelia Road⟧. ⟦b:omnibus viīs sēmitīsque essedāriōs ex silvīs ēmittēbat⟧, 5, 19, 2, ⟦i:he kept sending his chariot men out by all possible highways and byways⟧. ⟦b:hīs pontibus pābulātum mittēbat⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 40, 1, ⟦i:by these bridges he sent foraging⟧. ⟦b:frūmentum Tiberī vēnit⟧, L. 2, 34, 5, ⟦i:some grain came by the Tiber⟧. ⟦b:lupus Ēsquilīna portā ingressus per portam Capēnam prope intāctus ēvāserat⟧, L. 33, 26, 9, ⟦i:a wolf that came in town by the Esquiline gate had got out through the Capene gate, almost unscathed⟧. This construction gives rise to some adverbs: see ⟦r707:707⟧. The ablative of the route is sometimes used with a substantive of action (⟦r1301:1301⟧): as, ⟦b:nāvigātiō īnferō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 9, 5, 1, ⟦i:the cruise by the lower sea⟧. ⟦b:eōdem flūmine invectiō⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 5, 70, ⟦i:entrance by the same river⟧.

title: The Ablative of Instrument or Means
text:
⟦#1377⟧
The ablative is used to denote the instrument or means: as,
⟦b:pugnābant armīs⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 3, 103, ⟦i:they fought with arms⟧. ⟦b:clārē oculīs videō, sum pernīx pedibus, manibus mōbilis⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 630, ⟦i:I can see distinctly with my eyes, I’m nimble with my legs, and active with my arms⟧. ⟦b:iuvābō aut rē tē aut operā aut cōnsiliō bonō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 19, ⟦i:I’ll help thee either with my purse or hand or good advice⟧. ⟦b:lacte et carne vīvunt, pellibusque sunt vestītī⟧, 5, 14, 2, ⟦i:they live on milk and meat, and they are clad in skins⟧. ⟦b:contentus paucīs lēctōribus⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 10, 74, ⟦i:content with readers few⟧. ⟦b:centēnāque arbore flūctum verberat⟧, V. 10, 207, ⟦i:and with an hundred beams at every stroke the wave he smites⟧. Rarely with substantives denoting action (⟦r1301:1301⟧): as, ⟦b:gestōrēs linguīs, audītōrēs auribus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 429, ⟦i:reporters with their tongues and listeners with their ears⟧. ⟦b:tenerīs labellīs mollēs morsiunculae⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 67a, ⟦i:caressing bites with velvet lips⟧.
⟦#1378⟧
When the instrument is a person, the accusative with ⟦b:per⟧ is used: as, ⟦b:haec quoque per explōrātōrēs ad hostēs dēferuntur⟧, 6, 7, 9, ⟦i:this too is reported to the enemy through the medium of scouts⟧. Or a circumlocution, such as ⟦b:virtūte⟧, ⟦b:beneficiō⟧, ⟦b:benignitāte⟧, or especially ⟦b:operā⟧, with a genitive or possessive; as, ⟦b:deūm virtūte multa bona bene parta habēmus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 346, ⟦i:thanks to the gods, we’ve many a pretty penny prettily put by⟧. ⟦b:meā operā Tarentum recēpistī⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 11, ⟦i:It was through me you got Tarentum back⟧. Rarely the ablative of a person, the person being then regarded as a thing: as, ⟦b:iacent suīs testibus⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 47, ⟦i:they are cast by their own witnesses⟧.
⟦#1379⟧
The instrumental ablative is used with the five deponents ⟦b:fruor⟧, ⟦b:fungor⟧, ⟦b:potior⟧, ⟦b:ūtor⟧, ⟦b:vēscor⟧, and several of their compounds, and with ⟦b:ūsus est⟧ and ⟦b:opus est⟧: as,
⟦b:pāce numquam fruēmur⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 7, 19, ⟦i:we never shall enjoy ourselves with peace⟧, i.e. ⟦i:we never shall enjoy peace⟧. ⟦b:fungar vice cōtis⟧, H. ⟦i:AP.⟧ 304, ⟦i:I’ll play the whetstone’s part⟧. ⟦b:castrīs nostrī potītī sunt⟧, 1, 26, 4, ⟦i:our people made themselves masters of the camp⟧. ⟦b:vestrā operā ūtar⟧, L. 3, 46, 8, ⟦i:I will avail myself of your services⟧. ⟦b:carne vēscor⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 90, ⟦i:I live on meat⟧. ⟦b:opust chlamyde⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 734, ⟦i:there is a job with a cloak⟧, i.e. ⟦i:we need a cloak⟧.
⟦#1380⟧
Instead of the instrumental ablative, some of the above verbs take the accusative occasionally in old and post-Augustan Latin: thus, in Plautus, Terence, Cato, always ⟦b:abūtor⟧, also ⟦b:fungor⟧, except once in Terence; ⟦b:fruor⟧ in Cato and Terence, and ⟦b:perfungor⟧ in Lucretius, once each; ⟦b:potior⟧ twice in Plautus and three times in Terence, often also the genitive (⟦r1292:1292⟧). The gerundive of these verbs is commonly used personally in the passive, as if the verbs were regularly used transitively (⟦r2244:2244⟧).
⟦#1381⟧
⟦b:ūtor⟧ often has a second predicative ablative: as, ⟦b:administrīs druidibus ūtuntur⟧, 6, 16, 2, ⟦i:they use the druids as assistants⟧. ⟦b:facilī mē ūtētur patre⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 217, ⟦i:an easy-going father he will find in me⟧.
⟦#1382⟧
⟦b:ūsus est⟧ and ⟦b:opus est⟧ sometimes take a neuter participle, especially in old Latin: as, ⟦b:vīsō opust cautōst opus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 225, ⟦i:there’s need of sight, there’s need of care⟧. Sometimes the ablative with a predicate participle: as, ⟦b:celeriter mī eō homine conventōst opus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cur.⟧ 302, ⟦i:I needs must see that man at once⟧.
⟦#1383⟧
With ⟦b:opus est⟧, the thing wanted is often made the subject nominative or subject accusative, with ⟦b:opus⟧ in the predicate: as, ⟦b:dux nōbīs et auctor opus est⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 6, 4, ⟦i:we need a leader and adviser⟧. Usually so when the thing needed is a neuter adjective or neuter pronoun: as, ⟦b:multa sibī̆ opus esse⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 126, ⟦i:that he needed much⟧. A genitive dependent on ⟦b:opus⟧ is found once or twice in late Latin (⟦r1227:1227⟧).
⟦#1384⟧
⟦b:ūsus est⟧ is employed chiefly in comedy, but also once or twice in Cicero, Lucretius, Vergil, and Livy. Once with the accusative: ⟦b:ūsust hominem astūtum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 385, ⟦i:there’s need of a sharp man⟧.

title: The Ablative of Specification
text:
⟦#1385⟧
The instrumental ablative is used to denote that in respect of which an assertion or a term is to be taken: as,
⟦b:temporibus errāstī⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 23, ⟦i:you have slipped up in your chronology⟧. ⟦b:excellēbat āctiōne⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 215, ⟦i:his forte lay in delivery⟧. ⟦b:Helvētiī reliquōs Gallōs virtūte praecēdunt⟧, 1, 1, 4, ⟦i:the Helvetians outdo the rest of the Kelts in bravery⟧. ⟦b:hī omnēs linguā, īnstitūtīs, lēgibus inter sē differunt⟧, 1, 1, 2, ⟦i:these people all differ from each other in language, usages, and laws⟧. ⟦b:sunt quīdam hominēs nōn rē sed nōmine⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 105, ⟦i:some people are human beings not in reality but in name⟧. ⟦b:ūna Suēba nātiōne, altera Nōrica⟧, 1, 53, 4, ⟦i:one woman a Suebe by birth, the other Noric⟧. ⟦b:vīcistis cochleam tarditūdine⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 532, ⟦i:you’ve beaten snail in slowness⟧. ⟦b:dēmēns iūdiciō volgī⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 6, 97, ⟦i:mad in the judgement of the world⟧. ⟦b:sapiunt me͡ā sententiā⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 335, ⟦i:in my opinion they are wise⟧. ⟦b:meā quidem sententiā⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 56, ⟦i:in my humble opinion⟧. ⟦b:quis iūre perītior commemorārī potest?⟧ ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 107, ⟦i:who can be named that is better versed in the law?⟧

title: The Ablative of Fulness
text:
⟦#1386⟧
The instrumental ablative is used with verbs of abounding, filling, and furnishing: as,
⟦b:vīlla abundat porcō, haedō, āgnō⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 56, ⟦i:the country place is running over with swine, kid, and lamb⟧. ⟦b:tōtum montem hominibus complērī iussit⟧, 1, 24, 3, ⟦i:he gave orders for the whole mountain to be covered over with men⟧. ⟦b:Māgōnem poenā adfēcērunt⟧, N. 23, 8, 2, ⟦i:they visited Mago with punishment⟧. ⟦b:legiōnēs nimis pulcrīs armīs praeditās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 218, ⟦i:brigades in goodliest arms arrayed⟧. ⟦b:cōnsulārī imperiō praeditus⟧, ⟦i:Pis.⟧ 55, ⟦i:vested with the authority of consul⟧. For the genitive with ⟦b:compleō⟧ and ⟦b:impleō⟧, see ⟦r1293:1293⟧.
⟦#1387⟧
The ablative is sometimes used with adjectives of fulness, instead of the regular genitive (⟦r1263:1263⟧). Thus, in later Latin, rarely with ⟦b:plēnus⟧: as, ⟦b:maxima quaeque domus servīs est plēna superbīs⟧, J. 5, 66, ⟦i:a grand establishment is always full of stuck-up slaves⟧. ⟦b:et ille quidem plēnus annīs abiīt, plēnus honōribus⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 2, 1, 7, ⟦i:well, as for him, he has passed away, full of years and full of honours⟧. So in Cicero and Caesar, once each. Also with ⟦b:dīves⟧ in poetry, and, from Livy on, in prose. With ⟦b:refertus⟧, the ablative of things is common, while persons are usually in the genitive (⟦r1263:1263⟧). With ⟦b:onustus⟧, the ablative is generally used, rarely the genitive.

title: The Ablative of Measure, Exchange, and Price
text:
⟦#1388⟧
The instrumental ablative is used with verbs of measuring and of exchanging, and in expressions of value and price: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:quod magnōs hominēs virtūte mētīmur⟧, N. 18, 1, 1, ⟦i:because we gauge great men by their merit⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:nēmō nisi vīctor pāce bellum mūtāvit⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 58, 15, ⟦i:nobody except a conqueror has ever exchanged war for peace⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:haec sīgna sēstertiūm sex mīllibus quīngentīs esse vēndita⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 12, ⟦i:that these statues were sold for sixty-five hundred sesterces⟧. ⟦b:aestimāvit dēnāriīs III⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 214, ⟦i:he valued it at three denars⟧. ⟦b:trīgintā mīllibus dīxistis eum habitāre⟧, ⟦i:Cael.⟧ 17, ⟦i:you have said he pays thirty thousand rent⟧. ⟦b:quod nōn opus est, āsse cārum est⟧, Cato in Sen. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 94, 28, ⟦i:what you don’t need, at a penny is dear⟧. ⟦b:hem, istūc verbum, mea voluptās, vīlest vīgintī minīs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 297, ⟦i:bless me, that compliment, my charmer, were at twenty minas cheap⟧.
⟦#1389⟧
With ⟦b:mūtō⟧ and ⟦b:commūtō⟧, the ablative usually denotes the thing received. But sometimes in Plautus, and especially in Horace, Livy, and late prose, it denotes the thing parted with: as, ⟦b:cūr valle permūtem Sabīnā dīvitiās operōsiōrēs?⟧ H. 3, 1, 47, ⟦i:why change my Sabine dale for wealth that brings more care?⟧ Similarly with ⟦b:cum⟧ in the prose of Cicero’s age: as, ⟦b:mortem cum vītā commūtāre⟧, Sulp. in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 4, 5, 3, ⟦i:to exchange life for death⟧.
⟦#1390⟧
The ablative of price or value is thus used chiefly with verbs or verbal expressions of bargaining, buying or selling, hiring or letting, costing, being cheap or dear. Also with ⟦b:aestimō⟧, of a definite price, and sometimes ⟦b:magnō⟧, ⟦b:permagnō⟧ (⟦r1273:1273⟧).
⟦#1391⟧
The ablatives thus used, are (⟦i:a.⟧) those of general substantives of value and price, such as ⟦b:pretium⟧, (⟦i:b.⟧) numerical designations of money, or (⟦i:c.⟧) neuter adjectives of quantity, ⟦b:magnō⟧, ⟦b:permagnō⟧, ⟦b:quam plūrimō⟧, ⟦b:parvō⟧, ⟦b:minimō⟧, ⟦b:nihilō⟧, ⟦b:nōnnihilō⟧: as, ⟦b:magnō decumās vēndidī⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 40, ⟦i:I sold the tithes at a high figure⟧. For ⟦b:tantī⟧ and ⟦b:quantī⟧, ⟦b:plūris⟧ and ⟦b:minōris⟧, see ⟦r1274:1274⟧.
⟦#1392⟧
The ablative is also used with ⟦b:dignus⟧ and ⟦b:indignus⟧: as,
⟦b:dignī maiōrum locō⟧, ⟦i:Agr.⟧ 2, 1, ⟦i:well worthy of the high standing of their ancestors⟧. ⟦b:nūlla vōx est audīta populī Rōmānī maiestāte indigna⟧, 7, 17, 3, ⟦i:not a word was heard out of keeping with the grandeur of Rome⟧. See also ⟦b:dignor⟧ in the dictionary. Similarly in Plautus with ⟦b:condignē⟧, ⟦b:decōrus⟧, ⟦b:decet⟧, ⟦b:aequē⟧, ⟦b:aequos⟧. For the genitive with ⟦b:dignus⟧, see ⟦r1269:1269⟧; for the accusative with ⟦b:dignus⟧ and a form of ⟦b:sum⟧, 1144.

title: The Ablative of the Amount of Difference
text:
⟦#1393⟧
The instrumental ablative is used to denote the amount of difference.
This ablative is used with any words whatever of comparative or of superlative meaning: as, ⟦b:ūnō diē longiōrem mēnsem faciunt aut bīduō⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 129, ⟦i:they make the month longer by a day, or even by two days⟧. ⟦b:ubī̆ adbibit plūs paulō⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 220, ⟦i:when he has drunk a drop too much⟧. ⟦b:nummō dīvitior⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 1323, ⟦i:a penny richer⟧. ⟦b:bīduō post⟧, 1, 47, 1, ⟦i:two days after⟧. ⟦b:multīs ante diēbus,⟧ 7, 9, 4, ⟦i:many days before⟧. ⟦b:paucīs ante diēbus⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 3, ⟦i:a few days ago⟧. ⟦b:nimiō praestat⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 396, ⟦i:‘t is ever so much better⟧. ⟦b:multō mālim⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 184, ⟦i:I would much rather⟧. ⟦b:multō maxima pars⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 17, ⟦i:the largest part by far⟧.
⟦#1394⟧
In expressions of time, the accusative is sometimes used with ⟦b:post⟧, less frequently with ⟦b:ante⟧, as prepositions, instead of the ablative of difference: as, ⟦b:post paucōs diēs⟧, L. 21, 51, 2, ⟦b:post diēs paucōs⟧, L. 37, 13, 6, ⟦b:paucōs post diēs⟧, L. 33, 39, 2, ⟦i:after a few days⟧. ⟦b:paucōs ante diēs⟧, L. 39, 28, 4, ⟦b:diēs ante paucōs⟧, L. 31, 24, 5, ⟦i:a few days before⟧. With this prepositional construction, ordinals are common: as, ⟦b:post diem tertium⟧, 4, 9, 1, ⟦i:after the third day⟧, according to the Roman way of reckoning, i.e. the next day but one.
⟦#1395⟧
(1.) When the time before or after which anything occurs is denoted by a substantive, the substantive is put in the accusative with ⟦b:ante⟧ or ⟦b:post⟧: as,
⟦b:paulō ante tertiam vigiliam⟧, 7, 24, 2, ⟦i:a little before the third watch⟧. ⟦b:bīduō ante vīctōriam⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 10, 14, 1, ⟦i:the day but one before the victory⟧. ⟦b:paucīs diēbus post mortem Āfricānī⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 3, ⟦i:a few days after the death of Africanus⟧.
⟦#1396⟧
Sometimes in late writers, as Tacitus, Pliny the younger, and Suetonius, a genitive is loosely used: as, ⟦b:sextum post clādis annum⟧, Ta. 1, 62, i.e. ⟦b:sextō post clādem annō⟧, ⟦i:six years after the humiliating defeat⟧. ⟦b:post decimum mortis annum⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 6, 10, 3, ⟦i:ten years after his death⟧. Similarly ⟦b:intrā sextum adoptiōnis diem⟧, Suet. ⟦i:Galb.⟧ 17, ⟦i:not longer than six days after the adoption-day⟧.
⟦#1397⟧
(2.) When the time before or after which anything occurs is denoted by a sentence, the sentence may be introduced:
(⟦i:a.⟧) By ⟦b:quam⟧: as, ⟦b:post diem tertium gesta rēs est quam dīxerat⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 44, ⟦i:it took place two days after he said it⟧. With ⟦b:quam⟧, ⟦b:post⟧ is sometimes omitted. Or (⟦i:b.⟧) less frequently by ⟦b:cum⟧: as, ⟦b:quem trīduō, cum hās dabam litterās, exspectābam⟧, Planc. in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 10, 23, 3, ⟦i:I am looking for him three days after this writing⟧ (⟦r1601:1601⟧). For a relative pronoun sentence, see ⟦r1354:1354⟧.
⟦#1398⟧
Verbs of surpassing sometimes have an accusative of extent (⟦r1151:1151⟧): as, ⟦b:mīrāmur hunc hominem tantum excellere cēterīs?⟧ ⟦i:IP.⟧ 39, ⟦i:are we surprised that this man so far outshines everybody else?⟧ With comparatives, the accusative is rare: as, ⟦b:aliquantum inīquior⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 201, ⟦i:somewhat too hard⟧. Similarly ⟦b:permultum ante⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 3, 11, 1, ⟦i:long long before⟧.
⟦#1399⟧
In numerical designations of distance, the words ⟦b:intervāllum⟧ and ⟦b:spatium⟧ are regularly put in the ablative: as, ⟦b:rēx VI mīlium passuum intervāllō ā Saburrā cōnsēderat⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 38, 3, ⟦i:the king had pitched six miles away from Saburra⟧. So sometimes ⟦b:mīlle⟧: as, ⟦b:mīlibus passuum VI a Caesaris castrīs sub monte cōnsēdit⟧, 1, 48, 1. See ⟦r1152:1152⟧.

title: Two or More Ablatives Combined
text:
⟦#1400⟧
Two or more ablatives denoting different relations are often combined in the same sentence: as,
⟦b:Menippus, meō iūdiciō⟧ (⟦r1385:1385⟧) ⟦b:tōtā Asiā⟧ (⟦r1346:1346⟧) ⟦b:illīs temporibus⟧ (⟦r1350:1350⟧) ⟦b:disertissimus⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 315, ⟦i:Menippus, in my opinion the most gifted speaker of that day in all Asia⟧. ⟦b:hāc habitā ōrātiōne⟧ (⟦r1362:1362⟧) ⟦b:mīlitibus studiō⟧ (⟦r1316:1316⟧) ⟦b:pugnae ardentibus⟧ (⟦r1370:1370⟧) ⟦b:tubā⟧ (⟦r1377:1377⟧) ⟦b:sīgnum dedit⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 90, 4, ⟦i:seeing that his soldiers were hot for battle after this speech, he gave the signal by trumpet⟧.

title: Use of Cases with Prepositions
text:
⟦#1401⟧
Two cases, the accusative and the ablative, are used with prepositions.
⟦#1402⟧
Prepositions were originally adverbs which served to define more exactly the meaning of a verb.
Thus, ⟦b:endo⟧, ⟦i:in⟧, ⟦i:on⟧, the older form of ⟦b:in⟧, is an adverb, in an injunction occurring in a law of the Twelve Tables, 451 B.C., ⟦b:manum endo iacitō⟧, ⟦i:let him lay hand on⟧. Similarly, ⟦b:trāns⟧, ⟦i:over⟧, in ⟦b:trānsque datō⟧, ⟦i:and he must hand over⟧, i.e. ⟦b:trāditōque⟧.
⟦#1403⟧
In the course of time such adverbs became verbal prefixes; the verbs compounded with them may take the case, accusative or ablative, required by the meaning of the compound. Thus, ⟦b:amīcōs adeō⟧, ⟦i:I go to my friends⟧ (⟦r1137:1137⟧); ⟦b:urbe exeō⟧, ⟦i:I go out of town⟧ (⟦r1302:1302⟧).
⟦#1404⟧
For distinctness or emphasis, the prefix of the verb may be repeated before the case: as, ⟦b:ad amīcōs adeō⟧; ⟦b:ex urbe exeō⟧. And when it is thus separately expressed before the case, it may be dropped from the verb: as, ⟦b:ad amīcōs eō⟧; ⟦b:ex urbe eō⟧.
⟦#1405⟧
The preposition thus detached from the verb becomes an attendant on a substantive, and serves to show the relation of the substantive in a sentence more distinctly than the case alone could.
⟦#1406⟧
A great many adverbs which are never used in composition with a verb likewise become prepositions: as, ⟦b:apud⟧, ⟦b:circiter⟧, ⟦b:īnfrā⟧, ⟦b:iūxtā⟧, ⟦b:pōne⟧, ⟦b:propter⟧, &c., &c. The inflected forms of substantives, ⟦b:prīdiē⟧, ⟦b:postrīdiē⟧ (⟦r1413:1413⟧), ⟦b:tenus⟧ (⟦r1420:1420⟧), and ⟦b:fīnī⟧ (⟦r1419:1419⟧), are also sometimes used as prepositions. And ⟦b:vicem⟧ (⟦r1145:1145⟧), ⟦b:causā⟧, ⟦b:grātiā⟧, ⟦b:nōmine⟧, ⟦b:ergō⟧ (⟦r1257:1257⟧), resemble prepositions closely in meaning.
⟦#1407⟧
A trace of the original adverbial use of prepositions is sometimes retained, chiefly in poetry, when the prefix is separated from its word by what is called ⟦i:Tmesis⟧: as, ⟦b:īre inque gredī⟧, i.e. ⟦b:ingredīque⟧, Lucr. 4, 887, ⟦i:to walk and to step off⟧. ⟦b:per mihī̆ mīrum vīsum est⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 214, ⟦i:passing strange it seemed to me⟧.
⟦#1408⟧
Even such words as are used almost exclusively as prepositions sometimes retain their original adverbial meaning also: as, ⟦b:adque adque⟧, E. in Gell. 10, 29, 2, ⟦i:and up and up⟧, ⟦i:and on and on⟧, or ⟦i:and nearer still and still more near⟧. ⟦b:occīsīs ad hominum mīlibus quattuor⟧, 2, 33, 5, ⟦i:about four thousand men being killed⟧. ⟦b:susque dēque⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 14, 6, 1, ⟦i:up and down⟧, ⟦i:topsy turvy⟧, ⟦i:no matter how⟧.
⟦#1409⟧
On the other hand, some verbal prefixes are never used as separate prepositions with a substantive. These are called ⟦i:Inseparable Prepositions⟧; they are: ⟦b:amb-⟧, ⟦i:round⟧, ⟦b:an-⟧, ⟦i:up⟧, ⟦b:dis-⟧, ⟦i:in two⟧, ⟦b:por-⟧, ⟦i:towards⟧, ⟦b:rē̆d-⟧, ⟦i:back⟧. Usually also ⟦b:sēd-⟧, ⟦i:apart⟧ (⟦r1417:1417⟧).

title: Prepositions used with the Accusative
text:
⟦#1410⟧
The accusative is accompanied by the following prepositions:
⟦b:ad⟧, ⟦i:to⟧, ⟦b:adversus⟧ or ⟦b:adversum⟧, ⟦i:towards⟧, ⟦i:against⟧, ⟦b:ante⟧, in composition also ⟦b:antid-⟧, ⟦i:before⟧, ⟦b:apud⟧, ⟦i:near⟧, ⟦i:at⟧, ⟦b:circā⟧, ⟦b:circum⟧, ⟦b:circiter⟧, ⟦i:round⟧, ⟦i:about⟧, ⟦b:cis⟧, ⟦b:citrā⟧, ⟦i:this side of⟧, ⟦b:contrā⟧, ⟦i:opposite to⟧, ⟦b:ergā⟧, ⟦i:towards⟧, ⟦b:extrā⟧, ⟦i:outside⟧, ⟦b:īnfrā⟧, ⟦i:below⟧, ⟦b:inter⟧, ⟦i:between⟧, ⟦b:intrā⟧, ⟦i:within⟧, ⟦b:iūxtā⟧, ⟦i:near⟧, ⟦b:ob⟧, ⟦i:against⟧, ⟦b:penes⟧, ⟦i:in the possession of⟧, ⟦b:per⟧, ⟦i:through⟧, ⟦b:pōne⟧, ⟦b:post⟧, in Plautus ⟦b:postid⟧, ⟦b:poste⟧, ⟦b:pos⟧, ⟦i:behind⟧, ⟦b:praeter⟧, ⟦i:past⟧, ⟦b:prope⟧ (⟦b:propius⟧, ⟦b:proximē⟧), ⟦b:propter⟧, ⟦i:near⟧, ⟦b:secundum⟧, ⟦i:after⟧, ⟦b:subter⟧, ⟦i:under⟧, ⟦b:suprā⟧, ⟦i:above⟧, ⟦b:trāns⟧, ⟦i:across⟧, ⟦b:uls⟧, ⟦b:ultrā⟧, ⟦i:beyond⟧. For the various shades of meaning and applications of these prepositions, see the dictionary.
⟦#1411⟧
Prepositions which accompany the accusative may be easily remembered in this order:
⟦b:ante⟧, ⟦b:apud⟧, ⟦b:ad⟧, ⟦b:adversum⟧,
⟦b:circum⟧, ⟦b:cis⟧, ⟦b:ob⟧, ⟦b:trāns⟧, ⟦b:secundum⟧,
⟦b:penes⟧, ⟦b:pōne⟧, ⟦b:prope⟧, ⟦b:per⟧,
⟦b:post⟧, and all in ⟦b:-ā⟧ and ⟦b:-ter⟧.
⟦#1412⟧
Of the above named words some are not used as prepositions till a relatively late period.
Thus, ⟦b:īnfrā⟧ is first used as a preposition by Terence and once only; ⟦b:circā⟧ somewhat before and ⟦b:citrā⟧ about Cicero’s time; ⟦b:ultrā⟧ first by Cato; ⟦b:iūxtā⟧ by Varro. In Cicero ⟦b:iūxtā⟧ is still used only as an adverb, in Caesar and Nepos as a preposition.
⟦#1413⟧
The substantive forms ⟦b:prīdiē⟧, ⟦i:the day before⟧, and ⟦b:postrīdiē⟧, ⟦i:the day after⟧, are sometimes used with an accusative like prepositions, mostly in Cicero, to denote dates: as, ⟦b:prīdiē nōnās Māiās⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 2, 11, 2, ⟦i:the day before the nones of May⟧, i.e. ⟦i:6 May⟧. ⟦b:postrīdiē lūdōs Apollinārīs⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 16, 4, 1, ⟦i:the day after the games of Apollo⟧, i.e. ⟦i:6 July⟧. For the genitive with these words, see ⟦r1232:1232⟧.
⟦#1414⟧
The adverb ⟦b:vorsus⟧ or ⟦b:versus⟧, ⟦i:wards⟧, occurs as a post positive (⟦r1434:1434⟧) preposition rarely: once in Sallust, ⟦b:Aegyptum vorsus⟧, J. 19, 3, ⟦i:Egyptwards⟧, in Cicero a few times, twice in Pliny the elder. ⟦b:usque⟧, ⟦i:even to⟧, occurs with names of towns in Terence (once), Cicero, and later; with appellatives in Cato (once) and late writers.
⟦#1415⟧
⟦b:clam⟧, ⟦i:secretly⟧, is ordinarily an adverb. But in old Latin it is used often as a preposition, ⟦i:unknown to⟧, with an accusative of a person. Terence has once the diminutive form ⟦b:clanculum⟧, ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 52. With the ablative only in the MSS. of Caesar, once, ⟦b:clam vōbīs⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 32, 8, ⟦i:without your knowledge⟧, and in ⟦i:Bell. Afr.⟧ 11, 4.
⟦#1416⟧
⟦b:subter⟧, ⟦i:under⟧, is used in poetry, once by Catullus and once by Vergil, with the locative ablative: as, ⟦b:Rhoetēō subter lītore⟧, Cat. 65, 7, ⟦i:beneath Rhoeteum’s strand⟧.

title: Prepositions used with the Ablative
text:
⟦#1417⟧
The ablative is accompanied by the following prepositions:
⟦b:abs⟧, ⟦b:ab⟧, or ⟦b:ā⟧, ⟦i:from⟧, ⟦b:cōram⟧, ⟦i:face to face⟧, ⟦b:dē⟧, ⟦i:down from⟧, ⟦i:from⟧, ⟦i:of⟧, ⟦b:ex⟧ or ⟦b:ē⟧, ⟦i:out of⟧, ⟦b:prae⟧, ⟦i:at the fore⟧, ⟦i:in front of⟧, ⟦b:prō⟧, ⟦i:before⟧, ⟦b:quom⟧ or ⟦b:cum⟧, ⟦i:with⟧, ⟦b:sine⟧, ⟦i:without⟧. In official or legal language, also ⟦b:sēd⟧ or ⟦b:sē⟧, ⟦i:without⟧. For the different classes of ablatives with these prepositions, see ⟦r1297:1297-1300⟧; for the various shades of meanings and applications, see the dictionary.
⟦#1418⟧
Prepositions which accompany the ablative may be easily remembered in this order:
⟦b:abs⟧ (⟦b:ab⟧, ⟦b:ā⟧), ⟦b:cum⟧, ⟦b:cōram⟧, ⟦b:dē⟧,
⟦b:prae⟧, ⟦b:prō⟧, ⟦b:sine⟧, ⟦b:ex⟧ (or ⟦b:ē⟧).
⟦#1419⟧
The ablative ⟦b:fīnī⟧, ⟦i:as far as⟧, is used in old Latin as a preposition with the ablative: as, ⟦b:osse fīnī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 859, ⟦i:down to the bone⟧. ⟦b:operītō terrā rādīcibus fīnī⟧, Cato, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 28, 2, ⟦i:cover with loam the length of the roots⟧. Also, as a real substantive, with a genitive (⟦r1255:1255⟧): as, ⟦b:ānsārum īnfimārum fīnī⟧, Cato, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 113, 2, ⟦i:up to the bottom of the handles⟧. Rarely ⟦b:fīne⟧, and before the genitive: as, ⟦b:fīne genūs⟧, O. 10, 537, ⟦i:as far as the knee⟧.
⟦#1420⟧
⟦b:tenus⟧, ⟦i:the length⟧, was originally a substantive accusative (⟦r1151:1151⟧). From Cicero on, it is used as a preposition with the ablative, and standing after its case: as, ⟦b:Taurō tenus⟧, ⟦i:D.⟧ 36, ⟦i:not further than Taurus⟧. ⟦b:pectoribus tenus⟧, L. 21, 54, 9, ⟦i:quite up to the breast⟧. ⟦b:hāctenus⟧, ⟦i:thus far⟧, ⟦i:only thus far⟧. Also, as a real substantive, with a genitive, usually a plural, mostly in verse (⟦r1232:1232⟧): as, ⟦b:labrōrum tenus⟧, Lucr. 1, 940, ⟦i:the length of the lips⟧, ⟦i:up to the lips⟧. ⟦b:Cūmārum tenus⟧, Cael. in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 8, 1, 2, ⟦i:as far as Cumae⟧.
⟦#1421⟧
The adverbs ⟦b:palam⟧, ⟦i:in presence of⟧, ⟦b:procul⟧, ⟦i:apart from⟧, either ⟦i:near⟧ or ⟦i:far⟧, ⟦b:simul⟧, ⟦i:with⟧, are rarely used in poetry and late prose as prepositions with the ablative. ⟦b:coram⟧ occurs but once as a preposition (inscriptional) before Cicero’s time. ⟦b:absque⟧ with the ablative occurs once each in Cicero and Quintilian; in Plautus and Terence only in a coordinate protasis (⟦r1701:1701⟧; ⟦r2110:2110⟧).

title: Prepositions used with the Accusative or the Ablative
text:
⟦#1422⟧
Two cases, the accusative and the ablative, are accompanied by the prepositions in, older ⟦b:endo⟧, ⟦b:indu⟧, ⟦i:into⟧, ⟦i:in⟧, ⟦b:sub⟧, ⟦i:under⟧, and ⟦b:super⟧, ⟦i:over⟧, ⟦i:on⟧.
⟦#1423⟧
(1.) ⟦b:in⟧ and ⟦b:sub⟧ accompany the accusative of the end of motion, the locative ablative of rest: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:in cūriam vēnimus⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 138, ⟦i:we went to the senate-house⟧. ⟦b:in vincla coniectus est⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 17, ⟦i:he was put in irons⟧. ⟦b:hīc pāgus eius exercitum sub iugum mīserat⟧, 1, 12, 5, ⟦i:this canton had sent his army under the yoke⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:erimus in castrīs⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 12, 28, ⟦i:we shall be in camp⟧. ⟦b:viridī membra sub arbutō strātus⟧, H. 1, 1, 21, ⟦i:stretched out—his limbs—all under an arbute green⟧.
⟦#1424⟧
Verbs of rest sometimes have ⟦b:in⟧ with the accusative, because of an implied idea of motion. And, conversely, verbs of motion sometimes have ⟦b:in⟧ with the ablative, because of an implied idea of rest: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:mihi in mentem fuit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 180, ⟦i:it popped into my head⟧, i.e. came in and is in (compare ⟦b:venithoc mī in mentem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 226. ⟦b:in eius potestātem venīre nōlēbant⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 150. ⟦b:in eōrum potestātem portum futūrum intellegēbant⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 98, ⟦i:they knew full well the haven would get under the control of these people⟧). (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:Caesar exercitum in hībernīs conlocāvit⟧, 3, 29, 3, ⟦i:Caesar put the army away in winter quarters⟧, i.e. put them into and left them in. ⟦b:eam in lectō conlocārunt⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 593, ⟦i:they laid the lady on her couch⟧. So commonly with ⟦b:locō⟧, ⟦b:conlocō⟧, ⟦b:statuō⟧, ⟦b:cōnstituō⟧, ⟦b:pōnō⟧, and its compounds. For ⟦b:expōnō⟧ and ⟦b:impōnō⟧, see the dictionary.
⟦#1425⟧
(2.) ⟦b:super⟧ accompanies the ablative when it has colloquially the sense of ⟦b:dē⟧, ⟦i:about⟧, ⟦i:in reference to⟧: as, ⟦b:hāc super rē scrībam ad tē Rēgiō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 16, 6, 1, ⟦i:I’ll write you about this from Regium⟧. In other senses, the accusative, but sometimes in poetry the ablative, chiefly in the sense of ⟦i:on⟧: as, ⟦b:ligna super focō largē repōnēns⟧, H. 1, 9, 5, ⟦i:piling on hearth the faggots high⟧. ⟦b:nocte super mediā⟧, V. 9, 61, ⟦i:at dead of night⟧. ⟦b:paulum silvae super hīs⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 6, 3, ⟦i:a bit of wood to crown the whole⟧.

title: Combination of Substantives by a Preposition
text:
⟦#1426⟧
(1.) Two substantives are sometimes connected by a preposition, to indicate certain attributive relations (⟦r1043:1043⟧); such are particularly:
(⟦i:a.⟧) Place: as, ⟦b:illam pugnam nāvālem ad Tenedum⟧, ⟦i:Mur.⟧ 33, ⟦i:the sea-fight off Tenedus⟧. ⟦b:excessum ē vītā⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 3, 60, ⟦i:the departure from life⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) Source, origin, material: as, ⟦b:ex Aethiopiā ancillulam⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 165, ⟦i:a lady’s maid from Aethiopia⟧. ⟦b:pōcula ex aurō⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 62, ⟦i:bowls of gold⟧ (⟦r1314:1314⟧). (⟦i:c.⟧) Direction of action, connection, separation: as, ⟦b:amor in patriam⟧, ⟦i:Fl.⟧ 103, ⟦i:love of country⟧. ⟦b:vestra ergā mē voluntās⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 1, ⟦i:your good will towards me⟧. ⟦b:proelium cum Tūscīs ad Iāniculum⟧, L. 2, 52, 7, ⟦i:the battle with the Tuscans at Janiculum⟧. ⟦b:vir sine metū⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 48, ⟦i:a man devoid of fear⟧ (⟦r1043:1043⟧).
⟦#1427⟧
(2.) Very commonly, however, other constructions are used, even to indicate the relations above: as,
⟦b:bellum Venetōrum⟧, 3, 16, 1, ⟦i:war with the Venetans⟧ (⟦r1231:1231⟧). ⟦b:bellō Cassiānō⟧, 1, 13, 2, ⟦i:in the war with Cassius⟧ (⟦r1233:1233⟧). ⟦b:in aureīs pōculīs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 54, ⟦i:in golden bowls⟧ (⟦r1233:1233⟧). ⟦b:scūtīs ex cortice factīs⟧, 2, 33, 2, ⟦i:with long shields made out of bark⟧ (⟦r1314:1314⟧). ⟦b:post vīctōriam eius bellī, quod cum Persīs fuit⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 49, ⟦i:after the victory in the war with the Persians⟧.
⟦#1428⟧
Prepositional expressions are sometimes used predicatively: as, ⟦b:sunt omnēs sine maculā⟧, ⟦i:Pl.⟧ 6, 14, ⟦i:they are all without spot or blemish⟧. And sometimes they are equivalent to adjectives: as, ⟦b:contrā nātūram⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 4, 11, ⟦i:unnatural⟧, ⟦b:suprā hominem⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 34, ⟦i:superhuman⟧. Or to substantives: as, ⟦b:sine pondere⟧, O. 1, 20, ⟦i:things without weight⟧. Or to adverbs: as, ⟦b:sine labōre⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 461, ⟦i:easily⟧.

title: Repetition or Omission of a Preposition with several Substantives
text:
⟦#1429⟧
(1.) A preposition is often repeated with emphasis before two or more substantives: as,
⟦b:in labōre atque in dolōre⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 685, ⟦i:in toil and in trouble⟧. Particularly so with ⟦b:et . . . et⟧, ⟦b:aut . . . aut⟧, ⟦b:nōn sōlum . . . sed etiam⟧, ⟦b:nōn minus ... quam⟧, &c., &c.: as, ⟦b:et ex urbe et ex agrīs⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 21, ⟦i:from Rome and from the country too⟧.
⟦#1430⟧
(2.) A preposition is often used with the first only of two or more substantives: as, ⟦b:in labōre ac dolōre⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 41, ⟦i:in toil and trouble⟧. ⟦b:incidit in eandem invidiam quam pater suus⟧, N. 5, 3, 1, ⟦i:he fell under the selfsame ban as his father⟧. Particularly when the second is in apposition: as, ⟦b:cum duōbus ducibus, Pyrrhō et Hannibale⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 28, ⟦i:with two commanders, Pyrrhus and Hannibal⟧.

title: Two Prepositions with one Substantive
text:
⟦#1431⟧
(1.) When two prepositions belong to one and the same substantive, the substantive is expressed with the first. With the second, the substantive is repeated, or its place is taken by a pronoun: as,
⟦b:contrā lēgem prōque lēge⟧, L. 34, 8, 1, ⟦i:against the law and for the law⟧. ⟦b:partim contrā Avītum, partim prō hōc⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 88, ⟦i:partly against Avitus, partly for him⟧. If, however, the two prepositions accompany the same case, the substantive need not be repeated: as, ⟦b:intrā extrāque mūnītiōnēs⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 72, 2, ⟦i:inside and outside the works⟧.
⟦#1432⟧
(2.) The second preposition is often used adverbially, without any substantive: as, ⟦b:et in corpore et extrā⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 68, ⟦i:both in the body and outside⟧.

title: Position of Prepositions
text:
⟦#1433⟧
In general a preposition precedes its case: see ⟦r178:178⟧.
⟦#1434⟧
Disyllabic prepositions sometimes follow their substantives. Thus, in Cicero, ⟦b:contrā⟧, ⟦b:ultrā⟧, and ⟦b:sine⟧, sometimes stand after a relative; so likewise ⟦b:inter⟧ in Cicero, Caesar, and Sallust; occasionally also ⟦b:penes⟧ and ⟦b:propter⟧. For ⟦b:versus⟧, see ⟦r1414:1414⟧; for ⟦b:fīnī⟧, 1419; for ⟦b:tenus⟧, 1420.
⟦#1435⟧
Of monosyllables, ⟦b:ad⟧ and ⟦b:dē⟧ often follow a relative. Also ⟦b:cum⟧ often in Cicero and Sallust, and regularly in Caesar. With a personal or a reflexive pronoun, ⟦b:cum⟧ regularly follows, as ⟦b:mēcum⟧, ⟦b:nōbīscum⟧, ⟦b:sēcum⟧.
⟦#1436⟧
In poetry and late prose, prepositions are freely put after their cases.
⟦#1437⟧
In oaths and adjurations, ⟦b:per⟧ is often separated from its proper accusative by the accusative of the object: as, ⟦b:per tē de͡ōs ōrō⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 538, ⟦i:I beg thee by the gods⟧, ⟦i:in the gods’ name⟧.

title: Use of Adverbs
text:
⟦#1438⟧
Adverbs qualify verbs, adjectives, or adverbs.
(⟦i:a.⟧) With verbs, all sorts of adverbs are used: as, of Place: ⟦b:quis istīc habet?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 114, ⟦i:who lives in there?⟧ Time: ⟦b:tum dentēs mihi cadēbant prīmulum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 1116, ⟦i:my teeth were just beginning then to go⟧. Number: ⟦b:bis cōnsul fuerat P. Āfricānus⟧, ⟦i:Mur.⟧ 58, ⟦i:Africanus had twice been consul⟧. Degree, Amount: ⟦b:Ubiī magnopere ōrābant⟧, 4, 16, 5, ⟦i:the Ubians earnestly entreated⟧. ⟦b:Dumnorīx plūrimum poterat⟧, 1, 9, 3, ⟦i:Dumnorix was all-powerful⟧. Manner: ⟦b:bene quiēvit, libenter cibum sūmpsit⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 3, 16, 4, ⟦i:he has slept beautifully, he has relished his food⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) With adjectives and adverbs, oftenest adverbs of degree or amount only, or their equivalents, such as ⟦b:bene⟧, ⟦b:ēgregiē⟧, &c.: as, ⟦b:valdē dīligēns⟧, ⟦i:Ac.⟧ 2, 98, ⟦i:very particular⟧. ⟦b:ēgregiē fortis⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 268, ⟦i:exceptionally brave⟧. Adverbs of manner, however, are also used, especially in poetry: as, ⟦b:turpiter hīrtum⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 3, 22, ⟦i:disreputably rough⟧, i.e. disreputable and rough.
⟦#1439⟧
An adverb is sometimes used with the meaning of an adjective: as,
⟦b:reliquīs deincēps diēbus⟧, 3, 29, 1, ⟦i:the remaining successive days⟧. ⟦b:dē suīs prīvātim rēbus⟧, 5, 3, 5, ⟦i:in relation to their personal interests⟧. ⟦b:undique silvae⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 1, 6, 2, ⟦i:the surrounding woods⟧. Particularly when the substantive expresses character, like an adjective: as, ⟦b:vērē Metellus⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 130, ⟦i:a trueblooded Metellus⟧. ⟦b:rūsticānus vir, sed plānē vir⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 53, ⟦i:a country man, but every inch a man⟧.
⟦#1440⟧
Perfect participles used as substantives are commonly qualified by an adverb, and not by an adjective. Particularly so ⟦b:dictum⟧, ⟦b:factum⟧, ⟦b:inventum⟧, ⟦b:respōnsum⟧, with ⟦b:bene⟧ and ⟦b:male⟧, and their synonymes: as, ⟦b:rēctē ac turpiter factum⟧, 7, 80, 5, ⟦i:heroism and cowardice⟧. ⟦b:bene facta male locāta male facta arbitror⟧, E. in ⟦i:Off.⟧ 2, 62, ⟦i:good deeds ill put, bad deeds I count⟧. In superlative qualifications, however, the adjective is preferred.
⟦#1441⟧
Other substantives also may be qualified by an adverb, when a verb construction or a participle is implied: as, ⟦b:C. Flāminius cōnsul iterum⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 1, 77, ⟦i:Flaminius in his second consulship⟧. ⟦b:ō totiēns servos⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 7, 70, ⟦i:time and again a slave⟧. ⟦b:ictū comminus⟧, ⟦i:Caecin.⟧ 43, ⟦i:by a hand-to-hand blow⟧. ⟦b:pūblicē testem⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 156, ⟦i:a government witness⟧. ⟦b:populum lātē rēgem⟧, V. 1, 21, ⟦i:a nation regnant wide⟧. ⟦b:lātē tyrannus⟧, H. 3, 17, 9, ⟦i:lord paramount far and near⟧.
⟦#1442⟧
An adverb sometimes takes the place of a substantive: as, ⟦b:cum amīcī partim dēseruerint mē, partim etiam prōdiderint⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 1, 3, 5, ⟦i:since my friends have some of them abandoned me, and others again have actually betrayed me⟧, i.e. ⟦b:aliī . . . aliī⟧. ⟦b:postquam satis tūta circā vidēbantur⟧, L. 1, 58, 2, ⟦i:finding every thing round about looked pretty safe⟧, i.e. ⟦b:quae circā erant⟧. ⟦b:palam laudārēs, sēcrēta male audiēbant⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 1, 10, ⟦i:his outward walk you would have admired; his private life was in bad odour⟧, i.e. ⟦b:quae palam fīēbant⟧.

title: Negative Adverbs
text:
⟦#1443⟧
(1.) The negative oftenest used in declaration or interrogation is ⟦b:nōn⟧, ⟦i:not⟧: as,
⟦b:nōn metuō mihi⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 225, ⟦i:I fear not for myself⟧. ⟦b:nōn semper imbrēs nūbibus hīspidōs mānant in agrōs⟧, H. 2, 9, 1, ⟦i:not always from the clouds do showers on stubbly fields come dripping dropping down⟧. ⟦b:nōn dīcēs hodiē?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 7, 21, ⟦i:will you not say without delay?⟧
⟦#1444⟧
⟦b:nōn⟧ is a modification of ⟦b:noenum⟧ or ⟦b:noenu⟧, compounded of ⟦b:ne⟧, ⟦i:no⟧, and the accusative ⟦b:oinom⟧ or ⟦b:oenum⟧, the older form of ⟦b:ūnum⟧, ⟦i:one thing⟧. ⟦b:noenum⟧ occurs in Plautus twice, in Ennius, Lucilius, Afranius, and Varro, once each, and ⟦b:noenu⟧ occurs twice in Lucretius (⟦r99:99⟧).
⟦#1445⟧
Negation is often expressed by other compounds of ⟦b:ne⟧. In such cases the Latin idiom frequently differs from the English, and a transfer of the negative is required in translation.
Such compounds are: (⟦i:a.⟧) Verbs, such as ⟦b:negō⟧, ⟦b:nequeō⟧, ⟦b:nesciō⟧, ⟦b:nōlō⟧: as, ⟦b:negat vērum esse⟧, ⟦i:Mur.⟧ 74, ⟦i:he maintains it is not true⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) Nouns, such as ⟦b:nēmō⟧, ⟦b:neuter⟧, ⟦b:nūllus⟧, ⟦b:nihil⟧: as, ⟦b:nēminī meus adventus labōrī fuit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 16, ⟦i:my visit did not trouble anybody⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) Adverbs, such as ⟦b:numquam⟧, ⟦b:nusquam⟧. (⟦i:d.⟧) Similarly, the conjunction ⟦b:neque⟧ is used for ⟦i:and not⟧, ⟦i:but not⟧, unless a single word is to be emphasized or contrasted: as, ⟦b:nec frūstrā⟧, 8, 5, 3, ⟦i:and not in vain⟧.
⟦#1446⟧
A form ⟦b:nec⟧ is used rarely in old Latin in the sense of ⟦b:nōn⟧: as, ⟦b:tū dīs nec rēctē dīcis⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 119, ⟦i:thou dost abuse the gods⟧, i.e. ⟦b:nōn rēctē⟧ or ⟦b:male dīcis⟧. After Plautus’s time, ⟦b:nec⟧ for ⟦b:nōn⟧ occurs in a few set combinations, such as ⟦b:nec opīnāns⟧, ⟦i:not expecting⟧, and, from Livy on, ⟦b:necdum⟧, ⟦i:not yet⟧, i.e. ⟦b:nōndum⟧.
⟦#1447⟧
The form ⟦b:nē⟧ usually introduces an imperative or a subjunctive, as will be explained further on. But ⟦b:nē⟧ is also used in the combination ⟦b:nē . . . quidem⟧, ⟦i:not even⟧, ⟦i:not . . . either⟧, with the emphatic word between ⟦b:nē⟧ and ⟦b:quidem⟧: as, ⟦b:nē tum quidem⟧, 1, 50, 2, ⟦i:not even then⟧. ⟦b:nē Vorēnus quidem sēsē vāllō continet⟧, 5, 44, 6, ⟦i:Vorenus did not keep inside the palisade either⟧.
⟦#1448⟧
The adjective ⟦b:nūllus⟧ is sometimes used, chiefly in colloquial language, for ⟦b:nōn⟧ or ⟦b:nē⟧ (⟦r1051:1051⟧): as, ⟦b:Philotīmus nūllus vēnit⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 11, 24, 4, ⟦i:no Philotimus has shown himself⟧. ⟦b:nūllus crēduās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 606, ⟦i:you needn’t believe it at all⟧.
⟦#1449⟧
(2.) The negative ⟦b:haut⟧ or ⟦b:haud⟧, ⟦i:not⟧, is used principally with adjectives and adverbs, less frequently with verbs: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:haud mediocris vir⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 2, 55, ⟦i:no ordinary man⟧. ⟦b:rem haud sānē difficilem⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 4, ⟦i:a thing not particularly hard⟧. ⟦b:haud procul⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 15, ⟦i:not far⟧. In all periods of the language often combined with ⟦b:quisquam⟧, ⟦b:ūllus⟧, ⟦b:umquam⟧, ⟦b:usquam⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) In old Latin ⟦b:haud⟧ is freely used with all sorts of verbs, especially with ⟦b:possum⟧. In Cicero, it occurs here and there with a few verbs, such as ⟦b:adsentior⟧, ⟦b:errō⟧, ⟦b:īgnōrō⟧, ⟦b:nītor⟧, ⟦b:amō⟧, but is principally confined to ⟦b:sciō⟧, in the combination ⟦b:haud sciō an⟧, ⟦i:I don’t know but⟧ (⟦r1782:1782⟧). Caesar uses ⟦b:haud⟧ once only, and then in this combination.
⟦#1450⟧
A shorter form, ⟦b:hau⟧, occurs often in old Latin, and a few times in the classical period: as, ⟦b:heic est sepulcrum hau pulcrum pulcrai fēminae⟧, CIL. I, 1007, 2, on the burial site of a woman, ⟦i:here is the site not sightly of a sightly dame⟧. In Plautus it is juxtaposed with ⟦b:sciō⟧, making ⟦b:hausciō⟧, i.e. ⟦b:nesciō⟧.
⟦#1451⟧
(3.) Negation may also be intimated by such words as ⟦b:vix⟧, ⟦i:hardly⟧, ⟦b:parum⟧, ⟦i:not . . . enough⟧, ⟦i:not quite⟧, ⟦b:minus⟧, ⟦i:less⟧, ⟦i:not⟧, ⟦b:minimē⟧, ⟦i:least of all⟧, ⟦b:male⟧, &c.
⟦#1452⟧
Two negatives in the same sentence are usually equivalent to an affirmative.
Thus, with ⟦b:nōn⟧ first, an indefinite affirmative: as, ⟦b:nōn nēmō⟧, ⟦i:somebody⟧, ⟦i:a certain gentleman⟧, ⟦i:one or another⟧. ⟦b:nōn nūllus⟧, ⟦i:some⟧. ⟦b:nōn nihil⟧, ⟦i:something⟧, ⟦i:somewhat⟧. ⟦b:nōn numquam⟧, ⟦i:sometimes⟧. With ⟦b:nōn⟧ second, a universal affirmative: as, ⟦b:nēmō nōn⟧, ⟦i:everybody⟧, ⟦i:every human being⟧. ⟦b:nūllus nōn⟧, ⟦i:every⟧. ⟦b:nihil nōn⟧, ⟦i:every thing⟧. ⟦b:numquam nōn⟧, ⟦i:always⟧. ⟦b:nōn possum nōn cōnfitērī⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 9, 14, 1, ⟦i:I must confess⟧. ⟦b:nēmō īgnōrat⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 111, ⟦i:everybody knows⟧.
⟦#1453⟧
Sometimes, however, in old Latin, a second negation is used merely to emphasize the negative idea: as, ⟦b:lapideō sunt corde multī, quōs nōn miseret nēminis⟧, E. in Fest. p. 162, ⟦i:there’s many a man with heart of stone, that feels for nobody⟧. For doubled negatives in compound sentences, see ⟦r1660:1660⟧.

title: The Positive
text:
⟦#1454⟧
The positive sometimes expresses an idea of disproportion: as,
⟦b:prō multitūdine hominum angustōs sē fīnīs habēre arbitrābantur⟧, 1, 2, 5, ⟦i:in view of their large numbers they thought they had a cramped place to live in⟧. Generally, however, disproportion is expressed as in 1460 or 1461.

title: The Comparative
text:
⟦#1455⟧
When two things only are compared, the comparative is used: as,
