⟦b:uter igitur melior?⟧ ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 133, ⟦i:which of the two then is the better?⟧ ⟦b:uter est īnsānior hōrum?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 3, 102, ⟦i:which of these two is crazier?⟧ ⟦b:uter erātis, tūn an ille, maior?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 1119, ⟦i:you were—which of the two the bigger, thou or he?⟧
⟦#1456⟧
The superlative is sometimes loosely used when only two things are meant: as, ⟦b:Numitōrī, quī stirpis maximus erat, rēgnum lēgat⟧, L. 1, 3, 10, ⟦i:to Numitor, who was the eldest of the family, he bequeaths the crown⟧, of two brothers, Numitor and Amulius. ⟦b:id me͡ā minumē rēfert, quī sum nātū maxumus⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 881, ⟦i:that is of small concern to me, who am the eldest son⟧, says Demea, who has only one brother.
⟦#1457⟧
From Cicero on, an adjective or adverb is sometimes compared with another adjective or adverb. In such comparisons ⟦b:quam⟧ is always used.
In this case: (⟦i:a.⟧) Both members may have the positive form, the first with ⟦b:magis⟧: as, ⟦b:Celer disertus magis est quam sapiēns⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 10, 1, 4, ⟦i:Celer is more eloquent than wise⟧. ⟦b:magis audācter quam parātē⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 241, ⟦i:with more assurance than preparation⟧. Or (⟦i:b.⟧) Both members may have the comparative suffix: as, ⟦b:lubentius quam vērius⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 78, ⟦i:with greater satisfaction than truth⟧. ⟦b:pestilentia minācior quam perniciōsior⟧, L. 4, 52, 3, ⟦i:a plague more alarming than destructive⟧.
⟦#1458⟧
But sometimes the second member is put in the positive, even when the first has the comparative suffix: as, ⟦b:ācrius quam cōnsīderātē⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 1, 83, ⟦i:with more spirit than deliberation⟧. And sometimes both members: as, ⟦b:clārīs maiōribus quam vetustīs⟧, Ta. 4, 61, ⟦i:of a house famous rather than ancient⟧.
⟦#1459⟧
The comparative may be modified by ablatives of difference, such as ⟦b:multō⟧, ⟦i:far⟧, ⟦b:aliquantō⟧, ⟦i:considerably⟧, ⟦b:paullō⟧ or ⟦b:paulō⟧, ⟦i:a little⟧, ⟦b:nimiō⟧, ⟦i:too much⟧, ⟦i:ever so much⟧ (⟦r1393:1393⟧). Also by ⟦b:etiam⟧, ⟦i:even⟧, ⟦i:still⟧, and in Catullus, Sallust, Vergil, and later Latin by ⟦b:longē⟧, ⟦i:far⟧, ⟦b:adhūc⟧, ⟦i:still⟧.
⟦#1460⟧
The comparative of an adjective or adverb often denotes that which is more than usual or more than is right: as,
⟦b:solēre aiunt rēgēs Persārum plūrēs uxōrēs habēre⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 76, ⟦i:they say the Persian kings generally have several wives⟧. ⟦b:senectūs est nātūrā loquācior⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 55, ⟦i:age is naturally rather garrulous⟧. ⟦b:stomachābātur senex, sī quid asperius dīxeram⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 93, ⟦i:the old gentleman always got provoked if I said anything a bit rough⟧.
⟦#1461⟧
The comparative of disproportion is often defined by some added expression: as,
⟦b:prīvātīs maiōra focīs⟧, J. 4, 66, ⟦i:something too great for private hearths⟧ (⟦r1321:1321⟧). ⟦b:flāgrantior aequō nōn dēbet dolor esse virī⟧, J. 13, 11, ⟦i:the indignation of a man must not be over hot⟧ (⟦r1330:1330⟧). In Livy and Tacitus by ⟦b:quam prō⟧ with the ablative: see the dictionary. Sometimes a new sentence is added: as, ⟦b:sum avidior, quam satis est, glōriae⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 9, 14, 2, ⟦i:I am over greedy of glory⟧. For ⟦b:quam ut⟧ or ⟦b:quam quī⟧, see ⟦r1896:1896⟧.
⟦#1462⟧
The comparative with a sentence of negative import is often preferred to the superlative with a positive sentence: as,
⟦b:elephantō bēluārum nūlla prūdentior⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 97, ⟦i:of the larger beasts not one is more sagacious than the elephant⟧, or ⟦i:the elephant is the most sagacious of beasts⟧. ⟦b:sequāmur Polybium, quō nēmō fuit dīligentior⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 2, 27, ⟦i:let us follow Polybius, the most scrupulous of men⟧. For ⟦b:nēmō⟧ or ⟦b:quis⟧, the more emphatic ⟦b:nihil⟧ or ⟦b:quid⟧ is often used: as, ⟦b:Phaedrō nihil ēlegantius, nihil hūmānius⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 93, ⟦i:Phaedrus was the most refined and sympathetic of men⟧.
⟦#1463⟧
In colloquial language, a comparative suffix is sometimes emphasized by the addition of ⟦b:magis⟧: as, ⟦b:mollior magis⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 422, ⟦i:more tenderer⟧. And sometimes by a mixture of construction, the comparative is modified by ⟦b:aequē⟧, like the positive: as, ⟦b:homo mē miserior nūllus est aequē⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Mer.⟧ 335, ⟦i:there’s not a man so woebegone as I⟧, for ⟦b:miserior⟧ alone, or ⟦b:aequē miser⟧.
⟦#1464⟧
The comparative with the ablative is particularly common, when a thing is illustrated by some striking typical object, usually an object of nature. In such illustrations, the positive with ⟦i:as⟧ is commonly used in English: as, ⟦b:lūce clārius⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 186, ⟦i:plain as day⟧. ⟦b:ō fōns Bandusiae, splendidior vitrō⟧, H. 3, 13, 1, ⟦i:ye waters of Bandusia, as glittering as glass⟧. ⟦b:melle dulcior ōrātiō⟧, E. in ⟦i:CM.⟧ 31, ⟦i:words sweet as honey⟧. ⟦b:ventīs ōcior⟧, V. 5, 319, ⟦i:quick as the winds⟧. ⟦b:vacca candidior nivibus⟧, O. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 3, 5, 10, ⟦i:a cow as white as driven snow⟧. ⟦b:caelum pice nigrius⟧, O. ⟦i:H.⟧ 17, 7, ⟦i:a sky as black as pitch⟧. ⟦b:dūrior ferrō et saxō⟧, O. 14, 712, ⟦i:as hard as steel and stone⟧.

title: The Superlative
text:
⟦#1465⟧
When more than two things are compared, the superlative is used to represent a quality as belonging in the highest degree to an individual or to a number of a class: as,
⟦b:proximī sunt Germānīs⟧, 1, 1, 3, ⟦i:they live the nearest to the Germans⟧. ⟦b:hōrum omnium fortissimī⟧, 1, 1, 3, ⟦i:the bravest of these all⟧.
⟦#1466⟧
The superlative may be strengthened by the addition of such words as ⟦b:ūnus⟧, ⟦i:preeminently⟧, usually with a genitive, ⟦b:maximē⟧, ⟦b:quam⟧, with or without a form of ⟦b:possum⟧, ⟦i:as possible⟧, &c., &c. (⟦r1892:1892⟧). In old Latin by ⟦b:multō⟧; from Cicero on, by ⟦b:longē⟧, ⟦i:far⟧, and ⟦b:vel⟧, ⟦i:perhaps⟧, ⟦i:even⟧: as,
⟦b:cōnfirmāverim rem ūnam esse omnium difficillimam⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 25, ⟦i:I am not afraid to avouch it is the one hardest thing in the world⟧. ⟦b:longē nōbilissimus⟧, 1, 2, 1, ⟦i:the man of highest birth by far⟧. ⟦b:quam maximīs potest itineribus in Galliam contendit⟧, 1, 7, 1, ⟦i:he pushes into Gaul by the quickest marches he can⟧. ⟦b:quam mātūrrimē⟧, 1, 33, 4, ⟦i:as early as possible⟧.
⟦#1467⟧
The superlative is also used to denote a very high degree of the quality.
This superlative, called the ⟦i:Absolute Superlative⟧, or the ⟦i:Superlative of Eminence⟧, may be translated by the positive with some such word as ⟦i:most⟧, ⟦i:very⟧: as, ⟦b:homo turpissimus⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 16, ⟦i:an utterly unprincipled man⟧. Often best by the positive alone: as, ⟦b:vir fortissimus, Pīsō Aquītānus⟧, 4, 12, 4, ⟦i:the heroic Piso of Aquitain⟧ (⟦r1044:1044⟧).
⟦#1468⟧
In exaggerated style, the superlative of eminence may be capped by a comparative: as, ⟦b:stultior stultissumō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 907, ⟦i:a greater than the greatest fool⟧. ⟦b:ego miserior sum quam tū, quae es miserrima⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 14, 3, 1, ⟦i:I am myself more unhappy than you, who are a most unhappy woman⟧.

title: The Active Voice
text:
⟦#1469⟧
In the active voice, the subject is represented as performing the action of the verb.
⟦#1470⟧
By action is meant the operation of any verb, whether active or passive, and whether used intransitively or transitively.
⟦#1471⟧
The active of one verb sometimes serves as the passive of another: thus, ⟦b:pereō⟧, ⟦i:go to destruction⟧, ⟦i:die⟧, serves as the passive of ⟦b:perdō⟧, ⟦i:destroy⟧, and ⟦b:vēneō⟧, ⟦i:go to sale⟧, ⟦i:am sold⟧, as the passive of ⟦b:vēndō⟧, ⟦i:put for sale⟧, ⟦i:sell⟧. Similarly ⟦b:fīō⟧, ⟦i:become⟧, ⟦i:get to be⟧, ⟦i:am made⟧, is used in the present system as the passive of ⟦b:faciō⟧, ⟦i:make⟧ (⟦r788:788⟧).

title: The Passive Voice
text:
⟦#1472⟧
In the passive voice, the subject is represented as acted upon.
⟦#1473⟧
The object accusative of the active voice becomes the subject of the passive voice (⟦r1125:1125⟧); and the predicate accusative of the active voice becomes a predicate nominative with the passive voice (⟦r1167:1167⟧).
Thus (⟦i:a.⟧) in the active construction: ⟦b:illum laudābunt bonī, hunc etiam ipsī culpābunt malī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 397, ⟦i:the one the good will praise, the other e’en the bad themselves will blame⟧. In the passive: ⟦b:laudātur ab hīs, culpātur ab illīs⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 2, 11, ⟦i:he’s praised by some, by others blamed⟧. Active: ⟦b:cīvēs Rōmānōs interficiunt⟧, 7, 3, 1, ⟦i:they slay some citizens of Rome⟧. Passive: ⟦b:Indutiomarus interficitur⟧, 5, 58, 6, ⟦i:Indutiomarus is slain⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) Active: ⟦b:mīlitēs certiōrēs facit⟧, 3, 5, 3, ⟦i:he informs the soldiers⟧. Passive: ⟦b:certior factus est⟧, 2, 34, ⟦i:he was informed⟧.
⟦#1474⟧
Verbs which have two accusatives, one of the person and one of the thing in the active voice, generally have the person as subject in the passive, less frequently the thing: see ⟦r1171:1171⟧.
⟦#1475⟧
An emphasizing or defining accusative, or an accusative of extent or duration, is occasionally made the subject of a passive: as,
⟦b:haec illīc est pugnāta pugna⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 253, ⟦i:this fight was fought off there⟧ (⟦r1140:1140⟧). ⟦b:tōta mihī dormītur hiems⟧, Mart. 13, 59, 1, ⟦i:all winter long by me is slept⟧, i.e. ⟦b:tōtam dormiō hiemem⟧ (⟦r1151:1151⟧).
⟦#1476⟧
The person by whom the action is done is put in the ablative with ⟦b:ab⟧ or ⟦b:ā⟧ (⟦r1318:1318⟧); the thing by which it is done is put in the instrumental ablative (⟦r1377:1377⟧); as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:nōn numquam latrō ā viātōre occīditur⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 55, ⟦i:once in a while the robber gets killed by the wayfarer⟧. ⟦b:respondit, ā cīve sē spoliārī mālle quam ab hoste vēnīre⟧, Quintil. 12, 1, 43, ⟦i:he said in reply that he would rather be plundered by a Roman than sold by an enemy⟧ (⟦r1471:1471⟧). (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:ūnīus virī prūdentiā Graecia līberāta est⟧, N. 2, 5, 3, ⟦i:Greece was saved from slavery by the sagacity of a single man⟧, i.e. Themistocles. Very often, however, the person or thing is not expressed, particularly with impersonals.
⟦#1477⟧
When the person is represented as a mere instrument, the ablative is used without ⟦b:ab⟧ (⟦r1378:1378⟧); and when collectives, animals, or things without life are personified, the ablative takes ⟦b:ab⟧ (⟦r1318:1318⟧): as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:neque vērō minus Platō dēlectātus est Diōne⟧, N. 10, 2, 3, ⟦i:and Plato on his part was just as much bewitched with Dion⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:eius ōrātiō ā multitūdine et ā forō dēvorābātur⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 283, ⟦i:his oratory was swallowed whole by the untutored many and by the bar⟧.
⟦#1478⟧
Sometimes the person by whom the action is done is indicated by the dative of the possessor: see ⟦r1216:1216⟧. And regularly with the gerund and gerundive construction (⟦r2243:2243⟧).
⟦#1479⟧
Only verbs of transitive use have ordinarily a complete passive. Verbs of intransitive use have only the impersonal forms of the passive (⟦r1034:1034⟧): as,
⟦b:diū atque ācriter pugnātum est⟧, 1, 26, 1, ⟦i:there was long and sharp fighting⟧. ⟦b:tōtīs trepidātur castrīs⟧, 6, 37, 6, ⟦i:all through the camp there was tumult and affright⟧. ⟦b:mihī̆ quidem persuādērī numquam potuit, animōs ēmorī⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 80, ⟦i:for my part, I never could be convinced that the soul becomes extinct at death⟧ (⟦r1181:1181⟧). Similarly verbs which have a transitive use may also be used impersonally: as, ⟦b:di͡ēs noctīsque ēstur, bibitur⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 235, ⟦i:there is eating and drinking all day and all night⟧ (⟦r1133:1133⟧).
⟦#1480⟧
The complementary dative of a verb in the active voice is in poetry very rarely made the subject of a passive verb: as, ⟦b:invideor⟧, H. ⟦i:AP.⟧ 56, ⟦i:I am envied⟧. ⟦b:imperor⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 5, 21, ⟦i:I charge myself⟧.
⟦#1481⟧
The passive had originally a reflexive meaning, which is still to be seen in the passive of many verbs: as,
⟦b:exercēbātur plūrimum currendō et lūctandō⟧, N. 15, 2, 4, ⟦i:he took a great deal of exercise in running and wrestling⟧. ⟦b:dēnsōs fertur in hostīs⟧, V. 2, 511, ⟦i:he tries to charge upon the serried foes⟧. ⟦b:quod semper movētur, aeternum est⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 53, ⟦i:anything that is always moving, is eternal⟧.
⟦#1482⟧
The present participle of reflexives is sometimes used in a reflexive sense: as, ⟦b:exercēns⟧, ⟦i:exercising oneself⟧, ⟦i:exercising⟧, ⟦b:ferēns⟧, ⟦i:tearing along⟧, ⟦b:vehēns⟧, ⟦i:riding⟧, and ⟦b:invehēns⟧, ⟦i:mounted on⟧, ⟦b:pāscēns⟧, ⟦i:browsing⟧, ⟦b:versāns⟧, ⟦i:playing⟧, ⟦i:being⟧, ⟦b:volvēns⟧, ⟦i:rolling⟧. Also the gerund: as, ⟦b:iūs vehendī⟧, ⟦i:the privilege of riding⟧.
⟦#1483⟧
Passive forms of ⟦b:coepī⟧ and ⟦b:dēsinō⟧ are commonly used in the perfect system, when a dependent infinitive is passive: as,
⟦b:litterīs ōrātiō est coepta mandārī⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 26, ⟦i:oratory began to be put in black and white⟧. ⟦b:veterēs ōrātiōnēs legī sunt dēsitae⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 123, ⟦i:the old speeches ceased to be read⟧. But the active forms are sometimes used by Cornificius, Sallust, and Livy, and regularly by Tacitus. The active forms are used with ⟦b:fierī⟧ also, which is not passive (⟦r789:789⟧); but even with ⟦b:fierī⟧, Livy uses the passive forms.
⟦#1484⟧
Similar attractions with a passive infinitive occur in ⟦b:potestur⟧, &c., ⟦b:quītur⟧ and ⟦b:quitus sum⟧, ⟦b:nequītur⟧, &c., rarely, and mostly in old Latin: as, ⟦b:fōrma in tenebrīs nōscī nōn quitast⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 572, ⟦i:her shape could hardly be distinguished in the dark⟧.
⟦#1485⟧
Some perfect participles have an active meaning: as, ⟦b:adultus⟧, ⟦i:grown up⟧. See ⟦r907:907⟧, and also in the dictionary ⟦b:cautus⟧, ⟦b:cōnsultus⟧, ⟦b:concrētus⟧, ⟦b:dēflāgrātus⟧, ⟦b:incōnsīderātus⟧, ⟦b:occāsus⟧, ⟦b:nūpta⟧.

title: Deponents
text:
⟦#1486⟧
Many verbs have only passive inflections, but with the meaning of active inflections. Such verbs are called ⟦i:Deponents⟧.
⟦#1487⟧
In many deponents, a reflexive, passive, or reciprocal action is still clearly to be seen: as,
⟦b:nāscor⟧, ⟦i:am born⟧; ⟦b:moror⟧, ⟦i:delay myself⟧, ⟦i:get delayed⟧; ⟦b:ūtor⟧, ⟦i:avail myself⟧; ⟦b:amplectimur⟧, ⟦i:hug each other⟧; ⟦b:fābulāmur⟧, ⟦i:talk together⟧; ⟦b:partīmur⟧, ⟦i:share with one another⟧.
⟦#1488⟧
Some verbs have both active and deponent inflections: as, ⟦b:adsentiō⟧, ⟦i:agree⟧, more commonly ⟦b:adsentior⟧. ⟦b:mereō⟧, ⟦i:earn⟧, and ⟦b:mereor⟧, ⟦i:deserve⟧. See also in the dictionary ⟦b:altercor⟧, ⟦b:auguror⟧, ⟦b:comitor⟧, ⟦b:cōnflīctor⟧, ⟦b:fabricor⟧, ⟦b:faeneror⟧, ⟦b:mūneror⟧, ⟦b:ōscitor⟧, ⟦b:palpor⟧, ⟦b:populor⟧, ⟦b:revertor⟧. The following have active inflections in the present system and deponent inflections in the perfect system: ⟦b:audeō⟧, ⟦b:cōnfīdō⟧ and ⟦b:diffīdō⟧, ⟦b:gaudeō⟧, ⟦b:soleō⟧: see also ⟦r801:801⟧.
⟦#1489⟧
In old Latin especially, many verbs which afterwards became fixed as deponents occur with active inflections also: as, ⟦b:adūlō⟧, ⟦b:arbitrō⟧, ⟦b:aucupō⟧, ⟦b:auspicō⟧, ⟦b:lūctō⟧, ⟦b:lūdificō⟧, ⟦b:morō⟧, ⟦b:partiō⟧, ⟦b:venerō⟧, &c., &c.
⟦#1490⟧
Verbs which are usually deponent are rarely found with a passive meaning: as, ⟦b:Sūllānās rēs dēfendere crīminor⟧, ⟦i:LAgr.⟧ 3, 13, ⟦i:I am charged with defending Sulla’s policy⟧.
⟦#1491⟧
When it is desirable to express the passive of a deponent, a synonyme is sometimes used: thus, the passive of ⟦b:mīror⟧, ⟦i:admire⟧, may sometimes be represented by ⟦b:laudor⟧, ⟦i:am praised⟧. Or some circumlocution: as, ⟦b:habet venerātiōnem quidquid excellit⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 45, ⟦i:anything best in its kind is looked on with respect⟧, as passive of ⟦b:veneror⟧. ⟦b:familia in suspīciōnem est vocāta⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 10, ⟦i:the household was suspected⟧, as passive of ⟦b:suspicor⟧.
⟦#1492⟧
The perfect participle of deponents is sometimes used with a passive meaning. Some of the commonest of these participles are: ⟦b:adeptus⟧, ⟦b:commentus⟧, ⟦b:complexus⟧, ⟦b:cōnfessus⟧, ⟦b:ēmentītus⟧, ⟦b:expertus⟧, ⟦b:meditātus⟧, ⟦b:opīnātus⟧, ⟦b:pactus⟧, ⟦b:partītus⟧, ⟦b:testātus⟧, &c., &c.

title: Declarations
text:
⟦#1493⟧
The indicative mood is used in simple, absolute declarations: as,
⟦b:arma virumque canō⟧, V. 1, 1, ⟦i:arms and the man I sing⟧. ⟦b:leve fit quod bene fertur onus⟧, O. ⟦i:A.⟧ 4, 2, 10, ⟦i:light gets the load that’s bravely borne⟧.
⟦#1494⟧
The negative used with the indicative is commonly ⟦b:nōn⟧, ⟦i:not⟧ (⟦r1443:1443⟧). For other negative expressions, see ⟦r1445:1445-1451⟧.
⟦#1495⟧
Certain verbs and verbal expressions denoting ability, duty, propriety, necessity, and the like, mostly with an infinitive, are regularly put in the indicative, even when the action of the infinitive is not performed.
This applies to declarations, questions, or exclamations: as, (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:possum dē ichneumonum ūtilitāte dīcere, sed nōlō esse longus⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 101, ⟦i:I might expatiate on the usefulness of the ichneumon, but I do not care to be long-winded⟧. ⟦b:inter ferās satius est aetātem dēgere quam in hāc tantā immānitāte versārī⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 150, ⟦i:it would be better to pass your days in the midst of howling beasts than to live and move among such brutish men⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:stultī erat sperāre⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2. 23, ⟦i:it would have been folly to hope⟧. ⟦b:quid enim facere poterāmus?⟧ ⟦i:Pis.⟧ 13, ⟦i:for what else could we have done?⟧ (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:licuit uxōrem genere summō dūcere⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 680, ⟦i:I might have married a wife of high degree⟧. ⟦b:nōn potuit pīctor rēctius dēscrībere eius fōrmam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 402, ⟦i:no painter could have hit his likeness more exactly⟧. (⟦i:d.⟧) ⟦b:quantō melius fuerat prōmissum patris nōn esse servātum⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 94, ⟦i:how much better it would have been, for the father’s word not to have been kept⟧.
⟦#1496⟧
The principal verbs and verbal expressions thus used are: (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:possum⟧, ⟦b:licet⟧, ⟦b:dēbeō⟧, ⟦b:oportet⟧, ⟦b:convenit⟧, ⟦b:decet⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:aequum⟧, ⟦b:aequius⟧, ⟦b:iūstum⟧, ⟦b:fās⟧, ⟦b:necesse est⟧; ⟦b:cōnsentāneum⟧, ⟦b:satis⟧, ⟦b:satius⟧, ⟦b:optābile⟧, ⟦b:optābilius est⟧; ⟦b:ūtilius⟧, ⟦b:melius⟧, ⟦b:optimum⟧, ⟦b:pār⟧, ⟦b:rēctum est⟧; ⟦b:facile⟧, ⟦b:difficile⟧, ⟦b:grave⟧, ⟦b:īnfīnītum⟧, ⟦b:longum⟧, ⟦b:magnum est⟧; ⟦b:est⟧ with the predicative genitive, or a possessive pronoun (⟦r1237:1237⟧). (⟦i:c.⟧) Similarly, but without an infinitive, forms of ⟦b:sum⟧ with a gerund, a gerundive, or a future participle.
⟦#1497⟧
The imperfect of most of the above verbs and verbal expressions often relates to action not performed at the present time: as,
⟦b:hīs aliās poteram subnectere causās; sed eundum est⟧, J. 3, 315, ⟦i:to these I might add other grounds; but I must go⟧. The context must determine whether the imperfect relates (⟦i:a.⟧) to action not performed either in the present as here, or in the past as in 1495, or (⟦i:b.⟧) to action performed in the past: as, ⟦b:sollicitāre poterat, audēbat⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 16, ⟦i:he had at once the assurance and the ability to play the tempter’s part⟧.
⟦#1498⟧
Forms of ⟦b:possum⟧ are sometimes put in the subjunctive (⟦r1554:1554⟧). Thus, ⟦b:possim⟧, &c., often (⟦r1556:1556⟧), also ⟦b:possem⟧, &c., usually of present time (⟦r1560:1560⟧), less frequently of past time (⟦r1559:1559⟧), ⟦b:potuissem⟧, &c., particularly in sentences of negative import (⟦r1561:1561⟧), rarely ⟦b:potuerim⟧, &c. (⟦r1558:1558⟧). Sometimes also ⟦b:dēbērem⟧, &c., of present time (⟦r1560:1560⟧), ⟦b:dēbuissem⟧, &c., chiefly in apodosis.

title: The Indicative Mood: Questions
text:
⟦#1499⟧
The indicative is the mood ordinarily used in enquiries and in exclamations: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:huic ego ‘studēs?’ inquam. respondit ‘etiam.’ ‘ubī̆?’ ‘Mediōlānī.’ ‘cūr nōn hīc?’ ‘quia nūllōs hīc praeceptōrēs habēmus,’⟧ Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 4, 13, 3, ⟦i:said I to the boy, ‘do you go to school?’ ‘yes, sir,’ said he; ‘where?’ ‘at Mediolanum;’ ‘why not here?’ ‘oh because we haven’t any teachers here.’⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:ut ego tuum amōrem et dolōrem dēsīderō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 3, 11, 12, ⟦i:how I always feel the absence of your affectionate sympathy⟧.
⟦#1500⟧
Questions and exclamations are used much more freely in Latin than in English. Particularly common are two questions, of which the first is short and general, leading up to the real question: as,
⟦b:sed quid ais? ubi nunc adulēscēns habet?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 156, ⟦i:but tell me, where is the youngster living now?⟧ ⟦b:estne? vīcī? et tibī̆ saepe litterās dō?⟧ Cael. in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 8, 3, 1, ⟦i:is it true? have I beaten? and do I write to you often?⟧ The real question is often preceded by ⟦b:quid est⟧, ⟦b:quid dīcis⟧, or by ⟦b:quid⟧, ⟦b:quid vērō⟧, ⟦b:quid tum⟧, ⟦b:quid posteā⟧, ⟦b:quid igitur⟧, ⟦b:quid ergō⟧, &c., &c.: as, ⟦b:quid? canis nōnne similis lupō?⟧ ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 97, ⟦i:why, is not the dog like the wolf?⟧
⟦#1501⟧
There are two kinds of questions: (1.) Such questions as call for the answer ⟦i:yes⟧ or ⟦i:no⟧ in English: as, ⟦i:is he gone?⟧ These may conveniently be called ⟦i:Yes or No Questions⟧. (2.) Questions introduced by an interrogative pronoun, or by a word derived from an interrogative pronoun: as, ⟦i:who is gone? where is he?⟧ These are called ⟦i:Pronoun Questions⟧.

title: The Indicative Mood: Yes or No Questions
text:
⟦#1502⟧
(1.) Yes or No questions are sometimes put without any interrogative particle: as,
⟦b:Thraex est Gallīna Syrō pār?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 5, 44, of two gladiators, ⟦i:is Thracian Bantam for the Syrian a match?⟧ Often intimating censure: as, ⟦b:rogās?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 634, ⟦i:dost ask?⟧ or ⟦i:what an absurd question⟧. ⟦b:prōmpsistī tū illī vīnum? :: nōn prōmpsī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 830, ⟦i:thou hast been broaching wine for him? :: not I⟧. Especially with ⟦b:nōn⟧: as, ⟦b:patēre tua cōnsilia nōn sentīs?⟧ ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 1, ⟦i:you don’t see that your schemes are out?⟧ It is often doubtful whether such sentences are questions, exclamations, or declarations.
⟦#1503⟧
(2.) Yes or No questions are usually introduced by one of the interrogative particles ⟦b:-ne⟧ or ⟦b:-n⟧, ⟦b:nōnne⟧, ⟦b:num⟧, ⟦b:an⟧, ⟦b:anne⟧.
⟦#1504⟧
A question with ⟦b:-ne⟧ or ⟦b:-n⟧ may enquire simply, without any implication as to the character of the answer, or it may either expect an affirmative answer like ⟦b:nōnne⟧, or less frequently a negative answer like ⟦b:num⟧: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:valen?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 50, ⟦i:art well?⟧ ⟦b:habētin aurum?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 269, ⟦i:have you got the gold?⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:iussīn in splendōrem darī bullās hās foribus?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 426, ⟦i:didn’t I give orders to polish up the bosses of the door?⟧ ⟦b:facitne ut dixī?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 526, ⟦i:isn’t he acting as I said?⟧ (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:istō immēnsō spatiō quaerō, Balbe, cūr Pronoea vestra cessāverit. labōremne fugiēbat?⟧ ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 22, ⟦i:I want to know, Balbus, why your people’s Providence lay idle all that immeasurable time; it was work she was shirking, was it?⟧ ⟦b:quid, mundum praeter hunc umquamne vīdistī? negābis⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 96, ⟦i:tell me, did you ever see any universe except this one? you will say no⟧.
⟦#1505⟧
Sometimes the ⟦b:-ne⟧ of an interrogative sentence is transferred to a following relative, chiefly in Plautus and Terence: as, ⟦b:rogās? quīne arrabōnem ā mē accēpistī ob mulierem?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 860, ⟦i:how can you ask, when you have got the hansel for the girl from me?⟧ Similarly, ⟦b:ō sērī studiōrum, quīne putētis difficile⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 10, 21, ⟦i:what laggards at your books, to think it hard⟧, i.e. ⟦b:nōnne estis sērī studiōrum, quī putētis difficile?⟧ Compare 1569.
⟦#1506⟧
To a question with ⟦b:nōnne⟧, a positive answer is usually expected, seldom a negative: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:nōnne meministī? :: meminī vērō⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 10, ⟦i:don’t you remember? :: oh yes⟧. Sometimes a second or third question also has ⟦b:nōnne⟧, but oftener ⟦b:nōn⟧: as, ⟦b:nōnne ad tē L. Lentulus, nōn Q. Sanga, nōn L. Torquātus vēnit?⟧ ⟦i:Pis.⟧ 77, ⟦i:did not Lentulus and Sanga and Torquatus come to see you?⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:nōnne cōgitās?⟧ ⟦i:RA.⟧ 80, ⟦i:do you bear in mind?⟧ ⟦b:nōnne⟧ is rare in Plautus, comparatively so in Terence, but very common in classical Latin.
⟦#1507⟧
To a question with ⟦b:num⟧ a negative answer is generally expected. Less frequently either a positive or a negative answer indifferently: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:num negāre audēs?⟧ ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 8, ⟦i:do you undertake to deny it?⟧ ⟦b:num, tibi cum faucēs ūrit sitis, aurea quaeris pōcula?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 2, 114, ⟦i:when thirst thy throat consumes, dost call for cups of gold?⟧ Rarely ⟦b:numne⟧: as, ⟦b:quid, deum ipsum numne vīdistī?⟧ ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 88, ⟦i:tell me, did you ever see god in person?⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:sed quid ais? num obdormīvistī dūdum?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 620, ⟦i:but harkee, wert asleep a while ago?⟧ ⟦b:numquīd vīs?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 192, ⟦i:hast any further wish?⟧
⟦#1508⟧
A question with ⟦b:an⟧, less often ⟦b:anne⟧, or if negative, with ⟦b:an nōn⟧, usually challenges or comments emphatically on something previously expressed or implied: as,
⟦b:an habent quās gallīnae manūs?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 29, ⟦i:what, what, do hens have hands?⟧ ⟦b:an⟧ is also particularly common in argumentative language, in anticipating, criticising, or refuting an opponent: as, ⟦b:quid dīcis? an bellō Siciliam virtūte tuā līberātam?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 5, ⟦i:what do you say? possibly that it was by your prowess that Sicily was rid of the war?⟧ ⟦b:at vērō Cn. Pompēī voluntātem ā mē aliēnābat ōrātiō mea. an ille quemquam plūs dīlēxit?⟧ ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 38, ⟦i:but it may be urged that my way of speaking estranged Pompey from me. why, was there anybody the man loved more?⟧ In old Latin, ⟦b:an⟧ is oftener used in a single than in an alternative question, while in classical Latin it is rather the reverse.
⟦#1509⟧
(3.) Yes or No questions are sometimes introduced by ⟦b:ecquis⟧, ⟦b:ecquō⟧, ⟦b:ecquandō⟧, or ⟦b:ēn umquam⟧: as,
⟦i:heus, ecquis hīc est?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 420, ⟦i:hollo, is e’er a person here?⟧ ⟦b:ecquid animadvertis hōrum silentium?⟧ ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 20, ⟦i:do you possibly observe the silence of this audience?⟧ (⟦r1144:1144⟧). ⟦b:ō pater, ēn umquam aspiciam tē?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 588, ⟦i:O father, shall I ever set mine eyes on thee?⟧
⟦#1510⟧
(4.) In Plautus, ⟦b:satin⟧ or ⟦b:satin ut⟧, ⟦i:really⟧, ⟦i:actually⟧, sometimes becomes a mere interrogative or exclamatory particle: as, ⟦b:satin abiīt ille?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 481, ⟦i:has that man really gone his way?⟧

title: Positive and Negative Answers
text:
⟦#1511⟧
There are no two current Latin words corresponding exactly with ⟦i:yes⟧ and ⟦i:no⟧ in answers.
⟦#1512⟧
(1.) A positive answer is expressed by some emphatic word of the question, repeated with such change as the context may require: as,
⟦b:an nōn dīxī esse hoc futūrum? :: dīxtī⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 621, ⟦i:didn’t I say that this would be? :: you did⟧. ⟦b:hūc abiīt Clītiphō :: sōlus? :: sōlus⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 904, ⟦i:here Clitipho repaired :: alone? :: alone⟧. The repeated word may be emphasized by ⟦b:sānē⟧, ⟦b:vērō⟧: as, ⟦b:dāsne manēre animōs post mortem? :: dō vērō⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 25, ⟦i:do you grant that the soul lives on after death? :: oh yes⟧. Often, however, adverbs are used, without the repetition, such as ⟦b:certē⟧, ⟦b:certō⟧, ⟦b:etiam⟧, ⟦b:factum⟧, ⟦b:ita⟧, ⟦b:ita enimvērō⟧, ⟦b:ita vērō⟧, ⟦b:sānē⟧, ⟦b:sānē quidem⟧, ⟦b:scīlicet⟧, ⟦i:oh of course⟧, ⟦b:vērō⟧, rarely ⟦b:vērum⟧.
⟦#1513⟧
(2.) A negative answer is expressed by a similar repetition, with ⟦b:nōn⟧ or some other negative added: as,
⟦b:estne frāter intus? :: nōn est⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 569. ⟦i:is brother in? :: he’s not⟧. Or, without repetition, by such words as ⟦b:nōn⟧, ⟦b:nōn ita⟧, ⟦b:nōn quidem⟧, ⟦b:nōn hercle vērō⟧, ⟦b:minimē⟧, ⟦b:minimē quidem⟧, ⟦b:minimē vērō⟧, ⟦b:nihil minus⟧.
⟦#1514⟧
⟦b:immō⟧ introduces a sentence rectifying a mistake, implied doubt, or understatement in a question: as, ⟦b:nūllane habēs vitia? :: immō alia, et fortasse minōra⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 3, 20, ⟦i:have you no faults? :: I beg your pardon, other faults, and peradventure lesser ones⟧. ⟦b:causa igitur nōn bona est? immō optima⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 9, 7, 4, ⟦i:isn’t the cause a good one then? good? yes, more than good, very good⟧.

title: The Indicative Mood: Alternative Questions
text:
⟦#1515⟧
The alternative question belongs properly under the head of the compound sentence. But as the interrogative particles employed in the single question are also used in the alternative question, the alternative question is most conveniently considered here.
⟦#1516⟧
In old English, the first of two alternative questions is often introduced by the interrogative particle ⟦i:whether⟧, and the second by ⟦i:or⟧: as, ⟦i:whether is it easier to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee, or to say Arise?⟧ In modern English, ⟦i:whether⟧ is not used thus.
⟦#1517⟧
The history of the Latin alternative question is just the reverse of the English. In old Latin, the first question is very often put without any interrogative particle. Later, in the classical period, the use of ⟦b:-ne⟧, or oftener of ⟦b:utrum⟧, etymologically the same as ⟦i:whether⟧, is overwhelmingly predominant.
⟦#1518⟧
In the simplest form of the alternative sentence, neither question is introduced by an interrogative particle: as,
⟦b:quid agō? adeō, maneō?⟧ T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 736, ⟦i:what shall I do? go up and speak, or wait?⟧ (⟦r1531:1531⟧).
⟦#1519⟧
Of two alternative questions, the first either has no interrogative particle at all, or is more commonly introduced by ⟦b:utrum⟧, ⟦b:-ne⟧, or ⟦b:-n⟧. The second is introduced by ⟦b:an⟧, rarely by ⟦b:anne⟧, or if it is negative, by ⟦b:an nōn⟧: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:album an ātrum vīnum pōtās?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 915, ⟦i:do you take light wine or dark?⟧ ⟦b:Tacitus es an Plīnius?⟧ Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 9, 23, 3, ⟦i:are you Tacitus or Pliny?⟧ ⟦b:sortiētur an nōn?⟧ ⟦i:PC.⟧ 37, ⟦i:will he draw lots or not?⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:iam id porrō utrum libentēs an invītī dabant?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 118, ⟦i:then furthermore did they offer it voluntarily or did they consent to give it under stress?⟧ ⟦b:utrum cētera nōmina in cōdicem acceptī et expēnsī dīgesta habēs an nōn?⟧ ⟦i:RC.⟧ 9, ⟦i:have you all other items methodically posted in your ledger or not?⟧ (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:servosne es an līber?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 343, ⟦i:art bond or free?⟧ ⟦b:esne tū an nōn es ab illō mīlitī Macedoniō?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 616, ⟦i:art thou or art thou not the Macedonian captain’s man?⟧ ⟦b:videōn Clīniam an nōn?⟧ T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 405, ⟦i:do I see Clinia or not?⟧
⟦#1520⟧
⟦b:necne⟧ for ⟦b:an nōn⟧ is rare: as, ⟦b:sēmina praetereā linquontur necne animāī corpore in exanimō?⟧ Lucr. 3, 713, ⟦i:are seeds moreover left or not of soul within the lifeless frame?⟧ Twice in Cicero: as, ⟦b:sunt haec tua verba necne?⟧ ⟦i:TD.⟧ 3, 41, ⟦i:are these your words or not?⟧ But ⟦b:necne⟧ is common in indirect questions.
⟦#1521⟧
Instead of a single second question with ⟦b:an⟧, several questions may be used if the thought requires it, each introduced by ⟦b:an⟧.
⟦#1522⟧
Sometimes an introductory ⟦b:utrum⟧ precedes two alternative questions with ⟦b:-ne⟧ and ⟦b:an⟧: as, ⟦b:utrum tū māsne an fēmina ’s?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 104, ⟦i:which is it, art thou man or maid?⟧ This construction has its origin in questions in which ⟦b:utrum⟧ is used as a live pronoun: as, ⟦b:utrum māvīs? statimne nōs vēla facere an paululum rēmigāre?⟧ ⟦i:TD.⟧ 4, 9, ⟦i:which would you rather do, have us make sail at once, or row just a little bit?⟧ In Horace and late prose, ⟦b:utrumne . . . an⟧ is found a few times.
⟦#1523⟧
Sometimes a second alternative question is not put at all: as, ⟦b:utrum hōc bellum nōn est?⟧ ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 8, 7, in old English, ⟦i:whether is not this war?⟧
⟦#1524⟧
Two or more separate questions asked with ⟦b:-ne . . . -ne⟧, or with ⟦b:num ... num⟧, must not be mistaken for alternative questions: as, ⟦b:num Homērum, num Hēsiodum coēgit obmūtēscere senectūs?⟧ ⟦i:CM.⟧ 23, ⟦i:did length of days compel either Homer or Hesiod to hush his voice?⟧ (⟦r1692:1692⟧).
⟦#1525⟧
An alternative question is answered by repeating one member or some part of it, with such changes as the context may require.

title: The Indicative Mood: Pronoun Questions
text:
⟦#1526⟧
Pronoun questions or exclamations are introduced by interrogative pronouns, or words of pronoun origin.
Such words are: (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:quis⟧, ⟦b:quī⟧, ⟦b:quoius⟧, ⟦b:uter⟧, ⟦b:quālis⟧, ⟦b:quantus⟧, ⟦b:quotus⟧: as, ⟦b:quid rīdēs?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 5, 3, ⟦i:why dost thou laugh?⟧ (⟦r1144:1144⟧). ⟦b:uter est īnsānior hōrum?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 3, 102, ⟦i:which of these is the greater crank?⟧ ⟦b:hōra quota est?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 6, 44, ⟦i:what’s o’clock?⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) Or ⟦b:unde⟧, ⟦b:ubī̆⟧, ⟦b:quō⟧, ⟦b:quōr⟧ or ⟦b:cūr⟧, ⟦b:quī⟧ ablative, ⟦i:how⟧, ⟦b:quīn⟧, ⟦i:why not⟧, ⟦b:quam⟧, ⟦i:how⟧, ⟦b:quandō⟧, ⟦b:quotiēns⟧: as, ⟦b:unde venīs et quō tendis?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 9, 62, ⟦i:whence dost thou come, and whither art thou bound?⟧ ⟦b:deus fallī quī potuit?⟧ ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 76, ⟦i:how could a god have been taken in?⟧ (⟦r1495:1495⟧). ⟦b:quam bellum erat cōnfitērī nescīre⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 84, ⟦i:how pretty it would have been to own up that you did not know⟧ (⟦r1495:1495⟧).
⟦#1527⟧
Sometimes ⟦b:quīn⟧ loses its interrogative force, and introduces an impatient imperative, particularly in Plautus and Terence, or an indicative of sudden declaration of something obvious or startling: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:quīn mē aspice⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 172, ⟦i:why look me over, won’t you?⟧ i.e. ⟦b:mē aspice, quīn aspicis?⟧ So twice in Cicero’s orations. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:quīn discupiō dīcere⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 932, ⟦i:why I am bursting with desire to tell⟧.
⟦#1528⟧
In Plautus, Terence, Horace, and Livy, ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦i:how⟧, also is used in questions: as, ⟦b:ut valēs?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 1304, ⟦i:how do you do?⟧ ⟦b:ut sēsē in Samniō rēs habent?⟧ L. 10, 18, 11, ⟦i:how is every thing in Samnium?⟧ Very commonly, and in Cicero only so, in exclamations also: as, ⟦b:ut fortūnātī sunt fabrī ferrāriī, quī apud carbōnēs adsident; semper calent⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 531, ⟦i:what lucky dogs the blacksmiths be, that sit by redhot coals; they’re always warm⟧.
⟦#1529⟧
In poetry, ⟦b:quis⟧, ⟦b:uter⟧, and ⟦b:quantus⟧ are found a few times with ⟦b:-ne⟧ attached; as, ⟦b:uterne ad cāsūs dubiōs fīdet sibi certius?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 2, 107, ⟦i:which of the two in doubtful straits will better in himself confide?⟧
⟦#1530⟧
Two or more questions or exclamations are sometimes united with one and the same verb: as,
⟦b:unde quō vēnī?⟧ H. 3, 27, 37, ⟦i:whence whither am I come?⟧ ⟦b:quot diēs quam frīgidīs rēbus absūmpsī⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 1, 9, 3, ⟦i:how many days have I frittered away in utter vapidities⟧. ⟦b:quantae quotiēns occāsiōnēs quam praeclārae fuērunt⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 38, ⟦i:what great chances there were, time and again, splendid ones too⟧.

title: Some Applications of Questions
text:
⟦#1531⟧
A question in the indicative present or future may be used to intimate command or exhortation, deliberation, or appeal: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:abin hinc?⟧ T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 861, ⟦i:will you get out of this?⟧ ⟦b:abin an nōn? :: abeō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 660, ⟦i:will you begone or not? :: I’ll go⟧. ⟦b:quīn abīs?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 1087, ⟦i:why won’t you begone?⟧ or ⟦i:get you gone⟧, ⟦i:begone⟧. ⟦b:nōn tacēs?⟧ T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 987, ⟦i:won’t you just hold your tongue?⟧ ⟦b:ecquis currit pollinctōrem arcēssere?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 910, ⟦i:won’t some one run to fetch the undertaker man?⟧ ⟦b:quīn cōnscendimus equōs?⟧ L. 1, 57, 7, ⟦i:why not mount?⟧ or ⟦i:to horse, to horse⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:quid est, Crasse, īmusne sessum?⟧ ⟦i:DO.⟧ 3, 17, ⟦i:what say you, Crassus, shall we go and take a seat?⟧ ⟦b:quoi dōnō lepidum novum libellum?⟧ Cat. 1, 1, ⟦i:unto whom shall I give the neat new booklet?⟧ ⟦b:quid agō? adeō, maneō?⟧ T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 736, ⟦i:what shall I do? go up and speak, or wait?⟧ (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:eōn? vocō hūc hominem? :: ī, vocā⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 774, ⟦i:shall I go, and shall I call him here? :: go call him⟧. See also ⟦r1623:1623⟧. Such indicative questions occur particularly in old Latin, in Catullus, in Cicero’s early works and letters, and in Vergil.
⟦#1532⟧
Some set forms occur repeatedly, especially in questions of curiosity, surprise, incredulity, wrath, or captiousness: as,
⟦b:sed quid ais?⟧ T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 575, ⟦i:but apropos⟧, or ⟦i:but by the way⟧ (⟦r1500:1500⟧). ⟦b:quid istīc?⟧ T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 572, ⟦i:well, well, have it your way⟧: compare ⟦b:quid istīc verba facimus?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:E.⟧ 141. ⟦b:ain tū?⟧ ⟦i:Br.⟧ 152, ⟦i:no, not seriously?⟧ ⟦b:itane?⟧ T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 1058, ⟦i:not really?⟧ Frequently ⟦b:egone⟧: as, ⟦b:quid nunc facere cōgitās? :: egone?⟧ T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 608, ⟦i:what do you think of doing now? :: what, I?⟧ In Plautus, threats are sometimes introduced by ⟦b:scīn quō modō?⟧ ⟦i:do you know how?⟧ i.e. at your peril.
⟦#1533⟧
A question is sometimes united with a participle, or an ablative absolute, or thrown into a subordinate sentence: as,
⟦b:quem frūctum petentēs scīre cupimus illa quō modō moveantur?⟧ ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 3, 37, ⟦i:with what practical end in view do we seek to know how yon bodies in the sky keep in motion?⟧ ⟦b:quā frequentiā prōsequente crēditis nōs illinc profectōs?⟧ L. 7, 30, 21, ⟦i:by what multitudes do you think we were seen off when we left that town?⟧ ⟦b:‘hominēs’ inquit ‘ēmistī.’ quid utī faceret?⟧ ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 84, ⟦i:‘you bought up men’ says he; with what purpose?⟧

title: The Infinitive of Intimation
text:
⟦#1534⟧
The infinitive is principally used in subordination, and will be spoken of under that head. One use, however, of the present infinitive in main sentences, as a kind of substitute for a past indicative, requires mention here.
⟦#1535⟧
In animated narration, the present infinitive with a subject in the nominative sometimes takes the place of the imperfect or perfect indicative: as,
⟦b:interim cōtīdiē Caesar Aeduōs frūmentum flāgitāre⟧, 1, 16, 1, ⟦i:there was Caesar meantime every day dunning and dunning the Aeduans for the grain⟧. ⟦b:Diodōrus sordidātus circum hospitēs cursāre, rem omnibus nārrāre⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 41, ⟦i:Diodorus kept running round in sackcloth and ashes from friend to friend, telling his tale to everybody⟧. ⟦b:intereā Catilīna in prīmā aciē versārī, labōrantibus succurrere⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 60, 4, ⟦i:Catiline meantime bustling round in the forefront of battle, helping them that were sore bestead⟧. ⟦b:tum vērō ingentī sonō caelum strepere, et micāre ignēs, metū omnēs torpēre⟧, L. 21, 58, 5, ⟦i:at this crisis the welkin ringing with a dreadful roar, fires flashing, everybody paralyzed with fear⟧. This infinitive occurs in almost all writers, for instance, Plautus, Terence, Cicero, Horace, and particularly Sallust, Livy, and Tacitus. Less commonly in Caesar. Usually two or more infinitives are combined, and infinitives are freely mixed with indicatives. The subject is never in the second person.
⟦#1536⟧
This infinitive is used to sketch or outline persistent, striking, or portentous action, where description fails; and as it merely ⟦i:intimates⟧ the action, without distinct declaration, and without notation of time, number, or person, it is called the ⟦i:Infinitive of Intimation⟧. It cannot be adequately represented in English.
⟦#1537⟧
The infinitive of intimation is sometimes used without a subject, when emphasis centres in the action alone; as,
⟦b:ubī̆ turrim procul cōnstituī vīdērunt, inrīdēre ex mūrō⟧, 2, 30, 3, ⟦i:when they saw the tower planted some way off, jeer after jeer from the wall⟧. ⟦b:tum spectāculum horribile in campīs patentibus: sequī fugere, occīdī capī⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 101, 11, ⟦i:then a heartrending spectacle in the open fields: chasing and racing, killing and catching⟧.
⟦#1538⟧
Terence and Petronius have it in questions: as, ⟦b:rēx tē ergō in oculīs :: scīlicet :: gestāre? :: vērō⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 401, ⟦i:your king then always bearing you :: of course, of course :: in eye? :: oh yes⟧. ⟦b:quī morī timōre nisi ego?⟧ Petr. 62.
⟦#1539⟧
It may be mentioned here, that the infinitive of intimation is sometimes used from Sallust on in relative clauses and with ⟦b:cum⟧, ⟦i:when⟧. Also by Tacitus in a temporal protasis with ⟦b:ubī̆⟧, ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦b:dōnec⟧, or ⟦b:postquam⟧, co-ordinated with a present or imperfect indicative protasis: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:cingēbātur interim mīlite domus, cum Libō vocāre percussōrem⟧, Ta. 2, 31, ⟦i:the house meantime was encompassed with soldiers, when Libo called for somebody to kill him⟧ (⟦r1869:1869⟧). (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:ubī̆ crūdēscere sēditiō et ā convīciīs ad tēla trānsībant, inicī catēnās Flāviānō iubet⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 3, 10, ⟦i:when the riot was waxing hot, and they were proceeding from invectives to open violence, he orders Flavian to be clapped in irons⟧ (⟦r1933:1933⟧).

title: Wish
text:
⟦#1540⟧
The subjunctive may be used to express a wish.
Wishes are often introduced by ⟦b:utinam⟧, in old and poetical Latin also by ⟦b:utī⟧, ⟦b:ut⟧, and curses in old Latin by ⟦b:quī⟧; these words were originally interrogative, ⟦i:how⟧. Sometimes the wish is limited by ⟦b:modo⟧, ⟦i:only⟧. In negative wishes ⟦b:nē⟧ is used, either alone, or preceded by ⟦b:utinam⟧ or ⟦b:modo⟧; rarely ⟦b:nōn⟧, or the old-fashioned ⟦b:nec⟧, ⟦i:not⟧ (⟦r1446:1446⟧).
⟦#1541⟧
(1.) The present and perfect represent a wish as practicable; although a hopeless wish may, of course, if the speaker chooses, be represented as practicable: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:tē spectem, suprēma mihī cum vēnerit hōra⟧, Tib. 1, 1, 59, ⟦i:on thee I’d gaze, when my last hour shall come⟧. ⟦b:utinam illum diem videam⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 3, 3, ⟦i:I hope I may see the day⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:utinam cōnēre⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 101, ⟦i:I hope you may make the effort⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:dī vortant bene quod agās⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 196, ⟦i:may gods speed well whate’er you undertake⟧. ⟦b:quī illum dī omnēs perduint⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 123, ⟦i:him may all gods fordo⟧. ⟦b:ō utinam hībernae duplicentur tempora brūmae⟧, Prop. 1, 8, 9, ⟦i:oh that the winter’s time may doubled be⟧. ⟦b:utinam revīvīscat frāter⟧, Gell. 10, 6, 2, ⟦i:I hope my brother may rise from his grave⟧. ⟦b:nē istūc Iuppiter sīrit⟧, L. 28, 28, 11, ⟦i:now Jupiter forefend⟧. The perfect is found principally in old Latin.
⟦#1542⟧
The present is very common in asseveration: as,
⟦b:peream, nisi sollicitus sum⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 15, 19, 4, ⟦i:may I die, if I am not worried⟧. ⟦b:sollicitat, ita vīvam, me tua valētūdō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 20, ⟦i:your state of health worries me, as I hope to live⟧. ⟦b:ita vīvam, ut maximōs sūmptūs faciō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 5, 15, 2, ⟦i:as I hope to be saved, I am making great outlays⟧. See also ⟦r1622:1622⟧.
⟦#1543⟧
The perfect subjunctive sometimes refers to past action now completed: as, ⟦b:utinam abierit malam crucem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 799, ⟦i:I hope he’s got him to the bitter cross⟧ (⟦r1165:1165⟧). ⟦b:utinam spem implēverim⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 1, 10, 3, ⟦i:I hope I may have fulfilled the expectations⟧.
⟦#1544⟧
(2.) The imperfect represents a wish as hopeless in the present or immediate future, the pluperfect represents it as unfulfilled in the past: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:tēcum lūdere sīcut ipsa possem⟧, Cat. 2, 9, ⟦i:could I with thee but play, e’en as thy mistress’ self⟧, to Lesbia’s sparrow. ⟦b:utinam ego tertius vōbīs amīcus adscrīberer⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 63, ⟦i:would that I could be enrolled with you myself, as the third friend⟧, says tyrant Dionysius to Damon and Phintias. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:utinam mē mortuum prius vīdissēs⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 1, 3, 1, ⟦i:I wish you had seen me dead first⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:utinam nē in nemore Pēliō secūribus caesa accēdisset abiēgna ad terram trabēs⟧, E. in Cornif. 2, 34, ⟦i:had but, in Pelion’s grove, by axes felled, ne’er fallen to the earth the beam of fir⟧, i.e. for the Argo. ⟦b:utinam ille omnīs sēcum cōpiās ēdūxisset⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 4, ⟦i:I only wish the man had marched out all his train-bands with him⟧.
⟦#1545⟧
In old or poetical Latin, the imperfect sometimes denotes unfulfilled past action, like the usual pluperfect; as, ⟦b:utinam in Siciliā perbīterēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 494, ⟦i:would thou hadst died in Sicily⟧. ⟦b:utinam tē dī prius perderent⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 537, ⟦i:I wish the gods had cut thee off before⟧. See ⟦r2075:2075⟧.
⟦#1546⟧
In poetry, a wish is sometimes thrown into the form of a conditional protasis with ⟦b:sī⟧ or ⟦b:ō sī⟧: as, ⟦b:ō sī urnam argentī fōrs quae mihi mōnstret⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 6, 10, ⟦i:oh if some chance a pot of money may to me reveal⟧.

title: Exhortation, Direction, Statement of Propriety
text:
⟦#1547⟧
The subjunctive may be used to express an exhortation, a direction, or a statement of propriety.
The subjunctive of exhortation is sometimes preceded in old Latin by ⟦b:utī⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧, originally interrogative. In negative exhortations or directions, ⟦b:nē⟧, ⟦b:nēmō⟧, ⟦b:nihil⟧, or ⟦b:numquam⟧, &c., is used, rarely ⟦b:nōn⟧.
⟦#1548⟧
(1.) The present expresses what is to be done or is not to be done in the future: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:hoc quod coepī prīmum ēnārrem⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 273, ⟦i:first let me tell the story I’ve begun⟧. ⟦b:taceam nunc iam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 1058, ⟦i:let me now hold my tongue⟧. ⟦b:cōnsīdāmus hīc in umbrā⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 2, 7, ⟦i:let us sit down here in the shade⟧. ⟦b:nē difficilia optēmus⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 15, ⟦i:let us not hanker after impossibilities⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) HAICE · VTEI · IN · COVENTIONID · EXDEICATIS, CIL. I, 196, 23, ⟦i:this you are to proclaim in public assembly⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:nōmina dēclīnāre et verba in prīmīs puerī sciant⟧, Quintil. 1, 4, 22, ⟦i:first and foremost boys are to know how to inflect nouns and verbs⟧. ⟦b:utī adserventur magnā dīligentiā,⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 115, ⟦i:let them be watched with all due care⟧. ⟦b:nē quis tamquam parva fastīdiat grammaticēs elementa⟧, Quintil. 1, 4, 6, ⟦i:let no man look down on the rudiments of grammar fancying them insignificant⟧.
⟦#1549⟧
(2.) The perfect subjunctive is rare: as, ⟦b:idem dictum sit⟧, Quintil. 1, 1, 8, ⟦i:the same be said, once for all⟧. Mostly in prohibitions: as, ⟦b:morātus sit nēmō quō minus abeant⟧, L. 9, 11, 13, ⟦i:let no man hinder them from going away⟧.
⟦#1550⟧
In positive commands, the second person singular often has a definite subject in old or epistolary Latin, and particularly ⟦b:sīs⟧, for the imperative ⟦b:es⟧ or ⟦b:estō⟧. Usually however an indefinite subject (⟦r1030:1030⟧): as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:eās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 519, ⟦i:be off⟧. ⟦b:hīc apud nōs hodiē cēnēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 1129, ⟦i:dine here with us today⟧. ⟦b:cautus sīs, mī Tirō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 9, 4, ⟦i:you must be careful, dear Tiro⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:istō bonō ūtāre, dum adsit⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 33, ⟦i:enjoy this blessing while you have it with you⟧.
⟦#1551⟧
When a prohibition is expressed in the subjunctive, the second person of the present is often used in old Latin, sometimes the perfect. Later, however, the perfect is generally prevalent. In the classical period, the present is almost confined to poetry. For the imperative in prohibitions, see ⟦r1581:1581-1586⟧.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:nē illum verberēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 747, ⟦i:you mustn’t thrash the man⟧. Once in Horace: ⟦b:nē sīs patruos mihī⟧, ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 3, 88, ⟦i:don’t play stern governor to me⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:nē trānsierīs Ibērum⟧, L. 21, 44, 6, ⟦i:do not cross the Iberus⟧. ⟦b:quod dubitās nē fēcerīs⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 1, 18, 5, ⟦i:what you have doubt about, never do⟧.
⟦#1552⟧
(3.) The imperfect or (but not in old Latin) pluperfect subjunctive is sometimes used to express past obligation or necessity: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) Imperfect: ⟦b:quae hīc erant cūrārēs⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 230, ⟦i:thou shouldst have looked to matters here⟧. ⟦b:paterētur⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 202, ⟦i:he should have stood it⟧. ⟦b:quod sī meīs incommodīs laetābantur, urbis tamen perīculō commovērentur⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 54, ⟦i:well, if they did gloat over my mishaps, still they ought to have been touched by the danger to Rome⟧. ⟦b:crās īrēs potius⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 710, ⟦i:you’d better have gone tomorrow⟧, i.e. have resolved to go tomorrow. ⟦b:poenās penderēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 427, ⟦i:thou hadst to pay a penalty⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) Pluperfect: ⟦b:restitissēs, rēpugnāssēs, mortem pugnāns oppetīssēs⟧, Poet. in ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 45, ⟦i:thou shouldst have made a stand, fought back, and fighting met thy fate⟧. ⟦b:quid facere dēbuistī? frūmentum nē ēmissēs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 195, ⟦i:what ought you to have done? you should not have bought any wheat⟧. Usually, however, past obligation or necessity is expressed by the gerundive construction, or by some separate verb meaning ⟦i:ought⟧ (⟦r1496:1496⟧).

title: Willingness, Assumption, Concession
text:
⟦#1553⟧
The subjunctive of desire may be used to denote willingness, assumption, or concession: as,
⟦b:ōderint dum metuant⟧, Poet. in Suet. ⟦i:Cal.⟧ 30, ⟦i:they are welcome to hate, as long as they fear⟧. ⟦b:nē sit sānē summum malum dolor, malum certē est,⟧ ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 14, ⟦i:grant for aught I care that pain is not the worst evil, an evil it certainly is⟧. ⟦b:nīl fēcerit, estō⟧, J. 6, 222, ⟦i:he may be guiltless, be it so⟧.

title: The Subjunctive of Action Conceivable
text:
⟦#1554⟧
The subjunctive is often used to represent action as conceivable, without asserting that it actually takes place.
In some of its applications, this subjunctive is often more exactly defined by an expression of doubt or of assurance: as, ⟦b:fors fuat an⟧ in Plautus, ⟦b:forsitan⟧ from Terence on (rarely ⟦b:forsan⟧, ⟦b:fors⟧), ⟦b:fortasse⟧, ⟦i:may be⟧, ⟦i:perhaps⟧; ⟦b:opīnor⟧, ⟦b:haud sciō an⟧, ⟦i:I fancy⟧; ⟦b:facile⟧, ⟦i:easily⟧, ⟦b:sine ūllā dubitātiōne⟧, ⟦i:unhesitatingly⟧, &c., &c. The negative used with this subjunctive is ⟦b:nōn⟧.
⟦#1555⟧
This subjunctive is particularly common in guarded or diffident statements: thus, ⟦b:velim⟧, ⟦i:I could wish⟧, ⟦b:nōlim⟧, ⟦i:I should not be willing⟧, ⟦b:mālim⟧, ⟦i:I would rather⟧, ⟦b:dīxerim⟧, ⟦i:I should say⟧, are often preferred to a blunter ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦i:I insist⟧, ⟦b:nōlō⟧, ⟦i:I won’t⟧, ⟦b:mālō⟧, ⟦i:I prefer⟧, or ⟦b:dīcō⟧, ⟦i:I say⟧.
⟦#1556⟧
The present denotes action in an indefinite future: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:ego forsitan in grege adnumerer⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 89, ⟦i:as for me, I might perhaps be counted in the common herd⟧. ⟦b:mūtuom argentum rogem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 758, ⟦i:money I might borrow⟧. ⟦b:haud sciō an rēctē dīcāmus⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 58, ⟦i:I rather think we may say with propriety⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) The second person singular generally has an imaginary subject (⟦r1030:1030⟧): as, ⟦b:dīcās hīc forsitan⟧, J. 1, 150, ⟦i:here peradventure thou mayst say⟧, i.e. anybody may say. ⟦b:rogēs mē quid sit deus, auctōre ūtar Simōnidē⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 60, ⟦i:you may ask me what god is; I should follow the lead of Simonides⟧. ⟦b:migrantīs cernās⟧, V. 4, 401, ⟦i:thou canst descry them on the move⟧ (⟦r1635:1635⟧). Often with some generalizing word, such as ⟦b:saepe⟧, ⟦b:numquam⟧, ⟦b:plūrēs⟧: as, ⟦b:saepe videās⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 4, 86, ⟦i:thou oft canst see⟧. ⟦b:Fortūnam citius reperiās quam retineās⟧, Publil. Syr. 168, ⟦i:dame Fortune thou mayst sooner find than bind⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:nunc aliquis dīcat mihi⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 3, 19, ⟦i:now somebody may say to me⟧ (more commonly ⟦b:dīcet aliquis⟧, ⟦b:dīcēs⟧, ⟦r1620:1620⟧). ⟦b:forsitan aliquis dīcat⟧, L. 5, 52, 5, ⟦i:perhaps somebody may say⟧. ⟦b:hoc vōbīs incrēdibile videātur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 109, ⟦i:this may seem incredible to you⟧.
⟦#1557⟧
(1.) The perfect seldom occurs in old Latin. Later, it is rarely used of past time. In this use it resembles the perfect of concession (⟦r1553:1553⟧): as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:forsitan temere fēcerim⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 31, ⟦i:peradventure I may have acted rashly⟧. ⟦b:errāverim fortasse⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 1, 23, 2, ⟦i:I may have been mistaken perhaps⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:concēdō; forsitan aliquis aliquandō eius modī quippiam fēcerit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 78, ⟦i:I grant it; perhaps somebody, at some time or other, may have done something of the sort⟧. ⟦b:haec ipsa forsitan fuerint nōn necessāria⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 52, ⟦i:even this may perhaps have been superfluous⟧.
⟦#1558⟧
(2.) The perfect is oftenest used with a future meaning, and particularly the first person singular active of verbs meaning ⟦i:think⟧ or ⟦i:say⟧: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:nōn facile dīxerim⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 121, ⟦i:I could not readily say⟧. ⟦b:hoc sine ūllā dubitātiōne cōnfirmāverim⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 25, ⟦i:this I can assert without any hesitation⟧. ⟦b:pāce tuā dīxerim⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 12, ⟦i:by your leave I would say⟧. The first person plural occurs first in Cornificius, and is rare: as, ⟦b:hunc deum rīte beātum dīxerīmus⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 52, ⟦i:such a god we should be right in pronouncing happy⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:plānē perfectum Dēmosthenem facile dīxerīs⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 35, ⟦i:you would readily pronounce Demosthenes absolutely perfect⟧ (⟦r1030:1030⟧). ⟦b:tū vērō eum nec nimis valdē umquam nec nimis saepe laudāverīs⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 3, 1, ⟦i:oh no, rest assured you never can praise him too emphatically nor too often⟧. ⟦b:conluviem istam nōn nisi metū coērcuerīs⟧, Ta. 14, 44, ⟦i:such a motley rabble you can only keep under by terrorism⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:forsitan quispiam dīxerit⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 29, ⟦i:perhaps somebody may say⟧.
⟦#1559⟧
(1.) The imperfect properly denotes action which might have taken place in the past: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:nōn ego hoc ferrem calidus iuventā cōnsule Plancō⟧, H. 3, 14, 27, ⟦i:this I should not have brooked in my hot youth, in Plancus’ consulate⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) The second person singular, particularly of verbs meaning ⟦i:see⟧, ⟦i:make out⟧, ⟦i:think⟧, ⟦i:say⟧, generally has an imaginary subject (⟦r1030:1030⟧): as, ⟦b:vidērēs⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 8, 77, ⟦i:thou mightst have seen⟧. ⟦b:cernerēs⟧, L. 22, 7, 12, ⟦i:you might have descried⟧. ⟦b:nescīrēs⟧, L. 3, 35, 3, ⟦i:you could not have told⟧. ⟦b:tē columen rē̆ī pūblicae dīcerēs intuērī⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 19, ⟦i:you would have sworn you were gazing on a pillar of the state⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:quī vidēret, urbem captam dīceret⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 52, ⟦i:anybody who saw it, would have said it was a captured city⟧. ⟦b:dīcī hoc in tē nōn potest, posset in Tarquiniō, cum rēgnō esset expulsus⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 88, ⟦i:this cannot be said in your case; it might have been said in Tarquin’s, when he was driven from the throne⟧. ⟦b:numquam faceret⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 121, ⟦i:he never would have done it⟧.
⟦#1560⟧
(2.) The imperfect often denotes action not performed at the present time; so especially ⟦b:vellem⟧ (⟦b:nōllem⟧, ⟦b:māllem⟧): as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:nimis vellem habēre perticam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 589, ⟦i:I wish so much I had a stick⟧. ⟦b:vellem adesse posset Panaetius; quaererem ex eō⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 81, ⟦i:I only wish Panaetius could be with us: I should ask him⟧ (Panaetius was dead). ⟦b:cuperem voltum vidēre tuum⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 4, 16, 7, ⟦i:I should like to see the expression of your face⟧. ⟦b:māllem Cerberum metuerēs⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 12, ⟦i:I would rather you stood in dread of Cerberus⟧. ⟦b:possem idem facere⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 84, ⟦i:I could do the same⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:melius sequerēre cupīdine captam⟧, O. 14, 28, ⟦i:better for thee it were a loving bride to woo⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:in hāc fortūnā perūtilis eius opera esset⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 9, 17, 2, ⟦i:in the present pinch his services would be extremely valuable⟧.
⟦#1561⟧
The pluperfect represents action which did not take place in the past: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:vellem quidem licēret: hoc dīxissem⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 138, ⟦i:I only wish it were allowed; I should have said so and so⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:dedissēs huic animō pār corpus, fēcisset quod optābat⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 1, 12, 8, ⟦i:you might have given this spirit a body to match; he would have done what he craved to do⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:urbēs et rēgna celeriter tanta nēquitia dēvorāre potuisset⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 67, ⟦i:such colossal prodigality might have been capable of swallowing down cities and kingdoms speedily⟧. ⟦b:vīcissent inprobōs bonī; quid deinde?⟧ ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 43, ⟦i:the good might have overpowered the bad; what next?⟧
⟦#1562⟧
It may be mentioned here, that the subjunctive of action conceivable often extends to subordinate sentences: see ⟦r1731:1731⟧.

title: Mood: Questions
text:
⟦#1563⟧
I. The subjunctive is often used to ask what action or whether any action is desired, commanded, proper, or necessary.
In many instances a negative answer or no answer at all is expected The negative is ⟦b:nē⟧, sometimes ⟦b:nōn⟧.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:quō mē vertam?⟧ ⟦i:Scaur.⟧ 19, ⟦i:which way shall I turn?⟧ ⟦b:quid faciam, praescrībe :: quiēscās :: nē faciam, inquis, omnīnō versūs?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 1, 5, ⟦i:lay down the law, what I’m to do :: keep still :: wilt have me write, sayst thou, no verse at all?⟧ ⟦b:quid igitur faciam? nōn eam?⟧ T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 46, ⟦i:what then am I to do? not go?⟧ ⟦b:quid nī meminerim?⟧ ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 273, ⟦i:why should not I remember?⟧ or ⟦i:of course I remember⟧. ⟦b:huic cēdāmus? huius condiciōnēs audiāmus?⟧ ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 13, 16, ⟦i:shall we bow the knee to him? shall we listen to his terms?⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:quid tandem mē facere decuit? quiēscerem et paterer?⟧ L. 42, 41, 12, ⟦i:what in the world ought I to have done? keep inactive and stand it?⟧
⟦#1564⟧
Such questions sometimes have the alternative form: as, ⟦b:Corinthiīs bellum indīcāmus, an nōn?⟧ ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 1, 17, ⟦i:are we to declare war against Corinth, or not?⟧ ⟦b:utrum indicāre mē e͡i thēnsaurum aequom fuit, an ego alium dominum paterer fierī hīsce aedibus?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 175, ⟦i:should I have pointed out the hoard to him, or should I have allowed another to become the owner of this house?⟧ here ⟦b:paterer⟧ is equivalent to ⟦b:aequom fuit patī⟧ (⟦r1495:1495⟧).
⟦#1565⟧
II. The subjunctive is often used to ask whether action is conceivable: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:quis putet celeritātem ingenī L. Brūtō dēfuisse?⟧ ⟦i:Br.⟧ 53, ⟦i:who can suppose that Brutus lacked ready wit?⟧ i.e. ⟦b:nēmō putet⟧ (⟦r1556:1556⟧), ⟦b:putābit⟧ (⟦r1620:1620⟧), or ⟦b:putāre potest⟧. ⟦b:sī enim Zēnōnī licuit, cūr nōn liceat Catōnī?⟧ ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 3, 15, ⟦i:for if it was allowed Zeno, why should not it be allowed Cato?⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:hoc tantum bellum quis umquam arbitrārētur ab ūnō imperātōre cōnficī posse?⟧ ⟦i:IP.⟧ 31, ⟦i:who would ever have dreamed that this stupendous war could be brought to a close by a single commander?⟧ The imperfect sometimes denotes action not performed at the present time (⟦r1560:1560⟧): ⟦b:quis enim cīvis rēgī nōn favēret?⟧ ⟦i:D.⟧ 6, ⟦i:for what Roman would not feel for the king?⟧ (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:ego tē vidēre nōluerim?⟧ ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 1, 3, 1, ⟦i:I have objected to seeing you?⟧
⟦#1566⟧
The subjunctive is often used in interrogative outbursts of surprise, disapprobation, indignation, or captious rejoinder. In such questions a pronoun, ⟦b:ego⟧, ⟦b:tū⟧ (⟦b:ille⟧), is usually expressed. The negative is ⟦b:nōn⟧.
This subjunctive occurs in Plautus and Terence, in Cicero, oftenest the letters, in Horace, Vergil, and Livy. Not in Caesar nor Sallust.
⟦#1567⟧
(1.) The question may have no interrogative word, or may have ⟦b:-ne⟧, especially in comedy: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:nōn tacēs? :: taceam?⟧ T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 987, ⟦i:you hold your tongue :: I hold my tongue?⟧ ⟦b:nē flē :: egone illum nōn fleam?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 139, ⟦i:weep not :: what, I not weep for him?⟧ ⟦b:tū pulsēs omne quod obstat?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 6, 30, ⟦i:what, you, sir, punch whatever’s in your way?⟧ ⟦b:faveās tū hostī? ille litterās ad tē mittat?⟧ ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 7, 5, ⟦i:you, sir, sympathize with the enemy? he correspond with you?⟧ ⟦b:sapiēnsne nōn timeat?⟧ ⟦i:Ac.⟧ 2, 135, ⟦i:a sage not be afraid?⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:ego mihī̆ umquam bonōrum praesidium dēfutūrum putārem?⟧ ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 94, ⟦i:could I have dreamed that I should ever lack the protection of the patriotic?⟧ (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:‘apud exercitum mihī̆ fuerīs’ inquit ‘tot annōs?’⟧ ⟦i:Mur.⟧ 21, ⟦i:‘to think of your having been with the army, bless my soul?’ says he, ‘so many years.’⟧ (⟦i:d.⟧) ⟦b:mihī̆ cuiusquam salūs tantī fuisset, ut meam neglegerem?⟧ ⟦i:Sull.⟧ 45, ⟦i:could anybody’s safety have been so important in my eyes as to make me disregard my own?⟧
⟦#1568⟧
(2.) The question may have ⟦b:utī⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧: as,
⟦b:tē ut ūlla rēs frangat? tū ut umquam tē corrigās?⟧ ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 22, ⟦i:any thing break you down? you ever reform?⟧ ⟦b:pater ut obesse fīlīo dēbeat?⟧ ⟦i:Planc.⟧ 31, ⟦i:a father morally bound to work against his son?⟧
⟦#1569⟧
(3.) The question with ⟦b:utī⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧ is sometimes attended by a remnant of another question with ⟦b:-ne⟧ or ⟦b:-n⟧. In this combination, ⟦b:-ne⟧ either precedes, joined to an emphatic word, or it is attached directly to ⟦b:utī⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:egone ut tē interpellem?⟧ ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 42, ⟦i:what I? interrupt you?⟧ ⟦b:illīne ut impūne concitent fīnitima bella?⟧ L. 4, 2, 12, ⟦i:what, they be allowed to stir up border warfare with impunity?⟧ ⟦b:virgō haec līberast :: meane ancilla lībera ut sit, quam ego numquam ēmīsī manū?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Cur.⟧ 615, ⟦i:this girl is free :: my servant-girl? she to be free, when I have never set her free?⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:utne tegam spurcō Dāmae latus?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 5, 18, ⟦i:what, I’m to shield a nasty Dama’s side?⟧ ⟦b:somnium. utine haec īgnōrāret su͡om patrem?⟧ T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 874, ⟦i:oh bosh, not to have known the father that begat her?⟧ See ⟦r1505:1505⟧ and ⟦r1532:1532⟧.
⟦#1570⟧
It may be mentioned here, that the interrogative subjunctive is often used in subordinate sentences: see ⟦r1731:1731⟧.

title: Command
text:
⟦#1571⟧
The second person of the imperative mood is used in commands, either particular or general.
Commands are very often attended by a vocative or vocative nominative, or by ⟦b:tū⟧, ⟦i:sir⟧, ⟦i:sirrah⟧, or ⟦b:vōs⟧, ⟦i:gentlemen⟧, ⟦i:you people⟧ (⟦r1118:1118⟧). They are of various kinds, as follows: (⟦i:a.⟧) Order, often to an inferior: thus, to an official: ⟦b:līctor, conligā manūs⟧, ⟦i:Rab.⟧ 13, L. 1, 26, 7, Gell. 12, 3, 2, ⟦i:lictor, tie up his wrists⟧. To soldiers: as, ⟦b:dēsilīte mīlitēs⟧, 4, 25, 3, ⟦i:overboard, my men⟧. ⟦b:sīgnifer, statue sīgnum⟧, L. 5, 55, 1, ⟦i:standardbearer, plant your standard⟧. ⟦b:īnfer mīles sīgnum⟧, L. 6, 8, 1, ⟦i:advance your standard, man⟧, or ⟦i:charge⟧. To sailors: as, ⟦b:hūc dīrigite nāvēs⟧, L. 29, 27, 13, ⟦i:head your galleys this way⟧. To slaves: as, ⟦b:convorrite aedēs scōpīs, agite strēnuē⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 10, ⟦i:sweep up the house with brooms, be brisk⟧. Also to an equal: as, ⟦b:aperīte aliquis⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Mer.⟧ 130, ⟦i:open the door there somebody⟧ (⟦r1080:1080⟧). Or to a superior: as, ⟦b:heus, exī, Phaedrome⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cur.⟧ 276, ⟦i:ho Phaedromus, come out⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) Exhortation, entreaty, summons, request, prayer, imprecation, wish, concession, &c.: as, ⟦b:vōs vōbīs cōnsulite⟧, 7, 50, 5, ⟦i:every man of you for himself⟧. ⟦b:ēs, bibe, animō obsequere⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 677, ⟦i:eat, drink, and be merry⟧. ⟦b:sperne voluptātēs⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 2, 55, ⟦i:scorn thou delights⟧. ⟦b:quīn tū ī intrō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 815, ⟦i:go in, go in, won’t you go in?⟧ (⟦r1527:1527⟧). ⟦b:patent portae, proficīscere, ēdūc tēcum etiam omnīs tuōs⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 10, ⟦i:the gates are open, march forth; take out all your myrmidons with you too⟧. ⟦b:audī, Iuppiter⟧, L. 1, 32, 6, ⟦i:bow down thine ear, Jupiter⟧. ⟦b:ī in crucem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 940, ⟦i:get you gone to the cross⟧. ⟦b:vīve valēque⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 5, 109, ⟦i:long live and thrive⟧, or ⟦i:farewell⟧. ⟦b:tibī̆ habē⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 690, ⟦i:you keep it yourself⟧.
⟦#1572⟧
The imperative is often softened by the addition of ⟦b:amābō⟧, ⟦b:obsecrō⟧, ⟦b:quaesō⟧, ⟦i:prithee⟧, ⟦i:I beg⟧, or ⟦b:sīs⟧, ⟦b:sultis⟧, ⟦b:sōdēs⟧, ⟦i:please⟧ (⟦r97:97⟧). It is sharpened by ⟦b:age⟧, ⟦b:agedum⟧ or ⟦b:agidum⟧, ⟦b:age sīs⟧, ⟦i:mark me⟧, or ⟦b:ī⟧, ⟦i:go⟧, ⟦i:come on⟧, or by ⟦b:modo⟧, ⟦i:only⟧. The concessive imperative sometimes has ⟦b:sānē⟧, ⟦i:for all me⟧.
⟦#1573⟧
In Plautus and Terence, the enclitic ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:a while⟧, ⟦i:a minute⟧, ⟦i:just⟧, is often attached to the imperative: as, ⟦b:manedum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 585, ⟦i:wait a minute⟧. In classical Latin, ⟦b:dum⟧ is retained with ⟦b:age⟧ and ⟦b:agite⟧: as, ⟦b:agedum cōnferte cum illīus vītā P. Sūllae⟧, ⟦i:Sull.⟧ 72, ⟦i:come now, compare Sulla’s life with that man’s⟧ (⟦r1075:1075⟧).
⟦#1574⟧
It may be mentioned here, that the imperative is often used in the protasis of a conditional sentence: as,
⟦b:tolle hanc opīniōnem, lūctum sustuleris⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 30, ⟦i:do away with this notion, and you will do away with mourning for the dead⟧. Once only in old Latin, but often in late Latin, with a copulative: as, ⟦b:perge, ac facile ecfēceris⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 695, ⟦i:start on, and you will do it easily⟧.
⟦#1575⟧
(1.) The third person, and the longer forms of the second person, are used particularly in laws, legal documents, and treaties, and also in impressive general rules and maxims: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:rēgiō imperiō duō suntō⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 3, 8, ⟦i:there shall be two men vested with the power of kings⟧. ⟦b:amīcitia rēgī Antiochō cum populō Rōmānō hīs lēgibus estō⟧, L. 38, 38, 1, ⟦i:there shall be amity between king Antiochus and Rome on the following terms⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:vīcīnīs bonus estō⟧, Cato, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 4, ⟦i:always be good to your neighbours⟧. ⟦b:mōribus vīvitō antīquīs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 295, ⟦i:live thou in old-time ways⟧. The longer forms are often called the ⟦i:Future Imperative⟧.
⟦#1576⟧
(2.) The longer forms of the second person are also sometimes used in the ordinary speech of everyday life: as, ⟦b:cavētō⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 1, 3, 8, ⟦i:beware⟧. In old Latin, often ⟦b:ēs⟧, ⟦i:be thou⟧, but in classical Latin, oftener ⟦b:estō⟧ (or ⟦b:sīs⟧). Usually ⟦b:habētō⟧, meaning ⟦i:keep⟧, or ⟦i:consider⟧, regularly ⟦b:scītō⟧, ⟦b:scītōte⟧, ⟦i:you must know⟧ (⟦r846:846⟧). In verse, the long forms may sometimes be due to the metre: as, ⟦b:hīc hodiē cēnātō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 1417, ⟦i:take dinner here today⟧. ⟦b:pār prō parī refertō⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 445, ⟦i:pay tit for tat⟧. But also without such necessity: as, ⟦b:aufertō intrō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tru.⟧ 914, ⟦i:take it within⟧. ⟦b:quiētus estō, inquam⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 713, ⟦i:be not concerned, I say⟧.
⟦#1577⟧
(3.) It may be mentioned here, that the longer forms are very often used in the apodosis of a complex sentence, particularly with a future or a future perfect protasis: as,
⟦b:sī iste ībit, ītō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 863, ⟦i:if he shall go, go thou⟧. ⟦b:medicō mercēdis quantum poscet, prōmittī iubētō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 14, 1, ⟦i:you must order your medical man to be promised all he shall charge in the way of a fee⟧. ⟦b:ubī̆ nihil erit quod scrībās, id ipsum scrībitō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 4, 8b, 4, ⟦i:when you don’t have anything to write, then write just that⟧. ⟦b:cum ego P. Grānium testem prōdūxerō, refellitō, sī poteris⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 154, ⟦i:when I put Granius on the witness stand, refute him if you can⟧.
⟦#1578⟧
In such combinations, however, the shorter forms are sometimes found: as, ⟦b:ubi volēs, accerse⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 848, ⟦i:fetch me when you will⟧. And conversely the longer forms are also found with a present protasis: as, ⟦b:ūnum illud vidētō, sī mē amās⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 1, 2, ⟦i:attend to this one thing, an thou lovest me⟧.
⟦#1579⟧
A command is sometimes expressed by the subjunctive, accompanying ⟦b:fac⟧, ⟦b:facitō⟧, ⟦b:fac ut⟧, ⟦b:facitō ut⟧, ⟦b:cūrā ut⟧, ⟦b:cūrātō ut⟧, ⟦b:vidē⟧, ⟦b:vidē ut⟧, ⟦b:volō⟧, or particularly ⟦b:velim⟧: as,
⟦b:magnum fac animum habeās et spem bonam⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 1, 2, 16, ⟦i:see that you keep up an heroic soul and unabated hope⟧ (⟦r1712:1712⟧). ⟦b:fac cōgitēs⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 11, 3, 4, ⟦i:see that you bear in mind⟧. ⟦b:cūrā ut valeās⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 12, 29, 3, ⟦i:take good care of yourself⟧. ⟦b:velim exīstimēs⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 12, 29, 2, ⟦i:I should like to have you consider⟧. For commands in the subjunctive alone, see ⟦r1547:1547⟧; in the future indicative, 1624; in the form of a question, 1531.
⟦#1580⟧
A periphrastic perfect passive form is rare: as, ⟦b:iūre caesus estō⟧, Twelve Tables in Macrob. ⟦i:Sat.⟧ 1, 4, 19, ⟦i:he shall be regarded as killed with justifying circumstances⟧. ⟦b:probē factum estō⟧, L. 22, 10, 6, ⟦i:let it be considered justified⟧. ⟦b:at vōs admonitī nostrīs quoque cāsibus este⟧, O. ⟦i:Tr.⟧ 4, 8, 51, ⟦i:but be ye warned by our misfortunes too⟧.

title: Prohibition
text:
⟦#1581⟧
(1.) In prohibitions with the second person, the imperative with ⟦b:nē⟧ is used in old Latin, and with ⟦b:nēve⟧ as a connective, rarely ⟦b:neque⟧: as,
⟦b:nē flē⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 139, ⟦i:weep not⟧. ⟦b:nē saevī tantō opere⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 868, ⟦i:be not thus wroth⟧. Sometimes in classical poetry also, in imitation of old style: as, ⟦b:nē saevī, magna sacerdōs⟧, V. 6, 544, ⟦i:rave not, thou priestess grand⟧. Once in Livy: ⟦b:nē timēte⟧, 3, 2, 9, ⟦i:be not afraid⟧.
⟦#1582⟧
From Ovid on, ⟦b:nōn⟧ is used a few times for ⟦b:nē⟧: as, ⟦b:nōn cārīs aurēs onerāte lapillīs⟧, O. ⟦i:AA.⟧ 3, 129, ⟦i:load not with precious stones your ears⟧.
⟦#1583⟧
(2.) Prohibitions in the second person are usually expressed by ⟦b:nōlī⟧ or ⟦b:nōlīte⟧ with the infinitive, particularly in classical prose: as,
⟦b:obiūrgāre nōlī⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 3, 11, 2, ⟦i:don’t scold⟧. ⟦b:nōlīte id velle quod fierī nōn potest⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 7, 25, ⟦i:don’t yearn after the unattainable⟧.
⟦#1584⟧
In poetry, equivalents for ⟦b:nōlī⟧ are sometimes used with the infinitive, such as ⟦b:fuge⟧, ⟦b:parce⟧ or ⟦b:comperce⟧, ⟦b:conpesce⟧, ⟦b:mitte⟧ or ⟦b:omitte⟧, ⟦b:absiste⟧: as, ⟦b:quid sit futūrum crās, fuge quaerere⟧, H. 1, 9, 13, ⟦i:what fate the morrow brings, forbear to ask⟧. Livy has once ⟦b:parce⟧, 34, 32, 20.
⟦#1585⟧
(3.) A prohibition in the second person is often expressed by the subjunctive accompanying ⟦b:cavē̆⟧, ⟦b:fac nē⟧, ⟦b:vidē nē⟧, ⟦b:vidētō nē⟧, ⟦b:cūrā nē⟧, ⟦b:cūrātō nē⟧, or ⟦b:nōlim⟧, and in old Latin ⟦b:cavē̆ nē⟧: as,
⟦b:cavē festīnēs⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 12, 6, ⟦i:don’t be in a hurry⟧. ⟦b:cavētō nē suscēnseās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 372, ⟦i:see that thou beest not wroth⟧. ⟦b:hoc nōlim mē iocārī putēs⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 9, 15, 4, ⟦i:I should hate to have you think I am saying this in fun⟧. For prohibitions in the second person with ⟦b:nē⟧ and the present or perfect subjunctive, see ⟦r1551:1551⟧. For the subjunctive coordinated with ⟦b:cavē̆⟧, see ⟦r1711:1711⟧.
⟦#1586⟧
In law language, prohibitions are expressed by the third person of the imperative with ⟦b:nē⟧, and with ⟦b:nēve⟧ as a connective: as,
⟦b:hominem mortuom in urbe nē sepelītō nēve ūritō⟧, Twelve Tables in ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 2, 58, ⟦i:he shall not bury nor yet shall he burn a dead man in town⟧. ⟦b:mulierēs genās nē rāduntō nēve lessum fūneris ergō habentō⟧, Twelve Tables in ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 2, 59, ⟦i:women shall not tear their cheeks nor shall they keen in lamentation for the dead⟧ (⟦r1257:1257⟧). Likewise with ⟦b:nēmō⟧: as, ⟦b:nēminī pārentō⟧, Twelve Tables in ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 3, 8, ⟦i:they shall not be subject to anybody⟧. See also ⟦r1548:1548⟧.

title: The Tenses of the Indicative: The Present Tense
text:
⟦#1587⟧
The present indicative represents action as going on at the time of speaking or writing: as,
⟦b:scrībō⟧, ⟦i:I write⟧, or ⟦i:I am writing⟧. ⟦b:nunc prīmum audiō⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 936, ⟦i:for the first time I hear⟧. ⟦b:notat ad caedem ūnum quemque nostrūm⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 2, ⟦i:he is marking us out for death, each and all⟧. ⟦b:domus aedificātur⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 4, 2, 7, ⟦i:the house is building⟧.
⟦#1588⟧
The present is used to denote action customary or repeated at any time, or a general truth: as,
⟦b:agrī cultūrae nōn student⟧, 6, 22, 1, ⟦i:they do not apply themselves to farming⟧. ⟦b:virī in uxōrēs vītae necisque habent potestātem⟧, 6, 19, 3, ⟦i:the married men have power of life and death over their wives⟧. ⟦b:probitās laudātur et alget⟧, J. 1, 74, ⟦i:uprightness gets extolled, and left out in the cold⟧. ⟦b:dum vītant stultī vitia, in contrāria currunt⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 2, 24, ⟦i:while fools essay a vice to shun, into its opposite they run⟧. ⟦b:mors sōla fatētur quantula sint hominum corpuscula⟧, J. 10, 172, ⟦i:death is the only thing that tells what pygmy things men’s bodies be⟧. ⟦b:stultōrum plēna sunt omnia⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 9, 22, 4, ⟦i:the world is full of fools⟧. ⟦b:rīsū ineptō rēs ineptior nūllast⟧, Cat. 39, 16, ⟦i:there’s nothing sillier than a silly laugh⟧.
⟦#1589⟧
The present, when accompanied by some expression of duration of time, is often used to denote action which has been going on some time and is still going on.
This present is translated by the English perfect: as, ⟦b:Lilybaeī multōs iam annōs habitat⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 38, ⟦i:he has lived at Lilybaeum this many a year⟧. ⟦b:iam dūdum auscultō⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 7, 1, ⟦i:I have been listening for an age⟧. ⟦b:satis diū hōc iam saxum vorsō⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 1085, ⟦i:I’ve trundled at this boulder long enough as ’t is⟧. ⟦b:nimium diū tē castra dēsīderant⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 10, ⟦i:the camp has felt your absence altogether too long⟧. ⟦b:iam diū īgnōrō quid agās⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 7, 9, 1, ⟦i:I have not known this long time how you are getting on⟧. This use extends to the subjunctive and to nouns of the verb also. But if the action is conceived as completed, the perfect is used: as, ⟦b:sērō resistimus ē̆ī quem per annōs decem aluimus⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 7, 5, 5, ⟦i:it is too late to oppose a man whom we have been supporting ten long years⟧.
⟦#1590⟧
The present is often used to represent past action as going on now. This is called the ⟦i:Present of Vivid Narration⟧: as,
⟦b:trānsfīgitur scūtum Puliōni et verūtum in balteō dēfīgitur. āvertit hīc cāsus vāgīnam, inpedītumque hostēs circumsistunt⟧, 5, 44, 7, ⟦i:Pulio has his shield run through, and a javelin sticks fast in his sword belt. This mischance puts his scabbard out of reach, and the enemy encompass him in this hampered condition⟧. This present often stands side by side with a past tense. It is common in subordinate sentences also.
⟦#1591⟧
The present is sometimes used in brief historical or personal memoranda, to note incidents day by day or year by year as they occur. This is called the ⟦i:Annalistic Present⟧: as,
⟦b:Proca deinde rēgnat. is Numitōrem prōcreat. Numitōrī rēgnum vetustum Silviae gentis lēgat⟧, L. 1, 3, 9, ⟦i:after this Proca is king; this man begets Numitor; to Numitor he bequeaths the ancient throne of the Silvian race⟧. ⟦b:duplicātur cīvium numerus. Caelius additur urbī mōns⟧, L. 1, 30, 1, ⟦i:number of citizens doubled; Mt. Caelius added to city⟧. ⟦b:in Māmurrārum lassī deinde urbe manēmus⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 5, 37, ⟦i:in the Mamurras’ city then forspent we sleep⟧. Particularly common with dates: as, ⟦b:A. Vergīnius inde et T. Vetusius cōnsulātum ineunt⟧, L. 2, 28, 1, ⟦i:then Verginius and Vetusius enter on the consulship⟧. ⟦b:M. Sīlānō L. Nōrbānō cōnsulibus Germānicus Aegyptum proficīscitur⟧, Ta. 2, 59, ⟦i:in the consulship of Silanus and Norbanus, Germanicus leaves for Egypt⟧.
⟦#1592⟧
Verbs of hearing, seeing, and saying are often put in the present, even when they refer to action really past: as,
⟦b:audiō Valerium Mārtiālem dēcessisse⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 3, 21, 1, ⟦i:I hear that Martial is dead⟧, i.e. the epigrammatist, 102 A.D. Particularly of things mentioned in books, or in quoting what an author says: as, ⟦b:Hercyniam silvam, quam Eratosthenī nōtam esse videō⟧, 6, 24, 2, ⟦i:the Hercynian forest, which I see was known to Eratosthenes⟧. ⟦b:Platō ‘ēscam malōrum’ appellat voluptātem⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 44, ⟦i:Plato calls pleasure the ‘bait of sin.’⟧
⟦#1593⟧
The present is sometimes loosely used of future action: as,
⟦b:crās est mihī̆ iūdicium⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 338, ⟦i:tomorrow I’ve a case in court⟧. ⟦b:ego sȳcophantam iam condūcō dē forō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 815, ⟦i:for me, a sharper from the market place I’ll straight engage⟧. ⟦b:quam mox inruimus?⟧ T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 788, ⟦i:how soon do we pitch in?⟧ This present is also used in subordinate sentences with ⟦b:antequam⟧ and ⟦b:priusquam⟧ (⟦r1912:1912⟧, ⟦r1915:1915⟧), with ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:until⟧ (⟦r2006:2006⟧), and sometimes with ⟦b:sī⟧.

title: The Imperfect Tense
text:
⟦#1594⟧
The imperfect indicative represents action as going on in past time: as,
⟦b:scrībēbam⟧, ⟦i:I was writing⟧, or ⟦i:I wrote⟧. ⟦b:ei mihi quālis erat⟧, V. 2, 274, ⟦i:woe’s me, how ghastly he appeared⟧. ⟦b:multōsque per annōs errābant āctī fātīs⟧, V. 1, 31, ⟦i:and they for many a year were roaming round, by fates pursued⟧.
⟦#1595⟧
The imperfect often denotes past action lasting while something else occurred: as,
⟦b:an tum erās cōnsul, cum mea domus ardēbat?⟧ ⟦i:Pis.⟧ 26, ⟦i:were you perhaps consul at the time my house was burning down?⟧ ⟦b:neque vērō tum īgnōrābat sē ad exquīsīta supplicia proficīscī⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 100, ⟦i:and all the time he knew perfectly well that he was starting off to suffer studied torments⟧.
⟦#1596⟧
The imperfect is used to denote repeated or customary past action or condition: as,
⟦b:commentābar dēclāmitāns cōtīdiē⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 310, ⟦i:I always practised speaking my compositions every day⟧. ⟦b:noctū ambulābat in pūblicō Themistoclēs⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 4, 44, ⟦i:Themistocles used to promenade the streets nights⟧.
⟦#1597⟧
The imperfect, when accompanied by some expression of duration of time, is used to denote action which had been going on for some time, and was still going on.
This imperfect, which is translated by the English pluperfect, is analogous to the present in 1589: as, ⟦b:pater grandis nātū iam diū lectō tenēbātur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 16, ⟦i:his aged father had long been bedridden⟧. ⟦b:hōram amplius iam permultī hominēs mōliēbantur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 95, ⟦i:something over an hour a good many men had been prizing away⟧. But if the action is conceived as completed at a past time, the pluperfect is used: as, ⟦b:diem iam quīntum cibō caruerat⟧, 6, 38, 1, ⟦i:four whole days he had gone without eating⟧.
⟦#1598⟧
In a few examples, the imperfect is used to denote action suddenly recognized, though going on before: as, ⟦b:ehem, Parmenō, tūn hīc erās?⟧ T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 340, ⟦i:why bless me, Parmeno, were you here all this time?⟧
⟦#1599⟧
In descriptions of place or in general truths, where the present might be expected, the imperfect is sometimes used, by assimilation to past action in the context: as, ⟦b:ipsum erat oppidum Alesia in colle summō⟧, 7, 69, 1, ⟦i:Alesia proper was situated on the top of a hill⟧. Often also in subordinate sentences.
⟦#1600⟧
For the imperfect indicative of certain verbs relating to action not performed at the present time, see ⟦r1497:1497⟧; for the conative use, see ⟦r2302:2302⟧.
⟦#1601⟧
In letters, the imperfect may denote action at the time of writing, the writer transferring himself to the time of the reader: as,
⟦b:haec tibi dictābam post fānum putre Vacūnae⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 10, 49, ⟦i:I dictate this for thee behind Vacuna’s crumbling shrine⟧. ⟦b:nihil habēbam quod scrīberem⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 9, 10, 1, ⟦i:I have nothing to write⟧. Similarly in the delivery of messages: as, ⟦b:scrībae ōrābant⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 6, 36, ⟦i:the clerks request⟧. The present, however, is very often used where the imperfect would be applicable. Compare 1616.

title: The Tenses of the Indicative: The Perfect Tense
text:
⟦#1602⟧
The Latin perfect indicative represents two English tenses: thus, the preterite, ⟦i:I wrote⟧, and the perfect, ⟦i:I have written⟧, are both expressed by the perfect ⟦b:scrīpsī⟧. In the first sense, this perfect is called the ⟦i:Historical Perfect⟧; in the second sense, it is called the ⟦i:Perfect Definite⟧.

title: The Historical Perfect
text:
⟦#1603⟧
The historical perfect simply expresses action as having occurred at an indefinite past time, without implying anything as to the duration of the action: as,
⟦b:scrīpsī⟧, ⟦i:I wrote⟧. ⟦b:vēnī, vīdī, vīcī⟧, Caesar in Suet. ⟦i:Iul.⟧ 37, ⟦i:came, saw, overcame⟧. ⟦b:apud Helvētiōs longē nōbilissimus fuit Orgetorīx⟧, 1, 2, 1, ⟦i:among the Helvetians, the man of highest birth by all odds was Orgetorix⟧. ⟦b:Diodōrus prope triennium domō caruit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 41, ⟦i:for nearly three years Diodorus had to keep away from home⟧. ⟦b:in Graeciā mūsicī flōruērunt, discēbantque id omnēs⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 4, ⟦i:in Greece musicians stood high, and everybody studied the art⟧ (⟦r1596:1596⟧).
⟦#1604⟧
It may be mentioned here, that in subordinate sentences the historical perfect is sometimes loosely used from the writer’s point of view, instead of the more exact pluperfect demanded by the context: as, ⟦b:aliquantum spatiī ex eō locō, ubī̆ pugnātum est, aufūgerat⟧, L. 1, 25, 8, ⟦i:he had run off some distance from the spot where the fighting had occurred⟧. See ⟦r1925:1925⟧.

title: The Perfect Definite
text:
⟦#1605⟧
The perfect definite expresses action which is already completed at the present time, and the effects of which are regarded as continuing: as,
⟦b:scrīpsī⟧, ⟦i:I have written⟧. ⟦b:dīxērunt⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 73, ⟦b:dīxēre⟧, Quintil. 1, 5, 43, ⟦i:they have finished speaking⟧. ⟦b:spectātōrēs, fābula haec est ācta⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 1181, ⟦i:ladies and gentlemen, this play is done⟧.
⟦#1606⟧
In old Latin, ⟦b:habeō⟧ with the perfect participle is sometimes equivalent to a periphrastic perfect: as, ⟦b:illa omnia missa habeō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 602, ⟦i:I’ve dropped all that⟧, i.e. ⟦b:mīsī⟧. But in classical Latin, the participle and a tense of ⟦b:habeō⟧ are more or less distinct in their force: as, ⟦b:Caesar aciem īnstrūctam habuit⟧, 1, 48, 3, ⟦i:Caesar kept his line drawn up⟧, not ⟦i:had drawn up⟧. Compare 2297.
⟦#1607⟧
With verbs of inceptive meaning the perfect definite is equivalent to the English present: as,
⟦b:cōnsistō⟧, ⟦i:take my stand⟧, ⟦b:cōnstitī⟧, ⟦i:stand⟧, ⟦b:cōnsuēscō⟧, ⟦i:get used⟧, ⟦b:cōnsuēvī⟧, ⟦i:am used⟧, ⟦b:nōscō⟧, ⟦i:learn⟧, ⟦b:nōvī⟧, ⟦i:know⟧. Similarly ⟦b:meminī⟧, ⟦i:remember⟧, and ⟦b:ōdī⟧, ⟦i:hate⟧. The pluperfect of such verbs is represented by the English imperfect, and the future perfect by the English future.
⟦#1608⟧
The perfect often denotes a present resulting state: as, ⟦b:vīcīne, periī, interiī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 1031, ⟦i:my neighbour, I am dead and gone⟧.
