Particularly in the passive voice: as, ⟦b:Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs⟧, 1, 1, 1, ⟦i:Gaul, including everything under the name, is divided into three parts⟧. Compare 1615.
⟦#1609⟧
In the perfect passive, forms of ⟦b:fuī⟧, &c., are sometimes used to represent a state no longer existing: as, ⟦b:monumentō statua superimposita fuit, quam dēiectam nūper vīdimus ipsī⟧, L. 38, 56, 3, ⟦i:on the monument there once stood a statue which I saw not long ago with my own eyes, lying flat on the ground⟧. Similarly, in the pluperfect, ⟦b:fueram⟧, &c.: as, ⟦b:arma quae fīxa in parietibus fuerant, ea sunt humī inventa⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 1, 74, ⟦i:the arms which had once been fastened on the walls were found on the floor⟧. Sometimes, however, forms of ⟦b:fuī⟧, &c., ⟦b:fueram⟧, &c., and ⟦b:fuerō⟧, &c., are used by Plautus, Cicero, especially in his letters, Nepos, Sallust, and particularly Livy, in passives and deponents, quite in the sense of ⟦b:sum⟧, &c.
⟦#1610⟧
The perfect of some verbs may imply a negative idea emphatically by understatement, as:
⟦b:fuit Īlium⟧, V. 2, 325, ⟦i:Ilium has been⟧, i.e. Ilium is no more. ⟦b:vīximus, flōruimus⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 14, 4, 5, ⟦i:we have lived our life, we have had our day⟧. ⟦b:fīlium ūnicum adulēscentulum habeō. āh, quid dīxī? habēre mē? immō habuī⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 93, ⟦i:I have one only son, a growing boy. Ah me, what did I say, I have? Oh no, have had.⟧
⟦#1611⟧
The perfect may denote an action often done, or never done: as,
⟦b:iam saepe hominēs patriam cārōsque parentēs prōdiderunt⟧, Lucr. 3, 85, ⟦i:time and again have men their land betrayed and parents dear⟧. ⟦b:nōn aeris acervus et aurī dēdūxit corpore febrīs⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 2, 47, ⟦i:no pile of brass and gold hath fevers from the body drawn⟧. ⟦b:multī, cum obesse vellent, prōfuērunt et, cum prōdesse, obfuērunt⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 70, ⟦i:many a man has done good, when he meant to do harm, and when he meant to do good, has done harm⟧. Common from Cicero, Sallust, and Catullus on, especially in poetry.
⟦#1612⟧
The perfect is sometimes used as a lively future perfect to express completed future action: as,
⟦b:quam mox coctumst prandium?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 342, ⟦i:how soon is lunch all cooked?⟧ ⟦b:cui sī esse in urbe licēbit, vīcimus⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 14, 20, 3, ⟦i:if he shall be allowed to stay in town, the day is ours⟧. ⟦b:periī, sī mē aspexerit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 320, ⟦i:I’m gone, if he lays eyes on me⟧.
⟦#1613⟧
It may be mentioned here, that the perfect is regularly used in a subordinate sentence denoting time anterior to a present of repeated action (⟦r1588:1588⟧). In such sentences the present is preferred in English: as,
⟦b:reliquī, quī domī mānsērunt, sē atque illōs alunt⟧, 4, 1, 5, ⟦i:the others, that stay at home, always support themselves and the above-mentioned also⟧. ⟦b:sī quī aut prīvātus aut populus eōrum dēcrētō nōn stetit, sacrificiīs interdīcunt⟧, 6, 13, 6, ⟦i:if any man or any community does not abide by their decree, they always debar them from sacrifices⟧. So also with ⟦b:quom⟧ or ⟦b:cum⟧, ⟦b:quotiēns⟧, ⟦b:simul atque⟧, ⟦b:ubī̆⟧. Compare 1618.

title: The Pluperfect Tense
text:
⟦#1614⟧
The pluperfect indicative expresses past action, completed before another past action expressed or understood: as,
⟦b:scrīpseram⟧, ⟦i:I had written⟧. ⟦b:Pyrrhī temporibus iam Apollō versūs facere dēsierat⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 116, ⟦i:in Pyrrhus’s day Apollo had quite given up making poetry⟧. ⟦b:mortuus erat Āgis rēx. fīlium relīquerat Leōtychidem⟧, N. 17, 1, 4, ⟦i:Agis the king had died; he had left a son Leotychides⟧.
⟦#1615⟧
The pluperfect often expresses a past resulting state: as,
⟦b:castra oportūnīs locīs erant posita⟧, 7, 69, 7, ⟦i:the camp was pitched on favourable ground⟧. ⟦b:ita ūnō tempore et longās nāvēs aestus complēverat, et onerāriās tempestās adflīctābat⟧, 4, 29, 2, ⟦i:thus at one and the same time the tide had filled the men-of-war, and the gale of wind kept knocking the transports about⟧. This use is analogous to that of the perfect in 1608.
⟦#1616⟧
In letters, the pluperfect is sometimes used to denote action occurring previous to the time of writing, the writer transferring himself to the time of the reader: as,
⟦b:ūnam adhūc ā tē epistolam accēperam⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 7, 12, 1, ⟦i:I have only had one letter from you thus far⟧. This use is analogous to that of the imperfect in 1601, and very often, where this pluperfect would be applicable, the perfect is used.
⟦#1617⟧
The pluperfect is sometimes used where the perfect would be expected. Particularly so when it anticipates a past tense to follow in a new sentence: as, ⟦b:quod factum prīmō populārīs coniūrātiōnis concusserat. neque tamen Catilīnae furor minuēbātur⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 24, 1, ⟦i:this terrified the conspirators at first; and yet Catiline’s frenzy was not getting abated⟧. Verbs of saying are also often put in the pluperfect in subordinate sentences referring to a preceding statement: as, ⟦b:Epidamniēnsis ille, quem dūdum dīxeram, adoptat illum puerum surruptīcium⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men. prol.⟧ 57, ⟦i:said man of Epidamnus that I named erewhile adopts said kidnapped boy⟧.
⟦#1618⟧
It may be mentioned here, that the pluperfect is used in a subordinate sentence denoting time anterior to a past tense of repeated action. In such sentences the preterite is preferred in English: as,
⟦b:hostēs ubī̆ aliquōs singulārēs cōnspexerant, incitātīs equīs adoriēbantur⟧, 4, 26, 2, ⟦i:every time the enemy caught sight of detached parties, they would always charge full gallop⟧. Compare the analogous perfect in 1613.

title: The Tenses of the Indicative: The Future Tense
text:
⟦#1619⟧
The future indicative expresses future action, either momentary or continuous: as,
⟦b:scrībam⟧, ⟦i:I shall write⟧, ⟦i:I shall be writing⟧, or ⟦i:I will write⟧, ⟦i:I will be writing⟧. The future commonly expresses either prediction, or will, determination, promise, threat: as, (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:tuās litterās exspectābō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 5, 7, ⟦i:I shall be on the lookout for letters from you⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:vīvum tē nōn relinquam; moriēre virgīs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 85, ⟦i:I will not leave you alive; you shall die under the rod⟧. But separate forms to mark the sharp distinction which exists between ⟦i:shall⟧ and ⟦i:will⟧ in the English future and future perfect are utterly unknown in Latin: thus, in ⟦b:occīdar equidem, sed victus nōn perībō⟧, Cornif. 4, 65, ⟦i:I shall be murdered, to be sure, but I will not die a vanquished man⟧, the difference between the prediction contained in ⟦i:I shall⟧, and the determination contained in ⟦i:I will⟧, cannot be expressed in Latin by the future indicative.
⟦#1620⟧
The future is often used in diffident assertion, to express an assumption, a belief, conviction, or concession, of the speaker himself, without implying its universal acceptance: as,
⟦b:dīcēs⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 60, ⟦i:you will say⟧. ⟦b:dīcet aliquis⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 3, 46, ⟦i:somebody will say⟧ (⟦r1556:1556⟧). ⟦b:dabit hoc Zēnōnī Polemō⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 4, 51, ⟦i:Polemo will concede this point to Zeno⟧. ⟦b:excūdent aliī spīrantia mollius aera, crēdō equidem⟧, V. 6, 847, ⟦i:with greater grace, I well believe, shall others shape the bronze that breathes⟧. Particularly in conclusions: as, ⟦b:sequētur igitur vel ad supplicium beāta vīta virtūtem⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 87, ⟦i:happiness then will walk with goodness even to the scaffold⟧. Or in general truths: as, ⟦b:cantābit vacuus cōram latrōne viātor⟧, J. 10, 22, ⟦i:the pourë man whan he goth by the weye, bifore the thevës he may synge and pleye⟧.
⟦#1621⟧
The future sometimes predicts that a thing not yet known to be true will prove to be true: as, ⟦b:haec erit bonō genere nāta⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 645, ⟦i:this maid, you’ll find, is come of honest stock⟧, i.e. ⟦b:esse reperiētur⟧. Compare the imperfect in 1598.
⟦#1622⟧
In Plautus and Terence, the future is sometimes used in protestations, wishes, or thanks: as, ⟦b:ita mē dī amābunt⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 749, ⟦i:so help me heaven⟧. ⟦b:dī tē amābunt⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 278, ⟦i:the gods shall bless thee⟧. Usually, however, the subjunctive: see ⟦r1542:1542⟧ and ⟦r1541:1541⟧.
⟦#1623⟧
The future is sometimes used in questions of deliberation or appeal: as, ⟦b:dēdēmus ergō Hannibalem?⟧ L. 21, 10, 11, ⟦i:are we then to surrender Hannibal?⟧ ⟦b:hancine ego ad rem nātam memorābō?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 188, ⟦i:am I to say that I was born for such a fate?⟧ Oftener the present subjunctive (⟦r1563:1563⟧), or sometimes the present indicative (⟦r1531:1531⟧).
⟦#1624⟧
The future is sometimes used, particularly in the second person, to express an exhortation, a direction, a request, a command, or with ⟦b:nōn⟧ a prohibition: as,
⟦b:crās ferrāmenta Teānum tollētis⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 1, 86, ⟦i:tomorrow to Teanum you will take your tools⟧. ⟦b:bonā veniā mē audiēs⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 59, ⟦i:you will listen to me with kind indulgence⟧. ⟦b:tū intereā nōn cessābis⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 5, 12, 10, ⟦i:meantime you will not be inactive⟧. ⟦b:haec igitur tibī̆ erunt cūrae⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 3, 9, 4, ⟦i:you will attend to this then⟧, i.e. ⟦b:haec cūrābis⟧.
⟦#1625⟧
It may be mentioned here, that the future is used in sentences subordinate to a future, an imperative, or a subjunctive implying a future: as,
⟦b:profectō nihil accipiam iniūriae, sī tū aderis⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 5, 18, 3, ⟦i:I am sure I shall suffer no harm, if you are with me⟧. ⟦b:ut mēd esse volēs, ita erō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 239, ⟦i:as you will have me be, so will I be⟧. ⟦b:ut is quī audiet, cōgitet plūra, quam videat⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 242, ⟦i:so that the hearer may imagine more than he sees⟧. But sometimes a present is used (⟦r1593:1593⟧).

title: The Future Perfect Tense
text:
⟦#1626⟧
The future perfect indicative expresses completed future action: as,
⟦b:scrīpserō⟧, ⟦i:I shall have written⟧, or ⟦i:I will have written⟧. The future perfect is very common in Latin, particularly in protasis with a relative, with ⟦b:cum⟧, ⟦b:ubī̆⟧, &c., with ⟦b:antequam⟧ or ⟦b:priusquam⟧, with ⟦b:ut (... ita)⟧, ⟦i:as (... so)⟧, or with ⟦b:sī⟧, to express action anterior in time to a future; in English, this future perfect is usually represented by a loose present or perfect: as, ⟦b:quicquid fēceris, adprobābō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 3, 3, 2, ⟦i:whatever you do, I shall think right⟧. Examples will be given further on, in speaking of the complex sentence.
⟦#1627⟧
It may be mentioned here that the future perfect in protasis and apodosis both denotes two actions occurring at one and the same time; these actions are usually identical: as,
⟦b:quī Antōnium oppresserit, is hoc bellum taeterrimum cōnfēcerit⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 10, 19, 2, ⟦i:the man that puts down Antony will put an end to this cruel war⟧, i.e. putting down Antony will be ending the war. ⟦b:respīrārō, sī tē vīderō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 2, 24, 5, ⟦i:I shall take breath again, if I set eyes on you⟧.
⟦#1628⟧
The future perfect sometimes denotes a future resulting state: as,
⟦b:molestus certē e͡i fuerō⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 641, ⟦i:at all events I shall have proved a bane to him⟧. ⟦b:meum rē̆ī pūblicae atque imperātōrī officium praestiterō⟧, 4, 25, 3, ⟦i:I will have my duty all done to country and commander too⟧.
⟦#1629⟧
The future perfect is sometimes used to express rapidity of future action, often with the implication of assurance, promise, or threat: as,
⟦b:abierō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 590, ⟦i:I’ll instantly be gone⟧. ⟦b:iam hūc revēnerō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 863, ⟦i:B.⟧ 1066, ⟦i:I’ll be back here again forthwith⟧. ⟦b:prīmus impetus castra cēperit⟧, L. 25, 38, 17, ⟦i:the first rush will see the camp carried⟧.
⟦#1630⟧
The future perfect often denotes action postponed to a more convenient season, or thrown upon another person.
Often thus with ⟦b:post⟧, ⟦b:aliās⟧, and particularly ⟦b:mox⟧: as, ⟦b:vōbīs post nārrāverō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 721, ⟦i:I’ll tell you by and by⟧, i.e. I won’t tell you now. ⟦b:ad frātrem mox īerō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 194, ⟦i:I’ll to my brother’s by and by⟧, i.e. not yet. ⟦b:fuerit ista eius dēlīberātiō⟧, L. 1, 23, 8, ⟦i:that is a question for him to settle⟧, i.e. not me. Especially ⟦b:vīderō⟧: as, ⟦b:quae fuerit causa, mox vīderō⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 1, 35, ⟦i:what the reason was, I won’t consider now⟧. ⟦b:rēctē secusne aliās vīderimus⟧, ⟦i:Ac.⟧ 2, 135, ⟦i:whether right or not, we will consider some other time⟧, i.e. never. ⟦b:vōs vīderitis⟧, L. 1, 58, 10, ⟦i:that is a question for you⟧, i.e. not me.
⟦#1631⟧
The future perfect sometimes denotes action which will have occurred while something else takes place: as,
⟦b:nōn erō vōbīs morae: tībīcen vōs intereā hīc dēlectāverit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 573a, ⟦i:I will not keep you long; meantime the piper will have entertained you here⟧. ⟦b:tū invītā mulierēs, ego accīverō puerōs⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 5, 1, 3, ⟦i:do you, sir, invite the ladies, and I will meantime have fetched the children⟧.
⟦#1632⟧
The future perfect is often not perceptibly different from the future, especially in the first person singular in old Latin: as,
⟦b:ego mihī prōvīderō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 526, ⟦i:I’ll look out for myself⟧. ⟦b:erōs in obsidiōne linquet, inimīcūm animōs auxerit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 280, ⟦i:he’ll leave his owners in a state of siege, he’ll swell the courage of the enemy⟧. Similarly Cicero, in the protases ⟦b:sī potuerō⟧, ⟦b:sī voluerō⟧, ⟦b:sī licuerit⟧, ⟦b:sī placuerit⟧.

title: The Future Active Participle with sum
text:
⟦#1633⟧
The future active participle combined with the tenses of ⟦b:sum⟧ expresses action impending, resolved on, or destined, at the time indicated by the tense of the verb: as,
⟦b:cum hōc equite pugnātūrī estis⟧, L. 21, 40, 10, ⟦i:with this kind of cavalry are you going to fight⟧. ⟦b:bellum scrīptūrus sum, quod populus Rōmānus cum Iugurthā gessit⟧, Sall. ⟦i:I.⟧ 5, 1, ⟦i:I purpose to write the history of the war that the people of Rome carried on with Jugurtha⟧. ⟦b:fīet illud, quod futūrum est⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 21, ⟦i:whatever is destined to be, will be⟧. ⟦b:Delphōs petiīt, ubī̆ columnās, quibus impositūrī statuās rēgis Perseī fuerant, suīs statuīs dēstināvit⟧, L. 45, 27, 6, ⟦i:he went to Delphi, where he appropriated for his own statues the pillars on which they had intended to put statues of king Perses⟧.

title: Use of the Verb: The Tenses of the Subjunctive
text:
⟦#1634⟧
In simple sentences, the tenses of the subjunctive correspond in general to the same tenses of the indicative. But the present has a future meaning; the imperfect sometimes expresses past, sometimes present action; and the perfect sometimes expresses past action, and sometimes future action.
⟦#1635⟧
The present subjunctive is sometimes used in reference to past action, like the indicative present of vivid narration (⟦r1590:1590⟧): as, ⟦b:migrantīs cernās⟧, V. 4, 401, ⟦i:you can descry them swarming out⟧ (⟦r1556:1556⟧). ⟦b:comprehendī iussit; quis nōn pertimēscat?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 14, ⟦i:he ordered them to be arrested; who would not be thoroughly scared?⟧ (⟦r1565:1565⟧). See also ⟦r2075:2075⟧.

title: The Compound Sentence, or Coordination
text:
⟦#1636⟧
Two or more independent simple sentences may be coordinated to form a compound sentence in one of two ways: either without a connective, or with a connective.
What applies to the coordination of sentences, also applies to the coordination of the parts of sentences in abridged sentences (⟦r1057:1057⟧).

title: The Compound Sentence, or Coordination: Without a Connective
text:
⟦#1637⟧
When simple sentences or parts of sentences are coordinated without any connective, this mode of arrangement is called ⟦i:Asyndetic Coordination⟧ or ⟦i:Asyndeton⟧.
Asyndeton, whether in unabridged or in abridged sentences, is more usual with three or more members than with two. It occurs particularly often in Plautus, Terence, Ennius, and Cato, also in Cicero, especially in his early works and letters.
⟦#1638⟧
The sentences in which asyndeton occurs are commonly such as might be connected by words meaning ⟦i:and⟧ or ⟦i:but⟧; less often by words meaning ⟦i:as⟧, ⟦i:for⟧, &c. Asyndeton is especially common:
⟦#1639⟧
(a.) In animated narration of events happening at the same moment, in description, and in climaxes. Also in mention of colleagues in office, and in many set phrases and formulas: as,
⟦b:vēnī, vīdī, vīcī⟧, Caesar in Suet. ⟦i:Iul.⟧ 37, ⟦i:came, saw, overcame⟧. ⟦b:nostrī celeriter ad arma concurrunt, vāllum cōnscendunt⟧, 5, 39, 3, ⟦i:our men rush speedily to arms, clamber up the palisade⟧. ⟦b:huic s. c. intercessit C. Caelius, C. Pānsa, tribūnī pl.⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 8, 8, 7, ⟦i:this decree of the senate was objected to by Caelius and Pansa, tribunes of the commons⟧. ⟦b:hī ferre agere plēbem⟧, L. 3, 37, 7, ⟦i:there were these people worrying and harrying the commons⟧ (⟦r1535:1535⟧).
⟦#1640⟧
(b.) In contrasts or antitheses: as,
⟦b:opīniōnis commenta dēlet diēs, nātūrae iūdicia cōnfirmat⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 5, ⟦i:the fictions of speculation are swept away by time, but the judgements of nature are confirmed⟧. Particularly when either member is positive, the other negative: ⟦b:vincere scīs, Hannibal, victōriā ūtī nescīs⟧, L. 22, 51, 4, ⟦i:you know how to conquer, Hannibal, but not how to use victory⟧, says Maharbal after Cannae, 216 B.C.
⟦#1641⟧
Asyndeton is very common with two or more imperatives: as, ⟦b:ēgredere ex urbe, Catilīna, līberā rem pūblicam metū, in exsilium proficīscere⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 20, ⟦i:go forth from Rome, Catiline, relieve the commonwealth from its fear, depart into exile⟧. Particularly when the first is ⟦b:age⟧, ⟦i:come on⟧, ⟦i:mark me⟧, or ⟦b:ī⟧, ⟦i:go⟧ (⟦r1572:1572⟧). But from Horace on, ⟦b:ī nunc⟧, ⟦i:go to now⟧, is followed by ⟦b:et⟧ with a second imperative in derisive orders. In old Latin, the imperatives may be joined by ⟦b:et⟧ or even ⟦b:atque⟧.
⟦#1642⟧
Asyndeton is also common with parentheses. These often take the place of a modern foot-note: as, ⟦b:lēgātus capite vēlātō fīlō (lānae vēlāmen est) ‘audī, Iuppiter,’ inquit⟧, L. 1, 32, 6, ⟦i:the envoy with his head covered with a ‘filum’ (that is to say a wrap of wool) says ‘bow down thine ear, Jupiter.’⟧ Parentheses however are often introduced, from Terence on by ⟦b:nam⟧, and from Sallust and Cicero on, by ⟦b:et⟧, ⟦b:neque⟧, ⟦b:autem⟧, ⟦b:enim⟧, &c.
⟦#1643⟧
Simple sentences or parts of sentences may be connected by copulative, disjunctive, or adversative conjunctions.

title: Copulative Conjunctions
text:
⟦#1644⟧
Copulative conjunctions denote union, and connect both the sentences and their meaning. They are ⟦b:et⟧, ⟦b:-que⟧, ⟦b:atque⟧ or ⟦b:ac⟧, ⟦i:and⟧, and ⟦b:neque⟧ or ⟦b:nec⟧, ⟦i:neither⟧.
⟦#1645⟧
(1.) ⟦b:et⟧, ⟦i:and⟧, is the commonest copulative, and connects either likes or unlikes; with two members only, it is either used between them, or is prefixed for emphasis to both: as,
⟦b:Dumnorīx apud Sēquanōs plūrimum poterat et Helvētiīs erat amīcus⟧, 1, 9, 3, ⟦i:Dumnorix was very influential among the Sequani and a friend to the Helvetians⟧. ⟦b:Dēmocritus alba discernere et ātra nōn poterat⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 114, ⟦i:Democritus could not tell white and black apart⟧. ⟦b:et discipulus et magister perhibēbantur inprobī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 425, ⟦i:both pupil and master were rated as knaves⟧.
⟦#1646⟧
With three or more members, ⟦b:et⟧ is either used between the members or, frequently, prefixed for emphasis to all. Often, however, it is omitted throughout (⟦r1637:1637⟧), or a third member is appended by ⟦b:-que⟧ (⟦r1651:1651⟧): as,
⟦b:persuādent Rauricīs et Tulingīs et Latovicīs utī ūnā cum hīs proficīscantur⟧, 1, 5, 4, ⟦i:they induce the Rauricans, Tulingans, and Latovicans to join them in their march⟧. ⟦b:is et in custōdiam cīvēs Rōmānōs dedit et supplicātiōnem mihī̆ dēcrēvit et indicēs maximīs praemiīs adfēcit⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 10, ⟦i:this person voted in the first place to put Roman citizens in ward, then to decree a thanksgiving in my honour, and lastly to reward the informers with liberal gifts⟧.
⟦#1647⟧
Two members belonging closely together as a pair, and connected by ⟦b:et⟧, ⟦b:atque⟧, or ⟦b:-que⟧, are sometimes put asyndetically with another member or members: as,
⟦b:Aeduī ferunt sē dēiectōs prīncipātū; queruntur fortūnae commūtātiōnem et Caesaris indulgentiam in sē requīrunt⟧, 7, 63, 8, ⟦i:the Aeduans set forth that they were cast down from the chief place; they complain of the change of fortune, and say they miss Caesar’s former kindness to them⟧. ⟦b:nūntiātum est equitēs Ariovistī propius tumulum accēdere et ad nostrōs adequitāre; lapidēs in nostrōs conicere⟧, 1, 46, 1, ⟦i:it was reported that Ariovistus’s cavalry were moving nearer the hillock and galloping up to the Romans; that they were throwing stones at our men⟧.
⟦#1648⟧
⟦b:et⟧ has sometimes the meaning of ⟦i:also⟧ or of ⟦i:and also⟧, particularly when there is a change of speakers, or before a pronoun: as, ⟦b:et hoc sciō⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 1, 12, 11, ⟦i:I know that too⟧. Sometimes also after ⟦b:vērum⟧, ⟦b:nam⟧, and ⟦b:simul⟧, especially when a pronoun follows. Not in Caesar.
⟦#1649⟧
(2.) ⟦b:-que⟧, ⟦i:and⟧, combines members which belong together and make a whole, though they may be different or opposed to each other; the second member is often a mere appendage: as,
⟦b:rogat ōratque tē⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 144, ⟦i:he begs and entreats you⟧, or ⟦i:he earnestly entreats you⟧. ⟦b:lībertī servolīque nōbilium⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 141, ⟦i:the freedmen and slaves of the great⟧, or ⟦i:retainers, bond and free⟧. ⟦b:omnēs ea, quae bona videntur, sequuntur fugiuntque contrāria⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 4, 12, ⟦i:everybody runs after what seems good and avoids the opposite⟧. ⟦b:-que⟧ is usually put after the first word of the new member. It is particularly common in old or legal style.
⟦#1650⟧
The combination ⟦b:-que . . . -que⟧, ⟦i:both . . . and⟧, is very common in poetry: as, ⟦b:noctēsque diēsque⟧, E. in ⟦i:CM.⟧ 1, ⟦i:both night and day⟧. In prose, it is used by Sallust when the first word is a pronoun: as, ⟦b:mēque rēgnumque meum⟧, ⟦i:I.⟧ 10, 2, ⟦i:both myself and my throne⟧; and by Livy to connect two relative sentences: as, ⟦b:omnēs quīque Rōmae quīque in exercitū erant⟧, 22, 26, 5, ⟦i:everybody, both people in Rome and people in the army⟧.
⟦#1651⟧
After two members without a connective, a third member is sometimes appended by ⟦b:-que⟧: as,
⟦b:satis habēbat hostem rapīnīs, pābulātiōnibus, populātiōnibusque prohibēre⟧, 1, 15, 4, ⟦i:he was satisfied with keeping the enemy from plundering, foraging, and ravaging⟧.
⟦#1652⟧
(3.) ⟦b:atque⟧, or before any consonant except ⟦b:h⟧ often ⟦b:ac⟧, ⟦i:and⟧, ⟦i:and besides⟧, adds something belonging essentially to what goes before, but more important as a supplement or extension; as,
⟦b:sē ex nāvī prōiēcit atque in hostēs aquilam ferre coepit⟧, 4, 25, 4, ⟦i:he sprang overboard and furthermore proceeded to bear the eagle upon the enemy⟧. ⟦b:magna dīs immortālibus habenda est atque huic Iovī Statōrī grātia⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 11, ⟦i:we owe a great debt of gratitude to the gods immortal in general, and to yon Jove the Stayer in particular⟧. ⟦b:atque . . . atque⟧ occurs for ⟦b:et . . . et⟧ once in Vergil, and once in Silius Italicus.
⟦#1653⟧
⟦b:atque⟧ is used in comparisons, after words of likeness and unlikeness: as,
⟦b:parī spatiō trānsmissus, atque ex Galliā est in Britanniam⟧, 5, 13, 2, ⟦i:the journey across is just as long as it is from Gaul to Britain⟧. ⟦b:īdemque iussērunt simulācrum Iovis facere maius et contrā, atque anteā fuerat, ad orientem convertere⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 20, ⟦i:and they furthermore gave orders to make a statue of Jupiter, a bigger one, and to turn it round to the east, the opposite of the way it originally faced⟧. Sometimes ⟦b:et⟧ is thus used after ⟦b:alius⟧, ⟦b:aliter⟧, ⟦b:aequē⟧, ⟦b:pariter⟧, &c.: see the dictionary.
⟦#1654⟧
With adjectives and adverbs in the comparative degree, ⟦b:atque⟧ sometimes takes the place of ⟦b:quam⟧ ⟦i:than⟧, when the first member of comparison is negative (⟦r1895:1895⟧): as, ⟦b:amīcior mihi nūllus vīvit atque is est⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Mer.⟧ 897, ⟦i:I have no greater friend alive than that man is⟧. So in Plautus, Terence, Lucretius, Catullus, Vergil, rarely in Cicero, and in Horace even when the first member is positive.
⟦#1655⟧
A sentence is often introduced by ⟦b:et⟧, ⟦b:-que⟧, or ⟦b:atque⟧, where ⟦i:but⟧ would be used in English, particularly so when a positive sentence follows a negative one: as,
⟦b:Sōcratēs nec patrōnum quaesīvit nec iūdicibus supplex fuit adhibuitque līberam contumāciam⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 71, ⟦i:Socrates did not try to find an advocate nor bow the knee to his judges, but he was plain-spoken and defiant⟧. ⟦b:nostrōrum mīlitum impetum hostēs ferre nōn potuērunt ac terga vertērunt⟧, 4, 35, 2, ⟦i:the enemy could not stand the dash of our people, but turned their backs⟧. ⟦b:hominis nē Graecī quidem ac Mȳsī potius⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 1, 1, 19, ⟦i:a creature who is not even a Greek, but more of a Mysian⟧.
⟦#1656⟧
Two sentences, one of which would ordinarily be introduced by a subordinating temporal conjunction, are sometimes, mostly in poetry, coordinated by ⟦b:et⟧ or ⟦b:-que⟧: as, ⟦b:dīxit et in silvam pennīs ablāta refūgit⟧, V. 3, 258, ⟦i:she spake, and on her pinions sweeping, vanished to the wood⟧, i.e. ⟦b:simul atque dīxit, refūgit⟧.
⟦#1657⟧
(4.) ⟦b:neque⟧ or ⟦b:nec⟧, ⟦i:neither⟧, ⟦i:nor⟧, ⟦i:and . . . not⟧, ⟦i:but . . . not⟧, is used as a negative copulative, sometimes as a negative adversative: as,
⟦b:opīniōnibus volgī rapimur in errōrem nec vēra cernimus⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 2, 43, ⟦i:we are swept into error by the delusions of the world and cannot make out the truth⟧. ⟦b:nōn enim temere nec fortuī̆tō creātī sumus⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 118, ⟦i:for we were not created at adventure nor by accident⟧. ⟦b:subsidiō suīs iērunt collemque cēpērunt, neque nostrōrum mīlitum impetum sustinēre potuērunt⟧, 7, 62, 8, ⟦i:they went to aid their people and carried the hill, but they could not stand the fiery onset of our soldiers⟧. ⟦b:neque⟧ or ⟦b:nec⟧ is often repeated: as, ⟦b:nec meliōrēs nec beātiōrēs esse possumus⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 1, 32, ⟦i:we can neither be better nor wiser⟧.
⟦#1658⟧
⟦b:nec⟧ is rarely used in the sense of ⟦b:nē . . . quidem⟧, ⟦i:not even⟧, ⟦i:not . . . either⟧: as, ⟦b:nec nunc⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 3, 262, ⟦i:not even now⟧, a free quotation of ⟦b:nē nunc quidem⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 46. ⟦b:nec . . . quidem⟧, ⟦i:and not even⟧, is used once or twice for the common ⟦b:ac nē . . . quidem⟧ or ⟦b:et nē . . . quidem⟧.
⟦#1659⟧
Instead of ⟦b:neque⟧ or ⟦b:nec⟧, ⟦i:and not⟧, the copulatives ⟦b:et⟧, ⟦b:atque⟧, rarely ⟦b:-que⟧, followed by a negative, ⟦b:nōn⟧, ⟦b:nēmō⟧, ⟦b:nihil⟧, &c., are sometimes used in Cicero and Livy, less often in old Latin, and rarely in Caesar and Sallust: as, ⟦b:quid tū fēcissēs, sī tē Tarentum et nōn Samarobrīvam mīsissem?⟧ ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 7, 12, 1, ⟦i:what would you have done, if I had sent you to Tarentum, and not to Samarobriva?⟧ Particularly thus ⟦b:et nōn⟧, or oftener ⟦b:ac nōn⟧, in corrections. But ordinarily ⟦b:neque⟧ or ⟦b:nec⟧ is preferred to ⟦b:et nōn⟧, and ⟦b:nec quisquam⟧, &c., to ⟦b:et nēmō⟧, &c. (⟦r1445:1445⟧).
⟦#1660⟧
When ⟦b:neque⟧ is followed by another negative, the assertion is positive (⟦r1452:1452⟧): as,
⟦b:nec hoc ille nōn vīdit⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 4, 60, ⟦i:and the man did not fail to see this⟧. This positive use begins with Varro. In old Latin two negatives, and particularly ⟦b:neque . . . haud⟧, are often used, as in old English, to strengthen the negation (⟦r1453:1453⟧).
⟦#1661⟧
After a general negative, a word may be emphasized by ⟦b:nē ... quidem⟧ or ⟦b:nōn modo⟧, or the parts of a compound sentence may be distributed by ⟦b:neque . . . neque⟧, without destroying the negation: as,
⟦b:nihil in locīs commūnibus, nē in fānīs quidem, nihil istum neque prīvātī neque pūblicī tōtā in Siciliā relīquisse⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 2, ⟦i:that the defendant has left nothing untouched in public places, no, not even in the temples, nothing either in the way of private or of public property, in all Sicily⟧. Similarly when a coordinate member is appended with ⟦b:neque⟧: as, ⟦b:nequeō satis mīrārī neque conicere⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 547, ⟦i:I can’t quite puzzle out or guess⟧.

title: Combination of Different Copulatives
text:
⟦#1662⟧
Different copulatives are sometimes combined, as follows.
⟦#1663⟧
(1.) The affirmative copulatives ⟦b:et⟧ and ⟦b:-que⟧ are sometimes combined, particularly in abridged sentences: as,
⟦b:et Epamīnōndās praeclārē cecinisse dīcitur, Themistoclēsque est habitus indoctior⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 4, ⟦i:Epaminondas in the first place is said to have played beautifully, and Themistocles was not considered exactly an educated man⟧. This combination is used by Cicero rarely, by Horace in the satires, and rarely by late writers.
⟦#1664⟧
The sequence ⟦b:-que . . . et⟧ is rare in old Latin, and not used by Caesar, Vergil, or Horace. ⟦b:-que . . . atque⟧ is first used by Lucretius, then by Vergil, Ovid, Livy, and Tacitus.
⟦#1665⟧
(2.) Affirmative and negative copulatives are sometimes combined. Thus ⟦b:neque⟧ or ⟦b:nec⟧ combined with ⟦b:et⟧, in the sequences ⟦b:neque . . . et⟧ and ⟦b:et . . . neque⟧, which is rare in old Latin, is common in Cicero: as,
⟦b:nec mīror et gaudeō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 10, 1, 4, ⟦i:in the first place I am not surprised, and in the second place I feel glad⟧; ⟦b:neque . . . et nōn⟧, however, is rare. ⟦b:patēbat via et certa neque longa⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 11, 4, ⟦i:there lay a road open at once plain and not long⟧. ⟦b:neque . . . -que⟧ begins with Cicero, but is rare (⟦r1655:1655⟧), ⟦b:neque . . . ac⟧ begins with Tacitus.
⟦#1666⟧
Of all the Latin writers, Tacitus aims most at variety by combination of asyndeton and by the use of different copulatives: as, ⟦b:rēgem Rhamsēn Libyā Aethiopiā Mēdīsque et Persīs et Bactriānō ac Scythā potītum⟧, 2, 60, ⟦i:that king Rhamses got control of Libya and Aethiopia and the Medes and Persians, and the Bactrian and Scythian⟧.

title: Disjunctive Conjunctions
text:
⟦#1667⟧
Disjunctive conjunctions connect the sentences, but disconnect the meaning. They are ⟦b:aut⟧, ⟦b:vel⟧, ⟦b:sīve⟧ or ⟦b:seu⟧, ⟦b:-ve⟧, and ⟦b:an⟧, ⟦i:or⟧. Of these conjunctions, ⟦b:aut⟧, ⟦b:vel⟧, and ⟦b:sīve⟧ are often placed before two or more members of a sentence in the sense of ⟦i:either . . . or⟧. And in poetry, ⟦b:-ve . . . -ve⟧ sometimes occurs.
⟦#1668⟧
(1.) ⟦b:aut⟧, ⟦i:or⟧, sometimes ⟦i:or even⟧, ⟦i:or at least⟧, is used between two members which are to be represented as essentially different in meaning, and of which one excludes the other: as,
⟦b:hīc vincendum aut moriendum, mīlitēs, est⟧, L. 21, 43, 5, ⟦i:here you must conquer, my men, or die⟧. ⟦b:hōrae mōmentō cita mors venit aut victōria laeta⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 1, 7, ⟦i:within an hour’s brief turn comes speedy death or victory glad⟧. ⟦b:aut vīvam aut moriar⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 483, ⟦i:I shall either live or die⟧. ⟦b:sīderibus dubiīs aut illō tempore quō sē frīgida circumagunt pigrī serrāca Boōtae⟧, J. 5, 22, ⟦i:when stars blink faint, or even at the time when round rolls slow Boötes’ frigid wain⟧. ⟦b:quā rē vī aut clam agendum est⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 10, 12, 5 [10, 12b, 2], ⟦i:so we must use force, or at any rate secrecy⟧. Sometimes ⟦b:aut⟧ connects kindred ideas: as, ⟦b:equī ictī aut vulnerātī cōnsternābantur⟧, L. 21, 33, 6, ⟦i:the horses kept getting frantic from being hit or wounded⟧.
⟦#1669⟧
⟦b:aut⟧, in the sense of ⟦i:otherwise⟧, ⟦i:or else⟧, sometimes introduces a statement of what necessarily follows, if something else is not done: as,
⟦b:audendum est aliquid ūniversīs, aut omnia singulīs patienda⟧, L. 6, 18, 7, ⟦i:you must make some bold dash collectively, or else you must suffer every thing individually⟧. ⟦b:vel⟧ is also occasionally used in this sense.
⟦#1670⟧
(2.) ⟦b:vel⟧, ⟦i:or⟧, introduces an alternative as a matter of choice or preference, and often relates merely to the selection of an expression: as,
⟦b:eius modī coniūnctiōnem tēctōrum oppidum vel urbem appellāvērunt⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 1, 41, ⟦i:such a collection of dwelling-houses they called, well, a town or a city, whichever you please⟧. ⟦b:vel imperātōre vel mīlite mē ūtiminī⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 20, 16, ⟦i:use me as your generalissimo or as a private, whichever you will⟧. ⟦b:Catilīnam ex urbe vel ēiēcimus vel ēmīsimus vel ipsum ēgredientem verbīs prōsecūtī sumus⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 1, ⟦i:we have—what shall I say?—driven Catiline out of town, or allowed him to go out, or, when he was going out of his own accord, wished him a pleasant journey⟧. ⟦b:vel⟧ is often followed by ⟦b:etiam⟧, ⟦b:potius⟧, or ⟦b:dīcam⟧. From Tacitus on, ⟦b:vel⟧ is sometimes used in the sense of ⟦b:aut⟧: as, ⟦b:vincendum vel cadendum esse⟧, Ta. 14, 35, ⟦i:they must do or die⟧ (⟦r1668:1668⟧).
⟦#1671⟧
⟦b:vel⟧ is sometimes used in the sense of ⟦i:if you will⟧, ⟦i:even⟧, or ⟦i:perhaps⟧, especially before superlatives, or in the sense of ⟦i:for instance⟧: as,
⟦b:huius domus est vel optima Messānae, nōtissima quidem certē⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 3, ⟦i:this gentleman’s house is perhaps the finest in all Messana, at any rate the best known⟧. ⟦b:amant tēd omnēs mulierēs, neque iniūriā: vel illae, quae here palliō mē reprehendērunt⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 58, ⟦i:the girls all idolize you, well they may; for instance those that buttonholed me yesterday⟧.
⟦#1672⟧
(3.) ⟦b:sīve⟧ or ⟦b:seu⟧, ⟦i:or⟧, used as a disjunctive conjunction, denotes a distinction which is not essential, or the speaker’s uncertainty as to some matter of detail; when used once only, it is chiefly in corrections, often with ⟦b:potius⟧, ⟦i:rather⟧, added; as,
⟦b:is Ascanius urbem mātrī seu novercae relīquit⟧, L. 1, 3, 3, ⟦i:said Ascanius left the city to his mother, or his stepmother, if you prefer⟧. ⟦b:dīxit Pompēius, sīve voluit⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 2, 3, 2, ⟦i:Pompey made a speech, or rather attempted to make one⟧.
⟦#1673⟧
⟦b:sīve⟧ is often repeated in the sense of ⟦i:either⟧, or ⟦i:no matter whether . . . or⟧: as,
⟦b:ita sīve cāsū sīve cōnsiliō deōrum, quae pars calamitātem populō Rōmānō intulerat, ea prīnceps poenās persolvit⟧, 1, 12, 6, ⟦i:thus, no matter whether from chance or through special providence, the part which had done damage to Rome was the first to pay penalty in full⟧.
⟦#1674⟧
(4.) ⟦b:-ve⟧ rarely connects main sentences, usually only the less important parts of the sentence, or, oftener still, subordinate sentences: as,
⟦b:cūr timeam dubitemve locum dēfendere?⟧ J. 1, 103, ⟦i:why should I fear or hesitate to stand my ground?⟧ ⟦b:Appius ad mē bis terve litterās mīserat⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 6, 1, 2, ⟦i:Appius had written me two or three times⟧. With ⟦b:nē⟧ it forms ⟦b:nēve⟧ or ⟦b:neu⟧, which is used as a continuation of ⟦b:nē⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧: see ⟦r1581:1581⟧; 1586; 1947.
⟦#1675⟧
(5.) The interrogative particle ⟦b:an⟧ sometimes becomes a disjunctive conjunction, ⟦i:or⟧, ⟦i:or possibly⟧, ⟦i:or perhaps⟧: as, ⟦b:Simōnidēs an quis alius⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 104, ⟦i:Simonides or possibly somebody else⟧. Common in Cicero, though not so in his speeches, and in Livy, commonest in Tacitus.

title: Adversative Conjunctions
text:
⟦#1676⟧
Adversative conjunctions connect the sentences, but contrast the meaning. They are ⟦b:autem⟧, ⟦i:on the other hand⟧, ⟦b:sed⟧, ⟦b:vērum⟧, ⟦b:cēterum⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, ⟦b:vērō⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, ⟦i:indeed⟧, ⟦b:at⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, ⟦b:tamen⟧, ⟦b:nihilō minus⟧, ⟦i:nevertheless⟧.
Of these conjunctions, ⟦b:autem⟧ and ⟦b:vērō⟧ are put after one word, or sometimes after two closely connected words; ⟦b:tamen⟧ is put either at the beginning, or after an emphatic word.
⟦#1677⟧
(1.) ⟦b:autem⟧, ⟦i:again⟧, ⟦i:on the other hand⟧, ⟦i:however⟧, simply continues the discourse by a statement appended to the preceding, without setting it aside: as,
⟦b:hōrum prīncipibus pecūniās, cīvitātī autem imperium tōtīus prōvinciae pollicētur⟧, 7, 64, 8, ⟦i:to the chieftains of this nation on the one hand he promises moneys, and to the community on the other hand the hegemony of the whole province⟧. The opposition in a sentence introduced by ⟦b:autem⟧, ⟦i:again⟧, is often so weak that a copulative, ⟦i:and⟧, might be used: as, ⟦b:ille quī Dī̆ogenem adulēscēns, post autem Panaetium audierat⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 24, ⟦i:the man who in his early youth had sat at the feet of Diogenes, and afterwards of Panaetius⟧. ⟦b:autem⟧ is oftenest used in philosophical or didactic discourse, less frequently in history, oratory, or poetry.
⟦#1678⟧
⟦b:autem⟧ is often used in questions: as, ⟦b:metuō crēdere :: crēdere autem?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 304, ⟦i:I am afraid to trust :: trust, do you say?⟧
⟦#1679⟧
(2.) ⟦b:sed⟧ or ⟦b:set⟧, and ⟦b:vērum⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, are used either in restriction, or, after a negative, in direct opposition: as,
⟦b:vēra dīcō, sed nēquīquam, quoniam nōn vīs crēdere⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 835, ⟦i:I tell the truth, but all in vain, since you are bent not to believe⟧. ⟦b:nōn ego erus tibī, sed servos sum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 241, ⟦i:I am not your master, but your slave⟧.
⟦#1680⟧
⟦b:nōn modo⟧, or ⟦b:nōn sōlum⟧, ⟦i:not only⟧, ⟦i:not alone⟧, is followed by ⟦b:sed etiam⟧ or ⟦b:vērum etiam⟧, ⟦i:but also⟧, by ⟦b:sed . . . quoque⟧, ⟦i:but ... as well⟧, or sometimes by ⟦b:sed⟧ or ⟦b:vērum⟧ alone: as,
⟦b:quī nōn sōlum interfuit hīs rēbus, sed etiam praefuit⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 1, 8, 1, ⟦i:who has not had a hand only in these matters, but complete charge⟧. ⟦b:quī omnibus negōtiīs nōn interfuit sōlum, sed praefuit⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 1, 6, 1. ⟦b:nōn tantum⟧ is sometimes used by Livy, and once or twice by Cicero, but not by Caesar or Sallust, for ⟦b:nōn modo⟧. Livy and Tacitus sometimes omit ⟦b:sed⟧ or ⟦b:vērum⟧.
⟦#1681⟧
⟦b:nōn modo⟧ has sometimes the meaning of ⟦b:nōn dīcam⟧: as, ⟦b:nōn modo ad certam mortem, sed in magnum vītae discrīmen⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 45, ⟦i:I won’t say to certain death, but to great risk of life⟧.
⟦#1682⟧
⟦b:nōn modo⟧ or ⟦b:nōn sōlum⟧, when attended by another negative, may also be followed by ⟦b:sed nē . . . quidem⟧, ⟦i:but not even⟧, or ⟦b:sed vix⟧, ⟦i:but hardly⟧: as,
⟦b:nōn modo tibī̆ nōn īrāscor, sed nē reprehendō quidem factum tuum⟧, ⟦i:Sull.⟧ 50, ⟦i:so far from being angry with you I do not even criticise your action⟧. When both members have the same predicate, usually placed last, the negation in ⟦b:nē . . . quidem⟧ or ⟦b:vix⟧ usually applies to the first member also: as, ⟦b:tālis vir nōn modo facere, sed nē cōgitāre quidem quicquam audēbit, quod nōn audeat praedicāre⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 77, ⟦i:a man of this kind will not only not venture to do, but not even to conceive anything which he would not venture to trumpet to the world⟧, or ⟦i:will not venture to conceive, much less do⟧.
⟦#1683⟧
(3.) ⟦b:cēterum⟧ is sometimes used in the sense of ⟦b:sed⟧, in Terence, Sallust, and Livy. Sometimes also in the sense of ⟦b:sed rē vērā⟧, in Sallust and Tacitus, to contrast reality with pretence.
⟦#1684⟧
(4.) ⟦b:vērō⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, ⟦i:indeed⟧, introduces an emphatic contrast or a climax: as,
⟦b:sed sunt haec leviōra, illa vērō gravia atque magna⟧, ⟦i:Pl.⟧ 86, ⟦i:however, all this is less important, but the following is weighty and great⟧. ⟦b:scīmus mūsicēn nostrīs mōribus abesse ā prīncipis persōnā, saltāre vērō etiam in vitiīs pōnī⟧, N. 15, 1, 2, ⟦i:we know that, according to our Roman code of ethics, music is not in keeping with the character of an eminent man, and as to dancing, why that is classed among vices⟧. In Plautus, ⟦b:vērō⟧ is only used as an adverb; its use as an adversative conjunction begins with Terence. In the historians, ⟦b:vērō⟧ is often equivalent to ⟦b:autem⟧.
⟦#1685⟧
(5.) ⟦b:at⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, denotes emphatic lively opposition, an objection, or a contrast: as,
⟦b:brevis ā nātūrā nōbīs vīta data est; at memoria bene redditae vītae sempiterna⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 14, 32, ⟦i:a short life hath been given by nature unto man; but the memory of a life laid down in a good cause endureth for ever⟧. ⟦b:at⟧ is often used before a word indicating a person or a place, to shift the scene, especially in history. In law language, ⟦b:ast⟧ sometimes occurs, and ⟦b:ast⟧ is also sometimes used, generally for the metre, in Vergil, Horace, and late poetry.
⟦#1686⟧
(6.) ⟦b:tamen⟧, ⟦b:nihilō minus⟧, ⟦i:nevertheless⟧.
⟦b:accūsātus capitis absolvitur, multātur tamen pecūniā⟧, N. 4, 2, 6, ⟦i:he is accused on a capital charge and acquitted, but is nevertheless fined in a sum of money⟧. ⟦b:minus dolendum fuit rē nōn perfectā, sed poeniendum certē nihilō minus⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 19, ⟦i:there was less occasion for sorrow because the thing was not done, but certainly none the less for punishment⟧.

title: Other Words As Connectives
text:
⟦#1687⟧
Instead of a conjunction, other words are often used as connectives: as, ⟦b:pars . . . pars⟧, ⟦b:aliī . . . aliī⟧; adverbs of order or time: as, ⟦b:prīmum⟧, ⟦i:first⟧, or ⟦b:prīmō⟧, ⟦i:at first⟧ ⟦b:... deinde . . . tum⟧, &c.; and particularly adverbs in pairs: as, ⟦b:modo . . . modo⟧, ⟦b:tum . . . tum,⟧ less frequently ⟦b:quā . . . quā⟧, ⟦b:simul . . . simul⟧: as,
⟦b:multitūdō pars prōcurrit in viās, pars in vestibulīs stat, pars ex tēctīs prōspectant⟧, L. 24, 21, 8, ⟦i:part of the throng runs out into the streets, others stand in the fore-courts, others gaze from the house-tops⟧. ⟦b:prōferēbant aliī purpuram, tūs aliī, gemmās aliī⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 146, ⟦i:they produced some of them purple, others frankincense, others precious stones⟧. ⟦b:prīmō pecūniae, deinde imperī cupīdō crēvit⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 10, 3, ⟦i:at first a love of money waxed strong, then of power⟧. ⟦b:tum hoc mihī̆ probābilius, tum illud vidētur⟧, ⟦i:Ac.⟧ 2, 134, ⟦i:one minute this seems to me more likely, and another minute that⟧.
⟦#1688⟧
Simple sentences may also be coordinated by words denoting inference or cause, such as ⟦b:ergō⟧, ⟦b:igitur⟧, ⟦b:itaque⟧, ⟦i:therefore⟧; ⟦b:nam⟧, ⟦b:namque⟧, ⟦b:enim⟧, ⟦i:for⟧, ⟦b:etenim⟧, ⟦i:for you see⟧: as,
⟦b:adfectus animī in bonō virō laudābilis, et vīta igitur laudābilis bonī virī, et honesta ergō, quoniam laudābilis⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 47, ⟦i:the disposition in a good man is praiseworthy, and the life therefore of a good man is praiseworthy, and virtuous accordingly, seeing it is praiseworthy⟧. Of these words, ⟦b:nam⟧, ⟦b:namque⟧, and ⟦b:itaque⟧ are usually put first in the sentence; ⟦b:enim⟧ and ⟦b:igitur⟧, usually after one word, rarely after two. But in Plautus regularly, and generally in Terence, ⟦b:enim⟧ has the meaning of ⟦i:indeed⟧, ⟦i:verily⟧, ⟦i:truly⟧, ⟦i:depend upon it⟧, and may stand at the beginning.
⟦#1689⟧
In Plautus, the combination ⟦b:ergō igitur⟧ occurs, and in Terence and Livy, ⟦b:itaque ergō⟧: as, ⟦b:itaque ergō cōnsulibus diēs dicta est⟧, L. 3, 31, 5, ⟦i:accordingly then a day was set for the trial of the consuls⟧.
⟦#1690⟧
The interrogative ⟦b:quippe⟧, ⟦i:why?⟧ losing its interrogative meaning, is also used as a coordinating word, ⟦i:why⟧, or ⟦i:for⟧: as, ⟦b:hōc genus omne maestum ac sollicitum est cantōris morte Tigellī: quippe benignus erat⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 2, 2, ⟦i:such worthies all are sad, are woebegone over Tigellius the minstrel’s death; why he was generosity itself⟧.
⟦#1691⟧
Simple sentences may also be coordinated by pronominal words, such as ⟦b:hinc⟧, ⟦b:inde⟧, ⟦i:hence⟧, ⟦b:eō⟧, ⟦b:ideō⟧, ⟦b:idcircō⟧, ⟦b:proptereā⟧, ⟦i:so⟧, ⟦i:on that account⟧, &c.: as,
⟦b:nocte perveniēbant; eō custōdiās hostium fallēbant⟧, L. 23, 19, 10, ⟦i:they got there in the night; in that way they eluded the enemy’s pickets⟧. But ⟦b:eō⟧ and ⟦b:ideō⟧ are not used thus by Cicero, Caesar, or Sallust, or ⟦b:idcircō⟧ and ⟦b:proptereā⟧ by Cicero or Caesar.
⟦#1692⟧
In animated rhetorical discourse any word repeated with emphasis may serve as a copulative; this is called ⟦i:Anaphora⟧: as,
⟦b:mīles in forum, mīles in cūriam comitābātur⟧, Ta. 1, 7, ⟦i:soldiers went with him to the forum, soldiers to the senate chamber⟧. ⟦b:ēreptī estis ex interitū, ēreptī sine sanguine, sine exercitū, sine dīmicātiōne⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 23, ⟦i:you are rescued from death, rescued without bloodshed, without an army, without a struggle⟧.

title: The Intermediate Coordinate Sentence
text:
⟦#1693⟧
A sentence coordinate in form with another sentence is often equivalent in meaning to a subordinate sentence. Such sentences are called ⟦i:Intermediate Coordinate Sentences⟧.
The most varied relations of a subordinate sentence may be thus expressed by a coordinate sentence, and the combination of the two coordinate sentences is in sense equivalent to a complex sentence.
⟦#1694⟧
Such coordinated sentences are a survival of a more primitive state of the language. They occur oftenest in Plautus and Terence, in Cicero’s philosophical works and letters, in Horace’s satires and epistles, and in Juvenal. In general they have been superseded by complex sentences, even in the oldest specimens of the language.
⟦#1695⟧
I. The relation of the two members may not be indicated by the mood, but left to be determined from the context.
Thus, in the combination ⟦b:amat, sapit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 995, ⟦i:he is in love, he shows his sense⟧, the two members ⟦b:amat⟧ and ⟦b:sapit⟧ are alike in form. But in sense, ⟦b:sapit⟧ is the main member and ⟦b:amat⟧ is the subordinate member. Just what the relation of the ⟦b:amat⟧ is, whether it is ⟦b:sī amat⟧, ⟦i:if he is in love⟧, ⟦b:cum amat⟧, ⟦i:when he is in love⟧, ⟦b:quod amat⟧, ⟦i:because he is in love⟧, or ⟦b:etsī amat⟧, ⟦i:though he is in love⟧, &c., &c., is left to the reader to make out. The following are some of the commonest combinations of this class:
⟦#1696⟧
(1.) The coordinated member may stand instead of the commoner accusative and infinitive with a verb of perceiving, thinking, knowing, or saying (⟦r2175:2175⟧). Such are ⟦b:crēdō⟧, ⟦b:fateor⟧, ⟦b:opīnor⟧, ⟦b:putō⟧, ⟦b:certum est⟧, &c.: as,
⟦b:lūdōs mē facitis, intellegō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 802, ⟦i:you are making game of me, I am aware⟧. ⟦b:nārrō tibī̆: plānē relēgātus mihī̆ videor⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 2, 11, 1, ⟦i:I tell you what, I seem to myself regularly banished⟧. ⟦b:spērō, servābit fidem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:E.⟧ 124, ⟦i:I hope he’ll keep his word⟧ (⟦r2235:2235⟧).
⟦#1697⟧
(2.) The coordinated member may be a direct question or an exclamation.
Thus (⟦i:a.⟧) in enquiries calling for an answer: as, ⟦b:sīgnī dīc quid est⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 421, ⟦i:tell me, what is there in the shape of seal?⟧ (⟦r1251:1251⟧). Or (⟦i:b.⟧) in ejaculation: as, ⟦b:viden ut astat furcifer?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 1172, ⟦i:seest how the knave is posing there?⟧ ⟦b:vidēte quaesō, quid potest pecūnia⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 410, ⟦i:see pray how all-commanding money is⟧. This construction occurs oftenest in comedy, and with an imperative meaning ⟦i:say⟧, ⟦i:tell⟧, or ⟦i:look⟧. The subordinate construction is the rule: see ⟦r1773:1773⟧.
⟦#1698⟧
(3.) The coordinated member rarely represents a relative sentence (⟦r1816:1816⟧): as,
⟦b:urbs antīqua fuit, Tyriī tenuēre colōnī⟧, V. 1, 12, ⟦i:there was an ancient town, which Tyrian settlers held⟧. ⟦b:est locus, Hesperiam Graī cōgnōmine dīcunt⟧, V. 1, 530, ⟦i:there is a place, the Greeks by name Hesperia call⟧, imitated from ⟦b:est locus Hesperiam quam mortālēs perhibēbant⟧, E. in Macrob. ⟦i:Sat.⟧ 6, 1, ⟦i:there is a place which sons of men Hesperia called⟧.
⟦#1699⟧
(4.) The coordinated member may represent a subordinate temporal member: as,
⟦b:vēnit hiemps, teritur Sicuōnia bāca trapētis⟧, V. ⟦i:G.⟧ 2, 519, ⟦i:has winter come, in mills is Sicyon’s olive ground⟧ (⟦r1860:1860⟧). ⟦b:vix prōram attigerat, rumpit Sāturnia fūnem⟧, V. 12, 650, ⟦i:scarce had he touched the prow, Saturnia snaps the rope⟧, i.e. ⟦b:cum rumpit⟧ (⟦r1869:1869⟧). ⟦b:lūcēbat iam ferē, prōcēdit in medium⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 94, ⟦i:it was just about light, when he presents himself before them⟧. ⟦b:fuit ōrnandus in Mānīliā lēge Pompēius; temperātā ōrātiōne ōrnandī cōpiam persecūtī sumus⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 102, ⟦i:when I had to glorify Pompey in the matter of the Manilius law, I went through the ample material for glorification in moderate language⟧.
⟦#1700⟧
(5.) The coordinated member may be equivalent to a member with ⟦b:ut⟧, expressing result (⟦r1965:1965⟧): as,
⟦b:iam faxō sciēs⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 663, ⟦i:I’ll let you know at once⟧, i.e. ⟦b:sciās⟧ (⟦r1712:1712⟧) or ⟦b:ut sciās⟧ (⟦r1965:1965⟧). ⟦b:iam faxō hīc erunt⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 715, ⟦i:I’ll warrant they shall soon be here⟧. ⟦b:adeō rēs rediīt, adulēscentulus victus est⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 113, ⟦i:things came to such a pass the youngster was put down⟧. ⟦b:cētera dē genere hōc, adeō sunt multa, loquācem dēlassāre valent Fabium⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 1, 11, ⟦i:the other cases of the kind, so plentiful are they, might tire the gabbling Fabius out⟧. ⟦b:ita haec ūmōre tigna pūtent, nōn videor mihi sarcīre posse aedīs meās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 146, ⟦i:so sopping rotten are these joists, I don’t think I can patch my house⟧. ⟦b:ita avidō ingeniō fuit, numquam indicāre id fīliō voluit suō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul. prol.⟧ 9, ⟦i:so niggardly was he, he’d never point it out to his own son⟧. ⟦b:tanta incepta rēs est, haud somnīculōsē hoc agundumst⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 227, ⟦i:so big a job have we begun, not drowsily must this be done⟧.
⟦#1701⟧
(6.) The coordinated member may be equivalent to a conditional protasis: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:fīliam quis habet, pecūniā opus est⟧, ⟦i:Par.⟧ 44, ⟦i:a man has a daughter, he needs money⟧. ⟦b:trīstis es, indignor⟧, O. ⟦i:Tr.⟧ 4, 3, 33, ⟦i:if you are sad, I feel provoked⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:sī iste ībit, ītō; stābit, astātō simul⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 863, ⟦i:if he shall move, move thou; but shall he stand, stand by his side⟧. ⟦b:in caelum, iusseris, ībit⟧, J. 3, 78, ⟦i:say but the word, he’ll mount the sky⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:subdūc cibum ūnum diem āthlētae, Iovem Olympium inplōrābit⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 40, ⟦i:cut off an athlete from his food just a day, he will pray to Jupiter aloft in Olympus⟧ (⟦r1574:1574⟧). (⟦i:d.⟧) ⟦b:Zēnōnem rogēs, respondeat totidem verbīs⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 4, 69, ⟦i:you may ask Zeno, he would answer in just as many words⟧ (⟦r1556:1556⟧). (⟦i:e.⟧) ⟦b:tū quoque magnam partem opere in tantō, sineret dolor, Īcare, habērēs⟧, V. 6, 31, ⟦i:thou too a goodly space in work so vast, had grief allowed, O Icarus, hadst filled⟧ (⟦r1559:1559⟧). ⟦b:at darēs hanc vim M. Crassō, in forō saltāret⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 75, ⟦i:but had you given this chance to Crassus, he would have capered in the market place⟧ (⟦r1559:1559⟧). ⟦b:nam absque tē esset, hodiē numquam ad sōlem occāsum vīverem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 1022, ⟦i:for were it not for you, I ne’er should live this blessed day till set of sun⟧ (⟦r1560:1560⟧, ⟦r2110:2110⟧). (⟦i:f.⟧) ⟦b:ūnā fuissēmus, cōnsilium certē nōn dēfuisset⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 9, 6, 6, ⟦i:had we been together, we certainly should not have lacked a programme⟧ (⟦r1561:1561⟧).
⟦#1702⟧
(7.) The coordinated member may be equivalent to a concession: as,
⟦b:id fortasse nōn perfēcimus, cōnātī quidem sumus⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 210; ⟦i:though we have perhaps not attained unto this, yet we have attempted it⟧. ⟦b:ergō illī intellegunt quid Epicūrus dīcat, ego nōn intellegō?⟧ ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 13, ⟦i:do those gentlemen then understand what Epicurus means, and I not?⟧
⟦#1703⟧
(8.) The coordinated member may denote efficient cause or reason: as,
⟦b:peregrīnus ego sum, Sauream nōn nōvī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 464, ⟦i:I am a stranger, and I don’t know Saurea⟧. ⟦b:mulier es, audācter iūrās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 836, ⟦i:because you are a woman, you are bold to swear⟧. ⟦b:tacent, satis laudant⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 476, ⟦i:their silence is sufficient praise⟧.
⟦#1704⟧
(9.) The coordinated member may represent the protasis of a comparative sentence with ⟦b:ut⟧ (⟦r1937:1937⟧): as,
⟦b:ita mē dī ament, honestust⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 474, ⟦i:so help me heaven, he is a proper man⟧. ⟦b:sollicitat, ita vīvam, mē tua, mī Tirō, valētūdō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 20, ⟦i:your health, dear Tiro, keeps me fidgety, as I hope to live⟧.
⟦#1705⟧
II. The subordinate idea is often indicated by the subjunctive of desire coordinated with another verb, usually with one which has a different subject.
Thus, the combination ⟦b:amēs: oportet⟧, ⟦i:you should love; it is right⟧ (⟦r1547:1547⟧), in which the two verbs are used separately, blends into one whole, ⟦b:amēs oportet⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 35, ⟦i:it is right you should love⟧. The verb with which the subjunctive is coordinated specifies more exactly the general idea of desire contained in the subjunctive itself. The tense of the coordinate subjunctive is regulated by that of the other verb.
⟦#1706⟧
The negative employed with coordinated subjunctives is the adverb ⟦b:nē⟧, ⟦i:not⟧.
Thus, the combination ⟦b:vidē: nē mē lūdās⟧, ⟦i:see to it; don’t you fool me⟧ (⟦r1547:1547⟧), in which the two verbs are used separately, blends into one whole, ⟦b:vidē nē mē lūdās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cur.⟧ 325, ⟦i:see to it you don’t fool me⟧. Similarly, ⟦b:metuō: nē peccet⟧, ⟦i:I am afraid; let her not slip up⟧ (⟦r1548:1548⟧), becomes ⟦b:metuō nē peccet⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 624, ⟦i:I am afraid she may slip up⟧. From its frequent use in sentences of subordinate meaning, ⟦b:nē⟧ came at an early period to be regarded as a subordinating conjunction also, ⟦i:lest⟧, ⟦i:that . . . not⟧, as well as an adverb, and took the place of the less usual ⟦b:ut nē⟧. Hence members with ⟦b:nē⟧ are more conveniently treated under the head of subordination (⟦r1947:1947⟧).
⟦#1707⟧
(1.) The subjunctive is often coordinated with verbs of wishing. Such are ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:nōlō⟧, rarely ⟦b:mālō⟧, ⟦b:optō⟧, ⟦b:placet⟧, &c.: as,
⟦b:animum advortās volō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 388, ⟦i:I wish you would pay heed⟧ (⟦r1548:1548⟧). ⟦b:quid vīs faciam?⟧ T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 846, ⟦i:what wilt thou I should do?⟧ (⟦r1563:1563⟧). ⟦b:vin conmūtēmus? tuam ego dūcam et tū meam?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 59, ⟦i:would you like to swap? I take your wife, and you take mine?⟧ (⟦r1563:1563⟧). ⟦b:mālō tē sapiēns hostis metuat, quam stultī cīvēs laudent⟧, L. 22, 39, 20, ⟦i:I would rather a wise enemy should fear you, than stupid fellow-citizens admire you⟧ (⟦r1548:1548⟧). Coordination is the rule with ⟦b:velim⟧, ⟦b:vellem⟧, &c., used in the sense of ⟦b:utinam⟧ (⟦r1540:1540⟧): as, ⟦b:dē Menedēmō vellem vērum fuisset, dē rēgīnā velim vērum sit⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 15, 4, 4, ⟦i:about Menedemus I could wish it had been true, about the queen I hope it may be true⟧. ⟦b:tellūs optem prius īma dehīscat⟧, V. 4, 24, ⟦i:I would the earth to deepest depths might sooner yawn⟧. ⟦b:L. Domitius dīxit placēre sībī̆ sententiās dē singulīs ferrent⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 83, 3, ⟦i:Domitius said his view was they should vote on the men separately⟧.
⟦#1708⟧
(2.) The subjunctive is often coordinated with verbs of request, entreaty, encouragement, exhortation, charge, direction, command. Such are ⟦b:precor⟧, ⟦b:rogō⟧, ⟦b:ōrō⟧, ⟦b:petō⟧, ⟦b:hortor⟧, ⟦b:postulō⟧, ⟦b:moneō⟧, ⟦b:cēnseō⟧; ⟦b:mandō⟧, ⟦b:imperō⟧, ⟦b:praecipiō⟧, ⟦b:dēcernō⟧; and chiefly in old Latin, ⟦b:iubeō⟧: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:reddās incolumem precor⟧, H. 1, 3, 7, ⟦i:deliver him up safe I pray⟧. ⟦b:rogat fīnem ōrandī faciat⟧, 1, 20, 5, ⟦i:he requests him to make an end of entreaty⟧. ⟦b:ā tē id quod suēstī petō, mē absentem dēfendās⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 15, 8, ⟦i:I ask you to do as you always do, stand up for me when I am away⟧. ⟦b:nōn hortor sōlum sed etiam rogō atque ōrō, tē colligās virumque praebeās⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 5, 18, 1, ⟦i:I not only exhort you, but more than that I beg and entreat you, pull yourself together and quit you like a man⟧. ⟦b:postulō etiam atque etiam cōnsīderēs quō prōgrediāre⟧, L. 3, 45, 10, ⟦i:I charge you think again and again what you are coming to⟧. ⟦b:tē moneō videās, quid agās. magnō opere cēnseō, dēsistās⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 174, ⟦i:I advise you to consider what you are doing. I earnestly recommend you to stop⟧. ⟦b:hunc admonet iter cautē faciat⟧, 5, 49, 3, ⟦i:he warns him he must pursue his march with care⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:huic mandat Rēmōs adeat⟧, 3, 11, 2, ⟦i:he directs him to go to the Remans⟧. ⟦b:praecipit ūnum omnēs peterent Indutiomarum⟧, 5, 58, 5, ⟦i:he says they must all concentrate their attack on Indutiomarus⟧. ⟦b:huic imperat quās possit adeat cīvitātēs⟧, 4, 21, 8, ⟦i:he orders him to visit such communities as he can⟧. ⟦b:senātus dēcrēvit darent operam cōnsulēs nē quid rēs pūblica dētrīmentī caperet⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 29, 2, ⟦i:the senate decreed the consuls must see to it that the commonwealth received no harm⟧. ⟦b:iube maneat⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 737, ⟦i:tell her she must stay⟧. ⟦b:mīlitēs certiōrēs facit, paulisper intermitterent proelium⟧, 3, 5, 3, ⟦i:he tells the soldiers they must stop fighting a little while⟧. ⟦b:abī, nūntiā patribus urbem Rōmānam mūniant⟧, L. 22, 49, 10, ⟦i:go tell the fathers they must fortify Rome town⟧. ⟦b:dīxī equidem in carcerem īrēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 624, ⟦i:I’m sure I told you you must go to jail⟧. ⟦b:scrībit Labiēnō cum legiōne veniat⟧, 5, 46, 3, ⟦i:he writes to Labienus he must come with a legion⟧. ⟦b:lēgātiōnem mittunt sī velit suōs recipere, obsidēs sibī̆ remittat⟧, 3, 8, 5, ⟦i:they send an embassy, if he wishes to get his own men back, he must send back the hostages to them⟧.
⟦#1709⟧
(3.) The subjunctive is often coordinated with expressions of propriety or necessity. Such are ⟦b:oportet⟧, ⟦b:optumum est⟧, ⟦b:opus est⟧, ⟦b:decet⟧, ⟦b:necesse est⟧.
⟦b:mē ipsum amēs oportet, nōn mea⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 85, ⟦i:it is myself you should love, not my possessions⟧. ⟦b:quoniam habēs istum equom, aut ēmerīs oportet, aut hērēditāte possideās, aut surripuerīs necesse est⟧, ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 1, 84, ⟦i:since you are in possession of that horse, you must either have bought him or inherited him, or else you must necessarily have stolen him⟧. ⟦b:sed taceam optumumst⟧, Pl. ⟦i:E.⟧ 60, ⟦i:but I’d best hold my tongue⟧. ⟦b:nihil opust rescīscat⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Mer.⟧ 1004, ⟦i:she needn’t find it out at all⟧. ⟦b:condemnētur necesse est⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 111, ⟦i:be condemned he needs must⟧.
⟦#1710⟧
(4.) The subjunctive is sometimes coordinated with verbs of permission or concession. Such are ⟦b:permittō⟧ in Sallust and Livy, ⟦b:concēdō⟧, also ⟦b:sinō⟧, mostly in the imperative, chiefly in old Latin and poetry, and the impersonal ⟦b:licet⟧ (used thus often in Cicero, rarely before or after): as,
⟦b:supplēmentum scrīberent cōnsulēs, permissum⟧, L. 27, 22, 11, ⟦i:leave was given that the consuls might fill up the army⟧. ⟦b:sine sciam⟧, L. 2, 40, 5, ⟦i:let me know⟧. ⟦b:sine modo adveniat senex⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 11, ⟦i:let but the old man come⟧. ⟦b:fremant omnēs licet, dīcam quod sentiō⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 195, ⟦i:though everybody may growl, I will say what I think⟧. See ⟦r1904:1904⟧.
⟦#1711⟧
(5.) The subjunctive is often coordinated with the imperative ⟦b:cavē̆⟧, ⟦b:cavētō⟧, ⟦b:cavēte⟧, ⟦i:beware⟧, used in the sense of ⟦b:nē⟧ (⟦r1585:1585⟧): as,
⟦b:cavē faciās⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 13, 33, 4, ⟦i:don’t do it⟧. ⟦b:cave dīrumpātis⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen. prol.⟧ 117, ⟦i:don’t break it off⟧ (⟦r1075:1075⟧).
⟦#1712⟧
(6.) The subjunctive is often coordinated with verbs of giving, persuading, accomplishing, taking care. In this case the subjunctive has the meaning of purpose or result. Such are the imperative ⟦b:cedo⟧, and ⟦b:dō⟧, ⟦b:persuādeō⟧, ⟦b:impetrō⟧, ⟦b:cūrō⟧, also ⟦b:faciō⟧, particularly ⟦b:fac⟧ and ⟦b:facitō⟧: as,
⟦b:cedo bibam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 373, ⟦i:give me to drink⟧. ⟦b:date bibat tībīcinī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 757, ⟦i:give the piper to drink⟧. ⟦b:huic Sp. Albīnus persuādet rēgnum Numidiae ā senātū petat⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 35, 2, ⟦i:Albinus induces him to ask of the senate the throne of Numidia⟧. ⟦b:tandem inpetrāvī abīret⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 591, ⟦i:at last I’ve coaxed him to clear out⟧. ⟦b:fac sciam⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 7, 16, 3, ⟦i:let me know⟧. ⟦b:faxō sciās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 644, ⟦i:I’ll let you know⟧, much oftener ⟦b:sciēs⟧ or ⟦b:scībis⟧ (⟦r1700:1700⟧). ⟦b:fac bellus revertāre⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 18, 1, ⟦i:mind you come back a beauty⟧ (⟦r1579:1579⟧).
⟦#1713⟧
A subjunctive is now and then loosely coordinated with verbs in general, to indicate the purpose of the action: as,
⟦b:ēvocāte hūc Sōsiam, Blepharōnem arcēssat⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 949, ⟦i:call Sosia here, let him fetch Blepharo⟧. ⟦b:clārē advorsum fābulābor, hic auscultet quae loquar⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 300, ⟦i:I’ll speak distinctly face to face, that he may hear what I shall say⟧. ⟦b:operam hanc subrupuī tibī̆, ex mē scīrēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 523, ⟦i:I did this secretly for you, that you might learn from me⟧. ⟦b:manibus date līlia plēnīs, purpureōs spargam flōrēs⟧, V. 6, 883, ⟦i:lilies in handfuls give, I fain would scatter purple flowers⟧, that is, ⟦i:that I may scatter⟧.

title: The Complex Sentence, or Subordination
text:
⟦#1714⟧
In a complex sentence, that is one consisting of a main and a subordinate sentence, the subordinate member is introduced by some subordinating word: such are,
I. Interrogative words, in indirect questions; II. Relative pronouns; III. Relative conjunctive particles, or conjunctive particles not of relative origin.
⟦#1715⟧
Subordinate sentences may have the value of a substantive, usually as subject or as object; of an attributive; or of an adverb or adverbial adjunct: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:eādem nocte accidit ut esset lūna plēna⟧, 4, 29, 1, ⟦i:it came to pass the same night that there was a full moon⟧. ⟦b:videō quid agās⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 17, ⟦i:I see what you are driving at⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:fundus quī est in agrō, quī Sabīnus vocātur, eum meum esse aiō⟧, ⟦i:Mur.⟧ 26, ⟦i:the estate which is in the territory which is called Sabine, that I maintain is mine⟧, lawyers’ wordiness for ⟦b:fundus Sabīnus⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:cum advesperāsceret, ad pontem Mulvium pervēnērunt⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 5, ⟦i:when it was getting dark, they reached the Mulvius bridge⟧, i.e. ⟦b:vesperī⟧, or ⟦b:prīmō vespere⟧.
⟦#1716⟧
Subordinate sentences which express time or place, are called ⟦i:Temporal⟧ or ⟦i:Local⟧ sentences; comparison or manner, ⟦i:Comparative⟧ or ⟦i:Modal⟧ sentences; condition, cause, or concession, ⟦i:Conditional⟧, ⟦i:Causal⟧, or ⟦i:Concessive⟧ sentences; purpose, ⟦i:Final⟧ sentences; result, ⟦i:Consecutive⟧ sentences.
⟦#1717⟧
In a main sentence, the indicative present, future, and future perfect, and the imperative, are called ⟦i:Primary Tenses⟧; the indicative imperfect, historical perfect, and pluperfect, and the infinitive of intimation, are called ⟦i:Secondary Tenses⟧. The perfect definite and the present of vivid narration are sometimes regarded as primary tenses, oftener as secondary tenses.
⟦#1718⟧
Verbs which have an implication of futurity, such as those meaning ⟦i:can⟧, ⟦i:ought⟧, ⟦i:must⟧, &c., with an infinitive, also subjunctives of wish (⟦r1540:1540⟧) or of exhortation (⟦r1547:1547⟧), may be called ⟦i:Virtual Futures⟧.
⟦#1719⟧
Sometimes the subjunctive serves as a main sentence: see ⟦r1762:1762⟧; sometimes a noun of the verb: see ⟦r1766:1766⟧.

title: Mood of the Subordinate Sentence
text:
⟦#1720⟧
The indicative and the subjunctive are both used in subordinate sentences, as will be shown in the treatment of the several words of subordination. Some general uses may be mentioned collectively here.

title: Mood of the Subordinate Sentence: The Indicative Mood
text:
⟦#1721⟧
The indicative is ordinarily used in sentences introduced by a relative pronoun, or by a causal conjunctive word other than ⟦b:cum⟧.
⟦b:pontem, quī erat ad Genāvam, iubet rescindī⟧, 1, 7, 2, ⟦i:he orders the bridge which was near Geneva torn up⟧. ⟦b:concēdō, quia necesse est⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 145, ⟦i:I give up, because I have to⟧. In sentences of this class, however, the subjunctive is often required, particularly in indirect discourse (⟦r1722:1722⟧), or in cases of attraction (⟦r1728:1728⟧).

title: The Subjunctive of Indirect Discourse and of Attraction
text:
⟦#1722⟧
The subjunctive is used in relative, causal, temporal, and conditional sentences in indirect discourse, and in cases of attraction.
⟦#1723⟧
A direct quotation or question gives the words of the original speaker without alteration. When the original words of a quotation or question are changed to conform to the construction of the sentence in which they are quoted, it is called ⟦i:Indirect Discourse⟧.
⟦#1724⟧
In the complete form of indirect discourse, the subjunctive is subordinate to an infinitive or an accusative with the infinitive, dependent on a verb of saying or thinking (⟦r2175:2175⟧): as,
⟦b:negat Epicūrus iūcundē posse vīvī, nisi cum virtūte vīvātur⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 3, 49, ⟦i:Epicurus avers there is no living happily, without living virtuously⟧; directly, ⟦b:iūcundē vīvī nōn potest, nisi cum virtūte vīvitur⟧. ⟦b:Sōcratēs dīcere solēbat, omnēs in eō quod scīrent, satis esse ēloquentēs⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 63, ⟦i:Socrates used to maintain that all men were eloquent enough in a matter they knew⟧; directly, ⟦b:omnēs in eō quod sciunt satis sunt ēloquentēs⟧.
⟦#1725⟧
The idea of saying or thinking is often not formally expressed in the main sentence, and the indirect discourse is intimated by the subordinate subjunctive only: as,
⟦b:noctū ambulābat in pūblicō Themistoclēs, quod somnum capere nōn posset⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 4, 44, ⟦i:Themistocles used to walk the streets nights, ‘because he could not sleep,’⟧ given as Themistocles’s reason; the writer’s would be ⟦b:poterat⟧. ⟦b:Paetus omnēs librōs, quōs frāter suus relīquisset, mihī̆ dōnāvit⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 2, 1, 12, ⟦i:Paetus made me a present of all the books ‘that his brother had left.’⟧ ⟦b:dum reliquae nāvēs eō convenīrent, in ancorīs expectāvit⟧, 4, 23, 4, ⟦i:he waited at anchor till the rest of the vessels should gather there⟧ (⟦r2005:2005⟧). ⟦b:pervēnit priusquam Pompēius sentīre posset⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 67, 4, ⟦i:he got there before Pompey should be able to learn of his coming⟧ (⟦r1919:1919⟧). ⟦b:Xerxēs praemium prōposuit, quī invēnisset novam voluptātem⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 20, ⟦i:Xerxes offered a reward to anybody who should devise a new form of entertainment⟧ (⟦r2110:2110⟧).
⟦#1726⟧
A speaker or writer may quote his own thoughts in the indirect form, like another person’s: as, ⟦b:haec tibi dictābam post fānum putre Vacūnae, exceptō quod nōn simul essēs, cētera laetus⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 10, 49, ⟦i:I write thee this behind Vacuna’s mouldering pile, in all else well, except that thou’rt not here the while⟧ (⟦r1601:1601⟧).
⟦#1727⟧
Instead of an intimation of indirect discourse by a mere subjunctive, a verb of thinking or saying is sometimes introduced by ⟦b:quī⟧, or especially ⟦b:quod⟧, sometimes by ⟦b:cum⟧, and put illogically itself in the subjunctive: as, ⟦b:litterās, quās mē sibī̆ mīsisse dīceret, recitāvit⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 7, ⟦i:he read off a letter, which he said I sent him⟧, i.e. ⟦b:quās mīsissem⟧. ⟦b:impetrāre nōn potuī, quod religiōne sē impedīrī dīcerent⟧, Sulpicius in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 4, 12, 3, ⟦i:I could not get leave, because they said they were hampered by religious scruple⟧, i.e. ⟦b:quod impedīrentur⟧. ⟦b:cum dīceret⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 83, ⟦i:saying as he did⟧. This construction is common in Cicero, somewhat so in Caesar, rare in Sallust.
⟦#1728⟧
The subjunctive is used in sentences expressing an essential part of the thought, which are subordinate to another subjunctive, or to an infinitive. This is called the ⟦i:Subjunctive of Attraction⟧, or ⟦i:of Assimilation⟧: as,
⟦b:vereor nē, dum minuere velim labōrem, augeam⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 1, 12, ⟦i:I am afraid I may make the work harder, while I am aiming to make it less⟧. ⟦b:sī sōlōs eōs dīcerēs miserōs, quibus moriendum esset, nēminem eōrum, quī vīverent exciperēs⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 9, ⟦i:if you should pronounce only such people unhappy as had to die, you would not except one of those who were living⟧. ⟦b:mōs est Syrācūsīs, ut sī quā dē rē ad senātum referātur, dīcat sententiam quī velit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 142, ⟦i:it is the custom at Syracuse, that if any question is discussed in the senate, anybody who pleases may express his opinion⟧. ⟦b:sapiēns nōn dubitat, sī ita melius sit, migrāre dē vītā⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 1, 62, ⟦i:the sage does not hesitate, if this be the better course, to withdraw from life⟧. ⟦b:mōs est Athēnīs laudārī in cōntiōne eōs, quī sint in proeliīs interfectī⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 151, ⟦i:it is the custom in Athens to eulogize in public assembly such as have fallen in action⟧.
⟦#1729⟧
The indicative is kept in subordinate statements added or vouched for by the person reporting, and also in circumlocutions equivalent to a substantive: as,
⟦b:nūntiātum est Ariovistum ad occupandum Vesontiōnem, quod est oppidum maximum Sēquanōrum, contendere⟧, 1, 38, 1, ⟦i:it was reported that Ariovistus was pressing on to seize Vesontio, which is the most considerable town of the Sequans⟧. ⟦b:prūdentissima cīvitās Athēniēnsium, dum ea rērum potīta est, fuisse trāditur⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 70, ⟦i:Athens is said to have been passing wise, as long as she held the hegemony⟧. ⟦b:vīs, quae restant, mē loquī?⟧ T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 195, ⟦i:wilt have me tell the rest?⟧ i.e. ⟦b:relicua⟧. ⟦b:fierī potest, ut id quod sentit polītē ēloquī nōn possit⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 6, ⟦i:it may be that he cannot express his thought in polished style⟧, i.e. ⟦b:sententiam suam⟧.

title: The Subjunctive of Repeated Action
text:
⟦#1730⟧
The subjunctive is sometimes used in relative, temporal, or conditional sentences, to express action repeated or occurring at no particular time: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:neque aliter sī faciat, ūllam inter suōs habet auctōritātem⟧, 6, 11, 4, ⟦i:and if he does not do this, he never has any ascendancy at all over his people⟧. With the present and perfect, however, this subjunctive is confined principally to the indefinite second person singular (⟦r1030:1030⟧): as, ⟦b:bonus sēgnior fit, ubī̆ neglegās⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 31, 28, ⟦i:the good man always gets slacker, when you are neglectful⟧. ⟦b:sīquoi mūtuom quid dederīs, fit prō propriō perditum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 1050, ⟦i:if you’ve lent anything to any man, ’tis not your own, but lost⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) The imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive begin with Catullus and Caesar, and get to be common with Livy and Tacitus: as, ⟦b:sī quis prehenderētur, cōnsēnsū mīlitum ēripiēbātur⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 110, 4, ⟦i:every time a man was taken up, he was rescued by the joint action of the rank and file⟧. ⟦b:quemcumque līctor prēndisset, tribūnus mittī iubēbat⟧, L. 3, 11, 2, ⟦i:every man the lictor arrested, a tribune would order released⟧.

title: The Subjunctive as in the Simple Sentence
text:
⟦#1731⟧
The subjunctive of wish, of action conceivable, or of interrogation, is sometimes used in a subordinate sentence exactly as in main sentences: as,
⟦b:haec diē nātālī meō scrīpsī, quō utinam susceptus nōn essem⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 11, 9, 3, ⟦i:this I have written on my birthday, on which day I wish I had never been lifted from the ground⟧ (⟦r1544:1544⟧). ⟦b:ut videās⟧, Lucr. 3, 348, ⟦i:so that you can see⟧ (⟦r1556:1556⟧). ⟦b:neque id faciō, ut forsitan quibusdam videar, simulātiōne,⟧ ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 1, 8, 2, ⟦i:nor do I do it, as perhaps I may seem to some to do, from hypocrisy⟧ (⟦r1556:1556⟧). ⟦b:etiamst paucīs vōs quod monitōs voluerim⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 53, ⟦i:there’s one point more, on which I’d have you briefly warned⟧ (⟦r1558:1558⟧). ⟦b:erant eiusmodī sitūs oppidōrum, ut neque pedibus aditum habērent neque nāvibus, quod minuente aestū nāvēs in vadīs adflīctārentur⟧, 3, 12, 1, ⟦i:the towns were so situated that there was no access to them by land, nor by boat either, because at ebb tide vessels would pound on the shoals⟧ (⟦r1559:1559⟧). ⟦b:vix erat hoc imperātum, cum illum spoliātum vidērēs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 86, ⟦i:hardly was the order from his lips, when you might have seen the man stript⟧ (⟦r1559:1559⟧). ⟦b:quō mē vertam nesciō⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 4, ⟦i:I don’t know which way to turn⟧ (⟦r1563:1563⟧).

title: The Tenses of the Indicative
text:
⟦#1732⟧
I. The tense of a subordinate indicative often indicates a close relation of time with the tense of the leading verb, particularly in cases of repeated contemporaneous or antecedent action. The subordinate sentence in such combinations is said to have ⟦i:Relative⟧ time.
⟦#1733⟧
(1.) The subordinate indicative tense may express action concurrent with the main action. Two concurrent sentences are usually put in the same tense.
Concurrent action is said to be (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦i:congruent⟧, when two actions merely cover the same time: as, ⟦b:dum legō, adsentior⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 24, ⟦i:as long as I am reading, I assent⟧. ⟦b:dum necesse erat, ūnus omnia poterat⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 139, ⟦i:so long as it had to be, one man controlled the world⟧. ⟦b:dum Latīnae loquentur litterae, quercus huic locō nōn deerit⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 1, 2, ⟦i:as long as Latin literature has the gift of speech, this spot will not lack its oak⟧. ⟦b:vīxit, dum vīxit, bene⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 461, ⟦i:he lived well all the time he lived⟧. ⟦b:quoad potuit, fortissimē restitit⟧, 4, 12, 5, ⟦i:as long as he could, he made a manful stand⟧. Or (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦i:coincident⟧, when one action is virtually the same as the other: as, ⟦b:cum tacent, clāmant⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 21, ⟦i:while they are dumb, they cry out⟧, i.e. their silence is as telling as a shout. ⟦b:fēcistī mihī̆ pergrātum, quod Serāpiōnis librum mīsistī⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 2, 4, 1, ⟦i:you have obliged me very much by sending Serapio’s book⟧.
⟦#1734⟧
(2.) The subordinate indicative tense may express action contemporaneous, antecedent, or subsequent, in relation to the main action.
⟦#1735⟧
(a.) Action contemporaneous with a main present is expressed by a present, with a main future or virtual future, by a future, with a main secondary tense by an imperfect: as,
⟦b:quod est, eō decet ūtī⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 27, ⟦i:what you have, that you should avail yourself of⟧. ⟦b:hōrologium mittam, sī erit sūdum⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 18, 3, ⟦i:I will send the clock, if it is pleasant⟧ (⟦r1625:1625⟧). ⟦b:paulātim dabis, sī sapiēs⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 870, ⟦i:you’ll give in driblets, if you are wise⟧. ⟦b:cum relaxāre animōs volent, caveant intemperantiam⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 122, ⟦i:when they want to unbend, let them beware of excess⟧ (⟦r1625:1625⟧; ⟦r1718:1718⟧). ⟦b:omnia deerant, quae ad reficiendās nāvēs erant ūsuī⟧, 4, 29, 4, ⟦i:they were out of everything that was serviceable for repairing their vessels⟧.
⟦#1736⟧
(b.) Action antecedent to a main present is expressed by a perfect, to a main future or virtual future by a future perfect, to a main secondary tense by a pluperfect: as,
⟦b:quōcumque aspexistī tuae tibī̆ occurrunt iniūriae⟧, ⟦i:Par.⟧ 18, ⟦i:wherever you turn your gaze, you are confronted by your own abominable acts⟧. ⟦b:cum posuī librum, adsēnsiō omnis ēlābitur⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 24, ⟦i:when I drop the book, all assent melts away⟧ (⟦r1860:1860⟧). ⟦b:quicquid fēceris, adprobābō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 3, 3, 2, ⟦i:no matter what you do, I shall think it well⟧ (⟦r1626:1626⟧). ⟦b:ut quisque istīus animum offenderat, in lautumiās statim coniciēbātur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 143, ⟦i:any man that wounded his sensibilities was always flung into the quarries without any ado⟧.
⟦#1737⟧
(c.) Action subsequent to a main present is expressed by the future participle with a present form of ⟦b:sum⟧, to a main future or virtual future by the future participle with a future form of ⟦b:sum⟧, and to a main secondary tense by the future participle with an imperfect form of ⟦b:sum⟧: as,
⟦b:decem diēs sunt ante lūdōs, quōs Cn. Pompēius factūrus est⟧, ⟦i:V. a. pr⟧. 31, ⟦i:there are ten days before the shows which Pompey is to manage⟧. ⟦b:attentōs faciēmus, sī dēmōnstrābimus ea, quae dictūrī erimus, magna esse⟧, ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 1, 23, ⟦i:we shall make people attentive if we show that what we are going to say is important⟧. ⟦b:rēx, quia nōn interfutūrus nāvālī certāminī erat, Magnēsiam concessit⟧, L. 36, 43, 9, ⟦i:as the king was not to have a hand in the action at sea, he moved off to Magnesia⟧.
⟦#1738⟧
II. A subordinate indicative tense is said to be ⟦i:Independent⟧ when it simply expresses time of its own, without any close relation to the time of the main action.
Such independent tenses may denote general present action: as, ⟦b:ībam forte viā sacrā, sīcut meus est mōs⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 9, 1, ⟦i:in Sacred Street, as is my wont, I happened to be promenading⟧ (relatively, ⟦b:erat mōs⟧, ⟦r1735:1735⟧). ⟦b:nōn mē appellābis, sī sapis⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 515, ⟦i:you won’t address me, if you have sense⟧ (relatively, ⟦b:sī sapiēs⟧, ⟦r1735:1735⟧). Or past action, either continuous, completed, or indefinite: as, ⟦b:ut mōs fuit Bī̆thȳniae rēgibus, lectīcā ferēbātur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 27, ⟦i:he regularly rode in a litter, as was the practice of the despots of Bithynia⟧; here ⟦b:fuit⟧ denotes action simply as past, without further definition of time (⟦r1603:1603⟧), whereas ⟦b:erat⟧, relative to the time of ⟦b:ferēbātur⟧, would imply ⟦i:which was then the practice⟧ (⟦r1595:1595⟧).
⟦#1739⟧
With ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:in the time while⟧, an independent present is used: see ⟦r1995:1995⟧. With ⟦b:postquam⟧, &c., ⟦i:after⟧, an independent perfect is used of a single action; see ⟦r1925:1925⟧.

title: Tense of the Subordinate Sentence: The Tenses of the Subjunctive
text:
⟦#1740⟧
Subordinate subjunctive sentences were originally independent coordinate sentences, in the tense required to express the thought. By degrees the subordinate sentence blended closely with the main sentence, and the combination of the two was regarded as one whole.
⟦#1741⟧
I. The time of the subordinate subjunctive is usually ⟦i:Relative⟧, that is either contemporaneous, antecedent, or subsequent, in relation to that of the main action.
⟦#1742⟧
Action contemporaneous with the main action is expressed by a present or imperfect subjunctive. Action antecedent is expressed by a perfect or a pluperfect subjunctive. Action subsequent is expressed by the future participle with a form of ⟦b:sim⟧ or of ⟦b:essem⟧.
⟦#1743⟧
Subordinate sentences with verbs of will or aim, with verbs of fear, also final sentences and many consecutive sentences are expressed in Latin as contemporaneous with the main action, not as subsequent to it.
⟦#1744⟧
II. The main and subordinate sentences may express wholly different spheres of time by tenses not commonly used together, when the thought requires it. In such cases the tense of the subordinate member is called ⟦i:Independent⟧, like the analogous tenses of the indicative (⟦r1738:1738⟧).
⟦#1745⟧
The use of subordinate subjunctive tenses relatively to the main tense, or what is commonly called the ⟦i:Sequence of Tenses⟧, is as follows:

title: Tense subordinate to an Indicative
text:
⟦#1746⟧
(1.) The present, or perfect subjunctive, or the future participle with a form of ⟦b:sim⟧, is used in sentences subordinate to a primary tense (⟦r1717:1717⟧): as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:tē hortor, ut Rōmam pergās⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 1, 3, 4, ⟦i:I urge you to repair to Rome⟧. ⟦b:cūrā, ut quam prīmum veniās⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 4, 10, 1, ⟦i:mind that you come as soon as you can⟧. ⟦b:ego quid accēperim sciō⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 58, ⟦i:I know what I have received⟧. ⟦b:quam sum sollicitus quidnam futūrum sit⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 8, 6, 3, ⟦i:how anxious I am to know what in the world is to come⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:in eum locum rēs dēducta est ut salvī esse nequeāmus⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 12, 1, ⟦i:to such a pass has it come that we cannot be saved⟧. ⟦b:an oblītus es quid initiō dīxerim?⟧ ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 2, ⟦i:have you possibly forgotten what I said at the start?⟧ ⟦b:quoniam in eam ratiōnem vītae nōs fortūna dēdūxit, ut sempiternus sermō dē nōbīs futūrus sit, caveāmus⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 1, 1, 38, ⟦i:since fortune has set us in such a walk of life that we are to be eternally talked about, let us be on our guard⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:efficiam, ut intellegātis⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 7, ⟦i:I will see that you understand⟧. ⟦b:dīcent quid statuerint⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 175, ⟦i:they will tell what they decided on⟧. ⟦b:quae fuerit causa, mox vīderō⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 1, 35, ⟦i:what the reason was I won’t consider till by and by⟧ (⟦r1630:1630⟧). ⟦b:tē disertum putābō, sī ostenderis quō modō sīs eōs inter sīcāriōs dēfēnsūrus⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 8, ⟦i:I shall think you a most effective speaker, if you show how you are going to defend them on the charge of murder⟧.
⟦#1747⟧
(2.) The imperfect, or pluperfect subjunctive, or the future participle with a form of ⟦b:essem⟧, is used in sentences subordinate to a secondary tense (⟦r1717:1717⟧): as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:hīs rēbus fīēbat, ut minus lātē vagārentur⟧, 1, 2, 4, ⟦i:so it came to pass that they did not roam round much⟧. ⟦b:docēbat, ut tōtīus Galliae prīncipātum Aeduī tenuissent⟧, 1, 43, 6, ⟦i:he showed how the Aeduans had had the mastery over all Gaul⟧. ⟦b:Flaccus quid aliī posteā factūrī essent scīre nōn poterat⟧, Fl. 33, ⟦i:Flaccus could not tell what other people would do in the future⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:is cīvitātī persuāsit, ut dē fīnibus suīs cum omnibus cōpiīs exīrent⟧, 1, 2, 1, ⟦i:this man prevailed on his community to emigrate from their place of abode, bag and baggage⟧. ⟦b:quās rēs in Hispāniā gessisset, disseruit⟧, L. 28, 38, 2, ⟦i:he discoursed on his military career in Spain⟧. ⟦b:an Lacedaemoniī quaesīvērunt num sē esset morī prohibitūrus?⟧ TD. 5, 42, ⟦i:did the Spartans ask whether he was going to prevent them from dying?⟧ (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:Ariovistus tantōs sibī̆ spīritūs sūmpserat, ut ferendus nōn vidērētur⟧, 1, 33, 5, ⟦i:Ariovistus had put on such high and mighty airs that he seemed intolerable⟧. ⟦b:hīc pāgus, cum domō exīsset patrum nostrōrum memoriā, L.
