⟦b:quoniam⟧, compounded of ⟦b:quom⟧ and ⟦b:iam⟧, ⟦i:when now⟧, refers primarily to time, but is seldom so used and only by early writers. The temporal meaning passed early into an exclusively causal meaning, ⟦i:since⟧. In both meanings it regularly introduces the indicative (⟦r1721:1721⟧). For special reasons, however, the subjunctive is used, as in indirect discourse (⟦r1725:1725⟧), or by attraction (⟦r1728:1728⟧).
⟦#1883⟧
(1.) ⟦b:quoniam⟧, ⟦i:when now⟧, used of time in early Latin, has sometimes as a correlative ⟦b:continuō⟧, ⟦b:subitō⟧, or ⟦b:extemplō⟧; it usually introduces the present indicative (⟦r1590:1590⟧): as,
⟦b:is quoniam moritur, numquam indicāre id fīliō voluit suō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 9, ⟦i:when he was on his dying bed, he ne’er would point it out to his own son⟧, of a hidden treasure. ⟦b:quoniam sentiō quae rēs gererētur, nāvem extemplō statuimus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 290, ⟦i:when now I saw what was doing, we stopped the ship at once⟧.
⟦#1884⟧
(2.) ⟦b:quoniam⟧, ⟦i:since⟧, ⟦i:seeing that⟧, ⟦i:now that⟧, with the indicative, introduces a reason, usually one known to the person addressed, or one generally known: as,
⟦b:vēra dīcō, sed nēquīquam, quoniam nōn vīs crēdere⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 835, ⟦i:the truth I speak, but all in vain, since thou wilt not believe⟧. ⟦b:vōs, Quirītēs, quoniam iam nox est, in vestra tecta discēdite⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 29, ⟦i:do you, citizens, since it is now grown dark, depart and go to your own several homes⟧. ⟦b:quoniam in eam ratiōnem vītae nōs fortūna dēdūxit, ut sempiternus sermō dē nōbīs futūrus sit, caveāmus⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 1, 1, 38, ⟦i:since fortune has set us in such a walk of life that we are to be eternally talked about, let us be on our guard⟧. Often in transition: as, ⟦b:quoniam dē genere bellī dīxī, nunc dē magnitūdine pauca dīcam⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 20, ⟦i:since I have finished speaking about the character of the war, I will now speak briefly about its extent⟧. With the subjunctive in indirect discourse (⟦r1725:1725⟧): as, ⟦b:crēbrīs Pompēī litterīs castīgābantur, quoniam prīmō venientem Caesarem nōn prohibuissent⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 25, 3, ⟦i:they were rebuked in numerous letters of Pompey, ‘because they had not kept Caesar off as soon as he came.’⟧

title: quotiēns, quotiēnscumque
text:
⟦#1885⟧
The relative particle ⟦b:quotiēns⟧ (⟦r711:711⟧), or ⟦b:quotiēnscumque⟧, ⟦i:every time that⟧, ⟦i:whenever⟧, introduces the indicative: as,
⟦b:quotiēns quaeque cohors prōcurrerat, magnus numerus hostium cadēbat⟧, 5, 34, 2, ⟦i:as the cohorts successively charged, a great number of the enemy fell every time⟧. ⟦b:quoius quotiēns sepulcrum vidēs, sacruficās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:E.⟧ 175, ⟦i:every time you see her tomb, you offer sacrifice⟧. ⟦b:nec quotiēnscumque mē vīderit, ingemīscet⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 146, ⟦i:neither shall he fall a-groaning whenever he sees me⟧ (⟦r1736:1736⟧). ⟦b:quotiēnsque⟧ is late and rare.
⟦#1886⟧
⟦b:quotiēns⟧ has sometimes as a correlative ⟦b:totiēns⟧, or a combination with ⟦b:tot⟧ which is equivalent to ⟦b:totiēns⟧: as, ⟦b:quotiēns dīcimus, totiēns dē nōbīs iūdicātur⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 125, ⟦i:every time we make a speech, the world sits in judgement on us⟧. ⟦b:sī tot cōnsulibus meruisset, quotiēns ipse cōnsul fuit⟧, ⟦i:Balb.⟧ 47, ⟦i:if he had been in the army as many years as he was consul⟧.
⟦#1887⟧
The subjunctive imperfect and pluperfect are common in the later writers to indicate repeated action (⟦r1730:1730⟧): as, ⟦b:quotiēns super tālī negōtiō cōnsultāret, ēditā domūs parte ac lībertī ūnīus cōnscientiā ūtēbātur⟧, ⟦i:Ta.⟧ 6, 27, ⟦i:whenever he had recourse to astrologers, it was in the upper part of his house and with the cognizance of only a single freedman⟧.

title: quam
text:
⟦#1888⟧
⟦b:quam⟧, ⟦i:as⟧ or ⟦i:than⟧, introduces an indicative protasis in periods of comparison. For special reasons, however, the subjunctive is used, as by attraction (⟦r1728:1728⟧), or of action conceivable (⟦r1731:1731⟧); see also ⟦r1896:1896, 1897⟧.
But usually periods of comparison are abridged (⟦r1057:1057⟧) by the omission of the verb or of other parts in the protasis (⟦r1325:1325⟧).

title: quam: With the Indicative
text:
⟦#1889⟧
(1.) ⟦b:quam⟧, ⟦i:as⟧, is used in the protasis of a comparative period of equality, generally with ⟦b:tam⟧ as correlative in the apodosis: as,
⟦b:tam facile vincēs quam pirum volpēs comēst⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 559, ⟦i:you’ll beat as easily as Reynard eats a pear⟧. ⟦b:tam excoctam reddam atque ātram quam carbōst⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 849, ⟦i:I’ll have her stewed all out and black as is a coal⟧. From Cicero on, the apodosis is in general negative or interrogative: as, ⟦b:quōrum neutrum tam facile quam tū arbitrāris concēditur⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 1, 10, ⟦i:neither of these points is as readily granted as you suppose⟧. ⟦b:quid est ōrātōrī tam necessārium quam vōx?⟧ ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 251, ⟦i:what is so indispensable to the speaker as voice?⟧ Otherwise ⟦b:nōn minus . . . quam⟧, ⟦i:no less than⟧, ⟦i:just as much⟧, or ⟦b:nōn magis . . . quam⟧, ⟦i:just as little⟧ or ⟦i:just as much⟧, is often preferred to ⟦b:tam . . . quam⟧: as, ⟦b:accēpī nōn minus interdum ōrātōrium esse tacēre quam dīcere⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 7, 6, 7, ⟦i:I have observed that silence is sometimes quite as eloquent as speech⟧. ⟦b:nōn magis mihī̆ deerit inimīcus quam Verrī dēfuit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 162, ⟦i:I shall lack an enemy as little as Verres did⟧. ⟦b:domus erat nōn dominō magis ōrnāmentō quam cīvitātī⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 5, ⟦i:the house was as much a pride to the state as to its owner⟧.
⟦#1890⟧
Instead of ⟦b:tam⟧, another correlative is sometimes used in the apodosis. Thus, ⟦b:aequē . . . quam⟧ occurs in Plautus and in Livy and later writers, generally after a negative expression; ⟦b:perinde . . . quam⟧ in Tacitus and Suetonius; ⟦b:iūxtā ... quam⟧ once in Livy. Sometimes the apodosis contains no correlative.
⟦#1891⟧
⟦b:tam . . . quam⟧ become by abridgement coordinating words: as,
⟦b:tam vēra quam falsa cernimus⟧, ⟦i:Ac.⟧ 2, 111, ⟦i:we make out things both true and false⟧.
⟦#1892⟧
The highest possible degree is expressed by ⟦b:tam . . . quam quī⟧ and a superlative without a verb; or by ⟦b:quam⟧ and a superlative with or without a form of ⟦b:possum⟧ (⟦r1466:1466⟧); sometimes by ⟦b:quantus⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:tam sum misericors quam vōs; tam mītis quam quī lēnissimus⟧, ⟦i:Sull.⟧ 87, ⟦i:I am as tender-hearted as you; as mild as the gentlest man living⟧. ⟦b:tam sum amīcus rē̆ī pūblicae quam quī maximē⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 5, 2, 6, ⟦i:I am as devoted a patriot as anybody can be⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:quam maximīs potest itineribus in Galliam contendit⟧, 1, 7, 1, ⟦i:he pushes into Gaul by as rapid marches as he can⟧. ⟦b:cōnstituērunt iūmentōrum quam maximum numerum coëmere⟧, 1, 3, 1, ⟦i:they determined to buy up the greatest possible number of beasts of burden⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:tanta est inter eōs, quanta maxima potest esse, mōrum distantia⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 74, ⟦i:there is the greatest possible difference of character between them⟧. Or without any superlative: ⟦b:fuge domum quantum potest⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 850, ⟦i:run home as quick as e’er you can⟧. ⟦b:ut potuī accūrātissimē tē tūtātus sum⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 5, 17, 2, ⟦i:I defended you as carefully as I could⟧.
⟦#1893⟧
⟦b:quam . . . tam⟧, with two comparatives or superlatives, is equivalent to the more common ⟦b:quō . . . eō⟧ with two comparatives (⟦r1973:1973⟧): as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:magis quam id reputō, tam magis ūror⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 1091, ⟦i:the more I think it over, the sorer do I feel⟧. This use is found in Plautus, Lucretius, and Vergil. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:quam quisque pessumē fēcit, tam maxumē tūtus est⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 31, 14, ⟦i:the worse a man has acted, the safer he always is⟧. This use is found in Plautus, Terence, Cato, Varro, and Sallust.
⟦#1894⟧
(2.) ⟦b:quam⟧, ⟦i:than⟧, is used in the protasis of a comparative period of inequality, with a comparative in the apodosis: as,
⟦b:meliōrem quam ego sum suppōnō tibī̆⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cu.⟧ 256, ⟦i:I give you in my place a better man than I am⟧. ⟦b:plūra dīxī quam voluī⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 79, ⟦i:I have said more than I intended⟧. ⟦b:Antōniō quam est, volō peius esse⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 15, 3, 2, ⟦i:I hope Antony may be worse off than he is⟧. ⟦b:doctrīna paulō dūrior quam nātūra patitur⟧, ⟦i:Mur.⟧ 60, ⟦i:principles somewhat sterner than nature doth support⟧. ⟦b:potius sērō quam numquam⟧, L. 4, 2, 11, ⟦i:better late than never⟧. ⟦b:corpus patiēns algōris suprā quam cuiquam crēdibile est⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 5, 3, ⟦i:a constitution capable of enduring cold beyond what anybody could believe⟧. ⟦b:suprā quam⟧ is found in Cicero, Sallust, and often in late writers; ⟦b:īnfrā⟧ and ⟦b:ultrā quam⟧ in Cicero, Livy, and late writers (⟦b:īnfrā quam⟧ also in Varro); ⟦b:extrā quam⟧ in Ennius, Cato, and in legal and official language in Cicero and Livy.
⟦#1895⟧
⟦b:quam⟧ is also used with some virtual comparatives: thus, ⟦b:nihil aliud⟧, ⟦b:nōn aliud quam⟧, ⟦i:no other than⟧, often as adverb, ⟦i:only⟧; ⟦b:secus quam⟧ with a negative, ⟦i:not otherwise than⟧; ⟦b:bis tantō quam⟧, ⟦i:twice as much as⟧; and ⟦b:prae quam⟧ in old Latin, ⟦i:in comparison with how⟧; and similar phrases: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:per bīduum nihil aliud quam stetērunt parātī ad pugnandum⟧, L. 34, 46, 7, ⟦i:for two days they merely stood in battle array⟧. This use occurs first in Sallust, then in Nepos, Livy, and later writers. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:mihī̆ erit cūrae nē quid fīat secus quam volumus⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 6, 2, 2, ⟦i:I will see to it that nothing be done save as we wish⟧. This use occurs in Plautus, Terence, Sallust, Cicero, Livy, and later writers. With both ⟦b:aliud⟧ and ⟦b:secus⟧ the clause is rarely positive, with ⟦b:aliud⟧ not before Livy. For ⟦b:atque⟧ (⟦b:ac⟧) instead of ⟦b:quam⟧ when the first clause is negative, see ⟦r1654:1654⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:bis tantō valeō quam valuī prius⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Merc.⟧ 297, ⟦i:I am twice as capable as I was before⟧. (⟦i:d.⟧) ⟦b:nīl hōc quidem est trīgintā minae, prae quam aliōs sūmptūs facit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 981, ⟦i:oh, this is nothing, thirty minae, when you think what other sums he spends⟧. ⟦b:prae quam⟧ is found only in Plautus rarely. Similar phrases are: ⟦b:contrā quam⟧, in Cicero, Livy, and later writers; ⟦b:praeter quam⟧, in Plautus, Naevius, and frequently in other writers when followed by ⟦b:quod⟧ (⟦r1848:1848⟧); ⟦b:super quam quod⟧ (⟦r1848:1848⟧) and ⟦b:īnsuper quam⟧ in Livy; ⟦b:prō quam⟧ in Lucretius; ⟦b:advorsum quam⟧, once in Plautus. ⟦b:prae quam⟧ is sometimes followed by a relative clause: as, ⟦b:prae quam quod molestumst⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 634, ⟦i:compared with what is painful⟧. For ⟦b:ante⟧ (or ⟦b:prius⟧) and ⟦b:post quam⟧, see ⟦r1911:1911⟧, ⟦r1923:1923⟧.

title: quam: With the Subjunctive
text:
⟦#1896⟧
The subjunctive is used with ⟦b:quam⟧ or ⟦b:quam ut⟧ after comparatives denoting disproportion (⟦r1461:1461⟧): as,
⟦b:quicquid erat oneris Segestānīs impōnēbat, aliquantō amplius quam ferre possent⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 76, ⟦i:he would impose every possible burden on the Segestans, far too much for them to bear⟧. ⟦b:quis nōn intellegit Canachī sīgna rigidiōra esse, quam ut imitentur vēritātem?⟧ ⟦i:Br.⟧ 70, ⟦i:who does not feel that the statues of Canachus are too stiff to be true to nature?⟧ ⟦b:clārior rēs erat quam ut dissimulārī posset⟧, L. 26, 51, 11, ⟦i:the thing was too notorious to be hushed up⟧. Instead of ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦b:quī⟧ is also used by Livy and later writers: as, ⟦b:maior sum quam cui possit Fortūna nocēre⟧, O. 6, 195, ⟦i:too strong am I for Fortune to break down⟧, says infatuated Niobe. All these sentences are extensions of the subjunctive of action conceivable (⟦r1554:1554⟧, ⟦r1818:1818⟧).
⟦#1897⟧
The subjunctive is used in clauses introduced by ⟦b:potius quam⟧, ⟦i:rather than⟧, to denote action merely assumed. ⟦b:citius⟧, ⟦b:ante⟧, or ⟦b:prius⟧, ⟦i:sooner⟧, is sometimes used in the sense of ⟦b:potius⟧: as,
⟦b:potius quam tē inimīcum habeam, faciam ut iusseris⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 174, ⟦i:rather than make you my enemy, I will do as you tell me⟧. ⟦b:dēpugnā potius quam serviās⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 7, 7, 7, ⟦i:fight it out rather than be a slave⟧. ⟦b:potius vituperātiōnem incōnstantiae suscipiam, quam in tē sim crūdēlis⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 105, ⟦i:I will submit to the charge of inconsistency rather than be cruel towards you⟧. ⟦b:animam omittunt prius quam locō dēmigrent⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 240, ⟦i:they lose their lives sooner than yield their ground⟧. Livy has also ⟦b:potius quam ut⟧. All these sentences are extensions of the subjunctive of desire (⟦r1540:1540⟧, ⟦r1817:1817⟧).

title: quam: With the Infinitive
text:
⟦#1898⟧
When the main clause is an infinitive, ⟦b:quam⟧ is often followed by an infinitive: as,
⟦b:mālim morīrī me͡os quam mendīcārier⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Vid.⟧ 96, ⟦i:better my bairns be dead than begging bread⟧. ⟦b:vōcēs audiēbantur prius sē cortice ex arboribus vīctūrōs, quam Pompēium ē manibus dīmissūrōs⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 49, 1, ⟦i:shouts were heard that they would live on the bark of trees sooner than let Pompey slip through their fingers⟧.

title: quamquam
text:
⟦#1899⟧
(1.) ⟦b:quamquam⟧ is used in old Latin as an indefinite adverb, ⟦i:ever so much⟧, ⟦i:however much⟧: as,
⟦b:quamquam negōtiumst, sī quid veis, Dēmiphō, nōn sum occupātus umquam amīcō operam dare⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Mer.⟧ 287, ⟦i:however busy I may be⟧ (⟦r1814:1814⟧), ⟦i:if anything you wish, dear Demipho, I’m not too busy ever to a friend mine aid to lend⟧. ⟦b:id quoque possum ferre, quamquam iniūriumst⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 205, ⟦i:that also I can bear, however so unfair⟧. From an adverb, ⟦b:quamquam⟧ became a conjunction, ⟦i:although⟧.
⟦#1900⟧
(2.) ⟦b:quamquam⟧, ⟦i:although⟧, introduces the indicative in the concession of a definite fact. In the later writers it is also sometimes used with the subjunctive, sometimes with a participle or an adjective.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:quamquam premuntur aere aliēnō, dominātiōnem tamen exspectant⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 19, ⟦i:though they are staggering under debt, they yet look forward to being lords and masters⟧. ⟦b:quamquam nōn vēnit ad fīnem tam audāx inceptum, tamen haud omnīnō vānum fuit⟧, L. 10, 32, 5, ⟦i:though the bold attempt did not attain its purpose, yet it was not altogether fruitless⟧. This is the classical use; but see ⟦r1901:1901⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:nam et tribūnīs plēbis senātūs habendī iūs erat, quamquam senātōrēs nōn essent⟧, Varro in Gell. 14, 8, 2, ⟦i:for even the tribunes of the people, though they were not senators, had the right to hold a meeting of the senate⟧. ⟦b:haud cunctātus est Germānicus, quamquam fingī ea intellegeret⟧, Ta. 2, 26, ⟦i:Germanicus did not delay, though he was aware this was all made up⟧. This use is found first in Varro, often in the Augustan poets, sometimes in Livy, always in Juvenal. It does not become common before Tacitus and the younger Pliny. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:sequente, quamquam nōn probante, Amynandrō⟧, L. 31, 41, 7, ⟦i:Amynander accompanying though not approving⟧ (⟦r1374:1374⟧). ⟦b:nē Aquītānia quidem, quamquam in verba Othōnis obstricta, diū mānsit⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 1, 76, ⟦i:Aquitania, though bound by the oath of allegiance to Otho, did not hold out long either⟧. This use is found once each in Cicero and Sallust, half a dozen times in Livy, oftener in Tacitus.
⟦#1901⟧
The subjunctive is also used often with ⟦b:quamquam⟧ for special reasons, as by attraction (⟦r1728:1728⟧), in indirect discourse (⟦r1725:1725⟧), and of action conceivable (⟦r1731:1731⟧).
⟦#1902⟧
For ⟦b:quamquam⟧ appending a fresh main sentence, see ⟦r2153:2153⟧; for its use with the infinitive, 2317.

title: quam vīs or quamvīs
text:
⟦#1903⟧
⟦b:quam vīs⟧ or ⟦b:quamvīs⟧ is used as an indefinite adverb (⟦r712:712⟧), ⟦i:as much as you please⟧, and is often joined with an adjective or other adverb to take the place of a superlative: as,
⟦b:quam vīs rīdiculus est, ubī̆ uxor nōn adest⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 318, ⟦i:he’s as droll as you please when his wife isn’t by⟧. ⟦b:quamveis īnsipiēns poterat persentīscere⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Merc.⟧ 687, ⟦i:the veriest dullard could detect⟧. ⟦b:quamvīs paucī adīre audent⟧, 4, 2, 5, ⟦i:the merest handful dares attack⟧. ⟦b:quamvīs callidē⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 134, ⟦i:ever so craftily⟧. ⟦b:quamvīs⟧ is also sometimes used to strengthen a superlative (⟦r1466:1466⟧), though not in classical prose.
⟦#1904⟧
(1.) The indefinite adverb ⟦b:quam vīs⟧, ⟦i:as much as you please⟧, is often used in subjunctive clauses of concession or permission; such subjunctives are sometimes coordinated with ⟦b:licet⟧: as,
⟦b:quod turpe est, id quam vīs occultētur, tamen honestum fierī nūllō modō potest⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 78, ⟦i:if a thing is base, let it be hidden as much as you will, yet it cannot be made respectable⟧ (⟦r1553:1553⟧). ⟦b:locus hīc apud nōs, quam vīs subitō veniās, semper līber est⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 82, ⟦i:our house is always open, come as sudden as you may⟧ (⟦r1553:1553⟧). ⟦b:praeter eōs quam vīs ēnumerēs multōs licet, nōnnūllōs reperiēs perniciōsōs tribūnōs⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 3, 24, ⟦i:besides these you may tell off as many as you please, you will still find some dangerous tribunes⟧ (⟦r1710:1710⟧). The combination with ⟦b:licet⟧ occurs first in Lucretius, then in Cicero.
Instead of ⟦b:vīs⟧, other forms are sometimes used: as, ⟦b:volumus⟧, ⟦b:volent⟧, ⟦b:velit⟧, &c.: thus, ⟦b:quam volent facētī sint⟧, ⟦i:Cael.⟧ 67, ⟦i:they may be as witty as they please⟧ (⟦r1735:1735⟧). ⟦b:quam volet Epicūrus iocētur et dīcat sē nōn posse intellegere, numquam mē movēbit⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 46, ⟦i:Epicurus may joke and say he can’t understand it as much as he likes, he will never shake me⟧. From an adverb, ⟦b:quam vīs⟧ became a conjunction, ⟦i:however much⟧, ⟦i:even if⟧.
⟦#1905⟧
(2.) The subjunctive with the conjunction ⟦b:quamvīs⟧, ⟦i:however much⟧, ⟦i:even if⟧, ⟦i:though⟧, denotes action merely assumed; when the action is to be denoted as real, ⟦b:ut⟧ or ⟦b:sīcut⟧ or the like, with the indicative, usually follows in the best prose (⟦r1943:1943⟧): as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:quamvīs sint hominēs quī Cn. Carbōnem ōderint, tamen hī dēbent quid metuendum sit cōgitāre⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 39, ⟦i:though there may be men who hate Carbo, still these men ought to consider what they have to fear⟧. ⟦b:nōn enim possīs, quamvīs excellās⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 73, ⟦i:you may not have the power, however eminent you may be⟧. This use begins with Cicero and Varro, and gets common in late writers. Not in Livy. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:illa quamvīs rīdicula essent, sīcut erant, mihī̆ tamen rīsum nōn mōvērunt⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 7, 32, 3, ⟦i:droll as this really was, it nevertheless did not make me laugh⟧. ⟦b:quamvīs enim multīs locīs dīcat Epicūrus, sīcutī dīcit, satis fortiter dē dolōre, tamen nōn id spectandum est quid dīcat⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 117, ⟦i:even though Epicurus really does speak in many places pretty heroically about pain, still we must not have an eye to what he says⟧. In the Augustan poets rarely, and often in Tacitus, the younger Pliny, and late writers, the subjunctive, without a parenthetical phrase introduced by ⟦b:ut⟧ or the like, is used of an action denoted as real: as, ⟦b:expalluit notābiliter, quamvīs palleat semper⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 1, 5, 13, ⟦i:he grew pale perceptibly, though he is always a pale man⟧. ⟦b:maestus erat, quamvīs laetitiam simulāret⟧, Ta. 15, 54, ⟦i:sad he was, though he pretended to be gay⟧.
⟦#1906⟧
⟦b:quamvīs⟧, ⟦i:even if⟧, ⟦i:though⟧, is also sometimes used with the indicative (⟦r1900:1900⟧): as,
⟦b:erat dignitāte rēgiā, quamvīs carēbat nōmine⟧, N. 1, 2, 3, ⟦i:he had the authority of a king, though not the title⟧. ⟦b:quamvīs tacet Hermogenēs, cantor est⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 3, 129, ⟦i:though he open not his mouth, Hermogenes remains a singer still⟧. This use occurs twice in Lucretius, once in Cicero, Nepos, and Livy each, in Varro, in the Augustan poets, and sometimes in late writers. Not in Tacitus, Pliny the younger, Juvenal, Martial, or Suetonius.
⟦#1907⟧
It may be mentioned here that the indefinite adverb ⟦b:quamlibet⟧, ⟦i:however you please⟧, is used in subjunctive clauses of concession or permission (⟦r1904:1904⟧) once or twice by Lucretius, Ovid, and Quintilian. Velleius has it with the participle, a construction sometimes found with ⟦b:quamvīs⟧ in late writers.

title: tamquam
text:
⟦#1908⟧
⟦b:tamquam⟧, ⟦i:just as⟧, introduces an indicative protasis in periods of comparison.
The ⟦b:tam⟧ properly belongs to the apodosis and is attracted to the protasis. ⟦b:tamquam⟧ has sometimes as correlative ⟦b:sīc⟧ or ⟦b:ita⟧.
⟦b:tē hortor ut tamquam poētae bonī solent, sīc tū in extrēmā parte mūneris tuī dīligentissimus sīs⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 1, 1, 46, ⟦i:I urge you to be very particular at the end of your task, just as good poets always are⟧. ⟦b:tamquam philosophōrum habent disciplinae ex ipsīs vocābula, parasītī ita ut Gnathōnicī vocentur⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 263, ⟦i:that so parasites may be called Gnathonites even as schools of philosophy are named from the masters⟧. Usually, however, ⟦b:ut⟧ (⟦r1944:1944⟧) or ⟦b:quemadmodum⟧ is used in this sense; and ⟦b:tamquam⟧ occurs oftenest in abridged sentences (⟦r1057:1057⟧), particularly to show that an illustration is untrue or figurative: as, ⟦b:Odyssīa Latīna est sīc tamquam opus aliquod Daedalī⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 71, ⟦i:the Odyssey in Latin is, you may say, a regular work of Daedalus⟧. ⟦b:oculī tamquam speculātōrēs altissimum locum obtinent⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 140, ⟦i:the eyes occupy the highest part, as a sort of watchmen⟧.
⟦#1909⟧
In late writers, especially in Tacitus, ⟦b:tamquam⟧ is often used to introduce a reason or motive, or a thought indirectly expressed: as,
⟦b:invīsus tamquam plūs quam cīvīlia agitāret⟧, Ta. 1, 12, ⟦i:hated on the ground that his designs were too lofty for a private citizen⟧ (⟦r1725:1725⟧). ⟦b:lēgātōs increpuit, tamquam nōn omnēs reōs perēgissent⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 3, 9, 36, ⟦i:he reproved the embassy ‘for not having completed the prosecution of all the defendants’⟧ (⟦r1852:1852⟧, ⟦r1725:1725⟧). ⟦b:suspectus tamquam ipse suās incenderit aedīs⟧, J. 3, 222, ⟦i:suspected of having set his own house afire⟧.
⟦#1910⟧
For ⟦b:tamquam⟧ instead of ⟦b:tamquam sī⟧, see ⟦r2118:2118⟧; with a participle, 2121.

title: antequam, priusquam
text:
⟦#1911⟧
⟦b:antequam⟧ and ⟦b:priusquam⟧ accompany both the indicative and the subjunctive.
⟦b:ante⟧ and ⟦b:prius⟧ properly belong to the apodosis, and regularly stand with it if it is negative; but otherwise they are usually attracted to the protasis.
⟦b:antequam⟧ is very seldom found in old Latin, and it is in general much rarer than ⟦b:priusquam⟧, except in Tacitus.

title: antequam, priusquam: In General Statements
text:
⟦#1912⟧
In general present statements, ⟦b:antequam⟧ and ⟦b:priusquam⟧ regularly introduce the perfect indicative or the present subjunctive: as,
⟦b:membrīs ūtimur priusquam didicimus cuius ea causā ūtilitātis habeāmus⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 3, 66, ⟦i:we always use our limbs before we learn for what purposes of utility we have them⟧ (⟦r1613:1613⟧). ⟦b:priusquam lūcet, adsunt⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 709, ⟦i:before ’tis light they’re always here⟧; here ⟦b:lūcet⟧ is equivalent to ⟦b:inlūxit⟧. ⟦b:ante vidēmus fulgōrem quam sonum audiāmus⟧, Sen. ⟦i:QN.⟧ 2, 12, 6, ⟦i:we always see the flash before we hear the sound⟧. ⟦b:priusquam sēmen mātūrum siet, secātō⟧, Cato, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 53, ⟦i:always cut before the seed is ripe⟧ (⟦r1575:1575⟧). With the perfect subjunctive in the indefinite second person (⟦r1030:1030⟧): as, ⟦b:hoc malum opprimit antequam prōspicere potuerīs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 39, ⟦i:this calamity always overwhelms you before you can anticipate it⟧ (⟦r1731:1731⟧, ⟦r1558:1558⟧). For ⟦b:prius quam⟧, ⟦i:sooner than⟧, see ⟦r1897:1897⟧.
⟦#1913⟧
The future indicative is used a few times in general statements by old and late writers, and the perfect subjunctive after a negative clause rarely by Tacitus: as, ⟦b:bovēs priusquam in viam agēs, pice cornua īnfima unguitō⟧, Cato, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 72, ⟦i:always smear the hoofs of your oxen with pitch before you drive them on the road⟧ (⟦r1625:1625⟧, ⟦r1577:1577⟧). ⟦b:deū̆m honor prīncipī nōn ante habētur quam agere inter hominēs dēsierit⟧, Ta. 15, 74, ⟦i:divine honours are not paid to an emperor before he has ceased to live among men⟧. Cicero has the perfect subjunctive in a definition: thus, ⟦b:prōvidentia, per quam futūrum aliquid vidētur antequam factum sit⟧, ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 2, 160, ⟦i:foresight is the faculty through which a future event is seen before it has taken place⟧. He also has the present indicative once: ⟦i:Div.⟧ 1, 120.
⟦#1914⟧
In general past statements ⟦b:antequam⟧ and ⟦b:priusquam⟧ introduce the subjunctive imperfect or pluperfect; but this use is very rare: as, ⟦b:dormīre priusquam somni cupīdō esset⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 13, 3, ⟦i:a-sleeping always before they felt sleepy⟧. ⟦b:ita saepe magna indolēs virtūtis, priusquam rē̆ī pūblicae prōdesse potuisset, extīncta est⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 5, 47, ⟦i:thus character of unusual promise was oftentimes cut off, before it could do the government any good⟧.

title: antequam, priusquam: In Particular Statements
text:
⟦#1915⟧
In particular present or future statements, ⟦b:antequam⟧ and ⟦b:priusquam⟧ introduce a present, either indicative or subjunctive; in future statements the future perfect is also used, and regularly when the main verb is future perfect: as,
⟦b:antequam ad sententiam redeō, dē mē pauca dīcam⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 20, ⟦i:before I come back to the motion, I will say a little about myself⟧ (⟦r1593:1593⟧). ⟦b:est etiam prius quam abīs quod volo loquī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 232, ⟦i:there’s something else I want to say before you go⟧. ⟦b:antequam veniat in Pontum, litterās ad Cn. Pompēium mittet⟧, ⟦i:Agr.⟧ 2, 53, ⟦i:before he reaches Pontus, he will send a letter to Pompey⟧. ⟦b:prius quam ad portam veniās, est pistrīlla⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 583, ⟦i:there’s a little bakery just before you get to the gate⟧. ⟦b:nihil contrā disputābō priusquam dīxerit⟧, ⟦i:Fl.⟧ 51, ⟦i:I will not argue to the contrary before he has spoken⟧ (⟦r1626:1626⟧). ⟦b:neque prius, quam dēbellāverō, absistam⟧, L. 49, 39, 9, ⟦i:and I will not leave off before I have brought the war to an end⟧. ⟦b:sī quid mihī̆ acciderit priusquam hōc tantum malī vīderō⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 99, ⟦i:if anything shall befall me before I see this great calamity⟧. ⟦b:neque prōmittō quicquam neque respondeō prius quam gnātum vīderō⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 1044, ⟦i:I’m not promising anything nor making any answer before I see my son⟧ (⟦r1593:1593⟧). Tacitus uses neither the present indicative nor the future perfect.
⟦#1916⟧
In old Latin the future and the perfect subjunctive also occur: as,
⟦b:prius quam quoiquam convīvae dabis, gustātō tūte prius⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 885, ⟦i:before you help a single guest, taste first yourself⟧; but Terence does not use the future, and it is found only once or twice later. ⟦b:nūllō pactō potest prius haec in aedīs recipī, quam illam āmīserim⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 1095. ⟦i:on no terms can I take my new love to the house, before I’ve let the old love drop⟧; but usually the perfect subjunctive is due to indirect discourse.
⟦#1917⟧
In particular past statements ⟦b:antequam⟧ and ⟦b:priusquam⟧ introduce the perfect indicative, especially when the apodosis is negative. The imperfect subjunctive rarely occurs, chiefly in late writers.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:omnia ista ante facta sunt quam iste Ītaliam attigit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 161, ⟦i:all these incidents occurred before the defendant set foot in Italy⟧. ⟦b:neque prius fugere dēstitērunt quam ad Rhēnum pervēnērunt⟧, 1, 53, 1, ⟦i:and they did not stay their flight before they fairly arrived at the Rhine⟧. ⟦b:prius quam hinc abiīt quīndecim mīles minās dederat⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 53, ⟦i:the captain had paid down fifteen minae before he left here⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:nec prius sunt vīsī quam castrīs adpropinquārent⟧, 6, 37, 2, ⟦i:they were not seen before they drew near to the camp⟧. This use of the imperfect subjunctive, not to be confounded with that mentioned in 1919, is not found in old Latin or in Cicero. It is found in Nepos and Livy.
⟦#1918⟧
The present indicative also occurs in particular past statements in old Latin: as, ⟦b:is priusquam moritur mihi dedit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cu.⟧ 637, ⟦i:before he died he gave it me⟧. The indicative imperfect occurs four times in Livy and once in late Latin, the pluperfect once in old Latin and once in Cicero.
⟦#1919⟧
When the action of the protasis was forestalled, or when action conceivable or purpose is expressed, ⟦b:antequam⟧ and ⟦b:priusquam⟧ regularly introduce the imperfect subjunctive in particular past statements: as,
⟦b:plērīque interfectī sunt, priusquam occultum hostem vidērent⟧, L. 35, 29, 3, ⟦i:most of them were slain before they could see the hidden enemy⟧. ⟦b:antequam verbum facerem, dē sellā surrēxit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 147, ⟦i:before I could utter a word he arose from his seat⟧. ⟦b:pervēnit priusquam Pompēius sentīre posset⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 67, 4, ⟦i:he arrived before Pompey should be able to learn of his coming⟧ (⟦r1725:1725⟧). The present and perfect subjunctive occur rarely, generally when the main clause contains a present of vivid narration (⟦r1590:1590⟧). The imperfect is not found in old Latin.
⟦#1920⟧
The perfect indicative or imperfect subjunctive with ⟦b:antequam⟧ is often used attributively with nouns denoting time: as,
⟦b:fābulam docuit, annō ipsō ante quam nātus est Ennius⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 72, ⟦i:he exhibited a play just a year before Ennius was born⟧. ⟦b:ducentīs annīs ante quam Rōmam caperent, in Ītaliam Gallī trānscendērunt⟧, L. 5, 33, 5, ⟦i:two hundred years before they took Rome, the Gauls crossed over to Italy⟧. The pluperfect also occurs, when the main verb is pluperfect: as, ⟦b:Stāiēnus bienniō antequam causam recēpisset, sescentīs mīllibus nummūm sē iūdicium conruptūrum dīxerat⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 68, ⟦i:Stajenus had said two years before he undertook the case, that he would bribe the court for six hundred thousand sesterces⟧.
⟦#1921⟧
The pluperfect subjunctive is rarely introduced by ⟦b:antequam⟧ or ⟦b:priusquam⟧ except in indirect discourse: as,
⟦b:antequam dē meō adventū audīre potuissent, in Macedoniam perrēxī⟧, ⟦i:Pl.⟧ 98, ⟦i:before they should be able to hear of my arrival, I proceeded to Macedonia⟧ (⟦r1725:1725⟧). ⟦b:āvertit equōs in castra priusquam pābula gustāssent Trōiae Xanthumque bibissent⟧, V. 1, 472, ⟦i:he drave the horses off to camp, or ever they should taste of Troja’s grass and Xanthus drink⟧ (⟦r1725:1725⟧).
⟦#1922⟧
It may be mentioned here that ⟦b:postrīdiē quam⟧ and ⟦b:prīdiē quam⟧ occur a few times in Plautus and Cicero with the indicative; ⟦b:postrīdiē quam⟧ with the indicative in Suetonius; and ⟦b:prīdiē quam⟧ with the subjunctive in Livy, Valerius Maximus, and Suetonius.

title: ubī̆, ut, cum prīmum, simul atque
text:
⟦#1923⟧
With ⟦b:posteā quam⟧, ⟦b:postquam⟧ (⟦b:posquam⟧), ⟦i:after⟧, the following words may conveniently be treated: ⟦b:ubī̆⟧, ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦i:when⟧; ⟦b:ubī̆ prīmum⟧, ⟦b:ut prīmum⟧, ⟦b:cum prīmum⟧, ⟦i:when first⟧, and in Plautus ⟦b:quom extemplō⟧; ⟦b:simul atque⟧ (or ⟦b:ac⟧, less frequently ⟦b:et⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧, or ⟦b:simul⟧ alone), ⟦i:at the same time with⟧, ⟦i:as soon as⟧.
⟦b:postquam⟧, ⟦b:ubī̆⟧, ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦b:cum prīmum⟧, ⟦b:simul atque⟧, accompany the indicative.
For examples of the use of tenses, see ⟦r1924:1924-1934⟧.
⟦#1924⟧
In clauses introduced by ⟦b:posteā quam⟧ or ⟦b:postquam⟧, the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive, found a dozen times in the manuscripts of Cicero’s works and elsewhere, is generally corrected in modern editions or usually the conjunctive particle is emended to ⟦b:posteā quom⟧ (⟦b:cum⟧). But the subjunctive may of course be used with this and the other particles mentioned in 1923 for special reasons, as with the indefinite second person (⟦r1731:1731⟧), by attraction (⟦r1728:1728⟧), and in indirect discourse (⟦r1725:1725⟧). For the subjunctive of repeated past action with ⟦b:ubī̆⟧ and ⟦b:ut⟧, see ⟦r1932:1932⟧. The infinitive of intimation occurs in Tacitus (⟦r1539:1539⟧): as, ⟦b:postquam exuī aequālitās, prōvēnēre dominātiōnēs⟧, Ta. 3, 26, ⟦i:after equality between man and man was dropped, there came a crop of tyrants⟧.
⟦#1925⟧
In narration the perfect indicative is regularly used in clauses introduced by ⟦b:postquam⟧, ⟦b:ubī̆⟧, ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦b:cum prīmum⟧, ⟦b:simul atque⟧ (⟦r1739:1739⟧): as,
⟦b:postquam tuās litterās lēgī, Postumia tua mē convēnit⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 4, 2, 1, ⟦i:after I read your letter, your Postumia called on me⟧. ⟦b:postquam aurum abstulimus, in nāvem cōnscendimus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 277, ⟦i:after we got away the money, we took ship⟧. ⟦b:ubī̆ ad ipsum vēnī dēvorticulum, cōnstitī⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 635, ⟦i:when I came exactly to the side street, I pulled up⟧. ⟦b:ubī̆ sē diūtius dūcī intellēxit, graviter eōs accūsat⟧, 1, 16, 5, ⟦i:when he came to see that he was put off a good while, he takes them roundly to task⟧. ⟦b:quī ut perōrāvit, surrēxit Clōdius⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 2, 3, 2, ⟦i:when he had finished speaking, up jumped Clodius⟧. ⟦b:ut abiī abs tē, fit forte obviam mihi Phormiō⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 617, ⟦i:when I left you, Phormio happened to fall in my way⟧. ⟦b:crīmen eius modī est, ut, cum prīmum ad mē dēlātum est, ūsūrum mē illō nōn putārem⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 158, ⟦i:the charge is of such a sort that, when first it was reported to me, I thought I should not use it⟧. ⟦b:cum prīmum Crētae lītus attigit, nūntiōs mīsit⟧, L. 37, 60, 4, ⟦i:as soon as he touched the shore of Crete, he sent messengers⟧. ⟦b:ut prīmum loquī posse coepī, inquam⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 6, 15, ⟦i:as soon as I began to be able to speak, I said⟧. ⟦b:quem simul atque oppidānī cōnspexērunt, mūrum complēre coepērunt⟧, 7, 12, 5, ⟦i:as soon as the garrison espied him, they began to man the wall⟧. ⟦b:at hostēs, ubī̆ prīmum nostrōs equitēs cōnspexērunt, impetū factō celeriter nostrōs perturbāvērunt⟧, 4, 12, 1, ⟦i:but as soon as the enemy caught sight of our cavalry, they attacked and threw our men into disorder⟧. The conjunction ⟦b:simul atque⟧ is very rarely found in old Latin.
⟦#1926⟧
The present indicative of vivid narration (⟦r1590:1590⟧) sometimes occurs: as,
⟦b:postquam iam puerī septuennēs sunt, pater onerāvit nāvim magnam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men. prol.⟧ 24, ⟦i:after the boys were seven year olds, their father freighted a big ship⟧. ⟦b:quid ait, ubi mē nōminās⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 303, ⟦i:what sayeth she when you name me?⟧ ⟦b:ubī̆ neutrī trānseundī initium faciunt, Caesar suōs in castra redūxit⟧, 2, 9, 2, ⟦i:neither party taking the initiative in crossing, Caesar marched his men back to camp⟧. Verbs of perceiving, especially ⟦b:videō⟧, occur oftenest in this use, which is common in Plautus and Terence: as, ⟦b:postquam videt nūptiās adparārī, missast ancilla īlicō⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 513, ⟦i:after she sees a marriage on foot, her maid is sent forthwith⟧. ⟦b:abeō ab illīs, postquam videō mē lūdificārier⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 487, ⟦i:seeing myself made game of, I leave them⟧. ⟦b:quem posteā quam videt nōn adesse, ardēre atque furere coepit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 92, ⟦i:seeing that the man does not appear, he began to rage and fume⟧. ⟦b:ubī̆ hoc videt, init cōnsilium importūnī tyrannī⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 103, ⟦i:seeing this, he adopted the policy of a savage tyrant⟧. Plautus uses also ⟦b:quom extemplō⟧. Such protases often take on a causal sense (see also ⟦r1930:1930⟧).
⟦#1927⟧
The present or perfect with ⟦b:postquam⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧ is sometimes used in expressions equivalent to an emphasized accusative or ablative of time, the main verb being ⟦b:est⟧ or ⟦b:sunt⟧: as, ⟦b:septingentī sunt annī postquam inclita condita Rōma est⟧, E. in Varro, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 3, 1, 2, ⟦i:’tis seven hundred years since glorious Rome was founded⟧. ⟦b:domō ut abiērunt hic tertius annus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 29, ⟦i:this is the third year since they left home⟧. ⟦b:annus est octāvus ut imperium obtinēs⟧, Ta. 14, 53, ⟦i:it is the eighth year since you acquired empire⟧. For a similar use of ⟦b:cum⟧, see ⟦r1871:1871⟧.
⟦#1928⟧
The pluperfect with ⟦b:postquam⟧, denoting resulting state (⟦r1615:1615⟧), occurs less frequently: as,
⟦b:tum cum P. Āfricānus, posteā quam bis cōnsul fuerat, L. Cottam in iūdicium vocābat⟧, ⟦i:Caecil.⟧ 69, ⟦i:at the time when Africanus, after he had twice been consul, was bringing Cotta to judgement⟧. ⟦b:postquam omnium oculōs occupāverat certāmen, tum āversam adoriuntur Rōmānam aciem⟧, L. 22, 48, 4, ⟦i:when every eye was fairly riveted on the engagement, that instant they fell upon the Romans in the rear⟧. Not in Plautus, once in Terence, and rare in classical writers.
⟦#1929⟧
The pluperfect, less frequently the perfect, with ⟦b:postquam⟧ is used attributively with nouns denoting time.
In this use ⟦b:post⟧ is often separated from ⟦b:quam⟧, and two constructions are possible: (⟦i:a.⟧) Ablative: ⟦b:annō post quam vōta erat aedēs Monētae dēdicātur⟧, L. 7, 28, 6, ⟦i:the temple of Moneta is dedicated a year after it was vowed⟧. Without ⟦b:post⟧: ⟦b:quadringentēsimō annō quam urbs Rōmanā condita erat, patriciī cōnsulēs magistrātum iniēre⟧, L. 7, 18, 1, ⟦i:four hundred years after Rome town was founded, patrician consuls entered into office⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) Accusative, with an ordinal, and ⟦b:post⟧ as a preposition, or, sometimes, ⟦b:intrā⟧: ⟦b:post diem tertium gesta rēs est quam dīxerat⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 44, ⟦i:the deed was done the next day but one after he said it⟧. See ⟦r2419:2419⟧.
⟦#1930⟧
The imperfect with ⟦b:postquam⟧ expresses action continuing into the time of the main action. Such a protasis, especially when negative, usually denotes the cause of the main action: as,
⟦b:Appius, postquam nēmō adībat, domum sē recēpit⟧, L. 3, 46, 9, ⟦i:Appius, finding that nobody presented himself, went back home⟧. ⟦b:posteā quam ē scaenā explōdēbātur, cōnfūgit in huius domum⟧, ⟦i:RC.⟧ 30, ⟦i:after being repeatedly hissed off the stage, he took refuge in my client’s house⟧.
In old Latin this use is found only once, in Plautus; it is most common in Livy, but occurs frequently in Tacitus. So occasionally the present, generally when the main action is present (see also ⟦r1926:1926⟧): as, ⟦b:postquam nec ab Rōmānīs vōbīs ūlla est spēs, nec vōs moenia dēfendunt, pācem adferō ad vōs⟧, L. 21, 13, 4, ⟦i:now that it has become plain that you have no hope from the Romans, and that your walls are no protection to you, I bring peace unto you⟧. ⟦b:postquam līberast, ubī̆ habitet dīcere admodum incertē sciō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:E.⟧ 505, ⟦i:now that she’s free, I’m quite too ill informed to say where she lives⟧. ⟦b:quae omnia intellegit nihil prōdesse, posteā quam testibus convincitur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 103, ⟦i:he knows that all this is fruitless, now that he is being refuted by witnesses⟧. The perfect with ⟦b:postquam⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧ occurs occasionally in this use with the present in the main clause: as, ⟦b:animus in tūtō locōst, postquam iste hinc abiīt⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 1052, ⟦i:my mind is easy, now that fellow’s gone⟧. ⟦b:nam ut in nāvī vecta’s, crēdō timida ‘s⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 106, ⟦i:for after your voyage, of course you’re nervous⟧.
⟦#1931⟧
⟦b:postquam⟧ and ⟦b:ut⟧ have sometimes the meaning of ⟦i:ever since⟧ or ⟦i:as long as⟧: as,
⟦b:postquam nātus sum, satur numquam fuī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 156, ⟦i:since I was born I’ve never had enough to eat⟧. ⟦b:tibī̆ umquam quicquam, postquam tuos sum, verbōrum dedī?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 925, ⟦i:have I once ever cheated you as long as I have been your slave?⟧ ⟦b:neque meum pedem intulī in aedīs, ut cum exercitū hinc profectus sum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 733, ⟦i:I have n’t set foot in the house ever since I marched out with the army⟧. ⟦b:ut illōs dē rē pūblicā librōs ēdidistī, nihil ā tē posteā accēpimus⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 19, ⟦i:we have had nothing from you since you published the work On the State⟧.

title: ubī̆, ut, simul atque
text:
⟦#1932⟧
⟦b:ubī̆⟧, ⟦b:ut⟧, or ⟦b:simul atque⟧ (⟦b:ac⟧) often introduces a clause denoting indefinite or repeated action: as,
⟦b:adeō obcaecat animōs fortūna, ubī̆ vim suam refringī nōn vult⟧, L. 5, 37, 1, ⟦i:so completely does fortune blind the mind when she will not have her power thwarted⟧. ⟦b:ubī̆ salūtātiō dēflūxit, litterīs mē involvō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 9, 20, 3, ⟦i:when my callers go, I always plunge into my book⟧ (⟦r1613:1613⟧). ⟦b:omnēs profectō mulierēs tē amant, ut quaeque aspexit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 1264, ⟦i:all the ladies love you, every time one spies you⟧. ⟦b:simul atque sē īnflēxit hīc rēx in dominātum iniūstiōrem, fit continuō tyrannus⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 2, 48, ⟦i:for the moment our king turns to a severer kind of mastery, he becomes a tyrant on the spot⟧. ⟦b:Messānam ut quisque nostrūm vēnerat, haec vīsere solēbat⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 5, ⟦i:any Roman, who visited Messana, invariably went to see these statues⟧ (⟦r1618:1618⟧). ⟦b:hostēs, ubī̆ aliquōs singulārēs cōnspexerant, adoriēbantur⟧, 4, 26, 2, ⟦i:every time the enemy saw some detached parties, they would charge⟧. The imperfect in this use is not common in classical writers, and occurs but once, with ⟦b:ubī̆⟧, in old Latin; the pluperfect is rare before the silver age. Clauses with ⟦b:ut⟧ generally contain some form of ⟦b:quisque⟧ (⟦r2396:2396⟧). Plautus uses ⟦b:quom extemplō⟧ with the present and perfect. The subjunctive is found with ⟦b:ubī̆⟧ and ⟦b:ut quisque⟧ in cases of repeated past action (⟦r1730:1730⟧).
⟦#1933⟧
⟦b:ubī̆⟧, ⟦b:ut⟧, or ⟦b:simul atque⟧ rarely introduces an imperfect or pluperfect of definite time: as,
⟦b:quid ubi reddēbās aurum, dīxistī patrī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 685, ⟦i:what did you tell your father when you were returning the money?⟧ ⟦b:ubī̆ lūx adventābat, tubicinēs sīgna canere⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 99, 1, ⟦i:when daylight was drawing on, the trumpeters sounded the call⟧. ⟦b:ubī̆ nēmō obvius ībat, plēnō gradū ad hostium castra tendunt⟧, L. 9, 45, 14, ⟦i:finding nobody came to meet them, they advanced double quick upon the enemy’s camp⟧ (⟦r1930:1930⟧). The use of these tenses referring to definite time is very rare in old Latin, and found only with ⟦b:ut⟧ in Cicero.
⟦#1934⟧
⟦b:ubī̆⟧ or ⟦b:simul atque⟧, referring to definite time, introduces the future or future perfect, when the apodosis is also future: as,
⟦b:simul et quid erit certī, scrībam ad tē⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 2, 20, 2, ⟦i:as soon as there is anything positive, I will write to you⟧. ⟦b:ego ad tē statim habēbō quod scrībam, simul ut vīderō Cūriōnem⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 10, 4, 12, ⟦i:I shall have something to write you, as soon as ever I see Curio⟧. ⟦b:nam ubī̆ mē aspiciet, ad carnuficem rapiet continuō senex⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 688, ⟦i:when the old man sees me, he’ll hurry me off to Jack Ketch without any ado⟧. ⟦b:ubi prīmum poterit, sē illinc subdūcet⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 628, ⟦i:she’ll steal away as soon as she can⟧. Plautus has also ⟦b:quom extemplō⟧ in this use, and Pliny the Younger ⟦b:ut primum⟧.

title: utī or ut
text:
⟦#1935⟧
The relative adverb ⟦b:utī⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧ (⟦r711:711⟧) is found in the oldest Latin in the form ⟦b:utei⟧, but ⟦b:ut⟧ was the prevalent form even in the time of Plautus. As a conjunctive particle, it accompanies both the indicative and the subjunctive. For ⟦b:ut⟧ in wishes, see ⟦r1540:1540⟧; in questions, 1568.

title: ut, where
text:
⟦#1936⟧
⟦b:utī⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧ in the rare signification of ⟦i:where⟧, accompanies the indicative: as, ⟦b:atque in eōpse adstās lapide, ut praecō praedicat⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 815, ⟦i:and there you stand right on the auction block, just where the crier always cries⟧. ⟦b:sīve in extrēmōs penetrābit Indōs, lītus ut longē resonante Eōā tunditur undā⟧, Cat. 11, 2, ⟦i:or shall he pierce to farthest Ind, where by the long-resounding eastern wave the strand is lashed⟧. In classical Latin, ⟦b:ut⟧ in this sense is used only by the poets, as here and there in Lucilius, Catullus, Cicero’s ⟦i:Aratēa⟧, and Vergil. ⟦b:ubī̆⟧ is the word regularly used. For ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦i:when⟧, see ⟦r1923:1923⟧.

title: ut, as
text:
⟦#1937⟧
The indicative is used in the protasis of a comparative period introduced by ⟦b:utī⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦i:as⟧.
⟦b:ut⟧ often has as a correlative ⟦b:ita⟧, ⟦b:item⟧, ⟦b:itidem⟧, ⟦b:sīc⟧, ⟦b:perinde⟧, or ⟦b:similiter⟧, and sometimes in old Latin and poetry ⟦b:aequē⟧, ⟦b:adaequē⟧, ⟦b:pariter⟧, ⟦b:nōn aliter⟧, ⟦b:nōn secus⟧, ⟦b:īdem⟧. ⟦b:sīc⟧ is sometimes drawn to the protasis, making ⟦b:sīcutī⟧, ⟦b:sīcut⟧; ⟦b:utī⟧ is sometimes strengthened by ⟦b:vel⟧, making ⟦b:velutī⟧, ⟦b:velut⟧, ⟦i:even as⟧, ⟦i:just as⟧. ⟦b:quemadmodum⟧ often, and ⟦b:quōmodo⟧ sometimes, stands for ⟦b:ut⟧. For the use of ⟦b:ut⟧ in old Latin in sentences in which classical Latin would employ the indirect question, see ⟦r1791:1791⟧. For coordinated comparative sentences without ⟦b:ut⟧, see ⟦r1704:1704⟧.
⟦b:perge ut īnstituistī⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 2, 22, ⟦i:go on as you have begun⟧. ⟦b:ut volēs mēd esse, ita erō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 240, ⟦i:as you will have me be, so will I be⟧ (⟦r1625:1625⟧). ⟦b:ut sēmentem fēceris, ita metēs⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 261, ⟦i:as you sow, y’are like to reap⟧ (⟦r1626:1626⟧). ⟦b:ut nōn omnem frūgem in omnī agrō reperīre possīs, sīc nōn omne facinus in omnī vītā nāscitur⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 75, ⟦i:every crime does not start into being in every life, any more than you can find every fruit in every field⟧ (⟦r1731:1731⟧). Also in asseverations: ⟦b:ita mē dī amābunt, ut ego hunc auscultō lubēns⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 496, ⟦i:so help me heaven, as I am glad to hear this man⟧ (⟦r1622:1622⟧).
⟦#1938⟧
⟦b:ut . . . ita⟧ or ⟦b:sīc⟧, ⟦i:as . . . so⟧, often stand where concessive and adversative conjunctions might be used; ⟦i:while . . . nevertheless⟧, ⟦i:although ... yet⟧, ⟦i:certainly . . . but⟧: as,
⟦b:ut nihil bonī est in morte, sīc certē nihil malī⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 14, ⟦i:while there is nothing good after death, yet certainly there is nothing bad⟧. ⟦b:quō factō sīcut glōriam auxit, ita grātiam minuit⟧, Suet. ⟦i:Oth.⟧ 1, ⟦i:by this action he increased his reputation, but lessened his popularity⟧. ⟦b:nec ut iniūstus in pāce rēx, ita dux bellī prāvus fuit⟧, L. 1, 53, 1, ⟦i:but while he was an unjust king in peace, he was not a bad leader in war⟧. This adversative correlation is found sometimes in Cicero, but is far more common in late writers.
⟦#1939⟧
⟦b:ut quisque⟧, commonly with a superlative expression, is used in the protasis of a comparative period of equality, with ⟦b:ita⟧ or ⟦b:sīc⟧ and commonly another superlative expression in the apodosis: as,
⟦b:ut quaeque rēs est turpissima, sīc maximē vindicanda est⟧, ⟦i:Caec.⟧ 7, ⟦i:the more disgraceful a thing is, the more emphatically does it call for punishment⟧. ⟦b:ut quisque optimē Graecē scīret, ita esse nēquissimum⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 265, ⟦i:that the better Greek scholar a man was, the greater rascal he always was⟧ (⟦r1722:1722⟧). This construction is often abridged: as, ⟦b:sapientissimus quisque aequissimō animō moritur⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 83, ⟦i:the sage always dies with perfect resignation⟧. ⟦b:optimus quisque praeceptor frequentiā gaudet⟧, Quint. 1, 2, 9, ⟦i:the best teachers always revel in large classes⟧. See ⟦r2397:2397⟧.
⟦#1940⟧
⟦b:ut⟧ often introduces a parenthetical idea, particularly a general truth or a habit which accounts for the special fact expressed in the main sentence: as,
⟦b:nēmō, ut opīnor, in culpā est⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 143, ⟦i:nobody, as I fancy, is to blame⟧. ⟦b:excitābat flūctūs in simpulō, ut dīcitur, Grātidius⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 3, 36, ⟦i:Gratidius was raising a tempest in a teapot, as the saying is⟧. ⟦b:paulisper, dum sē uxor, ut fit, comparat, commorātus est⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 28, ⟦i:he had to wait a bit, as is always the case, while his wife was putting on her things⟧. ⟦b:hōrum auctōritāte adductī, ut sunt Gallōrum subita cōnsilia, Trebium retinent⟧, 3, 8, 3, ⟦i:influenced by these people they detain Trebius, as might have been expected, sudden resolutions being always characteristic of the Gauls⟧. ⟦b:sēditiōne nūntiātā, ut erat laenā amictus, ita vēnit in cōntiōnem⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 56, ⟦i:an outbreak was reported, and he came to the meeting all accoutred as he was, with his sacrificial robe on⟧. Often elliptically: as, ⟦b:acūtī hominis, ut Siculī⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 15, ⟦i:a bright man, of course, being a Sicilian⟧. ⟦b:Aequōrum exercitus, ut quī permultōs annōs imbellēs ēgissent, trepidāre⟧, L. 9, 45, 10, ⟦i:the army of the Aequians alarmed and irresolute, and naturally, since they had passed a great many years without fighting⟧ (⟦r1824:1824⟧, ⟦r1827:1827⟧).
⟦#1941⟧
⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦i:as for example⟧, is used in illustrations, particularly in abridged sentences (⟦r1057:1057⟧): as,
⟦b:genus est quod plūrēs partēs amplectitur, ut ‘animal.’ pars est, quae subest generī, ut ‘equos,’⟧ ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 1, 32, ⟦i:a class is what embraces a number of parts, as ‘living thing’; a part is what is included in a class, as ‘horse.’⟧ ⟦b:sunt bēstiae in quibus inest aliquid simile virtūtis, ut in leōnibus, ut in canibus⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 5, 38, ⟦i:there are brutes in which there is a something like the moral quality of man, as for instance the lion and the dog⟧.
⟦#1942⟧
The parenthetical clause with ⟦b:ut⟧ or ⟦b:prout⟧ sometimes makes an allowance for the meaning of a word, usually an adjective, in the main sentence: as,
⟦b:cīvitās ampla atque flōrēns, ut est captus Germānōrum⟧, 4, 3, 3, ⟦i:a grand and prosperous community, that is according to German conceptions⟧. ⟦b:ut captus est servōrum, nōn malus⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 480, ⟦i:not a bad fellow, as slaves go⟧. ⟦b:Sthenius ab adulēscentiā haec comparārat, supellēctilem ex aere ēlegantiōrem, tabulās pīctās, etiam argentī bene factī prout Thermītānī hominis facultātēs ferēbant, satis⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 83, ⟦i:Sthenius had been a collector from early years of such things as artistic bronzes, pictures; also of curiously wrought silver a goodly amount, that is as the means of a Thermae man went⟧. Often in abridged sentences: as, ⟦b:scrīptor fuit, ut temporibus illīs, lūculentus⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 102, ⟦i:he was a brilliant historian for the times⟧. ⟦b:multae etiam, ut in homine Rōmānō, litterae⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 12, ⟦i:furthermore, extensive reading, that is for a Roman⟧. ⟦b:ut illīs temporibus, praedīves⟧, L. 4, 13, 1, ⟦i:a millionaire, for those times⟧.
⟦#1943⟧
⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦i:as indeed⟧, ⟦i:as in fact⟧, with the indicative, is used to represent that an action supposed, conceded, or commanded, really occurs: as,
⟦b:sit Ennius sānē, ut est certē, perfectior⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 76, ⟦i:grant, for aught I care, that Ennius is a more finished poet, as indeed he is⟧. ⟦b:utī erat rēs, Metellum esse ratī⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 69, 1, ⟦i:supposing that it was Metellus, as in fact it was⟧. This use begins in the classical period. It is found particularly with ⟦b:quamvīs⟧, 1905; with ⟦b:sī⟧, see ⟦r2017:2017⟧.
⟦#1944⟧
⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦i:as⟧, ⟦i:like⟧, sometimes shows that a noun used predicatively is not literally applicable, but expresses an imputed quality or character: as,
⟦b:Cicerō ea quae nunc ūsū veniunt cecinit ut vātēs⟧, N. 25, 16, 4, ⟦i:Cicero foretold what is now actually occurring, like a bard inspired⟧. ⟦b:canem et faelem ut deōs colunt⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 1, 32, ⟦i:they bow the knee to dog and cat as gods⟧. ⟦b:quod mē sīcut alterum parentem dīligit⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 5, 8, 4, ⟦i:because he loves me like a second father⟧. ⟦b:rēgiae virginēs, ut tōnstrīculae, tondēbant barbam patris⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 58, ⟦i:the princesses used to shave their father, just like common barber-girls⟧. In an untrue or a merely figurative comparison ⟦b:tamquam⟧ (⟦r1908:1908⟧) or ⟦b:quasi⟧ is used.
⟦#1945⟧
In old Latin, ⟦b:prae⟧ is combined with ⟦b:ut⟧: ⟦b:praeut⟧, ⟦i:compared with how⟧: as, ⟦b:parum etiam, praeut futūrumst, praedicās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 374, ⟦i:you say too little still compared with how ’twill be⟧. ⟦b:praeut⟧ is sometimes followed by a relative clause: as, ⟦b:lūdum iocumque dīcet fuisse illum alterum, praeut huius rabiēs quae dabit⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 300, ⟦i:he’ll say the other was but sport and play, compared with what this youth will in his frenzy do⟧.
⟦#1946⟧
In Plautus ⟦b:sīcut⟧, with the indicative, has once or twice the meaning of ⟦i:since⟧: as, ⟦b:quīn tū illam iubē abs tē abīre quō lubet: sīcut soror eius hūc gemina vēnit Ephesum⟧, ⟦i:MG.⟧ 974, ⟦i:why, bid her go away from you wherever she may choose, since her twin sister here to Ephesus is come⟧.

title: utī or ut. NEGATIVE ut nē, nē, or ut nōn
text:
⟦#1947⟧
The subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧ is: (A.) That of action desired (⟦r1540:1540⟧), in clauses of purpose; in these the negative is ⟦b:nē⟧, or sometimes ⟦b:ut nē⟧, and ⟦i:and that not⟧, ⟦b:nēve⟧ or ⟦b:neu⟧, rarely ⟦b:neque⟧ or ⟦b:nec⟧. ⟦b:ut nē⟧, though used at all periods (not by Caesar, Sallust, or Livy), is chiefly found in older Latin; afterwards ⟦b:nē⟧ alone took its place (⟦r1706:1706⟧). ⟦b:ut nōn⟧ is used when the negative belongs to a single word. (B.) That of action conceivable (⟦r1554:1554⟧), in clauses of result; in these the negative is ⟦b:ut nōn⟧, ⟦b:ut nēmō⟧, ⟦b:ut nūllus⟧, &c.; or with emphasis on the negative, ⟦b:nēmō ut⟧, ⟦b:nūllus ut⟧, ⟦b:nihil ut⟧; also ⟦b:vix ut⟧, ⟦b:paene ut⟧, ⟦b:prope ut⟧.
⟦#1948⟧
Final and consecutive clauses with ⟦b:ut⟧ are of two classes: I. Complementary clauses, that is, such as are an essential complement of certain specific verbs or expressions; such clauses have the value of a substantive, and may represent a subject, an object, or any oblique case. II. Pure final or consecutive clauses, in which the purpose or result of any action may be expressed, and which are not essential to complete the sense of a verb.

title: Complementary Final Clauses
text:
⟦#1949⟧
(1.) The subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧ or ⟦b:nē⟧ is used in clauses which serve to complete the sense of verbs of will or aim.
⟦#1950⟧
(a.) Verbs of will include those of desire, request, advice, resolution, stipulation, command, or permission.
Will may be suggested by a general verb or expression: as, ⟦b:dīcō⟧, ⟦b:respondeō⟧, ⟦b:nūntiō⟧, &c.; or denoted by specific ones, of which some of the commonest are: desire: ⟦b:volō⟧ (⟦b:mālō⟧), ⟦b:concupīscō⟧, ⟦b:optō⟧. request: ⟦b:petō⟧, ⟦b:postulō⟧, ⟦b:flāgitō⟧, ⟦b:ōrō⟧, ⟦b:rogō⟧, ⟦b:precor⟧, ⟦b:obsecrō⟧, ⟦b:implōrō⟧, ⟦b:instō⟧, ⟦i:urge⟧, ⟦b:invītō⟧. advice: ⟦b:suādeō⟧, ⟦b:persuādeō⟧, ⟦i:persuade⟧, ⟦b:moneō⟧, ⟦i:bid⟧, ⟦b:admoneō⟧, ⟦b:hortor⟧, ⟦b:cēnseō⟧, ⟦i:propose⟧, ⟦i:vote⟧. resolution, stipulation: ⟦b:dēcernō⟧, ⟦b:statuō⟧, ⟦i:decree⟧, ⟦b:cōnstituō⟧, ⟦b:placet⟧, ⟦b:sanciō⟧, ⟦b:pacīscor⟧, ⟦b:pepigī⟧. command: ⟦b:imperō⟧, ⟦b:praecipiō⟧, ⟦b:praescrībō⟧, ⟦b:mandō⟧, ⟦b:negōtium dō⟧, ⟦b:ēdīcō⟧, ⟦b:ferō⟧, ⟦b:caveō⟧, ⟦b:interdīcō⟧. permission: ⟦b:concēdō⟧, ⟦i:allow⟧, ⟦b:permittō⟧, ⟦b:committō⟧, ⟦b:potestātem faciō⟧, ⟦b:veniam dō⟧, ⟦b:sinō⟧, ⟦b:nōn patior⟧.
⟦#1951⟧
(b.) Verbs of aim include those of striving, accomplishing, or inducing; such are:
striving: ⟦b:agō⟧ or ⟦b:id agō⟧, ⟦b:animum indūcō⟧, ⟦b:temptō⟧, ⟦b:operam dō⟧, ⟦b:labōrō⟧, ⟦b:nītor⟧, ⟦b:ēnītor⟧, ⟦b:mōlior⟧, ⟦b:videō⟧, ⟦b:prōspiciō⟧, ⟦b:cūrō⟧, ⟦b:nihil antīquius habeō quam⟧, ⟦b:contendō⟧, ⟦b:studeō⟧, ⟦b:pūgnō⟧. accomplishing: ⟦b:faciō⟧ (⟦b:efficiō⟧, ⟦b:perficiō⟧), ⟦b:praestō⟧; ⟦b:mereō⟧; ⟦b:impetrō⟧, ⟦b:adsequor⟧, ⟦b:cōnsequor⟧, ⟦b:adipīscor⟧. inducing: ⟦b:moveō⟧, ⟦b:excitō⟧, ⟦b:incitō⟧, ⟦b:impellō⟧, ⟦b:perpellō⟧, ⟦b:cōgō⟧.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:optāvit ut in currum patris tollerētur⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 94, ⟦i:he asked to be lifted into his father’s chariot⟧. ⟦b:optō nē sē illa gēns moveat⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 12, 19, 2, ⟦i:I hope and pray that that nation may not stir⟧. ⟦b:Ubiī ōrābant, ut sibī̆ auxilium ferret⟧, 4, 16, 5, ⟦i:the Ubians begged that he would help them⟧. ⟦b:Pausaniās ōrāre coepit nē ēnūntiāret⟧, N. 4, 4, 6, ⟦i:Pausanias began to beg that he would not tell⟧. ⟦b:hortātus est utī in officiō manēret⟧, 5, 4, 2, ⟦i:he urged him to remain steadfast in duty⟧. ⟦b:hortātur eōs nē animō dēficiant⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 19, 1, ⟦i:he urges them not to get disheartened⟧ (⟦r1752:1752⟧). ⟦b:suīs, ut idem faciant, imperat⟧, 5, 37, 1, ⟦i:he orders his men to do the same⟧. ⟦b:suīs imperāvit nē quod omnīnō tēlum rēicerent⟧, 1, 46, 2, ⟦i:he ordered his men not to throw any weapon at all back⟧. ⟦b:huic permīsit, utī in hīs locīs legiōnem conlocāret⟧, 3, 1, 3, ⟦i:he allowed this man to quarter his legion in these parts⟧. ⟦b:neque suam neque populī Rōmānī cōnsuētūdinem patī, utī sociōs dēsereret⟧, 1, 45, 1, ⟦i:that his practice and that of the Roman nation would not allow him to desert his allies⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:neque id agere ut exercitum teneat ipse, sed nē illī habeant quō contrā sē ūtī possint⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 85, 11, ⟦i:and that his object was not to hold the army himself, but to prevent the other side from having an army which they could use against him⟧. ⟦b:XII nāvibus āmissīs, reliquīs ut nāvigārī commodē posset effēcit⟧, 4, 31, 3, ⟦i:a dozen vessels were lost, but he managed to sail comfortably with the rest⟧. ⟦b:eius bellī fāma effēcit nē sē pugnae committerent Sappīnātēs⟧, L. 5, 32, 4, ⟦i:the story of this war prevented the Sappinatians from hazarding an engagement⟧. ⟦b:sī ā Chrȳsogonō nōn impetrāmus ut pecūniā nostrā contentus sit, vītam nē petat⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 150, ⟦i:if we do not succeed in making Chrysogonus satisfied with our money without his aiming at our life⟧. ⟦b:Aulum spē pactiōnis perpulit, utī in abditās regiōnēs sēsē īnsequerētur⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 38, 2, ⟦i:Aulus he induced by the hope of a pecuniary settlement to follow him to distant regions⟧. ⟦b:Antōnium pactiōne prōvinciae perpulerat, nē contrā rem pūblicam sentīret⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 26, 4, ⟦i:by agreeing to let Antony have a province, he had induced him not to be disaffected toward the government⟧.
⟦#1952⟧
Many of these verbs often have a coordinated subjunctive (⟦r1705:1705-1713⟧), or, according to the meaning, admit other constructions, which must in general be learned by reading, or from the dictionary. The following points may be noticed:
⟦#1953⟧
(a.) The verbs of resolving, ⟦b:statuō⟧, ⟦b:cōnstituō⟧, and ⟦b:dēcernō⟧, and of striving, ⟦b:nītor⟧, and ⟦b:temptō⟧, have usually the complementary infinitive (⟦r2169:2169⟧), unless a new subject is introduced. For ⟦b:volō⟧ (⟦b:mālō⟧), and ⟦b:cupiō⟧, see also ⟦r2189:2189⟧; for ⟦b:iubeō⟧, ⟦b:vetō⟧, ⟦b:sinō⟧, and ⟦b:patior⟧, ⟦r2198:2198⟧. ⟦b:postulō⟧, ⟦i:expect⟧, often has the same construction as ⟦b:volō⟧, especially in old Latin (⟦r2194:2194⟧). For ⟦b:imperō⟧, see ⟦r2202:2202⟧.
⟦#1954⟧
(b.) Some of the above verbs, with the meaning ⟦i:think⟧ or ⟦i:say⟧, have the accusative with the infinitive (⟦r2175:2175⟧, ⟦r2195:2195⟧): as, ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:contendō⟧, ⟦i:maintain⟧, ⟦b:concēdō⟧, ⟦i:admit⟧, ⟦b:statuō⟧, ⟦i:assume⟧, ⟦b:dēcernō⟧, ⟦i:judge⟧, ⟦b:moneō⟧, ⟦i:remind⟧, ⟦b:persuādeō⟧, ⟦i:convince⟧.
⟦#1955⟧
(c.) Verbs of accomplishing sometimes express result rather than purpose, and when the result is negative, are completed by a clause with ⟦b:ut nōn⟧ (⟦r1965:1965⟧). For the infinitive with such verbs, see ⟦r2196:2196⟧.
⟦#1956⟧
⟦b:est⟧ with a predicate noun is sometimes equivalent to a verb of will or aim, and has the same construction.
So with words like ⟦b:iūs⟧, ⟦b:lēx⟧, ⟦b:mūnus⟧, &c.: as, ⟦b:iūs esse bellī ut quī vīcissent hīs quōs vīcissent imperārent⟧, 1, 36, 1, ⟦i:that rules of war entitled conquerors to lord it over conquered⟧. ⟦b:quis nescit prīmam esse historiae lēgem, nē quid falsī dīcere audeat?⟧ ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 62, ⟦i:who does not know that the first rule of history is that it shall not venture to say anything false?⟧ ⟦b:iūstitiae prīmum mūnus est ut nē cui quis noceat⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 20, ⟦i:the first duty of justice is that a man harm nobody⟧. ⟦b:nam id arbitror adprīmē in vītā esse ūtile, ‘ut nē quid nimis,’⟧ T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 60, ⟦i:for this I hold to be a rule in life that’s passing useful, ‘naught in overplus.’⟧
⟦#1957⟧
(2.) The subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧ or ⟦b:nē⟧ is used in clauses which complete expressions of fear, anxiety, or danger.
⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦i:that not⟧, ⟦i:may not⟧, and ⟦b:nē⟧, ⟦i:lest⟧, ⟦i:may⟧, were originally signs of a wish (⟦r1540:1540⟧): thus, ⟦b:vereor, ut fīat⟧, ⟦i:I am afraid; may it come to pass⟧, acquires the meaning of ⟦i:I am afraid it may not come to pass⟧ (⟦r1706:1706⟧); and ⟦b:vereor, nē fīat⟧, ⟦i:I am afraid; may it not come to pass⟧, of ⟦i:I am afraid it may come to pass⟧. ⟦b:metuō ut⟧ is common in old Latin, and is used by Horace, but not by Caesar or Sallust, once by Cicero in the orations. ⟦b:timeō ut⟧ is rare, and first used by Cicero. ⟦b:vereor ut⟧ is not uncommon.
⟦b:at vereor ut plācārī possit⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 965, ⟦i:but I’m afraid she can’t be reconciled⟧. ⟦b:nē uxor rescīscat metuit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 743, ⟦i:he is afraid his wife may find it out⟧. ⟦b:ō puer, ut sīs vītālis metuō, et maiōrum nē quis amīcus frīgore tē feriat⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 1, 60, ⟦i:my boy, you’ll not see length of days I fear, and that some grander friend may with his coldness cut you dead⟧. ⟦b:nēquid summā dēperdat metuēns aut ampliet ut rem⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 4, 31, ⟦i:in dread lest from his store he something lose or may not add to his estate⟧. ⟦b:metuō nē nōs nōsmet perdiderīmus uspiam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 428, ⟦i:I’m afraid we’ve lost ourselves somewhere⟧. ⟦b:sollicitus nē turba perēgerit orbem⟧, J. 5, 20, ⟦i:apprehensive that the throng may have finished its round⟧. ⟦b:nē nōn⟧ is often, though rarely in old Latin, used for ⟦b:ut⟧, and regularly when the expression of fear is negative: as, ⟦b:nōn vereor nē hoc officium meum P. Servīliō nōn probem⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 82, ⟦i:I have no fear but I may make my services acceptable in the eyes of Servilius⟧. For ⟦b:nōn metuō quīn⟧, see ⟦r1986:1986⟧.
⟦#1958⟧
⟦b:vereor nē⟧ is often equivalent to ⟦i:I rather think⟧, and ⟦b:vereor ut⟧ to ⟦i:hardly⟧. ⟦b:vidē (videāmus, videndum est) nē⟧, and similar expressions, are sometimes used for ⟦b:vereor nē⟧, to introduce something conjectured rather than proved: as,
⟦b:vereor nē barbarōrum rēx fuerit⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 1, 58, ⟦i:I rather think he was king over savages⟧. ⟦b:vidē nē mea coniectūra multō sit vērior,⟧ ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 97, ⟦i:I rather think my conjecture is in better keeping with the facts⟧.
⟦#1959⟧
Other constructions with expressions of fear are: (⟦i:a.⟧) Indirect question. (⟦i:b.⟧) Accusative with infinitive. (⟦i:c.⟧) Complementary infinitive: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:erī semper lēnitās verēbar quorsum ēvāderet⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 175, ⟦i:I was afraid how master’s always gentleness would end⟧. ⟦b:timeō quid sit⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 620, ⟦i:I have my fears what it may be⟧. ⟦b:timeō quid rērum gesserim⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 397, ⟦i:I am concerned to think what capers I have cut⟧. ⟦b:metuō quid agam⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 720, ⟦i:I’m scared and know not what to do⟧ (⟦r1731:1731⟧). (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:ego mē cupiditātis rēgnī crīmen subitūrum timērem?⟧ L. 2, 7, 9, ⟦i:was I to fear being charged with aspiring to a throne?⟧ (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:vereor cōram in ōs tē laudāre⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 269, ⟦i:I am afraid to disgrace you with praise to the face⟧ (⟦r2168:2168⟧).
⟦#1960⟧
(3.) The subjunctive with ⟦b:nē⟧ is used in clauses which serve to complete the sense of verbs of avoiding, hindering, and resisting.
Such are: avoiding: ⟦b:caveō⟧, ⟦b:mē ēripiō⟧, ⟦b:vītō⟧. hindering: ⟦b:intercēdō⟧, ⟦b:interdīcō⟧, ⟦b:recūsō⟧, ⟦b:repugnō⟧, ⟦b:temperō⟧; also the following which often have ⟦b:quōminus⟧ (⟦r1977:1977⟧): ⟦b:dēterreō⟧, ⟦b:impediō⟧, ⟦b:obsistō⟧, ⟦b:obstō⟧, ⟦b:officiō⟧, ⟦b:prohibeō⟧, ⟦b:teneō⟧. resisting: ⟦b:resistō⟧, ⟦b:repugnō⟧, ⟦b:recūsō⟧; with these last often ⟦b:quōminus⟧. Some of the above verbs when preceded by a negative also take ⟦b:quīn⟧ (⟦r1986:1986⟧); ⟦b:prohibeō⟧ and ⟦b:impediō⟧ have also the accusative with the infinitive (⟦r2203:2203⟧). For the subjunctive coordinated with ⟦b:cavē̆⟧, see ⟦r1711:1711⟧.
⟦b:nē quid eīs noceātur neu quis invītus sacrāmentum dīcere cōgātur ā Caesare cavētur⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 86, 4, ⟦i:all precaution is taken by Caesar that no harm be done them, and that nobody be compelled to take the oath against his will⟧. ⟦b:per eōs, nē causam dīceret, sē ēripuit⟧, 1, 4, 2, ⟦i:thanks to this display of retainers he succeeded in avoiding trial⟧. ⟦b:plūra nē scrībam, dolōre impedior⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 11, 13, 5, ⟦i:grief prevents me from writing more⟧. ⟦b:nē qua sibī̆ statua pōnerētur restitit⟧, N. 25, 3, 2, ⟦i:he objected to having a statue erected in his honour⟧.

title: Pure Final Clauses
text:
⟦#1961⟧
The subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧ or ⟦b:nē⟧ is used to denote the purpose of the main action.
The purpose is often indicated in the main sentence by an expression like ⟦b:ideō⟧, ⟦b:idcircō⟧, ⟦b:proptereā⟧, ⟦b:eā mente⟧, &c.
⟦b:vigilās dē nocte, ut tuīs cōnsultōribus respondeās⟧, ⟦i:Mur.⟧ 22, ⟦i:you have to get up early in the morning to give advice to your clients⟧. ⟦b:maiōrēs nostrī ab arātrō addūxērunt Cincinnātum, ut dictātor esset⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 12, ⟦i:our fathers brought Cincinnatus from his plough, to be dictator⟧. ⟦b:dīcam auctiōnis causam, ut damnō gaudeant⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 207, ⟦i:I’ll tell the reason for the sale, that o’er my losses they may gloat⟧. ⟦b:quīn etiam nē tōnsōrī collum committeret, tondēre fīliās suās docuit⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 58, ⟦i:why, he actually taught his own daughters to shave, so as not to trust his throat to a barber⟧. ⟦b:Caesar, nē graviōrī bellō occurreret, ad exercitum proficīscitur⟧, 4, 6, 1, ⟦i:to avoid facing war on a more formidable scale, Caesar goes to the army⟧. ⟦b:tē ulcīscar, ut nē inpūne in nōs inlūseris⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 941, ⟦i:I’ll be revenged on you, so that you shan’t play tricks on me for nothing⟧ (⟦r1947:1947⟧). ⟦b:nē īgnōrārētis esse aliquās pācis vōbīs condiciōnēs, ad vōs vēnī⟧, L. 21, 13, 2, ⟦i:I have come to you to let you know that you have some chances of peace⟧ (⟦r1754:1754⟧). ⟦b:ita mē gessī nē tibī̆ pudōrī essem⟧, L. 40, 15, 6, ⟦i:I comported myself in such a way that I might not be a mortification to you⟧. ⟦b:Mariōnem ad tē eō mīsī, ut tēcum ad mē venīret⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 1, 1, ⟦i:I sent Mario to you with the intention of having him come with you to me⟧. ⟦b:idcircō nēmō superiōrum attigit, ut hīc tolleret? ideō C. Claudius rettulit, ut C. Verrēs posset auferre?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 7, ⟦i:was that the reason why no former officials laid a finger on it, that this man might swoop it away? was that why Claudius returned it, that a Verres might carry it off?⟧ ⟦b:danda opera est, ut etiam singulīs cōnsulātur, sed ita, ut ea rēs aut prōsit aut certē nē obsit rē̆ī pūblicae⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 2, 72, ⟦i:we must be particular in regarding the interests of individuals as well, but with this restriction, that our action may benefit, or at any rate may not damage the country⟧.
⟦#1962⟧
The subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧ or ⟦b:nē⟧ is often used not to express the purpose of the main action, but in a parenthetical clause, as though dependant upon some verb unexpressed: as,
⟦b:ut in pauca cōnferam, testāmentō factō mulier moritur⟧, ⟦i:Caec.⟧ 17, ⟦i:to cut a long story short, the woman makes her will and dies⟧. ⟦b:sed ut hīc nē īgnōret, quae rēs agātur: dē nātūrā agēbāmus deōrum⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 17, ⟦i:but that our friend here may know what is up: we were just on the nature of the gods⟧. The tense is present, in late writers the perfect, as ⟦b:ut sīc dīxerim⟧, Quint. 1, 6, 1. Here may also be mentioned the use of ⟦b:nēdum⟧ (rarely ⟦b:nē⟧ or, from Livy on, ⟦b:nēdum ut⟧) with the present subjunctive (rarely the imperfect): as, ⟦b:satrapa numquam sufferre eius sūmptūs queat: nēdum tū possīs⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 452, ⟦i:a prince couldn’t stand her extravagance, much less could you⟧. This is found in Terence and Lucretius once each, in Cicero, and later; not in Caesar. The preceding clause is negative or involves a negative idea. From Livy on, the verb may be omitted: as, ⟦b:vix clāmōrem eōrum, nēdum impetum tulēre⟧, L. 34, 20, 7, ⟦i:they hardly stood their war cry, much less their charge⟧.
⟦#1963⟧
The subjunctive is used in an assumption or concession with ⟦b:ut⟧ or ⟦b:nē⟧, or if the negation belongs to a single word, with ⟦b:ut nōn⟧, ⟦b:nēmō⟧, &c.: as,
⟦b:ut taceam, quoivīs facile scītū est quam fuerim miser⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 296, ⟦i:even supposing I say nothing, anybody can understand how unhappy I was⟧. ⟦b:sed ut haec concēdantur, reliqua quī concēdī possunt?⟧ ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 41, ⟦i:but even supposing this be admitted, how can the rest be admitted?⟧ ⟦b:nē sit summum malum dolor, malum certē est⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 14, ⟦i:grant that suffering is not the chiefest evil, an evil it assuredly is⟧ (⟦r1553:1553⟧). ⟦b:vērum ut hoc nōn sit, tamen praeclārum spectāculum mihī̆ prōpōnō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 2, 15, 2, ⟦i:but suppose this be not the case, still I anticipate a gorgeous show⟧. ⟦b:ac iam ut omnia contrā opīniōnem acciderent, tamen sē plūrimum nāvibus posse perspiciēbant⟧, 3, 9, 6, ⟦i:and even supposing everything turned out contrary to expectation, still they saw clearly that they had the advantage by sea⟧. ⟦b:ut enim nēminem alium nisi T. Patinam rogāsset, scīre potuit prōdī flāminem necesse esse⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 46, ⟦i:for even supposing he had asked nobody but Patina, he might have known that a priest must be appointed⟧. This use is common in Cicero, not found in Plautus or Sallust.
⟦#1964⟧
The subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧ or ⟦b:nē⟧, generally with ⟦b:ita⟧ as a correlative, sometimes has the force of a proviso: as,
⟦b:ita probanda est clēmentia, ut adhibeātur sevēritās⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 88, ⟦i:mercy is to be commended, provided that strictness is employed⟧. ⟦b:satis memoriae meae tribuent, ut maiōribus meīs dignum crēdant⟧, Ta. 4, 38, ⟦i:they will pay respect enough to my memory, provided they consider me worthy of my ancestors⟧.

title: Complementary Consecutive Clauses
text:
⟦#1965⟧
The subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧ or ⟦b:ut nōn⟧ is used in clauses which serve to complete the sense of certain verbs and expressions, chiefly of bringing to pass, happening, and following.
Such are: (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:faciō⟧, ⟦b:efficiō⟧ (unless they imply purpose, ⟦r1951:1951⟧); ⟦b:fit⟧, ⟦b:accidit⟧, ⟦b:contingit⟧, ⟦b:ēvenit⟧, ⟦b:est⟧, ⟦i:it is the case⟧; similarly ⟦b:mōs est⟧, ⟦b:cōnsuētūdō est⟧, &c. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:proximum est⟧, ⟦b:reliquum est⟧, ⟦b:extrēmum est⟧, ⟦b:relinquitur⟧, ⟦b:restat⟧, ⟦b:accēdit⟧. Or, of logical sequence, ⟦b:sequitur⟧, ⟦b:efficitur⟧.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:fēcērunt ut cōnsimilis fugae profectiō vidērētur⟧, 2, 11, 1, ⟦i:they made their march look exactly like a stampede⟧. ⟦b:splendor vester facit ut peccāre sine summō perīculō nōn possītis⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 22, ⟦i:your conspicuous position makes it impossible for you to do wrong without great peril⟧. ⟦b:hīs rēbus fīēbat, ut minus lātē vagārentur⟧, 1, 2, 4, ⟦i:so it came to pass that they did not rove round much⟧. ⟦b:fit ut nātūrā ipsā ad ōrnātius dīcendī genus excitēmur⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 338, ⟦i:it is sometimes the case that we are roused to a loftier style in oratory by sheer circumstance⟧. ⟦b:potest fierī ut fallar⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 13, 73, 2, ⟦i:it is possible that I am mistaken⟧. ⟦b:fierī nōn potest ut eum tū nōn cōgnōverīs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 190, ⟦i:it must be the case that you have made his acquaintance yourself⟧. ⟦b:eādem nocte accidit, ut esset lūna plēna⟧, 4, 29, 1, ⟦i:it came to pass on the same night that there was a full moon⟧ (⟦r1758:1758⟧). ⟦b:negāvit mōris esse Graecōrum ut in convīviō virōrum accumberent mulierēs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 66, ⟦i:he said it was not etiquette among the Greeks for women to go to men’s dinner parties⟧. ⟦b:est hōc commūne vitium in līberīs cīvitātibus, ut invidia glōriae comes sit⟧, N. 12, 3, 3, ⟦i:this is a common trouble in free communities, that envy is the attendant of a great name⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:proximum est, ut doceam⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 73, ⟦i:my next task is to prove⟧. ⟦b:relinquēbātur ut neque longius ab āgmine legiōnum discēdī Caesar paterētur⟧, 5, 19, 3, ⟦i:the consequence was that Caesar could not allow any very distant excursion from the main line of march⟧. ⟦b:restat ut doceam omnia hominum causā facta esse⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 154, ⟦i:lastly, I must prove that everything is made for man⟧. ⟦b:accēdēbat ut tempestātem ferrent⟧, 3, 13, 9, ⟦i:then, too, they could stand the gale⟧. ⟦b:accēdit ut⟧ is not found in old Latin; for ⟦b:accēdit quod⟧, see ⟦r1845:1845⟧. ⟦b:ita efficitur ut omne corpus mortāle sit⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 30, ⟦i:thus it follows that every bodily substance is mortal⟧. ⟦b:sequitur⟧ and ⟦b:efficitur⟧, ⟦i:it follows⟧, often have the accusative with the infinitive (⟦r2207:2207⟧). For the subjunctive with ⟦b:quam ut⟧ after a comparative of disproportion, see ⟦r1896:1896⟧. For ⟦b:fore⟧ and ⟦b:futūrum esse ut⟧ as the periphrasis for the future infinitive, see ⟦r2233:2233⟧.
⟦#1966⟧
Verbs of happening may often be rendered best by compacter expressions: thus, ⟦b:hīs rēbus fīēbat ut⟧, ⟦i:consequently⟧; ⟦b:fit ut⟧, ⟦i:once in a while⟧, ⟦i:sometimes⟧, ⟦i:often⟧; ⟦b:fierī potest ut⟧, ⟦i:possibly⟧; ⟦b:accidit ut⟧, ⟦i:accidentally⟧, ⟦i:unfortunately⟧.
⟦#1967⟧
⟦b:faciō ut⟧, or with a negative, commonly ⟦b:committō ut⟧, is used in circumlocutions for emphasis: as,
⟦b:faciundum mihī̆ putāvī, ut tuīs litterīs brevī respondērem⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 3, 8, 1, ⟦i:I thought I ought to take hold and write a few lines in answer to your letter⟧. ⟦b:ego vērō nōn committam, ut tibī̆ causam recūsandī dem⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 233, ⟦i:no, no, sir, I will not be guilty, not I, of giving you an excuse to back out⟧. So particularly with ⟦b:invītus⟧, ⟦b:libenter⟧, ⟦b:prope⟧: as, ⟦b:invītus fēcī ut L. Flāminīnum ē senātū ēicerem⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 42, ⟦i:it was with great reluctance that I expelled Flamininus from the senate⟧.
⟦#1968⟧
A subjunctive clause with ⟦b:ut⟧ is often used to define a preceding idea indicated in a general way by a neuter pronoun: as,
⟦b:post eius mortem nihilō minus Helvētiī id, quod cōnstituerant, facere cōnantur, ut ē fīnibus suīs exeant⟧, 1, 5, 1, ⟦i:after his death the Helvetians attempted just the same to carry out their resolution of moving out of their abodes⟧ (⟦r1752:1752⟧). ⟦b:omnibus Gallīs idem esse faciendum, quod Helvētiī fēcerint, ut domō ēmigrent⟧, 1, 31, 14, ⟦i:that all the Gauls must do just as the Helvetians had done and move away from home⟧. ⟦b:Helvētiī, cum id, quod ipsī diēbus XX aegerrimē cōnfēcerant, ut flūmen trānsīrent, illum ūnō diē fēcisse intellegerent, lēgātōs mittunt⟧, 1, 13, 2, ⟦i:when the Helvetians learned that the Roman commander had done in a single day what they had found it hard themselves to do in twenty, namely cross the river, they sent deputies⟧ (⟦r1752:1752⟧). ⟦b:id aliquot dē causīs acciderat, ut subitō Gallī bellī renovandi cōnsilium caperent⟧, 3, 2, 2, ⟦i:it was due to a variety of reasons that the Gauls suddenly conceived the idea of making war again⟧ (⟦r1758:1758⟧). ⟦b:hocine bonī esse officium servī exīstumas, ut erī suī corrumpat et rem et fīlium?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 27, ⟦i:is this what you think the duty of a good slave, to waste his own master’s property and corrupt his son?⟧
⟦#1969⟧
⟦b:tantum abest⟧, ⟦i:so far from⟧, is sometimes followed by a double ⟦b:ut⟧, the first introducing an unreal, and the second a real action: as,
⟦b:tantum abest ut haec bēstiārum causā parāta sint, ut ipsās bēstiās hominum grātiā generātās esse videāmus⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 158, ⟦i:so far from these things being made for brutes, we see that brutes themselves were created for man⟧. This use, very rarely personal, begins with Cicero, and is common in his writings and in Livy. Not in Caesar, Sallust, or Tacitus. Sometimes instead of ⟦b:ut⟧ the second sentence is coordinated (⟦r1700:1700⟧): ⟦b:tantum abfuit ut īnflammārēs nostrōs animōs, somnum vix tenēbāmus⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 278, ⟦i:so far from your firing our heart, we could hardly keep awake⟧. Or, the idea is expressed by ⟦b:ita nōn . . . ut⟧: as, ⟦b:erat ita nōn timidus ad mortem, ut in aciē sit ob rem pūblicam interfectus⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 63, ⟦i:so far from being afraid of death, he fell in battle for his country⟧.

title: Pure Consecutive Clauses
text:
⟦#1970⟧
The subjunctive is used with ⟦b:ut⟧ or ⟦b:ut nōn⟧ to denote result.
The result may be the result of an action or of a thing named in the main sentence. The main sentence often has a correlative to ⟦b:ut⟧, expressing (⟦i:a.⟧) degree: as, ⟦b:tantus⟧, ⟦i:so great⟧, ⟦b:tam⟧, ⟦i:so⟧ (with adjectives or adverbs), ⟦b:adeō⟧, ⟦b:tantopere⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) quality: as, ⟦b:is⟧ (⟦b:hīc⟧, ⟦b:ille⟧, ⟦b:iste⟧), ⟦i:such⟧, ⟦b:tālis⟧, ⟦b:ita⟧, ⟦b:sīc⟧.
⟦b:mōns altissimus impendēbat, ut facile perpaucī prohibēre possent⟧, 1, 6, 1, ⟦i:an exceeding high mountain hung over, so that a very few could block the way⟧. ⟦b:dictitābant sē domō expulsōs, omnibus necessāriīs egēre rēbus, ut honestā praescrīptiōne rem turpissimam tegerent⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 32, 4, ⟦i:they stoutly declared that they were driven out of house and home, and lacked the necessaries of life, thus veiling dishonour under the name of respectability⟧.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:Ariovistus tantōs sibī̆ spīritūs sūmpserat, ut ferendus nōn vidērētur⟧, 1, 33, 5, ⟦i:Ariovistus had put on such high and mighty airs as to seem intolerable⟧. ⟦b:adeō angustō marī cōnflīxit, ut eius multitūdō nāvium explicārī nōn potuerit⟧, N. 2, 4, 5, ⟦i:he went into action in such cramped sea-room, that his armada could not deploy⟧, of Xerxes (⟦r1757:1757⟧).
(⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:eōs dēdūxī testēs ut dē istīus factō dubium esse nēminī possit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 91, ⟦i:I have brought such witnesses that nobody can entertain a doubt of the defendant’s guilt⟧. ⟦b:ita sē recipiēbat ut nihil nisi dē perniciē populī Rōmānī cōgitāret⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 4, 4, ⟦i:he retreated, it is true, but retreated with his mind running on nothing but how to ruin the country⟧. ⟦b:illa, ex tūribulīs quae ēvellerat, ita scītē in aureīs pōculīs inligābat, ut ea ad illam rem nāta esse dīcerēs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 54, ⟦i:what he had torn from the censers he attached to golden cups so cunningly that you would have said it was just made for that very purpose⟧ (⟦r1731:1731⟧, ⟦r1559:1559⟧).
For the imperfect subjunctive connected with a main general present, see ⟦r1751:1751⟧; for the independent present or perfect subjunctive with a main secondary tense, see ⟦r1757:1757⟧.

title: ubī̆
text:
⟦#1971⟧
⟦b:ubī̆⟧, in the sense of ⟦i:where⟧ (⟦r709:709⟧), has the ordinary construction of a relative (⟦r1812:1812-1831⟧). For ⟦b:ubī̆⟧, ⟦i:when⟧, see ⟦r1923:1923-1926⟧ and 1932-1934; as a synonym of ⟦b:sī⟧, ⟦i:if⟧, see ⟦r2110:2110⟧.

title: quō or quī
text:
⟦#1972⟧
⟦b:quō⟧, ⟦b:whereby⟧, ⟦b:wherewith⟧, or in old Latin sometimes ⟦b:quī⟧ (⟦r689:689⟧), is the instrumental ablative from the relative and interrogative stem ⟦b:qui-⟧. Combined with ⟦b:minus⟧, ⟦i:the less⟧, ⟦i:not⟧, ⟦b:quō⟧ gives ⟦b:quōminus⟧.

title: quō or quī: With the Indicative
text:
⟦#1973⟧
The indicative is used with ⟦b:quō⟧ and a comparative in the protasis of a comparative period, with ⟦b:eō⟧ or ⟦b:hōc⟧ and a comparative as correlative (⟦r1393:1393⟧): as,
⟦b:quō dēlictum maius est, eō poena est tardior⟧, ⟦i:Caec.⟧ 7, ⟦i:the greater the sin is, the slower is the punishment⟧. The ⟦b:eō⟧ or ⟦b:hōc⟧ is sometimes omitted: as, ⟦b:quō plūrēs sumus, plūribus rēbus egēbimus⟧, L. 34, 34, 6, ⟦i:the more numerous we are, the more things we shall need⟧. In late writers, the comparative is sometimes omitted in the main clause, very rarely in the subordinate clause. ⟦b:quantō . . . tantō⟧ are also used like ⟦b:quō . . . eō⟧: as, ⟦b:quantō diūtius cōnsīderō, tantō mihī̆ rēs vidētur obscūrior⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 60, ⟦i:the longer I puzzle over it, the more incomprehensible the question seems to me⟧. ⟦b:quantō magis extergeō, tenuius fit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 1301, ⟦i:the more I polish, the slimmer it gets⟧. This form is sometimes used with ⟦b:quisque⟧ or ⟦b:quis⟧ of indefinite persons, instead of the commoner ⟦b:ut . . . ita⟧ or ⟦b:sīc⟧ (⟦r1939:1939⟧): as, ⟦b:quō quisque est sollertior, hōc docet labōriōsius⟧, ⟦i:RC.⟧ 31, ⟦i:the brighter a man is, the more wearisome he finds teaching⟧. ⟦b:quō quisque est maior, magis est plācābilis īrae⟧, O. ⟦i:Tr.⟧ 3, 5, 31, ⟦i:the greater be the man, the easier ’tis his anger to appease⟧.

title: quō or quī: With the Subjunctive
text:
⟦#1974⟧
The subjunctive is used with ⟦b:quō⟧ to express purpose.
⟦b:quō⟧ differs but little in meaning from ⟦b:ut⟧ of purpose. It is used (⟦i:a.⟧) particularly in clauses containing a comparative expression, or (⟦i:b.⟧) in solemn law language.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:equitēs omnibus in locīs pugnant, quō sē legiōnāriīs mīlitibus praeferrent⟧, 2, 27, 2, ⟦i:the troopers fought on every kind of ground, hoping to outshine the regular infantry thereby⟧. ⟦b:medicō putō aliquid dandum esse, quō sit studiōsior⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 16, 4, 2, ⟦i:I think it would be well to fee your medical man, to make him more attentive⟧. ⟦b:id amābō adiūtā mē quō id fīat facilius⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 150, ⟦i:help me in that, I pray, that it may be the easier done⟧. ⟦b:sublāta erat celebritās virōrum ac mulierum, quō lāmentātiō minuerētur⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 2, 65, ⟦i:the large attendance of both sexes was done away with, to make the weeping and wailing less harrowing⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:hominī mortuō nē ossa legitō, quō pos fūnus faciat⟧, Twelve Tables in ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 2, 60, ⟦i:he shall not gather up the bones of a dead man, with intent to celebrate the funeral a second time⟧ (⟦r1586:1586⟧). ⟦b:quī eōrum coiīt, coierit, quō quis iūdiciō pūblicō condemnārētur⟧, law in ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 148, ⟦i:whosoever of that number conspired or shall have conspired to have anybody condemned in a criminal court⟧.
