Otherwise rarely used without a comparative expression, yet occasionally found thus in Plautus, Terence, Sallust, and Ovid: as, ⟦b:hanc simulant parere quō Chremētem absterreant⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 472, ⟦i:they’re pretending that she’s lying in, to frighten Chremes off⟧. So often in Tacitus.
⟦#1975⟧
⟦b:quō nē⟧, in a negative clause of purpose, is found in a disputed passage in Horace, but not again until late Latin. For ⟦b:nōn quō⟧, ⟦b:nōn eō quō⟧, introducing an untenable reason, see ⟦r1855:1855⟧.
⟦#1976⟧
In old Latin ⟦b:quī⟧, ⟦i:whereby⟧, ⟦i:wherewith⟧, ⟦i:withal⟧, is partly felt as a live relative pronoun in the ablative, and partly as a mere conjunction of purpose; as a pronoun it may even take a preposition; as a conjunction, it may refer to a plural antecedent (⟦r689:689⟧): as, ⟦b:quasi patriciīs puerīs aut monērulae aut anitēs aut cōturnīcēs dantur, quīcum lūsitent: itidem mī haec upupa, quī mē dēlectem datast⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 1002, ⟦i:as to the sons of gentlemen or daws or ducks or quails are given, wherewith to play; just so to me this crow is given, to entertain myself withal⟧. ⟦b:enim mihi quidem aequomst dari vehicla quī vehar⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 500, ⟦i:in sooth ‘t were fair that carriages be given me, to ride withal⟧. The indicative occurs where the subjunctive would be used in classical Latin: as, ⟦b:multa concurrunt simul, quī coniectūram hanc faciō⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 511, ⟦i:a thousand things combine whereby I come to this conjecture⟧.

title: quōminus
text:
⟦#1977⟧
The subjunctive with ⟦b:quōminus⟧ (⟦r1972:1972⟧) is used to complete the sense of verbs of hindering or resisting.
Such verbs are: ⟦b:impediō⟧, ⟦b:teneō⟧, ⟦i:hinder⟧, ⟦b:interclūdō⟧, ⟦b:dēterreō⟧, ⟦b:obstō⟧, ⟦b:obsistō⟧, ⟦b:resistō⟧, ⟦b:repugnō⟧, ⟦b:nōn recūsō⟧; these verbs often have a subjunctive with ⟦b:nē⟧ (⟦r1960:1960⟧). Cicero rarely and Caesar never uses ⟦b:quōminus⟧ with ⟦b:impediō⟧ or ⟦b:prohibeō⟧. For the accusative and infinitive with these verbs, see ⟦r2203:2203⟧. ⟦b:quōminus⟧ is also used with ⟦b:moveor⟧, ⟦i:am influenced⟧, ⟦b:fit⟧, ⟦i:it is owing to⟧, ⟦b:stat per aliquem⟧, ⟦i:somebody is responsible⟧, or indeed any expression implying hindrance. When the verb of hindering has a negative with it, ⟦b:quīn⟧ is often used; see ⟦r1986:1986⟧.
⟦b:nōn dēterret sapientem mors, quōminus rē̆ī pūblicae suīsque cōnsulat⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 91, ⟦i:death does not hinder the wise man from working for country and friends⟧. ⟦b:quid obstat, quōminus sit beātus?⟧ ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 95, ⟦i:what is to hinder his being happy?⟧ ⟦b:neque recūsāvit quōminus lēgis poenam subīret⟧, N. 15, 8, 2, ⟦i:and he did not decline to submit to the penalty of the law⟧. ⟦b:Caesar, ubī̆ cōgnōvit per Āfrānium stāre quōminus proeliō dīmicārētur, castra facere cōnstituit⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 41, 3, ⟦i:when Caesar learned that owing to Afranius there was no battle, he resolved to build a camp⟧. ⟦b:sī tē dolor corporis tenuit, quōminus ad lūdōs venīrēs, fortūnae magis tribuō quam sapientiae tuae⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 7, 1, 1, ⟦i:if it was bodily suffering that kept you from coming to the performances, I think more highly of your luck than of your sense⟧. Terence first uses ⟦b:quōminus⟧ thus, but only rarely. He also sometimes uses the parts separately so that the true relative and negative forces appear: as, ⟦b:sī sēnserō quicquam in hīs tē nūptiīs fallāciae cōnārī, quō fīant minus⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 196, ⟦i:if I catch you trying on any trick in the matter of this marriage through which it may not come off⟧ (⟦r1451:1451⟧).
⟦#1978⟧
In Tacitus, ⟦b:quōminus⟧ is sometimes found where ⟦b:quīn⟧ would be used in classical Latin (⟦r1986:1986⟧): as, ⟦b:nec dubitātum quōminus pācem concēderent⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 2, 45, ⟦i:there was no hesitation in granting peace⟧.
⟦#1979⟧
It may be mentioned here that ⟦b:quō sētius⟧ with the subjunctive, instead of ⟦b:quōminus⟧, is found twice in Cicero’s earliest extant prose, and twice in older Latin.

title: quīn
text:
⟦#1980⟧
⟦b:quīn⟧ is composed of ⟦b:quī⟧, the ablative or locative of the interrogative and relative stem ⟦b:qui-⟧ (⟦r689:689⟧), and ⟦b:-ne⟧, ⟦i:not⟧. It is used in simple sentences and as a conjunctive particle.
⟦#1981⟧
For the use of ⟦b:quīn⟧, ⟦i:why not⟧, in questions with the indicative, see ⟦r1526:1526⟧. Such questions have the sense of an affirmative command or exhortation (⟦r1531:1531⟧): as, ⟦b:quīn abīs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 1087, ⟦i:why won’t you begone?⟧ or ⟦i:get you gone⟧. ⟦b:quīn cōnscendimus equōs⟧, L. 1, 57, 7, ⟦i:why not mount⟧, or ⟦i:to horse, to horse⟧. For the use of ⟦b:quīn⟧ without interrogative force, see ⟦r1527:1527⟧.
⟦#1982⟧
⟦b:quīn⟧ is found occasionally with the subjunctive in a direct question in Plautus, Terence, Lucilius, Lucretius, Cicero, and Tacitus: thus, ⟦b:quīn ego hōc rogem?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 426, ⟦i:why shouldn’t I ask this?⟧ (⟦r1563:1563⟧).
⟦#1983⟧
The subjunctive with the conjunctive particle ⟦b:quīn⟧ is used, particularly in old Latin, in connection with the common formula ⟦b:nūlla causa est⟧ or its equivalents.
Such a subjunctive may be regarded as original (⟦r1786:1786⟧) or as due to the indirect form of question (⟦r1773:1773⟧).
⟦b:nūlla causast quīn mē condōnēs crucī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 1070, ⟦i:there’s no reason why you shouldn’t deliver me up to execution⟧. ⟦b:quīn dēcēdam, nūlla causa est⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 17, 1, ⟦i:there is no reason why I should not retire⟧. ⟦b:quid causaest quīn in pistrīnum rēctā proficīscar viā?⟧ T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 600, ⟦i:what’s the reason I don’t march straight into the mill?⟧ ⟦b:haud causificor quīn eam habeam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 755, ⟦i:I don’t quibble against keeping her⟧.
⟦#1984⟧
⟦b:mīrum quīn⟧ with the subjunctive is used by Plautus in sarcastic expressions where ⟦b:mīrum⟧ is ironical: as, ⟦b:mīrum quīn tū illō tēcum dīvitiās ferās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 495, ⟦i:strange enough, how you can’t take your money there with you⟧, that is to Hades.
⟦#1985⟧
The subjunctive with ⟦b:quīn⟧ (or ⟦b:ut nōn⟧) is used after ⟦b:nōn possum⟧, or ⟦b:nōn possum⟧ with an infinitive, usually ⟦b:facere⟧, and with ⟦b:fierī nōn potest⟧: as,
⟦b:nōn enim possum quīn exclāmem, eugē, eugē, Lȳsitelēs, πάλιν⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 705, ⟦i:upon my word I must cry bravo, bravo, Lysiteles; encore!⟧ ⟦b:facere nōn potuī quīn tibī̆ sententiam dēclārārem⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 6, 13, 1, ⟦i:I could not help giving you my views⟧. ⟦b:fierī nūllō modō poterat, quīn Cleomenī parcerētur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 104, ⟦i:it was impossible not to spare Cleomenes⟧. ⟦b:ēheu, nequeō quīn fleam, quom abs tē abeam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 1342, ⟦i:O well-a-day, I needs must weep, for that from thee I part⟧. ⟦b:nōn potuistī ūllō modō facere, ut mihī̆ illam epistulam nōn mitterēs⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 11, 21, 1, ⟦i:you could not get along at all without writing me that letter⟧ (⟦r1965:1965⟧).
⟦#1986⟧
The subjunctive with ⟦i:quīn⟧ is used in clauses which complete the sense of verbs of restraining, abstaining, delaying, or doubting, when such verbs have a negative, expressed or implied.
Such verbs are (⟦i:a.⟧) restraining: ⟦b:temperō mihī̆⟧, ⟦b:teneō⟧, ⟦i:restrain⟧, ⟦b:retineō⟧, ⟦b:contineō⟧, ⟦b:dēterreō⟧, ⟦b:reprimō⟧. abstaining: ⟦b:praetermittō⟧, ⟦b:intermittō⟧. delaying: ⟦b:cunctor⟧, ⟦b:differō⟧, ⟦b:exspectō⟧, ⟦b:recūsō⟧; ⟦b:nōn multum⟧, ⟦b:nihil⟧, ⟦b:paulum abest⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) doubting: ⟦b:dubitō⟧, ⟦b:dubium est⟧; a doubt may also be implied in other words, or forms of words: as, ⟦b:nōn metuō⟧, ⟦b:nōn abest suspīciō⟧, &c.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:neque sibī̆ hominēs barbarōs temperātūrōs exīstimābat, quīn in prōvinciam exīrent⟧, 1, 33, 4, ⟦i:and he thought, as they were savages, they would not restrain themselves, but would sally out into the province⟧. ⟦b:vix mē contineō quīn involem mōnstrō in capillum⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 859, ⟦i:I scarce can keep from flying at the caitiff’s hair⟧. ⟦b:nihil praetermīsī, quīn Pompēium ā Caesaris coniūnctiōne āvocārem⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 23, ⟦i:I left no stone unturned to prevent Pompey from joining Caesar⟧. ⟦b:abstinēre quīn attingās nōn queās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 915, ⟦i:you can’t keep from touching it⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:nōn dubitat, quīn tē ductūrum negēs⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 405, ⟦i:he doesn’t doubt that you’ll refuse to marry⟧. ⟦b:quis dubitet, quīn in virtūte dīvitiae sint?⟧ ⟦i:Par.⟧ 48, ⟦i:who can doubt that there is money in virtue?⟧ ⟦b:neque abest suspīciō quīn ipse sibī̆ mortem cōnscīverit⟧, 1, 4, 4, ⟦i:and ground is not wanting for the belief that he made away with himself⟧.
⟦#1987⟧
⟦b:nōn dubitō⟧ has other constructions: (⟦i:a.⟧) Indirect question. (⟦b:b.⟧) Accusative with the infinitive (in some authors: chiefly Nepos and Livy and later writers). (⟦i:c.⟧) Meaning ⟦i:not hesitate⟧, the infinitive alone (⟦r2169:2169⟧). ⟦b:quīn⟧ seldom follows this meaning.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:nōn dubitō, quid nōbīs agendum putēs⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 10, 1, 2, ⟦i:I have no doubt about what you think is our duty to do⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:neque enim dubitābant hostem ventūrum⟧, L. 22. 55, 2, ⟦i:for they firmly believed the enemy would come⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:quid dubitāmus pultāre?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 1117, ⟦i:why do we hesitate to knock?⟧ ⟦b:nōlīte dubitāre quīn huic crēdātis omnia⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 68, ⟦i:do not hesitate to trust all to him⟧.
⟦#1988⟧
The subjunctive with ⟦b:quīn⟧ is often used after general negative assertions, or questions implying a negative: as,
⟦b:nēmō fuit omnīnō mīlitum quīn vulnerārētur⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 53, 3, ⟦i:there was absolutely not a single soldier but was wounded⟧. ⟦b:nūllust Ephesī quīn sciat⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 336, ⟦i:there’s not a soul at Ephesus but knows⟧. ⟦b:quis in circum vēnit, quīn is ūnōquōque gradū dē avāritiā tuā commonērētur?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 154, ⟦i:who came to the circus without being reminded of your avarice at each and every step?⟧ ⟦b:nūlla fuit cīvitās quīn partem senātūs Cordubam mitteret, nōn cīvis Rōmānus quīn convenīret⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 19, 2, ⟦i:there was not a community but sent a part of its local senate to Corduba, not a Roman citizen, but went to the meeting⟧. For ⟦b:quī nōn⟧ after such expressions, see ⟦r1821:1821⟧. The main sentence often has ⟦b:tam⟧, ⟦b:ita⟧, ⟦b:sīc⟧, or ⟦b:tantus⟧: as, ⟦b:nēmō est tam fortis, quīn rē̆ī novitāte perturbētur⟧, 6, 39, 3, ⟦i:there was nobody so brave but was demoralized by the strangeness of the situation⟧. ⟦b:nīl tam difficilest quīn quaerendō investīgārī possiet⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 675, ⟦i:there’s naught so hard but may by searching be tracked out⟧. Instead of ⟦b:quīn⟧, ⟦b:ut nōn⟧ or ⟦b:quī nōn⟧ is often used in such combinations (⟦r1821:1821⟧).
⟦#1989⟧
The subjunctive in an untenable reason, negatively put, is sometimes introduced by ⟦b:nōn quīn⟧ instead of ⟦b:nōn quod nōn⟧ or ⟦b:nōn quō nōn⟧ (⟦r1855:1855⟧): as, ⟦b:nōn quīn parī virtūte aliī fuerint⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 7, 6, ⟦i:not that others may not have been his peers in virtue⟧.
⟦#1990⟧
⟦b:quīn⟧ is used very rarely instead of ⟦b:quōminus⟧ to introduce clauses completing the sense of verbs which have no negative expressed or implied: as, once each in the ⟦i:Bellum Alexandrīnum⟧, in Tacitus, and in Seneca’s prose.

title: dum, dōnec, quoad, quamdiū
text:
⟦#1991⟧
With the temporal particles ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:while⟧, ⟦i:until⟧, and ⟦b:dōnec⟧, ⟦i:until⟧ (in old Latin ⟦b:dōnicum⟧ and in Lucretius ⟦b:dōnique⟧), may be conveniently treated the relative ⟦b:quaad⟧ or ⟦b:quoad⟧ (that is ⟦b:quā⟧ or ⟦b:quō⟧ combined with ⟦b:ad⟧), ⟦i:while⟧, ⟦i:until⟧, and the comparative ⟦b:quamdiū⟧, ⟦i:as long as⟧.
⟦#1992⟧
⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:while⟧, means originally ⟦i:a while⟧ (⟦r1151:1151⟧): as, ⟦b:circumspice dum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 146, ⟦i:look round you a while⟧, ⟦i:a minute⟧, ⟦i:just look round⟧ (⟦r1573:1573⟧). ⟦b:dum servī meī perplacet mihi cōnsilium, dum haud placet⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Merc.⟧ 348, ⟦i:one while my slave’s plan suits me completely, another while it doesn’t suit⟧. ⟦b:dum . . . dum⟧, Accius in ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 89, ⟦i:one while . . . another⟧.
⟦#1993⟧
As a pure conjunctive particle, ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:while⟧, means either (A.) ⟦i:in the time while⟧, or (B.) ⟦i:all the time while⟧; in the latter sense ⟦b:quoad⟧ and ⟦b:quamdiū⟧ are also used. From ⟦i:all the time while⟧, ⟦b:dum⟧ comes to mean (C.) ⟦i:as long as⟧, ⟦i:provided⟧; and (D.) ⟦i:until⟧; in this sense ⟦b:quoad⟧ and ⟦b:dōnec⟧ are also used.
⟦#1994⟧
The indicative is used in a protasis introduced by ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦b:quoad⟧, or ⟦b:quamdiū⟧, ⟦i:while⟧; and the subjunctive in a protasis introduced by ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:provided⟧, or ⟦i:until⟧.
The subjunctive is also used for special reasons, as in indirect discourse (⟦r1725:1725⟧), by attraction (⟦r1728:1728⟧), of action conceivable (⟦r1731:1731⟧), or by late writers to express repeated past action (⟦r1730:1730⟧). See also ⟦r1997:1997⟧ and ⟦r2009:2009⟧, end.

title: dum, in the time while
text:
⟦#1995⟧
The present indicative is regularly used with ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:in the time while⟧ (⟦r1739:1739⟧).
⟦b:dum⟧ sometimes has as correlative ⟦b:subitō⟧, ⟦b:repente⟧; ⟦b:iam⟧, ⟦b:intereā⟧, &c.
The main verb may be present, future, or past; as, ⟦b:dum haec dīcit, abiīt hōra⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 341, ⟦i:while he thus prated, sped an hour away⟧. ⟦b:īnficī dēbet iīs artibus quās sī, dum est tener, combiberit, ad maiōra veniet parātior⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 3, 9, ⟦i:he should be imbued with such arts as will, if absorbed while he is young, render him the better equipped to deal with weightier business⟧. ⟦b:nunc rem ipsam, ut gesta sit, dum breviter vōbīs dēmōnstrō, attendite⟧, ⟦i:Tul.⟧ 13, ⟦i:now give your attention to the case itself, while I set forth to you briefly how it occurred⟧. ⟦b:dum in hīs locīs Caesar morātur, ad eum lēgātī vēnērunt⟧, 4, 22, 1, ⟦i:while Caesar tarried in these regions, some envoys came to him⟧. ⟦b:dum haec aguntur, vōce clārā exclāmat⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 1120, ⟦i:while this was going on, with clarion voice he cries aloud⟧. ⟦b:haec dum aguntur, intereā Cleomenēs iam ad Helōrī lītus pervēnerat⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 91, ⟦i:while this was going on, Cleomenes meantime had already arrived at the shore of Helorum⟧. The phrase ⟦b:dum haec geruntur⟧, ⟦i:meanwhile⟧, is often used by the historians to shift the scene: as, ⟦b:dum haec in Venetīs geruntur, Q. Titūrius Sabīnus in fīnēs Venellōrum pervēnit⟧, 3, 17, 1, ⟦i:while this was going on among the Veneti, Sabinus arrived in the territory of the Venelli⟧. The present indicative is sometimes retained in indirect discourse, chiefly in poetry or late prose: as, ⟦b:dīc, hospes, Spartae nōs tē hīc vīdisse iacentīs, dum sānctīs patriae lēgibus obsequimur⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 101, ⟦i:tell it at Sparta, friend, that thou hast seen us lying here, obedient to our country’s holy laws⟧. ⟦b:dīcit sēsē illī ānulum, dum lūctat, dētrāxisse⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 829, ⟦i:he says that, in the struggle, he pulled off her ring⟧.
⟦#1996⟧
The future is rare and chiefly confined to old Latin: as,
⟦b:animum advortite, dum huius argūmentum ēloquar cōmoediae⟧, Pl. ⟦i:prol. Am.⟧ 95, ⟦i:attention lend, while I set forth the subject of this comedy⟧. ⟦b:dum pauca dīcam, breviter attendite⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 163, ⟦i:while I speak briefly, give me your attention a few moments⟧.
⟦#1997⟧
The imperfect indicative is rare; the imperfect subjunctive is sometimes used, chiefly by the poets and historians: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:dum haec Vēīs agēbantur, interim capitōlium in ingentī perīculō fuit⟧, L. 5, 47, 1, ⟦i:while this was going on at Vei, the capital meanwhile was in terrible peril⟧. The pluperfect of resulting state is rarer: as, ⟦b:dum in ūnam partem oculōs hostium certāmen āverterat, plūribus locīs capitur mūrus⟧, L. 32, 24, 5, ⟦i:while the eyes of the enemy were turned away in one direction toward the fight, the wall is carried in several places⟧ (⟦r1615:1615⟧). (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:dum sē rēx āverteret, alter ēlātam secūrim in caput dēiēcit⟧, L. 1, 40, 7, ⟦i:while the king was looking another way, the second man raised his axe and brought it down on his head⟧.
⟦#1998⟧
The clause with ⟦b:dum⟧ often denotes the cause of the main action, particularly when the subjects of both verbs are the same and the action of the protasis is coincident with that of the apodosis (⟦r1733:1733⟧).
⟦b:dum docent, discunt⟧, Sen. ⟦i:E.⟧ 7, 8, ⟦i:while they are teaching, they are learning⟧, or, ⟦i:by teaching they learn⟧. ⟦b:nīmīrum didicī etiam, dum in istum inquīrō, artificum nōmina⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 4, ⟦i:preposterous as it may seem, in hunting up evidence against the defendant, I have actually learned artists’ names⟧. The main action is often one not anticipated or desired: as, ⟦b:ita dum pauca mancipia retinēre volt, fortūnās omnīs lībertātemque suam perdidit⟧, ⟦i:Caecil.⟧ 56, ⟦i:so in her attempt to keep a few human chattels, she sacrificed all her possessions and her own liberty⟧. ⟦b:dum vītant stultī vitia, in contrāria currunt⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 2, 24, ⟦i:while fools essay a vice to shun, into its opposite they run⟧. Sometimes with the perfect: as, ⟦b:dum Alexandrī similis esse voluit, L. Crassī inventus est dissimillimus⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 282, ⟦i:from his desire to be like Alexander, he came out just the opposite of Crassus⟧.

title: dum, quoad, quamdiū (dōnec), all the time while
text:
⟦#1999⟧
⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦b:quoad⟧, or ⟦b:quamdiū⟧, ⟦i:all the time while⟧, often has as correlative ⟦b:tamdiū⟧, ⟦b:tantum⟧, ⟦b:tantummodo⟧, ⟦b:tantisper⟧, ⟦b:usque⟧, or ⟦b:ita⟧. When ⟦b:tamdiū⟧ is used, ⟦b:quam⟧ often stands for ⟦b:quamdiū⟧.
⟦#2000⟧
(1.) When the main verb is present or future, the protasis with ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦b:quoad⟧, or ⟦b:quamdiū⟧, ⟦i:all the time while⟧, is usually in the same tense as the main verb: as,
⟦b:mane dum scrībit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 737, ⟦i:wait while he writes⟧. ⟦b:aegrōtō dum anima est, spēs esse dīcitur⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 9, 10, 3, ⟦i:as long as a sick man has breath he is said to have hope⟧. ⟦b:vidua vīvitō vel usque dum rēgnum optinēbit Iuppiter⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 727, ⟦i:may’st widowed live e’en long as Jupiter shall reign⟧. ⟦b:ego tē meum esse dīcī tantisper volō, dum quod tē dignumst faciēs⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 106, ⟦i:I’ll have thee called my son but just so long as thou shalt act as doth become thee⟧. ⟦b:dum Latīnae loquentur litterae, quercus huic locō nōn deerit⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 1, 2, ⟦i:as long as Latin literature has the gift of speech, this spot will not lack its oak⟧ (⟦r1733:1733⟧). ⟦b:quamdiū quisquam erit quī tē dēfendere audeat, vīvēs⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 6, ⟦i:as long as there shall be a soul who will venture to defend you, you shall live on⟧. ⟦b:discēs quamdiū volēs, tamdiū autem velle dēbēbis quoad tē quantum prōficiās nōn paenitēbit⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 2, ⟦i:you shall study as long as you want to, and it will be proper for you to want to, as long as you are satisfied with your progress⟧. ⟦b:dandum hordeum et furfurēs usque quaad erunt lactantēs⟧, Varro ⟦i:R. R.⟧ 2, 7, 12, ⟦i:give them barley and bran as long as they are sucklings⟧. ⟦b:quoad⟧, ⟦i:as long as⟧, is not found in Terence.
⟦#2001⟧
(2.) With ⟦b:quamdiū⟧ the perfect is used when the main verb is perfect; with ⟦b:dum⟧ or ⟦b:quoad⟧ the perfect or imperfect is used when the main verb is perfect or pluperfect, and the imperfect usually when the main verb is imperfect: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:quōrum quamdiū mānsit imitātiō, tamdiū genus illud dīcendī vīxit⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 94, ⟦i:as long as the imitation of these men lasted, so long was that style in vogue⟧. ⟦b:tenuit locum tamdiū quam ferre potuit labōrem⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 236, ⟦i:he held the position as long as he could stand the work⟧. In this use ⟦b:quamdiū⟧ is found first in Cicero.
(⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:vīxit, dum vīxit, bene⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 461, ⟦i:he lived well all the time he lived⟧ (⟦r1733:1733⟧). ⟦b:avus noster quoad vīxit, restitit M. Grātidiō⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 3, 36, ⟦i:our grandfather as long as he lived, opposed Gratidius⟧.
(⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:Massiliēnsēs quoad licēbat, circumvenīre nostrōs contendēbant⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 58, 1, ⟦i:as long as the Massilia people had a chance, they kept trying to surround our men⟧. ⟦b:dum necesse erat, rēsque ipsa cōgēbat, ūnus omnia poterat⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 139, ⟦i:as long as it had to be, and circumstances demanded, one man controlled the world⟧ (⟦r1733:1733⟧). From Sallust on, the present of vivid narration (⟦r1590:1590⟧) is occasionally found with ⟦b:dum⟧ in this sense.
⟦#2002⟧
In poetry and in late prose writers, beginning with Lucretius and Livy, ⟦b:dōnec⟧ is used in the sense of ⟦i:all the time while⟧, usually with the indicative, but sometimes with the subjunctive of repeated past action: as, ⟦b:dōnec grātus eram tibī, Persārum viguī rēge beātior⟧, H. 3, 9, 1, ⟦i:as long as I was loved of thee, I flourished happier than the Persians’ king⟧. ⟦b:dōnec armātī cōnfertīque abībant, peditum labor in persequendō fuit⟧, L. 6, 13, 4, ⟦i:as long as they were moving off under arms and in close array, the task of pursuit fell to the infantry⟧. ⟦b:vulgus trucīdātum est dōnec īra et diēs permānsit⟧, Ta. 1, 68, ⟦i:the rank and file were butchered as long as wrath and daylight held out⟧. ⟦b:nihil trepidābant, dōnec continentī velut ponte agerentur⟧, L. 21, 28, 10, ⟦i:the elephants were not a bit skittish as long as they were driven along what seemed a continuous bridge⟧ (⟦r1730:1730⟧). The future is rare: as, ⟦b:nātus enim dēbet quīcumque est velle manēre in vītā, dōnec retinēbit blanda voluptās⟧, Lucr. 5, 177, ⟦i:whoe’er is born must wish in life to abide, so long as him fond pleasure shall detain⟧. ⟦b:dōnec eris fēlīx, multōs numerābis amīcōs⟧, O. ⟦i:Tr.⟧ 1, 9, 5, ⟦i:as long as fortune smiles, thou troops shalt count of friends⟧.

title: dum, as long as, provided, so
text:
⟦#2003⟧
The present and imperfect subjunctive are used in provisos introduced by ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:as long as⟧, ⟦i:provided⟧, ⟦i:so⟧.
⟦b:dum⟧ is sometimes accompanied by ⟦b:modo⟧, ⟦i:only⟧, or ⟦b:quidem⟧, ⟦i:that is⟧; or (from Terence on) ⟦b:modo⟧ is used without ⟦b:dum⟧. The negative is ⟦b:nē⟧ (from Ovid on, sometimes ⟦b:nōn⟧); ⟦b:nē⟧ sometimes has as correlative ⟦b:ita⟧.
⟦b:ōderint dum metuant⟧, Poet. in Suet. ⟦i:Cal.⟧ 30, ⟦i:let them hate, so they fear⟧. ⟦b:absit, dum modo laude partā domum recipiat sē⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 644, ⟦i:let him go, so only he come home with glory won⟧. ⟦b:postulābant prō homine miserrimō, quī vel ipse sēsē in cruciātum darī cuperet, dum dē patris morte quaererētur⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 119, ⟦i:they made the request in behalf of a pitiable wretch, who would be only too glad to be put to the rack himself, so his father’s death might be investigated⟧. ⟦b:itaque dum locus comminus pugnandī darētur, aequō animō singulās bīnīs nāvibus obiciēbant⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 58, 4, ⟦i:therefore, so a chance was given to fight hand to hand, they did not mind pitting one of their vessels against two of the enemy’s⟧. ⟦b:sī ē̆ī permissum esset, ita id sacrum faceret, dum nē plūs quīnque sacrificiō interessent⟧, L. 39, 18, 9, ⟦i:if he were allowed, he might perform the sacrifice far better, provided that not more than five people should have a part in the ceremonial⟧. ⟦b:dum quidem nēquid percontēris quod nōn lubeat prōloquī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 211, ⟦i:provided at least you ask nothing that I may not like to disclose⟧. ⟦b:volet, cīvis modo haec sit⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 889, ⟦i:he’ll consent, only let her be a free born maid⟧. ⟦b:magnō mē metū līberābis, dum modo inter mē atque tē mūrus intersit⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 10, ⟦i:you will relieve me of great fear, provided only there be a wall interposed between you and myself⟧.
⟦#2004⟧
⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦b:quoad⟧ or ⟦b:dōnec⟧, ⟦i:until⟧, often has as correlative ⟦b:usque⟧, ⟦b:usque eō⟧, ⟦b:usque ad eum fīnem⟧ or ⟦b:tamdiū⟧.

title: dum, until
text:
⟦#2005⟧
The subjunctive present is used in a protasis introduced by ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:until⟧, when the main verb denotes either indefinite or present time, and the subjunctive imperfect when the main verb is past.
The subjunctive is an extension of the subjunctive of desire (⟦r1540:1540⟧); the clause denotes something expected or proposed.
⟦b:is dum veniat sedens ibī̆ opperībere⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 48, ⟦i:you shall sit there waiting till he comes⟧. ⟦b:ōrandī sunt, ut sī quam habent ulcīscendī vim, differant in tempus aliud, dum dēfervēscat īra⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 4, 78, ⟦i:we must always ask such people, if they have any chance to take vengeance, to put it off to some other time, till their rage cool down⟧. ⟦b:cēnseō latendum tantisper ibīdem, dum effervēscit haec grātulātiō et simul dum audiāmus, quemadmodum negōtium cōnfectum sit⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 9, 2, 4, ⟦i:I advise lying low where you are, while the present congratulation excitement is cooling off, and at the same time till we may hear how the job was done⟧. ⟦b:dum reliquae nāvēs eō convenīrent, in ancorīs exspectāvit⟧, 4, 23, 4, ⟦i:he waited at anchor till the rest of the vessels should gather there⟧ (⟦r1725:1725⟧). ⟦b:Verginius dum collēgam cōnsuleret morātus, dictātōrem dīxit⟧, L. 4, 21, 10, ⟦i:Verginius, after waiting till he should consult his colleague, appointed a dictator⟧. ⟦b:observāvit dum dormitāret canēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 170, ⟦i:he watched till the dog should be napping⟧.
⟦#2006⟧
The present indicative with ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:while⟧, is sometimes used where the subjunctive might be expected with ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:until⟧ (⟦r1593:1593⟧). Other indicative tenses are rarely thus used: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:expectābō, dum venit⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 206, ⟦i:I will wait while he comes⟧. ⟦b:ego hīc tantisper, dum exīs, tē opperiar⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 683, ⟦i:I’ll wait for you here a while till you come out⟧. ⟦b:ego in Arcānō opperior, dum ista cōgnōscō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 10, 3, ⟦i:for myself I am waiting at the Arcae place, till I ascertain this⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:mihī̆ quidem usque cūrae erit, quid agās, dum quid ēgerīs, scierō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 12, 19, 3, ⟦i:for me I shall be anxious all the time to know what you are doing, till I know what you have done⟧. ⟦b:mānsit in condiciōne usque ad eum fīnem dum iūdicēs rēiectī sunt⟧, ⟦i:V. a. pr.⟧ 16, ⟦i:he stuck to his bargain till the jurors were challenged⟧.

title: quoad, dōnec, until
text:
⟦#2007⟧
⟦b:quoad⟧ or ⟦b:dōnec⟧, ⟦i:until⟧, introduces a protasis in the present subjunctive when the main verb is present or future; and in the perfect indicative when the main verb is past or a general present.
⟦b:quoad⟧ is found once in Plautus with the imperfect subjunctive (⟦r2008:2008⟧); in other authors here and there with both moods; not in Tacitus. With ⟦b:dōnec⟧ the present subjunctive is found once in Plautus, rarely in late Latin and in poetry; the perfect indicative is found at all periods; the present indicative (⟦r1590:1590⟧), found once in Plautus, is poetic and late. But ⟦b:dōnec⟧ is rarely used by Cicero, and never by Caesar or Sallust. ⟦b:dōnicum⟧ is found in old Latin (not in Terence) with the indicative (⟦r2009:2009⟧), and once in Nepos with the subjunctive of indirect discourse. ⟦b:dōnique⟧ is found four times in Lucretius with the indicative, always before vowels (⟦r2009:2009⟧). ⟦b:dōneque⟧ and ⟦b:dōneque cum⟧ seem to occur a few times in Vitruvius.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:ego hīc cōgitō commorārī, quoad mē reficiam⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 7, 26, 2, ⟦i:I am thinking of staying here till I feel better⟧. ⟦b:ea continēbis, quoad ipse tē videam⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 13, 21, 4, ⟦i:you will keep this back till I see you myself⟧. ⟦b:expergēfactīque secuntur inānia saepe cervōrum simulācra, dōnec discussīs redeant errōribus ad sē⟧, Lucr. 4, 995, ⟦i:and when awakened, often they still keep hunting the shadowy forms of stags, until the delusion is shaken off and they come to themselves⟧. ⟦b:magnus mīrandusque cliēns sedet ad praetōria rēgis, dōnec Bīthȳnō libeat vigilāre tyrannō⟧, J. 10, 160, ⟦i:a vassal great and strange he sits in the king’s gate, till it may suit his oriental majesty to wake⟧. ⟦b:inter eadem pecora dēgunt, dōnec aetās sēparet ingenuōs⟧, Ta. ⟦i:G.⟧ 20, ⟦i:they always live among the same flocks and herds, till maturity puts the free-born by themselves⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:nostrī reppulērunt neque fīnem sequendī fēcērunt, quoad equitēs praecipitēs hostēs ēgērunt⟧, 5, 17, 3, ⟦i:our people routed them and did not give up the pursuit till the cavalry drove the enemy headlong⟧. ⟦b:Milō cum in senātū fuisset eō diē quoad senātus est dīmissus, domum vēnit⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 28, ⟦i:after staying in the senate that day till the senate adjourned, Milo went home⟧. ⟦b:numquam dēstitit ōrāre usque adeō dōnec perpulit⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 660, ⟦i:he never ceased to tease until he gained his point⟧. ⟦b:usque eō timuī, dōnec ad rēiciundōs iūdicēs vēnimus⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 17, ⟦i:I was afraid all the time till we came to challenging jurors⟧. The present indicative of vivid narration (⟦r1590:1590⟧) is found in Vergil and Livy: as, ⟦b:sociī cōnsurgere tōnsīs, dōnec rōstra tenent siccum et sēdēre carīnae omnēs innocuae⟧, V. 10, 299, ⟦i:with one accord the shipmates rose to oars, until the beaks dry land attain, and keels all sat unscathed⟧.
⟦#2008⟧
An imperfect subjunctive is rarely found with ⟦b:quoad⟧, ⟦i:until⟧ (⟦r1725:1725⟧): as, ⟦b:haec diēs praestitūtast, quoad referret⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 623, ⟦i:this day was set by which he was to pay⟧. ⟦b:exercēbātur currendō et lūctandō ad eum fīnem, quoad stāns complectī posset⟧, N. 15, 2, 5, ⟦i:he used to practise running and wrestling, till he could give a grip standing⟧. For ⟦b:dōnec⟧, see ⟦r2009:2009⟧ at the end.
⟦#2009⟧
Other constructions occur, chiefly in old Latin or poetry, with ⟦b:dōnec⟧, or ⟦b:dōnicum⟧, ⟦i:until⟧. (⟦i:a.⟧) The future perfect: as, ⟦b:haud dēsinam, dōnec perfēcerō hōc⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 419, ⟦i:I shall not stop till I have finished this⟧. ⟦b:dēlīcta maiōrum luēs, dōnec templa refēceris⟧, H. 3, 6, 1, ⟦i:for sins of sires thou shalt atone, till thou hast shrines repaired⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) The future: ⟦b:coquitō usque dōnec conmadēbit bene⟧, Cato, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 156, 5, ⟦i:boil until it is very soft⟧. ⟦b:ter centum rēgnābitur annōs, dōnec geminam partū dabit Īlia prōlem⟧, V. 1, 272, ⟦i:for thrice a hundred years there will be kings, till Ilia gives birth to twins⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) The perfect indicative, less frequently the present, introductory to a general present: ⟦b:impedit piscīs usque adeō, dōnicum ēdūxit forās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tru.⟧ 38, ⟦i:he always draws his net about the fish, until he’s brought them out⟧ (⟦r1613:1613⟧). ⟦b:usque mantant neque id faciunt, dōnicum parietēs ruont⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 116, ⟦i:they keep waiting and don’t do it until the walls are falling⟧. (⟦i:d.⟧) The pluperfect indicative: ⟦b:horriferīs accībant vōcibus Orcum, dōnique eōs vītā prīvārant vermina saeva⟧, Lucr. 5, 996, ⟦i:with horrid cries on Death they’d call till gripings sore had set them free from life⟧. The imperfect indicative is found once in Tacitus, who also has the infinitive of intimation (⟦r1539:1539⟧) once or twice. An imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive sometimes occurs where purpose is intimated, and in Livy and late Latin to express repeated past action: as, ⟦b:dōnec ēgregius properāret exsul⟧, H. 3, 5, 45, ⟦i:till he could hasten forth a peerless exile⟧. ⟦b:trepidātiōnis aliquantum ēdēbant, dōnec quiētem ipse timor fēcisset⟧, L. 21, 28, 11, ⟦i:the elephants always displayed some nervousness, till terror itself restored quiet⟧ (⟦r1730:1730⟧). But the habit of using the imperfect subjunctive is very common in Tacitus where neither purpose nor repetition is intimated: as ⟦b:neque proelium omīsit dōnec caderet⟧, Ta. 3, 20, ⟦i:he ceased not fighting till he fell⟧.

title: quandō
text:
⟦#2010⟧
⟦b:quandō⟧, originally a temporal particle, has the meaning ⟦i:when⟧, which readily passes over to a causal meaning, ⟦i:since⟧, ⟦i:because⟧. In both meanings it introduces the indicative. For special reasons, however, the subjunctive is used, as in indirect discourse (⟦r1725:1725⟧) or of action conceivable (⟦r1731:1731⟧). ⟦b:quandō⟧ is also used to introduce a conditional protasis (⟦r2110:2110⟧).
In simple sentences, temporal ⟦b:quandō⟧ is used in pronoun questions (⟦r1526:1526⟧). As an indefinite adverb it has the meaning ⟦i:ever⟧.

title: Temporal quandō
text:
⟦#2011⟧
⟦b:quandō⟧, ⟦i:when⟧, introduces a temporal clause with the indicative.
The time is often indefinite or iterative; so usually in old Latin. ⟦b:quandō⟧ often has ⟦b:tum⟧ as correlative.
⟦b:fīō Iuppiter quandō lubet⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 864, ⟦i:I turn into Jupiter at my sweet will⟧. ⟦b:laudātō quandō illud quod cupis effēcerō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cu.⟧ 364, ⟦i:cry your bravo when I’ve done what you desire⟧. ⟦b:quandō occāsiō illaec periīt, post sērō cupit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 249, ⟦i:when that chance is lost, he wants it all too late⟧ (⟦r1613:1613⟧). ⟦b:quandō omnēs creātī sunt, tum ad eōs deus fātur⟧, ⟦i:Tim.⟧ 40, ⟦i:when all were created, then to them spake the god⟧. ⟦b:quandō pars maior in eandem sententiam ībat, bellum erat cōnsēnsum⟧, L. 1, 32, 12, ⟦i:when the majority voted for the same motion, war was always agreed upon⟧. Temporal ⟦b:quandō⟧ is found sporadically at all periods; not in Terence or Caesar.
⟦#2012⟧
⟦b:quandōque⟧, ⟦i:whenever⟧, is found once in the Twelve Tables, a few times in Cicero (chiefly in legal formulae), three times in Horace, and here and there in later authors. Not in Caesar.

title: Causal quandō
text:
⟦#2013⟧
⟦b:quandō⟧, ⟦i:since⟧, ⟦i:seeing that⟧, introduces a causal clause with the indicative.
The reason is usually one known to the person addressed or one generally known (⟦r1884:1884⟧). ⟦b:quandō⟧ is often strengthened by ⟦b:quidem⟧.
⟦b:quandō hīc serviō, haec patriast mea⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 641, ⟦i:now that I am a slave here, this is my country⟧. ⟦b:quīn ergō abeis, quandō respōnsumst?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 1085, ⟦i:why don’t you go then, since you’ve had your answer?⟧ ⟦b:melius est, quandōquidem hoc numquam mī ipse voluit dīcere⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 639, ⟦i:better so, since he wouldn’t ever tell me about it of his own accord⟧. ⟦b:quandō mē in hunc locum dēdūxit ōrātiō, docēbō⟧. ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 43, ⟦i:seeing that my discourse has brought me to this point, I will show⟧. ⟦b:haec dētur cūra cēnsōribus, quandōquidem eōs in rē pūblicā semper volumus esse⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 3, 47, ⟦i:let this be the charge of the censors, seeing that we want such officers always in our state⟧. ⟦b:prō urbe ac penātibus dīmicandum esse, quandō Ītaliam tuērī nequīssent⟧, L. 22, 8, 7, ⟦i:that they must fight for home and country, now that they had failed to preserve Italy⟧ (⟦r1724:1724⟧). Causal ⟦b:quandō⟧ is found at all periods, though not in Caesar, and in Cicero’s orations only with ⟦b:quidem⟧.
⟦#2014⟧
⟦b:quandōque⟧, ⟦i:inasmuch as⟧, is used a few times in a formal or legal sense in Cicero and Livy: as, ⟦b:quandōque hīsce hominēs iniussū populī Rōmānī Quirītium foedus ictum īrī spopondērunt⟧, L. 9, 10, 9, ⟦i:inasmuch as these persons have promised that a covenant should be made, without the order of the Roman nation of Quirites⟧.

title: sī
text:
⟦#2015⟧
⟦b:sī⟧, in early Latin ⟦b:sei⟧, is originally a locative, meaning ⟦i:under those circumstances⟧, ⟦i:so⟧. With the enclitic ⟦b:-ce⟧, it forms ⟦b:sīce⟧ or ⟦b:sīc⟧, ⟦i:so⟧. The two are sometimes found as correlatives in colloquial style: as, ⟦b:sīc scrībēs aliquid, sī vacābis⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 12, 38, 2, ⟦i:so you shall have time, so you will write something⟧. See ⟦r708:708⟧.

title: Conditional Periods
text:
⟦#2016⟧
A protasis introduced by ⟦b:sī⟧, ⟦i:so⟧, ⟦i:if⟧, or ⟦b:nisi⟧, ⟦i:unless⟧, ⟦i:if not⟧, states a condition; the apodosis states action occurring under that condition. The conditional protasis and apodosis combined make a ⟦i:Conditional Period⟧.
Thus, ⟦b:sī diēs est⟧, ⟦i:if it is day⟧, is a conditional protasis; combined with an apodosis, ⟦b:lūcet⟧, ⟦i:it is light⟧, it makes a conditional period: ⟦b:sī diēs est, lūcet⟧, ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 1, 86, ⟦i:if it is day, it is light⟧.
⟦#2017⟧
A parenthesis with ⟦b:ut⟧ (⟦r1943:1943⟧) is added when the speaker asserts that the action of the protasis is not only assumed, but actually occurs: as, ⟦b:sī virtūs digna est glōriātiōne, ut est, beātus esse poterit virtūte ūnā praeditus⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 4, 51, ⟦i:if virtue is entitled to glorification, as it really is, he will find it possible to be happy in the possession of virtue alone⟧. ⟦b:sī nox opportūna est ēruptiōnī, sīcut est, haec profectō noctis aptissima hōra est⟧, L. 7, 35, 10, ⟦i:if night is always favourable for a sortie, and it always is, this particular hour of the night is surely the very best time⟧.
⟦#2018⟧
The apodosis is usually declarative. Often, however, it is interrogative, exclamatory, or imperative, or it may take any other form which the thought or the context may require. The apodosis has rarely a correlative to ⟦b:sī⟧: as, ⟦b:igitur⟧, ⟦i:it follows that⟧, ⟦b:idcircō⟧, ⟦i:for all that⟧, ⟦b:tum⟧, ⟦i:then⟧, ⟦b:ita⟧, ⟦b:sīc⟧, ⟦i:only⟧, ⟦b:eā condiciōne⟧, ⟦i:on condition⟧; ⟦b:at⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, ⟦b:tamen⟧, ⟦i:nevertheless⟧, ⟦b:certē⟧, ⟦b:saltem⟧, ⟦i:at any rate⟧, ⟦b:tum dēnique⟧, ⟦b:tum dēmum⟧, ⟦i:then and not till then⟧.
⟦#2019⟧
⟦b:sī⟧ is sometimes followed by ⟦b:quidem⟧ or, from Cicero on, by ⟦b:modo⟧: ⟦b:sī quidem⟧, ⟦i:that is if⟧, ⟦i:since⟧, ⟦i:even if⟧, ⟦b:sī modo⟧, ⟦i:if only⟧. ⟦b:sī tamen⟧, ⟦i:at least if⟧, is found in Lucretius, Sallust, the Augustan poets and in late writers. ⟦b:sīve ... sīve⟧ (⟦b:seu . . . seu⟧) or, in old Latin, ⟦b:sī . . . sīve⟧, ⟦i:whether . . . or⟧, with the indicative or the subjunctive of the indefinite second person (⟦r1556:1556⟧), leaves a choice between two cases possible. By abbreviation of the protasis ⟦b:sīve⟧ becomes a coordinating particle: see ⟦r1672:1672⟧.
⟦#2020⟧
The negative of ⟦b:sī⟧ is ⟦b:sī nōn⟧, ⟦i:if not⟧ (⟦b:sī nēmō⟧, ⟦b:sī nūllus⟧, &c.), or ⟦b:nisi⟧, ⟦i:unless⟧, ⟦i:if not⟧, used especially of an exception or after a negative, ⟦b:nisi sī⟧, chiefly in old, colloquial, or late Latin, or, particularly in solemn language or poetry, ⟦b:nī⟧ is sometimes used for ⟦b:nisi⟧. A restriction, usually an ironical afterthought, may be introduced by ⟦b:nisi forte⟧ (rare before Cicero) or ⟦b:nisi vērō⟧ (in Cicero and Pliny the Younger) with the indicative.
⟦b:nisi⟧ is sometimes found in an adversative sense in old and colloquial Latin, especially after ⟦b:nesciō⟧; from Cicero on, it may be strengthened by ⟦b:tamen⟧. For ⟦b:nisi quod⟧, see ⟦r1848:1848⟧.
⟦#2021⟧
When a second conditional period is opposed to a first, it is sometimes introduced by ⟦b:sī⟧ (or ⟦b:sī autem⟧), but usually by ⟦b:sīn⟧ (or ⟦b:sīn autem⟧). If the second period is negative, and its verb is not expressed, ⟦b:minus⟧ or ⟦b:aliter⟧ is preferred to ⟦b:nōn⟧.

title: Classes of Conditional Protases
text:
⟦#2022⟧
Conditional protases may be divided into two classes:
⟦#2023⟧
I. Indeterminate protases, that is such as merely suppose an action, without implying either its occurrence or its non-occurrence; these may take:
(A.) Any tense of the indicative required by the sense; or (B.) the present subjunctive, less frequently the perfect subjunctive, to express a condition in the future.
⟦#2024⟧
II. Protases of ACTION NON-OCCURRENT, that is such as suppose action not taking place. These take the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive.
Thus, in the period ⟦b:sī diēs est, lūcet⟧, ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 1, 86, ⟦i:if it is day, it is light⟧, the protasis ⟦i:if it is day⟧ is indeterminate, neither implying that ⟦i:it is⟧, or ⟦i:is not day⟧. But in ⟦b:sī vīveret, verba eius audīrētis⟧, ⟦i:if he were alive, you would hear his evidence⟧, ⟦i:RC.⟧ 42, the protasis denotes action non-occurrent, ⟦i:if he were alive⟧, implying ⟦i:but he is not⟧. The whole period, like the protasis, is either an ⟦i:Indeterminate Period⟧ or a ⟦i:Period of Action non-occurrent⟧.

title: Indicative Use
text:
⟦#2025⟧
The indicative in a conditional protasis may state present, past, or future time.
The mood and tense of the apodosis are determined by the sense. The following combinations occur:

title: Protasis in the Present
text:
⟦#2026⟧
⟦=⟧(a.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present.⟧
⟦b:sī sunt dī, beneficī in hominēs sunt⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 104, ⟦i:if there are gods, they are kind to men⟧. ⟦b:sī nescīs, tibī̆ īgnōscō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 10, 26, 3, ⟦i:if you do not know, I pardon you⟧. ⟦b:deus sum, sī hoc itast⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 843, ⟦i:I am a god, if this is so⟧. ⟦b:erus sī tuos domīst, quīn prōvocās?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 638, ⟦i:in case your master is at home, why don’t you call him out?⟧ ⟦b:hōc mortuō, aut sī quī ex reliquīs excellit dignitāte, succēdit, aut, sī sunt plūrēs parēs, dē prīncipātū contendunt⟧, 6, 13, 9, ⟦i:when this man dies, if there is any one of the rest superior in position, he always takes his place; or if there are several with equal claims, they have a contest about the supremacy⟧. ⟦b:sī vīs, potes⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 6, 39, ⟦i:you can, if you will⟧. ⟦b:in corpore sī quid eius modī est quod reliquō corporī noceat, id ūrī secārīque patimur⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 8, 15, ⟦i:in the human body if there is anything likely to damage the rest of the body, we always allow it to be cauterized and cut⟧. ⟦b:sī cui vēnae sīc moventur, is habet febrim⟧, ⟦i:Fat.⟧ 15, ⟦i:if a man’s pulse beats thus and so, he always has fever⟧. The present is sometimes loosely used of future time (⟦r1593:1593⟧): as, ⟦b:sī illum relinquō, e͡i͡us vītae timeō⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 210, ⟦i:if I desert him, I tremble for his life⟧. ⟦b:assequor omnia, sī properō; sī cunctor, āmittō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 10, 8, 5, ⟦i:I shall compass all my ends, if I hurry; if I delay, I shall lose everything⟧. ⟦b:castra nunc vōbīs hostium praedae dō, sī mihī̆ pollicēminī vōs fortiter operam nāvātūrōs⟧, L. 7, 16, 4, ⟦i:I give you the camp of the enemy as booty now, if you promise me you will quit you like men⟧.
⟦#2027⟧
⟦=⟧(b.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Perfect.⟧
⟦b:sī hominēs ratiōnem ā dīs datam in fraudem convertunt, nōn darī illam quam darī hūmānō generī melius fuit⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 78, ⟦i:if men apply reason, the gift of the gods, to purposes of mischief, it would have been better it should not be given to the human race than given⟧ (⟦r1495:1495⟧). The perfect of the apodosis is ordinarily used of future time (⟦r1612:1612⟧): as, ⟦b:occidī, sī tū vēra memorās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 369, ⟦i:I’m a dead man, if what you say is true⟧. ⟦b:nunc sī indicium faciō, interiī; sī taceō, interiī tamen⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 306, ⟦i:now if I tell, I’m dead and gone; if I keep dark, I’m dead and gone the same⟧. ⟦b:nī illōs hominēs expellō, ego occidī plānissumē⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 401, ⟦i:if I don’t drive those people off, all’s up with me⟧. ⟦b:nam sī argentum prius adfert, continuō nōs ambō exclūsī sumus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 360, ⟦i:for if he brings the money first, then we’re at once left out in the cold⟧.
⟦#2028⟧
⟦=⟧(c.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperfect.⟧
⟦b:sed sī domīst, Dēmaenetum volēbam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 452, ⟦i:but if he is at home, Demaenetus I wanted⟧. ⟦b:iam tum erat senex, senectūs sī verēcundōs facit⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 1023, ⟦i:he was already old, if age is what makes shamefastness⟧. ⟦b:sī singula vōs forte nōn movent, ūniversa certē tamen movēre dēbēbant⟧, ⟦i:DN⟧. 2, 163, ⟦i:if these points taken severally do not affect you, yet collectively they surely should have done so⟧ (⟦r1495:1495⟧).
⟦#2029⟧
⟦=⟧(d.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Pluperfect.⟧
⟦b:cesseram, sī aliēnam ā mē plēbem fuisse voltis, quae nōn fuit, invidiae⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 64, ⟦i:I had yielded, if you will have it that the commons were opposed to me, though they were not, to hatred⟧. ⟦b:hoc mī ūnum relicuom fuerat malum, sī puerum ut tollam cōgit⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 570, ⟦i:this was the only evil left in store for me, if he compels me to adopt the child⟧.
⟦#2030⟧
⟦=⟧(e.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Future.⟧
⟦b:sī interpellās, ego tacēbō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 1121, ⟦i:if you persist in breaking in, I’ll hold my tongue⟧. ⟦b:hīc tū sī laesum tē esse dīcis, patiar et concēdam; sī iniūriam tibī̆ factam quereris, dēfendam et negābō⟧, ⟦i:Caecil.⟧ 58, ⟦i:if you assert that you are hurt in this matter, I am perfectly willing to admit it; but if you complain that it is a violation of your rights, I shall stoutly maintain the contrary⟧. Often in this combination the present is loosely used of future time (⟦r1593:1593⟧): as, ⟦b:nunc sī ille hūc salvos revenit, reddam suom sibī̆; sī quid eō fuerit, habeō dōtem unde dem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 156, ⟦i:now if our absent friend comes safely back, I’ll give him back his own again; if anything befalls him, I’ve wherewith a dower to give⟧. ⟦b:nisi id cōnfestim facis, ego tē trādam magistrātuī⟧, N. 15, 4, 3, ⟦i:if you do not do it at once, I will hand you over to a magistrate⟧. ⟦b:sī pāce fruī volumus, bellum gerendum est; sī bellum omittimus, pāce numquam fruēmur⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 7, 19, ⟦i:if we wish to enjoy peace, we shall have to make war; if we give up war, we never shall enjoy peace⟧. ⟦b:convincam, sī negās⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 8, ⟦i:I will bring it home to you, if you deny it⟧. ⟦b:tibi dīvitiās dabō, sī impetrās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 1213, ⟦i:I’ll make you rich, if you succeed⟧.
⟦#2031⟧
⟦=⟧(f.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Future Perfect.⟧
⟦b:sī nequeō facere ut abeās, egomet abierō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 442, ⟦i:if I can’t make you go, I’ll instantly begone myself⟧ (⟦r1629:1629⟧). ⟦b:sī id nōn facis, ego quod mē in tē sit facere dignum invēnerō⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 107, ⟦i:if you don’t do it, I will have a proper course devised to use with you⟧.
⟦#2032⟧
⟦=⟧(g.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperative.⟧
⟦b:dā mihī̆ hoc, mel meum, sī mē amās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 244, ⟦i:give me this, honey mine, an thou lov’st me⟧. ⟦b:redargue mē, sī mentior⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 62, ⟦i:refute me, if I am not speaking the truth⟧. ⟦b:dēsilīte, mīlitēs, nisi vultis aquilam hostibus prōdere⟧, 4, 25, 3, ⟦i:jump overboard, men, unless you choose to abandon your eagle to the enemy⟧. ⟦b:nī iūdicātum facit, sēcum dūcitō, vincitō compedibus⟧, Twelve Tables in Gell. 20, 1, 45, ⟦i:unless he satisfies the judgement, the complainant shall take him with him, and put him in gyves⟧ (⟦r1593:1593⟧, ⟦r1575:1575⟧). ⟦b:quā rē, sī haec ita sunt, sīc mē colitōte ut deum⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 81, ⟦i:therefore, if this is so, you are to honour me as a god⟧.
⟦#2033⟧
⟦=⟧(h.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:sī quid habēs certius, velim scīre⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 4, 10, 1, ⟦i:if you have anything more definite, I should like to know⟧ (⟦r1554:1554⟧). ⟦b:sīn aliter animātus es, bene, quod agās, ēveniat tibī̆⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 715, ⟦i:but if you’re minded otherwise, may all you do betide you well⟧ (⟦r1540:1540⟧). ⟦b:quod sī nōn possumus facere, moriāmur⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 7, 14, ⟦i:if we cannot do it, let us die⟧ (⟦r1547:1547⟧). ⟦b:sī mihī̆ fīlius genitur, isque prius moritur, et cētera, tum mihī̆ ille sit hērēs⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 141, ⟦i:if a son is born to me, and the boy dies before &c., &c., then so and so is to be my heir⟧ (⟦r1593:1593⟧, ⟦r1548:1548⟧). ⟦b:sī est spēs nostrī reditūs, eam cōnfirmēs⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 14, 4, 3, ⟦i:if there is a hope of my coming back, strengthen that hope⟧ (⟦r1550:1550⟧). ⟦b:eum sī reddis mihi, praetereā ūnum nummum nē duīs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 331, ⟦i:if you restore my boy to me, you needn’t give one penny more⟧ (⟦r1551:1551⟧). ⟦b:sī hīc pernoctō, causae quid dīcam?⟧ T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 531, ⟦i:if I sleep here, what reason can I give⟧ (⟦r1563:1563⟧)?

title: Protasis in the Perfect
text:
⟦#2034⟧
⟦=⟧(a.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present.⟧
⟦b:sī quid vēnāle habuit Heius, sī id quantī aestimābat, tantī vēndidit, dēsinō quaerere cūr ēmeris⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 10, ⟦i:if Hejus had anything for sale, if he sold it at his own valuation, I stop enquiring why you bought⟧. ⟦b:sī vērē est ā nōbīs philosophia laudāta, eius trāctātiō optimō quōque dignissima est⟧, ⟦i:Ac.⟧ 2, 6, ⟦i:if philosophy has been extolled by me with justice, its study is eminently worthy of the good⟧. ⟦b:sī honōris causā statuam dedērunt, inimīcī nōn sunt⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 150, ⟦i:if they contributed a statue as a compliment, they are not enemies⟧. ⟦b:postēs quoiusmodī? . . . etiam nunc satis bonī sunt, sī sunt inductī pice⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 818, ⟦i:what think you of the posts? . . . they’re pretty good even now, if they are only smeared with pitch⟧. This combination is common in general conditional periods (⟦r1613:1613⟧): as, ⟦b:hominēs aegrī sī aquam gelidam bibērunt, prīmō relevārī videntur⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 31, ⟦i:if sick people drink cold water, at first they always seem refreshed⟧. ⟦b:sī quod est admissum facinus, īdem dēcernunt⟧, 6, 13, 5, ⟦i:if a crime has been committed, they also act as judges⟧. ⟦b:abiūrant, sī quid crēditumst⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cur.⟧ 496, ⟦i:they always swear they haven’t it, if anything is trusted them⟧. ⟦b:sī puer parvus occidit, aequō animō ferendum putant⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 93, ⟦i:if a baby dies, they always think the affliction should be borne with resignation⟧.
⟦#2035⟧
⟦=⟧(b.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Perfect.⟧
⟦b:sī peccāvī, īnsciēns fēcī⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 631, ⟦i:if I’ve done wrong, it was in ignorance⟧. ⟦b:haec bona in tabulās pūblicās sī rediērunt, tabulae pūblicae conruptae sunt⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 128, ⟦i:if this property has been entered on the state books, then the state books have been tampered with⟧. ⟦b:quō in bellō sī fuit error, commūnis ē̆ī fuit cum senātū⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 11, 34, ⟦i:if there was a mistake in this war, it was common to him and the senate⟧. ⟦b:interiī, sī abiīt⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 910, ⟦i:I’m lost, if he has gone⟧ (⟦r1608:1608⟧). Also in general periods (⟦r1613:1613⟧): as, ⟦b:animī sī quandō vēra vīdērunt, ūsī sunt fortūnā atque cāsū⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 108, ⟦i:if the mind has ever seen the truth, it has used in every case luck and chance⟧. ⟦b:studiōsē equidem ūtor nostrīs poētīs, sed sīcubi illī dēfēcērunt, vertī multa dē Graecīs⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 26, ⟦i:I use our own poets carefully, it is true: but whenever they have failed me, I have always translated a great deal from Greek⟧.
⟦#2036⟧
⟦=⟧(c.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Pluperfect.⟧
⟦b:sī illud iūre rogātum dīcere ausī sunt, oblītīne erant?⟧ ⟦i:PC.⟧ 45, ⟦i:if they ventured to say that that measure was brought forward in due form, had not they forgotten?⟧
⟦#2037⟧
⟦=⟧(d.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Future.⟧
⟦b:sī quis oriente canīculā nātus est, is in marī nōn moriētur⟧, ⟦i:if anybody is born when the dogstar is rising, he will never die at sea⟧ (general): ⟦b:sī Fabius oriente canīculā nātus est, Fabius in marī nōn moriētur⟧, ⟦i:Fat.⟧ 12, ⟦i:if Fabius was born when the dogstar was rising, Fabius will not die at sea⟧ (particular). ⟦b:sī parum intellēxtī, dīcam dēnuō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 1103, ⟦i:if you don’t understand, I’ll say again⟧. ⟦b:nōn ūtar eā cōnsuētūdine, sī quid est factum clēmenter, ut dissolūtē factum crīminer⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 19, ⟦i:I will not avail myself of the common practice, and if a thing has been done in a spirit of mercy, charge that it was done in a lax way⟧. ⟦b:nisi iam factum aliquid est per Flaccum, fīet ā mē⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 3, 11, 3, ⟦i:unless something or other has been done already through Flaccus, it will be done by me⟧.
⟦#2038⟧
⟦=⟧(e.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperative.⟧
⟦b:sī plūs minusve secuērunt, sē fraude estō⟧, Twelve Tables in Gell. 20, 1, 49, ⟦i:if they cut too much or too little, it shall be without penalty⟧ (⟦r1613:1613⟧). ⟦b:sī vīdistis, dīcite⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 323, ⟦i:if ye have seen, declare⟧. ⟦b:sī quid est peccātum ā nōbīs, prōfer⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 253, ⟦i:declare it, if we’ve erred at all⟧. ⟦b:sī numquam avārē pretium statuī artī meae, exemplum statuite in mē⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 48, ⟦i:if never like a miser I have set a price upon my art, a pattern set in me⟧. ⟦b:sī quōs propīnquus sanguī̆s patrōnōs dedit, iuvāte perīclitantem⟧, Ta. 3, 12, ⟦i:if relationship has made any of you his advocates, help him in his straits⟧.
⟦#2039⟧
⟦=⟧(f.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:sī nūlla colōris prīncipiīs est reddita nātūra, extemplō ratiōnem reddere possīs⟧, Lucr. 2, 757, ⟦i:if atoms have no colour, you might explain at once⟧ (⟦r1556:1556⟧). ⟦b:meritō maledīcās mī, sī nōn id ita factumst⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 572, ⟦i:you might with perfect right abuse me, if it is not so⟧ (⟦r1556:1556⟧).
⟦#2040⟧
⟦=⟧(g.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperfect Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:sī nēmō hāc praeteriīt, postquam intrō abiī, cistella hīc iacēret⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cist.⟧ 683, ⟦i:if nobody has passed along this way, since I went in, a casket must have been lying here⟧ (⟦r1560:1560⟧). ⟦b:nam cūr tam variae rēs possent esse requīrō, ex ūnō sī sunt ignī pūrōque creātae?⟧ Lucr. 1, 645, ⟦i:for how could things so motley be, I ask, if they are made of pure and simple fire⟧ (⟦r1565:1565⟧)?
⟦#2041⟧
⟦=⟧(h.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Pluperfect Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:sī Antōniō Crassus ēloquēns vīsus nōn est, tibī̆ numquam Cotta vīsus esset⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 106, ⟦i:if Antony did not hold Crassus eloquent, you would never have held Cotta so⟧ (⟦r1561:1561⟧).

title: Protasis in the Imperfect
text:
⟦#2042⟧
⟦=⟧(a.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present.⟧
⟦b:sī tum nōn pertimēscēbās, nē nunc quidem perhorrēscis?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 78, ⟦i:if you were not getting afraid then, are you not getting scared even now?⟧ ⟦b:sī quī senēs āc dēfōrmēs erant, eōs in hostium numerō dūcit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 64, ⟦i:if any were old and homely, he considers them in the light of enemies⟧ (⟦r1590:1590⟧). ⟦b:sī ad illum hērēditās veniēbat, vērī simile est ab illō necātum⟧, ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 1, 89, ⟦i:if the inheritance was coming to so and so, it is likely that the murder was committed by that man⟧. ⟦b:adulēscentī nihil est quod suscēnseam, sī illum minus nōrat⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 361, ⟦i:I have no cause for anger with the youth, if he was not acquainted with the man⟧.
⟦#2043⟧
⟦=⟧(b.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Perfect.⟧
⟦b:sed sī properābās magis, prīdiē nōs tē hūc dūxisse oportuit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 525, ⟦i:but if you were in greater haste, you should have brought us here the day before⟧.
⟦#2044⟧
⟦=⟧(c.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperfect.⟧
This combination is used chiefly of contemporaneous action (⟦r1732:1732⟧), in general conditional periods: as, ⟦b:sī quod erat grande vās, laetī adferēbant⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 47, ⟦i:if any good-sized vase was ever found, they would always bring it to him in high glee⟧. ⟦b:atque ea sī erant, magnam habēbās dīs grātiam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 143, ⟦i:and if them you ever had, you were monstrous grateful to the gods⟧. ⟦b:sī quae rēs erat maior, populus commovēbātur⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 105, ⟦i:if a thing of more than ordinary importance occurred, the populace was always aroused⟧. ⟦b:hī, sī quid erat dūrius, concurrēbant⟧, 1, 48, 6, ⟦i:whenever there was any pretty sharp work, these men would always fall to⟧. For the subjunctive in such protases, see ⟦r2071:2071⟧.
⟦#2045⟧
⟦=⟧(d.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Future.⟧
⟦b:flēbunt Germānicum etiam īgnōtī: vindicābitis vōs, sī mē potius quam fortūnam meam fovēbātis⟧, ⟦i:Ta.⟧ 2, 71, ⟦i:as for weeping for Germanicus, that will be done by strangers too; vengeance will be yours, if you honoured in me more the man than the position⟧. See ⟦i:Att.⟧ 14, 1, 1.
⟦#2046⟧
⟦=⟧(e.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:fāc animō magnō sīs, et sī turbidissima sapienter ferēbās, tranquilliōra laetē ferās⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 6, 14, 3, ⟦i:be of great heart, and if you bore anarchy like a stoic, bear a more orderly condition of things with good cheer⟧ (⟦r1550:1550⟧).
⟦#2047⟧
⟦=⟧(f.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperfect Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:sī amābās, invenīrēs mūtuom⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 286, ⟦i:you should have borrowed, if you were in love⟧ (⟦r1559:1559⟧). ⟦b:quod sī meīs incommodīs laetābantur, urbis tamen periculō commovērentur⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 54, ⟦i:if they did exult over my mishaps, still they ought to have been touched by the danger to Rome⟧ (⟦r1559:1559⟧).

title: Protasis in the Pluperfect
text:
⟦#2048⟧
⟦=⟧(a.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present.⟧
⟦b:sī hoc ita fātō datum erat, ut ad pācem petendam venīrem, laetor tē mihī̆ sorte potissimum datum, ā quō peterem⟧, L. 30, 30, 3, ⟦i:if it was so ordained by fate that I should come to sue for peace, I am glad that you are allotted me, of all men in the world, to sue from⟧.
⟦#2049⟧
⟦=⟧(b.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Perfect.⟧
⟦b:tum id, sī falsum fuerat, fīlius quōr nōn refellit?⟧ T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 400, ⟦i:if that had been untrue, why did not at the time your son disprove it?⟧ ⟦b:vel officiō, sī quid dēbuerat, vel errōrī, sī quid nescierat, satis factum esse dūxit⟧, ⟦i:D.⟧ 13, ⟦i:he thought he had done enough for duty, if he had been under any obligation, enough for delusion, if he had been acting under mistaken ignorance⟧.
⟦#2050⟧
⟦=⟧(c.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperfect.⟧
⟦b:sed in aedibus quid tibi meīs nam erat negōtī mē absente, nisi ego iusseram?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 427, ⟦i:but what business had you in my house in my absence, unless I had ordered?⟧ ⟦b:sī nihil in istā pugnā Rōsciī fēcerant, quam ob causam tantīs praemiīs dōnābantur?⟧ ⟦i:RA.⟧ 108, ⟦i:if the Rosciuses had not done service in that fight, why were they presented with such rewards?⟧ Often of antecedent action, in general conditional periods: as, ⟦b:sī quicquam caelātī adspexerat, manūs abstinēre, iūdicēs, nōn poterat⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 48, ⟦i:if he ever caught sight of a bit of chased work, why, gentlemen, he never could keep his hands off⟧. ⟦b:stomachābātur senex, sī quid asperius dīxeram⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 93, ⟦i:the old gentleman was always nettled, if I said anything harsh⟧. ⟦b:ac seu longum post tempus vēnerat hospes, sīve convīva per imbrem vīcīnus, bene erat nōn piscibus urbe petītīs⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 2, 118, ⟦i:and if a friend dropped in, after an absence long, or neighbour, come to take pot-luck upon a rainy day, we feasted not on fish brought out from town⟧. For the subjunctive in such protases, see ⟦r2071:2071⟧.
⟦#2051⟧
⟦=⟧(d.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperfect Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:ante sōlem exorientem nisi in palaestram vēnerās, haud mediocrīs poenās penderēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 426, ⟦i:ere sunrise so you came not to the wrestling school, amercement strong you had to pay⟧ (⟦r1552:1552⟧).

title: Protasis in the Future
text:
⟦#2052⟧
⟦=⟧(a.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present.⟧
⟦b:eam sei cūrābeis, perbonast⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Merc.⟧ 526, ⟦i:if you’ll take care of her, she is first-rate⟧. ⟦b:quod sī perferre nōn poterō, opprimī mē mālō⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 10, ⟦i:if I cannot succeed in bearing it, I would rather be crushed⟧.
⟦#2053⟧
⟦=⟧(b.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Perfect.⟧
⟦b:quam nisi dēfendēs, Rōmulus nōn bene vīdit avēs⟧, ⟦i:Prop.⟧ 4 (5), 6, 43, ⟦i:unless thou savest her, ’twas ill that Romulus espied his birds⟧. ⟦b:āctumst, sī quidem tū mē hīc lūdificābere⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 717, ⟦i:all’s up, that is in case you fool me here⟧ (⟦r1612:1612⟧). ⟦b:cui sī esse in urbe licēbit, vīcimus⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 14, 20, 3, ⟦i:if he shall be allowed to stay in town, the day is ours⟧ (⟦r1612:1612⟧).
⟦#2054⟧
⟦=⟧(c.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Future.⟧
⟦b:sī erum īnsimulābis malitiae, male audiēs⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 359, ⟦i:you’ll hear what you won’t like, if you insinuate anything wrong against master⟧. ⟦b:vīcīnīs bonus estō: sī tē libenter vīcīnitās vidēbit, facilius tua vēndēs; sī aedificābis, operīs, iūmentīs, māteriē adiuvābunt⟧, Cato, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 4, ⟦i:be obliging to your neighbours: if the neighbourhood looks on you with favour, you will find a readier sale for your produce; if you fall to building, they will help you with labour, draught animals, and building material⟧. ⟦b:sī id audēbis dīcere, causam inimīcī tuī sublevābis⟧, ⟦i:Caecil.⟧ 12, ⟦i:if you venture to say that, you will promote the cause of your enemy⟧. ⟦b:sī fortūna volet, fīēs dē rhētore cōnsul; sī volet haec eadem, fīēs dē cōnsule rhētor⟧, J. 7, 197, ⟦i:if fortune shall ordain, a magnate from a teacher thou shalt be; again shall she ordain, a teacher from a magnate shalt thou be⟧. ⟦b:nōn modo nōn laedētur causa nōbilitātis, sī istīs hominibus resistētis, vērum etiam ōrnābitur⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 138, ⟦i:the interests of the nobility will not be damaged, if you resist those creatures; oh no, on the contrary, they will be promoted⟧. The clause with ⟦b:sī⟧ is apt to take the future perfect (⟦r2061:2061⟧). The future in the apodosis often denotes action holding good at all times: as, ⟦b:dēfēnsor prīmum, sī poterit, dēbēbit vītam eius, quī īnsimulābitur, quam honestissimam dēmōnstrāre⟧, ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 2, 35, ⟦i:the advocate ought in the first place, if he can, to prove that the life of the accused is eminently respectable⟧. ⟦b:quod adsequēmur, sī cavēbimus nē in perturbātiōnēs incidāmus⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 131, ⟦i:we shall attain this end if we take care not to be subject to fits of passion⟧. Sometimes in exemplifications: ⟦b:sī patriam prōdere cōnābitur pater, silēbitne fīlius?⟧ ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 90, ⟦i:if a father shall try to betray his country, will the son keep silent?⟧ But see ⟦r2090:2090⟧.
⟦#2055⟧
⟦=⟧(d.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Future Perfect.⟧
⟦b:oculum ego ecfodiam tibī̆ :: dīcam tamen; nam sī sīc nōn licēbit, luscus dīxerō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 463, ⟦i:I’ll dig your eye out :: but I’ll speak, nathless; for if I may not as I am, I’ll say my say as one-eyed man⟧. ⟦b:sed sī tē aequō animō ferre accipiet, neclegentem fēceris⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 397, ⟦i:but if he sees you take it placidly, you’ll have him off his guard⟧. The more usual combination is as in 2062.
⟦#2056⟧
⟦=⟧(e.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperative.⟧
⟦b:vir tuos sī veniet, iube domī opperīrier⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cist.⟧ 592, ⟦i:in case your husband comes, tell him to wait at home⟧. Almost always the second imperative is used (⟦r1577:1577⟧): as, ⟦b:sī volet, suō vīvitō⟧, Twelve Tables in Gell. 20, 1, 45, ⟦i:if the prisoner wish, he may subsist on his own food⟧. ⟦b:sī veniet nūntius, facitō ut sciam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 148, ⟦i:if a messenger shall come, be sure you let me know⟧. ⟦b:sī dē mē ipsō plūra dīcere vidēbor, īgnōscitōte⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 31, ⟦i:if I seem to harp too much on myself, you must excuse me⟧.
⟦#2057⟧
⟦=⟧(f.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:sī quid erit, quod scrībendum putēs, velim faciās⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 11, 13, 5, ⟦i:if there shall be anything which you think worth writing, I wish you would write⟧ (⟦r1555:1555⟧). ⟦b:nam sī altera illaec magis īnstābit, forsitan nōs reiciat⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 717, ⟦i:for if the other lady presses more, perhaps he’ll throw us out⟧ (⟦r1554:1554⟧). ⟦b:peream, sī tē ferre poterunt⟧, Brut. in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 11, 23, 2, ⟦i:may I die, if they shall find it possible to endure you⟧ (⟦r1541:1541⟧). ⟦b:sī quandō illa dīcet ‘Phaedriam intrō mittāmus,’ Pamphilam cantātum prōvocēmus⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 441, ⟦i:if ever she shall say ‘let us have Phaedria in,’ then let us call out Pamphila to sing⟧ (⟦r1548:1548⟧). ⟦b:habeat, sī argentum dabit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 727, ⟦i:she’s welcome to them, if she pays the cash⟧ (⟦r1548:1548⟧).
⟦#2058⟧
⟦=⟧(g.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Perfect Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:sī mē audiētis, adulēscentēs, sōlem alterum nē metuerītis⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 1, 32, ⟦i:if you will hearken to me, my young friends, never fear a double sun⟧ (⟦r1551:1551⟧). ⟦b:sīn erit ille gemitus ēlāmentābilis, vix eum virum dīxerim⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 57, ⟦i:but if his groan be a long-drawn wail, I could scarcely call him a man⟧ (⟦r1558:1558⟧).

title: Protasis in the Future Perfect
text:
⟦#2059⟧
⟦=⟧(a.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present.⟧
⟦b:salvae sunt, sī istōs flūctūs dēvītāverint⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 168, ⟦i:they are saved, if they escape those waves⟧ (⟦r1593:1593⟧). ⟦b:rēx sum, sī ego illum hominem adlexerō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 671, ⟦i:I’m a millionaire, if I allure the man⟧ (⟦r1593:1593⟧). ⟦b:crīmen probāre tē cēnsēs posse, sī nē causam quidem maleficī prōtuleris?⟧ ⟦i:RA.⟧ 72, ⟦i:do you think you can prove your charge, if you do not even bring forward a motive for the crime?⟧ ⟦b:quod sī meam spem vīs improbōrum fefellerit, commendō vōbīs meum parvum fīlium⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 23, ⟦i:but if the might of the wicked disappoints my hope, unto your keeping do I commend the little son of mine⟧.
⟦#2060⟧
⟦=⟧(b.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Perfect.⟧
⟦b:victus sum, sī dīxeris⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 428, ⟦i:I am beaten if you tell⟧ (⟦r1612:1612⟧). ⟦b:sī sēnserit, periī⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 213, ⟦i:if he scents it, I’m done for⟧ (⟦r1612:1612⟧). ⟦b:sī cōnservātus erit, vīcimus⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 12, 6, 2, ⟦i:if he is saved, our success is assured⟧ (⟦r1612:1612⟧). ⟦b:tum, hercule, illō diē quō ego cōnsul sum creātus, male gesta rēs pūblica est, sī tuleritis⟧, L. 3, 19, 11, ⟦i:in that case it was indeed a bad day for the country when I was made consul, if you make the proposition⟧ (⟦r1608:1608⟧).
⟦#2061⟧
⟦=⟧(c.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Future.⟧
⟦b:perībō, sī nōn fēcerō, sī faxō vāpulābō⟧, Pl. in Gell. 3, 3, 8, ⟦i:I shall be done for if I don’t do it, if I do, I shall be done up too⟧ (⟦r1626:1626⟧). ⟦b:oculum ego ecfodiam tibī̆, sī verbum addideris⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 463, ⟦i:I’ll gouge your eye out for you, if you say another word⟧. ⟦b:sī tē interficī iusserō, residēbit in rē pūblicā reliqua coniūrātōrum manus⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 12, ⟦i:if I order you to be dispatched, the rest of the gang of conspirators will be left in the state⟧.
⟦#2062⟧
⟦=⟧(d.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Future Perfect.⟧
⟦b:sī dīxerō mendācium, solēns me͡o mōre fēcerō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 198, ⟦i:if fiction I relate, I shall have done but in my usual way⟧. ⟦b:sī tū argentum attuleris, cum illō perdiderō fidem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 376, ⟦i:if you, sir, bring the cash, I’ll break my word to him⟧. ⟦b:respīrārō, sī tē vīderō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 2, 24, 5, ⟦i:I shall be myself again, if I see you⟧. ⟦b:pergrātum mihī̆ fēceris, sī dē amīcitiā disputāris⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 16, ⟦i:you will do me a very great favour, if you will discourse on friendship⟧.
⟦#2063⟧
⟦=⟧(e.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperative.⟧
Generally the longer forms of the imperative are used (⟦r1577:1577⟧): ⟦b:patrōnus sī clientī fraudem fēcerit, sacer estō⟧, Twelve Tables in Serv. to V. 6, 609, ⟦i:if a patron shall cheat his client, let him be doomed⟧. ⟦b:servītum tibi mē abdūcitō, nī fēcerō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 520, ⟦i:if I don’t do it, take me off to be your slave⟧. ⟦b:hoc sī effēceris, quodvīs dōnum ā mē optātō⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 1056, ⟦i:if you do this, ask any gift you please of me⟧. ⟦b:sī mē adsequī potueris, ut tibī̆ vidēbitur, sepelītō⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 103, ⟦i:if you can ever find me, then bury me as you think best⟧. Rarely the shorter forms: ⟦b:inpinge pugnum, sī muttīverit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 800, ⟦i:drive your fist into him if he says booh⟧. ⟦b:sī tumidōs accēdere fastūs sēnseris, inceptō parce referque pedem⟧, O. ⟦i:AA.⟧ 1, 715, ⟦i:if thou shalt see disdain come swelling high, give o’er and beat retreat⟧.
⟦#2064⟧
⟦=⟧(f.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:sibī̆ habeat, sī nōn extemplō ab eō abdūxerō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 164, ⟦i:he may keep her, if I don’t carry her off that minute⟧ (⟦r1548:1548⟧). ⟦b:caecum mē ferrī cōnfitear, sī tē potuisse superārī dīxerō⟧, ⟦i:Planc.⟧ 6, ⟦i:if I say that you can be surpassed, I should own myself swept along like a blind man⟧ (⟦r1556:1556⟧). ⟦b:tum magis adsentiāre, sī ad maiōra pervēnerō⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 1, 62, ⟦i:you would agree all the more if I come at once to weightier points⟧ (⟦r1556:1556⟧).

title: Some Special Uses
text:
⟦#2065⟧
An indicative protasis with ⟦b:sī⟧ is often used to assume a general truth as a proof either for another general truth, or for a particular fact.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:sī voluptātis sēnsum capit, dolōrēs etiam capit⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 32, ⟦i:if it is susceptible of pleasure, it is also susceptible of pain⟧. ⟦b:sī omnēs, quī rē̆ī pūblicae cōnsulunt, cārī nōbīs esse dēbent, certē in prīmīs imperātōrēs. sī ferae partūs suōs dīligunt, quā nōs in līberōs nostrōs indulgentiā esse dēbēmus⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 168, ⟦i:if all people who are devoted to the public service are dear to us, then assuredly our military men ought always to be particularly dear. If wild beasts always love their young, how kind ought we always to be to our own children⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:sī pietātī summa tribuenda laus est, dēbētis movērī, cum Q. Metellum tam piē lūgēre videātis⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 167, ⟦i:if filial affection is always to be held in high honour, you ought to be touched in this instance, seeing such affectionate grief in Metellus⟧. ⟦b:sī nox opportūna est ēruptiōnī, sīcut est, haec profectō noctis aptissima hōra est⟧, L. 7, 35, 10, ⟦i:if night is always favourable for a sortie, and it always is, this particular hour of the night is the very best time⟧.
⟦#2066⟧
An indicative protasis with ⟦b:sī⟧ often assumes a fact, past or present, as an argument for another fact, or for a general truth.
In this case the apodosis, which is usually a question, often takes the subjunctive (⟦r1565:1565⟧).
⟦b:sī Sūlla potuit efficere, ut dictātor dīcerētur, cūr hīc nōn possit?⟧ ⟦i:Att.⟧ 9, 15, 2, ⟦i:if Sulla could succeed in being appointed dictator, why cannot this man?⟧ ⟦b:sī Zēnōnī licuit inaudītum rē̆ī nōmen impōnere, cūr nōn liceat Catōnī?⟧ ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 3, 15, ⟦i:if Zeno was allowed to give a new name to a thing, why should not Cato be allowed?⟧ ⟦b:quod sī Graecī leguntur ā Graecīs, quid est cūr nostrī ā nostrīs nōn legantur?⟧ ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 1, 6, ⟦i:but if Greeks are read by Greeks, why should not Romans be read by Romans?⟧
⟦#2067⟧
An indicative protasis with ⟦b:sī⟧ often assumes a fact which is declared in the apodosis to be no reason for another fact.
In this case the negative usually begins the period. ⟦b:sī⟧, for which ⟦b:quia⟧ or ⟦b:etsī⟧ is sometimes substituted, sometimes has ⟦b:idcircō⟧, ⟦b:īlicō⟧, or ⟦b:continuō⟧, rarely ⟦b:proptereā⟧ or ⟦b:ideō⟧, as correlative in the apodosis.
⟦b:nōn, sī tibī̆ anteā prōfuit, semper prōderit⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 8, 12, ⟦i:even if it has done you good in the past, that is no reason why it always will in the future⟧. ⟦b:nōn sī Opīmium dēfendistī, idcircō tē istī bonum cīvem putābunt⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 170, ⟦i:suppose you did defend Opimius, that is no reason why your friends will think you a patriot⟧. ⟦b:nec sī omne ēnūntiātum aut vērum aut falsum est, sequitur īlicō, esse causās immūtābilīs, quae prohibeant secus cadere atque cāsūrum sit⟧, ⟦i:Fat.⟧ 28, ⟦i:and even if every declaration is either true or false, it does not follow without any further ado that there are unchangeable causes to prevent a thing falling out different from the way it promises to fall out⟧. ⟦b:nōn continuō, sī mē in gregem sīcāriōrum contulī, sum sīcārius⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 94, ⟦i:it does not forthwith follow that if I have joined a band of bravoes, I am a bravo⟧.

title: mīror, mīrum sī
text:
⟦#2068⟧
⟦b:mīror⟧ or ⟦b:mīrum est⟧ (⟦b:mīra sunt⟧) may introduce a conditional protasis, instead of a clause with ⟦b:quod⟧ (⟦r1851:1851⟧) or the accusative with the infinitive (⟦r2188:2188⟧).
Generally the main clause is actually or virtually negatived: as, ⟦b:minus mīrandumst, illaec aetās sī quid illōrum facit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 409, ⟦i:’tis not to be wondered at, if youth does things like that⟧. ⟦b:idne tū mīrāre, sī patrissat fīlius?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 442, ⟦i:can you, sir, wonder at it if the son plays the father?⟧ ⟦b:nec mīrum sī ūtēbātur cōnsiliō⟧, ⟦i:Quinct.⟧ 18, ⟦i:and it is no wonder if he followed the advice⟧. ⟦b:mīrer, sī vāna vestra auctōritās est?⟧ L. 3, 21, 4, ⟦i:can I think it strange if your influence is of no account⟧ (⟦r1565:1565⟧)⟦i:?⟧ Rarely the main clause is positive: as, ⟦b:mīrābar hoc sī sīc abīret⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 175, ⟦i:I wondered if it was going to end so⟧ (⟦r1773:1773⟧). ⟦b:mīror sī quemquam amīcum habēre potuit⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 54, ⟦i:I wonder if he could have had a friend in the world⟧. In old colloquial style ⟦b:mīrum nī⟧ is found: as, ⟦b:mīrum nī hīc me exossāre cōgitat⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 319, ⟦i:strange that he doesn’t think of boning me⟧. ⟦b:ubi nunc ipsus? :: mīrum nī domīst⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 598, ⟦i:where is he now? :: at home of course⟧. So once in Livy: ⟦b:mīrum esse nī castra hostium oppugnentur⟧, L. 3, 28, 5, ⟦i:that he shouldn’t be surprised if the enemy’s camp were being stormed⟧ (⟦r1724:1724⟧). ⟦b:gaudeō sī⟧ is found once in Cicero, and ⟦b:terreō, metus est sī⟧, or the like occurs a few times in Tacitus. For ⟦b:sī⟧ in expressions of trial, hope, expectation, &c., see ⟦r1777:1777⟧.

title: The Subjunctive for the Indicative
text:
⟦#2069⟧
The indicative in the protasis is occasionally replaced by the subjunctive, as follows:
⟦#2070⟧
(1.) The present or perfect subjunctive is sometimes used in general present suppositions, regularly in the indefinite second person singular, rarely with other persons (⟦r1730:1730⟧): as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:nam dolī nōn dolī sunt nisi astū colās, sed malum maxumum, sī id palam prōvenit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 221, ⟦i:for tricks are never tricks, unless you handle them with craft, but damage dire, in case the thing gets out⟧; here the indicative ⟦b:prōvenit⟧ shows that ⟦b:colās⟧ is due to the person. ⟦b:nec calidae citius dēcēdunt corpore febrēs, textilibus sī in pīctūrīs ostrōque rubentī iactēris, quam sī in plēbēiā veste cubandum est⟧, Lucr. 2, 34, ⟦i:nor sooner will hot fevers leave the limbs, if on gay tapestries and blushing purple you should toss, than if perforce your bed you make on pallet rude⟧. ⟦b:quod est difficile, nisi speciem prae tē bonī virī ferās⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 2, 39, ⟦i:and this is a hard thing, unless you have the exterior of a good man⟧. ⟦b:nec habēre virtūtem satis est nisi ūtāre⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 1, 2, ⟦i:and to have virtue is not enough, unless one use it⟧. ⟦b:sīquoi mūtuom quid dederīs, fit prō propriō perditum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 1051, ⟦i:if aught you’ve lent to anyone, ’tis not your own, but lost⟧. ⟦b:nam nūllae magis rēs duae plūs negōtī habent, sī occēperīs exōrnāre⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 212, ⟦i:for no two things give more trouble if you once begin to fit them out⟧. ⟦b:nūlla est excūsātiō peccātī, sī amīcī causā peccāverīs⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 37, ⟦i:it is no excuse for a sin if you have sinned from friendship⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:suōs quisque opprimī nōn patitur, neque, aliter sī faciat, ūllam inter suōs habet auctōritātem⟧, 6, 11, 4, ⟦i:nobody suffers his vassals to be put down, and if he ever act otherwise, he has no influence among his people⟧. ⟦b:laeduntur artēriae, sī ācrī clāmōre compleantur⟧, Cornif. 3, 21, ⟦i:it always hurts the windpipe, if it be filled out with a sharp scream⟧. ⟦b:turpis excūsātiō est, sī quis contrā rem pūblicam sē amīcī causā fēcisse fateātur⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 40, ⟦i:it is always a discreditable apology, if a man confess that he has been unpatriotic from motives of friendship⟧. ⟦b:Britannī iniūncta imperiī mūnera impigrē obeunt, sī iniūriae absint⟧, Ta. ⟦i:Agr.⟧ 13, ⟦i:the Britons are always perfectly ready to perform the duties enjoined on them by the Roman government, if they be not maltreated⟧.
⟦#2071⟧
(2.) The imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive is sometimes used in general past suppositions (⟦r1730:1730⟧).
This use begins with Catullus and Caesar, the indicative being the regular classical construction (⟦r2044:2044⟧, ⟦r2050:2050⟧).
⟦b:chommoda dīcēbat, sī quandō commoda vellet dīcere Arrius⟧, Cat. 84, 1, ⟦i:hadvantages said Arrius, if advantages he ever meant to say⟧. ⟦b:sī quis prehenderētur, cōnsēnsū mīlitum ēripiēbātur⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 110, 4, ⟦i:every time a man was taken up, he was rescued by the joint action of the rank and file⟧. ⟦b:sīn autem locum tenēre vellent, nec virtūtī locus relinquēbātur, neque coniecta tēla vītāre poterant⟧, 5, 35, 4, ⟦i:but if on the other hand they undertook to hold their position, there was never any opening for bravery, nor could they ever dodge the shower of missiles⟧. ⟦b:sīn Numidae propius accessissent, ibī̆ virtūtem ostendere⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 58, 3, ⟦i:they showed forth their valour every time the Numidians drew near⟧ (⟦r1535:1535⟧).

title: Subjunctive Use
text:
⟦#2072⟧
The present or perfect subjunctive may be used in a conditional protasis of future time.
⟦#2073⟧
The apodosis is usually in the present subjunctive, less frequently in the perfect subjunctive. The imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive are rare (⟦r2089:2089⟧).
⟦#2074⟧
The indicative is sometimes used in the apodosis, especially in expressions of ability, duty, &c. (⟦r1495:1495⟧); ⟦b:nōn possum⟧ is regularly in the indicative when the protasis is also negative. For the future indicative the periphrastic form is sometimes used.
⟦#2075⟧
In the early period, before the imperfect subjunctive had been shifted to denote present time in conditional sentences (⟦r2091:2091⟧), the present subjunctive was used to express action non-occurrent in present time. Examples of this use are found in Plautus: as, ⟦b:sī honestē cēnseam tē facere posse, suādeam; vērum nōn potest; cave faxīs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 1371, ⟦i:if I thought that you could do the thing with credit to yourself, I should advise you to; but ’tis impossible; so don’t you do it⟧. ⟦b:vocem tē ad cēnam, nisi egomet cēnem forīs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 190, ⟦i:I should ask you home to dine, if I were not dining out myself⟧. Such sentences must not be confused with those in which an action from the nature of things impossible is represented as of possible occurrence.

title: Protasis in the Present Subjunctive
text:
⟦#2076⟧
⟦=⟧(a.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:at pigeat posteā nostrum erum, sī vōs eximat vinculīs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 203, ⟦i:but it may rue our master by and by, if he should take you out of bonds⟧. ⟦b:quid sī ēveniat dēsubitō prandium, ubī̆ ego tum accumbam?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 79, ⟦i:suppose a lunch should suddenly come off, where is your humble servant then to lie⟧ (⟦r1563:1563⟧)? ⟦b:hanc viam sī asperam esse negem, mentiar⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 100, ⟦i:if I say that this path is not rough, I should not tell the truth⟧. ⟦b:sī deus tē interroget, quid respondeās?⟧ ⟦i:Ac.⟧ 2, 80, ⟦i:if a god ask you, what would you answer?⟧ ⟦b:haec sī tēcum patria loquātur, nōnne impetrāre dēbeat?⟧ ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 19, ⟦i:if thy country plead with thee thus, ought she not to carry her point?⟧ ⟦b:sī existat hodiē ab īnferīs Lycūrgus, sē Spartam antīquam āgnōscere dīcat⟧, L. 39, 37, 3, ⟦i:if Lycurgus rise this day from the dead, he would say that he recognized the Sparta of yore⟧. ⟦b:eōs nōn cūrāre opīnor, quid agat hūmānum genus; nam sī cūrent, bene bonīs sit, male malīs, quod nunc abest⟧, E. in ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 104, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 79, ⟦i:but little care the gods, I trow, how fares the race of man; for should they care, the good were blest, the wicked curst; a thing that really cometh not to pass⟧.
⟦#2077⟧
⟦=⟧(b.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Perfect Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:sī aequom siet mē plūs sapere quam vōs, dederim vōbīs cōnsilium catum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:E.⟧ 257, ⟦i:if it becoming be for me to have more wit than ye, sage counsel might I give⟧ (⟦r1558:1558⟧). ⟦b:aufūgerim potius quam redeam, sī eō mihi redeundum sciam⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 424, ⟦i:I’d run away sooner than go back, if I should hear I had to⟧ (⟦r1558:1558⟧). ⟦b:nec satis sciō, nec sī sciam, dīcere ausim⟧, L. ⟦i:praef.⟧ 1, ⟦i:in the first place I do not know very well, and secondly if I should know, I should not venture to say⟧ (⟦r1555:1555⟧). ⟦b:iniussū tuō extrā ōrdinem numquam pugnāverim, nōn sī certam victōriam videam⟧, L. 7, 10, 2, ⟦i:without orders from you I never should fight out of ranks, no, not if I saw victory was certain⟧ (⟦r1558:1558⟧). ⟦b:tum vērō nēquīquam hāc dextrā capitōlium servāverim, si cīvem commīlitōnemque meum in vincula dūcī videam⟧, L. 6, 14, 4, ⟦i:upon my word, in that case I should prove to have saved the capital in vain, if I saw a townsman and brother-in-arms of mine haled to jail⟧. ⟦b:multōs circā ūnam rem ambitūs fēcerim, sī quae variant auctōrēs omnia exequī velim⟧, L. 27, 27, 12, ⟦i:I should make a long story about one subject, if I should undertake to go through all the different versions of the authorities⟧.
⟦#2078⟧
⟦=⟧(c.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present Indicative.⟧
⟦b:quī sī decem habeās linguās, mūtum esse addecet⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 128, ⟦i:if you should have a dozen tongues, ’tis fit you should be dumb⟧ (⟦r2074:2074⟧). ⟦b:sī prō peccātīs centum dūcat uxōrēs, parumst⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 1186, ⟦i:if he should wed a hundred wives in payment for his sins, ’tis not enough⟧. ⟦b:intrāre, sī possim, castra hostium volō⟧, L. 2, 12, 5, ⟦i:I propose to enter the camp of the enemy, if I be able⟧. ⟦b:tē neque dēbent adiuvāre, sī possint, neque possunt, sī velint⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 20, ⟦i:they ought not to help you, if they could, and cannot, if they would⟧. ⟦b:sī vōcem rērum nātūra repente mittat, quid respondēmus?⟧ Lucr. 3, 931, ⟦i:if Nature of a sudden lift her voice, what answer shall we make?⟧ ⟦b:sī quaerātur, idemne sit pertinācia et persevērantia, dēfīnītiōnibus iūdicandum est⟧, ⟦i:T.⟧ 87, ⟦i:if it be asked whether obstinacy and perseverance are the same, it must be settled by definitions⟧ (⟦r2074:2074⟧).
⟦#2079⟧
⟦=⟧(d.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Future.⟧
⟦b:quadrīgās sī īnscendās Iovis atque hinc fugiās, ita vix poteris effugere īnfortūnium⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 450, ⟦i:Jove’s four-in-hand if you should mount, and try to flee from here, even so you’ll scarce escape a dreadful doom⟧. ⟦b:sīquidem summum Iovem tē dīcās dētinuisse, malam rem effugiēs numquam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 414, ⟦i:e’en shouldst thou say imperial Jove detained thee, chastisement thou’lt ne’er avoid⟧. ⟦b:sī frāctus inlābātur orbis, inpavidum ferient ruīnae⟧, H. 3, 3, 7, ⟦i:should heaven’s vault crumbling fall, him all undaunted will its ruin strike⟧. ⟦b:neque tū hoc dīcere audēbis, nec sī cupiās, licēbit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 167, ⟦i:you will not dare to say this, sir, nor if you wish, will you be allowed⟧.
⟦#2080⟧
⟦=⟧(e.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Future Perfect.⟧
⟦b:nōn tantum, sī proeliō vincās, glōriae adiēceris, quantum adēmeris, sī quid adversī ēveniat⟧, L. 30, 30, 21, ⟦i:you will not acquire as much glory, if you succeed in battle, as you will lose, if any reverse occur⟧.
⟦#2081⟧
