⟦=⟧(f.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Periphrastic Future.⟧
⟦b:nōn latūrus sum, sī iubeās maxumē⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 1004, ⟦i:I don’t intend to be the bearer, should you urge me e’er so much⟧. ⟦b:quid, sī hostēs ad urbem veniant, factūrī estis?⟧ L. 3, 52, 7, ⟦i:suppose the enemy march on the town, what do you intend to do?⟧
⟦#2082⟧
⟦=⟧(g.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperfect Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:cantus et Lūnam dēdūcere temptat et faceret, sī nōn aera repulsa sonent⟧, Tib. 1, 8, 21, ⟦i:magic essays to draw Luna down and would succeed if clashing brass should not resound⟧ (⟦r1560:1560⟧). ⟦b:nē sī nāvigāre quidem velim, ita gubernārem, ut somniāverim; praesēns enim poena sit⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 122, ⟦i:again, suppose I undertake to go sailing, I should not lay my course as I may have dreamed; for the penalty would be swift⟧ (⟦r1560:1560⟧). ⟦b:sī hodiē bella sint, quāle Etrūscum fuit, quāle Gallicum; possētisne ferre Sextium cōnsulem esse?⟧ L. 6, 40, 17, ⟦i:suppose there be wars to-day like the Etruscan and the Gallic wars: could you bear to see Sextius consul⟧ (⟦r1565:1565⟧)?
⟦#2083⟧
⟦=⟧(h.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Pluperfect Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:carmina nī sint, ex umerō Pelopis nōn nituisset ebur⟧, Tib. 1, 4, 63, ⟦i:suppose there be no verse, from Pelops’ shoulder ne’er had ivory gleamed⟧ (⟦r1561:1561⟧).

title: Protasis in the Perfect Subjunctive
text:
⟦#2084⟧
⟦=⟧(a.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:dēbeam, crēdō, istī quicquam furciferō, sī id fēcerim⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 861, ⟦i:I should be, forsooth, responsible to the rogue, if I should do it⟧ (⟦r1556:1556⟧). ⟦b:sī dē caelō vīlla tācta siet, dē eā rē verba utī fīant⟧, Cato, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 14, 3, ⟦i:if the villa be struck by lightning, let there be utterances about the case⟧ (⟦r1547:1547⟧). ⟦b:sī ā corōnā relictus sim, nōn queam dīcere⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 192, ⟦i:if I should ever be abandoned by my audience, I should not be able to speak⟧. ⟦b:id sī acciderit, sīmus armātī⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 78, ⟦i:if this have happened, let us be on our guard⟧ (⟦r1548:1548⟧). ⟦b:cūr ego simulem mē, sī quid in hīs studiīs operae posuerim, perdidisse?⟧ ⟦i:Par.⟧ 33, ⟦i:why should I have the affectation to say that if I have spent any time in these pursuits, I have thrown it away⟧ (⟦r1563:1563⟧)? See also ⟦r2090:2090⟧.
⟦#2085⟧
⟦=⟧(b.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Perfect Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:sī paululum modo quid tē fūgerīt, ego perierim⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 316, ⟦i:should you have missed the smallest point, a dead man I should be⟧. See also ⟦r2090:2090⟧.
⟦#2086⟧
⟦=⟧(c.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Future Indicative.⟧
⟦b:sī forte līber fierī occēperim, mittam nūntium ad tē⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 1362, ⟦i:if haply I should be by way of getting free, I’ll send you word⟧. ⟦b:sī forte morbus amplior factus siet, servom intrō iisse dīcent Sōstratae⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 330, ⟦i:if her illness should get worse, they’ll say a slave of Sostrata’s went in there⟧.
⟦#2087⟧
⟦=⟧(d.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Periphrastic Future.⟧
⟦b:sī Vēīs incendium ortum sit, Fĭ̄dēnās inde quaesītūrī sumus?⟧ L. 5, 54, 1, ⟦i:if a fire break out at Vei, are we going to move from there to Fidenae?⟧
⟦#2088⟧
⟦=⟧(e.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperfect Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:sīquis hoc gnātō tuō tuos servos faxit, quālem habērēs grātiam?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 711, ⟦i:suppose a slave of yours has done this for a son of yours, how grateful should you have been?⟧

title: Conversion to Past Time
text:
⟦#2089⟧
An indeterminate subjunctive protasis is rarely thrown into the past, the present and perfect becoming respectively imperfect and pluperfect. In this case the form is the same as that of a protasis of action non-occurrent (⟦r2091:2091⟧), and the conversion occurs only when it is evident from the context that past action is supposed, which may or may not have occurred: as,
⟦b:cūr igitur et Camillus dolēret, sī haec post trecentōs et quīnquāgintā ferē annōs ēventūra putāret, et ego doleam, sī ad decem mīlia annōrum gentem aliquam urbe nostrā potītūram putem?⟧ ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 90, ⟦i:why then would Camillus have fretted, if he thought this would occur after a lapse of some three hundred and fifty years, and why should I fret, if I think that some nation may seize Rome some ten thousand years hence?⟧ ⟦b:erat sōla illa nāvis cōnstrāta; quae sī in praedōnum pugnā versārētur, urbis īnstar habēre inter illōs pīrāticōs myoparōnēs vidērētur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 89, ⟦i:this was the only vessel with a deck; and supposing she figured in the engagement with the corsairs, she would have loomed up like a town, surrounded by those pirate cock-boats⟧. ⟦b:Sardus habēbat ille Tigellius hoc; Caesar sī peteret nōn quicquam prōficeret⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 3, 4, ⟦i:Tigellius the Sardian had this way; supposing Caesar asked him, naught had he availed⟧.

title: Periods of Exemplification
text:
⟦#2090⟧
The present subjunctive is particularly common in exemplification. The perfect is sometimes used in the protasis, rarely in the apodosis: as,
⟦b:sī pater fāna expīlet, indicetne id magistrātibus fīlius?⟧ ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 90, ⟦i:if a father should plunder temples, would the son report it to the magistrates?⟧ ⟦b:sī quis pater familiās supplicium nōn sūmpserit, utrum is clēmēns an crūdēlissimus esse videātur?⟧ ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 12, ⟦i:assume for the sake of argument that a householder have not inflicted punishment, would he seem merciful, or a monster of cruelty?⟧ ⟦b:sī scierīs aspidem occultē latēre uspiam, et velle aliquem imprūdentem super eam adsīdere, improbē fēcerīs, nisi monuerīs nē adsīdat⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 59, ⟦i:suppose a man should know, e.g. that there was a snake hiding somewhere, and that somebody was going to sit down on the snake unawares; he would do wrong, if he did not tell him he must not sit down there⟧. In such periods the future is also used, but less frequently: see 2054.

title: Protases of Action Non-occurrent
text:
⟦#2091⟧
A conditional period in which the non-occurrence of the action is implied takes the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive both in the protasis and in the apodosis. The imperfect usually denotes present or indefinite time, and the pluperfect denotes past time.
For the present subjunctive in such conditions, see ⟦r2075:2075⟧.
⟦#2092⟧
The imperfect sometimes denotes past time (⟦r1559:1559⟧). When future time is referred to, the protasis is usually in the imperfect of the periphrastic future, commonly the subjunctive, but sometimes the indicative (⟦r2108:2108⟧).
⟦#2093⟧
The apodosis is very rarely in the present subjunctive (⟦r2098:2098⟧). The periphrastic future is sometimes used, commonly in the indicative (⟦r2097:2097⟧, ⟦r2100:2100⟧).

title: Protasis in the Imperfect Subjunctive
text:
⟦#2094⟧
⟦=⟧(a.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperfect Subjunctive.⟧
(a.) Protasis and apodosis both denoting present action; this is the usual application: ⟦b:sī intus esset, ēvocārem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 640, ⟦i:I should call him out, if he were in⟧. ⟦b:is iam prīdem est mortuus. sī vīveret, verba eius audīrētis⟧, ⟦i:RC.⟧ 42, ⟦i:that person has long been dead; if he were alive, you would hear his evidence⟧. ⟦b:adnuere tē videō; prōferrem librōs, sī negārēs⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 113, ⟦i:I see you nod assent; I should bring out the books, if you maintained the opposite⟧. ⟦b:sī L. Mummius aliquem istōrum vidēret Corinthium cupidissimē trāctantem, utrum illum cīvem excellentem, an ātriēnsem dīligentem putāret?⟧ ⟦i:Par.⟧ 38, ⟦i:if Mummius should see one of your connoisseurs nursing a piece of Corinthian, and going into perfect ecstasies over it, what would he think? that the man was a model citizen or a thoroughly competent indoor-man?⟧ ⟦b:quod sī semper optima tenēre possēmus, haud sānē cōnsiliō multum egērēmus⟧, ⟦i:OP.⟧ 89, ⟦i:now if we could always be in possession of what is best, we should not ever stand in any special need of reasoning⟧.
(b.) Protasis and apodosis both denoting past action: ⟦b:haec sī neque ego neque tū fēcimus, nōn siit egestās facere nōs; nam sī esset unde id fīeret, facerēmus; et tū illum tuom, sī essēs homō, sinerēs nunc facere⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 103, ⟦i:if neither you nor I have acted thus, ’twas poverty that stinted us; for if we’d had the means, we should have done so too; and you would let that boy of yours, if you were human, do it now⟧. Here ⟦b:esset⟧ refers to past time, ⟦b:essēs⟧ to present. ⟦b:num igitur eum, sī tum essēs, temerārium cīvem putārēs?⟧ ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 8, 14, ⟦i:would you therefore have thought him, if you had lived then, a hotheaded citizen?⟧ ⟦b:sī ūniversa prōvincia loquī posset, hāc vōce ūterētur; quoniam id nōn poterat, hārum rērum āctōrem ipsa dēlēgit⟧, ⟦i:Caecil.⟧ 19, ⟦i:if the collective province could have spoken, she would have used these words; but since she could not, she chose a manager for the case herself⟧.
⟦#2095⟧
⟦=⟧(b.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Pluperfect Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:invēnissēmus iam diū, sei vīveret⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 241, ⟦i:were he alive, we should have found him long ago⟧. ⟦b:sī mihi secundae rēs dē amōre meō essent, iam dūdum sciō vēnissent⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 230, ⟦i:if everything were well about my love, I know they would have been here long ago⟧. ⟦b:quae nisi essent in senibus, nōn summum cōnsilium maiōrēs nostrī appellāssent senātum⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 19, ⟦i:unless the elderly were in general characterized by these qualities, our ancestors would not have called the highest deliberative body the body of elders⟧.
⟦#2096⟧
⟦=⟧(c.) ⟦b:Periphrastic Apodosis.⟧
⟦b:quibus, sī Rōmae esset, facile contentus futūrus erat⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 12, 32, 2, ⟦i:with which, if he were in Rome, he would readily be satisfied⟧ (⟦r2093:2093⟧). ⟦b:quōs ego, sī tribūnī mē triumphāre prohibērent, testēs citātūrus fuī rērum ā mē gestārum⟧, L. 38, 47, 4, ⟦i:the very men whom I was to call to bear witness to my deeds, if the tribunes should refuse me a triumph⟧.

title: Protasis in the Pluperfect Subjunctive
text:
⟦#2097⟧
⟦=⟧(a.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperfect Subjunctive.⟧
(a.) Protasis denoting past, apodosis present action: ⟦b:sī ante voluissēs, essēs; nunc sērō cupis⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 568, ⟦i:if you had wished it before, you might be; as it is, you long too late⟧. ⟦b:sī nōn mēcum aetātem ēgisset, hodiē stulta vīveret⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 1320, ⟦i:if she hadn’t spent her life with me, she’d be a fool to-day⟧. ⟦b:sī tum illī respondēre voluissem, nunc rē̆ī pūblicae cōnsulere nōn possem⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 3, 33, ⟦i:if I had chosen to answer the man then, I should not be able to promote the public interest now⟧. ⟦b:quō quidem tempore sī meum cōnsilium valuisset, tū hodiē egērēs, nōs līberī essēmus⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 37, ⟦i:if by the way at that time my counsel had been regarded, you, sir, would be a beggar to-day and we should be free⟧.
(b.) Protasis and apodosis both referring to past: ⟦b:ōlim sī advēnissem, magis tū tum istūc dīcerēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 871, ⟦i:if I had come before, you’d have said so then all the more⟧. ⟦b:num igitur, sī ad centēsimum annum vīxisset, senectūtis eum suae paenitēret?⟧ ⟦i:CM.⟧ 19, ⟦i:suppose therefore he had lived to be a hundred, would he have regretted his years?⟧ ⟦b:Indōs aliāsque sī adiūnxisset gentēs, impedimentum maius quam auxilium traheret⟧, L. 9, 19, 5, ⟦i:if he had added the Indians and other nations, he would have found them a hindrance rather than a help in his train⟧.
⟦#2098⟧
⟦=⟧(b.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Pluperfect Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:sī appellāssēs, respondisset nōminī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 927, ⟦i:if you had called him, he’d have answered to his name⟧. ⟦b:nisi fūgissem, medium praemorsisset⟧, Pl. in Gell. 6, 9, 7, ⟦i:if I hadn’t run away, he’d have bitten me in two⟧. ⟦b:sī vēnissēs ad exercitum, ā tribūnīs vīsus essēs; nōn es autem ab hīs vīsus⟧; ⟦b:nōn es igitur ad exercitum profectus⟧, ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 1, 87, ⟦i:if you had come to the army, you would have been seen by the tribunes; but you have not been seen by them; therefore you have not been to the army⟧. ⟦b:sī beātus umquam fuisset, beātam vītam usque ad rogum pertulisset⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 3, 76, ⟦i:if he had ever been a child of fortune, he would have continued the life of bliss to the funeral pyre⟧. ⟦b:nisi mīlitēs essent dēfessī, omnēs hostium cōpiae dēlērī potuissent⟧, 7, 88, 6, ⟦i:unless the soldiers had been utterly exhausted, the entire force of the enemy might have been exterminated⟧ (⟦r2101:2101⟧). ⟦b:quod sī Catilīna in urbe remānsisset, dīmicandum nōbīs cum illō fuisset⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 17, ⟦i:but if Catiline had staid in town we should have had to fight with the villain⟧ (⟦r2101:2101⟧).
⟦#2099⟧
⟦=⟧(c.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Present Subjunctive.⟧
⟦b:vocem ego tē ad mē ad cēnam, frāter tuos nisi dīxisset mihī̆ tē apud sē cēnātūrum esse hodiē⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 510, ⟦i:I should like to invite you home to dinner, if my brother hadn’t told me that you were to dine with him to-day⟧.
⟦#2100⟧
⟦=⟧(d.) ⟦b:Periphrastic Apodosis.⟧
(a.) ⟦b:sī tacuisset, ego eram dictūrus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cist.⟧ 152, ⟦i:if she had held her peace, I was going to tell⟧ (⟦r2093:2093⟧). ⟦b:sī P. Sēstius occīsus esset, fuistisne ad arma itūrī?⟧ ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 81, ⟦i:if Sestius had been slain, were you disposed to rush to arms?⟧ ⟦b:conclāve illud, ubī̆ erat mānsūrus, sī īre perrēxisset, conruit⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 1, 26, ⟦i:the suite of rooms where he was going to spend the night, if he had pushed on, tumbled down⟧. ⟦b:Teucrās fuerat mersūra carīnās, nī prius in scopulum trānsfōrmāta foret⟧, O. 14, 72, ⟦i:she had gone on to sink the Trojan barks unless she had been changed into a rock⟧. (b.) ⟦b:quem sī vīcisset, habitūrus esset impūnitātem sempiternam⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 84, ⟦i:and if he overcame him, he would be likely to have exemption from punishment forever and ever⟧ (⟦r2093:2093⟧). ⟦b:aut nōn fātō interiīt exercitus, aut sī fātō, etiam sī obtemperāsset auspiciīs, idem ēventūrum fuisset⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 21, ⟦i:the destruction of his army was either not due to fate, or if to fate, it would have happened all the same, even if he had conformed to the auspices⟧.

title: Indicative Apodosis
text:
⟦#2101⟧
(1.) The apodosis of verbs of ability, duty, &c. (⟦r1495:1495-1497⟧), including the gerundive with ⟦b:sum⟧, is often in the indicative, the imperfect taking the place of the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive, and the perfect that of the pluperfect subjunctive. But the subjunctive is also found, especially ⟦b:possem⟧ rather than ⟦b:poteram⟧.
⟦#2102⟧
⟦=⟧(a.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperfect Indicative.⟧
(a.) Of present action: ⟦b:quod sī Rōmae Cn. Pompēius prīvātus esset, tamen ad tantum bellum is erat mittendus⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 50, ⟦i:now if Pompey were at Rome, in private station, still he would be the man to send to this important war⟧. ⟦b:quem patris locō, sī ūlla in tē pietās esset, colere dēbēbās⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 99, ⟦i:whom you ought to honour as a father, if you had any such thing as affection in you⟧.
(b.) Of past action: ⟦b:quid enim poterat Heius respondēre, sī esset improbus?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 16, ⟦i:for what answer could Hejus have given, if he were an unprincipled man?⟧ ⟦b:sī sordidam vestem habuissent, lūgentium Perseī cāsum praebēre speciem poterant⟧, L. 45, 20, 5, ⟦i:if they had worn dark clothing, they might have presented the mien of mourners for the fall of Perseus⟧.
⟦#2103⟧
⟦=⟧(b.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Perfect Indicative.⟧
⟦b:nōn potuit reperīre, sī ipsī sōlī quaerendās darēs, lepidiōrēs duās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 803, ⟦i:if you assigned the search to Sol himself, he couldn’t have found two jollier girls⟧. ⟦b:quō modo pultāre potuī sī nōn tangerem?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 462, ⟦i:how could I have knocked, if I hadn’t touched the door?⟧ ⟦b:licitumst, sī vellēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 566, ⟦i:you might have been, if you’d wished⟧. ⟦b:sī meum imperium exsequī voluissēs, interemptam oportuit⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 634, ⟦i:if you had been willing to follow my commands, she should have been dispatched⟧. ⟦b:cōnsul esse quī potuī, nisi eum vītae cursum tenuissem ā pueritiā?⟧ ⟦i:RP.⟧ 1, 10, ⟦i:how could I have been consul unless from boyhood I had taken that line in life?⟧ ⟦b:sī eum captīvitās in urbem pertrāxisset, Caesarem ipsum audīre potuit⟧, Ta. ⟦i:D.⟧ 17, ⟦i:if captivity had carried him to the city, he could have heard Caesar himself⟧. ⟦b:Antōnī gladiōs potuit contemnere, sī sīc omnia dīxisset⟧, J. 10, 123, ⟦i:Antonius’ swords he might have scorned, if all things he had worded so⟧. ⟦b:sī ūnum diem morātī essētis, moriendum omnibus fuit⟧, L. 2, 38, 5, ⟦i:if you had staid one day, you must all have died⟧.
⟦#2104⟧
(2.) Other verbs also sometimes have a past indicative apodosis, usually an imperfect or pluperfect, to denote an action very near to actual performance, which is interrupted by the action of the protasis.
Naturally such a protasis generally contains an actual or a virtual negative; but positive protases are found here and there, chiefly in late writers.
⟦#2105⟧
⟦=⟧(a.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Perfect Indicative.⟧
⟦b:paene in foveam dēcidī, nī hīc adessēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 594, ⟦i:I had almost fallen into a snare, unless you were here⟧. ⟦b:nec vēnī, nisi fāta locum sēdemque dedissent⟧, V. 11, 112, ⟦i:nor had I come, unless the fates a place and seat had given⟧. ⟦b:pōns sublicius iter paene hostibus dedit, nī ūnus vir fuisset Horātius Cocles⟧, L. 2, 10, 2, ⟦i:the pile-bridge all but gave a path to the enemy, had it not been for one heroic soul, Horatius Cocles⟧.
⟦#2106⟧
⟦=⟧(b.) ⟦b:Apodosis in the Imperfect Indicative.⟧
⟦b:quīn lābēbar longius, nisi mē retinuissem⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 1, 52, ⟦i:why, I was going to drift on still further, if I had not checked myself⟧. ⟦b:sī per L. Metellum licitum esset, mātrēs illōrum veniēbant⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 129, ⟦i:if Metellus had not prevented, the mothers of those people were just coming⟧; here the protasis may be held to contain a virtual negative; so in the last example on this page. ⟦b:castra excindere parābant, nī Mūciānus sextam legiōnem opposuisset⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 3, 46, ⟦i:they were preparing to destroy the camp, had not Mucianus checked them with the sixth legion⟧. ⟦b:sī dēstināta prōvēnissent, rēgnō imminēbat⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 4, 18, ⟦i:had his schemes succeeded, he was close upon the throne⟧.
⟦#2107⟧
⟦=⟧(c.) Apodosis in the Pluperfect Indicative.
⟦b:quīngentōs simul, nī hebes machaera foret, ūnō ictū occīderās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 52, ⟦i:five hundred, had your glaive not blunted been, at one fell swoop you’d slain⟧. ⟦b:praeclārē vīcerāmus, nisi Lepidus recēpisset Antōnium⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 12, 10, 3, ⟦i:we had gained a splendid victory, if Lepidus had not taken Antony under his protection⟧. ⟦b:quod ipsum fortūna ēripuerat, nisi ūnīus amīcī opēs subvēnissent⟧, ⟦i:RabP.⟧ 48, ⟦i:even this boon fortune had wrenched from him, unless he had been assisted by a single friend⟧. ⟦b:sī gladium nōn strīnxissem, tamen triumphum merueram⟧, L. 38, 49, 12, ⟦i:if I had not drawn my sword, I had still earned my triumph⟧. ⟦b:perierat imperium, sī Fabius tantum ausus esset quantum īra suādēbat⟧, Sen. ⟦i:de Ira⟧, 1, 11, 5, ⟦i:the empire had been lost, if Fabius had ventured as far as passion urged⟧.
⟦#2108⟧
⟦=⟧(3.) Periphrastic Protasis.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:ac sī tibī̆ nēmō respōnsūrus esset, tamen causam dēmōnstrāre nōn possēs⟧, ⟦i:Caecil.⟧ 43, ⟦i:and even supposing that nobody were going to answer you, still you would not be able to make the case good⟧ (⟦r2092:2092⟧). ⟦b:plūribus vōs, mīlitēs, hortārer, sī cum armātīs dīmicātiō futūra esset⟧, L. 24, 38, 9, ⟦i:I should exhort you at greater length, my men, if there was to be a tug with armed men⟧ (⟦r2092:2092⟧). (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:sī domum tuam expugnātūrus eram, nōn temperāssem vīnō in ūnum diem?⟧ L. 40, 14, 4, ⟦i:if I intended to capture your house, should I not have abstained from wine for a day⟧ (⟦r2092:2092⟧)?

title: Variation of the Protasis
text:
⟦#2109⟧
Instead of a conditional protasis with ⟦b:sī⟧ or ⟦b:nisi⟧, equivalents are often used.
⟦#2110⟧
Thus, the protasis may be coordinated (⟦r1701:1701⟧), or be introduced by a relative pronoun (⟦r1812:1812⟧), by ⟦b:quod⟧ (⟦r1843:1843⟧), ⟦b:cum⟧ (⟦r1859:1859⟧, ⟦r1860:1860⟧), ⟦b:ubī̆⟧ (⟦r1932:1932⟧), ⟦b:ut⟧ or ⟦b:nē⟧ (⟦r1963:1963⟧), ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦b:dum modo⟧, ⟦b:modo⟧ (⟦r2003:2003⟧), or ⟦b:quandō⟧ (⟦r2011:2011⟧). Or the protasis may be intimated by ⟦b:sine⟧, ⟦i:without⟧, ⟦b:cum⟧, ⟦i:with⟧, by a participle or ablative absolute, by a wish, or otherwise: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:nēmō umquam sine magnā spē immortālitātis sē prō patriā offerret ad mortem⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 32, ⟦i:nobody would ever expose himself to death for his country without a well-grounded conviction of immortality⟧. ⟦b:cum hāc dōte poteris vel mendīcō nūbere⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 396, ⟦i:with such a dowry you can e’en a beggar wed⟧. ⟦b:Sūlla, crēdō, hunc petentem repudiāsset⟧, ⟦i:Arch.⟧ 25, ⟦i:Sulla, I suppose, would have turned my client away, if he petitioned him⟧. ⟦b:quae legentem fefellissent, trānsferentem fugere nōn possunt⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 7, 9, 2, ⟦i:what would have escaped a reader can’t escape a translator⟧. ⟦b:vīvere ego Britannicō potiente rērum poteram?⟧ Ta. 13, 21, ⟦i:as for me, could I live, if Britannicus were on the throne⟧ (⟦r2102:2102⟧)? ⟦b:nisi tē salvō salvī esse nōn possumus⟧, ⟦i:Marc.⟧ 32, ⟦i:without you safe, safe we cannot be⟧. ⟦b:aspicerēs utinam, Sāturnia: mītior essēs⟧, O. 2, 435, ⟦i:would thou couldst see, Saturnia; thou wouldst gentler be⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:habet ōrātiōnem tālem cōnsul, quālem numquam Catilīna vīctor habuisset⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 28, ⟦i:he makes a speech—yes, and he a consul—such as a Catiline would never have made, if flushed with success⟧. ⟦b:revereāris occursum, nōn reformīdēs⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 1, 10, 7, ⟦i:you might well be abashed in his presence, but you would not be afraid⟧. ⟦b:dī immortālēs mentem illī perditō ac furiōsō dedērunt ut huic faceret insidiās; aliter perīre pestis illa nōn potuit⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 88, ⟦i:the immortal gods inspired that mad miscreant to waylay my client; otherwise, that monster could not have been destroyed⟧. For the use of ⟦b:absque⟧ in a coordinate protasis in Plautus and Terence, see ⟦r1701:1701⟧, ⟦r1421:1421⟧.
⟦#2111⟧
The verb of the protasis is sometimes omitted: as in abridged sentences (⟦r1057:1057⟧), or when it may be easily supplied (⟦r1036:1036⟧).
⟦b:aut enim nēmō, aut sī quisquam, ille sapiēns fuit⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 9, ⟦i:for either nobody or, if anybody, that was a wise man⟧. ⟦b:sī ēveniet, gaudēbimus: sīn secus, patiēmur⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cas.⟧ 377, ⟦i:if it shall come to pass, glad shall we be; if else, we shall endure⟧. ⟦b:mē voluisse, sī haec cīvitās est, cīvem esse mē; sī nōn, exsulem esse⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 7, 3, 5, ⟦i:that I wished, if this is a commonwealth, to be a citizen of it; if it is not, to be an exile⟧. ⟦b:sūmeret alicunde . . . sī nūllō aliō pactō, faenore⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 299, ⟦i:he could have got it from somebody or other . . . if in no other way, on usury⟧ (⟦r2113:2113⟧).

title: Variation of the Apodosis
text:
⟦#2112⟧
The apodosis is sometimes represented by the accusative of exclamation (⟦r1149:1149⟧), or the vocative: as,
⟦b:mortālem graphicum, sī servat fidem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 519, ⟦i:O what a pattern creature, if he keeps his word⟧. ⟦b:ō miserum tē, sī intellegis, miseriōrem, sī nōn intellegis, hoc litterīs mandārī⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 54, ⟦i:wretched man if you are aware, more wretched if you are not aware, that all this is put down in black and white⟧. ⟦b:inimīce lāmnae, Crīspe Sallustī, nisi temperātō splendeat ūsū⟧, H. 2, 2, 2, ⟦i:thou foe to bullion, Crispus Sallustius, so it shine not with tempered use⟧. Also the future participle in poetry and in prose from Livy on.
⟦#2113⟧
The verb of the apodosis, or the entire apodosis, is often omitted. In the latter case an appended verb might easily be mistaken for the apodosis.
⟦b:quid sī caelum ruat?⟧ T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 719, ⟦i:what if the sky should fall?⟧ ⟦b:quō mihi fortūnam, sī nōn concēditur ūtī?⟧ H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 5, 12, ⟦i:why wealth for me, if wealth I may not use?⟧ ⟦b:nisi restituissent statuās, vehementer minātur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 162, ⟦i:he threatens vengeance dire, if they did not put the statues back in their place⟧. ⟦b:quae supplicātiō sī cum cēterīs cōnferātur, hoc interest⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 15, ⟦i:if this thanksgiving be compared with all others, there would be found the following difference⟧. ⟦b:nōn edepol ubi terrārum sim sciō, sī quis roget⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 336, ⟦i:upon my word I don’t know where on earth I am, if anyone should ask⟧. ⟦b:sī Valeriō quī crēdat, quadrāgintā mīlia hostium sunt caesa⟧, L. 33, 10, 8, ⟦i:if anybody believe such a man as Valerius, there were forty thousand of the enemy slain⟧. A clause with ⟦b:sī⟧ or ⟦b:nisi⟧ is often used parenthetically: as, ⟦b:sī placet⟧, ⟦b:sī vidētur⟧, ⟦b:sīs⟧, ⟦b:sultis⟧, ⟦i:if you please⟧, ⟦b:sī quaeris⟧, ⟦i:if you must know⟧, ⟦i:in fact⟧, ⟦b:sī dīs placet⟧, ⟦i:please heaven⟧, ⟦b:nisi mē fallit⟧, ⟦i:if I am not mistaken⟧, &c., &c. For wishes introduced by ⟦b:ō sī⟧, without an apodosis, see ⟦r1546:1546⟧.
⟦#2114⟧
The apodosis is sometimes expanded by inserted expressions. So particularly by ⟦b:vereor nē⟧, equivalent to ⟦b:fortasse⟧ (⟦r1958:1958⟧), ⟦b:nōn dubitō quīn⟧, to ⟦b:profectō⟧ (⟦r1986:1986⟧), or a form of ⟦b:sum⟧ with a relative pronoun: as,
⟦b:quae cōnētur sī velim commemorāre, vereor nē quis exīstimet mē causam nōbilitātis voluisse laedere⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 135, ⟦i:if I should undertake to set forth his high and mighty schemes, possibly it might be thought that I wished to damage the cause of the conservatives⟧. ⟦b:sī tum P. Sēstius animam ēdidisset, nōn dubitō quīn aliquandō statua huic statuerētur⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 83, ⟦i:if Sestius had given up the ghost then, a statue would doubtless at some day have been set up in his honour⟧. ⟦b:quod ille sī repudiāsset, dubitātis quīn ē̆ī vīs esset adlāta?⟧ ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 62, ⟦i:if he had rejected this, have you any doubt that violent hands would have been laid on him?⟧ ⟦b:sescenta sunt quae memorem, sī sit ōtium⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 320, ⟦i:there are a thousand things that I could tell, if I had time⟧.
⟦#2115⟧
For expressions of trial, hope, or expectation, followed by a conditional protasis with ⟦b:sī⟧, see ⟦r1777:1777⟧.

title: etsī, tametsī (tamenetsī), etiamsī
text:
⟦#2116⟧
⟦b:etsī⟧, ⟦b:tametsī⟧, ⟦i:though⟧, ⟦b:etiamsī⟧, ⟦i:even if⟧, or sometimes simple ⟦b:sī⟧, ⟦i:if⟧, is used to introduce a concessive protasis. The verb of the protasis is either indicative or subjunctive; but the indicative is the prevailing construction, especially with ⟦b:etsī⟧. The apodosis often has ⟦b:tamen⟧ as an adversative correlative, even with ⟦b:tametsī⟧.
⟦b:etsī⟧ is rare in poetry; not in Sallust. Sometimes it is used like ⟦b:quamquam⟧ to append a fresh main sentence (⟦r2153:2153⟧). ⟦b:tametsī⟧ belongs chiefly to colloquial style, though Sallust often uses it; not in the Augustan poets or Tacitus. ⟦b:etiamsī⟧ is not found in Plautus or Caesar.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:nōn vīdī eam, etsī vīdī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 407, ⟦i:I saw her not, although I saw her⟧. ⟦b:quō mē habeam pactō, tametsī nōn quaeris, docēbō⟧, Lucilius in Gell. 18, 8, 2, ⟦i:I’ll tell you how I am, though you do not inquire⟧. ⟦b:etiamsī multī mēcum contendent, tamen omnīs superābō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 5, 8, 4, ⟦i:though I shall have many rivals, yet I will outdo them all⟧. ⟦b:tametsī causa postulat, tamen praeterībō⟧, ⟦i:Quinct.⟧ 13, ⟦i:though the case calls for it, still I will let it pass⟧. ⟦b:Caesar, etsī in hīs locīs mātūrae sunt hiemēs, tamen in Britanniam proficīscī contendit⟧, 4, 20, 1, ⟦i:though the winter always sets in early in these parts, nevertheless Caesar made haste to proceed to Britain⟧. ⟦b:Caesar, etsī intellegēbat, quā dē causā ea dīcerentur, Indutiomarum ad sē venīre iussit⟧, 5, 4, 1, ⟦i:though Caesar was aware of his motives in saying so, he directed Indutiomarus to come to him⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:etsī taceās, palam id quidem est⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 418, ⟦i:though you should hold your tongue, still that at least is plain⟧. ⟦b:etsī nihil aliud Sūllae nisi cōnsulātum abstulissētis, tamen eō contentōs vōs esse oportēbat⟧, ⟦i:Sull.⟧ 90, ⟦i:even though you had robbed Sulla of nothing but the consulship, still you ought to be satisfied with that⟧. ⟦b:equidem, etiamsī oppetenda mors esset, in patriā māllem quam in externīs locīs⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 4, 7, 4, ⟦i:for my part, even though death were to be faced, I should prefer it in my native land rather than abroad⟧.

title: quasi (quam sī), tamquam sī, ut or velut sī
text:
⟦#2117⟧
⟦b:sī⟧ following a word meaning ⟦i:than⟧ or ⟦i:as⟧ is used with the subjunctive in conditional comparisons.
In this use, ⟦b:quasi⟧ (⟦b:quam sī⟧ twice in Tacitus) and ⟦b:tamquam sī⟧ are found at all periods. ⟦b:ut sī⟧ is found in Terence once, in Cicero (not in the orations), once in Livy, sometimes in later writers. ⟦b:velut sī⟧ begins with Caesar; not in Cicero. ⟦b:ac sī⟧ is found once in the ⟦i:Bell. Hisp.⟧ and in late Latin.
⟦#2118⟧
⟦b:sī⟧ is often omitted after ⟦b:tamquam⟧, and (from Livy on) sometimes after ⟦b:velut⟧. After ⟦b:quasi⟧ it is sometimes inserted in Plautus, Lucretius, and late Latin. ⟦b:ceu⟧ is sometimes used, chiefly in poetry, for ⟦b:tamquam sī⟧. The main clause often has as correlative ⟦b:ita⟧, ⟦b:sīc⟧, ⟦b:perinde⟧, ⟦b:proinde⟧, ⟦b:similiter⟧, or ⟦b:nōn secus⟧.
⟦#2119⟧
The tense of the subjunctive is usually regulated by the sequence of tenses, in Cicero nearly always with ⟦b:quasi⟧ and ⟦b:tamquam sī⟧.
⟦b:quid mē sīc salūtās quasi dūdum nōn vīderīs?⟧ Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 682, ⟦i:why dost thou greet me thus as if but now thou hadst not looked on me?⟧ ⟦b:quid ego hīs testibus ūtor, quasi rēs dubia sit?⟧ ⟦i:Caecil.⟧ 14, ⟦i:why do I employ these witnesses, as if it were a case involving doubt?⟧ ⟦b:tamquam sī claudus sim, cum fūstīst ambulandum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 427, ⟦i:I have to take my walks with a stick, as if I were a lame man⟧. ⟦b:tamquam extrūderētur, ita cucurrit⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 10, 10, ⟦i:he rushed away as if he had been kicked out⟧. ⟦b:quod absentis Ariovistī crūdēlitātem, velut sī cōram adesset, horrērent⟧, 1, 32, 4, ⟦i:because they trembled at Ariovistus’s barbarity, absent as he was, just as if he stood before their eyes⟧. ⟦b:mē quoque iuvat, velut ipse in parte labōris ac perīculī fuerim, ad fīnem bellī Pūnicī pervēnisse⟧, L. 31, 1, 1, ⟦i:I feel glad myself at having finally reached the end of the Punic war, as if I had had a direct hand in the work and the danger⟧.
⟦#2120⟧
The imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive is sometimes used, even when the leading verb is in a primary tense, to mark action more distinctly as non-occurrent (⟦r2091:2091⟧): as,
⟦b:eius negōtium sīc velim suscipiās, ut sī esset rēs mea⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 14, ⟦i:I wish you would undertake his business, just as if it were my own affair⟧. ⟦b:mē audiās, precor, tamquam sī mihī̆ quirītantī intervēnissēs⟧, L. 40, 9, 7, ⟦i:listen to me, I pray you, as if you had come at a cry from me for help⟧. ⟦b:iūs iūrandum perinde aestimandum quam sī Iovem fefellisset⟧, Ta. 1, 73, ⟦i:as for the oath, it must be counted exactly as if he had broken one sworn on the name of Jupiter⟧. This is the more usual way in Cicero with ⟦b:ut sī⟧.
⟦#2121⟧
⟦b:quasi⟧, ⟦b:ut⟧, or, from Livy on, ⟦b:tamquam⟧ or ⟦b:velut⟧, ⟦i:as if⟧, is sometimes used with participle constructions, nouns, and abridged expressions: as,
⟦b:quasi temere dē rē pūblicā locūtus in carcerem coniectus est⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 6, ⟦i:on the ground that he had been speaking without good authority about a state matter, he was clapped in jail⟧. ⟦b:restitēre Rōmānī tamquam caelestī vōce iussī⟧, L. 1, 12, 7, ⟦i:the Romans halted as if bidden by a voice from heaven⟧. ⟦b:laetī, ut explōrātā victōriā, ad castra pergunt⟧, 3, 18, 8, ⟦i:in high spirits, as if victory were assured, they proceeded to the camp⟧.
⟦#2122⟧
In old Latin, ⟦b:quasi⟧ is found a few times for the original ⟦b:quam sī⟧ after a comparative: as, ⟦b:mē nēmō magis respiciet, quasi abhinc ducentōs annōs fuerim mortuos⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tru.⟧ 340, ⟦i:nobody will pay any more attention to me than if I had been dead two centuries⟧. It is also used (once in classical Latin, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 71) in periods of actual comparison, like ⟦b:tamquam⟧ (⟦r1908:1908⟧), with the indicative: as, ⟦b:senex ille illī dīxit, quasi ego nunc tibi dīcō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 545, ⟦i:that old man said to him, as I now say to you⟧. For its use in figurative comparisons, see ⟦r1908:1908⟧, ⟦r1944:1944⟧. For ⟦b:tamquam⟧ introducing a reason &c., see ⟦r1909:1909⟧, a late usage found rarely with ⟦b:quasi⟧ and ⟦b:ut⟧.

title: Connection of Separate Sentences or Periods
text:
⟦#2123⟧
Separate sentences or periods have a connective more commonly in Latin than in English. Sometimes, however, like the members of single periods, they are for special reasons put ⟦i:asyndetically⟧ (⟦r1637:1637⟧).

title: Connection of Separate Sentences or Periods: Without a Connective
text:
⟦#2124⟧
Asyndeton is common with two or more separate sentences or periods:
⟦#2125⟧
(a.) To represent a series of actions as occurring at the same moment: as,
⟦b:hīc diffīsus suae salūtī ex tabernāculō prōdit; videt imminēre hostēs; capit arma atque in portā cōnsistit; cōnsequuntur hunc centuriōnēs; relinquit animus Sextium gravibus acceptīs vulneribus⟧, 6, 38, 2, ⟦i:despairing of his life, he comes out of the tent; sees the enemy close at hand; seizes arms and takes his stand at the gate; the centurions rally round him; Sextius becomes unconscious, receiving severe wounds⟧.
⟦#2126⟧
(b.) When an occurrence is represented as consisting of many successive actions: the ⟦i:Enumerative Asyndeton⟧: as,
⟦b:perōrāvit aliquandō, adsēdit. surrēxī ego. respīrāre vīsus est, quod nōn alius potius dīceret. coepī dīcere. usque eō animadvertī, iūdicēs, eum aliās rēs agere, antequam Chrȳsogonum nōmināvi; quem simul atque attigī, statim homō sē ērēxit, mīrārī vīsus est. intellēxī quid eum pupugisset⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 60, ⟦i:after a while he wound up, took his seat; up rose your humble servant. He seemed to take courage from the fact it was nobody else. I began to speak. I noticed, gentlemen, that he was inattentive all along till I named Chrysogonus; but the moment I touched on him, the creature perked up at once, seemed to be surprised. I knew what the rub was.⟧
⟦#2127⟧
(c.) When the last sentence sums up the result of the preceding with emphasis: the ⟦i:Asyndeton of Summary⟧: as,
⟦b:hī dē suā salūte dēspērantēs, aut suam mortem miserābantur, aut parentēs suōs commendābant. plēna erant omnia timōris et lūctūs⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 41, 8, ⟦i:despairing of their lives, they either bewailed their own death, or strove to interest people in their parents. In short, it was one scene of terror and lamentation.⟧

title: Connection of Separate Sentences or Periods: With a Connective
text:
⟦#2128⟧
Separate sentences or periods may be connected: (1.) by pronominal words: (⟦i:a.⟧) demonstrative or determinative; (⟦i:b.⟧) relative; (2.) by conjunctions and adverbs.

title: Demonstrative and Determinative Words as Connectives
text:
⟦#2129⟧
⟦b:hīc⟧ and ⟦b:is⟧ serve as connectives at the beginning of a new period. In English the equivalent word is usually placed not at the beginning as a connective, but after some words.
⟦b:Gallia est dīvīsa in partēs trēs, quārum ūnam incolunt Belgae, aliam Aquītānī, tertiam Celtae. hī omnēs linguā, īnstitūtīs, lēgibus inter sē differunt⟧, 1, 1, 1, ⟦i:Gaul is divided into three parts, one of which is occupied by Belgians, another by Aquitanians, and the third by Kelts. In language, customs, and laws these are all different from each other.⟧ ⟦b:apud Helvētiōs nōbilissimus fuit Orgetorīx. is M. Messālā et M. Pīsōne cōnsulibus coniūrātiōnem nōbilitātis fēcit⟧, 1, 2, 1, ⟦i:among the Helvetians the man of highest rank was Orgetorix. In the consulship of Messala and Piso he got up a conspiracy among the nobles.⟧ ⟦b:angustōs sē fīnīs habēre arbitrābantur. hīs rēbus adductī cōnstituērunt ea quae ad proficīscendum pertinērent comparāre. ad eās rēs cōnficiendās biennium sibī̆ satis esse dūxērunt. ad eās rēs cōnficiendās Orgetorīx dēligitur. is sibī̆ lēgātiōnem suscēpit⟧, 1, 2, 5, ⟦i:they thought they had a narrow territory; so they resolved in consequence to make such preparations as were necessary for a move. They considered two years ample to do this. Orgetorix is chosen to do this. He took upon himself the office of envoy.⟧
⟦#2130⟧
Particularly common are demonstrative words at the beginning of a new period, to show that the first action necessarily took place or was natural.
⟦b:Dionȳsius tyrannus Syrācūsīs expulsus Corinthī puerōs docēbat; usque eō imperiō carēre nōn poterat⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 3, 27, ⟦i:after his expulsion from Syracuse, the tyrant Dionysius kept school at Corinth; so incapable was he of getting along without governing⟧.

title: Relatives as Connectives
text:
⟦#2131⟧
⟦b:quī⟧ serves to connect a new period when it may be translated by a demonstrative, or when it is equivalent to ⟦b:et is⟧, ⟦b:is autem⟧, ⟦b:is enim⟧, ⟦b:is igitur⟧: as,
⟦b:perpetrāret Anicētus prōmissa. quī nihil cunctātus poscit summam sceleris⟧, Ta. 14, 7, ⟦i:Anicetus must carry out his agreement. Without any ado he asks to have the entire management of the crime.⟧ For other examples, see ⟦r1835:1835⟧.
⟦#2132⟧
The neuter accusative ⟦b:quod⟧, ⟦i:as to that⟧, ⟦i:as to which⟧, ⟦i:whereas⟧, ⟦i:now⟧, ⟦i:so⟧, is used to connect a new period, especially before ⟦b:sī⟧, ⟦b:nisi⟧, ⟦b:etsī⟧, ⟦b:utinam⟧ (⟦r1837:1837⟧): as,
⟦b:quod sī tū valērēs, iam mihī̆ quaedam explōrāta essent⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 7, 2, 6, ⟦i:whereas if you were well yourself, some points would have been clear to me before this⟧. ⟦b:quod sī diūtius alātur contrōversia, fore utī pars cum parte cīvitātis cōnflīgat⟧, 7, 32, 5, ⟦i:now if the dispute be kept up any longer, one half of the community would quarrel with the other⟧. ⟦b:quod nisi mīlitēs essent dēfessī, omnēs hostium cōpiae dēlērī potuissent⟧, 7, 88, 6, ⟦i:so if the soldiers had not been utterly spent, all the forces of the enemy might have been exterminated⟧.

title: Conjunctions and Adverbs
text:
⟦#2133⟧
The conjunctions and adverbs used to coordinate sentences are: (⟦i:a.⟧) copulative and disjunctive; (⟦i:b.⟧) concessive and adversative; (⟦i:c.⟧) causal and illative.

title: et
text:
⟦#2134⟧
⟦b:et⟧, ⟦i:and⟧, simply adds, as in English (⟦r1645:1645⟧). But it is often used in such a connection that a modification of the translation is required to bring out the sense.
⟦#2135⟧
⟦b:et⟧ may continue the discourse with a concessive sentence, which is to be followed by an adversative. In such cases ⟦b:quidem⟧ often stands in the concessive sentence: as,
⟦b:prīmōrēs cīvitātis eadem ōrant. et cēterī quidem movēbant minus; postquam Sp. Lucrētius agere coepit, cōnsul abdicāvit sē cōnsulātū⟧, L. 2, 2, 8, ⟦i:the head men of the state make the same request. Now the others did not influence him much. But when Lucretius began to take steps the consul resigned his consulship.⟧
⟦#2136⟧
⟦b:et⟧, ⟦i:and strange to say⟧, ⟦i:and if you’d believe it⟧, introduces something unexpected: as,
⟦b:iamque trēs laureātae in urbe statuae, et adhūc raptābat Āfricam Tacfarinās⟧, Ta. 4, 23, ⟦i:there were already three triumphal statues in Rome, and, strange to say, Tacfarinas was still harrying Africa⟧.
⟦#2137⟧
⟦b:et⟧, ⟦i:and really⟧, ⟦i:and in fact⟧, ⟦i:and to be sure⟧; in this sense it is usually followed immediately by the verb: as,
⟦b:multa quae nōn volt videt. et multa fortasse quae volt!⟧ ⟦i:CM.⟧ 25, ⟦i:one sees much that one would not. Aye, and much perhaps that one would!⟧
⟦#2138⟧
⟦b:et⟧ introducing a sentence explaining in detail a general idea before given may be translated ⟦i:namely⟧: as,
⟦b:cōnsulēs religiō tenēbat, quod prōdigiīs aliquot nūntiātīs, nōn facile litābant. et ex Campāniā nūntiāta erant Capuae sepulchra aliquot dē caelō tācta⟧, L. 27, 23, 1, ⟦i:the consuls were detained by scruple, because several prodigies were reported, and they could not readily obtain good omens; namely from Campania it was reported that at Capua several tombs were struck by lightning⟧.
⟦#2139⟧
⟦b:et⟧, ⟦i:and also⟧, ⟦i:and besides⟧: as,
⟦b:Pūnicae quoque victōriae sīgnum octō ductī elephantī. et nōn minimum fuēre spectāculum praecēdentēs Sōsis et Moericus⟧, L. 26, 21, 9, ⟦i:as an emblem of the Punic victory also, elephants to the number of eight marched in parade. And furthermore not the least attractive part of the pageant were Sosis and Moericus, moving at the head of the line.⟧
⟦#2140⟧
⟦b:et⟧, ⟦i:and yet⟧, introduces a contrast or opposition: as,
⟦b:canōrum illud in vōce splendēscit etiam in senectūte, quod equidem adhūc nōn āmīsī; et vidētis annōs⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 28, ⟦i:the musical element in the voice actually improves in old age, and this I have not yet lost. And yet you see my years.⟧

title: neque or nec
text:
⟦#2141⟧
⟦b:nec⟧, ⟦i:and really . . . not⟧, ⟦i:and in fact . . . not⟧: as,
⟦b:magnō cum perīculō suō, quī forte patrum in forō erant, in eam turbam incidērunt. nec temperātum manibus foret, nī properē cōnsulēs intervēnissent⟧, L. 2, 23, 9, ⟦i:it was with great personal risk to such of the fathers as happened to be in the market place, that they got into the crowd. And in fact acts of violence would have occurred, unless the consuls had made haste to interfere.⟧
⟦#2142⟧
⟦b:nec⟧, ⟦i:and to be sure . . . not⟧: as,
⟦b:centum vīgintī līctōrēs cum fascibus secūrēs inligātās praeferēbant. nec attinuisse dēmī secūrem, cum sine prōvocātiōne creātī essent, interpretābantur⟧, L. 3, 36, 4, ⟦i:a hundred and twenty lictors with rods displayed axes bound in them. And to be sure they explained the matter thus, that there would have been no propriety in having the axe taken out, since the officers were appointed without any appeal.⟧
⟦#2143⟧
⟦b:nec⟧, ⟦i:not . . . either⟧, ⟦i:nor either⟧, ⟦i:neither⟧: as,
⟦b:eō annō vīs morbī levāta. neque ā pēnūriā frūmentī perīculum fuit⟧, L. 4, 25, 6, ⟦i:that year the violence of the plague grew less. Nor was there any danger from lack of grain either.⟧
⟦#2144⟧
⟦b:nec⟧, ⟦i:but . . . not⟧: as,
⟦b:missī tamen fētiālēs. nec eōrum verba sunt audīta⟧, L. 4, 30, 14, ⟦i:however the fetials were sent. But they were not listened to.⟧

title: -que
text:
⟦#2145⟧
⟦b:-que⟧, ⟦i:and likewise⟧: as,
⟦b:huic duōs flāminēs adiēcit. virginēsque Vestae lēgit⟧, L. 1, 20, 2, ⟦i:to this god he assigned two special priests. And he likewise chose maids for Vesta.⟧
⟦#2146⟧
⟦b:-que⟧, ⟦i:and in fact⟧, ⟦i:and so⟧, ⟦i:and in general⟧: as,
⟦b:tum quoque male pugnātum est. obsessaque urbs foret, nī Horātius esset revocātus⟧, L. 2, 51, 2, ⟦i:then also there was an unsuccessful engagement. And in fact Rome would have been besieged, unless Horatius had been recalled.⟧

title: atque or ac
text:
⟦#2147⟧
⟦b:atque⟧, ⟦i:and besides⟧, ⟦i:and more than that⟧, ⟦i:and actually⟧: as,
⟦b:ex quō efficitur animantem esse mundum. atque ex hōc quoque intellegī poterit in eō inesse intellegentiam, quod certē est mundus melior quam ūlla nātūra⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 32, ⟦i:from which it follows that the universe is alive. And more than that, we can see that it has sense from the following circumstance, that the universe is certainly superior to any element of the universe.⟧
⟦#2148⟧
⟦b:atque⟧, ⟦i:and so⟧, ⟦i:and consequently⟧: as,
⟦b:impedior religiōne quōminus expōnam quam multa P. Sēstius sēnserit. atque nihil dīcō praeter ūnum⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 8, ⟦i:I am prevented by scruples from setting forth how much Sestius was aware of. And so I will only say one thing.⟧

title: aut
text:
⟦#2149⟧
⟦b:aut⟧ is used to add a new sentence in the sense of ⟦b:aliōquī⟧, ⟦i:or else⟧, ⟦i:otherwise⟧, or as if ⟦b:nisi⟧, ⟦i:unless⟧, preceded: as,
⟦b:omnia bene sunt ē̆ī dīcenda, aut ēloquentiae nōmen relinquendum est⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 5, ⟦i:he must be able to speak well on all subjects, or else he must waive the name of an eloquent man⟧.

title: Concessive and Adversative
text:
⟦#2150⟧
A new concessive period is introduced by ⟦b:sānē⟧, ⟦b:quidem⟧, ⟦b:omnīnō⟧, ⟦i:to be sure⟧, or ⟦b:fortasse⟧, ⟦i:perhaps⟧: as,
⟦b:Plīnius et Cluvius nihil dubitātum dē fidē praefectī referunt. sānē Fabius inclīnat ad laudēs Senecae⟧, Ta. 13, 20, ⟦i:Pliny and Cluvius say that there was no doubt about the loyalty of the prefect. Fabius, it must be admitted, is always inclined to eulogize Seneca.⟧ ⟦b:id fortasse nōn perfēcimus; cōnātī quidem saepissimē sumus⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 210, ⟦i:perhaps we have not attained to it; still we have very often made the attempt⟧.
⟦#2151⟧
A new adversative sentence is introduced by ⟦b:autem⟧, ⟦i:again⟧, ⟦b:sed⟧, ⟦b:vērum⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, ⟦b:vērō⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, ⟦i:indeed⟧, ⟦b:at⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, or ⟦b:tamen⟧, ⟦b:nihilō minus⟧, ⟦i:nevertheless⟧.
These words when used to connect sentences have the same meaning as when used to connect the parts of a sentence (⟦r1676:1676⟧).
⟦#2152⟧
⟦b:atquī⟧, rarely ⟦b:atquīn⟧, ⟦i:and yet⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, is used chiefly in dialogue. It introduces a strong objection, sometimes in the form of a conditional protasis. From Cicero on, it is sometimes found after a question, to introduce an earnest denial.
⟦b:nōn sum apud mē :: atquī opus est nunc quom maxumē ut sīs⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 204, ⟦i:I’m all abroad :: but that’s just exactly where you must n’t be now⟧. ⟦b:nōn vereor condiscipulōrum nē quis exaudiat :: atquī cavendum est⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 1, 21, ⟦i:I’m not afraid of being overheard by any of my fellow-students :: and yet you must be on your guard⟧. ⟦b:sine veniat. atquī sī illam digitō attigerit ūnō, oculī īlicō ecfodientur⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 739, ⟦i:let him come on. But if he lays a finger on the maid, we’ll scratch his eyes out on the spot.⟧ ⟦b:quid vērō? modum statuārum habērī nūllum placet? atquī habeātur necesse est⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 144, ⟦i:what? is there, think you, to be no end to your statues? Yet there must be.⟧
⟦#2153⟧
⟦b:quamquam⟧, ⟦b:etsī⟧, ⟦b:tametsī⟧, ⟦i:though⟧, and ⟦b:nisi⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, are sometimes used to coordinate a new period, correcting the preceding: as,
⟦b:carēre sentientis est, nec sēnsus in mortuō, nē carēre quidem igitur in mortuō est. quamquam quid opus est in hōc philosophārī?⟧ ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 88, ⟦i:foregoing requires a sentient being, and there is no sensation in a dead man; therefore there is no foregoing either in a dead man. And yet what is the use of philosophizing over this?⟧ ⟦b:utram mālīs vidē; etsī cōnsilium quod cēpī rēctum esse sciō⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 326, ⟦i:of these two states choose which you will; though I am sure my plan’s the right one⟧. ⟦b:cūr ego nōn adsum? tametsī hoc minimē tibī̆ deest⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 7, 2, ⟦i:why am I not with you? though this is the very last thing you need⟧. ⟦b:spērābam dēfervisse adulēscentiam: ecce autem dē integrō! nisi quidquid est, volō hominem convenīre⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 152, ⟦i:I hoped his youthful passion had cooled down; yet here it is afresh! But be it what it may, I want to see the fellow⟧.

title: Causal and Illative
text:
⟦#2154⟧
⟦b:nam⟧, ⟦b:enim⟧, ⟦i:for⟧, or ⟦b:namque⟧, ⟦b:etenim⟧, ⟦i:for you see⟧, introduces a new period which gives the reason of the foregoing: as,
⟦b:quā quidem ex rē hominum multitūdō cōgnōscī potuit: nam minus hōrīs tribus mūnītiōnem perfēcērunt⟧, 5, 42, 4, ⟦i:and from this by the way their numbers could be gauged; for they made a breastwork in less than three hours⟧. ⟦b:quem meminisse potestis: annō enim ūndēvīcēsimō post eius mortem hī cōnsulēs factī sunt⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 14, ⟦i:you can remember him: for the present consuls were created only nineteen years after his death⟧.
⟦#2155⟧
The originally asseverative meaning of ⟦b:nam⟧ appears, even in the classical period, in colloquial language: as, ⟦b:tibī̆ ā mē nūlla ortast iniūria :: nam hercle etiam hoc restat⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 189, ⟦i:I’ve ne’er done you a wanton wrong :: aye verily that’s still to come⟧. In old Latin, it sometimes introduces a question: as, ⟦b:nam quae haec anus est?⟧ T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 732, ⟦i:why, who’s this old woman?⟧ Frequently it introduces an explanation or illustration, and, from Cicero on, a remark or question made in passing: as, ⟦b:sīc enim sēsē rēs habet: nam Odyssīa Latīna est sīc tamquam opus Daedalī⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 71, ⟦i:the case stands thus: the Odyssey in Latin is, you may say, a regular work of Daedalus⟧ (⟦r1908:1908⟧). ⟦b:vīvō Catōne multī ōrātōrēs flōruērunt: nam A. Albīnus⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 81, ⟦i:many orators flourished in Cato’s lifetime: for example, Albinus⟧. ⟦b:nam quid dē aedīle loquar?⟧ ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 95, ⟦i:for why speak of the aedile?⟧ ⟦b:enim⟧ does not differ essentially in use from ⟦b:nam⟧; for its meaning in old Latin, see ⟦r1688:1688⟧. ⟦b:namque⟧ is rare until Livy, and usually (always in old Latin) stands before a vowel. ⟦b:etenim⟧ is common only in classical Latin.
⟦#2156⟧
For ⟦b:quippe⟧, ⟦i:why⟧, often used as a coordinating word, see ⟦r1690:1690⟧.
⟦#2157⟧
⟦b:proinde⟧ or ⟦b:proin⟧, ⟦i:therefore⟧, ⟦i:so⟧, introduces a command or direction based upon the foregoing: as,
⟦b:ōrātiōnem spērat invēnisse sē, quī differat tē: proin tū fac apud tē ut siēs⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 407, ⟦i:he trusts he’s found some phrase wherewith he may confound you: so see you have your wits about you⟧. ⟦b:frūstrā meae vītae subvenīre cōnāminī. proinde abīte, dum est facultās⟧, 7, 50, 6, ⟦i:in vain ye try to save my life. So away, while ye have the power.⟧ ⟦b:iam undique silvae et sōlitūdō magna cōgitātiōnis incitāmenta sunt. proinde cum vēnābere, licēbit pugillārēs ferās⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 1, 6, 2, ⟦i:then again the surrounding woods and the loneliness are powerful stimulants to meditation. So when you go hunting, you can take a note book with you.⟧
⟦#2158⟧
A conclusion is denoted by ⟦b:ergō⟧, ⟦b:itaque⟧ or ⟦b:igitur⟧, ⟦i:therefore⟧, ⟦i:so⟧, introducing a new period: as,
⟦b:nihil est praestantius deō; ab eō igitur mundum necesse est regī. nūllī igitur est nātūrae subiectus deus. omnem ergō regit ipse nātūram⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 77, ⟦i:nothing is more excellent than god. Therefore the universe must be governed by him. Therefore god is in no respect subject to nature. Consequently he rules all nature himself.⟧ For the position of these words in their clauses, see ⟦r1688:1688⟧; for ⟦b:ergō igitur⟧ and ⟦b:itaque ergō⟧, 1689. For ⟦b:hinc⟧, ⟦b:inde⟧, ⟦b:eō⟧, ⟦b:ideō⟧, ⟦b:idcircō⟧, ⟦b:proptereā⟧, as coordinating words, see ⟦r1691:1691⟧.

title: Affirmative Coordination
text:
⟦#2159⟧
A new sentence affirmative of a foregoing is often introduced by an emphatic ⟦b:sīc⟧ or ⟦b:ita⟧.
These words often introduce a general truth which is deduced from the first statement.
⟦b:vīsne igitur tē īnspiciāmus ā puerō? sīc opīnor; ā prīncipiō ōrdiāmur⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 44, ⟦i:would you like to have us look into your record from boyhood? Yes, I think it would be well; let us begin at the beginning.⟧ ⟦b:quī dīligēbant hunc, illī favēbant. sīc est volgus: ex vēritāte pauca, ex opīniōne multa aestimat⟧, ⟦i:RC.⟧ 29, ⟦i:everybody who loved him, smiled on the other man. Yes, that is always the way of the world: it seldom judges by truth, often by hearsay.⟧

title: The Infinitive
text:
⟦#2160⟧
The infinitive is in its origin a verbal substantive.
⟦#2161⟧
The present infinitive active is an ancient dative, closely resembling in meaning and use the English infinitive with ⟦i:to⟧. It originally marked action merely in a general way, without indication of voice or tense. In virtue of this original timeless character, the present often represents action which is really past or future; in such cases the time must be inferred from the context.
⟦#2162⟧
The present infinitive active gradually approached the character of a verb, and the original substantive nature being forgotten, it was supplemented by a passive, and by forms for completed and for future action, active and passive.
⟦#2163⟧
The infinitive has furthermore two other properties of the verb: (⟦i:a.⟧) it is modified by an adverb, not by an adjective; and (⟦i:b.⟧) it is followed by the construction of its verb.

title: The Infinitive of Purpose
text:
⟦#2164⟧
The infinitive denotes purpose: (⟦i:a.⟧) when loosely added to a substantive in old Latin, (⟦i:b.⟧) with verbs of motion, ⟦b:eō⟧, ⟦b:veniō⟧, ⟦b:currō⟧, ⟦b:mittō⟧, in old or poetical Latin, and (⟦i:c.⟧) in the combination ⟦b:dō bibere⟧, ⟦i:give to drink⟧, in old, colloquial, or poetical Latin: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:occāsiō benefacta cumulāre⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 423, ⟦i:a chance to pile up kindnesses⟧. Parallel with a gerund: ⟦b:summa ēlūdendī occāsiōst mihi nunc senēs et Phaedriae cūram adimere argentāriam⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 885, ⟦i:I’ve now a splendid chance the greybeards of eluding and Phaedria to rescue from his money cares⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:recurre petere rē recentī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 1015, ⟦i:run back to get it ere it is too late⟧. ⟦b:voltisne eāmus vīsere?⟧ T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 102, ⟦i:do you think we’d better go to call?⟧ ⟦b:parasītum mīsī nudiusquārtus Cāriam petere argentum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cur.⟧ 206, ⟦i:my parasite I sent four days ago to Caria, to fetch the cash⟧. ⟦b:nec dulcēs occurrent ōscula nātī praeripere⟧, Lucr. 3, 895, ⟦i:nor shall thy children dear come running kiss on kiss to snatch⟧. ⟦b:nōn nōs ferrō Libycōs populāre penātīs vēnimus⟧, V. 1, 527, ⟦i:we are not come with steel to harry Libya’s hearths⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:bibere dā usque plēnīs cantharīs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 821, ⟦i:keep giving on to drink with brimming bowls⟧. ⟦b:bibere⟧ is thus used by Plautus, Terence, Cato, and Livy, and by Cicero once with ⟦b:ministrō⟧. In classical prose, purpose is expressed by the subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧ or a relative pronoun, or by a gerund or gerundive with ⟦b:ad⟧ or ⟦b:causā⟧.
⟦#2165⟧
In poetry, the infinitive of purpose is used with synonymes of ⟦b:dō⟧ also, and with verbs of leaving, taking away, taking up, &c.
⟦b:huic lōrīcam dōnat habēre⟧, V. 5, 259, ⟦i:on him a corselet he bestows to wear⟧. ⟦b:trīstitiam et metūs trādam protervīs in mare Crēticum portāre ventīs⟧, H. 1, 26, 1, ⟦i:sadness and fears I’ll to the wanton winds consign, to sweep into the Cretic sea⟧. ⟦b:quis sibi rēs gestās Augustī scrībere sūmit?⟧ H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 3, 7, ⟦i:who takes it on himself Augustus’ deeds to pen?⟧ ⟦b:quem virum aut hērōa lyrā vel ācrī tībiā sūmis celebrāre?⟧ H. 1, 12, 1, ⟦i:what hero or what demigod dost thou take up, to ring his praises on the rebec or the piercing pipe?⟧

title: The Infinitive with Adjectives
text:
⟦#2166⟧
The infinitive is sometimes used with adjectives, chiefly by poets of the Augustan age, and late prose writers, often in imitation of a Greek idiom: as,
⟦b:indoctum iuga ferre nostra⟧, H. 2, 6, 2, ⟦i:not taught our yoke to bear⟧. ⟦b:avidī committere pugnam⟧, O. 5, 75, ⟦i:hot to engage in fight⟧. ⟦b:sōlī cantāre perītī Arcades⟧, V. ⟦i:E.⟧ 10, 32, ⟦i:Arcadians alone in minstrelsy are skilled⟧. ⟦b:vitulus niveus vidērī⟧, H. 4, 2, 59, ⟦i:a bullock snow-white to behold⟧, i.e. ⟦b:vīsū⟧ (⟦r2274:2274⟧). These infinitives are of different kinds, some of them resembling a complementary infinitive, others a gerund or gerundive construction, the supine in ⟦b:-tū⟧ (⟦b:-sū⟧), &c., &c.
⟦#2167⟧
The infinitive is ordinarily used either as object or as subject of a verb.

title: The Complementary Infinitive
text:
⟦#2168⟧
The present infinitive is often used to complete the meaning of certain kinds of verbs which imply another action of the same subject: as,
⟦b:prō Pompēiō ēmorī possum⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 15, 3, ⟦i:I could die the death for Pompey⟧ (⟦r1495:1495⟧). ⟦b:quid habēs dīcere?⟧ ⟦i:Balb.⟧ 33, ⟦i:what have you to say?⟧ ⟦b:scīre volēbat⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 131, ⟦i:he wanted to know⟧. ⟦b:hoc facere dēbēs⟧, ⟦i:RabP.⟧ 7, ⟦i:you ought to do this⟧. ⟦b:Caesar Rhēnum trānsīre dēcrēverat⟧, 4, 17, 1, ⟦i:Caesar had resolved to cross the Rhine⟧. ⟦b:fugā salūtem petere contendērunt⟧, 3, 15, 2, ⟦i:they tried to save themselves by flight⟧. ⟦b:num negāre audēs?⟧ ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 8, ⟦i:do you dare deny it?⟧ ⟦b:vereor dīcere⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 323, ⟦i:I am afraid to tell⟧. ⟦b:num dubitās id facere?⟧ ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 13, ⟦i:do you hesitate to do that?⟧ ⟦b:mātūrat ab urbe proficīscī⟧, 1, 7, 1, ⟦i:he makes haste to leave Rome⟧. ⟦b:Dīviciācus Caesarem obsecrāre coepit⟧, 1, 20, 1, ⟦i:Diviciacus began to entreat Caesar⟧. ⟦b:Dolābella iniūriam facere persevērat⟧, ⟦i:Quint.⟧ 31, ⟦i:Dolabella persists in doing wrong⟧. ⟦b:illī pecūniam pollicērī nōn dēsistunt⟧, 6, 2, 1, ⟦i:these people did not stop offering money⟧. ⟦b:diem ēdictī obīre neglēxit⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 3, 20, ⟦i:he failed to keep the day named in the edict⟧. ⟦b:īrāscī amīcīs nōn temere soleō⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 8, 16, ⟦i:I am not apt to get provoked with friends without just cause⟧. ⟦b:illī rēgibus pārēre didicerant⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 3, 9, ⟦i:the men of old were trained to bow the knee to kings⟧ (⟦r1615:1615⟧). ⟦b:dextram cohibēre mementō⟧, J. 5, 71, ⟦i:remember that you keep hands off⟧.
⟦#2169⟧
The verbs or verbal expressions which are supplemented by an infinitive are chiefly such as mean ⟦i:can⟧, ⟦i:will⟧ or ⟦i:wish⟧, ⟦i:ought⟧, ⟦i:resolve⟧, ⟦i:endeavour⟧, ⟦i:dare⟧, ⟦i:fear⟧, ⟦i:hesitate⟧, ⟦i:hasten⟧, ⟦i:begin⟧, ⟦i:continue⟧, ⟦i:cease⟧, ⟦i:neglect⟧, ⟦i:am wont⟧, ⟦i:learn⟧, ⟦i:know how⟧, ⟦i:remember⟧, ⟦i:forget⟧, ⟦i:seem⟧. The infinitive in this combination contains the leading idea. For the occasional use of the perfect infinitive with some of these verbs, see ⟦r2223:2223⟧.
Some of the commonest of these verbs are ⟦b:possum⟧, ⟦b:queō⟧, ⟦b:nequeō⟧; ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:nōlō⟧, ⟦b:mālō⟧, ⟦b:cupiō⟧, ⟦b:studeō⟧; ⟦b:dēbeō⟧; ⟦b:cōgitō⟧, ⟦b:meditor⟧, ⟦b:statuō⟧, ⟦b:cōnstituō⟧, ⟦b:dēcernō⟧, ⟦b:parō⟧; ⟦b:cōnor⟧, ⟦b:nītor⟧, ⟦b:contendō⟧; ⟦b:audeō⟧; ⟦b:vereor⟧; ⟦b:cunctor⟧, ⟦b:dubitō⟧, ⟦b:festīnō⟧, ⟦b:mātūrō⟧, ⟦b:īnstituō⟧, ⟦b:coepī⟧, ⟦b:incipiō⟧, ⟦b:pergō⟧, ⟦b:persevērō⟧, ⟦b:dēsinō⟧, ⟦b:dēsistō⟧, ⟦b:omittō⟧, ⟦b:supersedeō⟧, ⟦b:neglegō⟧, ⟦b:nōn cūrō⟧; ⟦b:soleō⟧, ⟦b:adsuēscō⟧, ⟦b:cōnsuēscō⟧; ⟦b:discō⟧, ⟦b:sciō⟧, ⟦b:nesciō⟧, ⟦b:recordor⟧, ⟦b:meminī⟧, ⟦b:oblīvīscor⟧; ⟦b:videor⟧.
⟦#2170⟧
The infinitive is also used with many verbal expressions equivalent to the above verbs, such as ⟦b:habeō in animō⟧, ⟦b:cōnsilium est⟧, ⟦b:certum est⟧, ⟦b:parātus sum⟧, &c., &c., or with ⟦b:parātus⟧ alone, ⟦b:adsuēfactus⟧, &c., &c. Furthermore, in poetry and late prose, the place of many of the above verbs is often taken by livelier or fresher synonymes, such as ⟦b:valeō⟧ for ⟦b:possum⟧, from Lucretius on, ⟦b:ardeō⟧, ⟦i:burn⟧, for ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:cupiō⟧, or ⟦b:absiste⟧, ⟦b:fuge⟧, ⟦b:parce⟧, &c., for ⟦b:nōlī⟧ (⟦r1584:1584⟧), &c., &c.
⟦#2171⟧
A predicate noun used in the construction of the complementary infinitive, is put in the nominative: as,
⟦b:Aelius Stōicus esse voluit⟧, ⟦i:Br. 206⟧, ⟦i:Aelius wanted to be a Stoic⟧. ⟦b:esse quam vidērī bonus mālēbat⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 54, 6, ⟦i:he chose to be good rather than seem good⟧.

title: The Accusative with the Infinitive
text:
⟦#2172⟧
A very common form of a dependent sentence is that known as the ⟦i:Accusative with the Infinitive⟧.
Thus, of the two coordinate sentences ⟦b:sciō: iocāris tū nunc⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 1081, ⟦i:I know: you are jesting now⟧, the second may be put in a dependent form, the two sentences blending into one: ⟦b:sciō iocārī tē nunc⟧, ⟦i:I know you to be jesting now⟧.
⟦#2173⟧
The subject of an infinitive is put in the accusative.
Thus, in ⟦b:eum vident⟧, ⟦i:they see him⟧, ⟦b:eum⟧ is the object of ⟦b:vident⟧ (⟦r1134:1134⟧). If ⟦b:sedēre⟧ is added, ⟦b:eum vident sedēre⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 107, ⟦i:they see him sit⟧, or ⟦i:they see that he is sitting⟧, ⟦b:eum⟧ is at the same time the object of ⟦b:vident⟧ and the subject of ⟦b:sedēre⟧. But the accusative by degrees becoming detached from the main verb, and closely interlocked with the infinitive, the combination is extended to cases where the main verb is intransitive or passive.
⟦#2174⟧
A predicate noun referring to a subject accusative is itself put in the accusative: as,
⟦b:tē esse arbitror puerum probum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Most.⟧ 949, ⟦i:I think you are a good boy⟧. ⟦b:nēminem vīvum capī patiuntur⟧, 8, 35, 5, ⟦i:they do not allow anybody to be made prisoner alive⟧ (⟦r2198:2198⟧).

title: Verbs of Perceiving, Knowing, Thinking, and Saying
text:
⟦#2175⟧
The accusative with the infinitive is used with active verbs or verbal expressions of perceiving, knowing, thinking, and saying: as,
⟦b:patēre tua cōnsilia nōn sentīs?⟧ ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 1, ⟦i:you don’t feel that your plots are all out?⟧ ⟦b:huic fīlium scīs esse?⟧ T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 181, ⟦i:you are aware that this man has a son?⟧ ⟦b:Pompēiōs cōnsēdisse terrae mōtū audīvimus⟧, Sen. ⟦i:NQ.⟧ 6, 1, 1, ⟦i:we have heard that Pompei has been swallowed up by an earthquake⟧, 63 A.D., 17 years before its utter destruction. ⟦b:saepe audīvī inter ōs atque offam multa intervenīre posse⟧, Cato in Gell. 13, 18 (⟦r17:17⟧), 1, ⟦i:I have often heard ‘’twixt cup and lip there’s many a slip.’⟧ ⟦b:dīcit montem ab hostibus tenērī⟧, 1, 22, 2, ⟦i:he says the hill is held by the enemy⟧. ⟦b:dīxtin dūdum illam dīxisse, sē expectāre fīlium?⟧ T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 451, ⟦i:didn’t you say a while ago the woman said that she was looking for her son?⟧
Some of the commonest of these verbs are: (⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:audiō⟧, ⟦b:animadvertō⟧, ⟦b:sentiō⟧, ⟦b:videō⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:accipiō⟧, ⟦b:intellegō⟧, ⟦b:sciō⟧, ⟦b:nesciō⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:arbitror⟧, ⟦b:cēnseō⟧, ⟦b:cōgitō⟧, ⟦b:crēdō⟧, ⟦b:exīstimō⟧, ⟦b:meminī⟧, ⟦b:opīnor⟧, ⟦b:putō⟧, ⟦b:recordor⟧, ⟦b:suspicor⟧. (⟦i:d.⟧) ⟦b:adfirmō⟧, ⟦b:āiō⟧, ⟦b:dēmōnstrō⟧, ⟦b:dīcō⟧, ⟦b:disputō⟧, ⟦b:doceō⟧, ⟦b:fateor⟧, ⟦b:nārrō⟧, ⟦b:negō⟧, ⟦b:nūntiō⟧, ⟦b:ostendō⟧, ⟦b:prōmittō⟧, ⟦b:scrībō⟧, ⟦b:sīgnificō⟧, ⟦b:spērō⟧, ⟦b:trādō⟧. (⟦i:e.⟧) ⟦b:rūmor est⟧, ⟦b:nōn mē fugit⟧, ⟦b:certus sum⟧, ⟦b:nōn nescius sum⟧, &c., &c. Also occasionally verbs used in the sense of ⟦i:think⟧ or ⟦i:say⟧, as ⟦b:mittō⟧, ⟦i:send word⟧, and substantives or pronouns expressing a thought or judgement.
⟦#2176⟧
The accusative with the infinitive is sometimes introduced by a neuter pronoun, or by ⟦b:sīc⟧ or ⟦b:ita⟧: as, ⟦b:illud negābis, tē dē rē iūdicātā iūdicāvisse?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 81, ⟦i:will you deny this, that you sate in judgement on a matter that was already decided?⟧ ⟦b:sīc accēpimus, nūllum bellum fuisse⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 5, ⟦i:we have been told this, that there was not any war⟧. Sometimes by an ablative with ⟦b:dē⟧: as, ⟦b:dē hōc Verrī dīcitur, habēre eum perbona toreumata⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 38, ⟦i:about this man report is made to Verres that he had some choice bits of embossed work⟧.
⟦#2177⟧
(1.) Passive verbs of this class are commonly used personally in the third person of the present system, with the subject, and the predicate noun, if used, in the nominative: as,
⟦b:hī centum pāgōs habēre dīcuntur⟧, 4, 1, 4, ⟦i:these people are said to have a hundred cantons⟧. ⟦b:nūlla iam exīstimantur esse iūdicia⟧, ⟦i:V. a. pr.⟧ 43, ⟦i:there are thought to be no courts of law any longer⟧. ⟦b:pōns prope effectus nūntiābātur⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 62, 3, ⟦i:the bridge was reported to be well-nigh done⟧.
⟦#2178⟧
Such personal passives are much more common in the writers of Cicero’s day than in old Latin. Particularly so ⟦b:arguō⟧, ⟦b:audiō⟧, ⟦b:cōgnōscō⟧, ⟦b:comperiō⟧, ⟦b:concēdō⟧, ⟦b:dēfendō⟧, ⟦b:dēmōnstrō⟧, ⟦b:dīcō⟧, ⟦b:doceō⟧, ⟦b:excūsō⟧, ⟦b:exīstimō⟧, ⟦b:inveniō⟧, ⟦b:iūdicō⟧, ⟦b:līberō⟧, ⟦b:memorō⟧, ⟦b:negō⟧, ⟦b:nūntiō⟧, ⟦b:ostendō⟧, ⟦b:postulō⟧, ⟦b:putō⟧, ⟦b:reperiō⟧, ⟦b:trādō⟧.
⟦#2179⟧
(2.) With the first or second person the personal construction is rare: as, ⟦b:quod nōs bene ēmisse iūdicātī sumus⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 1, 13, 6, ⟦i:that we are thought to have made a good bargain⟧. ⟦b:cum inveniāre improbissimā ratiōne esse praedātus⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 3, ⟦i:when you prove to have been robbing most abominably⟧. But with ⟦b:videor⟧, ⟦i:seem⟧, the personal construction is the rule in all three persons, and in the perfect system as well as the present.
⟦#2180⟧
(3.) In the perfect system, and also usually in the gerundive construction (⟦r2246:2246⟧), verbs of this class are commonly impersonal: as,
⟦b:trāditum est Homērum caecum fuisse⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 114, ⟦i:the tradition is that Homer was blind⟧. ⟦b:ubī̆ tyrannus est, ibī̆ dīcendum est nūllam esse rem pūblicam⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 3, 43, ⟦i:wherever there is an absolute ruler, there we must maintain there is no commonwealth⟧.
⟦#2181⟧
(4.) With some verbs of this class, the impersonal construction is preferred even in the present system. Thus, commonly ⟦b:intellegitur⟧, ⟦i:it is understood⟧, as impersonal; regularly in classical Latin ⟦b:crēditur⟧; with a dative in Cicero and Caesar ⟦b:dīcitur⟧, ⟦b:nūntiātur⟧. The impersonals ⟦b:cernitur⟧, ⟦b:fertur⟧, ⟦b:memorātur⟧, ⟦b:prōditur⟧, ⟦b:vidētur⟧, are rare.
⟦#2182⟧
The personal construction is sometimes extended to other verbs or verbal expressions, especially in poetry: as, ⟦b:colligor⟧, O. ⟦i:A.⟧ 2, 6, 61, ⟦i:I am inferred⟧, for ⟦b:colligitur⟧. ⟦b:nōnnūllīs magistrātūs veniēbant in suspīciōnem nōs dēmorātī esse⟧, Lentulus in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 12, 15, 5, ⟦i:the magistrates were suspected by some of having delayed us⟧ (⟦r1491:1491⟧).
⟦#2183⟧
With verbs of thinking and saying the subject accusative is sometimes omitted.
(⟦i:a.⟧) Oftenest thus ⟦b:mē nōs⟧, ⟦b:tē vōs⟧, or ⟦b:sē⟧: as, ⟦b:stultē fēcisse fateor⟧, i.e. ⟦b:mē⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 1013, ⟦i:I own I’ve acted like a fool⟧. ⟦b:cōnfitēre vēnisse⟧, i.e. ⟦b:tē⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 61, ⟦i:confess you came⟧. ⟦b:quae imperārentur facere dīxērunt⟧, i.e. ⟦b:sē⟧, 2, 32, 3, ⟦i:they said they would do as ordered⟧ (⟦r2221:2221⟧). Often the future without ⟦b:esse⟧: as, ⟦b:refrāctūrōs carcerem minābantur⟧, i.e. ⟦b:sē⟧, L. 6, 17, 6, ⟦i:they threatened to break the jail open⟧, (⟦i:b.⟧) Less frequently an accusative of ⟦b:is⟧: as, ⟦b:oblītum crēdidī⟧, i.e. ⟦b:eum⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 9, 2, 1, ⟦i:I imagined he had forgotten⟧. Such omissions are common in old Latin, Cicero, Caesar, Livy, and in poetry.
⟦#2184⟧
When the accusative is not expressed, a predicate noun is sometimes put in the nominative, chiefly in poetry, in imitation of a Greek idiom: as,
⟦b:phasēlus ille quem vidētis, hospitēs, ait fuisse nāvium celerrimus⟧, Cat. 4, 1, ⟦i:the clipper you see yonder, friends, says she was once the fleetest of the fleet⟧. ⟦b:uxor invictī Iovis esse nescīs⟧, H. 3, 27, 73, ⟦i:thou knowest not thou art the bride of the unconquerable Jove⟧. Similarly with verbs of emotion (⟦r2187:2187⟧): as, ⟦b:gaudent esse rogātae⟧, O. ⟦i:AA.⟧ 1, 345, ⟦i:they are glad to have been asked⟧. ⟦b:gaudent perfūsī sanguine frātrum⟧, V. ⟦i:G.⟧ 2, 510, ⟦i:they’re glad to have been imbued with brothers’ blood⟧.

title: Verbs of Accusing
text:
⟦#2185⟧
The verbs of accusing, ⟦b:arguō⟧ and ⟦b:īnsimulō⟧, take the accusative with the infinitive like verbs of saying: as,
⟦b:cīvīs Rōmānōs necātōs esse arguō⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 149, ⟦i:my accusation is that Romans have been slain⟧. ⟦b:occīdisse patrem Sex. Rōscius arguitur⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 37, ⟦i:Roscius is charged with the murder of his father⟧. ⟦b:īnsimulāre coepērunt Epicratem litterās pūblicās corrūpisse⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 60, ⟦i:they began to accuse Epicrates of having falsified records of state⟧.

title: Verbs of Hoping, Promising, and Threatening
text:
⟦#2186⟧
The accusative with the future infinitive is used with verbs of hoping, promising, and threatening: as,
⟦b:id sēsē effectūrōs spērābant⟧, 7, 26, 2, ⟦i:they hoped to carry it out⟧. ⟦b:pollicentur sēsē ē̆ī dēditūrōs⟧, 5, 20, 2, ⟦i:they volunteer to surrender to him⟧. But sometimes the present infinitive alone: see ⟦r2236:2236⟧.

title: Verbs of Emotion
text:
⟦#2187⟧
The accusative with the infinitive is sometimes used with verbs of joy, grief, surprise, or wonder: as,
⟦b:venīre tū mē gaudēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 184, ⟦i:thou art glad I’m come⟧. ⟦b:doluī pācem repudiārī⟧, ⟦i:Marc.⟧ 14, ⟦i:I felt sorry peace was rejected⟧. These verbs often have the construction with ⟦b:quod⟧, or in old Latin with ⟦b:quia⟧ (⟦r1851:1851⟧).
⟦#2188⟧
Some of the commonest of these verbs are ⟦b:doleō⟧, ⟦b:gaudeō⟧, ⟦b:laetor⟧, ⟦b:mīror⟧, &c., &c.; and from Cicero on, ⟦b:angor⟧, ⟦b:indignor⟧, ⟦b:lūgeō⟧, ⟦b:sollicitō⟧.

title: Verbs of Desire
text:
⟦#2189⟧
(1.) The accusative with the infinitive is commonly used with ⟦b:volō⟧ (⟦b:mālō⟧, ⟦b:nōlō⟧), and ⟦b:cupiō⟧, when the subject of the infinitive is not the same as that of the verb: as,
⟦b:Catilīnam perīre voluī⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 8, 15, ⟦i:I wished Catiline to die⟧. ⟦b:māluit hominēs peccāre quam deōs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 22, ⟦i:he wanted men to sin rather than gods⟧. ⟦b:tē tuā fruī virtūte cupimus⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 331, ⟦i:we wish you to reap the benefit of your high character⟧.
⟦#2190⟧
(2.) Even when the subjects denote the same person, the accusative is sometimes used with the infinitive: as,
⟦b:ēmorī mē mālim⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 810, ⟦b:morī mē mālim⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 66, ⟦i:I’d rather die⟧. ⟦b:magnuficē volō mē virōs summōs accipere⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 167, ⟦i:I’m going to entertain some highborn gentlemen in style⟧. Oftenest when the infinitive is ⟦b:esse⟧, ⟦b:vidērī⟧, ⟦b:putārī⟧, or ⟦b:dīcī⟧: as, ⟦b:cupiō mē esse clēmentem, cupiō mē nōn dissolūtum vidērī⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 4, ⟦i:I wish to play the man of mercy, and yet I do not wish to seem over lax⟧. Rarely thus with ⟦b:dēsīderō⟧, ⟦b:nōlō⟧, ⟦b:optō⟧, and ⟦b:studeō⟧, and in Sallust with ⟦b:properō⟧.
⟦#2191⟧
For the perfect active with these verbs, see ⟦r2228:2228⟧; for the perfect passive, 2229.
⟦#2192⟧
⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:mālō⟧, and ⟦b:cupiō⟧ are often coordinated with the subjunctive of desire (⟦r1707:1707⟧). ⟦b:volō⟧ and ⟦b:mālō⟧ often have the subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧, particularly in old Latin (⟦r1950:1950⟧).
⟦#2193⟧
Verbs of resolving sometimes take the accusative with the infinitive: as, ⟦b:certum offirmāre est viam mē⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 454, ⟦i:I am resolved to hold the way⟧. So, from Cicero on, sometimes ⟦b:cēnseō⟧, ⟦b:dēcernō⟧, and ⟦b:sentiō⟧, in the exceptional sense of ⟦b:volō⟧ or ⟦b:iubeō⟧, ⟦i:think it best⟧: as, ⟦b:velle et cēnsēre eōs ab armīs discēdere⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 21, 4, ⟦i:that they wished and thought it best for those people to give up fighting⟧.
⟦#2194⟧
The accusative with the infinitive is sometimes used with verbs of demanding: as, ⟦b:hau postulō equidem mēd in lectō accumbere⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 488, ⟦i:I can’t expect, not I, to sprawl upon a couch⟧. ⟦b:hīc postulat sē absolvī?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 138, ⟦i:does this man ask to be acquitted?⟧ Similarly with ⟦b:ōrō⟧ and ⟦b:praecipiō⟧ in late writers.
⟦#2195⟧
The accusative with the infinitive is sometimes found with ⟦b:suādeō⟧ and ⟦b:persuādeō⟧ in Terence, Lucretius, and Vergil, and with ⟦b:precor⟧ in Ovid and late prose.

title: Verbs of Accomplishing
text:
⟦#2196⟧
Verbs of accomplishing rarely have the accusative with the infinitive: as, ⟦b:tālīs ōrātōrēs vidērī facit, quālīs ipsī sē vidērī volunt⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 142, of delivery, ⟦i:it makes orators appear just as they wish to appear themselves⟧. Oftenest in poetry. In prose usually the subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧ (⟦r1951:1951⟧).

title: Verbs of Teaching and Training
text:
⟦#2197⟧
The verbs of teaching and training, ⟦b:doceō⟧ and ⟦b:adsuēfaciō⟧, may take an accusative of a substantive and an infinitive expressing the thing taught: as,
⟦b:quīn etiam tondēre fīliās suās docuit⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 58, ⟦i:why more than that, he actually taught his own daughters to shave⟧, of Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse. ⟦b:equōs eōdem remanēre vestīgiō adsuēfēcērunt⟧, 4, 2, 3, ⟦i:they have their horses trained to stand stock-still⟧ (⟦r1608:1608⟧). Compare 1169.

title: Verbs of Bidding and Forbidding and of Allowing
text:
⟦#2198⟧
The accusative with the infinitive is used with ⟦b:iubeō⟧ and ⟦b:vetō⟧, ⟦b:sinō⟧ and ⟦b:patior⟧: as,
⟦b:mīlitēs ex oppidō exīre iussit⟧, 2, 33, 1, ⟦i:he ordered the soldiers to go out of the town⟧. ⟦b:pontem iubet rescindī⟧, 1, 7, 2, ⟦i:he orders the bridge torn up⟧. ⟦b:lēx peregrīnum vetat in mūrum ascendere⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 100, ⟦i:it is against the law for a foreigner to get up on the wall⟧. ⟦b:castra vāllō mūnīrī vetuit⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 41, 4, ⟦i:he gave orders that the camp should not be fortified with a palisade⟧. ⟦b:vīnum ad sē inportārī nōn sinunt⟧, 4, 2, 6, ⟦i:wine they will not allow to be brought into their country⟧. Cicero is the first to use ⟦b:vetō⟧ thus. Other constructions also occur with these words: see ⟦r1708:1708⟧, ⟦r1950:1950⟧, ⟦r1953:1953⟧, &c.
⟦#2199⟧
The person ordered or forbidden is often omitted, when stress is laid on the action merely, or when the person is obvious from the context: as, ⟦b:castra mūnīre iubet⟧, i.e. ⟦b:mīlitēs⟧, 2, 5, 6, ⟦i:he gives orders to construct a camp⟧. ⟦b:iussērunt prōnūntiāre⟧, i.e. ⟦b:tribūnōs et centuriōnēs⟧, 5, 33, 3, ⟦i:they gave orders to proclaim⟧. ⟦b:īdemque iussērunt simulācrum Iovis facere maius⟧, i.e. ⟦b:cōnsulēs⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 20, ⟦i:and they furthermore gave directions to make a statue of Jupiter, a bigger one⟧.
⟦#2200⟧
⟦b:iubeō⟧ is sometimes coordinated with the subjunctive, especially in old Latin (⟦r1708:1708⟧). Sometimes it has the subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧, especially in resolves of the people.
⟦#2201⟧
In the passive, ⟦b:iubeō⟧, ⟦b:vetō⟧, and ⟦b:sinō⟧ are used personally, the accusative of the person ordered or forbidden becoming nominative: as, ⟦b:iubentur scrībere exercitum⟧, L. 3, 30, 3, ⟦i:they are ordered to raise an army⟧. ⟦b:Nōlānī mūrōs adīre vetitī⟧, L. 23, 16, 9, ⟦i:the men of Nola were not allowed to go to the walls⟧. ⟦b:hīc accūsāre eum nōn est situs⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 95, ⟦i:this man was not allowed to accuse him⟧.
⟦#2202⟧
⟦b:imperō⟧ often has the accusative with a passive or deponent infinitive, or with ⟦b:fierī⟧: as, ⟦b:praesentem pecūniam solvī imperāvī⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 2, 4, 1, ⟦i:I have given orders for ready money to be paid⟧. Rarely with an active infinitive parallel with a passive: as, ⟦b:eō partem nāvium convenīre commeātumque comportārī imperat⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 42, 2, ⟦i:he orders part of the vessels to rendezvous there, and grain to be brought⟧. In the passive, a personal ⟦b:imperor⟧ occurs, like ⟦b:iubeor⟧ (⟦r2201:2201⟧): as, ⟦b:in lautumiās dēdūcī imperantur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 68, ⟦i:orders are given for them to be taken to the quarries⟧. See also ⟦r1950:1950⟧. ⟦b:permittō⟧ has sometimes the accusative with the infinitive from Tacitus on, usually the subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧ (⟦r1950:1950⟧).
⟦#2203⟧
The verbs of hindering, ⟦b:prohibeō⟧ and ⟦b:impediō⟧, sometimes have the accusative with the infinitive: as, ⟦b:barbarī nostrōs nāvibus ēgredī prohibēbant⟧, 4, 24, 1, ⟦i:the savages undertook to prevent our people from disembarking⟧. The infinitive used with ⟦b:prohibeō⟧ is usually passive or deponent. ⟦b:quid est igitur quod mē impediat ea quae probābilia mihī̆ videantur sequī?⟧ ⟦i:Off.⟧ 2, 8, ⟦i:what is there then to hinder me from following what seems to me to be probable?⟧ See also ⟦r1960:1960⟧ and ⟦r1977:1977⟧.

title: The Infinitive as a Substantive Accusative
text:
⟦#2204⟧
The accusative with the infinitive, or the infinitive alone, regarded as a neuter substantive, may be used as the object of a verb, or in apposition with the object: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:leporem gustāre fās nōn putant⟧, 5, 12, 6, ⟦i:tasting hare they count a sin⟧. ⟦b:errāre malum dūcimus⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 18, ⟦i:going astray we hold a bad thing⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:ad id quod īnstituistī, ōrātōrum genera distinguere aetātibus, istam dīligentiam esse accommodātam putō⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 74, ⟦i:I think your accurate scholarship is just the thing for your projected task—classifying public speakers chronologically⟧.
⟦#2205⟧
The infinitive as a substantive is rarely preceded by the preposition ⟦b:inter⟧ in late prose: as, ⟦b:multum interest inter dare et accipere⟧, Sen. ⟦i:Ben.⟧ 5, 10, 2, ⟦i:there is a vast difference between ‘give’ and ‘take.’⟧ Cicero has it thus once in a translation (⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 43). In poetry ⟦b:praeter⟧ is thus used rarely.
⟦#2206⟧
In poetry, the infinitive is used as a substantive object with such verbs as ⟦b:dō⟧, ⟦b:reddō⟧, ⟦b:adimō⟧, ⟦b:perdō⟧: as, ⟦b:hīc verērī perdidit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 158, ⟦i:this youth has lost his sense of shame⟧.

title: The Infinitive as Subject
text:
⟦#2207⟧
The accusative with the infinitive, or the infinitive alone, present or perfect, may be used as the subject of a verb, in apposition with the subject, or as a predicate nominative: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:mendācem memorem esse oportēre⟧, Quintil. 4, 2, 91, ⟦i:that a liar should have a good memory⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:sequitur illud, caedem senātum iūdicāsse contrā rem pūblicam esse factam⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 12, ⟦i:next comes this point, that the senate adjudged the homicide an offence against the state⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:exitus fuit ōrātiōnis, sibī̆ nūllam cum hīs amīcitiam esse posse⟧, 4, 8, 1, ⟦i:the end of the speech was that he could not have any friendship with these people⟧.
⟦#2208⟧
The infinitive is used as the subject (⟦i:a.⟧) with impersonal verbs, (⟦i:b.⟧) with ⟦b:est⟧, ⟦b:putātur⟧, ⟦b:habētur⟧, &c., and an abstract substantive, a genitive, or a neuter adjective in the predicate.
⟦#2209⟧
(a.) Some of the commonest impersonal verbs are ⟦b:appāret⟧, ⟦b:decet⟧, ⟦b:expedit⟧, ⟦b:licet⟧, ⟦b:lubet⟧, ⟦b:oportet⟧, ⟦b:praestat⟧, ⟦b:pudet⟧, ⟦b:rēfert⟧. Also in classical Latin, ⟦b:attinet⟧, ⟦b:condūcit⟧, ⟦b:cōnstat⟧, ⟦b:dēdecet⟧, ⟦b:exsistit⟧, ⟦b:fallit⟧, ⟦b:interest⟧, ⟦b:iuvat⟧, ⟦b:liquet⟧, ⟦b:obest⟧, ⟦b:paenitet⟧, ⟦b:patet⟧, ⟦b:pertinet⟧, ⟦b:placet⟧, ⟦b:displicet⟧, ⟦b:prōdest⟧, which are used as live verbs by Lucretius and Sallust also. Similarly in Plautus and Terence ⟦b:fortasse⟧.
⟦#2210⟧
The infinitive is occasionally used as a subject with verbs other than the above (⟦r2209:2209⟧): as, ⟦b:nōn cadit invidēre in sapientem⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 3, 21, ⟦i:envy does not square with our ideas of a sage⟧. ⟦b:carēre hoc sīgnificat, egēre eō quod habēre velīs⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 88, ⟦b:careō⟧ ⟦i:means not having what you would like to have⟧.
⟦#2211⟧
(b.) Some of the commonest abstracts used thus with ⟦b:est⟧ are ⟦b:fāma⟧, ⟦b:fās⟧ and ⟦b:nefās⟧, ⟦b:fidēs⟧, ⟦b:iūs⟧, ⟦b:laus⟧, ⟦b:opus⟧, ⟦b:mōs⟧, ⟦b:tempus⟧. From Cicero on, ⟦b:opīniō⟧ and ⟦b:prōverbium⟧. In Plautus, ⟦b:audācia⟧, ⟦b:cōnfīdentia⟧, ⟦b:miseria⟧, ⟦b:negōtium⟧, ⟦b:scelus⟧, &c. For genitives, see ⟦r1237:1237⟧. Neuter adjectives are such as ⟦b:aequum⟧, ⟦b:inīquum⟧, ⟦b:cōnsentāneum⟧, ⟦b:crēdibile⟧, ⟦b:incrēdibile⟧, ⟦b:manifestum⟧, ⟦b:necesse⟧, ⟦b:pār⟧, ⟦b:rēctum⟧, &c., &c.
⟦#2212⟧
The accusative is not expressed when it is indefinite, ⟦i:you⟧, ⟦i:a man⟧, ⟦i:a person⟧, ⟦i:anybody⟧, frequently also when it is implied in some other case in the sentence: as,
⟦b:nōn tam praeclārum est scīre Latīnē quam turpe nescīre⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 140, ⟦i:it is not so creditable to be a Latin scholar as it is disreputable not to be⟧. ⟦b:mihī̆ inter virtūtēs grammaticī habēbitur aliqua nescīre⟧, Quintil. 1, 8, 21, ⟦i:in my eyes it will be one merit in a classical scholar not to be omniscient⟧. ⟦b:temporī cēdere semper sapientis est habitum⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 4, 9, 2, ⟦i:bowing to the inevitable has always passed as a mark of wisdom⟧. ⟦b:peccāre licet nēminī⟧, ⟦i:Par.⟧ 20, ⟦i:no man is at liberty to sin⟧. An indefinite ⟦b:hominem⟧, ⟦b:aliquem⟧, or ⟦b:tē⟧, is rare: as, ⟦b:illa laus est, līberōs hominem ēducāre⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 703, ⟦i:it is a crown of glory for a man a family to rear⟧.
⟦#2213⟧
(1.) A predicate noun referring to the unexpressed indefinite subject of the infinitive is put in the accusative: as,
⟦b:nōn esse cupidum pecūnia est, nōn esse emācem vectīgal est, contentum vērō suīs rēbus esse maximae sunt dīvitiae⟧, ⟦i:Par.⟧ 51, ⟦i:for a man not to have desires, is money down, not to be eager to buy is an income; but to be satisfied with what you have is the greatest possible wealth⟧. A plural predicate is rare: as, ⟦b:esset ēgregium domesticīs esse contentōs⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 22, ⟦i:it would be a grand thing for people to be satisfied with home examples⟧.
⟦#2214⟧
(2.) When the subject of the infinitive is implied in a dative, a predicate noun may also be in the dative: as,
⟦b:mihī̆ neglegentī esse nōn licet⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 1, 17, 6, ⟦i:it will not do for me to be careless⟧. With a dative and licet, however, the predicate is sometimes in the accusative: as, ⟦b:quod sī cīvī Rōmānō licet esse Gādītānum⟧, ⟦i:Balb.⟧ 29, ⟦i:now if a Roman is allowed to be a Gaditanian⟧. Regularly so, when the subject is indefinite and not expressed (⟦r2212:2212⟧): as, ⟦b:haec praescrīpta servantem licet magnificē vīvere⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 92, ⟦i:a man who holds to these rules may live a noble life⟧.
⟦#2215⟧
The infinitive, used as a substantive in the nominative or accusative, sometimes has a neuter attribute.
Chiefly thus ⟦b:ipsum⟧, ⟦b:hoc ipsum⟧, ⟦b:tōtum hoc⟧: as, ⟦b:ipsum Latīnē loquī est in magnā laude pōnendum⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 140, ⟦i:just the mere ability of talking good Latin is to be accounted highly creditable⟧. Rarely a possessive, ⟦b:meum⟧, ⟦b:tuum⟧: as, ⟦b:ita tuom cōnfertō amāre nē tibi sit probrō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cur.⟧ 28, ⟦i:so shape thy wooing that it be to thee no shame⟧.

title: The Infinitive of Exclamation
text:
⟦#2216⟧
The infinitive alone, or the accusative with the infinitive, is sometimes used in exclamations of surprise, incredulity, disapproval, or lamentation: as,
