⟦b:nōn pudēre⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 233, ⟦i:not be ashamed⟧. ⟦b:sedēre tōtōs diēs in vīllā⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 12, 44, 2, ⟦i:sitting round whole days and days at the country place⟧. ⟦b:at tē Rōmae nōn fore⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 5, 20, 7, ⟦i:only to think you won’t be in Rome⟧. ⟦b:hoc posterīs memoriae trāditum īrī⟧, L. 3, 67, 1, ⟦i:to think this will be passed down to generations yet unborn⟧. Often with a ⟦b:-ne⟧, transferred from the unexpressed verb on which the infinitive depends (⟦r1503:1503⟧): as, ⟦b:tēne hoc, Accī, dīcere, tālī prūdentiā praeditum⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 84, ⟦i:what? you to say this, Accius, with your sound sense⟧. The exclamatory infinitive is chiefly confined to Plautus, Terence, and Cicero.
⟦#2217⟧
This infinitive has already been spoken of; see ⟦r1535:1535-1539⟧.

title: The Tenses of the Infinitive
text:
⟦#2218⟧
The present infinitive represents action as going on, the perfect as completed, and the future as not yet begun, at the time of the action of the verb to which the infinitive is attached.
The forms of the infinitive are commonly and conveniently called tenses, though this designation is not strictly applicable.

title: The Infinitive: The Present Tense
text:
⟦#2219⟧
In itself, the present infinitive denotes action merely as going on, without any reference to time. With some verbs, however, which look to the future, the present relates to action in the immediate future. With verbs of perceiving, knowing, thinking, and saying, it denotes action as going on at the time of the verb: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:facinus est vincīre cīvem Rōmānum⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 170, ⟦i:it is a crime to put a Roman in irons⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:audīre cupiō⟧, ⟦i:Caec.⟧ 33, ⟦i:I am eager to hear⟧. ⟦b:Antium mē recipere cōgitō a. d. V Nōn. Māi.⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 2, 9, 4, ⟦i:I am meditating going back to Antium the third of May⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:errāre eōs dīcunt⟧, 5, 41, 5, ⟦i:they say those people are mistaken⟧. ⟦b:tempus dīxī esse⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 687, ⟦i:I said it was time⟧. ⟦b:dīcēs tibī̆ Siculōs esse amīcōs?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 155, ⟦i:will you say the Sicilians are friends of yours?⟧
⟦#2220⟧
The present infinitive is sometimes used with ⟦b:meminī⟧, ⟦b:recordor⟧, ⟦b:memoriā teneō⟧, and with some analogous expressions, such as ⟦b:accēpimus⟧, ⟦b:fertur⟧, &c., to represent merely the occurrence of action really completed, without indicating its completion: as,
⟦b:meminī ad mē tē scrībere⟧, ⟦i:D.⟧ 38, ⟦i:I remember your writing to me⟧. ⟦b:meministis fierī senātūs cōnsultum⟧, ⟦i:Mur.⟧ 51, ⟦i:you remember a decree of the senate being passed⟧. ⟦b:sed ego īdem recordor longē omnibus anteferre Dēmosthenem⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 23, ⟦i:and yet I remember putting Demosthenes far above everybody else⟧. ⟦b:hanc accēpimus agrōs et nemora peragrāre⟧, ⟦i:HR.⟧ 24, ⟦i:we have heard of this goddess’s scouring fields and groves⟧. ⟦b:Q. Maximum accēpimus facile cēlāre, tacēre⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 108, ⟦i:we have heard of Fabius’s ready cleverness in keeping dark and holding his tongue⟧. But the perfect is used when the action is to be distinctly marked as completed: as, ⟦b:meministis mē ita distribuisse causam⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 122, ⟦i:you remember that I arranged the case thus⟧. Sometimes present and perfect are united: as, ⟦b:Helenē capere arma fertur, nec frātrēs ērubuisse deōs⟧, Prop. 3, 14, 19 (4, 13, 19), ⟦i:Helen is said to fly to arms, and not to have blushed in presence of her brother gods⟧. Here ⟦b:capere⟧ relates to the same completed action as the more exact ⟦b:ērubuisse⟧.
⟦#2221⟧
With verbs of saying, used in the narrower sense of promising, the present infinitive sometimes stands for the future (⟦r2236:2236⟧): as,
⟦b:crās māne argentum mihī̆ mīles dare sē dīxit⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 531, ⟦i:the soldier spoke of paying me the money early in the morning⟧. ⟦b:mē a͡ibat accersere⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 1118, ⟦i:he said he’d fetch me⟧ (⟦r2186:2186⟧). ⟦b:quae imperārentur facere dīxērunt⟧, 2, 32, 3, ⟦i:they agreed to do what was commanded⟧.
⟦#2222⟧
The present infinitive dependent on a past tense of ⟦b:dēbeō⟧, ⟦b:oportet⟧, ⟦b:possum⟧, often requires the English perfect infinitive in translation: as, ⟦b:quid enim facere poterāmus?⟧ ⟦i:Pis.⟧ 13, ⟦i:for what else could we have done?⟧ See, however, 1495. For the infinitive perfect, see ⟦r2230:2230⟧.

title: The Infinitive: The Perfect Tense
text:
⟦#2223⟧
(1.) The perfect active infinitive sometimes serves as a complement of ⟦b:dēbeō⟧, ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:possum⟧, &c. (⟦r2168:2168⟧): as,
⟦b:tametsī statim vīcisse dēbeō, tamen dē meō iūre dēcēdam⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 73, ⟦i:though I am entitled to come off victorious at once, yet I will waive my right⟧; compare ⟦b:vīcī⟧, ⟦i:I am victorious⟧, 1608. ⟦b:nīl vetitum fēcisse volet⟧, J. 14, 185, ⟦i:nothing forbidden will he wish to have done⟧; compare ⟦b:fēcī⟧, ⟦i:I am guilty⟧. ⟦b:unde illa potuit didicisse?⟧ ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 51, ⟦i:from what source could he have all that information acquired?⟧ ⟦b:bellum quod possumus ante hiemem perfēcisse⟧, L. 37, 19, 5, ⟦i:the war which we can have ended up before winter⟧.
⟦#2224⟧
(2.) In prohibitions, the perfect active infinitive often serves as a complement of ⟦b:nōlō⟧ or ⟦b:volō⟧ (⟦r2168:2168⟧).
Thus, in old Latin, ⟦b:nōlītō dēvellisse⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 872, ⟦i:do not have had it plucked⟧. Particularly so when dependent on ⟦b:nē velit⟧ or ⟦b:nē vellet⟧, in legal style: as, ⟦b:nē quis convēnisse sacrōrum causā velit⟧, L. 39, 14, 8, ⟦i:that nobody may presume to have banded with others for the observance of the mysteries⟧. BACAS · VIR · NEQVIS · ADIESE · VELET, CIL. I, 196, 7, inscription of 186 B.C., ⟦i:that no male should presume to have had resort to the Bacchants⟧ (⟦r765:765⟧; ⟦r48:48⟧). ⟦b:nē quid ēmisse velit īnsciente dominō⟧, Cato, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 5, 4, ⟦i:he must not venture to have bought anything without his master’s knowledge⟧, of a head farm-steward.
⟦#2225⟧
In poetry of the Augustan age, the complementary perfect infinitive active is sometimes dependent on a verb of will or effort, such as ⟦b:cūrō⟧, ⟦b:labōrō⟧, ⟦b:tendō⟧: as, ⟦b:tendentēs opācō Pēlion inposuisse Olympō⟧, H. 3, 4, 51, ⟦i:on shadowy Olympus striving Pelion to have piled⟧.
⟦#2226⟧
Any past tense of the indicative, when made dependent on a verb of perceiving, knowing, thinking, or saying, is represented by the perfect infinitive.
Thus, in ⟦b:Theophrastus scrībit Cīmōnem hospitālem fuisse: ita enim vīlicīs imperāvisse, ut omnia praebērentur⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 2, 64, ⟦i:Theophrastus says in his book that Cimon was the soul of hospitality: he had directed his stewards to furnish everything required⟧; the ⟦b:fuisse⟧ represents ⟦b:erat⟧ or ⟦b:fuit⟧, and the ⟦b:imperāvisse⟧ may represent ⟦b:imperābat⟧, ⟦b:imperāvit⟧, or perhaps ⟦b:imperāverat⟧, of direct discourse. ⟦b:praecō dīxisse prōnūntiat⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 75, ⟦i:the crier proclaims ‘speaking finished’⟧ (⟦r1605:1605⟧).
⟦#2227⟧
The perfect infinitive passive with ⟦b:fuisse⟧ denotes a past resulting state: as,
⟦b:dīcō Mithridātī cōpiās omnibus rēbus ōrnātās atque īnstrūctās fuisse, urbemque obsessam esse⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 20, ⟦i:I must tell you that Mithridates’s troops were completely armed and equipped, and that the town was under siege⟧. Here ⟦b:ōrnātās fuisse⟧ represents ⟦b:ōrnātae erant⟧ (⟦r1615:1615⟧), and ⟦b:obsessam esse⟧ represents ⟦b:obsidēbātur⟧ (⟦r1595:1595⟧).
⟦#2228⟧
(1.) The perfect active infinitive is sometimes used with ⟦b:nōlō⟧ or ⟦b:volō⟧, especially in poetry, when the subject of the infinitive is not the same as that of the verb (⟦r2189:2189⟧): as,
⟦b:hanc tē ad cēterās virtūtēs adiēcisse velim⟧, L. 30, 14, 6, ⟦i:I only wish you had this good quality added to the rest⟧.
⟦#2229⟧
(2.) ⟦b:volō⟧ often has an emphatic perfect passive infinitive, usually without ⟦b:esse⟧ (⟦r2230:2230⟧); less frequently ⟦b:cupiō⟧ and rarely ⟦b:nōlō⟧: as,
⟦b:factum volō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 495, ⟦i:As.⟧ 685, ⟦i:I want it done⟧, i.e. I will. ⟦b:illōs monitōs etiam atque etiam volō⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 27, ⟦i:I want those people cautioned over and over⟧. Particularly common in Cicero, not in Caesar or Sallust. Also with impersonal infinitives (⟦r1479:1479⟧): as ⟦b:oblīvīscere illum adversāriō tuō voluisse cōnsultum⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 16, 16c, 10, ⟦i:you must forget that the man wanted your enemy provided for⟧.
⟦#2230⟧
The perfect infinitive passive or deponent, commonly without ⟦b:esse⟧, is often used in Plautus, Terence, and Cicero, by assimilation with past tenses of verbs of propriety, such as ⟦b:aequum est⟧, ⟦b:convenit⟧, ⟦b:decet⟧, and ⟦b:oportet⟧: as, ⟦b:nōn oportuit relīctās⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 247, ⟦i:they shouldn’t have been left⟧. ⟦b:tē Iovī comprecātam oportuit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 739, ⟦i:you should have said your prayers to Jove⟧. The perfect active is less common: as, ⟦b:cāvisse oportuit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 944, ⟦i:you should have been upon your guard⟧. For ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:cupiō⟧, ⟦b:nōlō⟧, see ⟦r2229:2229⟧.
⟦#2231⟧
The perfect infinitive of completed action is very common with such expressions as ⟦b:satis est⟧, ⟦b:satis habeō⟧, ⟦b:iuvat⟧, ⟦b:melius est⟧, ⟦b:paenitet⟧, &c., also with verbs of emotion, such as ⟦b:gaudeō⟧, &c.: as, ⟦b:mē quoque iuvat ad fīnem bellī Pūnicī pervēnisse⟧, L. 31, 1, 1, ⟦i:I am delighted myself to have reached the end of the Punic war⟧. Oftentimes, however, in verse, the use of the perfect is partly due to the metre.

title: The Infinitive: The Future Tense
text:
⟦#2232⟧
The future infinitive is only used as a representative of the indicative, and not as a substantive.
⟦#2233⟧
For the future infinitive active or passive, a circumlocution with ⟦b:fore⟧ or ⟦b:futūrum esse⟧ with ⟦b:ut⟧ and the subjunctive present or imperfect is often used. This construction is necessary when the verb has no future participle or supine: as,
⟦b:spērō fore ut contingat id nōbīs⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 82, ⟦i:I hope we may be so fortunate⟧. ⟦b:clāmābant fore ut ipsī sē dī ulcīscerentur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 87, ⟦i:they cried out that the gods would avenge themselves⟧.
⟦#2234⟧
⟦b:fore⟧ with the perfect participle of a passive or deponent, represents the future perfect of direct discourse: as, ⟦b:dēbellātum mox fore rēbantur⟧, L. 23, 13, 6, ⟦i:they thought the war would soon be over⟧.
⟦#2235⟧
(1.) The future infinitive is commonly used with ⟦b:iūrō⟧, ⟦b:minor⟧, ⟦b:polliceor⟧, ⟦b:prōmittō⟧, and ⟦b:spērō⟧, especially when the leading verb and the infinitive have the same subject: as,
⟦b:iūrāvit sē nisi victōrem in castra nōn reversūrum⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 87, 5, ⟦i:he swore he would not come back to camp except as a victor⟧. ⟦b:quod sē factūrōs minābantur⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 13, 4, ⟦i:which they threatened they would do⟧. ⟦b:obsidēs datūrōs pollicitī sunt⟧, 4, 27, 1, ⟦i:they volunteered to give hostages⟧.
⟦#2236⟧
(2.) A looser present infinitive is sometimes used with the above verbs, especially in old Latin, generally without a subject accusative. Thus with ⟦b:iūrō⟧ by Cato and Plautus, and with ⟦b:minor⟧, ⟦i:proclaim with threats⟧, by Lucretius. Similarly ⟦b:dare pollicentur⟧, 6, 9, 7, ⟦i:they offer to give⟧. ⟦b:reliquōs dēterrērī spērāns⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 8, 3, ⟦i:hoping that the rest were scared⟧. ⟦b:spērō nostram amīcitiam nōn egēre testibus⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 2, ⟦i:I trust our friendship needs no witnesses⟧. As ⟦b:possum⟧ has no future infinitive, the present of this verb is necessarily used: as, ⟦b:tōtīus Galliae sēsē potīrī posse spērant⟧, 1, 3, 8, ⟦i:they hope to be able to get the control of the whole of Gaul⟧.

title: The Gerundive and Gerund
text:
⟦#2237⟧
The gerundive is a verbal adjective (⟦r899:899⟧). The gerund is a neuter verbal substantive, used only in the oblique cases of the singular. Both gerundives and gerunds express, in a noun form, the uncompleted action of the verb.
⟦#2238⟧
Gerundives and gerunds, like the English verbal in ⟦i:-ing⟧, were originally neither active nor passive (⟦r288:288⟧), but might stand for either an active or a passive. In time a prevailing passive meaning grew up in the gerundive, and a prevailing active meaning in the gerund.
A gerund may be followed by the same case as its verb; but for the gerund of verbs of transitive use, see ⟦r2242:2242⟧, ⟦r2255:2255⟧, ⟦r2259:2259⟧, ⟦r2265:2265⟧.
⟦#2239⟧
Both gerundives and gerunds are modified like verbs, by adverbs, not by adjectives.

title: The Gerundive Construction
text:
⟦#2240⟧
The gerundive expresses, in an adjective form, the uncompleted action of a verb of transitive use exerted on a substantive object, the substantive standing in the case required by the context, and the gerundive agreeing with it.
In this construction, which is called the ⟦i:gerundive construction⟧, the substantive and gerundive blend together in sense like the parts of a compound.
⟦b:male gerendō negōtiō in aere aliēnō vacillant⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 21, ⟦i:owing to bad business-managing they are staggering under debts⟧. ⟦b:studium agrī colendī⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 59, ⟦i:the occupation of land-tilling⟧. ⟦b:vir regendae rē̆ī pūblicae scientissimus⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 214, ⟦i:a man of great experience in state-managing⟧.

title: The Gerund
text:
⟦#2241⟧
The gerund expresses, in a substantive form, the uncompleted action of a verb which has no direct object.
⟦b:ars vīvendī⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 1, 42, ⟦i:the art of living⟧. ⟦b:nōn est locus ad tergiversandum⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 7, 1, 4, ⟦i:’tis no time for shill-I-shall-I-ing⟧. ⟦b:sum dēfessus quaeritandō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 1014, ⟦i:I’m all worn out with hunting⟧. ⟦b:sē experiendō didicisse⟧, Ta. 1, 11, ⟦i:he had learned by experience⟧.
⟦#2242⟧
Gerunds of verbs of transitive use are exceptionally found with a substantive object (2255, 2259, ⟦r2265:2265⟧), and regularly with neuter pronouns and neuter plural adjectives to avoid ambiguity (⟦r1106:1106⟧). See also ⟦r2247:2247⟧.
⟦b:agendī aliquid discendīque causā⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 5, 54, ⟦i:for the sake of doing or learning something⟧. ⟦b:faciendī aliquid vel nōn faciendī vēra ratiō⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 6, 27, 4, ⟦i:the true ground for doing or not doing a thing⟧. ⟦b:artem sē trādere vēra ac falsa dīiūdicandī⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 157, ⟦i:that he passed along the art of distinguishing between the true and the false⟧. ⟦b:regendī cūncta onus⟧, Ta. 1, 11, ⟦i:the burden of governing the world⟧.

title: Nominative
text:
⟦#2243⟧
The nominative of the gerundive construction, as the subject of ⟦b:sum⟧, denotes action which is to be done.
The combination acquires the meaning of obligation or propriety, and this meaning also passes over to the accusative with ⟦b:esse⟧. The person who has the action to do is put in the dative of the possessor (⟦r1215:1215⟧). Instead of the dative, the ablative with ⟦b:ab⟧ is sometimes used, particularly where the dative would be ambiguous.
⟦b:tibī̆ haec cūra suscipienda est⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 69, ⟦i:the undertaking of this care exists for you⟧, i.e., ⟦i:you must undertake this charge⟧. ⟦b:Caesarī omnia ūnō tempore erant agenda: vēxillum prōpōnendum, sīgnum tubā dandum, ab opere revocandī mīlitēs, aciēs īnstruenda, mīlitēs cohortandī, sīgnum dandum⟧, 2, 20, 1, ⟦i:for Caesar there was everything to be done at the same moment: the standard to be raised, bugle call given, soldiers summoned in from their work, line of battle to be formed, soldiers harangued, signal given for engagement⟧. ⟦b:quaerenda pecūnia prīmum est; virtūs post nummōs⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 1, 53, ⟦i:there is money-making to be the first aim: character second to dollars⟧. ⟦b:adeundus mihī̆ illic est homō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 1298, ⟦i:I must draw near this fellow⟧. ⟦b:Caesar statuit sibī̆ Rhēnum esse trānseundum⟧, 4, 16, 1, ⟦i:Caesar made up his mind that he must cross the Rhine⟧. ⟦b:ego istum iuvenem domī tenendum cēnseō⟧, L. 21, 3, 6, ⟦i:for my part, I think that young man ought to be kept at home⟧. ⟦b:ē̆ī ego ā mē referendam grātiam nōn putem?⟧ ⟦i:Planc.⟧ 78, ⟦i:should I not think that I ought to show my gratitude to him?⟧ ⟦b:quid ā mē amplius dīcendum putātis?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 60, ⟦i:what more do you think that I need say?⟧
⟦#2244⟧
⟦b:fruendus⟧, ⟦b:fungendus⟧, ⟦b:potiundus⟧, ⟦b:ūtendus⟧, ⟦b:vēscendus⟧, are also used in this construction, chiefly in the oblique cases; in the nominative the impersonal construction (⟦r2246:2246⟧) is usual. These verbs sometimes have a transitive use in old Latin (⟦r1380:1380⟧).
⟦b:nōn paranda nōbīs sōlum ea, sed fruenda etiam est⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 1, 3, ⟦i:that is a thing which we must not only obtain, but enjoy as well⟧, of wisdom. ⟦b:nec tamen est potiunda tibī⟧, O. 9, 754, ⟦i:she is not to be won by thee⟧. Examples of the oblique cases in this use are cited below.
⟦#2245⟧
⟦b:habeō⟧ with the gerundive, as an equivalent of ⟦b:est mihī̆⟧, ⟦b:est tibī̆⟧, &c. (⟦r2243:2243⟧), is sometimes found, chiefly in late writers and particularly in Tacitus: as,
⟦b:multī habent in praediīs, quibus frūmentum aut vīnum aliudve quid dēsit, inportandum⟧, Varro, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 1, 16, 2, ⟦i:many on whose estates corn or wine or something else is lacking, have to bring it in⟧. ⟦b:multum interest utrumne dē fūrtō dīcendum habeās an dē cīvibus trucīdātīs⟧, Ta. ⟦i:D.⟧ 37, ⟦i:it makes a great difference whether you have to speak about a theft or about the murder of Romans⟧. ⟦b:sī nunc prīmum statuendum habērēmus⟧, Ta. 14, 44, ⟦i:if we had to decide the point to-day for the first time⟧.
⟦#2246⟧
The neuter of verbs of intransitive use takes the impersonal construction with ⟦b:est⟧. Verbs ordinarily transitive also take the impersonal construction when used without an object.
⟦b:nunc est bibendum⟧, H. 1, 37, 1, ⟦i:now drinking exists⟧, i.e. ⟦i:now we must drink⟧. ⟦b:inambulandumst⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 682, ⟦i:I must be moving on⟧. ⟦b:ego amplius dēlīberandum cēnseō⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 457, ⟦i:I opine there must be more pondering⟧. ⟦b:linguae moderandumst mihī̆⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cu.⟧ 486, ⟦i:I must check my tongue⟧. ⟦b:omne animal cōnfitendum est esse mortāle⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 32, ⟦i:it must be admitted that every living thing is destined to die⟧. ⟦b:nēmō umquam sapiēns prōditōrī crēdendum putāvit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 38, ⟦i:no wise man ever held that a traitor was to be trusted⟧.
⟦#2247⟧
The impersonal construction with an object in the accusative, is old-fashioned and rare.
⟦b:canēs paucōs habendum⟧, Varro, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 1, 21, ⟦i:one should keep but few dogs⟧. ⟦b:aeternās quoniam poenās in morte timendumst⟧, Lucr. 1, 111, ⟦i:since punishment eterne they have in death to fear⟧. This construction occurs oftenest in Lucretius and Varro; once in Plautus, a few times in Cicero for special reasons, and here and there in later writers. Not in Caesar or Horace.
⟦#2248⟧
The gerundive sometimes acquires, in itself, the meaning of obligation or propriety, which it properly has only when combined with ⟦b:sum⟧, and becomes a mere adjective, used in any case.
⟦b:fōrmā expetendā līberālem virginem⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 521, ⟦i:a freeborn maid of shape delectable⟧. ⟦b:L. Brūtō, prīncipe huius maximē cōnservandī generis et nōminis⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 3, 11, ⟦i:Brutus, the first of this most highly cherished house and name⟧. ⟦b:huic timendō hostī obvius fuī⟧, L. 21, 41, 4, ⟦i:I met this dreadful foe⟧. ⟦b:Athēnās, multa vīsenda habentīs⟧, L. 45, 27, 11, ⟦i:Athens, which contains many sights worth a visit⟧. For ⟦b:volvendus⟧ &c., see ⟦r288:288⟧.
⟦#2249⟧
The attributive gerundive (⟦r2248:2248⟧), particularly with a negative, ⟦b:in-⟧ privative, or ⟦b:vix⟧, may denote possibility, like the verbal in ⟦b:-bilis⟧: as,
⟦b:labōrēs nōn fugiendōs⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 118, ⟦i:inevitable labours⟧. ⟦b:Polybius, haudquāquam spernendus auctor⟧, L. 30, 45, 5, ⟦i:Polybius, an authority by no means despicable⟧. ⟦b:īnfandum, rēgīna, iubēs renovāre dolōrem⟧, V. 2, 3, ⟦i:thou bidst me, queen, rehearse that woe unspeakable⟧. ⟦b:vix erat crēdendum⟧, 5, 28, 1, ⟦i:it was hardly credible⟧. ⟦b:praedicābile aliquid et glōriandum ac prae sē ferendum⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 49, ⟦i:something laudable and vauntable and displayable as well⟧.

title: Accusative
text:
⟦#2250⟧
(1.) The accusative of the gerundive construction is used with ⟦b:locō⟧ and ⟦b:condūcō⟧, with ⟦b:suscipiō⟧, ⟦b:habeō⟧, and ⟦b:cūrō⟧, and with verbs of giving or assigning.
With the verbs of giving or assigning (such as ⟦b:dō⟧, ⟦b:trādō⟧, ⟦b:committō⟧, ⟦b:attribuō⟧, ⟦b:dīvidō⟧, ⟦b:relinquō⟧, ⟦b:permittō⟧, ⟦b:dēnotō⟧), the emphasis often gravitates towards the substantive, and the gerundive, as an explanatory appendage, acquires the meaning of purpose. So in Plautus with the verbs of asking (⟦b:rogō⟧ and ⟦b:petō⟧); in Cicero with ⟦b:posco⟧.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:caedundum condūxī ego illum :: tum optumumst locēs efferendum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 567, ⟦i:I engaged him for killing :: then you’d better contract for his funeral⟧ (⟦r1709:1709⟧). ⟦b:sīgnum conlocandum cōnsulēs locāvērunt⟧, ⟦i:Cat.⟧ 3, 20, ⟦i:the consuls let out the erecting of the statue⟧. ⟦b:redemptor quī columnam illam condūxerat faciendam⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 47, ⟦i:the contractor who had undertaken the making of that pillar⟧. ⟦b:vellem suscēpissēs iuvenem regendum⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 10, 6, 2, ⟦i:I wish you had undertaken training the young man⟧. ⟦b:aedem habuit tuendam⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 130, ⟦i:he had the looking after the temple⟧. ⟦b:agrum dē nostrō patre colendum habēbat⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 364, ⟦i:he had the tilling of a farm from my father⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) COIRAVIT · BASILICAM · CALECANDAM, CIL. I, 1166, ⟦i:he superintended the town hall plastering⟧. ⟦b:pontem faciendum cūrat⟧, 1, 13, 1, ⟦i:he attends to a bridge’s being made⟧, i.e. ⟦i:has it made⟧. ⟦b:cōnsulibus senātus rem pūblicam dēfendendam dedit⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 8, 15, ⟦i:the senate entrusted the defence of the state to the consuls⟧. ⟦b:agrōs plēbī colendōs dedit⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 3, 16, ⟦i:he gave lands to the common people to till⟧. ⟦b:Antigonus Eumenem propīnquīs sepeliendum trādidit⟧, N. 18, 13, 4, ⟦i:Antigonus delivered Eumenes to his kinsfolk to be buried⟧. ⟦b:attribuit nōs trucīdandōs⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 13, ⟦i:us he handed over to be slaughtered⟧. ⟦b:sauciōs mīlitēs cūrandōs dīvidit patribus⟧, L. 2, 47, 12, ⟦i:he apportioned the wounded soldiers among the senators to cure⟧. ⟦b:haec porcīs comedenda relinquēs⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 7, 19, ⟦i:you’ll leave them to the pigs to eat⟧. ⟦b:cīvīs Rōmānōs trucīdandōs dēnotāvit⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 7, ⟦i:he specified Romans for slaughter⟧.
(⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:quae ūtenda vāsa semper vīcīnī rogant⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 96, ⟦i:traps that the neighbours are always asking the use of⟧. ⟦b:artoptam ex proxumō ūtendam petō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 400, ⟦i:I’m going for the use of a breadpan from next door⟧.
⟦#2251⟧
When such a verb is passive, the accusative becomes nominative.
⟦b:simulācrum Dī̆ānae tollendum locātur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 76, ⟦i:the moving of the statue of Diana is let out⟧. ⟦b:dīlaceranda ferīs dabor ālitibusque praeda⟧, Cat. 64, 152, ⟦i:I shall be given a prey for beasts and birds to tear⟧. ⟦b:trāditīque fētiālibus Caudium dūcendī⟧, L. 9, 10, 2, ⟦i:and they were delivered to the fetials to be taken to Caudium⟧.
⟦#2252⟧
(2.) The accusative of the gerundive construction or gerund is used with a preposition, usually ⟦b:ad⟧. If the verb is of transitive use, the gerundive is proper, not the gerund (⟦r2240:2240⟧).
This construction is used with verbs (including verbs of hindering), with substantives generally to denote purpose, and with adjectives which have the meaning of ⟦i:capable⟧, ⟦i:fit⟧, ⟦i:easy⟧, ⟦i:useful⟧, &c., &c.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:hic in noxiāst, ille ad dīcendam causam adest⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 266, ⟦i:when A’s in trouble, B turns up to make excuses for him⟧. ⟦b:ad pācem petendam ad Hannibalem vēnit⟧, L. 21, 13, 1, ⟦i:he is come to Hannibal to sue for peace⟧. ⟦b:ad eās rēs cōnficiendās Orgetorīx dēligitur⟧, 1, 3, 3, ⟦i:Orgetorix is chosen to do this⟧. ⟦b:dant sē ad lūdendum⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 5, 42, ⟦i:they devote themselves to playing⟧. ⟦b:palūs Rōmānōs ad īnsequendum tardābat⟧, 7, 26, 2, ⟦i:a morass hindered the Romans from pursuit⟧. ⟦b:ut peditēs ad trānseundum impedīrentur⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 62, 2, ⟦i:so that the infantry were hampered in crossing⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:causa ad obiūrgandum⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 150, ⟦i:a reason for finding fault⟧. ⟦b:spatium sūmāmus ad cōgitandum⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 4, 1, ⟦i:let us take time for thought⟧. ⟦b:alter occāsiōnem sibī̆ ad occupandam Asiam oblātam esse arbitrātur⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 4, ⟦i:the other thinks a chance is given him for seizing all Asia⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:homo nōn aptissimus ad iocandum⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 46, ⟦i:a man not very well fitted to be a joker⟧. ⟦b:nimis doctus illest ad male faciendum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:E.⟧ 378, ⟦i:too well the fellow’s trained at playing tricks⟧. ⟦b:ūtēbātur eō cibō quī esset facillimus ad concoquendum⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 64, ⟦i:he made use of the sort of food which was easiest to digest⟧.
⟦#2253⟧
Other prepositions are sometimes used: as, ⟦b:inter⟧, in old Latin, Vergil, Livy, and later writers; ⟦b:ob⟧, once in Ennius, rarely in Cicero and Sallust; ⟦b:in⟧ very rarely, but even in Cicero; ⟦b:ante⟧ (Vergil, Livy), ⟦b:circā⟧ (post-Augustan), ⟦b:propter⟧ (Varro, Val. Max.), all rare.
⟦b:mōrēs sē inter lūdendum dētegunt⟧, Quintil. 1, 3, 12, ⟦i:character discovers itself during play⟧. ⟦b:ob rem iūdicandam pecūniam accipere⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 78, ⟦i:to take money for passing judgement on a case⟧.

title: Dative
text:
⟦#2254⟧
The dative of the gerundive construction is used with adjectives, verbs, and phrases of ability, attention, and adaptation, with titles of office, and with ⟦b:comitia⟧, ⟦i:election⟧.
This construction is not very common in classical Latin, where few verbs and substantives take it instead of the usual ⟦b:ad⟧ and the accusative (⟦r2252:2252⟧). In old Latin, it is also joined to adjectives and participles; in Cicero it is thus used only with ⟦b:accommodātus⟧. From Livy on, the construction becomes a very favourite one. Caesar has it only as below and 3, 4, 1.
⟦b:tālīs iactandīs tuae sunt cōnsuētae manūs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Vid. your hands are used to throwing dice⟧. ⟦b:optumum operī faciundō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 757, ⟦i:most suitable for carrying on his trade⟧. ⟦b:praeesse agrō colendō⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 50, ⟦i:to superintend farm managing⟧. ⟦b:cum diēs vēnisset rogātiōnī ferendae⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 1, 14, 5, ⟦i:when the day came for proposing the bill⟧. ⟦b:hībernīs oppugnandīs hunc esse dictum diem⟧, 5, 27, 5, ⟦i:that this was the day set for attacking the winter quarters⟧. ⟦b:cōnsul plācandīs dīs habendōque dīlēctū dat operam⟧, L. 22, 2, 1, ⟦i:the consul devotes himself to propitiating the gods and raising troops⟧. ⟦b:Dēmosthenēs cūrātor mūrīs reficiendīs fuit⟧, ⟦i:OG.⟧ 19, ⟦i:Demosthenes was commissioner for repairing the walls⟧. ⟦b:IIIvirī rē̆ī pūblicae cōnstituendae⟧, L. ⟦i:Epit.⟧ 120, ⟦i:a commission of three for reorganizing the state⟧. ⟦b:comitia collēgae subrogandō habuit⟧, L. 2, 8, 3, ⟦i:he held an election for appointing a colleague⟧.
⟦#2255⟧
In the dative, a transitive gerund with an object in the accusative is found four times in Plautus; in Ovid, Livy, and Vitruvius once each.
⟦#2256⟧
Late writers sometimes use the dative of the gerundive construction instead of a final clause (⟦r1961:1961⟧): as,
⟦b:subdūcit ex aciē legiōnem faciendīs castrīs⟧, Ta. 2, 21, ⟦i:he withdraws a legion from the field to build a camp⟧. ⟦b:nīdum mollibus plūmīs cōnsternunt tepē̆faciendīs ōvīs, simul nē dūrus sit īnfantibus pullīs⟧, Plin. ⟦i:NH.⟧ 10, 92, ⟦i:they line the nest with soft feathers to warm the eggs, and also to prevent it from being uncomfortable to their young brood⟧.
⟦#2257⟧
The dative of the gerund is used chiefly by old and late writers, and is confined in the best prose to a few special phrases.
⟦b:ōsculandō meliust pausam fierī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 1205, ⟦i:’tis better that a stop be put to kissing⟧. ⟦b:tū nec solvendō erās⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 4, ⟦i:you were neither solvent⟧. SC · ARF, i.e. ⟦b:scrībendō arfuērunt⟧, CIL. I, 196, 2, ⟦i:there were present when the document was put in writing⟧. ⟦b:quod scrībendō adfuistī⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 15, 6, 2, ⟦i:because you were present at the writing⟧.

title: Genitive
text:
⟦#2258⟧
(1.) The genitive of the gerundive construction or gerund is used with substantives or adjectives.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:tacendī tempus est⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Poen.⟧ 741, ⟦i:it’s time to be still⟧. ⟦b:spēs potiundī oppidī⟧, 2, 7, 2, ⟦i:the hope of overpowering the town⟧ (⟦r2244:2244⟧). ⟦b:summa difficultās nāvigandī⟧, 3, 12, 5, ⟦i:the greatest difficulty in sailing⟧. ⟦b:proeliī committendī sīgnum dedit⟧, 2, 21, 3, ⟦i:he gave the signal for beginning the battle⟧. ⟦b:exemplō eōrum clādēs fuit ut Mārsī mitterent ōrātōrēs pācis petendae⟧, L. 9, 45, 18, ⟦i:their downfall was a warning to the Marsians to send envoys to sue for peace⟧. ⟦b:sīve nāvēs dēiciendī operis essent missae⟧, 4, 17, 10, ⟦i:or if vessels for breaking down the works had been sent⟧. Particularly with ⟦b:causā⟧, ⟦b:grātiā⟧, or rarely ⟦b:ergō⟧ (⟦r1257:1257⟧), to denote purpose: as, ⟦b:frūmentandī causā⟧, 4, 12, 1, ⟦i:for foraging⟧. ⟦b:vītandae suspīciōnis causā⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 19, ⟦i:to avoid suspicion⟧. ⟦b:mūneris fungendī grātiā⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 1, 27, ⟦i:for the sake of doing one’s duty⟧. ⟦b:illīusce sacrī coercendī ergō⟧, Cato, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 139, ⟦i:because of thinning out yon hallowed grove⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:quam cupida eram hūc redeundī⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 91, ⟦i:how eager I was to return here⟧. ⟦b:homine perītō dēfīniendī⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 60, ⟦i:a man accomplished in drawing distinctions⟧. ⟦b:perpessus est omnia potius quam cōnsciōs dēlendae tyrannidis indicāret⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 52, ⟦i:he stood out against the worst sooner than betray his confederates in the overthrow of the tyranny⟧. ⟦b:īnsuētus nāvigandī⟧, 5, 6, 3, ⟦i:unused to sailing⟧. ⟦b:studiōsus audiendī⟧, N. 15, 3, 2, ⟦i:an eager listener⟧. ⟦b:nescia tolerandī⟧, Ta. 3, 1, ⟦i:ignorant what patience was⟧. ⟦b:nandī pavidus⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 5, 14, ⟦i:afraid to swim⟧. With adjectives, the gerundive construction is not found in Plautus and Terence, and the gerund not in Plautus. Terence has the gerund with ⟦b:cupidus⟧, Cato with ⟦b:studiōsus⟧. The construction is of slow growth before Tacitus, who greatly developed it.
⟦#2259⟧
In the genitive, a transitive gerund with an object in the accusative is rare except in Plautus; ordinarily the gerundive is used (⟦r2240:2240⟧).
⟦b:tē dēfrūdandī causā⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 687, ⟦i:for the purpose of cheating you⟧. ⟦b:cupidus tē audiendī⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 16, ⟦i:eager to hear you⟧. ⟦b:summa ēlūdendī occāsiōst mihi nunc senēs⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 885, ⟦i:I’ve now a splendid chance the graybeards of eluding⟧. ⟦b:nē suī līberandī⟧ (⟦r2260:2260⟧) ⟦b:atque ulcīscendī Rōmānōs occāsiōnem dīmittant⟧, 5, 38, 2, ⟦i:that they should not let slip the chance of freeing themselves and taking vengeance on the Romans⟧. ⟦b:sīgnum colligendī vāsa dedit⟧, L. 24, 16, 14, ⟦i:he gave the signal to pack their things⟧.
⟦#2260⟧
⟦b:nostrī⟧, ⟦b:vostrī⟧ (or ⟦b:vestrī⟧), and ⟦b:suī⟧, being singular in form (⟦r649:649⟧) have often a singular gerundive.
⟦b:nōn tam suī cōnservandī quam tuōrum cōnsiliōrum reprimendōrum causā profūgērunt⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 7, ⟦i:they fled, not so much to protect themselves as to crush your plans⟧. ⟦b:vēnisse tempus ulcīscendī suī⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 28, ⟦i:that the time was come for them to revenge themselves⟧. ⟦b:vestrī adhortandī causā⟧, L. 21, 41, 1, ⟦i:for the purpose of encouraging you⟧.
⟦#2261⟧
Sometimes another genitive appears beside the genitive of the gerund, each perhaps dependent on the main word. This use is found in old Latin, Lucretius, Varro, and here and there in Cicero, as well as in late Latin.
⟦b:nōminandī istōrum tibī̆ erit cōpia⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 852, ⟦i:you will have a chance to name them⟧. ⟦b:poenārum solvendī tempus⟧, Lucr. 5, 1225, ⟦i:the time of paying penalties⟧. ⟦b:exemplōrum ēligendī potestās⟧, ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 2, 5, ⟦i:a chance of picking out examples⟧. ⟦b:lūcis tuendī cōpiam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 1008, ⟦i:a chance to look upon the light⟧.
⟦#2262⟧
(2.) The genitive of the gerundive construction is used predicatively with ⟦b:sum⟧.
⟦b:rēgium imperium, quod initiō cōnservandae libertātis fuerat⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 6, 7, ⟦i:the authority of the king, which had originally served to uphold freedom⟧. ⟦b:cētera in XII minuendī sūmptūs sunt lāmentātiōnisque fūnebris⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 2, 59, ⟦i:the rest of the contents of the Twelve Tables are conducive to the abating of extravagance and keening at funerals⟧. ⟦b:concordiam ōrdinum, quam dissolvendae tribūnīciae potestātis rentur esse⟧, L. 5, 3, 5, ⟦i:the union of the classes, which they believe serves to break down the power of the tribunes⟧. This use is not common. It is found rarely in Sallust and Cicero; chiefly in Livy.
⟦#2263⟧
The genitive of the gerundive construction, without a substantive or adjective (⟦r2258:2258⟧) or the verb ⟦b:sum⟧ (⟦r2262:2262⟧), is occasionally used to denote purpose: as,
⟦b:quae ille cēpit lēgum ac lībertātis subvortundae⟧, S. ⟦i:Fr. Phil.⟧ 10, ⟦i:which he began in order to overthrow freedom and the laws⟧, of civil war. ⟦b:ūnum vincīrī iubet, magis ūsurpandī iūris quam quia ūnīus culpa foret⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 4, 25, ⟦i:he ordered one into irons, more to vindicate his authority than because an individual was to blame⟧. This use occurs very rarely in Sallust, chiefly in Tacitus and late Latin. Once in Terence with the gerund.
⟦#2264⟧
Tacitus has the genitive of the gerundive construction two or three times with a judicial verb (⟦r1280:1280⟧) to denote the charge: as, ⟦b:occupandae rē̆ī pūblicae arguī nōn poterant⟧, Ta. 6, 10, ⟦i:they could not be charged with an attempt on the throne⟧.

title: Ablative
text:
⟦#2265⟧
In the ablative a transitive gerund with a substantive object is not uncommon.
⟦b:frātrem laudandō⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 1, 1, ⟦i:in quoting your brother⟧. ⟦b:largē partiendō praedam⟧, L. 21, 5, 5, ⟦i:by a lavish distribution of the spoil⟧. This use is particularly common in Livy. Not in Caesar.
⟦#2266⟧
(1.) The ablative of the gerundive construction or gerund denotes means, less often cause, rarely manner and circumstances, or time, or respect.
Means: ⟦b:Caesar dandō sublevandō īgnōscundō, Catō nihil largiundō glōriam adeptus est⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 54, 3, ⟦i:Caesar gained reputation by giving, helping, and pardoning, Cato by lavishing no gifts⟧. ⟦b:opprimī sustentandō ac prōlātandō nūllō pactō potest⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 6, ⟦i:it cannot be crushed by patience and procrastination⟧. Livy has this ablative with the adjective ⟦b:contentus⟧ (⟦r1377:1377⟧): ⟦b:nec iam possidendīs pūblicīs agrīs contentōs esse⟧, 6, 14, 11, ⟦i:that they were no longer satisfied with the occupation of the public lands⟧. Cause: ⟦b:aggerundā curvom aquā⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cas.⟧ 124, ⟦i:bowed with water carrying⟧. ⟦b:flendō turgidulī rubent ocellī⟧, Cat. 3, 18, ⟦i:with weeping red and swollen are her eyne⟧. Manner and circumstances: rare in old Latin and Cicero: not in Caesar: ⟦b:bellum ambulandō cōnfēcērunt⟧, Caelius in ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 8, 15, 1, ⟦i:they strolled through the war⟧. ⟦b:senex vincendō factus⟧, L. 30, 28, 5, ⟦i:maturing in victories⟧. Time: ⟦b:cum plausum meō nōmine recitandō dedissent⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 4, 1, 6, ⟦i:when they had applauded on the reading of my name⟧. ⟦b:partibus dīvidendīs ipsī regiō ēvēnit⟧, L. 25, 30, 6, ⟦i:at the distribution, the district fell to him⟧. Respect: ⟦b:Latīnē loquendō cuivīs erat pār⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 128, ⟦i:in his use of Latin he was a match for anybody⟧.
⟦#2267⟧
(2.) The ablative of the gerundive construction or gerund is also accompanied by a preposition, ⟦b:ab⟧, ⟦b:dē⟧, ⟦b:in⟧, or ⟦b:ex⟧; rarely by ⟦b:prō⟧.
⟦b:nūllum tempus illī umquam vacābat aut ā scrībendō aut ā cōgitandō⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 272, ⟦i:he never had any time free from writing or from thinking⟧. ⟦b:quod verbum ductum est ā nimis intuendō fortūnam alterīus⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 3, 20, ⟦i:a word which is derived from ‘looking too closely at’ another’s prosperity⟧, of the word ⟦b:invidia⟧. ⟦b:cōnsilium illud dē occlūdendīs aedibus⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 784, ⟦i:that idea about barring up the house⟧. ⟦b:nihil dē causā discendā praecipiunt⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 100, ⟦i:they give no instruction about studying up a case⟧. ⟦b:vostra ōrātiō in rē incipiundā⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 224, ⟦i:your remarks when we started in with this affair⟧. ⟦b:Āfricānī in rē gerundā celeritātem⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 25, ⟦i:Africanus’s swiftness in execution⟧. ⟦b:vix ex grātulandō ēminēbam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 504, ⟦i:I barely got my head above their congratulations⟧. ⟦b:quae virtūs ex prōvidendō est appellāta prūdentia⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 1, 60, ⟦i:a virtue which from ‘foreseeing’ is called foresight⟧. ⟦b:prō līberandā amīcā⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Per.⟧ 426, ⟦i:for setting free a leman⟧. ⟦b:prō ope ferendā⟧, L. 23, 28, 11, ⟦i:instead of going to the rescue⟧. In this use ⟦b:ab⟧ is not found in Plautus or Terence, nor ⟦b:prō⟧ in Terence. ⟦b:cum⟧ is found in Quintilian, ⟦b:super⟧ once in Horace, then in Tacitus, ⟦b:sine⟧ once in Varro.
⟦#2268⟧
With a comparative expression, the ablative of the gerundive is found once: ⟦b:nūllum officium referendā grātiā magis necessārium est⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 47, ⟦i:no obligation is more binding than the returning of a favour⟧. The gerundive construction in the ablative of separation (⟦r1302:1302⟧) is found rarely in Livy and Pliny the younger; Livy has also the gerund: as, ⟦b:Verminam absistere sequendō coēgit⟧, L. 29, 33, 8, ⟦i:he forced Vermina to abandon his pursuit⟧.

title: The Supine
text:
⟦#2269⟧
The supine is a verbal substantive. The form in ⟦b:-um⟧ is an accusative. The form in ⟦b:-ū⟧ is used sometimes as a dative, sometimes as an ablative.

title: The Supine in -um
text:
⟦#2270⟧
The supine in ⟦b:-um⟧ denotes purpose with verbs of motion (⟦r1166:1166⟧): as,
⟦b:abiīt piscātum⟧, Pl. ⟦b:R.⟧ 898, ⟦i:he’s gone a fishing⟧. ⟦b:neu noctū īrem obambulātum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 315, ⟦i:not to go a prowling by night⟧. ⟦b:legiōne ūnā frūmentātum missā⟧, 4, 32, 1, ⟦i:one legion being sent a foraging⟧. ⟦b:sessum it praetor⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 74, ⟦i:the praetor is going to take his seat⟧. ⟦b:spectātum veniunt, veniunt spectentur ut ipsae⟧, O. ⟦i:AA.⟧ 1, 99, ⟦i:they come to see and eke for to be seen⟧. This use is very common in Plautus and Terence, less common in Cicero and Caesar. It is found not infrequently in Sallust and particularly in Livy; sporadically in the Augustan poets. In late prose it is almost confined to archaistic writing. In classical Latin, purpose is more commonly expressed by the subjunctive with ⟦b:ut⟧ or a relative pronoun, or by a gerundive or gerund with ⟦b:ad⟧ or ⟦b:causā⟧. See also ⟦r2164:2164⟧.
⟦#2271⟧
The most common supines in ⟦b:-um⟧ are ⟦b:cubitum⟧, ⟦b:dormītum⟧, ⟦b:ēreptum⟧, ⟦b:frūmentātum⟧, ⟦b:grātulātum⟧, ⟦b:nūntiātum⟧, ⟦b:oppugnātum⟧, ⟦b:ōrātum⟧, ⟦b:pāstum⟧, ⟦b:perditum⟧, ⟦b:petītum⟧, ⟦b:salūtātum⟧, ⟦b:sessum⟧, ⟦b:supplicātum⟧. They are found chiefly with ⟦b:eō⟧ and ⟦b:veniō⟧. ⟦b:nūptum⟧ is also common with ⟦b:dō⟧, ⟦b:collocō⟧, &c., and supines are occasionally found with other verbs implying motion.
⟦#2272⟧
The supine in ⟦b:-um⟧ may be followed by the same construction as its verb: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) Accusative: ⟦b:deōs salūtātum atque uxōrem modo intrō dēvortor domum⟧, Pl. ⟦i:St.⟧ 534, ⟦i:I’ll just turn in home to greet my gods and my wife⟧. ⟦b:lēgātōs ad Caesarem mittunt rogātum auxilium⟧, 1, 11, 2, ⟦i:they send envoys to Caesar to beg aid⟧. ⟦b:oppugnātum patriam nostram veniunt⟧, L. 21, 41, 13, ⟦i:they come to assail our country⟧. Classical writers generally avoid this use of the accusative. (⟦i:b.⟧) Dative: ⟦b:servītum tibi mē abdūcitō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 520, ⟦i:take me away to slave for you⟧. ⟦b:nōn ego Grāīs servītum mātribus ībō⟧, V. 2, 786, ⟦i:not I shall go to be the serf of Grecian dames⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) Subordinate clause: ⟦b:lēgātī veniēbant: Aeduī questum quod Harūdēs fīnēs eōrum populārentur⟧, 1, 37, 1, ⟦i:envoys came: the Aeduans to complain ‘because the Harudians were laying their country waste’⟧ (⟦r1853:1853⟧). ⟦b:lēgātōs ad Caesarem mīsērunt ōrātum nē sē in hostium numerō dūceret⟧, 6, 32, 1, ⟦i:they sent envoys to Caesar to beg that he would not regard them in the light of enemies⟧.
⟦#2273⟧
The supine in ⟦b:-um⟧ followed by ⟦b:īrī⟧ forms the future passive infinitive: as,
⟦b:eum exceptum īrī putō⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 7, 22, 1, ⟦i:I think that there is a going to capture him⟧, i.e. ⟦i:that he is going to be captured⟧. Here ⟦b:īrī⟧ is used impersonally and ⟦b:eum⟧ is the object of ⟦b:exceptum⟧. This infinitive is found half a dozen times in old Latin, often in Cicero, rarely in other writers; not in the Augustan poets. For the common periphrasis, see ⟦r2233:2233⟧.

title: The Supine in -ū
text:
⟦#2274⟧
The supine in ⟦b:-ū⟧ is used with ⟦b:fās⟧, ⟦b:nefās⟧, and adjectives, chiefly of such meaning as ⟦i:easy⟧, ⟦i:good⟧, ⟦i:pleasant⟧, ⟦i:strange⟧, or their opposites.
Only a few supines in ⟦b:-ū⟧ are found; the commonest are ⟦b:audītū⟧, ⟦b:cōgnitū⟧, ⟦b:dictū⟧, ⟦b:factū⟧, ⟦b:inventū⟧, ⟦b:memorātū⟧, ⟦b:nātū⟧, ⟦b:vīsū⟧.
⟦b:sī hoc fās est dictū⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 38, ⟦i:if heaven allows us to say so⟧. ⟦b:difficile dictū est dē singulīs⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 1, 7, 2, ⟦i:it is hard to say in the case of individuals⟧. ⟦b:quaerunt quod optimum factū sit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 68, ⟦i:they ask what the best thing is to do⟧. ⟦b:quid est tam iocundum cōgnitū atque audītū?⟧ ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 31, ⟦i:what pleasure is greater to mind and ear?⟧ ⟦b:palpebrae mollissimae tāctū⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 142, ⟦i:the eyelids are very soft to the touch⟧. With such adjectives the dative is commonly used (⟦r1200:1200⟧); or, particularly with ⟦b:facilis⟧ or ⟦b:difficilis⟧, the gerundive construction with ⟦b:ad⟧ (⟦r2252:2252⟧); for the infinitive, see ⟦r2166:2166⟧. The supine in ⟦b:-ū⟧ is found chiefly in Cicero and Livy. Very rare in old Latin, Sallust, Caesar (who has only ⟦b:factū⟧ and ⟦b:nātū⟧), and the poets. From the elder Pliny and Tacitus on, it gets commoner.
⟦#2275⟧
The supine in ⟦b:-ū⟧ sometimes introduces a subordinate sentence, but it is never used with an object in the accusative.
⟦b:quoivīs facile scītū est quam fuerim miser⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 296, ⟦i:anybody can easily understand how unhappy I was⟧. ⟦b:incrēdibile memorātū est quam facile coaluerint⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 6, 2, ⟦i:it is an incredible tale how readily they grew into one⟧. ⟦b:vidētis nefās esse dictū miseram fuisse tālem senectūtem⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 13, ⟦i:you see that it were a sin to say that an old age like his was unhappy⟧.
⟦#2276⟧
The supine in ⟦b:-ū⟧ is found rarely with ⟦b:opus est⟧ (⟦r1379:1379⟧), ⟦b:dīgnus⟧ and ⟦b:indīgnus⟧ (⟦r1392:1392⟧): as,
⟦b:ita dictū opus est⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 941, ⟦i:thus thou must needs say⟧. ⟦b:nihil dignum dictū āctum hīs cōnsulibus⟧, L. 4, 30, 4, ⟦i:nothing worth mentioning was done this year⟧. For ⟦b:dignus⟧ with ⟦b:quī⟧ and the subjunctive, see ⟦r1819:1819⟧; for ⟦b:opus est⟧ with the infinitive, 2211.
⟦#2277⟧
In Plautus and Cato, the supine in ⟦b:-ū⟧ is very rarely used like an ablative of separation (⟦r1302:1302⟧): as, ⟦b:nunc opsonātū redeō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 288, ⟦i:I’m only just back from catering⟧. ⟦b:prīmus cubitū surgat, postrēmus cubitum eat⟧, Cato, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 5, 5, ⟦i:let him be first to get up from bed and last to go to bed⟧. Statius imitates this use in ⟦i:Ach.⟧ 1, 119.

title: The Participle
text:
⟦#2278⟧
The participle is a verbal adjective. Like the adjective, it is inflected to agree with its substantive. Like the verb, it may be modified by an adverb, it is active or passive, and it expresses action as continuing, completed, or future. It may also be followed by the same case as its verb.

title: Time of the Participle
text:
⟦#2279⟧
(1.) The time to which the participle refers is indicated by the verb of the sentence.
⟦b:āēr effluēns hūc et illūc ventōs efficit⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 101, ⟦i:the air by streaming to and fro produces winds⟧. ⟦b:convēnī hodiē adveniēns quendam⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 234, ⟦i:I met a man as I was coming to-day⟧. ⟦b:manūs tendentēs vītam ōrābant⟧, L. 44, 42, 4, ⟦i:with hands outstretched they begged their lives⟧. ⟦b:Croesus Halyn penetrāns magnam pervertet opum vim⟧, oracle in ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 115, ⟦i:Croesus, when Halys he shall cross, will overthrow a mighty realm⟧. ⟦b:benignitātem tu͡am mihī̆ expertō praedicās⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Merc.⟧ 289, ⟦i:thou vauntest to me who’ve proved thy courtesy⟧. ⟦b:cōnsecūtus id quod animō prōposuerat, receptuī canī iussit⟧, 7, 47, 1, ⟦i:having accomplished what he had designed, he gave orders to sound the retreat⟧. ⟦b:Dionȳsius Syrācūsīs expulsus Corinthī puerōs docēbat⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 3, 27, ⟦i:after his expulsion from Syracuse, Dionysius kept school at Corinth⟧. ⟦b:lēgātī dīxērunt sē rē dēlīberātā ad Caesarem reversūrōs⟧, 4, 9, 1, ⟦i:the envoys said that they would come back to Caesar after they had thought the matter over⟧.
⟦#2280⟧
(2.) The perfect participle of deponents is sometimes used with past tenses or their equivalents to denote incomplete contemporaneous action. So occasionally a perfect passive.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:Metellum esse ratī portās clausēre⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 69, 1, ⟦i:supposing that it was Metellus, they closed their gates⟧. ⟦b:gāvīsus illōs retinērī iussit⟧, 4, 13, 6, ⟦i:with pleasure he gave orders for their detention⟧. ⟦b:persuādent Rauracīs utī eōdem ūsī cōnsiliō proficīscantur⟧, 1, 5, 4, ⟦i:they coaxed the Rauraci to adopt the same plan and go⟧. ⟦b:sōlātus iussit sapientem pāscere barbam⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 3, 35, ⟦i:consoling me he bade me grow a philosophic beard⟧. This use is found in old Latin and in Cicero very rarely. Sallust and Caesar use a few verbs thus. It is not uncommon in the Augustan poets and Livy. In late writers, especially Tacitus, it is frequent. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:servum sub furcā caesum mediō ēgerat circō⟧, L. 2, 36, 1, ⟦i:he had driven a slave round, flogged under the fork, right in the circus⟧. With this compare ⟦b:servus per circum, cum virgīs caederētur, furcam ferēns ductus est⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 1, 55, ⟦i:a slave with the fork on his neck was driven through the circus, flogged with rods the while⟧ (⟦r1872:1872⟧). But the perfect passive has its ordinary force (⟦r2279:2279⟧) in ⟦b:verberibus caesum tē in pistrīnum dēdam⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 199, ⟦i:I’ll give you a flogging and then put you in the mill⟧.
⟦#2281⟧
For the perfect participle with forms of ⟦b:sum⟧ and ⟦b:fuī⟧, see ⟦r1608:1608⟧, ⟦r1609:1609⟧; for the conative present participle, 2301; reflexive, 1482.

title: The Attributive Participle
text:
⟦#2282⟧
The present or perfect participle is often used as an adjective to express a permanent condition: as,
⟦b:ācrem ōrātōrem, incēnsum et agentem et canōrum forī strepitus dēsīderat⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 317, ⟦i:the noisy forum requires an impetuous speaker, inspired and dramatic and sonorous⟧. ⟦b:L. Abuccius, homo adprīmē doctus⟧, Varro, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 3, 2, 17, ⟦i:Abuccius, an eminently learned man⟧. ⟦b:aliī facētī, flōrentēs etiam et ōrnātī⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 20, ⟦i:others are brilliant, even bright and elegant⟧. ⟦b:id tibī̆ renūntiō futūrum ut sīs sciēns⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 508, ⟦i:I give you notice this will happen, that you may be prepared⟧.
⟦#2283⟧
The future participle is found as an adjective in the Augustan poets and in late writers. Cicero, however, has ⟦b:futūrus⟧ in this use with ⟦b:rēs⟧ and a few other words, and has ⟦b:ventūrus⟧ once.
⟦b:dā mānsūram urbem⟧, V. 3, 85, ⟦i:grant a city that shall abide⟧. ⟦b:firmus pariēs et dūrātūrus⟧, Ta. ⟦i:D.⟧ 22, ⟦i:a strong and durable wall⟧. ⟦b:sīgna ostenduntur ā dīs rērum futūrārum⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 12, ⟦i:signs of future events are disclosed by the gods⟧. For the future participle with forms of ⟦b:sum⟧, see ⟦r1633:1633⟧.
⟦#2284⟧
Many participles have become complete adjectives, and as such are capable of composition or comparison, or take the case required by an adjective.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:nōmen invictī imperātōris⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 82, ⟦i:the invincible general’s name⟧. ⟦b:pūrus et īnsōns sī vīvō⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 6, 69, ⟦i:pure and guiltless if I live⟧ (⟦r749:749⟧). (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:solūtus venēficae scientiōris carmine⟧, H. ⟦i:Epod.⟧ 5, 71, ⟦i:freed by some craftier witch’s charm⟧. ⟦b:homo ērudītissimus, Verrēs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 126, ⟦i:Verres, most accomplished of men⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:tibi sum oboediēns⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 806, ⟦i:I’m your obedient⟧ (⟦r1200:1200⟧). ⟦b:tē cōnfīdō ea factūrum quae mihī̆ intellegēs maximē esse accommodāta⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 3, 3, 2, ⟦i:I feel confident that you will do what you shall feel most appropriate to my interests⟧ (⟦r1201:1201⟧). For the genitive with such participles, see ⟦r1266:1266⟧.
⟦#2285⟧
A perfect participle in agreement with a substantive often contains the leading idea, and may be translated like an abstract substantive with a genitive dependent. The nominative is rarely thus used. The present participle in this use is rare, the future late.
This construction expresses the completed action of the verb in precisely the same way that the gerundive construction (⟦r2240:2240⟧) expresses uncompleted action.
(⟦i:a.⟧) Joined with substantives: ⟦b:iniūriae retentōrum equitum Rōmānōrum⟧, 3, 10, 2, ⟦i:the outrages of Roman knights detained⟧, i.e. ⟦i:in the detention of Roman knights⟧. ⟦b:servātī cōnsulis decus⟧, L. 21, 46, 10, ⟦i:the credit of saving the consul⟧. ⟦b:male administrātae prōvinciae urgēbātur⟧, Ta. 6, 29, ⟦i:he was charged with maladministration of his province⟧. ⟦b:ō quid solūtīs est beātius cūrīs?⟧ Cat. 31, 7, ⟦i:oh what is sweeter than the putting off of care?⟧
(⟦i:b.⟧) Joined with prepositions: ⟦b:ab conditā urbe ad līberātam⟧, L. 1, 60, 3, ⟦i:from the foundation of the city to the liberation thereof⟧. ⟦b:post nātōs hominēs improbissimus⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 224, ⟦i:the greatest reprobate since the creation of man⟧. ⟦b:ante cīvitātem datam⟧, ⟦i:Arch.⟧ 9, ⟦i:before the gift of the citizenship⟧.
(⟦i:c.⟧) In the nominative: very rare before Livy: ⟦b:dēpressa hostium classis⟧, ⟦i:Arch.⟧ 21, ⟦i:the sinking of the enemy’s fleet⟧. ⟦b:angēbant ingentis spīritūs virum Sicilia Sardiniaque āmissae⟧, L. 21, 1, 5, ⟦i:what tortured the high-souled hero was the loss of Sicily and Sardinia⟧. ⟦b:cuius turbāvit nitidōs exstīnctus passer ocellōs⟧, J. 6, 7, ⟦i:whose sparkling eyne the sparrow’s death bedimmed⟧.
⟦#2286⟧
This use of the participle, though old, is not common before Livy, who, like Tacitus, has it frequently, both with substantives and with prepositions. Very rare in Caesar, rare in Cicero, who, however, uses it both with substantives and with a few prepositions. In old Latin (not in Terence), it is found with the substantives ⟦b:opus⟧ and ⟦b:ūsus⟧, in Cato with ⟦b:post⟧, in Varro with ⟦b:propter⟧: as, ⟦b:mī homine conventōst opus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cur.⟧ 302, ⟦i:I needs must see the man⟧. ⟦b:propter mare congelātum⟧, Varro, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 1, 2, 4, ⟦i:by reason of the freezing of the sea water⟧. For the participle alone with ⟦b:ūsus est⟧ and ⟦b:opus est⟧, see ⟦r1382:1382⟧.

title: The Substantive Participle
text:
⟦#2287⟧
Participles sometimes become substantives, especially the perfect participle: as,
⟦b:vīvit gnāta⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 749, ⟦i:your daughter’s alive⟧. ⟦b:dē dēmēnsō suō⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 43, ⟦i:out of his allowance⟧. ⟦b:īnstitūtum tenēbimus⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 4,7, ⟦i:we will hold to our fundamental idea⟧. Adverbs, not adjectives, are commonly used to qualify perfect participles used as substantives; for examples, see ⟦r1440:1440⟧. The masculine singular is rarely used as a substantive; the neuter, both singular and plural, is common, particularly with prepositions.
⟦#2288⟧
The masculine plural of the perfect participle, when used as a substantive, generally denotes a definite class of persons: as,
⟦b:ut damnātī in integrum restituantur, vīnctī solvantur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 12, ⟦i:that the condemned go scot-free, the imprisoned are set at liberty⟧. ⟦b:Catilīna cum expedītīs in prīmā aciē vorsārī⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 60, 4, ⟦i:Catiline bustling round in the van with the light infantry⟧. ⟦b:ēvocātīs equōs sūmit⟧, 7, 65, 5, ⟦i:he took away the veterans’ horses⟧. Rarely not denoting a definite class: as, ⟦b:missī intercipiuntur⟧, 5, 40, 1, ⟦i:the men who had been sent⟧ (i.e. on a particular occasion) ⟦i:are cut off⟧.
⟦#2289⟧
The perfect participle alone sometimes serves as the subject of a sentence instead of an abstract substantive (⟦r2285:2285⟧): as,
⟦b:nōtum furēns quid fēmina possit⟧, V. 5, 6, ⟦i:the knowledge of what a woman in her wrath can do⟧. ⟦b:prōnūntiātum repente nē quis violārētur, multitūdinem exuit armīs⟧, L. 4, 59, 7, ⟦i:the sudden proclamation that nobody was to be harmed, deprived the people of their weapons⟧. This use is found chiefly in Livy, once or twice in Cicero; not in Caesar or Sallust. See ⟦r1382:1382⟧.
⟦#2290⟧
The present participle is rarely a substantive in the nominative and ablative singular, but often in the other cases.
⟦b:in cōnstituentibus rem pūblicam⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 45, ⟦i:among the founders of a state⟧. ⟦b:multae īnsectantēs dēpellunt⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 127, ⟦i:many drive off their pursuers⟧. ⟦b:nec praeterita nec praesentia abs tē, sed futūra exspectō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 8, 1, ⟦i:I do not expect from you the past or the present, but the future⟧.
⟦#2291⟧
The genitive plural of the present participle is often best translated by an English abstract: as,
⟦b:cachinnōs inrīdentium commovēbat⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 216, ⟦i:he provoked guffaws of derision⟧. ⟦b:mixtōs terrentium paventiumque clāmōrēs⟧, L. 22, 5, 4, ⟦i:mingled cries of exultation and terror⟧. ⟦b:prīmō gaudentium impetū⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 1, 4, ⟦i:in the first outburst of joy⟧.
⟦#2292⟧
The future participle is very rarely used as a substantive.
⟦b:audītūrum dictūrī cūra dēlectat⟧, Quintil. 11, 3, 157, ⟦i:deliberation on the part of one who is on the point of speaking attracts his prospective hearer⟧. ⟦b:havē̆, imperātor, moritūrī tē salūtant⟧, Suet. ⟦i:Claud.⟧ 21, ⟦i:emperor, all hail! the doomed give thee greeting⟧. This use is found in late writers, as in Tacitus and Curtius once each, and half a dozen times in Pliny the younger. Cicero and Sallust have ⟦b:futūrus⟧ thus (⟦r2283:2283⟧): as, ⟦b:abs tē futūra exspectō⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 2, 8, 1, ⟦i:from you I expect the future⟧. ⟦b:supplicia in post futūrōs composuit⟧, S. ⟦i:Fr. Lep.⟧ 6, ⟦i:he invented penalties for men unborn⟧.

title: The Appositive Participle
text:
⟦#2293⟧
The appositive participle is a loose substitute for a subordinate sentence introduced by a relative or by a conjunctive particle.
⟦#2294⟧
(1.) The appositive participle may represent a relative sentence: as,
⟦b:nōvī ego Epicūrēōs omnia sigilla venerantēs⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 85, ⟦i:why, I know Epicureans who bow the knee to all sorts of graven images⟧. ⟦b:Conōn mūrōs dīrutōs ā Lȳsandrō reficiendōs cūrat⟧, N. 9, 4, 5, ⟦i:Conon superintended the rebuilding of the walls which had been destroyed by Lysander⟧. The future participle is poetic and late (⟦r2283:2283⟧): as, ⟦b:servēs itūrum Caesarem in Britannōs⟧, H. 1, 35, 29, ⟦i:guard Caesar who against the Britons is to march⟧.
⟦#2295⟧
(2.) The appositive participle, representing other sentences, may express various relations: as, (⟦i:a.⟧) time, (⟦i:b.⟧) cause or means, (⟦i:c.⟧) purpose, (⟦i:d.⟧) concession, (⟦i:e.⟧) hypothesis, (⟦i:f.⟧) description or the manner of an action, like an adverb.
For the ablative absolute in such relations, see ⟦r1362:1362-1374⟧, particularly 1367.
(⟦i:a.⟧) Time: ⟦b:vehemēns sum exoriēns, quom occidō vehementior⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 71, ⟦i:furious am I at my rising, when I set more furious still⟧. ⟦b:occīsus est ā cēnā rediēns⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 97, ⟦i:he was murdered on his way home from a dinner-party⟧. ⟦b:ūnam noctem sōlam praedōnēs commorātī, accedēre incipiunt Syrācūsās⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 95, ⟦i:the freebooters, after tarrying but one night, began to draw near Syracuse⟧. The future is late (⟦r2283:2283⟧): as, ⟦b:prīmum omnium virōrum fortium itūrī in proelia canunt⟧, Ta. ⟦i:G.⟧ 3, ⟦i:as the chief of all brave heroes, they sing of him when they are on the point of going to battle⟧, of Hercules.
(⟦i:b.⟧) Cause or means: ⟦b:mōtum exspectāns dīlectum habēre īnstituit⟧, 6, 1, 1, ⟦i:since he anticipated a rising, he determined on recruiting troops⟧. ⟦b:moveor tālī amīcō orbātus⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 10, ⟦i:I am certainly affected at being bereaved of such a friend⟧. ⟦b:dextrā datā fidem futūrae amīcitiae sanxisse⟧, L. 1, 1, 8, ⟦i:by giving his right hand he gave a pledge of future friendship⟧. ⟦b:quae contuēns animus accēdit ad cōgnitiōnem deōrum⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 153, ⟦i:through the contemplation of these, the mind arrives at a knowledge of the gods⟧. The future participle is late: as, ⟦b:neque illīs iūdicium aut vēritās, quippe eōdem diē dīversa parī certāmine postulātūrīs⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 1, 32, ⟦i:they had neither sound judgement nor sincerity, since on the same day they were to make conflicting demands with equal vehemence⟧.
(⟦i:c.⟧) Purpose: the future participle, commonly with a verb of motion: ⟦b:ad Clūsium vēnērunt, legiōnem Rōmānam castraque oppugnātūrī⟧, L. 10, 26, 7, ⟦i:they came to the neighbourhood of Clusium, to assail the Roman legion and camp⟧. ⟦b:ascendit ipse, lātūrus auxilium⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 6, 16, 9, ⟦i:he went aboard in person to go to the rescue⟧. ⟦b:laetō complērant lītora coetū vīsūrī Aeneadas⟧, V. 5, 107, ⟦i:in happy company they’d filled the strand to see Aeneas’ men⟧. ⟦b:rediēre omnēs Bonōniam, rursus cōnsiliātūrī⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 2, 53, ⟦i:they all went back to Bologna for a second consultation⟧. This use appears first in C. Gracchus as cited by Gellius, then once in Cicero and Sallust each, and a few times in the poets. From Livy on, it grows commoner. In the poets, Livy, and Tacitus, it is sometimes joined with a conditional idea or protasis: as, ⟦b:ēgreditur castrīs Rōmānus, vāllum invāsūrus nī cōpia pugnae fieret⟧, L. 3, 60, 8, ⟦i:the Roman marches out of camp, proposing to assault the stockade unless battle were offered⟧.
(⟦i:d.⟧) Concession: ⟦b:quī mortālis nātus condiciōnem postulēs immortālium⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 3, 36, ⟦i:thou who, though born to die, layest claim to the state of the deathless⟧. ⟦b:bēstiīs, quibus ipsa terra fundit pāstūs abundantīs nihil labōrantibus⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 111, ⟦i:the beasts, on which, though they toil not, earth lavishes sustenance in profusion⟧. Often with ⟦b:tamen⟧ or the like accompanying the verb: as, ⟦b:ibī̆ vehementissimē perturbātus Lentulus tamen et sīgnum et manum suam cōgnōvit⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 12, ⟦i:thereupon Lentulus, though thrown into the most extreme confusion, did yet recognize his own hand and seal⟧. For ⟦b:quamquam⟧ and ⟦b:quamvīs⟧, see ⟦r1900:1900⟧, ⟦r1907:1907⟧. Ovid and Propertius sometimes have ⟦b:licet⟧ (⟦r1710:1710⟧): as, ⟦b:isque, licet caelī regiōne remōtōs, mente deōs adiīt⟧, O. 15, 62, ⟦i:he in the spirit to the gods drew nigh, though they are far away in heaven’s domain⟧. The future participle is rare and late.
(⟦i:e.⟧) Hypothesis: ⟦b:quid igitur mihī̆ ferārum laniātus oberit nihil sentientī?⟧ ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 104, ⟦i:what hurt will the clawing of wild beasts do me if I have no feeling?⟧ ⟦b:appārēbat nōn admissōs prōtinus Carthāginem itūrōs⟧, L. 21, 9, 4, ⟦i:it grew obvious that, if not given audience, they would go to Carthage forthwith⟧. For other examples, see ⟦r2110:2110⟧. For the participle with ⟦b:quasi⟧ or ⟦b:ut⟧, and in late writers with ⟦b:tamquam⟧ or ⟦b:velut⟧, see ⟦r2121:2121⟧. The future participle is rare and late.
(⟦i:f.⟧) Description or manner: ⟦b:haec properantēs scrīpsimus⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 4, 4a, ⟦i:I have written this hastily⟧, i.e. ⟦i:in haste yours truly⟧. ⟦b:dictātor et magister equitum triumphantēs in urbem rediēre⟧, L. 2, 20, 13, ⟦i:the dictator and his master of the horse returned to the city in triumph⟧. ⟦b:incendēbat haec flētū et pectus verberāns⟧, Ta. 1, 23, ⟦i:he lent passion to his words with tears and beating of his breast⟧. ⟦b:vīnctōs aspiciunt catēnīs līberōs suōs⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 108, ⟦i:they behold their own children held in bondage⟧.
⟦#2296⟧
The participle with a negative may be translated by ⟦i:without⟧: as,
⟦b:id illa ūnivorsum abripiet haud existumāns quantō labōre partum⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 45, ⟦i:my lady’ll grab it all without a thought of all the toil it cost to get⟧. ⟦b:nōn rogātōs ultrō offerre auxilium⟧, L. 34, 23, 3, ⟦i:that without being asked, they offer assistance of their own accord⟧.

title: The Predicative Participle
text:
⟦#2297⟧
⟦b:habeō⟧ is sometimes used with certain perfect participles to express an action continuing in its consequences, ⟦b:faciō⟧, ⟦b:dō⟧, and in old Latin ⟦b:reddō⟧ and ⟦b:cūrō⟧, with a perfect participle, are emphatic substitutes for the verb to which the participle belongs.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:quae nōs nostramque adulēscentiam habent dēspicātam et quae nōs semper omnibus cruciant modīs⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 383, ⟦i:who hold us and our youth in scorn and torment us in every way⟧. ⟦b:in eā prōvinciā pecūniās magnās collocātās habent⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 18, ⟦i:they have invested large funds in that province⟧. ⟦b:Clōdiī animum perspectum habeō, cōgnitum, iūdicātum⟧, ⟦i:ad Br.⟧ 1, 1, 1, ⟦i:Clodius’s mind I have looked into thoroughly, probed, formed a judgement on⟧. ⟦b:clausum lacū ac montibus et circumfūsum suīs cōpiīs habuit hostem⟧, L. 22, 4, 5, ⟦i:his enemy he had shut in by lake and mountains and surrounded by his troops⟧. See also ⟦r1606:1606⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:missa haec face⟧, T. ⟦i:Ad.⟧ 906, ⟦i:let this pass⟧. ⟦b:vērum haec missa faciō⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 76, ⟦i:but I let this pass⟧. ⟦b:Mānlium missum fēcit⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 112, ⟦i:he let Manlius go⟧. ⟦b:factum et cūrātum dabō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cas.⟧ 439, ⟦i:I’ll have it done and seen to⟧. ⟦b:strātās legiōnēs Latīnōrum dabō⟧, L. 8, 6, 6, ⟦i:I will lay the Latin legions low⟧. ⟦b:ego iam tē commōtum reddam⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 864, ⟦i:I’ll soon have you worked up⟧. ⟦b:inventum tibī cūrābō tu͡om Pamphilum⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 684, ⟦i:I’ll have your Pamphilus looked up for you⟧. In classical writers, ⟦b:faciō⟧ only is found in this use and only with the participle of ⟦b:mittō⟧; ⟦b:dō⟧ occurs in late writers; ⟦b:reddō⟧ and ⟦b:cūrō⟧ only in old Latin. All these verbs are usually in the future tense or its equivalent. For ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:cupiō⟧, and ⟦b:nōlō⟧ with the infinitive passive without ⟦b:esse⟧, see ⟦r2229:2229⟧.
⟦#2298⟧
The present participle is used predicatively with verbs signifying ⟦i:represent⟧, and with verbs denoting the exercise of the senses or mind: as,
⟦b:facit Sōcratem disputantem⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 31, ⟦i:he represents Socrates discussing⟧. ⟦b:quasi ipsōs indūxī loquentēs⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 3, ⟦i:I have brought on the men themselves as speaking⟧. ⟦b:nōn illum miserum, īgnārum cāsūs suī, redeuntem ā cēnā vidētis?⟧ ⟦i:RA.⟧ 98, ⟦i:do you not see the poor man, little dreaming of his fate, returning from the dinner?⟧ ⟦b:nōn audīvit dracōnem loquentem⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 141, ⟦i:he did not hear the serpent speaking⟧. This use is found in Plautus, Terence, Cicero, Sallust, Horace, Nepos, Vitruvius, and Livy. Once in Piso (consul 133 B.C.), as cited by Gellius, 7, 9, 6. Verbs denoting the exercise of the senses or mind take the accusative with the infinitive to denote the fact or action; see ⟦r2175:2175⟧. For ⟦b:audiō⟧ with ⟦b:cum⟧, see ⟦r1870:1870⟧. For the infinitive without ⟦b:esse⟧ with verbs of emotion, see ⟦r2184:2184⟧.
⟦#2299⟧
A passive with a verb meaning ⟦i:represent⟧ is expressed, for lack of a present passive participle, by the infinitive (⟦r2175:2175⟧). The infinitive active is rare.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:cōnstruī ā deō atque aedificārī mundum facit⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 19, ⟦i:he represents the world being put together and built by the gods⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:poētae impendēre saxum Tantalō faciunt⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 4, 35, ⟦i:the poets represent a rock hanging over Tantalus⟧. Rarely the participle (⟦r2298:2298⟧) and the infinitive are united: as, ⟦b:Polyphēmum Homērus cum ariete conloquentem facit eiusque laudāre fortūnās⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 115, ⟦i:Homer represents Polyphemus chatting with the ram and his envy of the ram’s estate⟧. But the perfect infinitive active must be used when the action is to be distinctly marked as completed, for lack of a perfect active participle: as, ⟦b:fēcit Dolābella Verrem accēpisse⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 100, ⟦i:Dolabella represented Verres as having received⟧.

title: Some Occasional Peculiarities of Verbs
text:
⟦#2300⟧
In many cases where in English a verb like ⟦i:wish⟧ or ⟦i:try to have⟧ a thing done, ⟦i:can⟧, ⟦i:must⟧, or ⟦i:am allowed to⟧, is used, the equivalent Latin verb is omitted. As this use generally extends through the entire system of the verb, examples of the nouns of the verb and of subordinate sentences thus used, are conveniently included here.

title: The Conative Use
text:
⟦#2301⟧
A verb is sometimes used to denote action proposed, attempted, or begun, but not necessarily carried out. This is called the ⟦i:Conative Use⟧ of the verb: as,
⟦b:ancillās dēdō⟧, T. ⟦i:Hec.⟧ 773, ⟦i:I try to give⟧, or ⟦i:I offer up the servant girls⟧. ⟦b:sine ūllā dubitātiōne condemnant⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 75, ⟦i:without a moment’s hesitation they vote to condemn⟧. ⟦b:dum id inpetrant⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 233, ⟦i:as long as they’re trying to get it⟧. ⟦b:sī plācēs inlacrimābilem Plūtōna⟧, H. 2, 14, 5, ⟦i:shouldst thou the stonyhearted Pluto strive to melt⟧. ⟦b:sī discēdās⟧, J. 7. 50, ⟦i:should you attempt to leave⟧. ⟦b:in cūriam abiēcit, quam vīvus ēverterat⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 90, ⟦i:he shoved the corpse into the senate house, which the man in his lifetime had done his best to overthrow⟧. ⟦b:adsurgentem rēgem umbōne resupīnat⟧, L. 4, 19, 5, ⟦i:with the boss of his shield he put the king flat on his back, when he tried to get up⟧.
⟦#2302⟧
This use is particularly common in the imperfect indicative: as,
⟦b:nostrōs ingredī prohibēbant⟧, 5, 9, 6, ⟦i:they tried to stop our people from getting in⟧. ⟦b:Apellēs faciēbat⟧, Plin. ⟦i:NH. praef.⟧ 26, ⟦i:Apelles undertook to do this⟧, or ⟦i:an attempt of Apelles’s⟧. ⟦b:sēdābant tumultūs, sēdandō interdum movēbant⟧, L. 3, 15, 7, ⟦i:they tried to quell the riotings, but by trying they started them once in a while afresh⟧. ⟦b:num dubitās id mē imperante facere, quod iam tuā sponte faciēbās?⟧ ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 13, ⟦i:do you possibly hesitate to do at my command what you wanted to do, as it was, yourself?⟧ The conative use is not very common in old Latin, but more frequent from Cicero and Caesar on.
⟦#2303⟧
When the conative use is to be expressed more distinctly, a form of ⟦b:volō⟧ or ⟦b:cōnor⟧ is used, or a frequentative, like ⟦b:vēnditō⟧, ⟦i:try to sell⟧, ⟦b:adventō⟧, ⟦i:strive to come⟧.

title: The Causative Use
text:
⟦#2304⟧
A verb is sometimes used to denote not what the subject actually does himself, but what he has another do. This is called the ⟦i:Causative Use⟧ of the verb: as,
⟦b:animī causā mihi nāvem faciam⟧, Pl. ⟦i:R.⟧ 932, ⟦i:just for diversion I’ll build me a yacht⟧. ⟦b:cum vellet sibī̆ ānulum facere, aurificem iussit vocārī⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 56, ⟦i:wanting to make him a ring, he ordered a goldsmith to be called⟧. ⟦b:complūrēs pauperēs mortuōs suō sūmptū extulit⟧, N. 5, 4, 3, ⟦i:he buried a good many poor dead people at his own expense⟧, i.e. had them buried. Also in the passive: as, ⟦b:tondēmur⟧, Quintil. 1, 6, 44, ⟦i:we get shaved⟧. When greater exactness is required, having a thing done may be expressed more distinctly by ⟦b:faciō⟧ (⟦r1965:1965⟧), by ⟦b:cūrō⟧ (⟦r2250:2250⟧), or by ⟦b:iubeō⟧.

title: The Potential Use
text:
⟦#2305⟧
A verb is sometimes used to indicate action that can be done, and especially action that can be done at any time. This is called the ⟦i:Potential Use⟧ of the verb: as,
⟦b:clārē oculīs videō⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 630, ⟦i:I can see distinctly⟧. ⟦b:proptereā quod inter fīnēs Helvētiōrum et Allobrogum Rhodanus fluit isque nōnnūllīs locīs vadō trānsītur⟧, 1, 6, 2, ⟦i:because the Rhone runs between the district of the Helvetians and Allobrogans, and the river in some places can be forded⟧, or ⟦i:is fordable⟧. Particularly with a negative: as, ⟦b:apertē adūlantem nēmō nōn videt⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 99, ⟦i:an open flatterer anybody can see through⟧. ⟦b:nōn facile dīiūdicātur amor vērus et fīctus⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 9, 16, 2, ⟦i:real love and pretended love cannot easily be told apart⟧. ⟦b:ubī̆ Crassus animadvertit, suās cōpiās nōn facile dīdūcī, nōn cunctandum exīstimāvit⟧, 3, 23, 7, ⟦i:when Crassus saw that his forces could not easily be divided, he thought he ought to lose no time⟧. ⟦b:quoniam prōpositum nōn tenuerat⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 65, 4, ⟦i:seeing that he had not succeeded in carrying out his plan⟧. Sometimes this idea is expressed by the subjunctive (⟦r1554:1554⟧).

title: The Obligatory Use
text:
⟦#2306⟧
A verb is sometimes used to denote obligatory action. This is called the ⟦i:Obligatory Use⟧ of the verb: as,
⟦b:paulisper commorātus est⟧, ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 28, ⟦i:he had to wait⟧. ⟦b:aegra trahēbant corpora⟧, V. 3, 140, ⟦i:they had to drag their sickly frames along⟧. ⟦b:caruī patriā⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 145, ⟦i:I had to keep away from the country of my birth⟧. ⟦b:senātor populī Rōmānī pernoctāvit in pūblicō⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 25, ⟦i:a senator of Rome was fain to sleep in the streets⟧. ⟦b:serēmus aliquid in dērelictō solō⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 16, ⟦i:we shall have to sow something in an abandoned field⟧. ⟦b:erat summa inopia pābulī, adeō ut foliīs equōs alerent⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 58, 3, ⟦i:there was an utter lack of fodder, so that they were fain to feed their horses on leaves⟧.

title: The Permissive Use
text:
⟦#2307⟧
A verb is sometimes used to denote permitted action. This is called the ⟦i:Permissive Use⟧ of the verb: as,
⟦b:Verrēsne habēbit domī suae candēlābrum Iovis?⟧ ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 71, ⟦i:shall Verres be allowed to have at his house a candelabra of Jupiter?⟧ ⟦b:petit ut ipse dē eō statuat⟧, 1, 19, 5, ⟦i:he asks to be allowed to sit in judgement himself on the man⟧. ⟦b:Pīsō ōrāvit ut manēret⟧, Ta. 2, 81, ⟦i:Piso asked to be allowed to stay⟧.

title: (Ōrātiō Oblīqua.)
text:
⟦#2308⟧
The speech or thought of another, quoted in his own words, is called ⟦i:Direct Discourse⟧ (⟦r1723:1723⟧).
⟦#2309⟧
The speech or thought of another, dependent on a verb of saying or thinking, is called ⟦i:Indirect Discourse⟧ (⟦r1723:1723⟧).
One may, of course, quote his own words or thoughts indirectly, as well as those of another (⟦r1726:1726⟧).
⟦#2310⟧
The verb of thinking or saying is often not distinctly expressed, but only implied in the context (⟦r1725:1725⟧).
⟦#2311⟧
The principles which govern the change of direct discourse into indirect discourse have been already set forth in the foregoing pages; but, for the convenience of the learner, they are here put together.

title: Main Sentences
text:
⟦#2312⟧
Declarative sentences of direct discourse are put in the accusative with the infinitive, and interrogative and imperative sentences of direct discourse are put in the subjunctive, in indirect discourse.
(⟦i:a.⟧) For examples of declarative sentences, see ⟦r2175:2175-2184⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) Interrogative (⟦r1773:1773⟧): ⟦b:quid vellet? cūr in suās possessiōnēs venīret?⟧ 1, 44, 7, ⟦i:what did he mean? why this movement into his property?⟧ from Ariovistus’s reply to Caesar. ⟦b:dictātor litterās ad senātum mīsit: deum benignitāte Vēiōs iam fore in potestāte populī Rōmānī; quid dē praedā faciendum cēnsērent?⟧ L. 5, 20, 1, ⟦i:the dictator sent this letter to the senate: through the bounty of the gods Vei would soon belong to the Roman nation; what did they think should be done about the booty?⟧
(⟦i:c.⟧) Imperative (⟦r1547:1547⟧): ⟦b:Cicerō respondit: sī ab armīs discēdere velint, sē adiūtōre ūtantur lēgātōsque ad Caesarem mittant⟧, 5, 41, 7, ⟦i:Cicero replied: if they wished to lay down their arms, let them take his advice and send envoys to Caesar⟧. ⟦b:nūntius ē̆ī domō vēnit: bellum Athēniēnsēs et Boeōtōs indīxisse Lacedaemoniīs; quārē venīre nē dubitāret⟧, N. 17, 4, 1, ⟦i:a message reached him from home: the Athenians and Boeotians had declared war on the Lacedaemonians; so he was to come without delay⟧. See also ⟦r1707:1707⟧, ⟦r1708:1708⟧.
⟦#2313⟧
Rhetorical questions (that is, declarations made for effect in the form of questions) in the first or third person in the direct discourse are put in the accusative with the infinitive in indirect discourse: as,
⟦b:sī veteris contumēliae oblīvīscī vellet, num etiam recentium iniūriārum memoriam dēpōnere posse?⟧ 1, 14, 3, ⟦i:if he were inclined to disregard the old affront, could he also forget their fresh insults?⟧ from Caesar’s reply to the Helvetians. ⟦b:haud mīrum esse Superbō ē̆ī inditum Rōmae cōgnōmen: an quicquam superbius esse quam lūdificārī sīc omne nōmen Latīnum? cui nōn appārēre adfectāre eum imperium in Latīnōs?⟧ L. 1, 50, 3, ⟦i:no wonder Rome dubbed him ‘the Proud’: could there be a greater sign of pride than this mockery of the whole Latin nation? who did not see that he aspired to dominion over the Latins?⟧ This use is not found in old Latin. It occurs once or twice in Cicero’s letters and a few times in Caesar. In Livy and late writers, it is not uncommon. Such questions in the second person require the subjunctive (⟦r2312:2312⟧).
⟦#2314⟧
Questions which are in the subjunctive in direct discourse retain the subjunctive in indirect discourse: as,
⟦b:quod vērō ad amīcitiam populī Rōmānī attulissent, id iīs ēripī quis patī posset?⟧ 1, 43, 8, ⟦i:who could allow them to be stripped of what they had possessed when they became the friends of the Roman nation?⟧ (⟦r1565:1565⟧).

title: Subordinate Sentences
text:
⟦#2315⟧
The verb of a subordinate sentence, introduced by a relative word or a conjunctive particle, stands in the subjunctive in indirect discourse (⟦r1722:1722⟧).
For the indicative with ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦i:in the time while⟧, retained in indirect discourse, see ⟦r1995:1995⟧.
⟦b:sapientissimum esse dīcunt eum, cui quod opus sit ipsī veniat in mentem; proximē accēdere illum quī alterīus bene inventīs obtemperet⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 84, ⟦i:they say he is the wisest man who thinks out of himself what is expedient; and that the man who avails himself of the wise devices of another comes next⟧. ⟦b:ad haec Ariovistus respondit: iūs esse bellī, ut quī vīcissent iīs quōs vīcissent, quemadmodum vellent imperārent⟧, 1, 36, 1, ⟦i:to this Ariovistus answered: that it was the right of war for the conquerors to dictate to the conquered such terms as they pleased⟧.
⟦#2316⟧
Relative sentences equivalent to main sentences (⟦r1835:1835⟧) may be put in the accusative with the infinitive: as,
⟦b:ūnum medium diem fuisse, quem tōtum Galbam in cōnsīderandā causā compōnendāque posuisse⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 87, ⟦i:that a single day intervened and that this whole day Galba employed in studying up and arranging the case⟧. This use is found in Cicero, rarely in Caesar, in Livy, and a few times in other authors. Not in old Latin.
⟦#2317⟧
So also sentences introduced by certain conjunctive particles are occasionally put in the accusative with the infinitive: as,
⟦b:id quod saepe dictum est: ut mare ventōrum vī agitārī atque turbārī, sīc populum Rōmānum hominum sēditiōsōrum vōcibus concitārī⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 138, ⟦i:the oft-repeated saying: as the sea is ruffled and tossed by the mighty winds, so the people of Rome are stirred up by the talk of agitators⟧. ⟦b:honōrificum id mīlitibus fore, quōrum favōrem ut largitiōne et ambitū male adquīrī, ita per bonās artēs haud spernendum⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 1, 17, ⟦i:that would be a mark of respect to the troops, and their good will, though usually won by bribery and corruption, was certainly no small gain if honourably come by⟧. ⟦b:fugere senātum testēs tabulās pūblicās cēnsūs cuiusque, cum interim obaerātam plēbem obiectārī aliīs atque aliīs hostibus⟧, L. 6, 27, 6, ⟦i:that the senate sought to avoid evidence of each man’s property through making public returns, while at the same time the commons lay bankrupt and at the mercy of one enemy after another⟧. ⟦b:ut⟧ and ⟦b:quemadmodum⟧ are found with this infinitive in Cicero, Livy, and Tacitus; ⟦b:cum interim⟧ and ⟦b:sī nōn⟧ in Livy; ⟦b:quia⟧ in Livy and Seneca; ⟦b:quamquam⟧ in Livy and Tacitus; ⟦b:nisi forte⟧ in Tacitus. For ⟦b:quam⟧ with the infinitive, see ⟦r1898:1898⟧.
⟦#2318⟧
Relative sentences which are not a part of the quotation, but an addition of the writer’s, or which are a circumlocution equivalent to a substantive, are marked by the indicative (⟦r1729:1729⟧): as,
⟦b:Condrūsōs, Eburōnēs, Caeroesōs, Paemānōs, quī ūnō nōmine Germānī appellantur, arbitrārī ad XL mīlia⟧, 2, 4, 10, ⟦i:that they reckoned the Condrusians, Eburonians, Caeroesians and Paemanians (who are all called by one name Germans) at forty thousand⟧. For other examples of such sentences, see ⟦r1729:1729⟧.
⟦#2319⟧
Sentences containing the thought of another, introduced by a relative pronoun or by causal, temporal, or other conjunctive particles, take the subjunctive, though not appended to the accusative with the infinitive (⟦r1725:1725⟧): as,
⟦b:numquis, quod bonus vir esset, grātiās dīs ēgit umquam?⟧ ⟦i:DN.⟧ 3, 87, ⟦i:did anybody ever thank the gods ‘because he was a good man’?⟧ (⟦r1853:1853⟧). ⟦b:mihī̆ loquitur nec rēctē quia tibī̆ aurum reddidī et quia nōn tē dēfraudāverim⟧, Pl. ⟦i:B.⟧ 735, ⟦i:he’s always pitching into me because I returned you the money and ‘because I didn’t do you out of it’⟧ (⟦r1856:1856⟧, ⟦r1853:1853⟧). ⟦b:aedem Dīiovī vōvit, sī eō diē hostēs fūdisset⟧, L. 31, 21, 12, ⟦i:he vowed a temple to infernal Jove, ‘if he should rout the enemy on that day.’⟧ For other examples, see ⟦r1725:1725⟧, ⟦r1852:1852⟧, ⟦r1853:1853⟧, ⟦r1884:1884⟧, &c.
⟦#2320⟧
Sometimes a verb of saying or thinking is added, and is itself irrationally put in the subjunctive. For examples, see ⟦r1727:1727⟧.

title: Tense: Of the Infinitive
text:
⟦#2321⟧
The tenses of the infinitive follow their usual law (⟦r2218:2218⟧), representing the action as present, past, or future, from the speaker’s point of view.
⟦b:nūntiātum est Ariovistum ad occupandum Vesontiōnem contendere trīduīque viam ā suīs fīnibus prōfēcisse⟧, 1, 38, 1, ⟦i:it was reported that Ariovistus was pressing on⟧ (⟦r2219:2219⟧) ⟦i:to seize Vesontio, and that he had done a three days’ journey from his own borders⟧ (⟦r2226:2226⟧). ⟦b:fāma est āram esse in vestibulō templī⟧, L. 24, 3, 7, ⟦i:rumour has it that there is an altar in the vestibule of the temple⟧ (⟦r2219:2219⟧). ⟦b:lēgāti haec sē ad suōs relātūrōs dīxērunt⟧, 4, 9, 1, ⟦i:the envoys said they would report this to their countrymen⟧ (⟦r2232:2232⟧). For other examples, see ⟦r2175:2175-2203⟧; for the infinitive equivalent of the indicative imperfect and pluperfect, see ⟦r2226:2226⟧, ⟦r2227:2227⟧.

title: Tense: Of the Subjunctive
text:
⟦#2322⟧
The tenses of the subjunctive follow the law of the sequence of tenses; see ⟦r1745:1745⟧.
The tenses are usually imperfect or pluperfect, as the verb introducing a quotation is usually past.
⟦b:Sōcratēs dīcere solēbat, omnēs in eō quod scīrent, satis esse ēloquentēs⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 63, ⟦i:Socrates used to maintain that all men were eloquent enough in a matter which they understood⟧ (⟦r1766:1766⟧). ⟦b:dīcēbam quoad metuerēs, omnia tē prōmissūrum⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 89, ⟦i:I said that as long as you were afraid, you would promise everything⟧ (⟦r1771:1771⟧). ⟦b:cōgnōvit Suēbōs posteā quam pontem fierī comperissent, nūntiōs in omnēs partēs dīmīsisse⟧, 4, 19, 2, ⟦i:he ascertained that after the Suebans had learned of the building of the bridge, they had sent out messengers in every direction⟧ (⟦r1772:1772⟧). For other examples, see ⟦r1746:1746-1772⟧.
⟦#2323⟧
But the present and perfect subjunctive are often used, especially when the main verb is present, or for vividness after a secondary tense.
⟦b:Alexandrum Philippus accūsat quod largitiōne benevolentiam Macedonum cōnsectētur⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 2, 53, ⟦i:Philip accuses Alexander of courting the favour of the Macedonians by the use of money⟧ (⟦r1746:1746⟧, ⟦r1853:1853⟧). ⟦b:initium quod huic cum mātre fuerit simultātis audīstis⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 17, ⟦i:you have heard the origin of the enmity which was between the defendant and his mother⟧ (⟦r1746:1746⟧). ⟦b:Ariovistus respondit: stīpendium capere iūre bellī quod victōrēs victīs imponere cōnsuerint⟧, 1, 44, 1, ⟦i:Ariovistus answered that it was by the laws of war that he took the tribute which victors were wont to lay upon the vanquished⟧ (⟦r1755:1755⟧). For other examples, see ⟦r1746:1746-1772⟧.
⟦#2324⟧
The future of direct discourse is represented in indirect discourse by the imperfect, and the future perfect by the pluperfect subjunctive.
⟦b:sē quod ē rē pūblicā esset factūrum⟧, L. 28, 45,3, ⟦i:that he would do what should be for the interests of the state⟧ (⟦r1766:1766⟧). ⟦b:sē nōn ante coeptūrum quam ignem in rēgiīs castrīs cōnspexisset⟧, L. 30, 5, 5, ⟦i:that he would not begin before he saw fire in the royal camp⟧ (⟦r1766:1766⟧, ⟦r1921:1921⟧). The present or perfect subjunctive also is found when the main verb requires. For other examples, see ⟦r1746:1746-1772⟧.

title: Pronoun
text:
⟦#2325⟧
⟦b:ego⟧ and ⟦b:nōs⟧, of direct discourse, are represented by ⟦b:sē⟧ in indirect discourse, and ⟦b:meus⟧ and ⟦b:noster⟧ by ⟦b:suus⟧. ⟦b:tū⟧ and ⟦b:vōs⟧, of direct discourse, are represented in indirect discourse by ⟦b:ille⟧, or, when less emphatic, by ⟦b:is⟧.
For the use of the reflexive pronoun, see ⟦r2338:2338-2342⟧.
