⟦b:sē prius in Galliam vēnisse quam populum Rōmānum⟧, 1, 44, 7, ⟦i:that he came into Gaul before the Roman nation⟧, said Ariovistus of himself. ⟦b:sē ā patribus maiōribusque suīs didicisse⟧, 1, 13, 6, ⟦i:that they had learned from their fathers and ancestors⟧, said the Helvetians of themselves. ⟦b:trānsīsse Rhēnum sēsē nōn suā sponte⟧, 1, 44, 1, ⟦i:that he had crossed the Rhine not of his own accord⟧, was the assertion of Ariovistus. ⟦b:quī nisi dēcēdat, sēsē illum nōn prō amīcō sed hoste habitūrum. quod sī eum interfēcerit, multīs sēsē prīncipibus populī Rōmānī grātum esse factūrum⟧, 1, 44, 11, ⟦i:that unless he withdrew, he should consider him not a friend but a foe. Why, if he killed him, he should do a favour to numerous leading men in the Roman nation⟧. Here Ariovistus is reported as speaking to Caesar.

title: Protasis
text:
⟦#2326⟧
The protasis of every kind (⟦r2023:2023⟧, ⟦r2024:2024⟧) has the verb in the subjunctive in indirect discourse (⟦r2315:2315⟧).
⟦#2327⟧
The tense of the protasis is generally imperfect or pluperfect (⟦r2322:2322⟧): as,
⟦b:Ariovistus respondit: sī ipse populō Rōmānō nōn praescrīberet, nōn oportēre sēsē ā populō Rōmānō impedīrī⟧, 1, 36, 1, ⟦i:Ariovistus answered: if he did not dictate to the Roman nation, no more ought the Roman nation to interfere with him⟧ (⟦r2026:2026⟧). ⟦b:quae sī fēcisset, Pompēium in Hispāniās itūrum⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 10, 3, ⟦i:if he did that, Pompey would go to the Spains⟧ (⟦r2061:2061⟧).
⟦#2328⟧
But indeterminate protases (⟦r2023:2023⟧) are sometimes put in the present or perfect subjunctive in indirect discourse, even with a main secondary tense: as,
⟦b:Ariovistus respondit: sī iterum experīrī velint, sē parātum esse dēcertāre⟧, 1, 44, 1, ⟦i:Ariovistus answered that if the Romans wanted to try again, he was ready to fight it out⟧ (⟦r2026:2026⟧). ⟦b:quī nisi dēcēdat, sēsē illum prō hoste habitūrum⟧, 1, 44, 11, ⟦i:that unless he withdrew, he should consider him an enemy⟧ (⟦r2054:2054⟧).
⟦#2329⟧
Protases of action non-occurrent (⟦r2024:2024⟧) remain in the imperfect or pluperfect, even with a main primary tense.
⟦b:licet Varrō Mūsās, Aelī Stilōnis sententiā, Plautīnō dīcat sermōne locutūrās fuisse sī Latīnē loquī vellent⟧, Quintil. 10, 1, 99, ⟦i:though Varro, following Stilo’s dictum, may say that the Muses would have spoken in the style of Plautus, if they had wanted to speak Latin⟧ (⟦r2095:2095⟧). ⟦b:quaeret ab accūsātōribus quid factūrī essent, sī in eō locō fuissent⟧, Cornif. 2, 22, ⟦i:he will ask the accusers what they would have done if they had been in that predicament⟧ (⟦r2099:2099⟧).

title: Apodosis
text:
⟦#2330⟧
In indeterminate conditional periods (⟦r2023:2023⟧), the apodosis simply follows the general rule (⟦r2312:2312⟧): as,
⟦b:Iovem sīc aiunt philosophī, sī Graecē loquātur, loquī⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 121, ⟦i:the philosophers say that this is Jove’s style of speaking, if Jove speaks Greek⟧ (⟦r2026:2026⟧). ⟦b:sīn bellō persequī persevērāret, reminīscerētur prīstinae virtūtis Helvētiōrum⟧, 1, 13, 4, ⟦i:if he persisted in following them up with war, let him call to mind the old time valour of the Helvetians⟧ (⟦r2056:2056⟧). ⟦b:in prōvinciīs intellegēbant sī is quī esset cum imperiō emere vellet, fore utī quod quisque vellet quantī vellet auferret⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 10, ⟦i:in the provinces they saw that if a man clothed in authority should wish to be a buyer, he would carry off every time whatever he wished at what he wished⟧ (2233; 2054 or 2076). ⟦b:futūrum esse, nisi prōvīsum esset, ut Rōma caperētur⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 1, 101, ⟦i:that unless precaution was taken, Rome would be captured⟧ (⟦r2233:2233⟧, ⟦r2061:2061⟧). For other examples, see ⟦r2327:2327⟧, ⟦r2328:2328⟧.
⟦#2331⟧
In conditional periods of action non-occurrent (⟦r2024:2024⟧), the future participle with ⟦b:fuisse⟧, is used in apodoses of the active voice: as,
⟦b:an Cn. Pompēium cēnsēs maximārum rērum glōriā laetātūrum fuisse, sī scīret sē in sōlitūdine Aegyptiōrum trucīdātum īrī⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 22, ⟦i:do you suppose that Pompey would have taken any pleasure in the fame which his peerless exploits brought him if he had known that he was going to be butchered in the wilds of Egypt?⟧
In one instance, found in Caesar, the future participle with ⟦b:esse⟧ occurs, representing the imperfect subjunctive of present time (⟦r2091:2091⟧):
⟦b:Caesarem arbitrārī profectum in Ītaliam; neque aliter Carnūtēs interficiundī Tasgetiī cōnsilium fuisse captūrōs, neque Eburōnēs, sī ille adesset, ad castra ventūrōs esse⟧, 5, 29, 2, ⟦i:that he thought Caesar was gone into Italy; otherwise, the Carnutes would not have formed their design of killing Tasgetius, and the Eburones, if he were at hand, would not be assaulting the camp⟧. Here the context shows that ⟦b:ventūrōs esse⟧ represents the imperfect subjunctive. But ordinarily it might seem to represent the future indicative. Hence, to avoid ambiguity, the Romans generally did not try to express present time in apodoses of this class in indirect discourse.
⟦#2332⟧
The perfect infinitive is exceptionally used; this is based upon the indicative in apodosis (⟦r2104:2104⟧).
⟦b:memoriā teneō solitum ipsum nārrāre sē studium philosophiae ācrius hausisse, nī prūdentia mātris incēnsum animum coërcuisset⟧, Ta. ⟦i:Agr.⟧ 4, ⟦i:I remember that he used to say that he had drunk in the study of philosophy with too great eagerness, had not his discreet mother checked his ardent soul⟧ (2105 or 2107).
⟦#2333⟧
⟦b:possum⟧, in the apodosis of a conditional period of action non-occurrent (⟦r2101:2101⟧), is regularly put in the perfect infinitive in indirect discourse: as,
⟦b:Platōnem exīstimō, sī genus forēnse dīcendī trāctāre voluisset, gravissimē potuisse dīcere⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 4, ⟦i:I think that if Plato had only chosen to cultivate forensic eloquence, he might have been a most impressive speaker⟧ (⟦r2103:2103⟧). ⟦b:cum dīcerent sē potuisse in amplissimum locum pervenīre, sī sua studia ad honōrēs petendōs cōnferre voluissent⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 153, ⟦i:saying they might have risen to the proudest position, if they had only chosen to apply their energies to a political career⟧ (⟦r2103:2103⟧).
⟦#2334⟧
⟦b:futūrum fuisse ut⟧ with the imperfect subjunctive is rarely used in apodoses of the passive voice (⟦r2331:2331⟧): as,
⟦b:Theophrastus accūsāsse nātūram dīcitur quod hominibus tam exiguam vītam dedisset: quōrum sī aetās potuisset esse longinquior, futūrum fuisse ut omnī doctrīnā hominum vīta ērudīrētur⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 3, 69, ⟦i:it is said that Theophrastus took nature to task ‘for giving man such a short life; if the period could have been longer man’s life would have been informed with knowledge of every sort’⟧ (⟦r2099:2099⟧). See also Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 101, 2.

title: The Personal Pronoun
text:
⟦#2335⟧
For the use of the nominatives ⟦b:ego tū⟧, ⟦b:nōs vōs⟧, see ⟦r1029:1029⟧. The genitive plurals ⟦b:nostrū̆m⟧ and ⟦b:vestrū̆m⟧ are used as partitive, ⟦b:nostrī⟧ and ⟦b:vestrī⟧ as objective genitives: as,
⟦b:nēmō nostrūm⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 55, ⟦i:not one of us⟧ (⟦r1242:1242⟧). ⟦b:ab utrīsque vestrūm⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 11, 21, 5, ⟦i:by each of you⟧ (⟦r1243:1243⟧). ⟦b:grāta mihī̆ vehementer est memoria nostrī tua⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 12, 17, 1, ⟦i:your remembrance of me is exceedingly agreeable to me⟧ (⟦r1260:1260⟧). ⟦b:nostrī nōsmet paenitet⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 172, ⟦i:we’re discontented with our lot⟧ (⟦r1283:1283⟧). For the adjective instead of the possessive or objective genitive, see ⟦r1234:1234⟧, ⟦r1262:1262⟧.

title: The Reflexive sē and suus
text:
⟦#2336⟧
The reflexive regularly refers to the subject of the verb: as,
⟦b:fugae sēsē mandābant⟧, 2, 24, 2, ⟦i:they betook themselves to flight⟧. ⟦b:animō servit, nōn sibī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 308, ⟦i:he serves his passions, not his better self⟧. ⟦b:est amāns suī virtūs⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 98, ⟦i:virtue is fond of itself⟧. ⟦b:dūcit sēcum ūnā virginem⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 229, ⟦i:he is leading a girl along with him⟧. ⟦b:Caesar cōpiās suās dīvīsit⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 97, 3, ⟦i:Caesar divided his forces⟧. For ⟦b:sē ipse⟧, see ⟦r2376:2376⟧; for ⟦b:sē⟧ or ⟦b:suus quisque⟧, 2397.
⟦#2337⟧
The reflexive sometimes refers to a word not the subject, when that word is specially emphasized or easily made out from the context. This holds chiefly of ⟦b:suus⟧, which is used with great freedom: as,
⟦b:Alexandrum uxor sua occīdit⟧, ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 2, 144, ⟦i:Alexander was murdered by his own wife⟧. ⟦b:dēsinant īnsidiārī domī suae cōnsulī⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 32, ⟦i:let them cease to waylay the consul in his own house and home⟧. ⟦b:suās rēs Syrācūsānīs restituit⟧, L. 29, 1, 17, ⟦i:he restored their property to the Syracuse people⟧.
⟦#2338⟧
In the construction of the accusative with the infinitive (⟦r2175:2175⟧), the reflexive is regularly used when the subject of the infinitive refers to the subject of the verb: as,
⟦b:Vārus imperium sē habēre dīxit⟧, ⟦i:Lig.⟧ 22, ⟦i:Varus said that he had authority⟧. ⟦b:id sēsē effectūrōs spērābant⟧, 7, 26, 2, ⟦i:they hoped to accomplish it⟧ (⟦r2235:2235⟧).
⟦#2339⟧
The reflexive, in this construction, sometimes refers to an emphasized word not the formal subject of the verb: as,
⟦b:canum custōdia quid sīgnificat aliud nisi sē ad hominum commoditātēs esse generātōs?⟧ ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 158, ⟦i:the watchfulness of the dog—does not it show that he was created for the convenience of man?⟧
⟦#2340⟧
When the subject of the infinitive is different from that of the verb, the reflexive sometimes refers to the subject of the verb, sometimes to that of the infinitive: as,
⟦b:Ariovistus respondit omnēs Galliae cīvitātēs ad sē oppugnandum vēnisse⟧, 1, 44, 1, ⟦i:Ariovistus answered that all the states of Gaul had come to attack him⟧, i.e. Ariovistus. ⟦b:nēminem sēcum sine suā perniciē contendisse⟧, 1, 36, 6, ⟦i:that no man had contended with him without his own undoing⟧; ⟦b:sēcum⟧ refers to Ariovistus, the subject of the main verb ⟦b:respondit⟧, ⟦b:suā⟧ to ⟦b:nēminem⟧.
⟦#2341⟧
In subordinate subjunctive clauses of purpose, indirect discourse, or indirect question, the reflexive refers to the subject of the main sentence: as,
⟦b:huic mandat, ut ad sē quam prīmum revertātur⟧, 4, 21, 2, ⟦i:he instructs him to come back to himself as soon as possible⟧. ⟦b:excruciābit mē erus, quia sibī nōn dīxerim⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 859, ⟦i:my master’ll torture me ‘because I have not told him.’⟧ ⟦b:Paetus omnīs librōs, quōs frāter suus relīquisset, mihī̆ dōnāvit⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 2, 1, 12, ⟦i:Paetus made me a present of all the books ‘that his brother left.’⟧ For the use of ⟦b:is⟧ for ⟦b:sē⟧, see ⟦r2370:2370⟧.
⟦#2342⟧
The reflexive, in such subordinate clauses, sometimes refers to an emphatic word not the main subject: as,
⟦b:identidem fēlīcem Priamum vocābat, quod superstes omnium suōrum exstitisset⟧, Suet. ⟦i:Tib.⟧ 62, ⟦i:he was for ever calling Priam ‘Fortune’s darling, because he outlived all his kith and kin.’⟧
⟦#2343⟧
The reflexive referring to the main subject is sometimes irregularly used in subordinate indicative clauses.
⟦b:Epamīnōndās ē̆ī, quī sibī̆ successerat, exercitum nōn trādidit⟧, ⟦i:Inv.⟧ 1, 55, ⟦i:Epaminondas did not deliver the army to his successor⟧. ⟦b:centum bovēs mīlitibus dōnō dedit, quī sēcum fuerant⟧, L. 7, 37, 3, ⟦i:he gave a hundred oxen to the soldiers who had been with him⟧.

title: Equivalents for a Reciprocal Pronoun
text:
⟦#2344⟧
The place of a reciprocal pronoun, ⟦i:each other⟧, is supplied by ⟦b:inter nōs⟧, ⟦b:inter vōs⟧, ⟦b:inter sē⟧, or by ⟦b:alter⟧ or ⟦b:alius⟧ followed by another case of the same word: as,
⟦b:inter nōs nātūrā cōniūnctī sumus⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 3, 66, ⟦i:we are united with each other by nature⟧. ⟦b:Cicerōnēs puerī amant inter sē⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 6, 1, 12, ⟦i:the Cicero boys are fond of each other⟧. ⟦b:cum alius aliī subsidium ferret⟧, 2, 26, 2, ⟦i:when they were helping each other⟧. For ⟦b:uterque⟧, see ⟦r2400:2400⟧. The reciprocal idea is sometimes expressed by the form of the verb: as, ⟦b:fulvā lūctantur harēnā⟧, V. 6, 643, ⟦i:they wrestle with each other on the yellow sand⟧ (⟦r1487:1487⟧).
⟦#2345⟧
From Livy on, ⟦b:invicem inter sē⟧, ⟦b:invicem sē⟧, or ⟦b:invicem⟧ alone, is often used in the expression of reciprocal relations: as,
⟦b:invicem inter sē grātantēs⟧, L. 9, 43, 17, ⟦i:mutually congratulating each other⟧. ⟦b:invicem sē antepōnendō⟧, Ta. ⟦i:Agr.⟧ 6, ⟦i:mutually preferring one another⟧. ⟦b:ut invicem ardentius dīligāmus⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 7, 20, 7, ⟦i:that we may love each other more ardently⟧.

title: The Possessive Pronoun
text:
⟦#2346⟧
The possessive of the personal and reflexive pronoun is regularly omitted, unless it is required for emphasis or contrast: as,
⟦b:ōra manūsque tuā lavimus, Fērōnia, lymphā⟧, H. S. 1, 5, 24, ⟦i:our hands and faces in thy rill, Feronia, we bathe⟧. The possessive sometimes has the meaning of ⟦i:proper⟧, ⟦i:appropriate⟧, ⟦i:favourable⟧; as, ⟦b:suō locō dīcam⟧, Quintil. 1, 1, 36, ⟦i:I shall tell in the proper place⟧. For the possessive pronoun used instead of the possessive or objective genitive, see ⟦r1234:1234⟧, ⟦r1262:1262⟧.

title: hīc
text:
⟦#2347⟧
⟦b:hīc⟧ points out what is near the speaker in place, time, or thought: as,
⟦b:hī domum mē ad sē auferent⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Men.⟧ 847, ⟦i:these fellows will hale me off to their house⟧. ⟦b:nōn mē exīstimāvī in hōc sermōne usque ad hanc aetātem esse ventūrum⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 232, ⟦i:I did not think that in this discourse I should get down to the present generation⟧. ⟦b:reliquum omne tempus huius annī⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 30, ⟦i:all the rest of this year⟧.
⟦#2348⟧
⟦b:hīc⟧ sometimes points out the speaker with pathos, or with emphasis, particularly in comedy.
⟦b:haec arma et hunc mīlitem propitiō flūmine accipiās⟧, L. 2, 10, 11, ⟦i:receive these arms and this soldier in thy gracious stream⟧, the prayer of Horatius Cocles to Father Tiber. ⟦b:tibī̆ erunt parāta verba, huic hominī verbera⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 356, ⟦i:you’ll get a chiding, this child a hiding⟧. ⟦b:fēcisset nī haec praesēnsisset canēs⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 172, ⟦i:and he’d have done it, unless this dog had got scent of it in time⟧, where the speaker means himself.
⟦#2349⟧
The neuter plural ⟦b:haec⟧ sometimes means ⟦i:the realm⟧, ⟦i:our country⟧, ⟦i:our state⟧, ⟦i:the⟧ [Roman] ⟦i:world⟧: as,
⟦b:haec, quae iam prīdem vastāre studēs⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 21, ⟦i:the realm which you have long sought to lay in ruins⟧. ⟦b:quī haec dēlēre cōnātī sunt⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 7, ⟦i:who have tried to destroy the state⟧. ⟦b:servus est nēmō quī nōn haec stāre cupiat⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 16, ⟦i:there lives no slave that wills not our country should abide⟧.
⟦#2350⟧
⟦b:hīc⟧, as expressing a familiar, every-day thing, occasionally has a shade of contempt, either alone, or with ⟦b:volgāris⟧, ⟦b:cottīdiānus⟧ or the like: as,
⟦b:mittit hominī mūnera satis largē, haec ad ūsum domesticum⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 62, ⟦i:he sent him some presents—pretty liberal ones, commonish things for household use⟧. ⟦b:mittō hāsce artīs volgārīs, coquōs, pistōrēs⟧, ⟦i:RA.⟧ 134, ⟦i:I’ll skip your everyday common occupations—such as cooks, bakers, &c., &c.⟧ ⟦b:taedet cottīdiānārum hārum fōrmārum⟧, T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 297, ⟦i:I’m sick of your everyday beauties⟧.
⟦#2351⟧
When ⟦b:hīc⟧ relates to the words of a sentence, it points out what has preceded or is to follow, or emphasizes a word referred to by a preceding relative.
For ⟦b:hīc⟧ used to introduce a new sentence, see ⟦r2129:2129⟧.
⟦b:haec habuī dē senectūte quae dīcerem⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 85, ⟦i:this was what I had to say on Old Age⟧. ⟦b:sed haec hāctenus; nunc ad ostenta veniāmus⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 2, 53, ⟦i:so much for this; let us now go on to portents⟧. ⟦b:fēcit pācem hīs condiciōnibus⟧, N. 8, 3, 1, ⟦i:he made peace on the following terms⟧. ⟦b:dīcitur locūtus in hanc ferē sententiam esse⟧, L. 6, 40, 2, ⟦i:it is said that he spoke to somewhat the following effect⟧. ⟦b:quaesierat ex mē Scīpiō quidnam sentīrem dē hōc quod duo sōlēs vīsōs esse cōnstāret⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 1, 19, ⟦i:Scipio had asked me what I thought about this, that it was generally agreed that two suns had been seen⟧.
⟦#2352⟧
⟦b:hīc⟧ and ⟦b:ille⟧ are often opposed, particularly in contrasts of classes: as,
⟦b:laudātur ab hīs, culpātur ab illīs⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 2, 11, ⟦i:one side praises him, the other condemns⟧. ⟦b:illud est album, hoc dulce, canōrum illud, hoc bene olēns, hoc asperum⟧, ⟦i:Ac.⟧ 2, 21, ⟦i:that is white, this is sweet, that sonorous, this fragrant, this rough⟧. ⟦b:ōrātor, nōn ille volgāris sed hīc excellēns⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 45, ⟦i:an orator, not of the common sort, but the superior one of whom we are speaking⟧.
⟦#2353⟧
In transitions, ⟦b:ille⟧ introduces a new thing, ⟦b:hīc⟧ denotes ⟦i:the aforementioned⟧: as,
⟦b:sed haec vetera; illud vērō recēns, Caesarem meō cōnsiliō interfectum⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 25, ⟦i:but this is all ancient history; here, however, is something new, that Caesar was killed at my suggestion⟧.
⟦#2354⟧
When ⟦b:hīc⟧ and ⟦b:ille⟧ refer to two different persons or things named in the sentence, ⟦b:hīc⟧ commonly refers to the nearer word, ⟦b:ille⟧ to the remoter word; or ⟦b:hīc⟧ sometimes refers to what is nearer the mind of the speaker, even though it be remoter in the sentence.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:Caesar beneficiīs ac mūnificentiā magnus habēbātur, integritāte vītae Catō. Ille mānsuētūdine et misericordiā clārus factus, huic sevēritās dignitātem addiderat⟧, S. ⟦i:C.⟧ 54, 2, ⟦i:Caesar was esteemed great for his liberality and generosity, Cato for his unsullied life. The former became famous through his humanity and mercy, the latter’s dignity was heightened by his austerity.⟧ (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:cavē Catōnī antepōnās nē istum quidem ipsum quem Apollō, ut ais, sapientissimum iūdicāvit: huius enim facta, illīus dicta laudantur⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 10, ⟦i:suffer not Cato to find a rival even in your man himself, whom, as you say, Apollo declared wisest of mankind; for our Cato is renowned for deeds, the other for doctrines⟧.
⟦#2355⟧
⟦b:hīc⟧ and ⟦b:ille⟧ are used together, chiefly in poetry, to explain something past by a present thing: as,
⟦b:hunc illum poscere fāta reor⟧, V. 7, 272, ⟦i:this I think is he whom the fates require⟧. ⟦b:hunc illum fātīs externā ab sēde profectum portendī generum⟧, V. 7, 255, ⟦i:this was the man whom destiny foretold should fare from foreign home to be his son-in-law⟧.

title: iste
text:
⟦#2356⟧
⟦b:iste⟧ points out something near to, belonging to, or imputed to the person addressed: as,
⟦b:cum istā sīs auctōritāte, nōn dēbēs adripere maledictum ex triviō⟧, ⟦i:Mur.⟧ 13, ⟦i:carrying the influence that you do, you ought not to take to street-corner abuse⟧. ⟦b:multae istārum arborum meā manū sunt satae⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 59, ⟦i:many of the trees you see there were planted by my own hand⟧. ⟦b:salem istum quō caret vestra nātiō, inrīdendīs nōbīs nōlītōte cōnsūmere⟧, ⟦i:ND.⟧ 2, 74, ⟦i:do not waste in ridiculing us that wit which your fraternity sadly needs⟧. Often with ⟦b:tuus⟧ or ⟦b:vester⟧: as, ⟦b:īsdem hīc sapiēns dē quō loquor oculīs quibus iste vester intuēbitur⟧, ⟦i:Ac.⟧ 2, 105, ⟦i:the sage of whom I speak will look with the same eyes as the sage you boast of⟧.
⟦#2357⟧
From its use in addressing opponents or in talking at them, ⟦b:iste⟧ is common in contemptuous phrases: as,
⟦b:tū istīs faucibus, istīs lateribus, istā gladiātōriā tōtīus corporis firmitāte⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 2, 63, ⟦i:you with that gullet of yours, those swollen flanks, that prizefighter’s bulky make-up⟧. ⟦b:nōn erit ista amīcitia, sed mercātūra quaedam⟧, ⟦i:ND.⟧ 1, 122, ⟦i:such a thing will not be a friendship, but a sort of traffic⟧.

title: ille
text:
⟦#2358⟧
⟦b:ille⟧ points to what is remote in place, time, or thought: as,
⟦b:ergō illī intellegunt quid Epicūrus dīcat, ego nōn intellegō?⟧ ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 13, ⟦i:do those gentlemen then understand what Epicurus means and I not?⟧ ⟦b:populus Rōmānus nihil aequē atque illam veterem iūdiciōrum vim gravitātemque requīrit⟧, ⟦i:Caecil.⟧ 8, ⟦i:the Roman people miss nothing so much as the ancient vigour and firmness attaching to public trials⟧. ⟦b:hīs autem dē rēbus sōl mē ille admonuit ut brevior essem⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 3, 209, ⟦i:but on these topics yonder sun has warned me to be pretty brief⟧. For other examples, see ⟦r2352:2352-2355⟧.
⟦#2359⟧
⟦b:ille⟧ is used to point out a celebrity, often one of the past. So, particularly without a proper name, in allusive style, referring to what is famed in story.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:hīc est ille Dēmosthenēs⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 103, ⟦i:this is the famous Demosthenes⟧. ⟦b:Athēniēnsis ille Themistoclēs⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 299, ⟦i:Themistocles the great, of Athens⟧. ⟦b:illud Solōnis⟧, ⟦i:CM.⟧ 50, ⟦i:Solon’s memorable words⟧. ⟦b:Mēdēa illa⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 22, ⟦i:Medea famed in story⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:vīribus ille cōnfīsus periīt⟧, J. 10, 10, ⟦i:the man in the story lost his life through confidence in his strength⟧. ⟦b:illae rēgiae lacrimae⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 3, 7, 13, ⟦i:the monarch’s historic tears⟧, of Xerxes.
⟦#2360⟧
Indicating change of subject, ⟦b:ille⟧ is ⟦i:this other man⟧. In such cases it is often best expressed in English by a proper name or a descriptive word.
⟦b:ad sē adulēscentem iussit venīre. at ille, ut ingressus est, cōnfestim gladium dēstrīnxit⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 112, ⟦i:he gave orders to admit the young man. But this other, the moment he entered, drew his sword.⟧ ⟦b:rūsticus expectat dum dēfluat amnis: at ille lābitur et lābētur⟧, H. ⟦i:E.⟧ 1, 2, 42, ⟦i:he is a peasant waiting for the river to go down: but the river flows and will flow on⟧.
⟦#2361⟧
In concessions, ⟦b:ille⟧ often precedes ⟦b:quidem⟧; in translation no pronoun is required.
⟦b:librī scrīptī incōnsīderātē ab optimīs illīs quidem virīs, sed nōn satis ērudītīs⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 6, ⟦i:books rashly written by men respectable enough but of insufficient education⟧. ⟦b:est tarda illa medicīna, sed tamen magna⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 3, 35, ⟦i:it is a powerful remedy, though slow in its working⟧. ⟦b:hīc⟧, ⟦b:is⟧, and ⟦b:iste⟧ are used rarely in this way.
⟦#2362⟧
In poetry ⟦b:ille⟧ may serve: (1.) To repeat a thing with emphasis: as,
⟦b:arma virumque canō Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs Ītaliam vēnit, multum ille et terrīs iactātus et altō⟧, V. 1, 1, ⟦i:arms and the man I sing, from Troja’s shore the first to come to Italy, much tossed that man by land and sea⟧.
⟦#2363⟧
(2.) To emphasize the second of two ideas: as,
⟦b:nunc dextrā ingemināns ictūs, nunc ille sinistrā⟧, V. 5, 457, ⟦i:now with his right redoubling blows, now mighty with his left⟧. ⟦b:nōn tamen Euryalī, non ille oblītus amōrum⟧, V. 5, 334, ⟦i:still not Euryalus forgetting, no, not he his love!⟧
⟦#2364⟧
(3.) As a provisional subject, to anticipate the real subject, and keep the attention in suspense till the real subject comes with emphasis: as,
⟦b:ac velut ille canum morsū dē montibus altīs āctus aper substitit⟧, V. 10, 707, ⟦i:and e’en as he, goaded by bite of hounds from mountains high, the boar hath paused⟧.

title: is
text:
⟦#2365⟧
⟦b:is⟧ refers to something named in the context. When some feeling is to be expressed, such as admiration, or oftener contempt, ⟦b:homō⟧ is often put for ⟦b:is⟧.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:petit ā rēge et eum plūribus verbīs rogat ut id ad sē mittat⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 64, ⟦i:he solicits the king and begs him at considerable length to send it to him⟧. ⟦b:nōndum mātūrus imperiō Ascanius erat, tamen id imperium ĕ̄ī ad pūberem aetātem incolume mānsit⟧, L. 1, 3, 1, ⟦i:Ascanius was not yet old enough for the throne, but that throne was kept safe for him till he came of age⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:ego hominem callidiōrem vīdī nēminem quam Phormiōnem. veniō ad hominem, ut dīcerem argentum opus esse⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 591, ⟦i:a shrewder man than Phormio I never saw, not I! I went to him to tell him that I needed money⟧. ⟦b:nēquam esse hominem et levem sciēbam⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 22, ⟦i:I knew the fellow was worthless and frivolous⟧.
⟦#2366⟧
(1.) ⟦b:is⟧ refers to something named before or after: as,
⟦b:eius omnis ōrātiō versāta est in eō, ut scrīptum plūrimum valēre oportēre dēfenderet⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 244, ⟦i:his whole speech turned on the contention that the written word should be paramount⟧. ⟦b:Melitēnsis Diodōrus est; is Lilybaeī multōs iam annōs habitat⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 38, ⟦i:Diodorus is from Melita; he has lived many years at Lilybaeum⟧. For other examples of is used to connect sentences, see ⟦r2129:2129⟧.
⟦#2367⟧
With a connective, ⟦b:is⟧ denotes an important addition: as,
⟦b:vincula et ea sempiterna⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 4, 7, ⟦i:imprisonment and that too perpetual⟧. ⟦b:annum iam audientem Cratippum idque Athēnīs⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 1, ⟦i:after a year’s study under Cratippus, and that too in Athens⟧. ⟦b:erant in eō plūrimae litterae nec eae volgārēs⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 265, ⟦i:he was a man of very deep reading and that of no common sort either⟧.
⟦#2368⟧
(2.) ⟦b:is⟧ indicates something explained or restricted by a relative or indefinite, ⟦b:quī⟧, ⟦b:quīcumque⟧, ⟦b:sī quis⟧: as,
⟦b:haec omnia is fēcī, quī sodālis Dolābellae eram⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 12, 14, 7, ⟦i:all this I did, I that was Dolabella’s bosom friend⟧ (⟦r1807:1807⟧). ⟦b:ūnus ex eō numerō quī ad caedem parātī erant⟧, S. ⟦i:I.⟧ 35, 6, ⟦i:one of the number that were ready to do murder⟧ (⟦r1804:1804⟧). ⟦b:neque is sum quī mortis perīculō terrear⟧, 5, 30, 2, ⟦i:but I am not the man to be scared by danger of death, no, not I⟧ (⟦r1818:1818⟧). ⟦b:quīcumque is est, ē̆ī mē profiteor inimīcum⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 10, 31, 3, ⟦i:whoever he may be, I proclaim myself his enemy⟧ (⟦r1814:1814⟧). ⟦b:cum ipse Aliēnus ex eā facultāte, sī quam habet, aliquantum dētrāctūrus sit⟧, ⟦i:Caecil.⟧ 49, ⟦i:seeing that even Alienus is to suppress some part of that eloquence, if any he may have⟧. See also ⟦r1795:1795⟧, ⟦r1798:1798⟧. For ⟦b:id quod⟧, see ⟦r1811:1811⟧.
⟦#2369⟧
For the use of ⟦b:is⟧ instead of a relative repeated in a different case, see ⟦r1833:1833⟧.
⟦#2370⟧
⟦b:is⟧ sometimes is loosely used for the reflexive ⟦b:sē⟧ (⟦r2341:2341⟧); here the point of view of the writer shows itself.
⟦b:Mīlēsiōs nāvem poposcit, quae eum Myndum prōsequerētur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 1, 86, ⟦i:he asked the Milesians for a ship to escort him to Myndus⟧. ⟦b:suōs omnēs castrīs continuit ignēsque fierī prohibuit, quō occultior esset eius adventus⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 3, 30, 5, ⟦i:he confined his troops to camp and forbade the kindling of fires, in order to keep his coming a greater secret⟧.

title: īdem
text:
⟦#2371⟧
⟦b:īdem⟧, ⟦i:the same⟧, often connects two different predicates to the same person or thing. In this case, it may be variously rendered by ⟦i:likewise⟧, ⟦i:also⟧, ⟦i:all the same⟧, ⟦i:on the other hand⟧, ⟦i:at once⟧, ⟦i:very⟧, ⟦i:nevertheless⟧.
⟦b:ūtēbātur eō cibō quī et suāvissimus esset et īdem facillimus ad concoquendum⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 64, ⟦i:he made use of such food as was both very dainty and likewise very easy to digest⟧. ⟦b:ita fīet ut nōn omnēs quī Atticē, eīdem bene dīcant⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 291, ⟦i:so it will be found that not all who speak Attic are also good speakers⟧. ⟦b:multī quī ut iūs suum et lībertātem tenērent volnera excēpērunt fortiter et tulērunt, īdem omissā contentiōne dolōrem morbī ferre nōn possunt⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 65, ⟦i:many who have met heroically and endured wounds, to preserve their rights and their freedom, are nevertheless, when no contest is involved, unable to bear the pain of a disease⟧.
⟦#2372⟧
⟦b:īdem⟧ is often used with other pronouns, ⟦b:hīc⟧, ⟦b:iste⟧, ⟦b:istūc⟧, ⟦b:ille⟧: as,
⟦b:haec eadem centuriōnibus mandābant⟧, 7, 17, 8, ⟦i:they confided these same sentiments to their centurions⟧. ⟦b:multae aliae idem istuc cupiunt⟧, Pl. ⟦i:MG.⟧ 1040, ⟦i:many other ladies want just what you want⟧.
⟦#2373⟧
⟦i:The same as⟧ is expressed by ⟦b:īdem⟧ followed by ⟦b:quī⟧, ⟦b:atque⟧ or ⟦b:ac⟧, ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦b:quasi⟧, ⟦b:cum⟧, sometimes in poetry by the dative.
⟦b:īdem sum quī semper fuī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 447, ⟦i:I’m the same man I’ve always been⟧. ⟦b:pōmārium sēminārium ad eundem modum atque oleāgineum facitō⟧, Cato, ⟦i:RR.⟧ 48, ⟦i:make your fruit-tree nursery in the same way as your nursery for olive-trees⟧ (⟦r1653:1653⟧). ⟦b:eīsdem ferē verbīs ut disputātum est⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 9, ⟦i:in pretty much the same words as were used in the actual argument⟧ (⟦r1937:1937⟧). ⟦b:ut eōdem locō rēs sit quasi ea pecūnia lēgāta nōn esset⟧, ⟦i:Leg.⟧ 2, 53, ⟦i:so that the position is the same as if the money had not been bequeathed⟧ (⟦r2120:2120⟧). ⟦b:tibī̆ mēcum in eōdem est pistrīnō vīvendum⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 2, 144, ⟦i:you must live in the same mill as I⟧. ⟦b:Homērus eādem aliīs sōpītu’ quiētest⟧, Lucr. 3, 1037, ⟦i:Homer sleeps the same sleep as others⟧.

title: ipse
text:
⟦#2374⟧
⟦b:ipse⟧, ⟦i:self⟧, is used in contrasts.
⟦#2375⟧
⟦b:ipse⟧ may contrast the chief person with subordinates, or a person with any thing belonging to him.
⟦b:Catilīna ipse pertimuit, profūgit; hī quid exspectant?⟧ ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 6, ⟦i:Catiline, their head, has fled in abject terror; his minions here, what wait they for?⟧ ⟦b:ē̆ī mūnītiōnī, quam fēcerat, T. Labiēnum lēgātum praefēcit; ipse in Ītaliam magnīs itineribus contendit⟧, 1, 10, 3, ⟦i:he put Labienus, his lieutenant, in charge of the fortification he had made; he hurried, himself, to Italy with forced marches⟧. ⟦b:tēmētī nihil adlātum intellegō :: at iam adferētur, sī ā forō ipsus redierit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 355, ⟦i:I see there’s no wine brought :: but it soon will be, if the governor comes back from down town⟧. ⟦b:‘ipse dīxit;’ “ipse” autem erat Pȳthagorās⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 10, ⟦i:‘the old man said so;’ now “the old man” was Pythagoras⟧. ⟦b:nāvis tantum iactūrā factā, incolumēs ipsī ēvāsērunt⟧, L. 30, 25, 8, ⟦i:the vessel only was lost, and the sailors escaped in safety⟧.
⟦#2376⟧
⟦b:ipse⟧ is often used with personals and reflexives agreeing with the emphatic word. But the nominative is usually preferred, especially when ⟦b:ipse⟧ stands before the other pronoun, or when it stands after ⟦b:per mē⟧, ⟦b:per sē⟧. After ⟦b:mēmet⟧, ⟦b:nōbīsmet⟧, ⟦b:nōsmet⟧, &c., it agrees with these words.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:neque enim potest exercitum is continēre imperātor, quī sē ipsum nōn continet⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 38, ⟦i:for no commander can keep his army under control who does not keep his own self under control⟧. ⟦b:mīles frātrem suum, dein sē ipsum interfēcit⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 3, 51, ⟦i:a soldier slew his own brother, then himself⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:ipse sē quisque dīligit⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 80, ⟦i:every man loves himself⟧. ⟦b:bellum per sē ipse, iniussū populī ac senātūs, fēcit⟧, L. 1, 49, 7, ⟦i:he made war on his own responsibility, without orders from the people and senate⟧. ⟦b:Iūnius necem sibī̆ ipse cōnscīvit⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 7, ⟦i:Junius killed himself⟧. ⟦b:nōn egeō medicīnā, mē ipse cōnsōlor⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 10, ⟦i:I need no medicine, I am my own comforter⟧. (⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:ut nōbīsmet ipsīs imperēmus⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 2, 47, ⟦i:that we should govern ourselves⟧.
⟦#2377⟧
⟦b:ipse⟧ alone sometimes stands for an emphatic ⟦b:sē⟧ or ⟦b:suus⟧: as,
⟦b:pertimuērunt nē ab ipsīs dēscīsceret et cum suīs in grātiam redīret⟧, N. 7, 5, 1, ⟦i:they were much afraid that he would abandon them and come into favour with his compatriots again⟧. ⟦b:ea molestissimē ferre hominēs dēbent, quae ipsōrum culpā contrācta sunt⟧, ⟦i:QFr.⟧ 1, 1, 2, ⟦i:people should be most vexed at things which are brought about through fault of their own⟧.
⟦#2378⟧
⟦b:ipse⟧ is used in many combinations where ⟦i:self⟧ is an inadequate translation. It may sometimes be translated by:
⟦#2379⟧
(1.) ⟦i:Actual⟧, ⟦i:positive⟧, ⟦i:even⟧.
⟦b:habet certōs suī studiōsōs, quōs valētūdō modo bona sit, tenuitās ipsa dēlectat⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 64, ⟦i:he has a clique of admirers, who are charmed by positive scragginess, provided the health be good⟧. ⟦b:hōc ipsum ēlegantius pōnī meliusque potuit⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 100, ⟦i:even this might have been put more logically and better⟧.
⟦#2380⟧
(2.) ⟦i:Regular⟧, ⟦i:proper⟧, ⟦i:real⟧.
⟦b:flagrantem invidiā propter interitum C. Gracchī ipse populus Rōmānus perīculō līberāvit⟧, ⟦i:Sest.⟧ 140, ⟦i:though greatly detested in consequence of the death of Gracchus, he was acquitted by the Roman people proper⟧. ⟦b:cīvēs Rōmānī permultī in illō oppidō cōniūnctissimō animō cum ipsīs Agrigentīnīs vīvunt⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 93, ⟦i:a great many Romans live in that town in most friendly relations with the natives of Agrigentum⟧.
⟦#2381⟧
(3.) ⟦i:As well⟧, ⟦i:likewise⟧, ⟦i:too⟧, for which, from Livy on, ⟦b:et ipse⟧ is used.
⟦b:hoc Rīpheus, hoc ipse Dymās, omnisque iuventūs laeta facit⟧, V. 2, 394, ⟦i:this Ripheus doth, this Dymas too, and all the youth alert⟧. ⟦b:cōgitātiō Locrōs urbem recipiendī, quae sub dēfectiōnem Ītaliae dēscīverat et ipsa ad Poenōs⟧, L. 29, 6, 1, ⟦i:a project for recovering the city of Locri, which, on the revolt of Italy, had likewise gone over to the Carthaginians⟧.
⟦#2382⟧
(4.) ⟦i:Alone⟧, ⟦i:mere⟧.
⟦b:nōn sōlum adventus malī, sed etiam metus ipse adfert calamitātem⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 15, ⟦i:not only the coming of misfortune, but even the mere dread of it brings disaster⟧.
⟦#2383⟧
(5.) ⟦i:Exactly⟧, ⟦i:just⟧, with numerals and dates, or ⟦i:right⟧, of place.
⟦b:annīs LXXXVI ipsīs ante mē cōnsulem⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 61, ⟦i:exactly 86 years before my consulship⟧. ⟦b:Kalendīs ipsīs Novembribus⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 8, ⟦i:on the 1st of November precisely⟧. ⟦b:in ipsō vadō dēprehēnsus Indutiomarus interficitur⟧, 5, 58, 6, ⟦i:right at the ford Indutiomarus is caught and killed⟧. ⟦b:suprā ipsum balneum habitō⟧, Sen. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 56, 1, ⟦i:I live right over a bath⟧.
⟦#2384⟧
(6.) ⟦i:Of oneself⟧, ⟦i:voluntarily⟧, ⟦i:of one’s own motion⟧.
⟦b:valvae subitō sē ipsae aperuērunt⟧, ⟦i:Div.⟧ 1, 74, ⟦i:the temple-door suddenly opened of itself⟧. ⟦b:Catilīnam vel ēiēcimus vel ēmīsimus vel ipsum ēgredientem verbīs prōsecūtī sumus⟧, ⟦i:C.⟧ 2, 1, ⟦i:we have driven Catiline out, or let him out, or, when he was going out of his own motion, wished him godspeed⟧.

title: uter and quis
text:
⟦#2385⟧
⟦b:uter⟧, ⟦i:whether⟧? ⟦i:which⟧? is used in questions about two things; ⟦b:quis⟧ and ⟦b:quī⟧, ⟦i:who⟧? ⟦i:what⟧? in questions about more than two, though sometimes loosely of two things.
⟦b:uter est īnsānior hōrum?⟧ H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 3, 102, ⟦i:which of these is the greater crank?⟧ ⟦b:praeclārē apud eundem est Platōnem, similiter facere eōs quī inter sē contenderent uter potius rem pūblicam administrāret, ut sī nautae certārent quis eōrum potissimum gubernāret⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 87, ⟦i:in the same Plato is the excellent saying that for people to fall out with one another about which of two men should manage a state, were just as if the crew of a ship should quarrel about which of them should be pilot⟧. ⟦b:ut quem velīs, nesciās⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 16, 14, 1, ⟦i:so that you don’t know which to choose, as between Octavian and Antony⟧.
⟦#2386⟧
⟦b:quis⟧ and ⟦b:quid⟧ ask to have a thing named; ⟦b:quī⟧ and ⟦b:quod⟧ to have it described. But see ⟦r685:685⟧.
⟦b:quis Diōnem Syrācosium doctrīnīs omnibus expolīvit? nōn Platō?⟧ ⟦i:DO.⟧ 3, 139, ⟦i:who refined Syracusan Dio with learning of every sort? was it not Plato?⟧ ⟦b:quid rīdēs⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 2, 5, 3, ⟦i:why dost thou laugh?⟧ (⟦r1144:1144⟧). ⟦b:quis fuit igitur?:: iste Chaerea.:: quī Chaerea?⟧ T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 823, ⟦i:who was he then?:: your precious Chaerea.:: what Chaerea?⟧ ⟦b:quem frūctum petentēs scīre cupimus illa quō modō moveantur?⟧ ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 3, 37, ⟦i:with what practical end in view do we seek to know how yon bodies in the sky keep in motion?⟧
⟦#2387⟧
The relative pronoun has already been treated; see ⟦r1792:1792-1837⟧.

title: quis or quī; quispiam
text:
⟦#2388⟧
⟦b:quis⟧ or ⟦b:quī⟧, a, ⟦i:some⟧, ⟦i:somebody⟧, always stands after one or more words of the sentence. ⟦b:quis⟧ or ⟦b:quī⟧ is used after ⟦b:sī⟧ (⟦b:nisi⟧, ⟦b:sīve⟧), ⟦b:nē⟧, ⟦b:num⟧, ⟦b:utrum⟧, ⟦b:an⟧, ⟦b:quō⟧, or ⟦b:quandō⟧, in preference to ⟦b:aliquis⟧, unless emphasis is intended.
⟦b:dīxerit quis⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 76, ⟦i:somebody may say⟧. ⟦b:malum quod tibī dī dabunt⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Am.⟧ 563, ⟦i:some curse the gods will bring upon thee⟧. ⟦b:hī, sī quid erat dūrius, concurrēbant; sī quī equō dēciderat, circumsistēbant⟧, 1, 48, 6, ⟦i:if there was ever any sharpish work, these men would rally; if a man fell from his horse, they would close round him⟧. ⟦b:praecipit atque interdīcit ūnum omnēs peterent Indutiomarum, neu quis quem vulneret⟧, 5, 58, 4, ⟦i:he charges them and forbids them; they were all to assail Indutiomarus alone; and nobody was to wound anybody⟧ (⟦r2402:2402⟧).
⟦#2389⟧
⟦b:quispiam⟧, ⟦i:a⟧, ⟦i:some⟧, ⟦i:one or another⟧.
⟦b:forsitan quispiam dīxerit⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 3, 29, ⟦i:peradventure somebody may say⟧. ⟦b:quispiam dīcet⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 3, 111, ⟦i:somebody will say⟧. ⟦b:cum quaepiam cohors impetum fēcerat, hostēs vēlōcissimē refugiēbant⟧, 5, 35, 1, ⟦i:every time one or another cohort charged, the enemy fled back quick speed⟧ (⟦r2394:2394⟧).

title: aliquis
text:
⟦#2390⟧
⟦b:aliquis⟧ or ⟦b:aliquī⟧ ⟦i:some one⟧, ⟦i:some one or other⟧, has always some affirmative emphasis, and is opposed to the idea of ⟦i:all⟧, ⟦i:much⟧, ⟦i:none⟧: as,
⟦b:nōn enim dēclāmātōrem aliquem dē lūdō, sed perfectissimum quaerimus⟧, ⟦i:O.⟧ 47, ⟦i:for it is not some spouter from school that we aim to find, but the ideal orator⟧. ⟦b:omnēs ut aliquam perniciōsam bēstiam fugiēbant⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 41, ⟦i:everybody avoided him, like some dangerous wild animal or other⟧. ⟦b:audē aliquid Gyarīs dīgnum sī vīs esse aliquid⟧, J. 1, 73, ⟦i:venture some deed that deserves transportation, if you care to be something grand⟧. ⟦b:nōn sine aliquā spē⟧, ⟦i:D.⟧ 7, ⟦i:not without some hope⟧. ⟦b:quaerō sitne aliqua āctiō an nūlla⟧, ⟦i:Caec.⟧ 33, ⟦i:I ask whether there is some ground for an action or none⟧. ⟦b:num igitur aliquis dolor post mortem est?⟧ ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 82, ⟦i:is there, then, some sense of pain after death?⟧ With emphasis after ⟦b:sī⟧ (⟦r2388:2388⟧): ⟦b:sī aliquid dē summā gravitāte Pompēius, multum de cupiditāte Caesar remīsisset, aliquam rem pūblicam nōbīs habēre licuisset⟧, ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 13, 2, ⟦i:if Pompey had sacrificed really something of his importance, and Caesar a good deal of his ambition, we might have had what would have been to some degree a commonwealth⟧.
⟦#2391⟧
⟦b:aliquis⟧ is sometimes equivalent to ⟦b:aliquis alius⟧: as,
⟦b:cum M. Pīsōne et cum Q. Pompēiō aut cum aliquō⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 310, ⟦i:with Piso or Pompey or some other man⟧. ⟦b:ea mihī cottīdiē aut tūre aut vīnō aut aliquī semper supplicat⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Aul. prol.⟧ 23, ⟦i:she always offers me incense or wine or something else every day⟧.

title: quīdam
text:
⟦#2392⟧
⟦b:quīdam⟧, ⟦i:a⟧, ⟦i:a certain⟧, denotes a thing which we cannot describe or do not care to.
⟦b:nōn inrīdiculē quīdam ex mīlitibus decimae legiōnis dīxit: plūs quam pollicitus esset, Caesarem facere⟧, 1, 42, 6, ⟦i:one of the privates of the Tenth said a very dry thing: that ‘Caesar was doing more than he engaged to.’⟧ ⟦b:accurrit quīdam nōtus mihi nōmine tantum⟧, H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 9, 3, ⟦i:up trots a man I knew by name alone⟧. ⟦b:assimilis quīdam mūgituī sonus⟧, Suet. ⟦i:Galb.⟧ 18, ⟦i:a mysterious sound like the lowing of a cow⟧. ⟦b:vidēmus nātūram suō quōdam itinere ad ultimum pervenīre⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 35, ⟦i:nature reaches perfection by a kind of road of her own⟧. Often in translations from Greek: as, ⟦b:aliīs librīs ratiōnem quandam per omnem nātūram rērum pertinentem vī dīvīnā esse adfectam putat⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 1, 36, ⟦i:in other works he supposes ‘a kind of Reason pervading all nature and endowed with divine power⟧, of Zeno’s doctrine.
⟦#2393⟧
⟦b:quīdam⟧ is often used to soften an exaggeration or a metaphor, sometimes to denote contempt.
⟦b:ēloquentissimōs hominēs innumerābilīs quōsdam nōminābat⟧, ⟦i:DO.⟧ 1, 91, ⟦i:great speakers he named, absolutely without number⟧. ⟦b:ad omnīs enim meōs impetūs quasi mūrus quīdam bonī nōmen imperātōris oppōnitur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 2, ⟦i:for against all assaults of mine the name of a good commander is set up, like a regular wall⟧. ⟦b:sed aliud quoddam fīlum ōrātiōnis tuae⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 25, ⟦i:but there is quite a different fibre to your speech⟧. ⟦b:nōn est eōrum urbānitāte quādam quasi colōrāta ōrātiō⟧, ⟦i:Br.⟧ 170, ⟦i:their language lacks the tinge of an indefinable metropolitan element⟧. ⟦b:Theomnāstus quīdam, homo rīdiculē īnsānus⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 148, ⟦i:a person of the name of Theomnastus, an absurd, crack-brained creature⟧.

title: quisque
text:
⟦#2394⟧
⟦b:quisque⟧, ⟦i:each⟧, ⟦i:each in particular⟧, ⟦i:each by himself⟧, applies what is stated of all to each several case, out of a number more than two.
⟦b:laudātī prō cōntiōne omnēs sunt, dōnātīque prō meritō quisque⟧, L. 38, 23, 11, ⟦i:they were collectively commended in assembly convened, and received presents, each in proportion to his deserts⟧. ⟦b:quotiēns quaeque cohors prōcurrerat, magnus numerus hostium cadēbat⟧, 5, 34, 2, ⟦i:as the cohorts successively charged, a great number of the enemy fell every time⟧ (⟦r2389:2389⟧). ⟦b:mēns cuiusque, is est quisque, nōn ea figūra quae digitō dēmōnstrārī potest⟧, ⟦i:RP.⟧ 6, 26, ⟦i:the mind of a man is always the man, and not that shape which can be pointed out by the finger⟧.
⟦#2395⟧
⟦b:quisque⟧ is sometimes used in a relative and demonstrative sentence both.
⟦b:quod cuique obtigit, id quisque teneat⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 21, ⟦i:let every man keep what he has got⟧. ⟦b:id enim est cuiusque proprium, quō quisque fruitur atque ūtitur⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 7, 30, 2, ⟦i:for that is always a man’s property which he has the enjoyment and use of⟧.
⟦#2396⟧
In a complex sentence, consisting of a main and a relative sentence, ⟦b:quisque⟧ is usually expressed but once, and then in the unemphatic relative sentence. In English, the equivalent of ⟦b:quisque⟧ goes with the main sentence.
⟦b:nēmō fuit quī nōn surrēxerit, tēlumque quod cuique fors offerēbat, adripuerit⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 95, ⟦i:not a man but sprang from his bed, and seized in every instance such a weapon as chance threw in his way⟧. ⟦b:theātrum cum commūne sit, rēctē tamen dīcī potest, eius esse eum locum, quem quisque occupārit⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 3, 67, ⟦i:though the theatre is open to all, still it may be said with perfect propriety, that each spectator is entitled to the seat he has taken⟧. ⟦b:Messānam ut quisque nostrūm vēnerat, haec vīsere solēbat⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 5, ⟦i:any Roman, who went to Messana, invariably went to see these statues⟧ (⟦r1939:1939⟧). ⟦b:eōrum ut quisque prīmus vēnerat, sub mūrō cōnsistēbat⟧, 7, 48, 2, ⟦i:as they successively arrived, each man of them took his stand under the wall⟧.
⟦#2397⟧
⟦b:quisque⟧ is often used with ⟦b:sē⟧ or ⟦b:suus⟧, superlatives, and ordinals, holding an unemphatic place ⟦i:after⟧ these words: as,
⟦b:ipse sē quisque dīligit⟧, ⟦i:L.⟧ 80, ⟦i:a man always loves his own self⟧. ⟦b:suos quoique mōs⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 454, ⟦i:every man his own way⟧. ⟦b:huic prō sē quisque nostrūm medērī velle dēbēmus⟧, ⟦i:L. Agr.⟧ 1, 26, ⟦i:this evil we ought to wish to remedy, according to our several abilities⟧. ⟦b:optimum quidque rārissimum est⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 2, 81, ⟦i:ever the fairest is the rarest⟧. ⟦b:nam in forō vix decumus quisquest, quī ipsus sēsē nōverit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Ps.⟧ 973, ⟦i:for in the marketplace there’s scarce one man in every ten that knows himself⟧. ⟦b:quīntō quōque annō Sicilia tōta cēnsētur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 139, ⟦i:at the end of every four years all Sicily is assessed⟧. ⟦b:quamquam prīmum quidque explicēmus⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 12, 1, 1, ⟦i:but stay—let me explain things successively⟧; or, ⟦i:one thing after another⟧. ⟦b:litterās mīsit, ut is ānulus ad sē prīmō quōque tempore adferrētur⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 58, ⟦i:he sent a letter directing said ring to be sent to him without delay⟧.
⟦#2398⟧
In old Latin ⟦b:quisque⟧ is sometimes equivalent to ⟦b:quīcumque⟧ or ⟦b:quisquis⟧, ⟦i:whoever⟧: as, ⟦b:quisque obviam huic occesserit īrātō, vāpulābit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 404, ⟦i:whoever meets him in his wrath will catch it⟧. In ⟦b:cuiusque generis⟧ and ⟦b:cuiusque modī⟧, it means ⟦i:any and every⟧: as, ⟦b:tot hominēs cuiusque modī⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 7, ⟦i:so many people of every sort⟧, i.e. ⟦b:cuicuimodī⟧. The neuter ⟦b:quidquid⟧ for ⟦b:quidque⟧ is not uncommon: as, ⟦b:cum prōcessit paulum et quātenus quicquid sē attingat perspicere coepit⟧, ⟦i:Fin.⟧ 5, 24, ⟦i:when it has progressed a little and has begun to discover how far each thing affects it⟧. Masculine ⟦b:quisquis⟧ for ⟦b:quisque⟧ is doubtful (see ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 6, 1, 1).

title: uterque
text:
⟦#2399⟧
⟦b:uterque⟧, ⟦i:each⟧, is used of two individuals, and ⟦b:utrīque⟧ of two sets or parties. But sometimes ⟦b:utrīque⟧ is used of two individuals.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:ut illa nātūra caelestis et terrā vacat et ūmōre, sīc utriusque hārum rērum hūmānus animus est expers⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 1, 65, ⟦i:even as the heavenly nature is free from the earthy and the humid, so the soul of man has no part in either of these qualities⟧ (⟦r1243:1243⟧). ⟦b:nūtū tremefactus uterque est polus⟧, O. ⟦i:F.⟧ 2, 489, ⟦i:at his nod trembled each pole⟧ (⟦r1243:1243⟧). ⟦b:Aetōliōrum utraeque manūs Hēraclēam sēsē inclūsērunt⟧, L. 36, 16, 5, ⟦i:both bands of the Aetolians shut themselves up in Heraclea⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:sex fīliī nōbīs, duae fīliae sunt, utraeque iam nūptae⟧, L. 42, 34, 4, ⟦i:we have six sons and two daughters, both already married⟧.
⟦#2400⟧
Reciprocal relations (⟦r2344:2344⟧) are sometimes expressed by ⟦b:uterque⟧ followed by a different case of ⟦b:alter⟧; rarely by ⟦b:uterque⟧ and a different case of the same word.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:quōrum uterque contempsit alterum⟧, ⟦i:Off.⟧ 1, 4, ⟦i:each of whom lightly esteemed the other⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:abdūcī nōn potest :: quī nōn potest? :: quia uterque utrīquest cordī⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 799, ⟦i:she’s not to be taken from him :: why isn’t she? :: because they’re heart to heart⟧. This doubling of ⟦b:uterque⟧ is found only half a dozen times; not in Cicero.
⟦b:quīvīs⟧ and ⟦b:quīlibet⟧; ⟦b:utervīs⟧ and ⟦b:uterlibet⟧.
⟦#2401⟧
⟦b:quīvīs⟧ and ⟦b:quīlibet⟧, ⟦i:any you please⟧, are used either in affirmative or negative sentences. When two are spoken of, ⟦b:utervīs⟧ or ⟦b:uterlibet⟧ is used.
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:ut quīvīs intellegere posset⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 17, ⟦i:so that any fool might know⟧. ⟦b:faciat quidlubet⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 464, ⟦i:let him do anything he likes⟧. (⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:quī utramvīs rēctē nōvit, ambās nōverit⟧, T. ⟦i:Andr. prol.⟧ 10, ⟦i:who knows either well, knows both⟧. ⟦b:utrumlibet ēlige⟧, ⟦i:Quinct.⟧ 81, ⟦i:choose either you like⟧.

title: quisquam and ūllus
text:
⟦#2402⟧
⟦b:quisquam⟧ (⟦r692:692⟧), ⟦i:a single one⟧, ⟦i:any one at all⟧, and ⟦b:ūllus⟧, ⟦i:any⟧, are used chiefly in negative sentences or in interrogative, conditional, and comparative sentences implying negation, or with ⟦b:sine⟧.
⟦b:vēnī Athēnās, neque mē quisquam ibī̆ adgnōvit⟧, ⟦i:TD.⟧ 5, 104, ⟦i:I came to Athens and not a person there knew me⟧ (⟦r1659:1659⟧). ⟦b:interdīcit omnibus, nē quemquam interficiant⟧, 7, 40, 4, ⟦i:he warns them collectively against killing any man at all⟧ (⟦r2388:2388⟧). ⟦b:hunc suā quisquam sententiā ex hāc urbe expellet?⟧ ⟦i:Mil.⟧ 104, ⟦i:will anybody at all, by his vote, banish this man from Rome?⟧ ⟦b:quis hoc fēcit ūllā in Scythiā tyrannus?⟧ ⟦i:Pis.⟧ 18, ⟦i:what tyrant ever did this in any Scythia?⟧ ⟦b:sī quisquam est timidus, is ego sum⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 6, 14, 1, ⟦i:if anybody is timid, I am the man⟧. ⟦b:quī saepius cum hoste cōnflīxit quam quisquam cum inimīcō concertāvit⟧, ⟦i:IP.⟧ 28, ⟦i:who has measured swords oftener with the enemy than anybody ever wrangled with an opponent in private life⟧. ⟦b:sine ūllō metū in ipsum portum penetrāre coepērunt⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 5, 96, ⟦i:without a bit of fear they began to make their way right into the harbour⟧. ⟦b:nēmō quisquam⟧ and ⟦b:nihil quicquam⟧ are old and late: as, ⟦b:lepidiōrem uxōrem nēmō quisquam habet⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cas.⟧ 1008, ⟦i:nobody has a jollier wife⟧. ⟦b:noster malī nīl quicquam prīmō⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 80, ⟦i:our young master didn’t make any trouble at first⟧.
⟦#2403⟧
⟦b:nēmō⟧ is generally used for ⟦b:nōn quisquam⟧, ⟦b:nēmō umquam⟧ for ⟦b:numquam quisquam⟧, ⟦b:nihil⟧ for ⟦b:nōn quicquam⟧, and ⟦b:nūllus⟧ for ⟦b:nōn ūllus⟧. If only two are spoken of, ⟦b:neuter⟧ is used. The plural ⟦b:neutrī⟧ is used of two parties.
⟦b:nēmōst miserior mē⟧, T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 263, ⟦i:no man’s unhappier than I⟧. ⟦b:nēmō igitur vir magnus sine aliquō adflātū dīvīnō umquam fuit⟧, ⟦i:DN.⟧ 2, 167, ⟦i:nobody who is a great man was ever without some divine inspiration⟧. ⟦b:ab nūllō ille līberālius quam ā Cluentiō trāctātus est⟧, ⟦i:Clu.⟧ 161, ⟦i:by no man has he been treated more generously than by Cluentius⟧. ⟦b:neutrum eōrum contrā alterum iuvāre⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 35, 5, ⟦i:to help neither of them against the other⟧. ⟦b:neutrī alterōs prīmō cernēbant⟧, L. 21, 46, 4, ⟦i:neither party saw the others at first⟧.
