title: Notation
text:
⟦#2406⟧
Numbers are noted by combinations of the characters I = 1; V = 5; X = 10; ↆ, later , , or L = 50; C = 100; D = 500; ↀ or , post-Augustan M = 1000.
⟦#2407⟧
Of these signs, V seems to be the half of X, which may be Etruscan in origin. The original signs for 50 and 1000 were taken from the Chalcidian Greek alphabet (⟦r18:18⟧, ⟦r19:19⟧), in which they represented sounds unknown to early Latin. Thus, ↆ, in the Chalcidian alphabet representing ⟦b:ch⟧ (⟦r49:49⟧), was used by the early Romans for 50, and became successively , , and L. The form ↆ, is found very rarely, oftener, in the Augustan period; is common during the last century of the republic and in the early empire; L, due to assimilation with the Roman letter, appears in the last century of the republic. The sign for 1000 was originally ↀ (Chalcidian ⟦b:ph⟧); it became (the common classical form), , or ; the form M as a numeral appears in the second century A.D., although M is found much earlier as an abbreviation for ⟦b:mīllia⟧ in M · P, that is ⟦b:mīllia passuum⟧. For 100, the sign (Chalcidian ⟦b:th⟧) may have been used originally; but C (the abbreviation for ⟦b:centum⟧) came into use at an early period. The sign D, = 500, is the half of ↀ.
⟦#2408⟧
To denote 10,000 the sign for 1000 was doubled: thus, ↂ, written also , , . Another circle was added to denote 100,000: thus, ↈ, written also , , . The halves of these signs were used for 5000 and 50,000: thus, ↁ and ↇ; variations of these last two signs are found, corresponding to the variations of the signs of which they are the halves.
⟦#2409⟧
From the last century of the republic on, thousands are sometimes indicated by a line drawn above a numeral, and hundreds of thousands by three lines enclosing a numeral: as, V̅ = 5000; = 1,000,000.
⟦#2410⟧
To distinguish numerals from ordinary letters, a line is often drawn above them: as, V͞I = 6. This practice is common in the Augustan period; earlier, a line is sometimes drawn across the numeral, as, = 2; = 500.
⟦#2411⟧
Of the two methods of writing the symbols for 4, 9, 14, 19, &c., the method by subtraction (IV, IX, XIV, XIX, &c.) is rarer, and is characteristic of private, not public inscriptions.

title: Some Forms of Numerals
text:
⟦#2412⟧
⟦b:quīnctus⟧, the older form of ⟦b:quīntus⟧ (⟦r170:170, 4⟧) is sometimes found in old and even in classical writers. Instead of ⟦b:septimus⟧ and ⟦b:decimus⟧, the older ⟦b:septumus⟧ and ⟦b:decumus⟧ are not uncommon (⟦r28:28⟧).
⟦#2413⟧
In the ordinals from ⟦i:twentieth⟧ upwards, the older forms ⟦b:vīcēnsumus⟧ or ⟦b:vīcēnsimus⟧, ⟦b:trīcēnsumus⟧ or ⟦b:trīcēnsimus⟧, &c., &c., are not infrequently found instead of ⟦b:vīcēsimus⟧, ⟦b:trīcēsimus⟧, &c., &c. (⟦r63:63⟧; ⟦r28:28⟧).
⟦#2414⟧
In the numeral adverbs from ⟦b:quīnquiēns⟧ upwards, later forms in ⟦b:-īēs⟧ (⟦r63:63⟧) are often found: as, ⟦b:quīnquiēs⟧, ⟦b:deciēs⟧, &c., &c.
⟦#2415⟧
In cardinals and ordinals from ⟦i:thirteen⟧ to ⟦i:seventeen⟧ inclusive, the larger number sometimes comes first, and in cardinals ⟦b:et⟧ is sometimes used, though rarely in Cicero.
⟦b:decem trēs⟧, L. 37, 30, 7, ⟦i:thirteen⟧. ⟦b:fundōs decem et trēs relīquit⟧, ⟦i:RA⟧. 20, ⟦i:he left thirteen farms⟧. Rarely the smaller number comes first with ⟦b:et⟧: as, ⟦b:dē tribus et decem fundīs⟧, ⟦i:RA⟧. 99, ⟦i:of the thirteen farms⟧.
⟦#2416⟧
Numbers from 18 to 99 inclusive which end in 8 or 9 are usually expressed by subtraction, as in the list (⟦r2405:2405⟧); less frequently (not in Cicero, rarely in classical writers) by addition: as, ⟦b:decem et octō⟧, 4, 19, 4; ⟦b:decem novem⟧, Ta. ⟦i:H.⟧ 2, 58.
⟦#2417⟧
In compound numbers from ⟦i:twenty-one⟧ to ⟦i:ninety-seven⟧ inclusive, except those which end in ⟦i:eight⟧ or ⟦i:nine⟧ (⟦r2416:2416⟧), the smaller number with et usually comes first or the larger number without ⟦b:et⟧, as in the list. But rarely the larger number comes first with ⟦b:et⟧: as, ⟦b:vīgintī et septem⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 4, 123, ⟦i:twenty and seven⟧.
⟦#2418⟧
In numbers from a ⟦i:hundred and one⟧ upwards, the larger number comes first, either with or without ⟦b:et⟧; but with distributives ⟦b:et⟧ is not used. With cardinals and ordinals the smaller number sometimes comes first with ⟦b:et⟧; as, ⟦b:iīs rēgiīs quadrāgintā annīs et ducentīs praeteritīs⟧, ⟦i:RP⟧. 2, 52, ⟦i:after these two hundred and forty years of monarchy were ended⟧.

title: Cardinals and Ordinals
text:
⟦#2419⟧
Dates are expressed either by cardinals with a plural substantive or by ordinals with a singular substantive: as,
⟦b:dictātor factus est annīs post Rōmam conditam CCCCXV⟧, ⟦i:Fam.⟧ 9, 21, 2, ⟦i:he was made dictator⟧ 415 U. C. (⟦r1393:1393⟧). ⟦b:annō trecentēsimō quīnquāgēsimō post Rōmam conditam, Nōnīs Iūnīs⟧, ⟦i:RP⟧. 1, 25, ⟦i:on the 5th of June⟧, 350 U. C. (⟦r1350:1350⟧). The ordinal is also used with a substantive not used in the singular: as, ⟦b:mancipia vēnībant Sāturnālibus tertiīs⟧, ⟦i:Att.⟧ 5, 20, 5, ⟦i:the slaves were sold on the third day of the Saturnalia⟧. As the Romans, however, had no fixed official era, they had no dates in the modern sense, and marked the year by the names of the consuls.

title: Distributives
text:
⟦#2420⟧
Distributives are used to denote an equal division among several persons or things, and in expressions of multiplication: as,
⟦b:bīnī senātōrēs singulīs cohortibus praepositī⟧, L. 3, 69, 8, ⟦i:two senators were put over every cohort⟧: sometimes when ⟦b:singulī⟧ is added, the cardinal is used, thus: ⟦b:singulīs cēnsōribus dēnāriī trecentī imperātī sunt⟧, ⟦i:V.⟧ 2, 137, ⟦i:every censor was assessed 300 denars⟧. ⟦b:bis bīna⟧, ⟦i:DN⟧. 2, 49, ⟦i:twice two⟧. Poets use multiplication freely, partly for variety, but mainly from metrical necessity.
⟦#2421⟧
Distributives are also used with substantives which have no singular, or which have a different meaning in the singular; but in this use ⟦i:one⟧ is always ⟦b:ūnī⟧, not ⟦b:singulī⟧, and ⟦i:three⟧ is often ⟦b:trīnī⟧, not ⟦b:ternī⟧: as,
⟦b:ut ūna castra iam facta ex bīnīs vidērentur⟧, Caes. ⟦i:C.⟧ 1, 74, 4, ⟦i:so that one camp seemed now to have been formed out of two⟧. ⟦b:trīnīs catēnīs vinctus⟧, 1, 53, 5, ⟦i:in triple irons⟧. Similarly with things in pairs, as: ⟦b:bovēs bīnī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Pers.⟧ 317, ⟦i:a yoke of oxen⟧.
⟦#2422⟧
Poets sometimes use the singular of distributives: as, ⟦b:centēnāque arbore flūctum verberat⟧, V. 10, 207, ⟦i:and with a hundred beams at every stroke the wave he smites⟧. ⟦b:duplicī nātūrā et corpore bīnō⟧, Lucr. 5, 879, ⟦i:twynatured and of body twain⟧. The plural is sometimes used in verse for the cardinal: ⟦b:centum bracchia . . . centēnāsque manūs⟧, V. 10, 565, ⟦i:a hundred arms . . . and hundred hands⟧.

title: Other Numerals
text:
⟦#2423⟧
Other numerical adjectives are ⟦i:multiplicatives⟧, ending in ⟦b:-plex⟧; they are: ⟦b:simplex⟧, ⟦i:onefold⟧, ⟦i:simple⟧, ⟦b:sēscuplex⟧, ⟦i:one and a half fold⟧, ⟦b:duplex⟧, ⟦b:triplex⟧, ⟦b:quadruplex⟧, ⟦b:quīncuplex⟧, ⟦b:septemplex⟧, ⟦b:decemplex⟧, ⟦b:centuplex⟧; and ⟦i:proportionals⟧, used mostly in the neuter as substantives: ⟦b:duplus⟧, ⟦i:twice as great⟧, ⟦b:triplus⟧, ⟦i:three times as great⟧, ⟦b:quadruplus⟧, ⟦b:septuplus⟧, ⟦b:octuplus⟧. Besides these there are other adjectives derived from numerals: as, ⟦b:prīmānus⟧, ⟦i:soldier of the first⟧: ⟦b:prīmārius⟧, ⟦i:first rate⟧: ⟦b:bīmus⟧, ⟦i:twinter⟧, ⟦i:two-year-old⟧; &c., &c.

title: Expression of Fractions
text:
⟦#2424⟧
⟦i:One half⟧ may be expressed by ⟦b:dīmidium⟧ or ⟦b:dīmidia pars⟧; other fractions with 1 as a numerator by ordinals, with or without ⟦b:pars⟧: as, ⟦b:tertia pars⟧ or ⟦b:tertia⟧, 1/3.
⟦#2425⟧
If the numerator is greater than 1 it is usually expressed by the cardinal feminine, with the ordinal feminine for the denominator: as, ⟦b:duae septimae⟧, 2/7. But besides these forms there are others, namely:
⟦#2426⟧
(1.) Fractions with a numerator less by 1 than the denominator, except 1/2, may be expressed by cardinals with ⟦b:partēs⟧, as, ⟦b:duae partēs⟧, 2/3; ⟦b:trēs partēs⟧, 3/4; ⟦b:quattuor partēs⟧, 4/5.
⟦#2427⟧
(2.) Fractions with 12 or its multiples as a denominator are expressed in business language by the parts of an ⟦b:ās⟧: thus,
1/12,  ⟦b:uncia⟧
1/6,  ⟦b:sextāns⟧
1/4,  ⟦b:quadrāns⟧
1/3,  ⟦b:triēns⟧
5/12,  ⟦b:quīncunx⟧
1/2,  ⟦b:sēmis⟧
7/12,  ⟦b:septunx⟧
2/3,  ⟦b:bēs⟧
3/4,  ⟦b:dōdrāns⟧
5/6,  ⟦b:dēxtāns⟧
11/12,  ⟦b:deūnx⟧
12/12,  ⟦b:ās⟧
⟦/⟧
⟦b:ex āsse hērēs⟧, Quintil. 7, 1, 20, ⟦i:heir to the whole⟧; ⟦b:relīquit hērēdēs ex bēsse nepōtem, ex tertiā parte neptem⟧, Plin. ⟦i:Ep.⟧ 7, 24, 2, ⟦i:she left her grandson heir to 2/3, her granddaughter to 1/3⟧. ⟦b:hērēdem ex dōdrante⟧, N. 25, 5, 2, ⟦i:heir to 3/4⟧.
⟦#2428⟧
Sometimes fractions are expressed by addition: as, ⟦b:dīmidia et quarta⟧, 3/4; ⟦b:pars tertia et septima⟧, 10/21; sometimes by division of the denominator: as, ⟦b:dīmidia quīnta⟧, 1/10.

title: Rules of Quantity: In Classical Latin
text:
⟦#2429⟧
The length of the vowel in some classes of syllables, as used in the classical period, may be conveniently fixed in the memory by the following rules. For the usage of older writers, see ⟦r126:126⟧, ⟦r129:129⟧, ⟦r132:132⟧ and 2464-2472. For the general principles of length of vowels and syllables, see ⟦r33:33-41⟧; 121-134; 177-178.

title: Monosyllables
text:
⟦#2430⟧
Monosyllables ending in a vowel or a single consonant have the vowel long: as,
⟦b:dōs⟧, ⟦b:sōl⟧; ⟦b:ā⟧ for ⟦b:ab⟧; ⟦b:ē⟧ for ⟦b:ex⟧ or ⟦b:ec-⟧, ⟦b:pēs⟧ for ⟦b:*peds⟧; ablative ⟦b:quā⟧, ⟦b:quī⟧; ⟦b:quīn⟧ for ⟦b:*quīne⟧; locative ⟦b:sei⟧, commonly ⟦b:sī⟧; ⟦b:sīc⟧ (⟦r708:708⟧); dative and ablative plural ⟦b:quīs⟧ (⟦r688:688⟧).

title: Rules of Quantity: Exceptions
text:
⟦#2431⟧
The vowel is short in:
⟦#2432⟧
(a.) Monosyllables ending in ⟦b:b⟧, ⟦b:d⟧, ⟦b:m⟧, and ⟦b:t⟧: as, ⟦b:ab⟧, ⟦b:ad⟧, ⟦b:dum⟧, ⟦b:dat⟧.
⟦#2433⟧
(b.) The indefinite ⟦b:qua⟧, N. and Ac.; the enclitics ⟦b:-que⟧ (rarely ⟦b:-quē⟧), ⟦b:-ne⟧, ⟦b:-ve⟧, ⟦b:-ce⟧; and in the words ⟦b:cor⟧, ⟦b:fel⟧, ⟦b:mel⟧; ⟦b:os⟧, ⟦i:bone⟧; ⟦b:ac⟧, ⟦b:vir⟧, ⟦b:is⟧, ⟦b:pol⟧, ⟦b:quis⟧ (N.); ⟦b:fac⟧, ⟦b:fer⟧, ⟦b:per⟧, ⟦b:ter⟧; ⟦b:an⟧, ⟦b:bis⟧, ⟦b:in⟧, ⟦b:cis⟧; ⟦b:nec⟧, ⟦b:vel⟧. N. ⟦b:hīc⟧ is rarely short (⟦r664:664⟧). For the quantity of ⟦b:es⟧, see ⟦r747:747⟧.

title: Penults
text:
⟦#2434⟧
Disyllabic perfects and perfect participles have the vowel of the penult long when it stands before a single consonant: as,
⟦b:vēnī⟧, ⟦b:vīdī⟧, ⟦b:vīcī⟧ (⟦r862:862⟧); ⟦b:fōvī⟧ (⟦r864:864⟧), ⟦b:fōtus⟧ (⟦r917:917⟧).

title: Prosody: Exceptions
text:
⟦#2435⟧
(a.) Nine perfects have the penult short (⟦r859:859-861⟧):
⟦b:bibī⟧, ⟦b:-fidī⟧
⟦b:dedī⟧, ⟦b:scidī⟧
⟦b:stetī⟧, ⟦b:stitī⟧
⟦b:tulī⟧, ⟦b:-tudī⟧, ⟦b:per-culī⟧.
⟦#2436⟧
(b.) Ten perfect participles have the penult short (⟦r918:918⟧; see also ⟦r919:919⟧):
⟦b:citus⟧, ⟦b:datus⟧
⟦b:itum⟧, ⟦b:ratus⟧
⟦b:-rutus⟧, ⟦b:satus⟧
⟦b:situs⟧, ⟦b:status⟧
⟦b:litus⟧, ⟦b:quitus⟧.

title: Ending in a Vowel
text:
⟦#2437⟧
In words of more than one syllable, final ⟦b:a⟧ and ⟦b:e⟧ are short; final ⟦b:o⟧, ⟦b:u⟧, and ⟦b:i⟧, are long: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) N. ⟦b:aquila⟧; Pl. N. and Ac. ⟦b:oppida⟧, ⟦b:cētera⟧, ⟦b:omnia⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) N. ⟦b:ille⟧; N. and Ac. ⟦b:rēte⟧; ⟦b:impūne⟧ (⟦r701:701⟧); V. ⟦b:bone⟧; Ab. ⟦b:tempore⟧; Inf. ⟦b:prōmere⟧; Imperat. ⟦b:rege⟧ (⟦r826:826⟧); Pres. Ind. and Imperat. ⟦b:querere⟧; Perf. ⟦b:rēxēre⟧.
(⟦i:c.⟧) N. ⟦b:sermō⟧; D. and Ab. ⟦b:verbō⟧; ⟦b:vērō⟧ (⟦r704:704⟧). ⟦b:iō⟧. ⟦b:regō⟧, ⟦b:erō⟧, ⟦b:amābō⟧, ⟦b:rēxerō⟧ (⟦r826:826⟧); ⟦b:estō⟧.
(⟦i:d.⟧) N. and Ac. ⟦b:cornū⟧ (⟦r587:587⟧); D. and Ab. ⟦b:metū⟧ (590, 425, ⟦r593:593⟧); ⟦b:diū⟧.
(⟦i:e.⟧) G. ⟦b:frūmentī⟧; V. ⟦b:Vergilī⟧ (⟦r459:459⟧); G. ⟦b:domī⟧ (⟦r594:594⟧); D. ⟦b:nūllī⟧, ⟦b:orbī⟧; Ab. ⟦b:sitī⟧ (⟦r554:554⟧). Imperat. ⟦b:vestī⟧ (⟦r845:845⟧). Inf. ⟦b:querī⟧, ⟦b:locārī⟧; Ind. Perf. ⟦b:rēxī⟧ (⟦r856:856⟧), ⟦b:rēxistī⟧.

title: Exceptions in a
text:
⟦#2438⟧
(a.) Final ⟦b:a⟧ is long in the ablative, in indeclinable words, and in the imperative: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) Ab. ⟦b:mēnsā⟧ (⟦r426:426⟧).
(⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:quadrāgintā⟧; many indeclinable words are ablatives: as, ⟦b:contrā⟧, ⟦b:iūxtā⟧, (⟦r707:707⟧). The indeclinable ⟦b:heia⟧, ⟦b:ita⟧, and ⟦b:quia⟧ (⟦r701:701⟧), have short ⟦b:a⟧.
(⟦i:c.⟧) Imperat. ⟦b:locā⟧ (⟦r845:845⟧). But ⟦b:puta⟧, ⟦i:for instance⟧, has short ⟦b:a⟧ (⟦r130:130, 4⟧).
⟦#2439⟧
(b.) Final ⟦b:a⟧ is long in some Greek nominatives and vocatives: as, N. ⟦b:Ēlectrā⟧; V. ⟦b:Aenēā⟧, ⟦b:Pallā⟧.

title: Exceptions in e
text:
⟦#2440⟧
(a.) Final ⟦b:e⟧ is long in cases of nouns with stems in ⟦b:-ē-⟧ (⟦r596:596⟧), in adverbs from stems in ⟦b:-o-⟧, and in the imperative singular active of verbs in ⟦b:-ēre⟧: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) ⟦b:diē⟧ (G., D., or Ab.), ⟦b:hodiē⟧, ⟦b:prīdiē⟧; see also ⟦r603:603⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) ⟦b:altē⟧ (⟦r705:705⟧); also ⟦b:ferē⟧, ⟦b:fermē⟧ and ⟦b:ohē⟧ or ⟦b:ōhē⟧; but ⟦b:e⟧ is always short in ⟦b:bene⟧ and ⟦b:male⟧; ⟦b:īnferne⟧ and ⟦b:superne⟧.
(⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:docē⟧ (⟦r845:845⟧); for ⟦b:cave⟧, see 130, 4.
⟦#2441⟧
(b.) Final ⟦b:e⟧ is long in the endings of some Greek nouns: as, N. ⟦b:crambē⟧, ⟦b:Circē⟧; V. ⟦b:Alcīdē⟧; Ne. Pl. N. and Ac. ⟦b:cētē⟧, ⟦b:melē⟧, ⟦b:pelagē⟧, ⟦b:tempē⟧.

title: Exceptions in o
text:
⟦#2442⟧
(a.) Final ⟦b:o⟧ is short in the nominatives ⟦b:ego⟧, ⟦b:duo⟧. It is sometimes shortened in ⟦b:homo⟧ (⟦r130:130, 3⟧) and in the nominative of other stems in ⟦b:-n-⟧ (⟦r484:484⟧, ⟦r485:485⟧): as, ⟦b:mentio⟧, ⟦b:Nāso⟧, ⟦b:virgo⟧. ⟦b:o⟧ is regularly short in ⟦b:endo⟧, in the ablatives ⟦b:cito⟧ and ⟦b:modo⟧, used as adverbs, and in many other words in late poetry: as, ⟦b:īlico⟧, ⟦b:immo⟧, ⟦b:ergo⟧, ⟦b:quando⟧, ⟦b:octo⟧, &c.; very rarely in the ablative of the gerund.
⟦#2443⟧
(b.) Before Ovid, ⟦b:o⟧ of the present indicative is regularly long. It is shortened only in the following words (⟦r130:130, 3⟧): in
⟦b:volo⟧, six times (Cat., 4 times; Hor., Prop.).
⟦b:scio⟧, twice (Verg.).
⟦b:nescio⟧, six times (Verg., twice; Hor., twice; Tib., Prop.);
and once each in ⟦b:eo⟧ and ⟦b:veto⟧ (Hor.), ⟦b:dēsino⟧ (Tib.), and ⟦b:findo⟧ (Prop.). From Ovid on, short ⟦b:o⟧ is not uncommon.
Short ⟦b:o⟧ in other forms of the verb is rare: as, ⟦b:dīxero⟧ (Hor.); ⟦b:esto⟧, ⟦b:ero⟧, ⟦b:dabo⟧ (Ov.); but ⟦b:o⟧ is always short in the imperative ⟦b:cedo⟧, ⟦i:give⟧, ⟦i:tell⟧.
⟦#2444⟧
Final ⟦b:u⟧ is short in ⟦b:indu⟧ and ⟦b:noenu⟧.

title: Exceptions in i
text:
⟦#2445⟧
(a.) Final ⟦b:i⟧ is short in ⟦b:nisi⟧, ⟦b:quasi⟧, and ⟦b:sīcuti⟧; also in the endings of some Greek nouns: as N. and Ac. ⟦b:sināpi⟧; V. ⟦b:Pari⟧, ⟦b:Amarylli⟧; D. ⟦b:Paridi⟧, ⟦b:Minōidi⟧; Pl. D. ⟦b:Trōasi⟧.
⟦#2446⟧
(b.) Final ⟦b:i⟧ is common in ⟦b:mihī̆⟧, ⟦b:tibī̆⟧, ⟦b:sibī̆⟧; ⟦b:ibī̆⟧, ⟦b:ubī̆⟧ (⟦r129:129, 2⟧).

title: Ending in a Single Consonant not s
text:
⟦#2447⟧
A final syllable ending in a single consonant not ⟦b:s⟧ has its vowel short: as,
⟦b:dōnec⟧. ⟦b:illud⟧. ⟦b:animal⟧ (⟦r536:536⟧); ⟦b:semel⟧. ⟦b:agmen⟧. ⟦b:calcar⟧ (⟦r537:537⟧); ⟦b:soror⟧, ⟦b:stultior⟧ (⟦r132:132⟧). ⟦b:moror⟧, ⟦b:loquar⟧, ⟦b:fatēbor⟧ (⟦r132:132⟧); ⟦b:regitur⟧, ⟦b:regimur⟧, ⟦b:reguntur⟧. ⟦b:regit⟧ (⟦r826:826⟧); ⟦b:amat⟧, ⟦b:sciat⟧, ⟦b:pōnēbat⟧; ⟦b:tinnit⟧, ⟦b:possit⟧; ⟦b:iacet⟧, ⟦b:neget⟧, ⟦b:esset⟧ (⟦r132:132⟧).

title: Appendix: Exceptions
text:
⟦#2448⟧
(a.) The last vowel is long in ⟦b:allēc⟧, and in compounds of ⟦b:pār⟧; in the contracted genitive plural of stems in ⟦b:-u-⟧: as ⟦b:currūm⟧; in all cases of ⟦b:illic⟧ and ⟦b:istic⟧ except the nominative masculine, in the adverbs ⟦b:illūc⟧ and ⟦b:istūc⟧, and sometimes in ⟦b:nihī̆l⟧. Also in the endings of some Greek nouns: as, N. ⟦b:āēr⟧, ⟦b:aethēr⟧, ⟦b:sīrēn⟧; Ac. ⟦b:Aenēān⟧.
⟦#2449⟧
(b.) In the short form of the genitive plural of stems in ⟦b:-o-⟧ and ⟦b:-ā-⟧, the vowel was originally long, but afterwards short: as, ⟦b:dīvŏ̄m⟧ (⟦r462:462⟧), ⟦b:caelicolū̆m⟧ (⟦r439:439⟧).
⟦#2450⟧
(c.) The last vowel is long in ⟦b:iīt⟧ and ⟦b:petiīt⟧ and their compounds.

title: Ending in s
text:
⟦#2451⟧
Final syllables in ⟦b:is⟧ and ⟦b:us⟧ have the vowel short; those in ⟦b:as⟧, ⟦b:es⟧, and ⟦b:os⟧, have the vowel long: as,
(⟦i:a.⟧) N. ⟦b:lapis⟧, ⟦b:fīnis⟧; G. ⟦b:lapidis⟧, ⟦b:fīnis⟧; ⟦b:magis⟧. Indic. Pres. ⟦b:regis⟧ (⟦r826:826⟧); Fut. ⟦b:eris⟧ (⟦r851:851⟧, ⟦r826:826⟧), ⟦b:eritis⟧, ⟦b:locābis⟧ (⟦r853:853⟧, ⟦r826:826⟧), ⟦b:locābitis⟧.
(⟦i:b.⟧) N. ⟦b:dominus⟧; ⟦b:currus⟧; N. and Ac. ⟦b:tempus⟧; ⟦b:prius⟧; ⟦b:rēgibus⟧; ⟦b:īmus⟧; ⟦b:regimus⟧.
(⟦i:c.⟧) ⟦b:aetās⟧; Pl. Ac. ⟦b:mēnsās⟧ (⟦r424:424⟧). Indic. Pres. ⟦b:locās⟧ (⟦r840:840⟧); Imp. ⟦b:erās⟧ (⟦r848:848⟧); ⟦b:regēbās⟧ (⟦r847:847⟧); Plup. ⟦b:rēxerās⟧ (⟦r880:880⟧); Subj. Pres. ⟦b:regās⟧, ⟦b:vestiās⟧, ⟦b:doceās⟧ (⟦r842:842⟧).
(⟦i:d.⟧) N. ⟦b:hērēs⟧; ⟦b:sēdēs⟧; ⟦b:nūbēs⟧; ⟦b:Cerēs⟧; ⟦b:fidēs⟧; Pl. N. and Ac. ⟦b:rēgēs⟧ (⟦r424:424⟧); Indic. Pres. ⟦b:docēs⟧ (⟦r840:840⟧); Fut. ⟦b:regēs⟧ (⟦r852:852⟧); Subj. Pres. ⟦b:siēs⟧ (⟦r841:841⟧); ⟦b:locēs⟧ (⟦r843:843⟧); Imp. ⟦b:essēs⟧ (⟦r850:850⟧); ⟦b:regerēs⟧ (⟦r849:849⟧); Plup. ⟦b:rēxissēs⟧ (⟦r881:881⟧).
(⟦i:e.⟧) N. ⟦b:custōs⟧; ⟦b:arbōs⟧; Pl. Ac. ⟦b:ventōs⟧ (⟦r424:424⟧).

title: Exceptions in is
text:
⟦#2452⟧
(a.) Final ⟦b:is⟧ has ⟦b:ī⟧ in all plural cases: as,
N. and Ac. ⟦b:omnīs⟧; D. and Ab. ⟦b:viīs⟧, ⟦b:locīs⟧ (108, ⟦i:a⟧), ⟦b:vōbīs⟧. Also in the nominatives singular ⟦b:Quirīs⟧ and ⟦b:Samnīs⟧, usually in ⟦b:sanguī̆s⟧ (⟦r486:486⟧), and twice in ⟦b:pulvī̆s⟧.
⟦#2453⟧
(b.) Final ⟦b:is⟧ has ⟦b:ī⟧ in the second person singular of verbs in ⟦b:-īre⟧, in ⟦b:māvīs⟧, in compounds of ⟦b:sīs⟧, and in all present subjunctives singular: as, ⟦b:duīs⟧, ⟦b:edīs⟧, ⟦b:velīs⟧, ⟦b:mālīs⟧, ⟦b:nōlīs⟧. For ⟦b:-rī̆s⟧ of the perfect subjunctive and the future perfect, see ⟦r877:877⟧, ⟦r878:878⟧, ⟦r883:883⟧, ⟦r884:884⟧.

title: Exceptions in us
text:
⟦#2454⟧
⟦b:u⟧ is long in the nominative singular of consonant stems with ⟦b:ū⟧ before the final stem consonant: as, ⟦b:tellūs⟧, stem ⟦b:tellūr-⟧; ⟦b:palūs⟧, once ⟦b:palus⟧ (Hor.), stem ⟦b:palūd-⟧; in the genitive singular and nominative and accusative plural of nouns with stems in ⟦b:-u-⟧: as, ⟦b:frūctūs⟧; and in the ending of some Greek names: as, N. ⟦b:Panthūs⟧; G. ⟦b:Sapphūs⟧.
⟦#2455⟧
Final ⟦b:as⟧ has short ⟦b:a⟧ in ⟦b:anas⟧ and in the ending of some Greek nouns: as, N. ⟦b:Īlias⟧; Pl. Ac. ⟦b:cratēras⟧.

title: Exceptions in es
text:
⟦#2456⟧
Final ⟦b:es⟧ has short ⟦b:e⟧ in the nominative singular of stems in ⟦b:-d-⟧ and ⟦b:-t-⟧ which have the genitive in ⟦b:-idis⟧, ⟦b:-itis⟧, and ⟦b:-etis⟧ (⟦r475:475⟧, ⟦r476:476⟧): as, ⟦b:praeses⟧, ⟦b:teges⟧, ⟦b:comes⟧ (but ⟦b:ē⟧ in ⟦b:abiēs⟧, ⟦b:ariēs⟧, and ⟦b:pariēs⟧), also, in ⟦b:penes⟧, in compounds of ⟦b:es⟧, ⟦i:thou art⟧, and in the endings of some Greek nouns: as, N. ⟦b:Cynosarges⟧; Pl. N. ⟦b:Arcades⟧, ⟦b:cratēres⟧.

title: Exceptions in os
text:
⟦#2457⟧
Final ⟦b:os⟧ has short ⟦b:o⟧ in the nominative of stems in ⟦b:-o-⟧: as, ⟦b:servos⟧, ⟦b:suos⟧, ⟦b:Dēlos⟧; also in ⟦b:compos⟧, ⟦b:impos⟧, and ⟦b:exos⟧; and in the endings of some Greek nouns: as, N. and Ac. ⟦b:epos⟧; G. ⟦b:chlamydos⟧, ⟦b:Erīnyos⟧.

title: Position
text:
⟦#2458⟧
For the general rule of position, see ⟦r177:177⟧, ⟦r178:178⟧; but, except in the thesis of a foot, a final syllable ending with a short vowel generally remains short before a word beginning with two consonants or a double consonant: as, ⟦b:molliă strāta⟧, ⟦b:nemorōsă Zacȳnthos⟧, ⟦b:lūcĕ smaragdī⟧.
In Horace such a final syllable is never lengthened before a word beginning with two consonants.

title: Hidden Quantity
text:
⟦#2459⟧
A vowel which stands before two consonants, or a double consonant, belonging to the same word, so that its natural quantity cannot be determined from the scansion of the word, is said to possess ⟦i:Hidden Quantity⟧.
⟦#2460⟧
The natural quantity of such a vowel may sometimes be ascertained: (⟦i:a.⟧) from the statements of ancient writers; (⟦i:b.⟧) from the way in which the vowel is written in Latin inscriptions (see ⟦r24:24⟧, 29); (⟦i:c.⟧) from the transliteration of the word into other languages, especially Greek; (⟦i:d.⟧) from the etymology of the word, or from a comparison of it with kindred words in other Indo-European languages; (⟦i:e.⟧) from comparison with derived words in the Romance languages. But all these kinds of evidence must be used with great caution.
⟦#2461⟧
For the length of a vowel before ⟦b:ns⟧, ⟦b:nf⟧, and certain other groups of consonants, see ⟦r122:122⟧.
⟦#2462⟧
In inceptive verbs (⟦r834:834⟧) the ending ⟦b:-scō⟧ is thought to be always preceded by a long vowel: as, ⟦b:crēscō⟧, ⟦b:nāscor⟧, ⟦b:proficīscor⟧.
⟦#2463⟧
In the perfect indicative active, perfect participle passive and kindred formations of verbs in ⟦b:-gō⟧ preceded by a short vowel, as ⟦b:agō⟧, ⟦b:regō⟧, the theme syllable shows a long vowel: as, ⟦b:lēxī⟧, ⟦b:rēxī⟧, ⟦b:tēxī⟧; ⟦b:āctus⟧, ⟦b:lēctus⟧; ⟦b:rēctor⟧; ⟦b:āctitō⟧.

title: Some Peculiarities of Quantity in Old Latin
text:
⟦#2464⟧
For the preservation of a long vowel in certain specific endings in old Latin, see ⟦r132:132⟧.
⟦#2465⟧
Final ⟦b:-āl⟧ is sometimes preserved long in the nominative singular: as, ⟦b:bacchānāl⟧ (Plaut.); also the syllable ⟦b:-es⟧ in the nominative singular of stems in ⟦b:-t-⟧ which have the genitive in ⟦b:-itis⟧ (⟦r477:477⟧): as ⟦b:mīlēs⟧ (Plaut.) 171, 1.
⟦#2466⟧
⟦b:Hic⟧, ⟦b:illic⟧ and ⟦b:istic⟧, when adverbs, have a long final syllable; but when nominative singular masculine, have the final syllable regularly short.
⟦#2467⟧
In Plautus ⟦b:frūstrā⟧ always where determinable (seven times) has the final syllable short. ⟦b:contrā⟧ sometimes has a short final syllable in old Latin.
⟦#2468⟧
In Latin poetry down to the time of Cicero, final ⟦b:s⟧ often does not “make position” before a following consonant (⟦r66:66⟧); as, ⟦b:tempŭs fert⟧ (Plaut.); ⟦b:magĭs stetisse⟧ (Ter.).
⟦#2469⟧
The first syllable of ⟦b:ille⟧, ⟦b:illic⟧ (the pronoun), ⟦b:quippe⟧, ⟦b:immō⟧, ⟦b:inde⟧, ⟦b:unde⟧, ⟦b:nempe⟧, ⟦b:omnis⟧, and perhaps ⟦b:iste⟧, is sometimes shortened.
In ⟦b:ille⟧, ⟦b:illic⟧, ⟦b:quippe⟧, and ⟦b:immō⟧ the shortening is, some hold, due to the fact that in common speech one of the double consonants was often pronounced faintly or not at all; while in ⟦b:inde⟧, ⟦b:unde⟧, ⟦b:nempe⟧, and ⟦b:omnis⟧ the nasal was very faintly sounded before the following consonant. But some authorities hold that always in ⟦b:nempe⟧, and sometimes in ⟦b:ille⟧, ⟦b:quippe⟧, ⟦b:inde⟧, ⟦b:unde⟧, and perhaps ⟦b:iste⟧, before an initial consonant final ⟦b:e⟧ disappears, and the word becomes a monosyllable.

title: Law of Iambic Shortening
text:
⟦#2470⟧
A long syllable, preceded by a short monosyllable or by a short initial syllable, and immediately preceded or followed by the verse-ictus, may be shortened: as, ⟦b:ét hŭnc⟧, ⟦b:dómŏ mē⟧, ⟦b:ad ŭxṓrem⟧, ⟦b:volŭntā́te⟧.
The short monosyllable may be a word which has become monosyllabic by elision: as, ⟦b:ég(o) hănc⟧.
⟦#2471⟧
If the syllable to be shortened is the first of a word of more than one syllable, or the second of a polysyllable, it must be one which is long by position, not by nature. There are some possible exceptions to this rule, such as ⟦b:verĕbā́minī⟧ (T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 902); but these are few and doubtful.
⟦#2472⟧
Iambic shortening took place not only in verse, but also to a considerable extent in common speech, particularly in iambic words (see ⟦r130:130⟧), in which the accent coöperated with the verse-ictus to produce the shortening.

title: Hiatus
text:
⟦#2473⟧
For hiatus within a word, and the means by which it is avoided, see ⟦r114:114-120⟧.
⟦#2474⟧
Hiatus between two words is much more common in old Latin than in writers of the classical period. The precise extent to which it is allowed by the early dramatists is matter of dispute. The following cases may be mentioned in which the Latin poets admit hiatus:
⟦#2475⟧
(1.) After interjections: as, ⟦b:hahahae homo⟧, T. ⟦i:Ph.⟧ 411; ⟦b:ō et praesidium⟧, H. 1, 1, 2.
⟦#2476⟧
(2.) After proper names, and words of Greek origin: as, ⟦b:ancillam ferre Venerī aut Cupīdinī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:As.⟧ 804; ⟦b:Thrēiciō Aquilōne⟧, H. ⟦i:Epod.⟧ 13, 3.
⟦#2477⟧
(3.) In the principal caesura of a verse. So especially in Plautus and Terence after the fourth foot of the iambic septenarius, and in Plautus in the principal break in the iambic octonarius, trochaic septenarius and trochaic octonarius.
⟦#2478⟧
(4.) Often in the dramatists where there is a change of speakers: as, ⟦b:quī potuit vidēre? :: oculīs :: quō pactō? :: hiantibus⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Merc.⟧ 182.
⟦#2479⟧
(5.) Probably sometimes in cases of repetition, enumeration, or sharp antithesis, and where there is an important pause in the sense: as, ⟦b:eam volt meretrīcem facere: ea mē dēperit⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cur.⟧ 46; ⟦b:sī pereō, hominum manibus periisse iuvābit⟧, V. 3, 606.
⟦#2480⟧
Vergil sometimes admits hiatus when the final syllable ending in a vowel is preceded or followed (or both) by two short syllables: as, ⟦b:lāmentīs gemitūque et fēmĭnĕō ŭlŭlātū⟧, V. 4, 667.

title: Elision
text:
⟦#2481⟧
For elision within a word, see ⟦r119:119⟧.
⟦#2482⟧
In verse a final vowel is generally elided before a vowel or ⟦b:h⟧: as,
⟦b:quidve moror, s(ī) omnīs ūn(ō) ōrdin(e) habētis Achīvōs⟧, V. 2, 102. Such a vowel was probably faintly sounded, not dropped altogether.
⟦#2483⟧
Elision is frequent in most of the early poets; but writers of the Augustan and succeeding ages regarded it with increasing disfavour. The elision of a long vowel before a short was in general avoided; but there are numerous exceptions.
⟦#2484⟧
Monosyllabic interjections do not suffer elision.
⟦#2485⟧
Monosyllables ending in a diphthong seldom suffer elision before a short vowel.
⟦#2486⟧
Diphthongs arising from Synizesis (⟦r2499:2499⟧) are sometimes elided in early Latin verse, but not in verse of the classical period.
⟦#2487⟧
The monosyllables ⟦b:quī⟧ (plural), ⟦b:dō⟧, ⟦b:stō⟧, ⟦b:rē⟧, ⟦b:spē⟧, are thought never to suffer elision before a short vowel.
⟦#2488⟧
The dactylic poets very rarely elide the final syllable of an iambic (⏑ –) or Cretic (– ⏑ –) word before a short vowel.
⟦#2489⟧
Elision seldom occurs if the syllable to be elided is immediately preceded by a vowel: as in ⟦b:de(am) et⟧.
⟦#2490⟧
The final syllable of a Greek word is rarely elided.
⟦#2491⟧
Elision is more common toward the beginning of a verse than toward the end.
⟦#2492⟧
Elision rarely occurs in the first syllable or last syllable of a verse; but see under Synapheia (⟦r2510:2510⟧), and for the elision of the enclitic ⟦b:-que⟧ or ⟦b:-ve⟧ at the end of a dactylic hexameter, see ⟦r2568:2568⟧.
⟦#2493⟧
Ecthlipsis (Gr. ἔκθλιψις, ⟦i:a squeezing out⟧). Final ⟦b:m⟧ and a preceding short vowel are usually elided before a vowel or ⟦b:h⟧: as,
⟦b:mōnstr(um) horrend(um) īnform(e) ingēns, cui lūmen ademptum⟧, V. 3, 658.
In such cases the ending was probably not cut off altogether, but was given a faint nasal sound.
⟦#2494⟧
Sometimes a monosyllable ending in a short vowel and ⟦b:m⟧ is not elided before a vowel: as ⟦b:quắm ego⟧ (Ter.); ⟦b:súnt cŭm odōre⟧ (Lucr.).
Such unelided monosyllables are most frequent in the early dramatists, and in them usually fall under the verse-ictus. See ⟦r61:61⟧.
⟦#2495⟧
The monosyllables ⟦b:dem⟧, ⟦b:stem⟧, ⟦b:rem⟧, ⟦b:spem⟧, ⟦b:sim⟧, are thought never to be elided before a short vowel.
⟦#2496⟧
After a word ending with a vowel, ⟦b:-m⟧, or ⟦b:-us⟧, the verb ⟦b:est⟧ often loses its ⟦b:e⟧: as, ⟦b:bonast⟧, ⟦b:bonumst⟧, ⟦b:bonust⟧, ⟦b:vīsust⟧. So, too, ⟦b:es⟧ sometimes loses its vowel: as ⟦b:homo’s⟧, ⟦b:adeptus’⟧. This usage reflects the actual pronunciation of common speech.
⟦#2497⟧
Semi-hiatus or Semi-elision. A long final vowel is sometimes shortened before a vowel. This may occur either in the arsis (⟦r2520:2520⟧), or in a resolved thesis: as, ⟦b:án quĭ amant⟧ (Verg.); ⟦b:léctulŏ ērudītulī⟧ (Cat.); ⟦b:nam quĭ́ aget⟧ (Ter.).
This kind of shortening is not frequent except in the early dramatists, who often shorten under the verse-ictus a monosyllable ending in a long vowel and followed by an initial vowel (as in the third example above).
⟦#2498⟧
Synaloepha (Greek συναλοιφή, ⟦i:a smearing together⟧) is a general term used to denote the means of avoiding hiatus. It includes elision and synizesis, though some grammarians use it in the same sense as synizesis.
⟦#2499⟧
⟦b:Synizesis⟧ (Greek συνίζεσις, ⟦i:a settling together⟧). Two vowels (or a vowel and a diphthong) which belong to different syllables sometimes coalesce so as to form one syllable. This is called ⟦i:Synizesis⟧, and is especially common in the early dramatists. Examples are: ⟦b:me͡o⟧, ⟦b:e͡adem⟧, ⟦b:cu͡ius⟧, ⟦b:aure͡i⟧. See ⟦r117:117⟧.
Some grammarians would include under Synizesis only cases in which a short vowel is subordinated to a following long; as ⟦b:tu͡o⟧.
⟦#2500⟧
The term ⟦i:Synaeresis⟧ (Greek συναίρεσις, ⟦i:a taking together⟧) is sometimes used as a synonym for Synizesis. The ancient grammarians, however, used it in the sense of Contraction (⟦r118:118⟧).
⟦#2501⟧
Dialysis (Greek διάλυσις, ⟦i:a breaking up⟧). Conversely, two vowels which usually form a diphthong are sometimes separated so as to form two syllables: as ⟦b:coëpī⟧ (Lucr.) for ⟦b:coepī⟧.
This, however, is really the survival of the original forms (⟦r120:120⟧).
⟦#2502⟧
The name Diaeresis (Greek διαίρεσις, ⟦i:a separating⟧) is sometimes used as a synonym for Dialysis; but it is better to restrict it to the meaning defined in 2542.
⟦#2503⟧
Hardening. A vocalic ⟦b:i⟧ or ⟦b:u⟧ is sometimes made consonantal before another vowel: as, ⟦b:abi͡ete⟧, ⟦b:ari͡ete⟧ (Verg.); ⟦b:cōnsili͡um⟧ (Hor.); ⟦b:omni͡a⟧ (Lucr.). See ⟦r117:117⟧ and ⟦r83:83⟧.
This usage is sometimes included under Synizesis (⟦r2499:2499⟧), while some grammarians term it Synaeresis (⟦r2500:2500⟧).
⟦#2504⟧
Softening. Conversely, a consonantal ⟦b:i⟧ or ⟦b:u⟧ sometimes becomes vocalized before a vowel, thus giving an additional syllable: as, ⟦b:silüae⟧ for ⟦b:silvae⟧ (Hor.); ⟦b:ēvolüisse⟧ for ⟦b:ēvolvisse⟧ (Ov.). See ⟦r52:52⟧.
This usage is sometimes included under the name Dialysis (⟦r2501:2501⟧).
⟦#2505⟧
Diastolé (Greek διαστολή, ⟦i:a drawing asunder⟧). A syllable which in verse of the classical period is generally short is sometimes used as long for metrical convenience. The syllable so employed generally falls under the verse-ictus, and in most cases is immediately followed by the principal caesura, or by a pause in the sense. Examples are:
⟦b:terga fatīgāmūs hastā, nec tarda senectus⟧, V. 9, 610.
⟦b:tum sīc Mercurium adloquitūr ac tālia mandat⟧, V. 4, 222.
⟦b:caeca timēt aliunde fāta⟧, H. 2, 13, 16.
In many such cases this lengthening is not arbitrary, but the “lengthened” syllable is one that was originally long (see ⟦r132:132⟧).
⟦#2506⟧
The enclitic ⟦b:-que⟧ is sometimes lengthened under the ictus when another ⟦b:-que⟧ precedes or follows in the arsis: as, ⟦b:cālōnēs famulīque metallīquḗ caculaeque⟧ (Accius).
⟦#2507⟧
Systolé (Greek συστολή, ⟦i:a drawing together⟧). Conversely a syllable which in verse is regularly long is sometimes shortened for metrical convenience: as, ⟦b:dedĕrunt⟧ (Hor.), ⟦b:nūllĭus⟧ (Hor.), imperat. ⟦b:commodă⟧ (Cat.).
In most cases this shortening is not arbitrary, but represents a pronunciation which was in actual use, especially among the common people.
⟦#2508⟧
Syncopé (Greek συγκοπή, ⟦i:a cutting short⟧). A short vowel is often dropped between two consonants: as, ⟦b:surpite⟧ for ⟦b:surripite⟧ (Hor.), ⟦b:repostum⟧ for ⟦b:repositum⟧ (Verg.).
This usage doubtless reflects the common pronunciation; see ⟦r110:110⟧, ⟦r111:111⟧.
⟦#2509⟧
Tmesis (Greek τμῆσις, ⟦i:a cutting⟧) is the separation of the parts of a word: as, ⟦b:septem subiecta triōnī⟧ = ⟦b:septemtriōnī subiecta⟧ (Verg.).
This usually occurs only in compounds; but early poets sometimes divided other words: as, ⟦b:saxō cere comminuit brum⟧ for ⟦b:saxō cerebrum comminuit⟧ (Ennius).
⟦#2510⟧
Synapheia (Greek συνάφεια, ⟦i:a joining together⟧) is the linking together of two verses belonging to the same system. Here elision or word division may occur at the end of the first verse: as,
⟦b:Iōve nōn probante u-⟧
⟦b:xōrius amnis⟧, H. 1, 2, 19.
⟦b:Iam licet veniās marīt(e),⟧
⟦b:uxor in thalamō tibī̆ est⟧, Cat. 61, 191.

title: Versification: By Herman W. Hayley, Ph.D
text:
⟦#2511⟧
Rhythm (Gr. ῥυθμός, from ῥεῖν, ⟦i:to flow⟧) is the effect of regularity produced by the discrimination of a movement or sound into uniform intervals of time. It is often marked by a stress or ⟦i:ictus⟧ recurring at fixed intervals.
Rhythm is by no means confined to verse. Music, dancing, and even the regular beat of a trip-hammer, have rhythm. Particular kinds of movement are often called rhythms, as anapaestic rhythms, dactylic rhythms, &c.
⟦#2512⟧
Metre (Gr. μέτρον, ⟦i:a measure⟧) is the definite measurement of verse by feet, lines, strophes, systems, &c.
⟦#2513⟧
Latin verse is quantitative, the rhythm depending upon the quantity of the syllables (but see ⟦r2548:2548⟧). The ictus naturally falls upon a long syllable (or its equivalent). English verse, on the other hand, is accentual, its rhythm depending upon the accent of words.

title: Quantity
text:
⟦#2514⟧
Signs of Quantity. A long syllable is indicated by –, a short one by ⏑. A syllable which varies in quantity, being sometimes long, sometimes short, is indicated by ⏓ or ⏒.
In the following metrical schemes, ⏓ indicates that the long is more usual or more strictly in accordance with the rhythm than the short. The reverse is indicated by ⏒.
⟦#2515⟧
The Unit of Measure is the duration of a short syllable and is called a ⟦i:Time⟧, ⟦i:Tempus⟧, or ⟦i:Mora⟧. The ⟦i:mora⟧ did not have an absolute length, but varied with the nature of the rhythm. For greater convenience, however, it is assumed that its length was uniform, and equalled that of an eighth note ♪ A long syllable, being equal to two shorts, has a length of two ⟦i:morae⟧, which is assumed to be the same as that of our quarter-note ♩ Hence in notation ⏑ = ♪ and – = ♩
⟦#2516⟧
Protraction. A long syllable may be prolonged (⟦i:Protraction⟧) so as to have a length of three ⟦i:morae⟧, in which case it is called a ⟦i:triseme⟧ (marked ⏗), or of four ⟦i:morae⟧, when it is termed a ⟦i:tetraseme⟧ (marked ⏘). See ⟦r2537:2537⟧ and ⟦r2541:2541⟧.
⟦#2517⟧
Correption. A long or short syllable may be shortened so as to occupy less than its normal time. This is called ⟦i:Correption⟧ (Lat. ⟦i:correptiō⟧, ⟦i:a shortening⟧). See ⟦r2523:2523⟧ and ⟦r2524:2524⟧.
⟦#2518⟧
Resolution and Contraction. In some kinds of verse a long syllable may be, as it were, broken up (⟦i:Resolution⟧) into the equivalent two shorts; and conversely two short syllables may in some cases be united (⟦i:Contraction⟧) into the equivalent long.

title: Feet
text:
⟦#2519⟧
Feet. Latin verse (like English) is measured by groups of syllables called ⟦i:Feet⟧. Each of these groups has a definite length of so many ⟦i:morae⟧ (⟦r2515:2515⟧).
It is theoretically more accurate to make the foot purely a time-division, as some authorities do; but the definition given above is sanctioned by established usage.
⟦#2520⟧
Arsis and Thesis. Every complete foot consists of two parts, an accented and an unaccented. The part on which the rhythmical accent or ⟦i:ictus⟧ falls is called the ⟦i:Thesis⟧ (Gr. θέσις, ⟦i:a setting down⟧). The unaccented part of the foot is termed the ⟦i:Arsis⟧ (Gr. ἄρσις, ⟦i:a raising⟧).
The name ⟦i:Thesis⟧ originally referred to the setting down of the foot in beating time or marching, or to the movement of the leader’s hand in making the downward beat; and ⟦i:Arsis⟧ in like manner meant the raising of the foot or hand. But the Roman grammarians misunderstood the Greek terms, supposing them to refer to the lowering and raising of the voice, and so interchanged them. Hence many modern writers prefer to use ⟦i:Arsis⟧ to denote the accented, and ⟦i:Thesis⟧ the unaccented, part of the foot.

text:

But these are of little practical importance, as most of them never are employed in Latin poetry, and the few which do occur are used only as substitutes for other feet.

title: Cyclic Feet
text:
⟦#2523⟧
A dactyl occurring in 3/8 time did not have the value of 2 ⟦i:morae⟧ + 1 + 1, but was given instead that of 1½ + ¾ + ¾; in other words both arsis and thesis suffered correption (⟦r2517:2517⟧), but the ratio between them remained unchanged. Such a dactyl is called ⟦i:cyclic⟧, and is marked – ⏖, or musically There is also a ⟦i:cyclic anapaest⟧, marked ⏖ – or
Some scholars, however, hold that the cyclic dactyl had approximately the value 1½ + ½ + 1, or , and mark it –⏑ ⏑. In like manner they mark the cyclic anapaest ⏑ ⏑–. The true nature of these cyclic feet is very uncertain.

title: Irrational Syllables and Feet
text:
⟦#2524⟧
A long syllable sometimes stands in place of a short. A syllable thus used is called ⟦i:irrational⟧ (marked >) because it destroys the normal ⟦b:ratio⟧ between arsis and thesis. The foot which contains such a syllable is itself called irrational. The most common irrational foot is the ⟦i:irrational spondee⟧ (– > when it stands for a trochee; >– when it replaces an iambus), which is found in iambic, trochaic, and logaoedic rhythms.
Probably the irrational long suffered a slight correption (⟦r2517:2517⟧), so that its duration was between that of the ordinary long and that of a short syllable.

title: Rhythms
text:
⟦#2525⟧
The different rhythms or metres are named trochaic, iambic, &c., according to their fundamental feet.
⟦#2526⟧
Much of the Latin poetry (though not by any means all) was written to be sung. The Greeks and Romans employed in their music not only common (or 2/4) time and triple (3/8, 3/4) time, but also 5/8 time, which last is very rarely used in modern music.
⟦#2527⟧
The Greek and Roman metricians divided the rhythms into three classes, according to the ratio between arsis and thesis in their fundamental feet. These classes were:— (⟦i:a.⟧) the ⟦i:Equal Class⟧ (γένος ἴσον, ⟦i:genus pār⟧) in which thesis and arsis are equal in duration, as in dactylics, anapaestics, &c.; (⟦i:b.⟧) the ⟦i:Double Class⟧ (γένος διπλάσιον, ⟦i:genus duplex⟧) in which the thesis has twice the duration of the arsis, as in trochaics, iambics, &c.; (⟦i:c.⟧) the ⟦i:Hemiolic Class⟧ (γένος ἡμιόλιον, ⟦i:genus sēscuplex⟧) in which the thesis has one and a half times the duration of the arsis, as in bacchiacs, cretics, etc.
⟦#2528⟧
Ascending and Descending Rhythms. Rhythms in which the thesis follows the arsis (as in iambics) are called ⟦i:ascending⟧; those in which it precedes the arsis (as in trochaics) are termed ⟦i:descending⟧.

title: Anacrusis
text:
⟦#2529⟧
The ancients recognized both ascending and descending rhythms (⟦r2528:2528⟧), and regarded the former class as at least equal in importance to the latter; but many modern scholars since the time of Bentley have preferred to treat all rhythms as descending, regarding the first arsis of an ascending rhythm as merely answering to a preliminary upward beat in music. Such an initial arsis was named by Gottfried Hermann ⟦i:Anacrūsis⟧ (Gr. ἀνάκρουσις, ⟦i:a striking up⟧).
Scholars have been influenced to adopt the anacrustic theory in its widest extent largely by the fact that in most modern music a measure must commence with a downward beat, a rule which did not hold in ancient music. By this theory an iambic verse becomes trochaic with anacrusis, an anapaestic verse dactylic with anacrusis, &c. But in many cases those kinds of verse which begin with an arsis were subject to different rules of construction from those which begin with a thesis. Hence it seems best to restrict anacrusis to logaoedic verse, in which it undoubtedly occurs.
⟦#2530⟧
The anacrusis may be a long syllable, a short syllable, or two shorts (but not two longs). It is often irrational (⟦r2524:2524⟧). In metrical schemes it is often set off from the rest of the verse by a vertical row of dots: thus, ⁝

title: Groups of Feet
text:
⟦#2531⟧
A group of two feet is called a ⟦i:dipody⟧, one of three a ⟦i:tripody⟧, one of four a ⟦i:tetrapody⟧, one of five a ⟦i:pentapody⟧, and one of six a ⟦i:hexapody⟧. The dipody is the measure of trochaic, iambic, and anapaestic verse. Other kinds of verse are measured by the single foot.
A single foot is sometimes called a ⟦i:monopody⟧. A group of three half feet, i.e. a foot and a half, is sometimes called a ⟦i:trithemimeris⟧, one of two and a half feet a ⟦i:penthemimeris⟧, one of three and a half a ⟦i:hephthemimeris⟧, &c.
⟦#2532⟧
A ⟦i:Rhythmical Series⟧, ⟦i:Rhythmical Sentence⟧, or ⟦i:Colon⟧ is a group of two or more feet (but not more than six) which are united into a rhythmic whole by strengthening one of the ictuses, so that it becomes the principal or dominant ictus of the whole group.
⟦#2533⟧
The Verse. A rhythmical series, or group of two (or even three) series, which forms a distinct and separate whole is called a ⟦i:Verse⟧. The final syllable of a verse must terminate a word (except in cases of synapheia, see ⟦r2510:2510⟧), and may be either long or short (whence it is termed ⟦i:syllaba anceps⟧) without regard to the rhythm. Hiatus (⟦r2474:2474⟧) is freely allowed at the end of a verse (though in rare cases elision occurs before a vowel at the beginning of the following verse; see ⟦r2492:2492⟧ and ⟦r2568:2568⟧).
A verse is generally (but not always) written as one line. Hence, the words “verse” and “line” are often used as synonyms.

title: Syllaba Anceps
text:
⟦#2534⟧
In the present work, the final syllable of each verse is marked long or short as the rhythm may require, without reference to its quantity in a given example; and in the general schemes it is to be understood that the final syllable is ⟦i:syllaba anceps⟧ (⟦r2533:2533⟧) unless the contrary is expressly stated.
⟦#2535⟧
Dicolic and Asynartetic Verses. A verse which consists of two rhythmical series (or cola) is called ⟦i:dicolic⟧. If the series of which the verse is made up are quasi-independent of each other, so that hiatus or syllaba anceps occurs in the caesura, the verse is styled ⟦i:asynartetic⟧ (Gr. ἀσυνάρτητος, ⟦i:not joined together⟧).
⟦#2536⟧
Names of Verses. Verses are called ⟦i:trochaic⟧, ⟦i:iambic⟧, ⟦i:dactylic⟧, &c., according to their fundamental (or characteristic) feet. A verse which contains one foot (or one dipody if iambic, trochaic, or anapaestic; see ⟦r2531:2531⟧) is called a ⟦i:monometer⟧, one of two a ⟦i:dimeter⟧, one of three a ⟦i:trimeter⟧, one of four a ⟦i:tetrameter⟧, one of five a ⟦i:pentameter⟧, and one of six a ⟦i:hexameter⟧.
Trochaic, iambic, and anapaestic verses are often named by Latin adjectives in ⟦i:-ārius⟧ (used as nouns) denoting the number of feet. Thus, such a verse of eight feet is called an ⟦i:octōnārius⟧, one of seven a ⟦i:septēnārius⟧, one of six a ⟦i:sēnārius⟧, &c. A short verse which is employed to close a system (⟦r2547:2547⟧), or to mark a metrical or musical transition between longer verses, is called a ⟦i:clausula⟧.

title: Catalexis, Pause, Syncope
text:
⟦#2537⟧
Catalexis. A verse, the last foot of which is incomplete, is said to suffer ⟦i:Catalexis⟧ (Gr. κατάληξις, ⟦i:a stopping short⟧) or to be ⟦i:catalectic⟧; one of which the last foot is complete is called ⟦i:acatalectic⟧.
It is usually the last part of the foot that is omitted; but (according to the theory now generally accepted) in catalectic iambic verses it is the last arsis that is omitted, the preceding thesis being protracted (⟦r2516:2516⟧) to compensate for the loss, thus: ⏑ ⏗́ –́
⟦#2538⟧
A verse in which both the last arsis and the next to the last are suppressed, so that a whole foot appears to be wanting, is called ⟦i:brachycatalectic⟧.
⟦#2539⟧
A verse is said to be catalectic ⟦i:in syllabam⟧, ⟦i:in disyllabum⟧, or ⟦i:in trisyllabum⟧, according to the number of syllables remaining in the last foot. Thus, the dactylic tetrameter – ⏑ ⏑ | – ⏑ ⏑ | – ⏑ ⏑ | – is catalectic ⟦i:in syllabam⟧, but – ⏑ ⏑ | – ⏑ ⏑ | – ⏑ ⏑ | – ⏑ is catalectic ⟦i:in disyllabum⟧.
⟦#2540⟧
Pauses. Theoretically all the feet (or dipodies; see ⟦r2531:2531⟧) into which a verse is divided must be equal in duration. Hence, when a final syllable (or two final syllables) is lost by catalexis, compensation is made for the loss by a pause at the end of the verse. Such a pause, which serves to fill out the last measure, answers to a ⟦i:rest⟧ in music.
A pause of one ⟦i:mora⟧ is often indicated by the sign ⌃, and one of two ⟦i:morae⟧ by ⌅.
⟦#2541⟧
Syncope is the omission of one or more arses in the body of a verse. Compensation is made for the suppression of an arsis by protracting (⟦r2516:2516⟧) the preceding thesis.

title: Caesura
text:
⟦#2542⟧
Caesura and Diaeresis. A ⟦i:Caesūra⟧ (literally ⟦i:a cutting⟧, from ⟦i:caedo⟧, ⟦i:I cut⟧) is the break in a verse produced by the ending of a word within a foot. When the end of a word coincides with the end of a foot, the break is called a ⟦i:Diaeresis⟧ (Gr. διαίρεσις, ⟦i:a separating⟧). A caesura is marked ‖, a diaeresis #.
The word ⟦i:caesura⟧ is often loosely used to include both caesura proper and diaeresis.
⟦#2543⟧
Strictly speaking, there is a caesura (or diaeresis, as the case may be) wherever a word ends within a verse; but the main incision in the verse is so much more important than the rest that it is often called the ⟦i:principal caesura⟧, or simply ⟦i:the caesura⟧.
⟦#2544⟧
Caesuras are named according to their position in the verse; thus a caesura after the third half-foot (i.e. in the second foot) is called ⟦i:trithemimeral⟧ (from Gr. τριθημιμερής, ⟦i:containing three halves⟧), one after the fifth half-foot (i.e. in the third foot) ⟦i:penthemimeral⟧ (Gr. πενθημιμερής, ⟦i:consisting of five halves⟧), one after the seventh half-foot (i.e. in the fourth foot) ⟦i:hephthemimeral⟧ (Gr. ἑφθημιμερής), &c.
The Latin names ⟦i:caesūra sēmiternāria⟧ (= the trithemimeral caesura), ⟦i:sēmiquīnāria⟧ (= the penthemimeral), ⟦i:sēmiseptēnāria⟧ (= the hepthemimeral), &c., are sometimes used. For the ⟦i:masculine⟧ and ⟦i:feminine⟧ caesuras, see ⟦r2557:2557⟧.

title: Strophe. System
text:
⟦#2545⟧
The Strophe. A fixed number of verses recurring in a regular order is called a ⟦i:Strophe⟧. A strophe commonly contains verses of different kinds, but some strophes are composed of verses which are all alike. The most common strophes in Latin poetry are either ⟦i:distichs⟧ (i.e. groups of two lines each), ⟦i:tristichs⟧ (of three lines each), or ⟦i:tetrastichs⟧ (of four).
Strophes and verses are frequently named after some poet who made use of them. So the Alcaic strophe (named after Alcaeus), the Sapphic strophe (named after Sappho), the Glyconic verse (named after Glycon), the Asclepiadean (after Asclepiades), the Phalaecean (after Phalaecus), the Pherecratean (after Pherecrates), &c.
⟦#2546⟧
A ⟦i:Stichic Series⟧ is a series of verses of the same kind not combined into strophes.
⟦#2547⟧
The System. A group of rhythmical series (see ⟦r2532:2532⟧) which is of greater extent than a verse is called a ⟦i:System⟧. Long systems, such as are common in Greek poetry, are comparatively rare in Latin verse.
Few verses have more than two rhythmical series; none more than three.
⟦#2548⟧
Although in all probability the Latin accent was mainly one of stress rather than of pitch, it seems to have been comparatively weak. Hence, when it conflicted with the metrical ictus, it could be the more easily disregarded. But accentual or semi-accentual poetry seems to have existed among the common people even in the Augustan age, and even in classical Latin verse in certain cases (as in the last part of the dactylic hexameter) conflict between ictus and accent was carefully avoided. After the third century A.D. the accent exerted a stronger and stronger influence upon versification, until in the Middle Ages the quantitative Latin verse was quite supplanted by the accentual.

title: Numeri Italici
text:
⟦#2549⟧
Some of the earliest remains of Latin literature are believed to show a rhythmical structure. These are chiefly prayers, imprecations, sacred songs and the like, couched in a set form of words. Of the rules according to which these ⟦b:carmina⟧ were composed, almost nothing is known. According to one theory, they are wholly accentual, and are composed of rhythmical series, each series containing four theses. Frequently an arsis is suppressed, and compensation for the omission is made by dwelling longer upon the thesis. As an example is given the prayer in Cato, ⟦i:Dē Rē Rūsticā⟧, 141:
⟦b:Mā́rs páter tḗ précor | quaésṓque útī síēs | vólēns própítiús⟧
⟦b:míhī́ dómṓ | fámiliaéque nóstraé⟧, &c.

title: The Saturnian
text:
⟦#2550⟧
The Saturnian is the best known and most important of the old Italian rhythms; but its nature long has been, and still is, matter of high dispute. There are two principal theories as to its character, the quantitative and the accentual, each of which is advocated by many distinguished scholars.
⟦#2551⟧
(1.) The Quantitative Theory. According to this theory, the Saturnian is a verse of six feet, with an anacrusis (⟦r2529:2529⟧). There is a break after the fourth arsis, or more rarely after the third thesis. Each thesis may be either a long syllable or two shorts; each arsis may be a short syllable, a long, or two shorts, but an arsis is not resolved before the principal break or at the end of the verse. Hiatus is common, especially at the principal break in the verse. A short final syllable may be lengthened by the influence of the verse-ictus. An arsis is frequently suppressed, especially the penultimate arsis. Two arses are never suppressed in the same half-verse, and rarely two in the same verse. Examples of the Saturnian, measured quantitatively, are:
⟦b:Dabúnt malúm Metéllī # Naéviṓ poḗtae.⟧
⟦b:Novém Iovís concórdēs # fī́liaé sorṓrēs.⟧ (Naevius.)
⟦b:Virúm mihī́, Camḗna, # ī́nsecḗ versū́tum.⟧ (Livius Andronicus.)
⟦b:E͡ōrúm sectám sequóntur # múltī mórtā́lēs.⟧
(Naevius.)
Compare in English: “The queén was ín the párlour, éating bréad and hóney.”
⟦#2552⟧
Most of the Roman grammarians who discussed the nature of the Saturnian seem to have regarded it as quantitative. In modern times the quantitative theory has been advocated by Ritschl, Buecheler, Havet, Christ, Lucian Mueller, W. Meyer, Reichardt and many others.
⟦#2553⟧
(2.) The Accentual Theory. According to this theory, the Saturnian is an accentual verse, constructed without regard to quantity. It is divided by the principal break into two halves, the first of which has three theses. The second half usually has three, but may have only two, in which case it is usually preceded by an anacrusis (⟦r2529:2529⟧). Two accented syllables are regularly separated by an unaccented syllable, but in strictly constructed Saturnians the second and third unaccented syllables are regularly separated by two unaccented ones. Hiatus was at first freely admitted, but in the Saturnians of the second century B.C. occurs only at the principal break. Examples of the Saturnian, measured according to this theory, are:
⟦b:Dábunt málum Metéllī # Naéviṓ poḗtae.⟧
⟦b:Nóvem Ióvis concórdēs # fī́liaé sorṓrēs.⟧ (Naevius.)
⟦b:Vírum míhi, Camḗna, # ī́nsecḗ versū́tum.⟧ (Livius Andronicus.)
⟦b:E͡ōrum séctam sequóntur # múltī mórtā́lēs.⟧ (Naevius.)
⟦#2554⟧
The accentual theory was held by the scholiast on V. ⟦i:G.⟧ 2, 385, and in modern times has been upheld (in one form or another) by O. Keller, Thurneysen, Westphal, Gleditsch, Lindsay and others. The brief statement given above agrees essentially with that of O. Keller. Gleditsch holds that each half-verse has four accents, as: ⟦b:Dábunt málum Métellī́ ‖ Naéviṓ poḗtaé⟧; Lindsay that the first hemistich has three accents and the second two, as: ⟦b:Dábunt málum Metéllī ‖ Naéviō poḗtae⟧. The whole question is still far from its final settlement.

title: Dactylic Rhythms
text:
⟦#2555⟧
These are descending rhythms belonging to the ⟦i:Equal Class⟧ (see ⟦r2527:2527⟧). In them the fundamental foot is the dactyl (–́ ⏑ ⏑), for which its metrical equivalent, the spondee (–́ –), is frequently substituted.

title: The Dactylic Hexameter
text:
⟦#2556⟧
The Dactylic Hexameter is the verse regularly employed in epic, didactic, and bucolic poetry, and is used by the Latin writers oftener than any other measure. It consists of six feet, the last of which is a spondee (but with the privilege of ⟦i:syllaba anceps⟧; see ⟦r2534:2534⟧). The fifth foot is usually a dactyl; but sometimes a spondee is employed, in which case the verse is called ⟦i:spondaic⟧. In each of the other four feet either a dactyl or a spondee may be used. The scheme is therefore:
–́ ⏔ | –́ ⏔ | –́ ⏔ | –́ ⏔ | –́ | –́ –
⟦#2557⟧
A caesura which comes immediately after the thesis of a foot is called ⟦i:masculine⟧; one which falls in the middle of the arsis (i.e. after the first short of a dactyl) is termed ⟦i:feminine⟧. The Roman writers show a strong preference for masculine principal caesuras, and in general their treatment of the caesura is more strict than that of the Greek poets.
⟦#2558⟧
The principal caesura in the Latin hexameter is most frequently the penthemimeral (⟦r2544:2544⟧): as in:
⟦b:Arma virumque canō ‖ Troiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs⟧ (V. 1, 1).
Next in order of frequency stands the hephthemimeral, which is usually accompanied by a secondary trithemimeral, and in many cases also by a feminine caesura in the third foot: as in the verse,
⟦b:Īnsīgnem ‖ pietāte ‖ virum ‖ tot adīre labōrēs⟧ (V. 1, 10).
If the secondary trithemimeral caesura is lacking, the penthemimeral is usually accompanied by a feminine caesura in the second foot. Sometimes, though more rarely, the principal break in the line is the feminine caesura in the third foot (often called the “caesura after the third trochee”), as in the verse
⟦b:Spargēns ūmida mella ‖ sopōriferumque papāver⟧ (V. 4, 486).
⟦#2559⟧
The diaeresis (see ⟦r2542:2542⟧) after the fourth foot (often called “bucolic diaeresis” from its use by pastoral writers) sometimes occurs, but is much less common in Latin hexameters than in Greek. An example is
⟦b:Dīc mihi, Dāmoetā, ‖ cuium pecus? # An Meliboeī?⟧ (V. ⟦i:E.⟧ 3, 1).
This diaeresis, though common in Juvenal, is rare in most of the Latin poets (even the bucolic), and when it does occur, it is usually accompanied by a penthemimeral caesura. Lucian Mueller and others deny that the bucolic diaeresis ever forms the principal break in a line.
⟦#2560⟧
When a line has several caesuras, it is often hard to determine which is the principal one. In general, masculine caesuras out-rank feminine; the penthemimeral takes precedence over the hephthemimeral, and the latter over all other caesuras. But if the hephthemimeral, or even one of the minor caesuras, coincides with an important pause in the sentence, it may out-rank the penthemimeral. Thus in the verse
⟦b:Paulāt(im) adnābam ‖ terrae; ‖ iam tūta tenēbam⟧ (V. 6, 358),
the principal caesura is after ⟦b:terrae⟧, not ⟦b:adnābam⟧.
Lines without a principal caesura are rare. An instance is
⟦b:Nōn quīvīs videt inmodulāta poēmata iūdex⟧ (H. ⟦i:AP.⟧ 263).
⟦#2561⟧
The great flexibility of the hexameter makes it an admirable vehicle of poetic expression. Accumulated spondees give the verse a slow and ponderous movement: as in the line
⟦b:Ill(ī) in|ter sē|sē ‖ ma|gnā vī | bracchia | tollunt⟧ (V. ⟦i:G.⟧ 4, 174).
The multiplication of dactyls imparts to the verse a comparatively rapid and impetuous motion, as in the famous verse
⟦b:Quadrupe|dante pu|trem ‖ soni|tū quatit | ungula | campum⟧ (V. 8, 596).
But even when dactyls are numerous, the Latin hexameter, “the stateliest measure ever moulded by the lips of man,” should not be read with the jerky 3/8 movement which is characteristic of the English hexameter.
⟦#2562⟧
The following passage may serve to illustrate the movement of the hexameter, and to show how the use of the different caesuras imparts variety to the measure:
⟦b:Ō soci|ī ‖ —nequ(e) e|n(im) īgnā|rī ‖ sumus | ante ma|lōrum—⟧
⟦b:ō pas|sī gravi|ōra, ‖ da|bit deus | hīs quoque | fīnem.⟧
⟦b:Vōs et | Scyllae|am ‖ rabi|em ‖ peni|tusque so|nantēs⟧
⟦b:accē|stis scopu|lōs, ‖ vōs | et Cȳ|clōpea | saxa⟧
⟦b:exper|tī; ‖ revo|cāt(e) ani|mōs, ‖ mae|stumque ti|mōrem⟧
⟦b:mittite: | forsan et | haec ‖ ō|lim ‖ memi|nisse iu|vābit.⟧ (V. 1, 198).
Compare in English:
Rolls and rages amain the restless, billowy ocean,
While with a roar that soundeth afar the white-maned breakers
Leap up against the cliffs, like foemen madly rejoicing.

title: Notes on the Hexameter
text:
⟦#2563⟧
(1.) In all probability, the hexameter was originally a composite verse, made up of two tripodies, or of a tetrapody and a dipody. Hence hiatus in the principal caesura is not very rare, even in the Augustan poets. The stress upon the first and fourth theses was probably stronger than that upon the other four.
⟦#2564⟧
(2.) In the second half of the hexameter, particularly in the fifth and sixth feet, verse-ictus and word-accent show a strong tendency to coincide.
⟦#2565⟧
(3.) A monosyllable rarely stands before the principal caesura or at the end of the verse. When the verse ends in a monosyllable, the thesis of the last foot is generally a monosyllable also, as in the line
⟦b:Crīspīnus minimō mē prōvocat; accipe, sī vīs⟧ (H. ⟦i:S.⟧ 1, 4, 14).
Exceptions to this rule sometimes occur when the poet wishes to produce a particular effect, as in
⟦b:Parturient montēs, nāscētur rīdiculus mūs⟧ (H. ⟦i:AP.⟧ 139).
⟦#2566⟧
(4.) A hexameter generally ends in a word of two or three syllables, almost never in one of four, rarely in one of five. But ⟦i:spondaic⟧ verses (⟦r2556:2556⟧) generally end with a word of four syllables, more rarely with one of three, almost never with one of two.
⟦#2567⟧
(5.) Spondaic verses are comparatively rare in Ennius and Lucretius, but become more frequent in Catullus. They are not common in Vergil, Horace, Propertius and Ovid, and do not occur at all in Tibullus. Persius has one spondaic verse, Valerius Flaccus one, Claudian five, Silius Italicus six, Statius seven. Ennius has lines composed entirely of spondees, and so in one instance (⟦r116:116, 3⟧) Catullus. Ennius also resolves the thesis of a dactyl in a few cases.
⟦#2568⟧
(6.) A verse which is connected with the following one by elision (⟦r2492:2492⟧) is called hypermetrical. Such verses are rare, and usually end with the enclitics ⟦b:-que⟧ or ⟦b:-ve⟧.
⟦#2569⟧
(7.) The dactylic hexameter was introduced into Latin literature by Ennius, and was further perfected by Lucilius, Lucretius, and Cicero, who took him as their model. Catullus and the group to which he belonged followed Alexandrian models more closely, while the great poets of the Augustan age carried the technique of the hexameter to its highest perfection. Horace in his lyric poetry treats the hexameter with great strictness; but in the Satires and Epistles he handles it with much freedom, imparting to the measure a more colloquial character by the frequent use of spondees and by less rigorous treatment of the caesura.

title: The Dactylic Pentameter
text:
⟦#2570⟧
The Dactylic Pentameter is a verse consisting of two catalectic dactylic tripodies, separated by a fixed diaeresis. Spondees are admitted in the first tripody, but not in the second. The final thesis of the first tripody is protracted to a tetraseme (⟦r2516:2516⟧) to compensate for the omission of the arsis. The scheme is therefore
–́ ⏔ | –́ ⏔ | ⏘́ # –́ ⏑ ⏑ | –́ ⏑ ⏑ | –́ ⌅
⟦#2571⟧
(1.) The verse is not asynartetic (⟦r2535:2535⟧), neither ⟦i:syllaba anceps⟧ nor hiatus being allowed at the end of the first tripody.
⟦#2572⟧
(2.) This verse is known as the pentameter because the ancient grammarians measured it
– ⏑ ⏑ | – ⏑ ⏑ | – – | ⏑ ⏑ – | ⏑ ⏑ –
⟦#2573⟧
The pentameter is rarely used except in combination with the hexameter, with which it forms the so-called ⟦i:Elegīac Distich⟧:
–́ ⏔ | – ⏔ | – ⏔ | –́ ⏔ | –́ ⏔ | –́ –
–́ ⏔ | –́ ⏔ | ⏘́ # –́ ⏑ ⏑ | –́ ⏑ ⏑ | –́ ⌅
⟦#2574⟧
The Elegiac Distich is used chiefly in elegiac poetry (whence the name), in amatory verse and in epigrams. The end of the pentameter generally coincides with a pause in the sense. As examples of the Elegiac Distich, the following may serve:
⟦b:Quam legis | ex il|lā ‖ tibi | vēnit e|pistola | terrā⟧
⟦b:lātus u|b(ī̆) aequore|īs # additur | Hister a|quīs.⟧
⟦b:Sī tibi | contige|rit ‖ cum | dulcī | vīta sa|lūte,⟧
⟦b:candida | fortū|nae # pars manet | ūna me|ae.⟧ O. ⟦i:Tr.⟧ 5, 7, 1.
Compare in English (but see ⟦r2561:2561⟧ ⟦i:ad fin.⟧):
“These lame hexameters the strong-winged music of Homer!
No—but a most burlesque, barbarous experiment . . .
Hexameters no worse than daring Germany gave us,
Barbarous experiment, barbarous hexameters.” (Tennyson).
⟦#2575⟧
The Elegiac Distich was introduced into Roman poetry by Ennius, who used it in epigrams. Varro employed it in his ⟦i:Saturae⟧, and Catullus seems to have been the first of the Latins who used it in Elegiac poetry. The elegiac and amatory poets of the Augustan age, especially Ovid, perfected it, and wielded it with unequalled grace and ease.
⟦#2576⟧
Ovid nearly always closes the pentameter with a disyllabic word; but earlier poets, especially Catullus, are less careful in this regard. Elision is less frequent in the pentameter than in the hexameter. It sometimes occurs in the main diaeresis of the pentameter, though rarely.

title: The Dactylic Tetrameter Acatalectic (or Alcmanian)
text:
⟦#2577⟧
This verse is chiefly used in composition with a trochaic tripody to form the Greater Archilochian verse (⟦r2677:2677⟧); but it occurs alone once in Terence (⟦i:Andria⟧ 625), and is employed in stichic series (⟦r2546:2546⟧) by Seneca. The scheme is:
–́ ⏔ | –́ ⏔ | –́ ⏔ | –́ ⏑ ⏑
An example is:
⟦b:hocine | crēdibi|l(e) aut memo|rābile⟧ (T. Andr. 625).
This verse is often called ⟦i:Alcmanian⟧ because it was used by the Greek poet Alcman.

title: The Dactylic Tetrameter Catalectic (or Archilochian)
text:
⟦#2578⟧
This verse consists of four dactylic feet, the last one being incomplete. The scheme is:
–́ ⏔ | –́ ⏔ | – | –́ ⏑ ⌃
An example is:
⟦b:Cármine | pérpetu|ṓ cele|brā́r(e) et⟧ (H. 1, 7, 6).
This verse differs from the preceding in that the last foot is always a trochee or spondee, never a dactyl. It is used only in the Alcmanian strophe (⟦r2724:2724⟧).

title: The Dactylic Trimeter Catalectic (or Lesser Archilochian)
text:
⟦#2579⟧
This verse has the scheme:
–́ ⏑ ⏑ | –́ ⏑ ⏑ | –́ ⌅
An example is:
⟦b:Árbori|búsque co | maé⟧ (H. 4, 7, 2).
It is used chiefly in the First Archilochian Strophe (see ⟦r2725:2725⟧). In form it is the same as the second half of the pentameter (⟦r2570:2570⟧).
⟦#2580⟧
These verses (⟦r2578:2578⟧, ⟦r2579:2579⟧) are often called ⟦i:Archilochian⟧ because they were first used by the Greek poet Archilochus.

title: Iambic Rhythms
text:
⟦#2581⟧
These are ascending rhythms (⟦r2528:2528⟧) in 3/8 time. The fundamental foot is the Iambus (⏑ –́), for which its metrical equivalent the tribrach ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑, the irrational spondee > –́, the irrational dactyl > ⏑́ ⏑, the cyclic anapaest ⏑ ⏑ –́, or the proceleusmatic ⏑ ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑ is sometimes substituted.
⟦#2582⟧
The Greek poets excluded all feet except the iambus and tribrach, and in comedy the anapaest, from the even places in iambic verse. The Latin poets were not so strict: but when one of the even feet was formed by a word or a word-ending, they did not usually allow the foot to be a spondee or an anapaest, but required it to be an iambus.

title: The Iambic Trimeter Or Senarius
text:
⟦#2583⟧
The Iambic Trimeter is the verse most frequently used by the Roman dramatists. It consists of six iambic feet, or three iambic dipodies. The ictus on the second thesis of each dipody was probably weaker than that upon the first thesis. Some ancient authorities, however, held that the ictus on the second thesis was the stronger. The last foot is always an iambus. The normal scheme is therefore:
⏑ –́ | ⏑ –̇ | ⏑ –́ | ⏑ –̇ | ⏑ –́ | ⏑ –̇
Some prefer (see ⟦r2529:2529⟧) to regard this verse as a trochaic trimeter catalectic with anacrusis. The normal scheme will then be:
⏑ ⁝ –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⏑ | –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⏑ | –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⌃
⟦#2584⟧
The Latin poets differ widely in their treatment of the Senarius, some (especially Plautus, Terence, and the other early dramatists) handling it with great freedom, while others (especially Phaedrus and Publilius Syrus) conform more closely to Greek models. We may therefore distinguish two periods:

title: Iambic Rhythms: Early Period
text:
⟦#2585⟧
Any one of the substitutions enumerated in 2581 is admitted in any foot except the last. The scheme is therefore:
⏑͐ –́  ⏑͐ –̇  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑͐ –̇  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑ –̇
⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑
> ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑̇ ⏑  > ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑̇ ⏑  [> ⏑́ ⏑]
⏑ ⏑ –́  ⏑ ⏑ –̇  ⏑ ⏑ –́  ⏑ ⏑ –̇  ⏑ ⏑ –́
⏑ ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑
⟦/⟧
The main caesura is usually penthemimeral (⟦r2544:2544⟧); but it is sometimes hephthemimeral, in which case there is generally a secondary caesura in, or diaeresis after, the second foot.
The following passage may serve to show the rhythm:
⟦b:Ubi vén|t(um) ad ae|dīs ‖ ést | Dromō | pultát | forēs;⟧
⟦b:anŭs quaé|dam prō|dit; ‖ haéc | ub(i) ape|rit ṓs|tium,⟧
⟦b:contínu(ō) | hic sē | coniḗ|cit ‖ in|tr(ō), ego cṓn|sequor;⟧
⟦b:anŭs fóri|bus ob|dit ‖ pés|sul(um), ad | lānám | redit.⟧
⟦b:Hīc scī́|rī potu|it ‖ aút | nusqu(am) ali|bī, Clī́|nia,⟧
⟦b:quō stúdi|ō vī|tam ‖ su͡ám | t(ē) absen|t(e) exḗ|gerit,⟧
⟦b:ubi d(ē) ín|prōvī|sōst ‖ ín|terven|tum múli|erī,⟧ &c. T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 275.
⏑ ⏑ –́  ⏑ –̇  > ‖ –́  ⏑ –̇  > –́  ⏑ –̇
⏑ ⏑ –́  > –̇  ⏑ ‖ –́  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ –́  ⏑ –̇
> ⏑́ ⏑  > –̇  > –́  ⏑ ‖ –̇  ⏑ ⏑ –́  ⏑ –̇
⏑ ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ –̇  > ‖ –́  ⏑ –̇  > –́  ⏑ –̇
> –́  > ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ‖ –́  > ⏑̇ ⏑  > –́  ⏑ –̇
> ⏑́ ⏑  > –̇  > ‖ –́  > –̇  > –́  ⏑ –̇
⏑ ⏑ –́  > –̇  > ‖ –́  > –̇  > ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ –̇
⟦/⟧
⟦#2586⟧
(1.) In the early dramatists, substitutions are very numerous, and lines which follow the normal scheme are rare. Substitutions are most frequent in the first foot.
⟦#2587⟧
(2.) Four shorts rarely stand in succession unless they belong to the same foot. Hence a dactyl or tribrach is seldom followed by an anapaest.
⟦#2588⟧
(3.) The dactyl and proceleusmatic are rare in the fifth foot. The proceleusmatic occurs chiefly in the first foot.
⟦#2589⟧
(4.) The fifth foot is very often a spondee. It must not be a pure iambus except (⟦i:a.⟧) when the line ends with a polysyllable of four or more syllables; (⟦i:b.⟧) when it ends with a word which forms a Cretic (⟦r2521:2521⟧); (⟦i:c.⟧) when it ends with an iambic word preceded by one which forms a Fourth Paeon (⟦r2521:2521⟧), or by an anapaestic word which is itself preceded by a final short syllable; (⟦i:d.⟧) when there is a change of speakers before the last foot; (⟦i:e.⟧) when elision occurs in the fifth or sixth foot.
⟦#2590⟧
(5.) The main caesura is rarely preceded by a monosyllable.
⟦#2591⟧
(6.) In the Senarius, and in the other iambic and trochaic verses of the early dramatists, a resolved arsis or thesis is usually placed so that its first syllable ⟦i:begins a word⟧, or so that the two shorts of the resolved arsis or thesis are ⟦i:enclosed⟧ by other syllables belonging to the same word. Hence a dactylic word with the ictus on the penult or ultima (e.g. ⟦b:tempóre⟧) rarely occurs. But there are occasional exceptions to the rule, especially in the case of words that are closely connected (e.g. a preposition with its case).

title: Later Period
text:
⟦#2592⟧
Later writers conform more closely to Greek usage, but differ from one another in the degree of strictness with which they follow it. The general scheme is:
⏑͐ –́  ⏑ –̇  ⏑͐ ‖ –́  ⏑ –̇  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑ –̇
⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ‖ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑
> ⏑́ ⏑  ⟦.⟧  > ‖ ⏑́ ⏑
[⏑ ⏑ –́]  [⏑ ⏑ –̇]
[⏑ ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑]
⟦/⟧
The main caesura is usually the penthemimeral (⟦r2544:2544⟧). The hephthemimeral sometimes occurs, but usually in connection with the penthemimeral, or with a diaeresis after the second foot. If the hephthemimeral is used without either of these, the second and third trochees of the line must form one word, as in
⟦b:ut gaú|det īn|sitī́|va ‖ dē|cerpḗns | pira.⟧ (H. ⟦i:Epod.⟧ 2, 19.)
⟦#2593⟧
(1.) The anapaest is rare in nearly all classical writers; Catullus does not admit it at all, and Horace only five times in all. The proceleusmatic is admitted in the first foot by Seneca, the author of the ⟦i:Octāvia⟧, Phaedrus, Publilius Syrus and Terentianus Maurus; other writers exclude it altogether. Catullus keeps the fifth foot pure, and Horace does not admit the tribrach in the fifth foot.
⟦#2594⟧
(2.) Catullus (4 and 29), Horace (⟦i:Epod.⟧ 16), Vergil (⟦i:Cat.⟧ 3, 4, 8), and the authors of the ⟦i:Priāpēa⟧ sometimes use the ⟦i:pure⟧ iambic trimeter, without resolutions or substitutions.
⟦#2595⟧
(3.) Phaedrus follows in part the earlier usage, admitting the spondee, dactyl, and anapaest, in every foot except the last. The dactyl he employs chiefly in the first, third, and fifth feet, the anapaest in the first and fifth. The proceleusmatic he admits only in the first.
⟦#2596⟧
The rhythm of the Senarius may be illustrated by the following lines:
But one amid the throng of eager listeners,
A sable form with scornful eye and look averse,
Out-stretched a lean fore-finger and bespake Haroun.

title: The Choliambus (or Scazon)
text:
⟦#2597⟧
The Choliambus is an iambic trimeter in which a trochee has been substituted for the final iambus. The penultimate syllable is therefore long instead of short. The caesura is generally the penthemimeral (⟦r2544:2544⟧). If it is hephthemimeral, there is regularly a diaeresis after the second foot. The scheme is:
⏑͐ –́  ⏑ –̇  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑ –̇  ⏑ –́  –́ ⏑
[⏑ ⏑́ ⏑]  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑
> ⏑́ ⏑  ⟦.⟧  > ⏑́ ⏑
⏑ ⏑ –́
⟦/⟧
An example is:
⟦b:Fulsḗ|re quon|dam ‖ cán|didī| tibī́ | sṓlēs.⟧ (Cat. 8, 3.)
⟦#2598⟧
(1). The anacrustic scheme (see ⟦r2529:2529⟧) of the choliambus is:
⏑ ⏑̆͐  –́ ⏑  –̇ ⏑͐  –́ ⏑  –̇ ⏑  ⏗́  –́ ⏑
⟦.⟧  ⏑́ ⏑ ⏑  ⏑̇ ⏑ ⏑  ⏑́ ⏑ ⏑  ⏑̇ ⏑ ⏑
⟦/⟧
i.e. trochaic trimeter with anacrusis (⟦r2529:2529⟧), syncope (⟦r2541:2541⟧), and protraction (⟦r2516:2516⟧).
⟦#2599⟧
(2.) Resolutions and substitutions are less common in the choliambus than in the ordinary trimeter. No monosyllable except ⟦b:est⟧ is admitted at the end of the line. The tribrach in the first foot is rare, and the fifth foot is regularly an iambus.
⟦#2600⟧
(3). The verse is named ⟦i:Choliambus⟧ (i.e. “lame” or “limping iambus”) or ⟦i:Scazon⟧ (“hobbler”) from its odd, limping movement. It is sometimes called Hipponactean from its inventor Hipponax, and is chiefly used to produce a satiric or ludicrous effect. It was introduced into Roman poetry by Cn. Mattius, and was employed by Varro, Catullus, Persius, Petronius, Martial, and others.

title: The Iambic Trimeter Catalectic
text:
⟦#2601⟧
The Iambic Trimeter Catalectic occurs in Horace (1, 4 and 2, 18). The caesura is regularly penthemimeral (⟦r2544:2544⟧). Resolutions are not admitted, except in one doubtful case, ⟦b:rēgumque puerīs⟧ (2, 18, 34), where ⟦b:pu͡erīs⟧ may be read (with synizesis: see ⟦r2499:2499⟧). The scheme is:
⏑͐ –́  ⏑ –̇  ⏑͐ ‖ –́  ⏑ –̇  ⏑ ⏗́ –̇
[⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑]
⟦/⟧
Examples are:
⟦b:Meā́ | renī|det ‖ ín | domō | lacū́|nar.⟧ (H. 2, 18, 2.)
⏑ –́ | ⏑ –̇ | ⏑ ‖ –́ | ⏑ –̇ | ⏑ ⏗́ –̇
⟦b:Seu pó|scit a|gnā sī́|ve mā|lit haé|dō.⟧ (H. 1, 4, 12.)
> –́ | ⏑ –̇ | > ‖ –́ | ⏑ –̇ | ⏑ ⏗́ –̇
⟦#2602⟧
(1.) The anacrustic scheme is:
⏑͐ ⁞ –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⏑͐ # –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⏑ | ⏗́ –̇ ⌃,
i.e. trochaic trimeter catalectic with anacrusis (⟦r2529:2529⟧), syncope (⟦r2541:2541⟧), and protraction (⟦r2516:2516⟧).
⟦#2603⟧
(2.) Horace seems to have changed his practice with reference to the first foot. In 1, 4 the first foot is a spondee in nine lines out of ten; in 2, 18, it is a spondee in only two lines out of twenty.

title: The Iambic Tetrameter Acatalectic (or Octonarius)
text:
⟦#2604⟧
This verse consists of four iambic dipodies, or eight complete iambic feet. The substitutions enumerated in 2581 are admitted in the first seven feet; but the last foot is always an iambus. The principal break in the line is usually a diaeresis after the fourth foot (which in that case must be a pure iambus), or a caesura after the arsis of the fifth. The full scheme is:
⏑͐ –́  ⏑͐ –̇  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑͐ –̇  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑͐ –̇  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑ –̇
⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑
> ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑̇ ⏑  > ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑̇ ⏑  > ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑̇ ⏑  > ⏑́ ⏑
⏖ –́  ⏑ ⏑ –̇  ⏑ ⏑ –́  ⏑ ⏑ –̇  ⏑ ⏑ –́  ⏑ ⏑ –̇  ⏑ ⏑ –́
⏖ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑
⟦/⟧
⟦#2605⟧
The following lines are examples of this metre:
⟦b:Enĭm vḗ|rō, Dā|ve, nī́l|locīst # sēgníti|ae neque | sōcór|diae,⟧
⟦b:quant(um) ín|tellē|xī módo | senis # sentén|tiam | dē nū́|ptiīs:⟧
⟦b:quae sī́|nōn a|stū prṓ|viden|tur ‖ m(ē)aút|erum | pessúm | dabunt.⟧ (T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 206.)
⏖ –́  > –̇  ⏑ –́  ⏑ –̇ # > ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑̇ ⏑  > –́  ⏑ –̇
> –́  > –̇  > ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ –̇ # > –́  ⏑ –̇  > –́  ⏑ –̇
> –́  > –̇  > –́  ⏑ –̇ | > ‖ –́  ⏑ –̇  > –́  ⏑ –̇
⟦/⟧
⟦#2606⟧
Compare in English:
He smote the rock, and forth a tide of crystal waters streamed amain;
Up sprang the flowrets from the ground, and Nature smiled o’er all the plain.
⟦#2607⟧
(1.) The iambic octonarius is chiefly a comic verse. Terence has about eight hundred lines in this measure, Plautus only about three hundred, Varro a few.
⟦#2608⟧
(2.) Substitutions are much less common than in the senarius, especially in the even feet.
⟦#2609⟧
(3.) When there is a diaeresis after the fourth foot, so that the line is divided into two equal halves, the verse is ⟦i:asynartetic⟧ (⟦r2535:2535⟧). There seems, however, to be no certain instance of hiatus in the diaeresis in the Terentian plays.

title: Early Usage
text:
⟦#2610⟧
The Iambic Septenarius consists of seven and a half iambic feet. In any of the complete feet the substitutes mentioned in 2581 are admitted. There is usually a diaeresis after the fourth foot, which in that case must be a pure iambus. If there is not such a diaeresis, there is generally a caesura after the arsis of the fifth foot. The scheme of substitution is:—
⏑͐ –́  ⏑͐ –̇  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑͐ –̇  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑͐ –̇  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑͐ ⌅
⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑
> ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑̇ ⏑  > ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑̇ ⏑  > ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑̇ ⏑  > ⏑́ ⏑
⏖ –́  ⏖ –̇  ⏖ –́  ⏖ –̇  ⏖ –́  ⏖ –̇  ⏖ –́
⏖ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏖ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏖ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏖ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏖ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏖ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏖ ⏑́ ⏑
⟦/⟧
⟦#2611⟧
Examples of the Septenarius are the lines:
⟦b:Spērā́|bit sūm|ptum síbi | senex ‖ levā́|t(um) ess(e) hā|runc ábi|tū:⟧
⟦b:n(ē) ill(e) haúd | scit hoc | paulúm | lucrī ‖ quant(um) ḗ|ī da|mn(ī) adpór|tet.⟧
⟦b:Tū nés|ciēs | quod scī́s, | Dromō, ‖ sī sápi|ēs. Mū|tum dī́|cēs.⟧
(T. ⟦i:Hau.⟧ 746.)
> –́  > –̇  > ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ –̇  ⏑ –́  > –̇  > ⏑́ ⏑  > ⌅
> –́  ⏑ –̇  > –́  ⏑ –̇  > –́  > –̇  > –́  ⏑ ⌅
> –́  ⏑ –̇  > –́  ⏑ –̇  > ⏑́ ⏑  > –̇  > –́  > ⌅
⟦/⟧
Compare in English:
“Now who be ye would cross Lochgyle, this dark and stormy water?” (Campbell.)
⟦#2612⟧
(1.) The Iambic Septenarius of the early comedy is not properly a “tetrameter catalectic” like the Greek, for the penultimate syllable is sometimes resolved, which is never the case in the Greek catalectic tetrameter. For the same reason the ordinary anacrustic (⟦r2529:2529⟧) scheme of the early Septenarius is erroneous; for a triseme cannot be resolved.
⟦#2613⟧
(2.) When there is a diaeresis after the fourth foot, the verse is asynartetic (see ⟦r2535:2535⟧).
⟦#2614⟧
(3.) The Septenarius seems not to have been used in tragedy.

title: Iambic Rhythms: Later Usage
text:
⟦#2615⟧
Varro and Catullus (⟦r25:25⟧) employ a form of the Septenarius which conforms more closely to Greek models, keeping the arses of the even feet pure and rarely admitting resolutions. There is regularly a diaeresis after the fourth foot. The scheme is:—
⏑͐ –́ | ⏑ –̇ | ⏑͐ –́ | ⏑ –̇ # ⏑͐ –́ | ⏑ –̇ | ⏑͐ ⏗́ –̇
or anacrustically (⟦r2529:2529⟧)
⏑͐ ⁞ –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⏑͐ | –́ ⏑ | –̇ ‖ ⏑͐ | –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⏑͐ | ⏗́ | –̇ ⌃
⟦#2616⟧
Catullus does not admit resolutions at all, save in one very doubtful case (⟦r25:25, 5⟧). Varro seems to admit them in the first foot only.

title: Iambic Dimeter Acatalectic (or Quaternarius)
text:
⟦#2617⟧
The Iambic Dimeter Acatalectic consists of two complete iambic dipodies or four iambic feet. In the first three feet the tribrach, irrational spondee, irrational dactyl and cyclic anapaest are admitted; but the proceleusmatic is very rare, except in the first foot of the ⟦i:Versus Reizianus⟧ (⟦r2625:2625⟧), (of which a Quaternarius forms the first colon). The scheme for substitution is:
⏑͐ –́  ⏑͐ –̇  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑ –̇
⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑
> ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑̇ ⏑  > ⏑́ ⏑
⏖ –́  ⏖ –̇  ⏖ –́
[⏖ ⏑́ ⏑]  [⏖ ⏑̇ ⏑]  ⏖ ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑]
⟦/⟧
Examples are:
⟦b:Rogitā́|re quasi | diffíci|le sit⟧
⏖ –́ | ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑ | > ⏑́ ⏑ | ⏑ –̇ (T. ⟦i:Eu.⟧ 209).
⟦b:Ast égo | vicis|sim rī́|serō⟧
> ⏑́ ⏑ | ⏑ –̇ | > –́ | ⏑ –̇ (H. ⟦i:Epod.⟧ 15, 24).
⟦b:Perū́n|xit hōc | Iā́|sonem⟧
⏑ –́ | ⏑ –̇ | ⏑ –́ | ⏑ –̇ (H. ⟦i:Epod.⟧ 3, 12).
⟦#2618⟧
(1.) The verse may also be regarded as a trochaic dimeter catalectic with anacrusis (⟦r2529:2529⟧), with the normal scheme:
⏑ ⁞ –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⏑ | –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⌃
⟦#2619⟧
(2.) Horace admits resolutions only four times, the tribrach once in the second foot and the dactyl thrice in the first.
⟦#2620⟧
(3.) Plautus (except in a few instances), Terence, and Horace employ the dimeter only as a ⟦i:clausula⟧ (⟦r2536:2536⟧) to longer verses. Petronius, Seneca, and Prudentius use it to form ⟦i:systems⟧ (⟦r2547:2547⟧); but it is rarely so employed by earlier writers.

title: The Iambic Dimeter Catalectic (or Ternarius)
text:
⟦#2621⟧
This is like the preceding verse, except that the last foot is incomplete. Examples are:—
⟦b:Nequ(e) íd | perspice|re quī́|vī⟧
⏑ –́ | > ⏑̇ ⏑ | ⏑ ⏗́ –̇ (Pl. ⟦i:Cap.⟧ 784).
⟦b:Date; móx | eg(o) hūc | revór|tor⟧
⏖ –́ | ⏑ –̇ | ⏑ ⏗́ –̇ (T. ⟦i:Andr.⟧ 485).
⟦#2622⟧
(1.) The verse may also be regarded as a syncopated catalectic trochaic dimeter with anacrusis (⟦r2529:2529⟧). The normal scheme will then be:—
⏑ ⁞ –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⏑ | ⏗́ | –̇ ⌃
⟦#2623⟧
(2.) Plautus and Terence use this verse as a ⟦i:clausula⟧ (⟦r2536:2536⟧). Petronius is the first who employs it to form ⟦i:systems⟧ (⟦r2547:2547⟧).

title: Other Iambic Verses
text:
⟦#2624⟧
Other short iambic verses, the acatalectic dipody (e.g. ⟦b:eg(o) ĭllūm | famē, | eg(o) ĭllúm | sitī⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Cas.⟧ 153), and the catalectic tripody (e.g. ⟦b:inóps | amā́|tor⟧, Pl. ⟦i:Tri.⟧ 256) sometimes occur, but are rare.

title: The Versus Reizianus
text:
⟦#2625⟧
This is a composite verse, consisting of two cola, an iambic dimeter acatalectic and an iambic tripody catalectic. The scheme is therefore,
⏑͐ –́  ⏑͐ –̇  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑ –̇ # ⏑͐ –́  ⏑͐ –́  ⏑ ⌅
⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑̇ ⏑  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑  [⏑ ⏑́ ⏑]  ⏑ ⏑́ ⏑
> ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑̇ ⏑  > ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑́ ⏑  > ⏑́ ⏑
⏖ –́  ⏖ –̇  ⏖ –́  ⏖ –́  ⏖ –́
⏖ ⏑́ ⏑  [⏖ ⏑̇ ⏑]  [⏖ ⏑́ ⏑]  ⏖ ⏑́ ⏑  ⏖ ⏑́ ⏑
⟦/⟧
Examples are:—
⟦b:Sed in aé|dibus | quid tíbi | meīs # n(am) erát | negṓ|tī⟧
⟦b:m(ē) absén|te, nis(i) e|go iús|seram? # volo scī́|re. Tac(ē) ér|gō⟧
⟦b:Quia vḗ|nimŭs coc|t(um) ad nū́|ptiās. # Quid tū́, | malŭm, cū́|rās.⟧ (Pl. ⟦i:Aul.⟧ 427.)
⟦#2626⟧
The nature of the second colon of this verse has long been disputed. Reiz and Christ treat it substantially as above; Studemund regards it as a syncopated iambic dimeter catalectic (⏑ – ⏑ ⏗ – ⏑), Spengel and Gleditsch as anapaestic, Leo as logaoedic, Klotz as sometimes logaoedic and sometimes anapaestic! The view of Christ (⟦i:Metrik⟧2, p. 348) seems, on the whole, the most reasonable, though the question cannot be said to be fully decided. The tribrach is rare in the second colon, but there seems to be a case in Plautus, ⟦i:R.⟧ 675 b.
⟦#2627⟧
For other iambic verses and combinations of verses, see special editions of the dramatists.

title: Trochaic Rhythms
text:
⟦#2628⟧
These are descending rhythms in 3/8 time. The fundamental foot is the trochee –́ ⏑, for which its metrical equivalent the tribrach ⏑́ ⏑ ⏑, the irrational spondee –́ >, the cyclic dactyl –́ ⏑ ⏑, the irrational anapaest ⏑́ ⏑ >, and (rarely) the proceleusmatic ⏑́ ⏑ ⏑ ⏑, are sometimes substituted.

title: The Trochaic Tetrameter Catalectic (or Septenarius)
text:
⟦#2629⟧
The Trochaic Tetrameter Catalectic is, next to the iambic trimeter, the verse most frequently used by the early Roman dramatists. It consists of seven and a half trochaic feet, or four trochaic dipodies (the last one being incomplete). The ictus on the second thesis of each dipody was probably weaker than that on the first thesis. The normal scheme is:—
–́ ⏑ | –̇ ⏑ | –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⏑ | –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⏑ | –́ ⏑ | –̇ ⌃
As in the case of the senarius, we may distinguish two periods in the usage:—

title: Trochaic Rhythms: Early Period
text:
⟦#2630⟧
The tribrach is admitted in any of the complete feet, and the irrational spondee, cyclic dactyl, and irrational anapaest in any of the first six feet.
